title: Samantha Steele regrets how she talked to police — but says 'justice prevailed'
summary: <p>A day after her acquittal on a DUI charge, Cook County Board of Review Commissioner Samantha Steele said her position of power hurt her more than it helped in the case, and she blasted the Cook County state’s attorney’s office for prosecuting her.</p><p>Steele said she felt “justice prevailed” when Judge Donald Suriano ruled Tuesday that the evidence against Steele amounted only to “suspicion of intoxication.”</p><p>“The state’s attorney had no real evidence to prosecute the case, but they chose to do that anyway, which is unfortunate for me,” Steele said. “It’s been a difficult year and a half to say the least.”</p><p>Instead of prosecuting her, Steele said “what [the state’s attorney’s office] should be doing is taking on ICE and providing people with the true sense of justice.” She echoed others who have called on Cook County’s top prosecutor to charge federal agents involved in aggressive immigration enforcement tactics in Chicago and the suburbs.</p><p>Chicago Police arrested Steele after she crashed a car on the North Side in November 2024, and the case against her finally went to trial Monday — weeks after she lost her re-election bid in the March Democratic primary.</p><p>The office of State’s Atty. Eileen O’Neill Burke said in a statement that the prosecution of Steele was no different than any other drunk-driving case in the county.</p><p>“In this matter, [the state’s attorney’s office] prosecuted the case because we believe the facts and the evidence demonstrated that the defendant violated the law,” according to the statement. “While the court ultimately rendered its verdict, our office remains committed to ensuring that all individuals are treated equally under the law.”</p><p>Police body-camera videos showed that Steele repeatedly invoked her position as an elected official at the scene of the crash, and she refused to submit to field sobriety tests. A police officer who responded to the crash alleged she made lewd remarks to him.</p><p>In the interview Wednesday, Steele denied making those comments but said she should have spoken in a different manner with the cops than what was shown in the videos.</p><p>“I regret the way I treated the officers,” Steele said. “I was shaken up. I was in a car accident, and I was trying to be jovial — which, after watching that, it didn’t come across that way.”</p><p>Steele said she did not mean to try to flex clout when she told police that she was a county elected official: “What was going on in my head was that I wanted them to know I knew my rights, and that I was not just someone that didn’t know what was going on.”</p><p>Steele’s defense lawyer, John Fotopoulos, said she simply exercised her rights to decline to cooperate.</p><p>“Any time you invoke your rights to the Constitution, a lot of times it’s not pretty,” he said. “It’s confrontational at times. Police officers, the government, doesn’t like when citizens invoke their rights.”</p><p>Fotopoulos said Chicago police “could have easily gone and requested a judge to issue a search warrant if they actually thought that she was under the influence of alcohol, and had the court order her to submit to blood or urine tests.”</p><p>Unlike his client, Fotopoulos did not criticize the state’s attorney’s office for prosecuting the case.</p><p>“I have the utmost respect for Eileen O'Neill Burke,” he said. “I think she’s doing a phenomenal job, but I can actually say if Eileen tried it herself, it still would be a ‘not guilty’ with what the evidence was.”</p><p>Steele said the long-running DUI case “definitely affected” her re-election bid and she would not totally rule out a political comeback attempt.</p><p>But she added, “In the end, I’m not a politician, right? I’m a messy person. I’m a normal person.”</p><p><i>Dan Mihalopoulos is an investigative reporter for WBEZ.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/05/samantha-steele-chicago-cook-county-board-of-review-crime-dui-drunk" >Cook County tax official Samantha Steele cleared of drunken driving charge</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/cook-county-review-board-primary-results" >Controversial Cook County Board of Review incumbent Samantha Steele loses to Democratic operative</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/11/23/cook-county-politician-board-of-review-samantha-steele-chicago-police" >In Samantha Steele’s DUI arrest, Cook County politician told Chicago cops, ‘I’m an elected official’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2024/11/11/cook-county-official-samantha-steele-dui-arrest-ravenswood-cpd" >Cook County official arrested, charged with driving while drunk in Chicago</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Rapid-responders in Chicago shift tactics as ICE enforcement continues at a lower profile
summary: <p>A calm has settled over the Chicago area this spring after months of chaos last fall, when masked federal immigration agents roamed neighborhoods, often deploying tear gas and other aggressive tactics while arresting people.</p><p>Groups of U.S. Border Patrol agents no longer are making surprise visits to Michigan Avenue or marching through Little Village, Back of the Yards and other neighborhoods. </p><p>But immigration enforcement hasn’t ended. A WBEZ / Chicago Sun-Times analysis of data from the Deportation Data Project, a collective of lawyers and academics, has found that 580 people have been detained in the Chicago area from Jan.1 through mid-March.</p><p>Organizers and other rapid-responders who try to warn people about immigration enforcement activity say they remain on high alert and are shifting tactics.</p><p>“This is going to be the new normal at least for the next couple years, and we just have to be always ready and always prepared,” said Mimi Guiracocha, a lead organizer with Pilsen Unidos por Ñuestro Orgullo, known by the acronym PUÑO, a rapid-response coalition based in the Lower West Side community.</p><p>Guiracocha is planning training sessions and deploying volunteer responders to verify immigration enforcement when she receives an alert. She and other organizers say they aim to be better prepared if large numbers of agents return to Chicago.</p><p>Building on lessons learned from last year in Chicago and Minneapolis, these new strategies include tapping new dispatch systems to speed responses when agents are spotted and encouraging block-by-block, hyperlocal communication. Also, some groups are training people to prepare for more aggressive enforcement tactics and to deal with the obstacles that immigrants might face if they are detained.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cristóbal Cavazos of Casa DuPage Workers Center drives arund Chicago’s west suburbs in 2025, responding to alerts about immigration enforcement activity.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Faster alert system</h3><p>Community leaders and rapid-responders say they are seeing more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall.</p><p>Cristóbal Cavazos, executive director of Casa DuPage Workers Center, an organization that documents immigration enforcement in the west suburbs, said the shift makes it harder for volunteers to track enforcement operations and get there quickly when they hear of them.</p><p>Cavazos said he’s seen as many as seven agents trying to arrest one person. That means people who weren't the original targets but are nearby might also get arrested.</p><p>Last year, Cavazos said he helped organize about 300 volunteer rapid-responders, who patrolled in Elgin, Villa Park and other suburbs. He said they used WhatsApp and then Signal messages to send people alerts about immigration enforcement. Those tools were helpful but not as practical when federal agents were spotted and rapid-responders needed to sound the alarm in real time, according to Cavazos, who said that, at times, the chats had too many comments, which slowed response times.</p><p>To alert people more quickly, Cavazos said his team is moving to a dispatch system using cellphone apps. Responders use the apps to provide live updates from their location, aiming to cut response times from the current 10 to 15 minutes to as few as five.</p><p>Cavazos got the idea for the dispatch system from the time he spent volunteering as a rapid-responder in Minneapolis in January. </p><p>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents "would be there, and people would be [on location] within one or two minutes,” Cavazos said. “They were just all over ICE like a cheap suit. That's community power.”</p><p>Some rapid-responders also are focusing on a narrower, block-by-block strategy to speed their responses to reports of immigration enforcement. Guiracocha said the aim is to use hyperlocal text chains and group chats for people to instantly alert their neighbors.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-620000" name="html-embed-module-620000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/28855661"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/28855661/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3>More training</h3><p><i>“Migra</i> watch” and “know your rights” training sessions have been around for years, but such sessions grew in popularity and evolved as federal enforcement escalated last fall.</p><p>Previously, a lot of the focus had been on showing people how to document an arrest or to ask for a warrant. Now, the training also includes planning for what to do after someone is arrested and taken to a detention center. </p><p>Data analyzed by WBEZ and the Sun-Times shows 1,341 people who were detained in the Chicago area from the start of Operation Midway Blitz through mid-March voluntarily agreed to self-deport. </p><p>Cavazos said he wants people to know they don't have to self-deport.</p><p>“Don’t talk, don’t sign, ask to speak to a lawyer,” is the advice Cavazos gives. His training sessions cover <i>habeas corpus</i> petitions, a legal process used to challenge the legality of a detention.</p><p>Participants also learn about the Castañon-Nava case, a 2022 settlement restricting federal immigration agents' authority to make warrantless arrests in Illinois and five other states. Agents are supposed to have probable cause that someone is in the country unlawfully and provide evidence that the person is a flight risk. Recent violations of this court order led a federal judge to order the release of immigrants who were illegally detained and 343 people have benefited from the case.</p><p>“Even up to now, people are getting released,” Guiracocha said. “We see those stories, and we put them in the training to say, this is why this matters.”</p><h3>Training to face aggressive tactics <b> </b></h3><p>Organizers said they try to convey the level of violence that immigrants and activists could face by role playing difficult arrest scenarios and teaching new deescalation tactics.</p><p>Those "really shifted from ‘these are the things that you can do if you see ICE’ to ‘ICE is unpredictable, and your safety is the No. 1 priority,’ ” said Rey Wences, senior director of deportation defense for the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights.</p><p>Wences said participants in training are told to follow protocols if shots are fired. They also learn how to protect themselves against chemical agents like tear gas and pepper spray, with an emphasis on using personal protective equipment. The training also shows people how to create an emergency plan in case they get hurt, arrested or deported.</p><p>During simulations, role-play participants act as agents and shout aggressive remarks to test a volunteer’s ability to remain firm without escalating the situation.</p><p>Some trainers describe the sessions as a “taste” of reality because it mirrors the chaos and crises that unfold when immigrants are being arrested. The sessions conclude with volunteers talking about their mental and emotional reactions to foster awareness and help people stay focused in case they find themselves facing aggressive tactics.</p><p>“There is no limit [to] the violence that these agents and this administration has on the community,” Guiracocha said. "I think [that] has been an awful lesson for us to learn but something that we can now use to prepare to equip ourselves."</p><p><i>Contributing: Lauren FitzPatrick, Alden Loury</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/29/standing-up-to-ice-in-suburban-chicago-the-peoples-patrol-puts-its-faith-in-resistance" >Standing up to ICE in the suburbs, the People’s Patrol puts its faith in resistance</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/28/broadview-detainees-operation-midway-blitz-self-deporting-high-rates-analysis-finds" >Broadview detainees during Operation Midway Blitz were self-deporting at alarming rates, analysis finds</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/05/volunteers-on-ice-patrol-in-pilsen-looking-for-agents" >Volunteers on ICE patrol in Pilsen, looking for agents</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

Sowacke</a></h5><p>Steps from the Red Line, Decibel quickly filled up Saturday night as the queue stretched down the block for the new nightclub’s opening weekend.</p><p>Those in line said they'd hoped to rekindle the flame that went out Nov. 19, 2023 — the day the historic Berlin nightclub closed after more than 40 years of serving the North Side LGBTQ community. Many wondered: Could new life settle in at 954 W. Belmont Ave.?</p><p>That new life is a dual-bar concept, The Belmont/Decibel, announced last year by HV Entertainment. The Belmont is a relaxed cocktail bar early in the evening, but after 10 p.m., a curtain is pulled back to reveal the revamped dance floor and transform into Decibel.</p><p>"It’s kinda surreal to be back here," said Andrew Rogers, 34. "I never thought I’d return to the space. Thankfully, it still has the same energy."</p><p>His friend, Riley Rogers, 37, agreed: "Having the sense of community is very important to me. Berlin brought so many queer and alt people together."</p><p>Later, music boomed from a DJ's set and body heat from the dancefloor fogged up the venue's windows.</p><p>"It’s not about the name — it’s about the vibes," bartender Derek Stuch said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdtithy-l-ju/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>After companies charged consumers higher prices on items due to the Trump administration's tariffs, what do you think of </b><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdtithy-l-tr/" target="_blank" ><b>companies getting refunds from the government</b></a><b>?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Respond to this newsletter</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). title: Close loophole on genetic discrimination in insurance
summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker envisions Illinois as a leader in life-science investment and jobs, highlighted by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinois.gov/news/release.html?releaseid=32279" target="_blank" >$1.5-billion partnership</a> announced in March with the biotherapeutics company CSL. </p><p>Breakthroughs from this type of work could equal lifesaving care but may remain unobtainable for many Illinoisans due to a lack of protections against genetic discrimination in insurance markets.</p><p>Genetic discrimination occurs when individuals are penalized for genetic risks, even if they <a class="Link" href="https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2788347" target="_blank" >never develop said condition</a>. The federal <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/110th-congress/house-bill/493" target="_blank" >Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act</a> protects Americans’ health insurance and employment. No such safeguards exist for life, disability or long-term care insurance. </p><p>Genetic testing is now an integral part of healthcare. This gap in protections creates a significant barrier to care. In fact, studies show that <a class="Link" href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35663290/" target="_blank" >fear of insurance discrimination</a> is a top reason patients decline genetic testing, a well-founded fear as shown in a 2025 study: <a class="Link" href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41288017/" target="_blank" >21% of the participating genetic counselors</a> reported a patient denied life insurance based on genetic testing results alone. </p><p>With skyrocketing healthcare costs, the use of genetic testing in medicine can shift the state’s health care burden from expensive, reactive treatment to more affordable, proactive treatments. This doesn’t just save lives; it puts money back into Illinoisans' wallets rather than the <a class="Link" href="https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/2025-life-mid-year-industry-commentary.pdf" target="_blank" >$22 billion</a> coffers of the insurance industry.</p><p>The Illinois Senate introduced new legislation, <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?GAID=18&DocNum=2799&DocTypeID=SB&LegId=164879&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >Senate Bill 2799</a>, to help protect Illinoisans’ genetic information from being used in life insurance, long-term care insurance and disability insurance policy determinations — the very safety nets that are critical for families. </p><p>For years, similar consumer protections have been blocked by claims of financial harm to the insurance industry — claims that lack empirical support. Other states, including Florida, have passed similar laws without seeing dramatic premium increases, according to <a class="Link" href="https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/2024-annual-life-industry-commentary.pdf" target="_blank" >2024 data from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners</a>.</p><p>Crucially, the Illinois bill does not prevent insurers from using a clinical diagnosis; it only prohibits the use of theoretical genetic risks. Genetic data is nuanced and requires specialized medical expertise to interpret. Allowing nonmedical professionals, like insurance brokers, to use this complex information to make life-altering financial decisions is scientifically unsound.</p><p>If Illinois is to remain a global biotechnology leader, our laws must protect the consumers driving that innovation. Passing legislation ensures the future of medicine in our state is defined by growth and privacy, not fear.</p><p><i>Rachel Campagna, president-elect, Illinois Society of Genetics Professionals</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-dd0000" name="module-dd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Stepping up for neighbors</h3><p>WBEZ's Chip Mitchell's story on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/01/chicago-immigration-midway-blitz-trump-children" >Isabel Conde</a> that ran in Sunday’s Sun-Times was deeply moving. A caring person, she stepped in and helped save a family. She is one of Chicago’s finest.</p><p>Since Ms. Conde gave so much of herself to others, can the rest of us in Chicago return the favor? She is going to grad school. She must have expenses. If the Sun-Times or some other organization could set up a fundraiser, I would be happy to contribute.</p><p><i>William Dodd Brown, Lincoln Square</i> </p><h3>Kind act in dark times</h3><p>Three homeless kids walking in a park, taken in by a stranger when their mother is detained by immigration agents: priceless.</p><p>The "Un"-United States of America: Shameful.</p><p><i>Sandra Minor, McHenry</i></p><h3>No American immune to gun violence </h3><p>I agree with Mr. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/05/01/police-officers-swedish-hospital-shooting-safe-t-act-electronic-monitoring-tom-weitzel" target="_blank" >Tom Weitzel</a>. We are living in a time of lawlessness and little accountability. I sympathize with the extremely dangerous job police officers have and can't imagine facing such a heavily armed public. As of April, 82 officers have been shot this year, according to Mr. Weitzel. <a class="Link" href="https://www.gunviolencearchive.org/" target="_blank" >Gun Violence Archive</a> data shows that 72 children newborn to 11 years old, and 278 teenagers 12-17 have been killed in shooting incidents this year.  Unlike policing, growing up in the United States shouldn't be such a dangerous activity.  When will we confront this shameful reality?</p><p><i>Sharon Marzano, Edgewater</i></p><h3>Low ‘Spirit’</h3><p>The latest victims in President Donald Trump's unconscionable war against Iran? The 17,000 hardworking Americans who are now former Spirit Airlines employees. Trump's ill-advised foreign adventure drove jet fuel prices up to such a high level that <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/spirit-airlines-trump-bailout-bankruptcy-37a4818e1b71c0905d022f669d85948c" target="_blank" >Spirit could no longer sustain operations</a>. How many more American workers will find their lives and careers being destroyed in the coming months as a result of Trump's criminal incompetence?</p><p><i>Chet Alexander, Alsip</i></p><h3>Papal pleasantries</h3><p>Chicagoan: Leo, how about them White Sox ?<br>Pope: I am very pleased with their progress.<br>Chicagoan: Leo, wadda ya think about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/04/12/trump-lambasts-pope-leo-xiv-extending-feud-over-iran-war-with-first-american-pontiff" target="_blank" >Donald Trump</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2026/04/19/catholic-white-house-comments-trump-vance-pope-leo" target="_blank" >JD Vance</a> dissin' you ?<br>Pope: I care not. I preach the Gospel.<br>Chicagoan: But Leo, they're warnin' you about what to say about world politics and religion.<br>Pope: Their comments are inane and have the impact of a flea on an elephant's hide.<br>Chicagoan: OK, Leo, but remember, if there's any trouble, I got a guy.<br>Pope: No need, I have billions of the faithful in my corner.<br>Chicagoan: That's great, but if it ain't enough you can always call on me.<br>Pope: No worries. I've got the chief Guy.</p><p><i>Philip S. Witt, Northbrook</i></p><h3>Would be more jazzed to see concert live</h3><p>I appreciated Erica Thompson's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/01/chicago-international-jazz-day-pope-leo-herbie-hancock-kurt-elling-lyric-opera" >reporting</a> in Monday's Sun -Times on the UNESCO International Jazz Day Global Concert that took place last week at the Lyric Opera House. I watched the livestream with great joy on my home computer. What is really "sticking in my craw," so to speak, were the number of empty seats on the main floor when the cameras panned across the audience. Everything that I read or heard prior to the performance indicated that all seats were accounted for and the general public could watch the livestream. As a senior citizen and lifelong Chicago jazz fan, I would have happily filled one of those empty seats!</p><p><i>Rocco P. Lotesto, Uptown</i><br></p>

title: Illinois State Police launches investigation into deadly ICE shooting of Silverio Villegas González
summary: <p>Illinois State Police has opened an investigation into the fatal shooting of Silverio Villegas González nearly eight months after he was killed by a federal immigration agent during a traffic stop in Franklin Park toward the start of Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>Franklin Park police asked ISP to investigate on Thursday, when a state commission released a damning report detailing the actions of federal agents during President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area last year.</p><p>The report urged Illinois law enforcement agencies to investigate and prosecute alleged crimes stemming from Midway Blitz.</p><p>The ISP probe is the most high-profile independent inquiry that’s been announced in response to the monthslong immigration enforcement operation, during which federal agents also shot <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/16/marimar-martinez-border-patrol-shooting-victim-chicago-congress-testimony" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a> in Brighton Park and routinely used <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/14/ice-bovino-border-patrol-homeland-security-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" >pummeling force and chemical irritants</a>.</p><p>It was launched amid a legal push to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" target="_blank" >install a special prosecutor</a> in the Cook County state’s attorney’s office to target the federal agents who carried out the campaign.</p><p>A coalition of elected officials, clergy, journalists and attorneys has argued that State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke “has an alliance with federal law enforcement that prevents her from taking action against the federal agents alleged to have committed crimes during Operation Midway Blitz.”</p><p>On Tuesday, O’Neill Burke’s office said prosecutors were contacted by ISP and will play a “supportive role” in the investigation, following the office's guidance for handling cases involving federal agents.</p><p>"We are unable to comment further on a pending law enforcement investigation," O'Neill Burke's office said in a statement.</p><p>Villegas González, a father and cook originally from Mexico, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/12/ice-officer-fatally-shoots-man-during-traffic-stop-in-chicago-suburb-authorities-say" target="_blank" >fatally shot</a> “at close range” on Sept. 12, 2025, according to an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >autopsy report</a>. He was allegedly attempting to flee the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who tried to stop his car.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-credit"><p>GoFundMe</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A bullet struck the back of Villegas González’s neck, the report found. He was rushed to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, where he was pronounced dead less than an hour later. </p><p>The FBI initially responded to the shooting scene and, according to ISP, was the “primary investigating agency.” ISP wouldn’t comment on the details of its new investigation. Franklin Park police didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. </p><p>The shooting happened just days after the Trump administration kicked off Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>Department of Homeland Security officials initially claimed an ICE agent had been “dragged a significant distance” by Villegas González’s car and suffered “severe injuries.” But in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/22/ice-officer-injuries-nothing-majo[…]dly-franklin-park-shooting-mexican-immigrant-chicago-video" target="_blank" >body camera footage</a> from the scene, the agent described his injuries as “nothing major.”</p><p>There have been mounting calls for Illinois law enforcement and prosecutors to hold federal agents accountable for the aggressive tactics deployed during Midway Blitz. Local agencies in Minnesota have taken a far more aggressive approach, swiftly launching investigations into the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.</p><p>The Cook County state’s attorney’s office has maintained it’s limited in its ability to conduct investigations. According to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >guidance released by the office</a> in February, law enforcement agencies should lead criminal investigations, then present evidence to prosecutors to review for charging.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Illinois Accountability Commission, assembled by Gov. JB Pritzker, has spent months conducting its own investigation, gathering testimony and reviewing video footage and legal records. The commission’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/30/pritzker-illinois-accountability-commission-operation-midway-blitz-trump-immigration" target="_blank" >final report</a>, released Thursday, found federal agents acted illegally and with impunity during its immigration enforcement efforts. </p><p>The report included a letter referring charges to O’Neill Burke, the Chicago Police Department, the Kane County state’s attorney, and the Elgin, Franklin Park and Evanston police departments.</p><p>O’Neill Burke responded that she couldn’t bring charges without a referral from a law enforcement agency.</p><p><i>Contributing: Jon Seidel</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/12/ice-officer-fatally-shoots-man-during-traffic-stop-in-chicago-suburb-authorities-say" target="_blank" >ICE officer fatally shoots man during traffic stop in Chicago suburb, authorities say</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/22/ice-officer-injuries-nothing-majo[…]dly-franklin-park-shooting-mexican-immigrant-chicago-video" target="_blank" >ICE officer said his injuries were ‘nothing major’ after deadly shooting near Chicago, video shows</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/30/pritzker-illinois-accountability-commission-operation-midway-blitz-trump-immigration" target="_blank" >Pritzker commission investigating Operation Midway Blitz ‘lays the foundation for real accountability’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Little Village sees 'really slow' Cinco de Mayo after parade is canceled for second straight year
summary: <p>Chicago's Cinco de Mayo parade once drew large crowds to Little Village, but this year's celebration was even more muted than last year according to business owners.</p><p>The annual holiday gathering in the heart of the city's Mexican community was canceled for the second year in a row due to immigration enforcement concerns, organizers said last month.</p><p>Small business owners said the parade has always been vital to their sales, but along 26th Street there was hardly any foot traffic early Tuesday afternoon, after fewer customers than usual were seen in the days leading up to the holiday.</p><p>For Francisca Alfaro Rodriguez, owner of Fran Arte y Estilo de Mexico, the parade used to draw customers into her store looking for traditional Mexican clothing. Instead, she said she barely sold anything during the holiday weekend.</p><p>“There used to be so much joy here,” Alfaro Rodriguez said. “There was pride in wearing Mexican attire.”</p><p>The parade, which commemorates Mexico’s unexpected victory over Napoleon III’s French army in the Battle of Puebla in 1862, has historically drawn hundreds to the neighborhood. But organizers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/20/cinco-de-mayo-parade-little-village-canceled-second-year" target="_blank" >told the Sun-Times</a> that Chicago’s Mexican community is still on edge in the wake of Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s deportation campaign in the Chicago area last fall.</p><p>Alfaro Rodriguez said sales have dropped nearly 90% since last year, and she was hoping the parade might help make up for it. Instead, the streets were largely empty on Tuesday.</p><p>“They say the raids have slowed down, but people are still not coming out,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div title: Departamento de Justicia desmantela programa de servicios legales para inmigrantes de bajos ingresos
summary: <p>Trece organizaciones sin fines de lucro con sede en Illinois están denunciando lo que dicen que es el desmantelamiento silencioso de un programa federal de muchos años que brinda asistencia legal a inmigrantes de bajos ingresos.</p><p>Durante más de 60 años, el Departamento de Justicia ha operado el Programa de Reconocimiento y Acreditación. Este programa permite que personas que no son abogados ofrezcan servicios legales y ha hecho que la representación asequible esté disponible para familias que no pueden permitirse un abogado privado.</p><p>Los abogados principales del Departamento de Justicia que dirigían el programa fueron reasignados abruptamente para trabajar como pasantes de derecho de nivel inicial, según el Proyecto Resurrección y una docena de otras agencias asociadas.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6d0000" name="module-6d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“El gobierno federal ha estado atacando a los inmigrantes, a nuestros vecinos, a nuestros maestros, a nuestros trabajadores desde el principio. Limitar la capacidad de las personas para vivir una vida plena, para participar en sus comunidades, al impedirles incluso tener acceso a un abogado cuando están en la corte es solo una forma más en que la administración federal está haciendo eso”, dijo Tovia Siegel, directora de organización y liderazgo de Justicia Inmigrante en el Proyecto Resurrección de Chicago.</p><p>El grupo indicó que no hubo advertencias previas para las más de 900 organizaciones sin fines de lucro y 2,600 representantes acreditados en todo el país que participan en el programa.</p><p>Siegel señaló que ya hay una necesidad masiva de representación, mientras que también hay una falta de debido proceso para los inmigrantes que solicitan beneficios mientras luchan contra la deportación.</p><p>“Lo que hace este programa es ampliar el acceso… a una representación legal de alta calidad y confiable a través de organizaciones sin fines de lucro, a una representación asequible, de bajo o ningún costo, un servicio realmente esencial que necesitan los inmigrantes”, dijo Siegel.</p><p>“El desmantelamiento de este programa es solo una forma más insidiosa en que la administración de Trump ha socavado la capacidad de las personas para tener debido proceso cuando enfrentan su día en la corte, cuando enfrentan una posible separación familiar o ser enviadas a un país en el que no creen que puedan estar seguros, o a veces, que ni siquiera han vivido”.</p><p>Liza Gutiérrez, directora de programas para inmigrantes de Partners for Our Communities en Palatine, dijo que es una gran pérdida no contar con el programa.</p><p>“Hemos estado luchando por la equidad al obtener representación para los más necesitados en nuestras comunidades. Cuando se trata de obtener representación para alivio migratorio, simplemente no hay suficiente y las personas no pueden permitirse contratar a un abogado tradicional”, dijo Gutiérrez, quien es representante acreditada por el Departamento de Justicia.</p><p>Sin el programa, Gutiérrez teme que los inmigrantes de bajos ingresos, desesperados por obtener estatus legal, puedan ser engañados por otros.</p><p>“Vemos personas que cobran entre $10,000 y $20,000 por presentar un caso de asilo, que sólo debería ser una tarifa anual de $100”, dijo Gutiérrez. “Esto significa que ahora las personas que están en la escala de ingresos más baja no podrán acceder a representación. Sabemos que esa representación es lo que hará que un caso sea ganable. Cuando te presentas a la corte sin representación, es muy probable que no ganes el caso”.</p><p>Un portavoz del Departamento de Justicia no respondió a las preguntas sobre el programa.</p><p>Otros grupos de Illinois que han firmado una carta en apoyo al programa son: Partners for Our Communities; Hanul Family Alliance; Binational Institute of Human Development; Spanish Community Center; Latino Policy Forum; AKWAABA QC; La Casa Norte; Chicago Workers Collaborative; FEDECMI/Casa Michoacan; Instituto del Progreso Latino; United African Organization; y Erie Neighborhood House.</p><p>Los grupos están pidiendo al Departamento de Justicia que reincorpore a los abogados principales a sus funciones en el programa de Reconocimiento y Acreditación. También están haciendo un llamado al Congreso para que ejerza su autoridad de supervisión y exija una contabilidad pública completa de los cambios en el programa.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
author: Michael Puente

title: Remaining 'Broadview Six' defendants move to disclose grand jury transcripts, drop conspiracy charges
summary: <p>Four remaining members of the so-called “Broadview Six” filed a motion Monday urging a federal judge to release grand jury transcripts, arguing that U.S. prosecutors have kept a felony conspiracy charge “alive and pending” after announcing that it would be dismissed.</p><p>The unredacted transcripts were set to be handed over last week to U.S. District Judge April Perry. Instead, prosecutors said they would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/29/broadview-ice-crime-chicago-trump-kat-abughezaleh" target="_blank" >drop the conspiracy charge</a> at the center of the protest case, one of the most high-profile prosecutions stemming from the Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign last year.</p><p>With the grand jury indictment seemingly dismissed, the judge decided she no longer needed to see the transcripts.</p><p>On Monday, defense attorneys for the four defendants said federal prosecutors are now keeping the conspiracy charge pending until misdemeanor charges of forcibly impeding a federal agent are settled at trial in less than a month. They filed a second motion Monday to dismiss the conspiracy charge.</p><p>Charged are former<b> </b>congressional<b> </b>candidate<b> </b>Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian<b> </b>Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt<b> </b>and Andre Martin, a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff.</p><p>Defense attorneys laid out three possibilities for what the unredacted transcripts could include: The assistant U.S. attorney either “mis-instructed” the grand jury on the law; failed to instruct the grand jury on the law at all; or there were other interactions between the assistant U.S. attorney and the grand jury that are “otherwise improper or prejudicial.”</p><p>The attorneys framed the prosecution as potentially politically motivated, tying it to the recent cases against former FBI Director James Comey and the Southern Poverty Law Center. They raised the possibility of the feds dropping the conspiracy charges in order to avoid disclosing the unredacted transcripts.</p><p>“This remarkable about-face, abandoning a high-profile indictment rather than submit to scrutiny its conduct before the grand jury comes at a time of mounting national distrust in the Department of Justice’s use of the grand jury process,” the motion states. “These actions only underscore the growing concern that the grand jury is being wielded not as an instrument of justice, but as a tool of unchecked prosecutorial power meant to persecute any perceived enemies of the current White House.”</p><p>The case stems from a protest last September at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in west suburban Broadview. Abughazaleh and others were seen on video pushing against a black SUV driven by a federal agent toward the facility.</p><p>Catherine Sharp, a former Cook County Board candidate, and musician Joselyn Walsh already had their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" ><u>charges dropped</u></a> in March.</p><p>Attorneys argued in the motion that the high-profile case had ripple effects beyond those charged, and it “impacted elections and potentially suppressed public dissent.”</p><p>The U.S. attorney’s office for the Northern District of Illinois didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The motion to disclose the transcripts isn’t a complete surprise. Defense attorneys immediately questioned the grand jury proceedings after the conspiracy charges were dropped and vowed not to back down in court.</p><p>Straw’s attorney, Christopher Parente, said, “The timing of the government's sudden decision to drop the felony indictment for the remaining Broadview 6 co-defendants — in lieu of presenting the requested unredacted grand jury transcripts to the Court — raises red flags about the government's presentation of the law to the grand jury.”</p><p>“Transparency around this presentation is essential, as the question of the government's use of grand juries has risen in national prominence, is material to this case and of consequence to the fair functioning of our justice system,” Parente said in a statement Monday.</p>
author: Mary Norkol

title: CeaseFire founder says anti-violence strategy he launched in Chicago can fight 'disease' of authoritarianism
summary: <p>Three decades ago, Dr. Gary Slutkin took on Chicago’s violence problem with a solution he called CeaseFire, which he said would inoculate the city from the “disease” of shootings as he did with public health emergencies like AIDS.</p><p>Now he’s applying the same thinking to an even broader problem: government authoritarianism.</p><p>Slutkin was scheduled to speak about his theory Monday night at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy.</p><p>In an interview beforehand, the epidemiologist turned international violence prevention expert says his concept of authoritarian violence as a disease is a natural extension of his earlier CeaseFire work, which he and others credit with decreases in violence in Chicago and elsewhere. </p><p>Many other anti-violence groups in Chicago have been based on the CeaseFire model of having "interrupters" negotiating truces on the street.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/public-safety/2025/06/06/violence-intervention-frederick-seaton-street-outreach-institute-nonviolence-chicago-cure-violence" target="_blank" >Why is Chicago violence plummeting? Some credit street outreach workers.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>According to Slutkin, crackdowns, political intimidation and dehumanizing rhetoric spread in waves, just like the epidemics of gun violence, AIDS and tuberculosis.</p><p>Slutkin presents his theory in his new book, "<a class="Link" href="https://tracking.us.nylas.com/l/ce7fe059b99a4b09ae2d994e444b9deb/2/3c0817a40f095504d1a33b056e312d12d34991990e8c3c955a6b30be20d6de8a?cache_buster=1777555150" target="_blank" ><u>The end of violence: Eliminating the World’s Most Dangerous Epidemic</u></a>."</p><p>He says authoritarian leaders are like “superspreaders” who use their power and platforms to “infect” their populations on a mass scale. State violence and imprisonment are symptoms of those diseased regimes, he says.</p><p>He says his book isn’t political in the sense that he’s not focusing on specific world leaders. He says he mentions President Donald Trump only once — in a section of the book about the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.</p><p>Still, many examples of the authoritarian violence Slutkin highlights have occurred during Trump’s most recent administration.</p><p>They include: Department of Homeland Security agents shooting and roughing up protesters and immigrants; U.S. military attacks on Venezuela, Iran and other countries; U.S. threats of taking over Greenland; and even cutbacks in U.S. food and health programs that he says will lead to a surge in deaths here and abroad.</p><p>“This was done in a very cruel way,” he says.</p><p>But he insists his focus isn’t on any one political figure.</p><p>“This isn’t about a person,” he says. “It’s about the disorder.”</p><p>Authoritarianism, he adds, is rising worldwide — not just in the United States, and in some places far more deeply entrenched.</p><p>In Chicago, long before formal “violence interrupter” programs took hold, communities relied on public education campaigns, neighborhood mobilization and social pressure to push back against violence.</p><p>During recent DHS immigration enforcement efforts, similar community responses surfaced in Chicago, Minnesota and other cities, where public backlash helped shape broader political reactions, including the Trump administration pulling back on its most aggressive immigration strategies, he says.</p><p>Change, he suggests, often starts at the ground level — with ordinary people questioning behavior, rejecting dehumanization and holding others accountable.</p><p>“It filters upward,” he says, describing how community pressure can influence institutions and even elected officials.</p><p>But sustaining that energy is difficult.</p><p>He points to “epidemic fatigue” — exhaustion that sets in when crises pile up, from economic uncertainty to immigration enforcement to the threat of war. The confusion, he says, can paralyze people.</p><p>The solution, in his view, is disciplined concentration on the problem: “Focus on the violence." That means educating the public, calling out harmful actions and challenging those who encourage or tolerate them. It also means rethinking protests not as attacks on individuals but as broader rejections of violent behavior itself.</p><p>Even those at the center of violence, he argues, often want to change. From gang leaders in U.S. cities to cartel figures in Latin America, many are trapped in what he calls a “stuck” system. Without alternatives, he says they remain locked in cycles of harm.</p><p>Authoritarian leaders may face a similar bind. With grim odds — exile, imprisonment or assassination — many act out of fear, he says, clinging to power as a means of survival.</p><p>“They need a way out,” Slutkin says — one that offers both safety and a path to save face.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cb0000" title: For May Day Chicago mom takes her family to a protest. ‘I have never heard of any right being won from home.’
summary: <p>At home Friday morning, Flor Ramirez moved between chores and preparations for the afternoon May Day march — packing tamales and cleaning out the family van to make sure there was enough room for the kids plus a friend she planned to pick up. Yessari, her 8-year-old daughter, said she especially liked watching her mother figure out how they’re going to dress up for the rally.</p><p>Last year, Flor Ramirez made butterflies for Yessari and her sister Saori to wear on their heads. “The butterflies symbolize freedom,” Yessari said. This year, using a stencil and glitter, their mom painted “ICE OUT” across the girl’s cheeks, one word on each side.</p><p>Flor Ramirez wasn’t always able to join the annual May Day rallies and marches that take place on May 1, a day recognized across the globe in defense of workers’ rights and in Chicago for immigrant rights as well.</p><p>In 2006, Ramirez, who’d recently arrived in the United States from Puebla, Mexico, wanted to join the May Day immigrant rights march but didn't know anyone who could take her. She was 18 years old and working at a Chipotle in Niles, IL.</p><p>Ramirez said the manager at Chipotle laughed when she requested the day off. He told her there were other ways to help. But Ramirez wanted to go.</p><p>“Fine,” she recalled him saying. “Go, but you don’t come back.”</p><p>Back then, she said, she used to listen to <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2006/06/15/5488198/the-power-of-spanish-language-radio" target="_blank" ><u>El Pistolero</u></a> on the radio, a program urging workers and immigrant families to show up for their rights as debate grew over a federal bill that would have <a class="Link" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Protection,_Anti-terrorism_and_Illegal_Immigration_Control_Act_of_2005" target="_blank" ><u>criminalized immigrants without legal status.</u></a></p><p>Now, nearly two decades later, Flor Ramirez along with her husband, Armando, and their 16-year-old son, Uri and daughters Saori, 10, and Yessari, 8 attended the May Day rally and march held at Union Park.</p><p>Twenty years ago, the threat was a bill that would have criminalized immigrants without legal status. Flor Ramirez says the threat now feels greater where even people with legal status, residency or citizenship are at risk.</p><p>Like many immigrant families, the Ramirez family is split across legal status and experiences: some of them were born in Mexico, some in the United States; some carry work permits or residency, or are U.S. citizens.</p><p>Flor and her husband, Armando, did not have legal status for years before receiving temporary protection from deportation and work authorization through Deferred Action for Labor Enforcement, or <a class="Link" href="https://immpolicytracking.org/policies/reported-uscis-ends-program-to-shield-workers-reporting-abuse/" target="_blank" ><u>DALE</u></a>, a 2023 Biden-era process created for immigrant workers involved in investigations of labor violations. The future of the program is now uncertain. The Trump administration stopped processing DALE requests last year, though workers who already received deferred action may remain protected until their protections expire.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The family arrived at Friday’s May Day march ready to make a lot of noise. Armando had fashioned home made drums from buckets he bought at Home Depot. The girls banged on tambourines while marching through Union Park. The music blared as the afternoon turned chilly and the girls bundled into blankets inside a wagon they had brought with in case they got tired.</p><p>Being at the May Day rally together with the whole family feels especially important to Ramirez this year because of what her family experienced during Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>In the fall her son Uri, a U.S. citizen, was waiting to be picked up from school when he got a text from his older brother that federal immigration agents were at a gas station near his school. So instead of leaving through the usual exit, Uri left through a different one, hoping the agents wouldn’t see him.</p><p>Flor later told him he had nothing to worry about.</p><p>“Mom,” he told her, “have you seen my face?”</p><p>“I was born here but…I still sort of felt afraid,” Uri said. “I still felt like I would be taken away from my family, my friends, my own home.</p><p>For the people who ask ‘ What is the point of marching on May Day? What has been accomplished?’ Flor Ramirez has an answer: “I have never heard of any right being won from home or from under the bed,” she said. That is the lesson she wants to pass down: that silence will not protect them.</p><p>If her children inherit anything from marching on May Day for immigrant rights, she wants it to be the opposite.</p><p>“Even if they don’t want us, our roots are already here. We are already a well-planted tree.”<br></p>

Some of those kids, who are citizens, moved in with relatives or friends. The Chicago High School for Agricultural Sciences junior has had turtles, vampire crabs, spiny eels, tarantulas and various fish as pets.</p><p>Now he's getting his first taste of what it’s like to raise a puppy.</p><p>Alan and a classmate are fostering puppies as part of a partnership between the school and the nonprofit PAWS Chicago, which culminates with an adoption event at the school’s Mount Greenwood campus on Saturday.</p><p>The students volunteered to care for the dogs to get them out of the shelter for a few days and raise awareness about the event — and also to get more experience working with animals. title: When immigration agents arrested a Chicago mother, a stranger stepped in to care for her 3 kids
summary: <p>When the 17-year-old let Isabel Conde visit, he and his sisters had been on their own for nearly four weeks.</p><p>The boy and the girls, ages 14 and 6, had been fending for themselves in the family’s Southwest Side apartment since immigration agents arrested their mother and moved her to a detention center in Kentucky.</p><p>“What I noticed right away was the girls huddled up together in the door frame of one of the bedrooms,” Conde says, recalling their embrace at the sight of an adult stranger in the home.</p><p>“I wanted to get all the basic facts,” Conde says.</p><p>“Financially, what was going to happen with their apartment? Medically, did they have health insurance? And, legally, what was going on with the mom’s case?”</p><p>During President Donald Trump’s second term, immigration agents have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/02/operation-midway-blitz-parents-children-immigration-detention-mental-health?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=01052025%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=01052025%20Morning%20Edition+CID_a6896837d6b9407a2c69df6cd912901d&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Trump%20deportation%20campaign%20will%20leave%20lasting%20mark%20on%20kids%20of%20detained%20parents%20experts%20say&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >taken away the parents</a> of thousands of U.S.-born children. Some of those kids, who are citizens, have moved in with relatives or family friends. Others have landed with strangers or languished in shelters.</p><p>The people who have opened their homes to care for these children often don’t know how long they'll be needed or what emotional fallout they’ll face when the kids leave.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bd0000" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1f1c099/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3908x2193+0+207/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F40%2F9a%2Fa0aa6cdb46838eecd59920afe595%2Fbroadviewfollow-092425-01.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A federal immigration agent sits in an SUV near the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview last September. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Conde, 27, heard the kids were living alone from a relative who came from the mother’s hometown in Puebla, Mexico.</p><p>The mother, 37, had entered the United States as a teenager in 2006.</p><p>All three of her children were born in Chicago. She worked in a factory and raised them on her own in Chicago Lawn.</p><p>The mother had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/17/ice-operation-midway-blitz-response-illinois-congressional-delegation-letter" target="_blank" >no criminal record</a>, but the immigration agents arrested her on Oct. 12, near their home. WBEZ agreed not to name the woman or her children to protect their safety.</p><p>When Conde visited the apartment weeks later, she started a list of all the adults in the kids’ lives — the people who might be able to take them in.</p><p>She learned the father of the two teens had returned to Mexico. The 6-year-old’s father remained in Chicago, but Conde didn’t think he was “able to care for her.”</p><p>Conde approached the kids’ aunts and uncles. She tried neighbors and their godparents. “No one was able to take all three of them,” she says.</p><p>Conde had worked for immigrant children as a paralegal. So she knew it was only a matter of time before someone called in the Illinois Department of Children and Family Services. The kids could end up in foster care or a shelter. They could be split apart.</p><p>A few nights after meeting the kids, Conde got a call from them.</p><p>“They were in a park and they shared with me that they left their home and were afraid because the father of the youngest was telling them he was going to separate them,” she says.</p><p>Conde was with her own mother: “We got in the car and drove immediately to that park.”</p><p>It was dark. The kids were pulling a wagon, loaded with clothes and a blanket. They were planning to sleep outside. The 17-year-old was pacing.</p><p>“They were scared,” Conde says.</p><p>Conde’s home, a Little Village apartment, had just two bedrooms. She decided it was big enough for all of them.</p><p>But she didn’t want to be accused of kidnapping. She wanted it known that she was taking in the kids for their safety.</p><p>So Conde and her mom packed them into the car and drove to the nearest police station.</p><p>When Conde got there, the father of the 6-year-old was already there. He wanted to take her, but the girl wanted to stay with her sister and brother.</p><p>“The police said we could figure this out between us or they could call the state,” Conde says, referring to that Illinois child welfare agency.</p><p>It took an hour but Conde, speaking Spanish, reached an agreement with the father in front of the officers: She would keep the children together and he could talk to his daughter on the phone whenever he wanted and arrange visits.</p><p>“I was able to take the kids to my house that night,” Conde says.</p><p>Conde’s own father had two extra beds — a queen and a twin. He brought them over and spread them across the living room, forming a “megabed” along with her couch, she says.</p><p>Conde brought in the kids’ wagon, full of clothes, and started a load of laundry.</p><p>She thought she would shelter the kids for just a few days, long enough to identify an adult who was willing and able to take them in.</p><p>Conde also took charge of getting their mother out of immigration detention.</p><p>The family had already spent thousands of dollars on a lawyer whose main advice was asking the mother to sign papers for a “voluntary” deportation, Conde says.</p><p>To Conde, that was a nonstarter. When she managed to reach the mother by phone, she says, “the first thing I told her was, ‘Do not sign anything. You have rights.’”</p><p>Conde found a pro-bono attorney.</p><p>But an immigration judge refused to release the mother on bond. So the attorney turned to the federal court system.</p><p>The legal battles stretched over weeks, then months.</p><p>Conde did her best for the kids.</p><p>“I would drive them to and from school every day,” she says, and would make sure they received the academic and social services they needed.</p><p>“Once we got temporary guardianship paperwork signed by their mom, I was able to start making sure that all of the medical needs were being met,” she says. “Then I got them into mental health therapy, each of them, because they had experienced a severe trauma.”</p><p>“My mom would come several nights a week and help me care for the kids,” Conde says. “She’s the art teacher at Ravenswood Elementary School, and they held a fundraiser for us. And I also tapped into community networks and mutual aid funds.”</p><p>With all the help, Conde could pay the rent on the family’s apartment, so it would be there if the kids’ mother were released.</p><p>“We took them to the ZooLights, the trampoline park, the children’s museum, the aquarium,” Conde says.</p><p>“The youngest grew out of her clothes right away,” Conde says. “She just hit a growth spurt. We had to get new clothes for everybody.”</p><p>“They had tamales with us at Thanksgiving, gifts for Christmas to open,” she says. “We just really made them a part of our family.”</p><p>But Conde was under increasing stress. Less than two weeks into the new year, she started graduate school. It wasn’t easy with the three children in her apartment.</p><p>“I would pray every night and ask that these children could be reunited with their mother,” she says.</p><p>On January 27, two-and-a-half months after Conde first took in the kids, a federal judge in Kentucky ruled the mother’s detention was unlawful. He ordered her immediate release.</p><p>The attorney arranged for volunteers in Kentucky to drive the mother to a spot in Indiana that Conde could reach.</p><p>“I immediately rented a van and picked up the kids from school and was like, ‘Guys, let’s go get your mom!’” Conde says.</p><p>The family was finally reunited.</p><p>Conde drove them back to her apartment. Her own folks came over and made the mother pozole, a Mexican stew.</p><p>“We gave her fresh clothes and then she just fell asleep with her kids in my living room,” Conde says.</p><p>The mother and kids stayed at Conde’s place a few days before returning to their home. It was ready for them because Conde had raised funds to pay the rent since October.</p><p>“They were back in their home and back together,” she says.</p><p>But Conde’s apartment suddenly felt empty.</p><p>“I loved them, and it was the goal all along to reunite them with their mom, but I missed them because we were all like a family for a while,” Conde says, her voice wavering. “I was really sad.”</p><p>This spring, the 17-year-old is graduating from high school. The 14-year-old is having a quinceañera. The younger girl is finishing kindergarten.</p><p>The mother’s immigration case remains pending but the next hearing has been postponed to 2028, giving her time to plan for any outcome. In the meantime, she has qualified for a work permit.</p><p>Conde has wrapped up her first semester of grad school. She’s looking forward to summer classes.</p><p>She gets to see the kids every now and then, but she still feels the loss.</p><p>“After protecting them for so long, I wanted to just keep being with them all the time,” Conde says. “But I knew that it was just the way of things and the way of love.”</p><p>She had to let them go.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/19/border-control-body-cameras-videos-midway-blitz-albany-park" target="_blank" >Border Patrol agent’s camera captures detainee’s lament: ‘We don’t have the opportunity that you have’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/28/border-patrol-gregory-bovino-cole-sheridan-broadview-ice" target="_blank" >‘His word means nothing’: Dismissed case reveals dishonesty of Border Patrol commander, protester says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/09/30/transcript-audio-gregory-bovino-arrestees-downtown-chicago-chosen-how-they-look" target="_blank" >Gregory Bovino says arrestees in Downtown Chicago chosen based partly on ‘how they look’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Pritzker commission investigating Operation Midway Blitz 'lays the foundation for real accountability'
summary: <p>Federal immigration agents acted illegally and with impunity to carry out President Donald Trump's aggressive deportation campaign in Chicago — and they did so with steadfast support from the president and his administration, a state accountability panel found. </p><p>After spending six months gathering testimony, video footage and legal records, the Illinois Accountability Commission <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/2026-04-iac-final-report.html" target="_blank" >put out its final report</a> Thursday examining Operation Midway Blitz and the alleged abuse carried out by federal agents in and around the city last fall. </p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker assembled the commission in October to investigate federal agents' conduct during Operation Midway Blitz. At a news conference Thursday, Pritzker said he assembled the panel of legal experts to conduct a thorough investigation when he realized the Trump administration wasn't going to hold agents accountable.</p><p>"These hearings and investigations demonstrated that Operation Midway Blitz was not an unfortunate collection of errors in judgment or limited abuses of power by individual bad actors," Pritzker said. "It was a carefully orchestrated, coordinated effort that started with Donald Trump and was executed by Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Tom Homan, Greg Bovino and others." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d00000" name="image-d00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9dea696/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fe3%2F6996284547e2b64fdccdd2c58e3c%2Fimg-9407.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/23e4c5c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fe3%2F6996284547e2b64fdccdd2c58e3c%2Fimg-9407.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2acc4cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fe3%2F6996284547e2b64fdccdd2c58e3c%2Fimg-9407.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Gov. JB Pritzker speaks at a podium " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2acc4cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fe3%2F6996284547e2b64fdccdd2c58e3c%2Fimg-9407.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c943ce7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fe3%2F6996284547e2b64fdccdd2c58e3c%2Fimg-9407.jpeg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2acc4cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fe3%2F6996284547e2b64fdccdd2c58e3c%2Fimg-9407.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Gov. JB Pritzker and his Illinois Accountability Commission discuss the panel’s final report that published Thursday. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kaitlin Washburn/Sun-Times </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> Earlier this week, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/27/pritzker-illinois-accountability-commission-operation-midway-blitz-hearing" target="_blank" >the commission conducted hearings</a> and brought in witnesses and victims to speak about several of the major flash points during Operation Midway Blitz. That included the confrontations between residents and federal agents in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/28/border-patrol-bodycam-video-tactics" target="_blank" >Little Village</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/24/immigration-agents-arrest-lake-view-protest-tear-gas" target="_blank" >Lake View</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/26/northwest-side-ice-arrests-tear-gas" target="_blank" >Old Irving Park</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/14/crash-involving-immigration-agents-in-east-side-leads-to-tear-gas-detentions" target="_blank" >East Side</a> and Evanston. </p><p>The report also names specific federal agents the commission alleges broke the law. One of those agents is Charles Exum, the Border Patrol agent who shot Marimar Martinez five times after a car with three CBP agents collided with her vehicle on Oct. 4 in Brighton Park. Martinez and her attorney Christopher Parente <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/28/illinois-accountability-commission-pritzker-federal-immigration-agents-ice-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >testified before the commission on Tuesday</a> about the shooting and its aftermath.</p><p>Other agents seen in several videos aren't named because the commission lacked the power to investigate all the agents involved, said Judge Rubén Castillo, the commission's chair. </p><p>That's why the report <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/IAC-Referral-Letter-04-2026.pdf" target="_blank" >includes a letter</a> referring charges to Cook County State's Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, the Chicago Police Department, the Kane County state's attorney, and the Elgin, Franklin Park and Evanston police departments. </p><p>"It is very clear to me," Castillo said at Thursday's news conference, "that the U.S. Justice Department will not be doing any investigating of these agents who committed these atrocities. So what is left? What is left is our local prosecutors, and in particular, our Cook County State's Attorney, and she will be referred this report. She has said that she hasn't been referred anything. Well, today she's going to be referred something, and it should be investigated." </p><p>And if Burke "doesn't want to investigate," Castillo said, she should "step aside and let a special prosecutor come in and do what needs to be done." </p><p>Castillo, a former U.S. district chief judge, is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" target="_blank" >among a coalition calling for</a> a special prosecutor to investigate federal agents.</p><p>The commission lacked both subpoena and prosecutorial power. It's now up to local law enforcement to carry on the commission's investigation, Pritzker said. </p><p>"The commission has done much of what is in its power to do, to lay the foundation for real accountability," he said. "It has gathered the evidence. It has heard from innocent victims. It has identified the culprits. But it will take the courage and conviction of all of us at every level of government to continue pressing forward, to ensure that these findings are met with action." </p><p>In response, Burke issued a statement Thursday maintaining that she can't bring charges until she has received a completed investigation from a law enforcement agency. </p><p>"We commend the bravery of every witness who testified about their harrowing experiences before the Illinois Accountability Commission," Burke said in the statement. "There is no doubt that Operation Midway Blitz has traumatized and harmed our communities. We look forward to receipt of the full report and will work with our local, state, and county law enforcement to review the material." </p><p>The final report includes <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/IAC-FinalReport-AppendixB-Policy-Reccommendations.pdf" target="_blank" >several other recommendations</a> for local, state and federal authorities, such as: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-aa4dab32-44cc-11f1-856d-7183ac2ad83b"><li>The Department of Homeland Security "must [rein] in agents’ use of chemical agents, physical force and vehicular pursuits." The department should also ensure all agents wear and use body worn cameras and prohibit agents from covering their faces and hiding their identity while on the job. <br></li><li>Congress "must amend the Immigration and Nationality Act to end warrantless arrests for civil enforcement matters and prohibit discriminatory stops that rely on race, ethnicity, workplace, accent or language." <br></li><li>The state of Illinois should work with local governments and nonprofits to "alleviate the economic damage caused by Operation Midway Blitz, expand access to legal services and family preparedness planning support, and prevent further disruption to civic life by immigration enforcement activities." </li></ul>

title: Review: Bruce Springsteen balances songs of defiance and resistance with messages of hope and unity
summary: <p>Bruce Springsteen brought his E Street Band to Chicago for a sold-out show on Wednesday night, marking the latest stop on the “Land of Hope and Dreams” tour. It was the most politically motivated pop concert hosted at the United Center since Nov. 2, 2024, when Stevie Wonder appeared during his tour named “Sing Your Song! As We Fix Our Nation’s Broken Heart.”</p><p>Wonder’s concert brimmed with hope and optimism days before the 2024 presidential election. Springsteen’s tone Wednesday was starkly different. Fifteen months into the Trump administration, the Boss arrived with songs of defiance and resistance.</p><p>Rock classics like “Born to Run” would come in due time. To begin, however, Springsteen had a message to convey.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" United Center.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Our democracy, our Constitution, [and] our rule of law are being challenged right now as never before by a reckless, incompetent, radical and racist administration,” said Springsteen. “We ask all of you to join with us in choosing hope over fear, democracy over authoritarianism, the rule of law over lawlessness, ethics over unbridled corruption, resistance over complacency, truth over lies, unity over division, and peace over war.”</p><p>The E Street Band then erupted into a strident cover of Edwyn Starr’s 1970 anthem “War,” featuring former Libertyville resident Tom Morello. As a founding member of Rage Against the Machine, the guitarist is no stranger to protest rock.</p><p>The band followed with Springsteen’s 1984 hit “Born in the U.S.A.,” about a Vietnam War veteran who encounters a lack of opportunity upon his return home. The song has often been mischaracterized as a patriotic anthem. Morello and Springsteen met at center stage to trade guitar solos as the song reached its fervent peak.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/11/14/review-tom-morello-and-friends-chicago-performance-vic-theatre" >Review: Tom Morello and Friends provide the soundtrack for the resistance in powerful set at Vic Theatre</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Springsteen’s prior local appearance in 2023 had packed Wrigley Field to the uppermost seats. That ballpark performance featured celebratory fare like “Rosalita” and “Mary’s Place.” Those were swapped on Wednesday for the turbulent power of songs like “The Ghost of Tom Joad” and the dramatic “American Skin (41 Shots).”</p><p>Nonetheless, the United Center set list offered fan favorites. In addition to the fire and brimstone of “Murder Incorporated,” crowd-pleasers included the sing-along stroll of “Hungry Heart.” The eventual encore was elevated by “Tenth Avenue Freeze-Out” with tributes to dearly departed band members, including saxophonist Clarence “The Big Man” Clemons and organist Danny Federici.</p><p>The heart of the show reflected Springsteen’s caustic opening remarks, though. The E Street Band covered the Clash’s anti-authoritarian “Clampdown” with brash punk spirit. “Anger can be power, know that you can use it,” sang Morello. Springsteen echoed the sentiment with his rebellious “Wrecking Ball.” “Hold tight to your anger,” he sang. “Don't fall to your fears.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div
