title: Man admits opening fire near border agents during Operation Midway Blitz
summary: <p>A man held for nearly six months on weapons charges admitted Monday that he fired a gun “in proximity of” U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents<b> </b>days before the deportation campaign known as Operation Midway Blitz <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/11/u-s-border-patrol-boss-greg-bovino-fellow-agents-expected-to-soon-leave-chicago" target="_blank" >began to wind down</a>.</p><p>Hector Gomez, 46, made the admission while pleading guilty to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/07/new-indictment-cites-shooting-near-border-patrol-agents-in-chicago-still-doesnt-charge-gunman" target="_blank" >illegally possessing a firearm</a> as a felon. Gomez also admitted that he is a Mexican citizen unlawfully present in the United States.</p><p>The claim that agents had been fired upon in early November was met with some skepticism, especially when no charges were announced against an alleged shooter. Even now, Gomez has admitted only to discharging his weapon “in proximity of”<b> </b>the agents, with no additional details.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/07/new-indictment-cites-shooting-near-border-patrol-agents-in-chicago-still-doesnt-charge-gunman" >New indictment cites shooting near Border Patrol agents in Chicago, still doesn’t charge gunman</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>There were no reports of anyone hit by gunfire<b> </b>in the Nov. 8 incident.</p><p>Still, federal prosecutors in Chicago now have their second guilty plea for a nonimmigration crime tied to Operation Midway Blitz. The feds <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >charged 32 known defendants</a> with such crimes. Twenty of them have been cleared, and four others are on track to have their cases dismissed.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/15/crime-chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-ice-border-patrol" target="_blank" >Anthony Gonzalez Alvarez</a> also pleaded guilty earlier this month to concealing information about a crime. In doing so, he admitted that he drove his Ford F-250<b> </b>into the rear of a vehicle driven by immigration officers.</p><p>Gomez entered his plea Monday before U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly, who scheduled Gomez’s sentencing for July 20. Gomez, who is in federal custody, spoke through a Spanish interpreter and told the judge he agreed with allegations read into the record by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jill<b> </b>Bhalakia.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s deportation blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The charge carries a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison. Kennelly noted the prosecution would also likely lead to Gomez’s deportation.</p><p>Gomez’s arrest came after a chaotic day in Little Village<b> </b>near the end of the monthslong deportation campaign in the Chicago area.</p><p>The Department of Homeland Security initially reported on social media that “an unknown male driving a black Jeep fired shots at agents and fled the scene.”</p><p>In court Monday,<b> </b>Gomez admitted that, at 9:30 a.m. on Nov 8, he fired “at least two rounds” near CBP agents while driving a black Jeep Wrangler. Gomez later parked the vehicle, got out and pointed the gun toward an unidentified victim before getting back into the Wrangler.</p>
author: Jon Seidel

title: Every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s immigration blitz
summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago have accused 32 known defendants of nonimmigration crimes tied to Operation Midway Blitz. Many were accused of assaulting or resisting federal agents or officers.</p><p>Two defendants have pleaded guilty. Twenty have been cleared. Grand jurors refused to indict at least three of the 20, and another member of that group was found not guilty at trial.</p><p>Meanwhile, prosecutors have entered into deferred-prosecution agreements with four additional defendants. In each of those cases, if that person abides by certain terms over a set period of time, the feds have agreed to drop the charges in that case as well.</p><p>The Chicago Sun-Times is tracking all of class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdliytk-l-h/" target="_blank" >Kaitlin Washburn</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdliytk-l-k/" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdliytk-l-o/" target="_blank" >Tom Schuba</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdliytk-l-b/" target="_blank" >Cindy Hernandez</a></h5><p><b>Fatal shooting</b>: A Chicago police officer was killed and another was "fighting for his life" after being wounded in a shooting Saturday morning at Endeavor Health Swedish Hospital, the city’s top cop said. The fatally shot officer was identified as John Bartholomew, 38, who worked for the police department for 10 years. No update was provided Sunday on the second officer, age 57, who has not been named.</p><p><b>Suspect charged</b>: Alphanso Talley, 26, was charged Sunday with murder, aggravated unlawful restraint, armed robbery, aggravated discharge of a firearm, possession of a firearm by a felon, aggravated battery of a peace officer, attempted murder, aggravated battery, escape and unlawful use of a weapon, according to a police source. He was expected in court Monday.</p><p><b>The timeline</b></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="line-height: inherit; margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px; margin-left: 24px; padding: 0px; list-style-type: disc;" id="rte-dff336a0-423e-11f1-a0ea-2f0911c208c3"><li><b>About 8 a.m.</b>: Roughly three hours before the shooting, the suspect robbed a convenience store in Albany Park. He was reportedly armed and had attacked a woman there. </li><li><b>Just before 9 a.m.</b>: Two suspects fled and one was arrested in Avondale. He asked to be taken to a hospital because he wasn’t feeling well.</li><li><b>Two hours later</b>, the shooting happened at Swedish.</li><li><b>10:50 a.m.</b>: The suspect shot Bartholomew and another officer, according to police. Officers responded to a call of an active shooter at Swedish at 10:53 a.m. and told SWAT teams to stand by.</li><li><b>10:58 a.m.</b>: Police confirmed an officer was shot and the suspect ran away on California Avenue.</li><li><b>11 a.m.</b>: Police confirmed two officers were shot and requested backup. How worried should you be?</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wdliytk-l-a/" target="_blank" >David Struett</a></h5><p><b>Bad bridges</b>: When the city reopened the State Street Bridge in March after nearly a year of emergency repairs, it provided a small bit of relief for traffic snarls along the Near North Side for much of 2025. Those traffic headaches were the result of the city’s unusual move to close five river bridges simultaneously to catch up on a backlog of necessary repairs.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: Exactly 100 of Chicago’s 601 bridges are listed in the same "poor" condition as the State Street Bridge, which unexpectedly shut down in April 2025 — several months before engineers were planning to carry out repairs. That’s 16.6% of all city bridges, well above the national average of 6.7%, according to a Sun-Times analysis of federal bridge inspection records.</p><p><b>Bottom line</b>: Bridge inspections are federally mandated at least every two years, and the results are publicly listed online. If the bridge is classified "structurally deficient" or "poor," that doesn’t mean it's at imminent risk of falling down. However, a poorly rated bridge must be inspected more often. Thompson</a></h5><p>On Saturday afternoon, Myron Stokes stood in a Bronzeville performance venue that's nearly 130 years old.</p><p>The room was dark, the walls were worn and the stage was vacant. But he said he could envision what the space was like in the 1920s, '30s and '40s.</p><p>"I hear the music, the dancing and the snapping of fingers," said Stokes, 56, of Oak Park, who also imagined what life may have been like for Black crowds back then.</p><p>Stokes was part of a group that explored the historic Forum Hall at 318-328 E. 43rd St., where jazz artists including Nat King Cole and Sun Ra played. The tour closed out a day of arts and activities, including performances in the soon-to-open Forum Cafe next door and a neighborhood walk to the homes and haunts of jazz icons.</p><p>The free event was part of Chicago’s monthlong celebration of UNESCO International Jazz Day, which culminates in an all-star global concert Thursday at Lyric Opera House.</p><p>Event organizers said they hoped attendees felt more connected to their communities and the people within.</p><p>"We want neighbors to meet each other," said Shani "Lady Sunshine" Smith of Calumet Heights, who led the outdoor tour. "We want people to know the histories of their communities and connect around that and take ownership of their communities."</p><p><a class="Link" title: Immigration raids upending Chicago's construction industry amid worker shortage, higher costs
summary: <p>Residential projects across Chicago are being postponed because construction companies are struggling to find reliable labor, prompting some contractors with projects west of Interstate 355 to operate with leaner crews and driving up day rates and overtime pay to attract workers.</p><p>President Donald Trump’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration" >immigration</a> enforcement has been affecting Chicago’s labor market, notably tradesmen like roofers, framers, concrete layers and landscapers.</p><p>The reverberations are difficult to aggregate given the off-the-books nature of the gray economy and insiders’ reluctance to speak out. But the ongoing threat of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol enforcement actions in Chicago have put added pressure on an industry already struggling with long-running worker shortages, stagnant wages and rising costs, construction experts say. </p><p>As a result, consumers are seeing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/31/lake-view-federal-cpd-immigration-raid" >project delays</a> and higher costs.</p><p>“When enforcement activity ramps up, even temporarily, employers tell us they see crews thin out almost overnight,” said Sam Mattingly, a former construction project manager who founded Indianapolis-based JobsinConstruction.com to help companies find workers. “ICE activity doesn't just reduce workforce numbers. It increases uncertainty, which discourages smaller contractors from taking on new projects. I don’t see the situation getting any better."</p><p>The worker shortage in Chicago and nationwide has been worsening for decades — fueled by an aging workforce, forces like the COVID-19 pandemic and the Great Recession and a dearth of younger workers entering the field, industry experts say.</p><p>Illinois faces a shortage of trade worker this year exceeding 200,000 jobs. Demand for certain positions are significant, including laborers (58,958), carpenters (42,113) and masons (19,907), according to data from Construction Industry Resources. </p><p>“There’s a clear shortage across every level of the trades, but it’s most acute at the journeyman level due to retirements and a thin pipeline behind them,” said Alicia Martin, president of the Illinois chapter of Associated Builders & Contractors. “The biggest gap is in experienced, highly skilled workers. And that’s not something you can solve quickly.”</p><p>Over the years, Chicago-area companies have become more reliant on foreign-born workers, according to federal data. In the Chicago-Naperville-Elgin market, 83,522 construction workers identified as foreign-born, 32.5% of the area's workforce, according to the latest U.S. Census Bureau figures.</p><p>For residential and smaller projects, day laborers have played a key role in meeting project deadlines and keeping costs lower for consumers, according to Nik Theodore, a University of Illinois Chicago professor who has studied the day labor industry since the early 2000s.</p><p>Before the proliferation of big home improvement stores, contractors would buy appliances and home furnishings from wholesalers at a much steeper discount than retailers could offer, allowing for a reliable profit.</p><p>That equation changed when big-box home stores like Menard’s, Home Depot and Lowe’s expanded nationwide, providing consumers with cheaper options on everything from cabinets to kitchen sinks. So labor costs became the competing factor for contractors, who started turning to day laborers, Theodore said.</p><p>“The industry has been struggling for skilled labor for years now, and immigrant workers in particular have been filling a number of the gaps, especially in occupations like drywall, plaster or roofing here in Chicago,” he said.</p><p>But challenging circumstances, in part fueled by the federal deportation efforts, have driven some employers to exploit workers, undercutting pay to $50 a day, compared to the average $150, or foregoing payment altogether after a day’s shift, according to the Albany Park nonprofit Latino Union of Chicago.</p><p>In the 1990s, Theodore said, the city’s first day labor site, a Shell gas station at Belmont Avenue and Pulaski Road, primarily attracted people of Polish descent and other Eastern Europeans. Today, the workforce is overwhelmingly Mexican, Central American and South Americans, with many day laborers congregating at a dozen or so hiring sites around Chicago outside Home Depots and few gas stations.</p><h3>‘Afraid to be outside,’ worker says </h3><p>On the North Side, a 40-year-old day laborer who said he doesn't have legal immigration status and declined to give his name for fear of deportation, said he has painted houses around the city and suburbs for 15 years. He said that, in October, he evaded an ICE raid in Avondale, where immigration officials picked up laborers and a female tamale vendor. He had been picked up at the same location in 2016 by federal agents and eventually released.</p><p>Since the most recent incident, he said he has kept a low profile and rarely leaves home except to look for work.</p><p>“I’m afraid to be outside,” he said through a translator from the Latino Union. “I’ve had to decline some work because of safety concerns. There's no work opportunities if I don’t go out.”</p><p>The painter and home repairman, who is appealing a 2016 deportation order, is one of about 800 day laborers affiliated with the Latino Union. The organization, one of the city’s oldest hiring centers — established in 2000 by female temporary workers — isn't a labor union. The organization provides job training and recruiting services for low-income immigrants and U.S.-born workers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" December.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Latino Union has ramped up worker rights awareness campaigns and training for volunteers to document immigration enforcement operations in the streets and alert workers of nearby sightings.</p><p>Immigration raids have affected Chicago’s day laborers before Trump took office, according to Miguel Alvelo Rivera, the Latino Union’s executive director, noting that the Obama administration also carried out mass deportations, though not on as large a scale.</p><p>“What this all really points to is a concerted but really badly coordinated attack on our communities, particularly working-class communities that are predominantly Black and brown,” he said.</p><p>Immigration enforcement has an immediate effect on day labor activity, the North Side worker said, with some large hiring sites seeing the number of people hoping to pick up work falling from 100 workers or more to a few dozen or less after raids.</p><p>But the workers come back, Rivera said: “Eventually, they have to show up again to be able to pay for rent, to be able to take care of themselves or their families."</p><p>The North Side resident said he's struggling to pay rent for a shared apartment and to provide for his mother in Mexico City.</p><h3>On the front lines</h3><p>Chicago attorney Kevin Herrera represents day laborers in immigration proceedings and worker claims. One of his clients, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/13/community-alleges-ice-targeted-day-laborer-demands-his-release" >Willian Gimenez</a>, was pulled over by ICE agents in September while driving to a barber shop in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/little-village" >Little Village</a>. Gimenez was handcuffed and taken to a detention center in Michigan, where he was kept for seven weeks before a judge ordered his release.</p><p>Community organizers and family members say they think he was targeted because Gimenez is one of five day laborers who filed a lawsuit last year against Home Depot and the city of Chicago. The workers said they were beaten by off-duty police officers working security and other employees from the Home Depot at 4555 S. Western Blvd. </p><p>In late January, an Illinois judge partially denied motions to dismiss the suit.</p><p>Herrera said some businesses benefit greatly from day laborers, attracting business as would-be employers stop to buy supplies as they look to hire workers.</p><p>“Home Depot, particularly, has been a huge beneficiary,” he said. “There's a real hypocrisy.”</p><p>The Atlanta-based home-improvement retailer posted revenue of $164.7 billion in fiscal year 2025, with a net profit of $14.2 billion. </p><p>Community organizers have pushed for boycott campaigns against Home Depot in Chicago, Los Angeles and other cities, accusing the retailer of cooperating with ICE. In January, a group of Home Depot investors asked the company to review its partnership with third-party surveillance vendors as it "already faces reputational risks stemming from frequent immigration enforcement raids occurring near its stores and heightened public concerns regarding data privacy," Reuters reported.</p><p>Home Depot says it has a longstanding policy prohibiting the sale of goods and services in their parking lots and doesn’t communicate with ICE or the Border Patrol.</p><p>“We aren’t notified that immigration enforcement activities are going to happen, and we aren’t involved in the operations," the company said in a written statement. "We cannot legally interfere with federal enforcement agencies, including preventing them from coming into our stores and parking lot."</p><h3>Exodus of workers</h3><p>Despite the construction industry’s increasing reliance on an immigrant workforce, there's no federal visa worker program.</p><p>The industry in 2024 employed 3.5 million foreign-born workers, nearly 30% of its workforce and the highest percentage of any sector, according to the Census Bureau.</p><p>“Since about 2012, our members’ top concern nationwide has been a shortage of construction workers,” said Brian Turmail of the Associated General Contractors of America.</p><p>Those concerns could grow as the immigrant population in the United States is declining for the first time in 50 years, according to government data analyzed by the Pew Research Center. The think tank estimates more than 1.2 million people have left the workforce since January 2025, when Trump started his second term.</p><p>Many were authorized to work under temporary protected status programs, according to Turmail.</p><p>“Twenty percent of those people, best we can tell, worked in construction,” he said.</p><p>The contractors group is backing two bipartisan legislative proposals that would create legal pathways for immigrants to work construction jobs in the United States, similar to the agriculture sector’s carve-out.</p><p>“No one should be surprised that undocumented workers work in construction,” Turmail said. “This is the logical consequence of decades of federal under investment in workforce development for fields like construction.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/20/cinco-de-mayo-parade-little-village-canceled-second-year" >Cinco de Mayo parade in Little Village canceled for second year as immigration enforcement concerns persist</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/08/06/migrant-day-laborers-chicago-police-department-lawsuit" >Migrant day laborers claim off-duty CPD officers detained, beat them while seeking work</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Ruling on whether to appoint a special prosecutor to probe Midway Blitz agents expected in coming weeks
summary: <p>A Cook County judge could decide next month whether to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" target="_blank" >appoint a special prosecutor</a> to investigate the federal agents who carried out the aggressive deportation campaign that shook the Chicago area last fall.</p><p>Cook County Circuit Judge Erica<b> </b>Reddick, the presiding judge of the criminal division, listened to nearly two hours of arguments Friday<b> </b>at the George N. Leighton courthouse<b> </b>before telling the attorneys she hopes to rule during a hearing May 11.</p><p>The judge questioned lawyers on both sides of the issue but did little to tip her hand. She asked if anyone had reported alleged crimes by agents to the police, and she tried to pin down how Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen<b> </b>O’Neill Burke’s office<b> </b>sees its role in any such probe.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" >Seeking special prosecutor to target ICE, coalition says O’Neill Burke turned ‘blind eye’ to feds’ violence</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Yvette<b> </b>Loizon, the chief assistant state’s attorney for policy and external affairs, acknowledged the public outrage stemming from the campaign known as Operation Midway Blitz. But, she said, “we’ve seen what lawlessness does.”</p><p>“When we want the law to bend so that it suits us, we create problems for everybody,” Loizon said during Friday’s argument.</p><p>Locke Bowman, an attorney who represents the coalition seeking a special prosecutor, pointed to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/21/oneill-burke-trump-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-chicago-cook-county" target="_blank" >O’Neill Burke’s refusal in August</a> to join other county officials in criticizing President Donald Trump, when the president threatened to deploy National Guard troops to Chicago.</p><p>“If she was unwilling to criticize the invasion of Cook County as it was about to happen,” Bowman asked, “what confidence can the citizens of Cook County have that now, in the aftermath, when violence has been perpetrated, when crimes have been committed, that she will be the person to step up and prosecute those who have committed crimes?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Friday at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Reddick’s ruling could be a crucial turning point in efforts to hold agents responsible for their conduct during the deportation campaign. If she were to appoint a special prosecutor, the law requires her<b> </b>to contact public agencies, like Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office or other counties, to see if someone is available at no cost before appointing a private attorney.</p><p>But if she were to side with O’Neill Burke, it would seem to vindicate the top prosecutor, who has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" target="_blank" >under pressure for much of this year</a> to hold the Midway Blitz agents accountable. Coalition attorneys say she has “abdicated her responsibility” by refusing to lead any such investigation.</p><p>But that raises questions about the discretion prosecutors have to decide which cases to pursue. There are also legal pitfalls when it comes to charging federal agents with crimes. For example, prosecuting federal agents in state court requires <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/can-state-officials-prosecute-the-feds-calls-grow-after-minneapolis-shooting" target="_blank" >showing they acted unreasonably</a> while fulfilling their duties.</p><p>Loizon on Friday called such issues “sticky wickets”<b> </b>and said O’Neill Burke tried to draw a “roadmap” to navigate them when she released protocols for such cases<b> </b>in February.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-cook-county-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-oneill-burke-loevy" >O’Neill Burke rejects bid for special prosecutor to target ICE, says it threatens to ‘thwart’ justice</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>O’Neill Burke has “repeatedly denounced the deplorable conduct of the Trump administration,” Loizon insisted, and even filed an amicus brief opposing the president when he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/10/09/federal-judge-set-to-hear-arguments-in-high-stakes-national-guard-hearing" target="_blank" >ultimately tried to follow through</a> on his National Guard threats.</p><p>The coalition seeking a special prosecutor is made up of more than 400 members,<b> </b>including U.S. Reps. Jesus<b> </b>“Chuy”<b> </b>Garcia, Jonathan<b> </b>Jackson and<b> </b>Delia<b> </b>Ramirez, all Democrats, and former U.S. District Chief Judge Ruben<b> </b>Castillo, who was appointed to the bench in 1994<b> </b>by President Bill Clinton.</p><p>The coalition also includes the Chicago News Guild, which represents journalists at the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>During Friday’s argument, Reddick asked coalition attorney Meg Gould whether individual complaints had been made to police departments about the agents’ actions. Gould told the judge she didn’t immediately have that information.</p><p>However, coalition attorney Steve Art later told reporters “we know that people have made complaints.”</p><div police. Loizon told her the office shouldn’t be the “primary investigators of crimes.”</p><p>“We can assist and support law enforcement when they are investigating crimes,” Loizon said. “… Our role is to support investigations.”</p><p>She said a <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoiscourts.gov/resources/bb31d7b0-e90c-4843-8486-c740ae2624ef/file" target="_blank" >2017 Illinois Supreme Court decision</a><b> </b>is<b> </b>“replete with statements that make it clear” that the high court was “discouraging prosecutors’ offices from being primary investigators in any case.”</p><p>No law enforcement agency has asked O'Neill Burke's office to review a case involving Midway Blitz agents' conduct, her team has said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/21/oneill-burke-trump-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-chicago-cook-county" >O’Neill Burke wouldn’t publicly denounce Trump because she wanted to ‘maintain’ ties with feds, emails show</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The judge also heard several references to the special prosecutor appointed to handle the shooting death of Laquan McDonald<b> </b>by Chicago police officer Jason Van Dyke. Loizon pointed out that then-Cook County State’s Attorney Anita<b> </b>Alvarez<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/5/5/18389589/alvarez-flip-flops-asks-for-special-prosecutor-in-mcdonald-case" target="_blank" >voluntarily<b> </b>recused<b> </b>from that case</a>.</p><p>A jury later found Van Dyke <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/10/5/18422864/16-shots-a-guilty-verdict-and-a-chicago-cop-goes-to-jail-for-killing-a-teen" target="_blank" >guilty<b> </b>of second-degree murder</a> in McDonald’s death.</p><p>Bowman said Friday there are sometimes circumstances, like the McDonald case, that<b> </b>“flow outside of the norm”<b> </b>— in which police are not engaged “for whatever reason.”<b> </b>He said O’Neill Burke has made clear that, in the absence of a separate police investigation, “she will not act.”</p><p>Bowman concluded by invoking the October<b> </b>shooting<b> </b>of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a><b> </b>in Chicago, and the September killing of<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" >Silverio<b> </b>Villegas<b> </b>Gonzalez</a><b> </b>in Franklin Park, both at the hands of immigration authorities.</p><p>In the end, the lawyer told the judge, “it’s up to you.”</p><p><i>Neither the reporter nor editors who worked on this story — including some represented by the News Guild — have been involved in the litigation described in this article.</i></p>

longstanding movement that involves not paying federal taxes. Some Chicagoans point to the government’s aggressive deportation efforts, the United States' support for Israel in the war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israel war against Iran as reasons for engaging in this kind of civil disobedience. </p><p><b>Getting organized</b>: "This definitely is our busiest tax season that I’ve witnessed," said Lincoln Rice, a Milwaukee organizer with the National War Tax Resistance Coordinating Committee, who hasn’t paid most of his federal taxes since 1998. The group provides training on tax resistance and consequences, which include threatening letters from the Internal Revenue Service, a monthly fine, and, in extreme cases, wage garnishment or prison time.</p><p><b>Zooming in</b>: Local attorney Rachel Cohen decided to not pay federal taxes, instead putting the owed amount into a high-yield savings account and paying only her state taxes. context</b>: Wrestling fans say the Eagles Club offered budget-friendly prices and free parking. And on the West Side, they can enjoy a set by trumpeter Victor Garcia in Austin, or a retrospective of Chicago jazz at the Garfield Park Conservatory.</p><p>And that’s only a sample of shows on "Neighborhood Jazz Night," which is part of UNESCO International Jazz Day programming.</p><p>Chicago is a first-time host for the celebration, which culminates in the All-Star Global Concert on Thursday at Lyric Opera House. That performance will feature more than 40 artists including Herbie Hancock, Kurt Elling, Dianne Reeves and Dee Dee Bridgewater.</p><p>But the large-scale show only captures some of Chicago’s jazz scene. Happening all month, a wealth of events — many of them free — have been exploring the history of jazz in the city, honoring homegrown talent and supporting local venues.</p><p>See our list of Jazz Day highlights for must-attend events.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiuuujl-l-ju/" target="_blank" ><b>JAZZ DAY HIGHLIGHTS HERE</b></a></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p> <br>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. title: Illinois marijuana firms will get a massive tax break from Trump administration's historic weed shift
summary: <p>The Trump administration's reclassification of medical marijuana will offer some Illinois weed firms a massive tax break, but industry leaders say more action is needed for comprehensive reform. </p><p>Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche signed an order that shifts state-licensed medical cannabis from a Schedule I — meant for drugs without medical use and a high potential for abuse — to the more loosely regulated Schedule III. It also applies to cannabis products approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.</p><p>The policy shift offers medical marijuana operators significant tax relief by allowing companies to deduct business expenses on their federal taxes. It also lowers the barrier for more cannabis research.</p><p>George Archos, founder and CEO of Verano, which operates 10 Zen Leaf dispensaries in the Chicago area and several more in the Midwest and Florida, said the company would save an estimated $80 million a year from the tax break.</p><p>“We could invest back into our operations, putting us on a level playing field with any other legal business,” Archos said.</p><p>Recreational cannabis remains a Schedule I drug, but Blanche’s order sets up an expedited Drug Enforcement Administration hearing process beginning June 29 to consider broader reclassification to Schedule III.</p><p>Rescheduling medical cannabis is a “long-overdue step that finally brings federal policy closer to the science,” said Charlie Bachtell, CEO of Cresco Labs, which operates 10 Sunnyside dispensaries in Illinois.</p><p>“This decision opens the door to expanded research, better data, more informed care, and broader access for those who need it most,” Bachtell said in a statement. “It is a win for all patients nationwide and will usher in a new era of healthcare, where cannabis is treated like any other medicine.”</p><p>The differing classifications for the same substance breaks a longstanding stance in the Controlled Substances Act, said Mike Feldman, general counsel for Nabis, the largest cannabis distributor in the U.S.</p><p>“[The order] creates a regime where the same product, in the same packaging, is federally Schedule III or Schedule I, depending on where it is purchased,” Feldman said. “That has never been how drug schedules work, for opioids, for psychedelics, for anything."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>An employee hands a customer their order at Zen Leaf Dispensary at 222 S Halsted St at Greektown, Thursday, April 23, 2026. Trump’s acting AG signed an order reclassifying state-licensed medical marijuana as a Schedule III drug, giving medical marijuana operators a tax break and lowering the barrier to more research.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But even reclassifying all types of cannabis isn’t going far enough to reform cannabis laws, said Betty Aldworth, chair of the Marijuana Policy Project.</p><p>“It does not resolve the fundamental contradictions between federal and state law. It does not address the ongoing reality of cash-only operations that put workers and communities at risk. It does not protect people from the legal consequences of cannabis use embedded in housing, immigration, employment, or family law,” Aldworth said in a statement.</p><p>“And it does not create a pathway for patients to access cannabis through insurance coverage, even when it may be safer or more effective than legal options.”</p><p>Kevin Sabet, president of Smart Approaches to Marijuana, which has been opposed to cannabis reclassification and legalization, called Blanche’s order an “injustice to the American people of unprecedented proportions” because of the massive tax breaks. He argued the move does nothing for cannabis research.</p><p>“What we would need for research is funding… And funding is not in any of these orders,” Sabet said.</p><p>He said the reclassification without further research reminds him of Big Tobacco putting profits over public health.</p><p>“It’s a massive industry that relies on addiction for profit and that’s what my worry is if we allow this to happen,” Sabet said.</p><p>All cannabis use remains federally illegal, though 24 states plus Washington D.C. have legalized adult recreational marijuana use, 40 allow medical marijuana use, and eight others allow low-THC cannabis or CBD oil for medical use. Only Idaho and Kansas ban marijuana outright.</p><p>Illinois has around 50,000 monthly medical marijuana patients, which is down from more than 70,000 in 2021 but is roughly the same as when the state legalized recreational use in 2020, state data shows.</p><p>The state collected $13 million in medical marijuana sales in February, down from $20 million at the same time last year and from its high of around $35 million collected monthly in 2021, according to state data. Illinois sold $105 million in recreational cannabis in February.</p>

>Bears’ exit from Chicago is closer to reality as House passes bill helping Arlington Heights bid</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-h/" target="_blank" >Tina Sfondeles</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-k/" target="_blank" >Mawa Iqbal</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-u/" target="_blank" >Matt Trunfio</a></h5><h5></h5><p><b>Arlington Heights Bears?</b>: In an attempt to keep the Chicago Bears from leaving for Indiana, Illinois lawmakers advanced a measure Wednesday that would give the team property tax certainty while also providing some property tax relief for homeowners.</p><p><b>The measure</b>: The House voted 78-32 to OK the megaproject proposal, which still needs approval from the Illinois Senate. It would incentivize the Bears to build a domed stadium in Arlington Heights by negotiating payments in lieu of property taxes based on assessments. It also directs those funds toward property tax relief for homeowners — near the megaproject and throughout Illinois.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The bill represents the first major legislative step toward ensuring the Bears stay in Illinois, after a monthslong tug of war between Illinois and the Hoosier state. The thorny details of infrastructure funding for Arlington Heights must still be dealt with before lawmakers' spring session adjourns next month.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-o/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>THE WATCHDOGS 👀</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-660000" name="image-660000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd8e901/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa5%2F27%2F87b7358e44b8b2c8e2fac262bd38%2Fbankfailure-260201-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/affd8dd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa5%2F27%2F87b7358e44b8b2c8e2fac262bd38%2Fbankfailure-260201-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dc0d191/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa5%2F27%2F87b7358e44b8b2c8e2fac262bd38%2Fbankfailure-260201-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Metropolitan Capital Bank and Trust, which declared bank failure, located at 9 E. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-q/" target="_blank" >Emmanuel Camarillo</a></h5><p><b>Union action</b>: Lunchroom workers represented by the union Unite Here Local 1 have been working to negotiate a contract with Chicago Public Schools for more than 11 months. To "sound the alarm" on what they see as unfair and unequal wages, they plan to protest Thursday. Several workers say they'll sit and block traffic downtown as an act of civil disobedience.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: The two biggest sticking points, according to Unite Here, are wages and staffing levels. Lunchroom workers including cooks, porters who clean kitchens and attendants who serve food are among the lowest-paid full-time workers in the school district. Their average salaries range from about $23,400 to $37,400, according to a recent CPS employee roster.</p><p><b>Zooming in</b>: Kimberly Penson, 61, is the sole cook at Greene Elementary School in Bridgeport. She has worked for CPS for 21 years and makes an annual salary of about $34,000. Penson says she feels deeply disrespected by the district’s leadership. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-f/" target="_blank" ><b>READ >Indie rockers Ratboys evolve from ‘country mouse’ to ‘city rat’ on latest album</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-ju/" target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>In other rat-related coverage, one of the most solid bands in the city's indie music scene, Ratboys, are in the midst of a banner run.</p><p>The quartet’s sixth record, "Singin’ to an Empty Chair," released Feb. 6, comprises 11 tracks drenched in twangy folk, pop-rock and distortion, and all beating with Midwestern heart. </p><p>It’s a similar vibe to 2023’s "The Window," which helped put the band on the map and led to their first headlining tour across the country; <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-tl/" target="_blank" >a Lollapalooza debut</a> a couple years later, not long after singer/guitarist Julia Steiner worked on the festival’s artist transport team; and an appearance on "CBS Saturday Sessions."</p><p>Ten years after forming at the University of Notre Dame, the band is going strong, having just wrapped a national tour and gearing up to play in Europe starting next month.</p><p>But Chicago is still home for Steiner, bassist Sean Neumann and drummer Marcus Nuccio.</p><p>"In Chicago, we all lift each other up. It feels very inclusive … and it’s been that way for a long time," Nuccio said of the city's music scene.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiujdhl-l-tr/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. From April 29-June 14 at Paramount Theatre, 23 E. Galena Blvd., Aurora. Heather Currie directs. From April 24-June 14 at Lifeline Theatre, 6912 N. Glenwood Ave. Tickets: $45. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://lifelinetheatre.com" target="_blank" ><u>lifelinetheatre.com</u></a>.</li><li><b>“Barbra & Judy Together Again” </b>features Barbra Streisand impressionist Steven Brinberg and Judy Garland interpreter Angela Ingersoll. The performance is a benefit for Season of Concern Chicago, the organization that provides financial assistance for theater artists affected by illness, injury or circumstance. At 7 p.m. April 27 at Studebaker Theater, Fine Arts Building, 410 S. Michigan Ave. Tickets: $50-$200. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://fineartsbuilding.com/events" target="_blank" ><u>fineartsbuilding.com/events</u></a>.</li><li>Saint Sebastian Players present<b> “I Hate Hamlet,”</b> Paul Rudnick’s comedy about an actor cast as Hamlet who is visited by the ghost of legendary actor John Barrymore. Zach Kunde directs. From April 24-May 17 at St. Bonaventure, 1625 W. Diversey Pkwy. Tickets: $35. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://saintsebastianplayers.org" target="_blank" ><u>saintsebastianplayers.org</u></a>.</li><li><b>“The Wedding Singer”</b> is a Tony Award-nominated musical about a 1980s wedding singer who is the life of the party until his fiancée flees. Amber Mak directs. From April 29-May 24 at Metropolis Performing Arts Centre, 111 W. Campbell St., Arlington Heights. Tickets: $25-$49. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://metropolisarts.com" target="_blank" ><u>metropolisarts.com</u></a>. <b></b></li></ul><h3><b>Dance</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-ccd62df1-3c1e-11f1-97f4-43fbcb901192"><li>The always remarkable <b>Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater</b> returns with performances of Medhi Walerski’s “Blink of an Eye,” Judith Jamison’s “A Case of You,” Fredrick Earl Mosley’s “Embrace,” Maija Garcia’s “Jazz Island,” Matthew Neenan’s “Difference Between,” Jamar Roberts’ “Song of the Anchorite” and each performance concludes with Ailey’s masterpiece “Revelations.” At 7:30 p.m. April 24, 1 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. April 25 and 3 p.m. April 26 at The Auditorium, 50 E. Ida B. Wells Dr. Tickets: $46+. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://auditoriumtheatre.org" target="_blank" ><u>auditoriumtheatre.org</u></a>.</li><li>Marcel Gbeffa and Sarah Trouche’s <b>“Didę” </b>is inspired by the Guèlèdè traditions whose ceremonies and masks pay homage to Ìyá Nlá, the Yoruba primordial spirit of all creation. At 7:30 p.m. April 24 at Dance Center of Columbia College, 1306 S. Michigan Ave. Tickets: $10-$100. Visit <a class="Link" href="http://dance.colum.edu" target="_blank" ><u>dance.colum.edu</u></a>.</li><li>Ede2 presents artistic director Rachel Molinaro’s <b>“The Little Dancer: A Reimagining of ‘Le Petit Prince,’”</b> the story of a pilot marooned in the desert where she meets a mysterious stranger. At 3:30 and 7 p.m. April 25 and 2 and 5 p.m. April 26 at Studio5, 1938 Dempster St., Evanston. Tickets: $11, $6 for ages 10 and under. title: Marimar Martinez, shot by CBP agent, testifies, urges accountability or 'more people are going to get hurt'
summary: <p>Marimar Martinez, the Chicago woman who was shot by a Border Patrol agent in October, testified Wednesday before the Homeland Security Committee in Washington, warning federal lawmakers that if immigration agents aren’t held accountable, “more people are going to get hurt.”</p><p>Martinez, 31, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" ><u>survived being shot</u></a> five times by Border Patrol agent Charles Exum after a car carrying three CBP agents collided with her vehicle Oct. 4 near 39th Street and Kedzie Avenue.</p><p>She said she was driving to donate clothes to a church that morning when she noticed an SUV that seemed to be driven by federal immigration agents who “had been invading my Hispanic neighborhood in recent weeks.”</p><p>After seeing uniformed Border Patrol agents in the car, Martinez said she followed the SUV, honked and shouted, “La migra,” to alert her neighbors of their presence.</p><p>Her car remained “two to three feet” to the left of the CBP vehicle when Exum veered into her lane. She made eye contact with Exum and “watched as he turned his steering wheel once again to his left and sideswiped my vehicle,” she said.</p><p>“I immediately froze, slammed on my brakes and stopped my car. The Border Patrol stopped just one to two car lengths ahead of me,” Martinez said. “At that moment, I believed I was in danger based on what I knew watching the news coverage of ICE agents … in Chicago.”</p><p>She drove forward, around the CBP agents as one agent pointed a gun at her, she said. She continued veering left until she struck a curb.</p><p>“I felt burning sensations in my arms and legs. Shortly after, I began to feel sharp impacts and burning sensation as I continued to drive past the Border Patrol agents. I could hear my back passenger window shatter,” Martinez said. “I looked down and noticed blood gushing out of my arms and legs and realized I had been shot multiple times.”</p><p>Wednesday was the first time <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/16/marimar-martinez-border-patrol-shooting-victim-chicago-congress-testimony" target="_blank" ><u>Martinez</u></a> testified before a committee. She was joined by the Rev. David Black, of the First Presbyterian Church of Chicago, who testified about when ICE agents fired pepper balls at him as he prayed outside the ICE processing facility in Broadview.</p><p>“What was done to me is only a reflection of what is being done to people in my community who have no culprit and no platform,” Black said. “On a daily basis, I witnessed the fear and the suffering of those who are being targeted by this violent campaign.”</p><p>George Retes Jr., a U.S. citizen who was tear gassed and arrested by ICE while on his way to work in southern California last July, and Ryan Ecklund, another U.S. citizen who was detained by ICE in January in Minnesota, also testified at Wednesday’s hearing.</p><p>Martinez first appeared before Congress at a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-goes-to-washington-wants-trump-officials-to-admit-not-a-domestic-terrorist" target="_blank" ><u>Feb. 3 public forum</u></a> organized in response to the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti at the hands of federal immigration officers in Minnesota. She told lawmakers then that she wanted federal agents held accountable, wanted to hear an apology and wanted the Trump administration to acknowledge she is “not a domestic terrorist.”</p><p>She reiterated that Wednesday, mainly asserting that she and “us Americans” want honesty, transparency and accountability from the Trump administration.</p><p>“Look at what happened to Renee [Good], look at what happened to Alex Pretti. It’s bound to happen sooner or later if we don’t hold these agents accountable for their actions. More people are going to get hurt,” Martinez said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/xmg8n9mcvzA?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Funding Lapse & Security Gaps: Assessing Harmful Impacts of the DHS Shutdown on Americans, Part II"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Wednesday’s hearing came at the request of committee Democrats who had also requested White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan appear.</p><p>The two Trump administration officials did not appear. All but one of the committee’s 17 Republican members, committee chairman Andrew Garbarino, R-NY, did not attend Wednesday’s hearing either.</p><p>The Homeland Security Committee hearing was called to discuss the impacts of the Department of Homeland Security shutdown that has now lasted 67 days, the longest partial government shutdown in history. Senate Democrats have blocked DHS funding and are calling for reforms to ICE and CBP tactics.</p><p>When questioned by Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, Martinez said she thinks about the October shooting “all the time,” she has “sometimes” lost sleep over it and had nightmares shortly after it happened. At one point, she stood up, removed her jacket and showed the lawmakers where on her body she was shot.</p><p>Martinez noted that after being shot, she continued driving about a mile to a mechanic shop, where workers helped her and called 911.</p><p>“Imagine if I would’ve stayed, I wouldn’t be here to testify. I wouldn’t,” Martinez said.</p><p>Exum apparently bragged to other CBP agents about shooting Martinez. In one text message previously shown in court, he wrote, “I fired 5 rounds and she had 7 holes. Put that in your book boys.”</p><p>Martinez said Wednesday it’s “not fair” that she was charged in relation to the shooting while Exum has not.</p><p>“I’ve been through hell and back, and I’ve fought for my freedom, I’ve fought for my voice,” Martinez said. “And these agents, Charles Exum has not even been held accountable for his actions. But when it comes to me, I had to fight. What about him?”</p><p>Toward the end of the roughly one-and-a-half hour hearing, Martinez said she wants Exum to be charged and tried for the shooting.</p><p>“I want the world to see my pain, my trauma, because this is not something to joke about, right,” Martinez said. “This is my life, we’re talking about my life.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/03/dhs-kristi-noem-senate-judiciary-committee-testimony-marimar-martinez-dick-durbin" target="_blank" ></a></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" ><u></u></a></p><p></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/05/trump-fires-noem-dhs-ice-border-patrol-markwayne-mullin" target="_blank" ></a></p>

title: Feds plan to use protest chants to prosecute Broadview ICE protesters — but balk at free speech defense
summary: <p>Federal prosecutors say the remaining members of the “Broadview Six” should be barred from making arguments about free speech rights when they go to trial<b> </b>next month — though the feds also plan to use protest chants caught on video as evidence against the group.</p><p>Prosecutors also argued there should be no references to the October<b> </b>shooting<b> </b>of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a> by a Border Patrol agent in Chicago, nor of the fatal shootings<b> </b>this year of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration authorities in Minnesota.</p><p>Meanwhile, defense attorneys asked<b> </b>U.S. District Judge April Perry to bar the feds from referring to their clients as “rioters,”<b> </b>“Antifa members”<b> </b>or<b> </b>“domestic terrorists.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" >Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants want conspiracy charge tossed, argue protesting isn’t a crime</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“They are inflammatory terms that carry strong political, social, and emotional connotations that risk unfairly biasing the jury against the defendants,”<b> </b>the defense attorneys wrote.</p><p>The arguments appeared in a series of motions filed Tuesday, five weeks ahead of the second federal trial to result from Operation Midway Blitz. Four people, including former congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >accused of a conspiracy</a> to impede a federal agent.</p><p>Also charged are Oak Park village trustee Brian<b> </b>Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andre<b> </b>Martin, a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff. The feds earlier this year <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped charges against two others</a> originally indicted in the case.</p><p>Questions about free speech have swirled since a grand jury handed up that indictment in October, in the heat of the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign last fall.<b> </b>Perry is still considering a defense request that she toss the conspiracy charge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" target="_blank" >based on the First Amendment</a>, which protects the freedom of speech, religion, assembly and the press. </p><p>Lawyers are next due back in Perry’s courtroom<b> </b>May 13. The trial is set to begin May 26.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d20000" name="image-d20000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bbe1361/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2286x1283+0+61/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2Fc8%2F7efede6e41d599881f57e7274e25%2Fkatscreenshot2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9424784/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2286x1283+0+61/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2Fc8%2F7efede6e41d599881f57e7274e25%2Fkatscreenshot2.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aeeca55/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2286x1283+0+61/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2Fc8%2F7efede6e41d599881f57e7274e25%2Fkatscreenshot2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Kat Abughazaleh appears in this screenshot of footage from outside an immigration holding facility in Broadview. title: Attacks on Jewish community highlight why all houses of worship need more protection
summary: <p>A Chicago man was recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-man-charged-with-threatening-shooting-at-synagogue" >charged</a> with threatening to "shoot up" a synagogue." For Jewish communities, this is not just another headline. It is a reminder that without serious investment in security, our institutions remain vulnerable.</p><p>At North Suburban Synagogue Beth El, where I serve as senior rabbi, we gather for connection and community. But like synagogues across the Chicago area, we do so knowing our safety cannot be taken for granted. We plan, train and coordinate with law enforcement. Still, the sense of security we have built can feel fragile.</p><p>Recent events underscore why. Synagogues abroad have been attacked with gunfire and explosives. Closer to home, an assailant targeted a <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/mar/30/michigan-synagogue-attacker-inspired-hezbollah" target="_blank" >synagogue near Detroit</a> while 140 children were inside. That attack did not become a tragedy in large part because of strong security measures already in place.</p><p>Jewish Americans are living with this reality every day. Parents think carefully about safety at schools. Congregants pay closer attention to entrances and exits. They do so because we have seen what happens when threats become reality. We’ve seen Jews murdered in synagogues in <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/US/pittsburgh-synagogue-mass-shooting-jury-reaches-verdict-death/story?id=101220141" target="_blank" >Pittsburgh</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/california-man-sentenced-life-followed-30-years-prison-federal-hate-crimes-related-2019-poway" target="_blank" >Poway</a>, at a Jewish community center in <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/man-who-shot-killed-three-people-kansas-jewish-sites-dies-n1266290" target="_blank" >Kansas</a>, at a kosher grocery store in <a class="Link" href="https://www.ktvu.com/news/officials-nj-kosher-deli-shooters-planned-attack-for-months" target="_blank" >New Jersey </a>and outside of a Jewish museum in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2025/05/21/2-staff-members-of-israeli-embassy-killed-in-shooting-near-jewish-museum-in-dc" target="_blank" >Washington, D.C.</a></p><p>The pattern is clear. Rhetoric escalates, followed by threats, and too often, violence. The question is not whether Jewish institutions are at risk, but rather whether we are doing enough to protect them.</p><p>The federal <a class="Link" href="https://www.fema.gov/grants/preparedness/nonprofit-security" target="_blank" >Nonprofit Security Grant program</a> is one of the most effective tools we have to prevent such tragedies. It funds cameras, reinforced doors and other critical protections. But each year, many more institutions apply for these grants than receive them. This means that synagogues across Illinois are left exposed because the funding is insufficient.</p><p>This is not only a Jewish issue. Churches, mosques and other houses of worship rely on this program as well. Protecting them is about upholding the basic American promise of safe and free religious life.</p><p>Congress should expand funding for this program and ensure funds are delivered quickly. Prevention depends on preparation. We cannot wait for the next attack to act.</p><p><i>Rabbi Michael Schwab, North Suburban Synagogue Beth El, Highland Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-820000" name="module-820000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Drug pricing program straying from mission </h3><p>Every day, I prescribe lifesaving medications for complex autoimmune diseases. The federal 340B Drug Pricing program was designed to ensure that cost was never a barrier to these types of medications for uninsured or underinsured individuals.</p><p>That’s why I support its original mission.</p><p>But from where I sit in a community-based practice, it’s clear the program is no longer operating as intended, and what’s happening should alarm anyone who wants to see it preserved.</p><p>The 340B program allows certain safety net hospitals and clinics known as “covered entities” to purchase eligible medications at steep discounts, bill payers the full price and keep the margin. The intent was to help these entities “stretch scarce federal resources as far as possible, reaching more eligible patients and providing more comprehensive services,” according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.hrsa.gov/opa" target="_blank" >Health Resources and Services Administration</a>.</p><p>But over the last decade, 340B has grown significantly in Illinois, from 34 covered entities in 2010 to 114 today. That’s more than half of Illinois hospitals.</p><p>At the same time, its footprint has expanded well beyond traditional safety net settings. Nearly half of Illinois 340B entities and contract pharmacies are now located in higher-income areas, far from the areas where they are needed most. Why? Because insurance reimbursements are generally higher, this means more 340B revenue for the covered entity.</p><p>The biggest problem is the lack of transparency into how 340B revenue is used. While many hospitals point to broader financial pressures, patients and policymakers alike deserve a clearer understanding of how 340B revenue is supporting access to care for our most vulnerable. This is especially true because state and employer health plans lose rebates on 340B drugs, which contributes to rising health care costs for employers and taxpayers across Illinois.</p><p>At the same time, our independent practices, which are often the most accessible and cost-effective sites of care, face mounting financial pressure without access to the same purchasing advantages. As care shifts into hospital systems, patients frequently encounter higher out-of-pocket costs.</p><p>None of this diminishes the importance of 340B. It underscores the need to ensure it is working as intended.</p><p>Illinois lawmakers should take a step back before advancing legislation that would lock in the program’s flaws. Instead, they should take a closer look at how 340B is functioning today, examine who benefits — and who bears the cost — and pursue targeted reforms that strengthen transparency, accountability and patient access.</p><p>That is how we preserve this program for the patients who need it most.</p><p><i>Dr. Erin Arnold, Skokie</i></p><h3>Right under the president’s nose </h3><h3></h3><p>When President Donald Trump secured his funding for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he promised they would go after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/12/operation-midway-blitz-ice-enforcement-chicago-actual-arrests" target="_blank" >“the worst of the worst,”</a> but he hasn't been able to find very many of those. Of course! They are all hiding in plain sight, in his Cabinet.</p><p><i>Bob Chicoine, Brookfield</i></p><h3>Be fair to Fox News</h3><h3></h3><p>I really enjoyed the story and the excellent way in which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/opinion/2026/04/15/transgender-women-mixup-sun-times-journalists-violet-miller-ellery-jones" >Ellery Jones</a> used humor to get her point across about being mixed up with her fellow transgender colleague. But (there it is: that inevitable, pesky, qualifying but), it seems only fair that when one references "misleading Fox News articles," one should give at least one example of a misleading article. Fair, however, does not seem to be in the lexicon of the mainstream news media these days. Thank you to Ms. Jones, though, for keeping Fox News in the public eye.</p><p><i>Sherry Szilage Stoffel, North Aurora</i><br></p>

painted around Chicago and the country</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wikjllt-l-ty/" target="_blank" >Genevieve Bookwalter</a></h5><h5></h5><p>You’ve probably seen her poetry by now.</p><p>Maybe it was spray-painted on the sidewalk outside a coffee shop or record store, or wheat-pasted on a utility pole that you walked by. Maybe you found the words within a giant heart painted inside an abandoned, run-down building you decided to explore.</p><p>The Pilsen artist known as Boots, whose real name is Kimberly Brown, has painted thousands of her original poetry snippets on sidewalks and elsewhere around Chicago since she began sharing her words with the world just before the pandemic.</p><p>Now, you can find her painted poetry while walking through towns in all 50 states, part of a project that Brown says has "become bigger than me at this point." All of them are tagged @poetrybyboots, which is her Instagram handle. The biggest number by far are in Chicago.</p><p>"It’s always extra special when my hometown appreciates it," says Brown, who receives tags, photos and messages nearly every day from fans who found her work. "It still blows my mind how many messages I’ll get."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wikjllt-l-tj/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wikjllt-l-ti/" target="_blank" >Should Illinois ban cellphones in classrooms during school hours?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"I think such a law, while popular, may be unenforceable. A better solution would be to jam the signal in classrooms; that way students cannot access distractions on their phones." — <i>Patricia Boughton</i></p><p>"I am a former Illinois student ... I believe with all the school shootings that go on around the country, these students need their phones. What if something happens to the teacher and no one else has a phone to call for help in that classroom? ... One more phone could save countless lives!" — <i>Gregory Bell-Bey</i></p><p>"I do think that cellphones should be banned during school hours. They provide a distraction from education and a barrier for teachers trying to communicate ... Schools should also ensure that students will have easy access to an office phone if they need to call their parents or guardians." — <i>Margaret McCoy</i></p><p>"I'm finishing my 22nd year as a CPS high school teacher. Brain rot is real. Critical thinking has atrophied. Attention spans are measured in seconds. Students are addicted to the dopamine hits endless scrolling or game-playing ... provide. I was an early adopter of Google Classroom, which I still use ... However, I now make paper copies and direct students to put their Chromebooks and phones away. It's a daily battle. I can't tell you how many times a student has told me, 'I'm talking to my mom." — <i>Sharon Marzano</i></p><p>"Absolutely! As an educator for more than 40 years, I can say ... It distracts students from focusing ... even if the phone is in a backpack and on silent, the temptation to check it is overwhelming. It fractures concentration, and over time leads to decreased attention span. It also contributes to diminished social skills, as kids are more focused on their devices than on human interaction. When phones are not allowed in school, teachers report students are way more engaged with learning and with one another." — <i>Anita Caref</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. title: Doc10 lost federal cash. The fest is still swinging big.
summary: <p>Chicago’s Doc10 film festival is best known for two things. It is one of the only documentary-exclusive film fests in the country, and the organizers have an uncanny knack for curating a menu of films that end up on annual shortlists for prestigious awards, including the Oscars.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2025/04/24/doc10-documentary-film-festival-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Last year’s festival</u></a>, which marked the group’s 10th anniversary, arrived at <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2024/12/03/for-chicago-documentary-filmmakers-its-a-steep-climb-to-streaming" target="_blank" ><u>a precarious time</u></a> in the documentary film industry. Political documentaries and more complex films have taken a backseat to celebrity-driven projects and true crime stories on major streaming platforms like Netflix. On the fundraising side, government grants for some projects landed in limbo<b> </b>after the Trump administration overhauled the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/02/14/trump-nea-grants-national-endowment-arts-chicago-theater-dance" target="_blank" ><u>National Endowment for the Arts</u></a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/04/04/trump-humanities-grants-chicago-illinois-culture-national-endowment" target="_blank" ><u>National Endowment for the Humanities</u></a>, leading to fewer filmmaker grants.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" data-module data-has-background ><a The barrage of cuts also impacted the Chicago Media Project (CMP), the group behind Doc10, which had its funding rescinded from the National Endowment of the Arts.</p><p>So heading into this year’s fest, which opens April 24, organizers faced a fresh urgency to program a festival that speaks to the current moment. They expanded programming to include “Speak Truth,” a series of film screenings and post-show discussions that feature films intended to provoke civic dialogue on urgent contemporary issues.</p><p>“We've always believed in the power of media to make change in the world,” said Paula Froehle, co-founder and CEO of the Chicago Media Project.</p><p>“The idea that came about last fall on the heels of the NEA rescinding funding, and us feeling somewhat targeted because of our DEI programming,” she said. One of the notable changes the Trump administration made to NEA funding was the refusal to pay for projects that promote what the administration describes as “DEI” or “gender ideology.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-000000" name="module-000000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://doc10.eventive.org/welcome" target="_blank" ><b><u>Doc10</u></b></a></h3><b>Where</b>: Davis Theatre, 4614 N. Film Festival</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Among the films the fest will screen in the “Speak Truth” series is director Steve Pink’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2024/10/31/adam-kinzinger-the-last-republican-documentary-steve-pink-streaming" target="_blank" ><u>“The Last Republican,”</u></a> which follows former Illinois Congressman Adam Kinzinger’s unwavering fight to hold President Donald Trump accountable for the January 6 insurrection. The screening on April 28 will include Kinzinger, via Zoom, and a panel discussion about fair elections and how everyday people can get involved in politics.</p><p>Chicago Media Project co-founder Steven Cohen said the idea this year is to flip the event from being just a film festival into also being an ideas festival. “Film is the galvanizing point and it's the reason people come together. But we go beyond there. We want Doc10 to not be the place where film is the end of the conversation, but the beginning of the conversation.”</p><p>Put simply, Cohen said, a running theme throughout this year's festival is
