But we go beyond there. We want Doc10 to not be the place where film is the end of the conversation, but the beginning of the conversation,” Doc10 Co-founder Steve Cohen (right) said. Here, he stands with fellow Doc10 co-founder Paula Froehle in 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Vee Sanders</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The line up of “Speak Truth” films also includes a slate of shorts with strong local ties. “ICE Under Watch,” screening May 3, is a collection of films by Chicago-based filmmakers that discuss immigration with a specific focus on Operation “Midway Blitz,” the monthslong federal immigration enforcement action that unfolded across the Chicago area last fall.</p><p>One of the docs in this series, “El Sueño,” is unfinished, but will screen a 10-minute excerpt. The project started with filmmaker Carlos Javier Ortiz filming Venezuelan refugees that were sent to Chicago in 2022 by Texas Governor Greg Abbott. Then, when Trump was reelected, Ortiz documented the rapid changes in immigration policy, leading up to events of Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>“I think for us, an important aspect of this film is that this is going to be Chicago’s historic memory,” said Alexandra Halkin, “El Sueño” producer. I think everybody that has been living in Chicago and dealing with the situation of [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] and border patrol, we all live through it one way or the other.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://player.vimeo.com/video/1147204272?app_id=122963" width="426" height="240" frameborder="0" allow="autoplay; fullscreen; picture-in-picture; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" title="Trailer El Sueño-ORTIZmp4"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Halkin said the four-year chunk of time the film covers starts with <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/race-class-communities/2022/08/31/texas-buses-dozens-of-migrants-to-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>the arrival of busloads</u></a> of Venezuelans sent from the border to Chicago in 2022 and ends with the 2026 midterm elections — a four-year chunk of “collective trauma.”</p><p>The ensuing discussion will focus on the power of media, collective organizing and solidarity in times of heightened enforcement and resistance.</p><p>This year’s official Doc10 selections serendipitously align with some of the themes from “Speak Truth,” even though senior programmer Anthony Kaufman said films are selected strictly based on merit. “It's finding the best films that we can, and then seeing what kind of themes emerge organically from the films themselves.”</p><p>Even so, the coveted 10 slots in the group of official selections contain films like “Everybody to Kenmure Street,” by award winning filmmaker Felipe Bustos Sierra. Set in the Scottish city of Glasgow, the documentary unfolds on a morning in May 2021, when immigration enforcement officers attempted to detain two community members.</p><p>The documentary uses reenactments and cell phone footage to depict the events of the day, during which what seemed like the entire community surrounded an immigration van and demanded the release of the detainees.</p><p>“Solidarity being worked out by people who didn't know each other — and you know, some were neighbors — but that, to me, was extraordinary,” said Sierra, the filmmaker, who screened his movie in Budapest days before Prime Minister Viktor Orbán <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/hungarys-orban-calls-for-his-partys-renewal-after-stunning-election-defeat" target="_blank" ><u>was defeated</u></a>. Of his time in Hungary, Sierra said, “I think the people getting to know about the protest itself, they keep saying, it’s healing and energizing.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/03645e1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3840x2155+0+2/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0d%2Fbf%2Fb5522eb44a20ab0fc453a2da5839%2Feverybody-to-kenmure-street-still-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9fa0eea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3840x2155+0+2/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0d%2Fbf%2Fb5522eb44a20ab0fc453a2da5839%2Feverybody-to-kenmure-street-still-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ba1d2a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3840x2155+0+2/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0d%2Fbf%2Fb5522eb44a20ab0fc453a2da5839%2Feverybody-to-kenmure-street-still-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A still from Everybody To Kenmure Street by Felipe Bustos Sierra, an official selection of the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Courtesy of Sundance Institute." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ba1d2a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3840x2155+0+2/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0d%2Fbf%2Fb5522eb44a20ab0fc453a2da5839%2Feverybody-to-kenmure-street-still-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7471d74/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3840x2155+0+2/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0d%2Fbf%2Fb5522eb44a20ab0fc453a2da5839%2Feverybody-to-kenmure-street-still-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ba1d2a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3840x2155+0+2/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0d%2Fbf%2Fb5522eb44a20ab0fc453a2da5839%2Feverybody-to-kenmure-street-still-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Everybody to Kenmure Street” unfolds on a Glasgow morning in May 2021, when immigration enforcement officers attempted to detain two community members.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Sundance Institute</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Typically, events like Doc10 would attempt to be as nonpartisan as possible. And while Cohen says the event itself doesn’t take a particular side, in the aftermath of losing government support, organizers now have more freedom to lean into opinions on fraught political topics.</p><p>“We’re obviously still nonpartisan, but that doesn't mean we can’t have a point of view,” said Cohen. “We're taking a point of view over things that shouldn't be controversial — like, we want free and fair elections. And democracy should be the winner in this next election.”</p><p>For the organizers, the strong stance is the result of feeling attacked.</p><p>“I just feel like when somebody threatens your livelihood, you gotta come back fighting bigger and stronger,” said Froehle. “There is power in numbers and people coming out. We have a great program that demonstrates how documentary filmmakers have the ability to spend more time with their subjects to get into the deeper, more intimate, emotional complexities of an experience.”</p>
author: Mike Davis | WBEZ

title: O'Neill Burke wouldn't denounce Trump because she wanted to 'maintain' relationship with feds, emails show
summary: <p>Cook County’s top prosecutor declined<b> </b>to criticize the Trump administration in the weeks leading up to Operation Midway Blitz because she wanted to keep her “excellent working relationships”<b> </b>with federal law enforcement, newly filed court records show.</p><p>It’s evidence that Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen<b> </b>O’Neill<b> </b>Burke<b> </b>has a conflict that justifies the installation of a special prosecutor who could investigate the federal agents behind last fall’s deportation campaign, a coalition of elected officials and community members argued. </p><p>"The State's Attorney has an alliance with federal law enforcement that prevents her from taking action against the federal agents alleged to have committed crimes during Operation Midway Blitz," its lawyers wrote<b> </b>in a 30-page court filing Friday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-cook-county-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-oneill-burke-loevy" >O’Neill Burke rejects bid for special prosecutor to target ICE, says it threatens to ‘thwart’ justice</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But O'Neill Burke's office insisted Monday she's<b> </b>"horrified by the thuggish and inappropriate conduct of [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement] agents in Chicago and elsewhere." </p><p>"The petition seeking a special prosecutor is frivolous, contains baseless allegations and gross misrepresentations of the law, and will make it more difficult for the Cook County State's Attorney's Office to successfully do its job protecting the public," O'Neill Burke's office said in a statement. </p><p>The fight over whether a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" target="_blank" >special prosecutor should be appointed</a> could come to a head soon, as Cook County Circuit Judge Erica<b> </b>Reddick<b> </b>is set to hear arguments Friday. She is the presiding judge<b> </b>of the court’s criminal division. O'Neill Burke's office promised a "comprehensive response"<b> </b>during the arguments.</p><p>The coalition seeking a special prosecutor pointed in its new filing to an Aug. 11 email. Sent by a member of the Justice Advisory Council, it discussed an effort by Cook County Board President Toni<b> </b>Preckwinkle’s office<b> </b>to get county agencies<b> </b>to sign on to a statement “responding to the recent actions and rhetoric coming out of the Trump administration.”</p><p>President Donald Trump<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/08/11/donald-trump-trump-federal-takeover-dc-police-national-guard-chicago-threat-jb-pritzker" target="_blank" >threatened<b> </b>that same day</a> to deploy the National Guard into Chicago. Trump eventually tried to follow through on that threat, but he was blocked<b> </b>first by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/10/09/federal-judge-set-to-hear-arguments-in-high-stakes-national-guard-hearing" target="_blank" >U.S. District Judge April Perry</a><b> </b>and eventually the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/12/23/supreme-court-trump-national-guard-illinois" target="_blank" >U.S. Supreme Court</a>.</p><p>Then-O'Neill Burke spokesman Matt<b> </b>McGrath<b> </b>responded<b> </b>Aug. 12, the morning after Trump’s threat.</p><p>“We obviously share concerns about Trump’s actions, rhetoric, and bluster,” he wrote. “At the same time the State’s Attorney’s top priority remains combating illegal guns, and to continue doing that effectively we need to maintain our excellent working relationships with the local (Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives) and other federal partners. So we will not be able to sign on.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fb0000" name="image-fb0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9481271/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3936x2209+0+212/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F29%2Fe67bc0c34d22ba9d56e96f32e594%2Fap25029702146868.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5107df9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3936x2209+0+212/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F29%2Fe67bc0c34d22ba9d56e96f32e594%2Fap25029702146868.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d2e98b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3936x2209+0+212/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F29%2Fe67bc0c34d22ba9d56e96f32e594%2Fap25029702146868.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="President Donald Trump speaks before signing the Laken Riley Act in the East Room of the White House, Wednesday, Jan. 29, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d2e98b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3936x2209+0+212/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F29%2Fe67bc0c34d22ba9d56e96f32e594%2Fap25029702146868.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a8b11fa/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3936x2209+0+212/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F29%2Fe67bc0c34d22ba9d56e96f32e594%2Fap25029702146868.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d2e98b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3936x2209+0+212/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F29%2Fe67bc0c34d22ba9d56e96f32e594%2Fap25029702146868.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>President Donald Trump speaks before signing the Laken Riley Act in the East Room of the White House on Jan. 29, 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Alex Brandon/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Operation Midway Blitz began four weeks after the email, a copy of which was filed Friday with the coalition’s latest brief in the special prosecutor litigation. </p><p>“If the state’s attorney felt that her conflict arising from federal collaborations prevented her from even opposing the Trump Administration’s threats to Chicago, then surely the same conflict prevents her from investigating and prosecuting federal agents who carried out those threats shortly thereafter,” the coalition’s attorneys wrote in their filing Friday.</p><p>The coalition seeking a special prosecutor is made up of more than 200 elected officials, clergy, journalists and attorneys. It includes the Chicago News Guild,<b> </b>which represents journalists at the Chicago Sun-Times. The effort is led in court by the Loevy and Loevy law firm.</p><p>Prosecuting federal agents in state court would require <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/can-state-officials-prosecute-the-feds-calls-grow-after-minneapolis-shooting" target="_blank" >showing they acted unreasonably</a> while fulfilling their duties. Meanwhile, prosecutors like O’Neill Burke are entrusted with discretion to choose which cases to pursue.</p><p>O’Neill Burke has insisted any investigation must be conducted by law enforcement. She’s also pointed to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoiscourts.gov/resources/bb31d7b0-e90c-4843-8486-c740ae2624ef/file" target="_blank" >2017 Illinois Supreme Court ruling</a> she says limits her own ability to investigate the agents.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" >Seeking special prosecutor to target ICE, coalition says O’Neill Burke turned ‘blind eye’ to feds’ violence</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The high court found that a state’s attorney’s duty to investigate is “limited to circumstances where other law enforcement agencies inadequately deal with such investigation … or where a law enforcement agency asks the state’s attorney for assistance.”</p><p>But the coalition argued Friday that “it is perfectly clear that local police are failing to investigate.” They pointed to the lack of any probe by the Franklin Park or Chicago police<b> </b>into the September killing of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" >Silverio<b> </b>Villegas<b> </b>Gonzalez</a><b> </b>by a federal agent.</p><p>The coalition argued that circumstances now are similar to those that led to special prosecutors in two previous high-profile cases: The death of Laquan<b> </b>McDonald<b> </b>at the hands of Chicago police officer Jason Van Dyke, and of David<b> </b>Koschman<b> </b>at the hands of former Mayor Richard M. Daley’s nephew<b> </b>Richard<b> </b>J. “R.J.”<b> </b>Vanecko.</p><p>“There is ample basis for the inference that the state’s attorney’s failure to act is because she is beholden to law enforcement and unwilling to risk impairing political and institutional relationships,” the coalition’s attorneys wrote.<b> </b>“Just as in those cases, a special prosecutor should be appointed here.”</p><p><i>Neither the reporters nor editors who worked on this story — including some represented by the News Guild — have been involved in the litigation described in this article.</i></p>
author: Sophie Sherry

title: Judge tosses lawsuit over Trump's push to deploy National Guard to Chicago after his Supreme Court loss
summary: <p>Six months after she blocked President Donald Trump’s efforts <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/10/09/federal-judge-set-to-hear-arguments-in-high-stakes-national-guard-hearing" target="_blank" >to deploy National Guard troops</a> into Chicago, a federal judge Monday confirmed that the orders triggering the deployment<b> </b>are no longer in effect<b> </b>and dismissed the lawsuit that challenged them.</p><p>U.S. District Judge April Perry ruled that the case is “moot,”<b> </b>meaning there’s no meaningful action left for her to take. But she warned that there are still “fail safes”<b> </b>built into the legal system, especially if it turns out there were “misrepresentations”<b> </b>from the Trump administration.</p><p>“The court cannot provide ongoing protection against hypothetical unlawful acts committed by the federal government,” Perry said.</p><p>The judge’s ruling comes despite a Dec. 31 social media post by Trump, commenting on his administration’s plans for Chicago, in which he promised “we will come back, perhaps in a much different and stronger form, when crime begins to soar again — Only a question of time!”</p><p>Perry told the courtroom, “I honestly don’t know what to make of those particular social media messages.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/12/23/supreme-court-trump-national-guard-illinois" >U.S. Supreme Court sides against Trump, won’t lift block on National Guard deployment in Illinois</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Given that the president’s comments were “about general crime control, which is not at all what this deployment was supposed to be about,” Perry said the president’s commentary was “not helpful enough” to find any exception in the law that would allow her to keep the case alive.</p><p>Attorney General Kwame<b> </b>Raoul<b> </b>later reacted to the ruling by saying American people “should not live under threat of military occupation simply because they live in a jurisdiction that has fallen out of a president's political favor.”</p><p>“I am pleased that today, the court has declared the Trump administration’s unlawful orders defunct and said it is absolutely clear that the administration cannot use the Illinois orders to federalize or deploy National Guard troops in Illinois,” Raoul said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-510000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by SAUL LOEB/AFP via Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Perry’s ruling brings to an end a historic lawsuit filed in the heat of the aggressive deportation campaign known as Operation Midway Blitz. The case eventually led to a rare defeat for the Trump administration <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/12/23/supreme-court-trump-national-guard-illinois" target="_blank" >before the U.S. Supreme Court</a>.</p><p>That’s despite a White House spokesperson’s claim that the president “exercised his lawful authority to protect federal officers and assets”<b> </b>amid<b> </b>“ongoing violent riots and lawlessness.”</p><p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago have yet to convict anyone of violence directed toward federal agents during Midway Blitz. One man <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/15/crime-chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-ice-border-patrol" target="_blank" >pleaded guilty</a> last week to concealing information about a crime, and in doing so he admitted he drove his Ford F-250<b> </b>into the rear passenger side of a federal vehicle.</p><p>The events in that case took place one day before Trump triggered deployment of the National Guard into Chicago.</p><p>Perry ruled Oct. 9 that the Trump administration’s “perception of events”<b> </b>around Chicago were “simply unreliable.” She found “no credible evidence that there is danger of rebellion in the state of Illinois,” nor that Trump was “unable … to execute the laws of the United States.”</p><p>The judge blocked deployment, and the Supreme Court eventually sided against Trump, as well.</p><p>Perry on Monday focused on whether deployment orders from Defense Secretary Pete<b> </b>Hegseth<b> </b>remained in effect. Justice Department lawyer Stephen<b> </b>Tagert told the judge they’d effectively been undone through an oral order by Hegseth on Dec. 31.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/10/09/federal-judge-set-to-hear-arguments-in-high-stakes-national-guard-hearing" >Federal judge hits Trump administration credibility in siding with city and state against National Guard deployment</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Much of Monday’s hearing revolved around whether Perry could view a record that documented Hegseth’s Dec. 31 order. Tagert said he was not authorized to immediately make it public, but might be able to obtain that clearance eventually. However, an attorney for the state of Illinois said he’d already obtained a copy through Gov. JB Pritzker’s office.</p><p>The lawyers eventually met with Perry in chambers. Then, she publicly read portions of the record documenting Hegseth’s order. Bottom line, she said, Hegseth’s oral order “killed”<b> </b>a previous extension of troop deployment<b> </b>through the middle of this month.</p><p>That, combined with the Supreme Court’s ruling in December, all meant that it “cannot reasonably be expected”<b> </b>that the Trump administration would try again to deploy troops under the orders issued last October. And she said she can’t rule on hypothetical scenarios.</p><p>“Things in Chicago are calm,”<b> </b>Perry said. “They have been calm for many, many months.”</p>
author: Jon Seidel

title: Cinco de Mayo parade in Little Village canceled for second year as immigration enforcement concerns persist
summary: <p>For the second year in a row, the annual Cinco de Mayo parade in Little Village has been canceled due to immigration enforcement concerns, organizers said.</p><p>The parade typically draws hundreds to the neighborhood and celebrates Mexico's victory over Napoleon III’s French army in the Battle of Puebla in 1862. But this year, Chicago's Mexican community is still on edge in the wake of "Operation Midway Blitz," the aggressive deportation campaign the Trump administration launched across the Chicago area last fall.</p><p>"Many families are experiencing fear and uncertainty due to increased immigration enforcement actions and the ongoing threat of raids," organizers with the Cermak Road Chamber of Commerce and Casa Puebla said in a statement.</p><p>People are still avoiding public gatherings out of fear, organizers said, adding, "there is nothing to celebrate."</p><p>The event was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/04/10/cinco-de-mayo-parade-canceled-immigration-chicago" >canceled last year,</a> too, for similar reasons. </p><p>"It was a difficult decision to make, but the safety of our community is more important,” organizer Hector Escobar told the Sun-Times last year.</p><p>Since then, Chicago and the suburbs were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/08/trump-chicago-crime-pritzker-national-guard-ice-truth-social" >targeted by masked federal agents</a>, who detained residents while at times deploying chemical irritants like tear gas. Widespread protests and grassroots efforts to protect immigrants followed. The ramped-up enforcement actions eventually waned, but the impact to Latino communities like Little Village, Pilsen and the Southeast Side has lingered.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/20/operation-midway-blitz-effects-latino-neighborhoods-pilsen-little-village-southeast-side" >Operation Midway Blitz fallout still being felt in Chicago’s Latino neighborhoods</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

After calling for backup and reporting that he and Rivera were fired upon, Baker tends to Rivera and carries her downstairs, where other officers are waiting.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: During an interview with COPA, Baker told investigators he was "best friends" with Rivera and that he "would never" intentionally shoot her. Thousands more in Lebanon and across the region have also been killed or injured.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: For weeks, Iranians studying or working at universities in the U.S. have struggled to focus on school and their jobs, distracted by the fear their loved ones abroad aren’t safe. Beltran Quan Kiu</a></h5><p>Just days before Afro-diaspora fusion restaurant Mahari celebrated its anniversary in January, it was named Best Neighborhood Restaurant at the 2026 Banchet Awards, beating out more established operators.</p><p>Mahari executive chef and owner Rahim Muhammad accepted the prize, shouting out Hyde Park, his birthplace, and adding, "We’re not from a large family or money … we’re just from the Chicago streets and we bring elegance from where we’re from."</p><p>Magic Johnson, Muhammad’s business partner and the eatery's director of community and culture, echoes the sentiment.</p><p>"I’ve been in Hyde Park since 2011 and the bond that I have with this community ... is something special," Johnson said.</p><p>Beyond its local roots, Mahari's team also wants to emphasize its diasporic connections — boasting a menu that's an ambitious medley of flavors, dishes and ingredients that crosses and crisscrosses borders, oceans and cultures.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wihiuhd-l-tt/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>On Friday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wihiuhd-l-td/" target="_blank" ><b>What’s the first vinyl album you ever bought, and from where?</b> </a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"'I Am Woman' by Helen Reddy, from Little’s Music in Oak Park. For a 10-year-old, $3.98 was a big chunk of birthday money." — <i>Marty Regan</i></p><p>"My first album was 'Tapestry' by Carole King, purchased from the local record store near North and Central Avenues in Chicago. I was so proud to buy it with my own money." — <i>Christine Bock</i></p><p>"The first album I recall purchasing was Jimmy Smith's 'The Cat,' in the mid-60s. Jazz organ and his visits to the Plugged Nickel in Old Town drove my desire to dive deeper into jazz." — <i>Richard Bell</i> </p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. Become a member to make stories like these free and available to everyone. Learn more at </i><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wihiuhd-l-th/" target="_blank" ><i>suntimes.com/member</i></a><i>.</i></p>

title: After Mather student and mom detained by ICE, a school and soccer community are left reeling
summary: <p>As 18-year-old Ricardo Navarrete worked diligently to make his soccer dreams come true, most days looked like this: Wake up, go to school, go to practice and repeat</p><p>The teen and his mother, Liliana Navarrete, left Colombia and arrived in Chicago as asylum seekers in 2022. Ricardo kept pursuing his lifelong passion for soccer, believing that the sport could help him and his family succeed in their new country, and that maybe one day he could play professionally.</p><p>He enrolled in school, found a local soccer club and became a standout player. Now a senior at Mather High School in West Ridge, Ricardo was ready for the next level. <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DU83cLsklx4/?img_index=2" target="_blank" ><u>He committed to playing</u></a> for community-college soccer powerhouse Truman College after graduation.</p><p>But Ricardo’s college plans are uncertain after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement took him and his mother into custody last month. Ricardo has described being held in cramped rooms with dozens of men and other tough conditions to friends and family.</p><p>The detention has left the Mather community and Ricardo’s soccer club teammates reeling. It’s a reminder that while widespread immigration enforcement in Chicago has lessened, President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign is still affecting families and students in the city.</p><p>Friends, family, teammates and community members held a rally for Ricardo and his mother on Thursday in West Ridge, calling for their release and an end to the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation strategy. They held signs that read “free our friend” and “estamos contigo Ricardo” — we’re with you Ricardo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Steven Navarrete spoke at a rally in West Ridge on Thursday about his brother Ricardo and his mother’s detention after they went for a routine check-in related to their asylum case.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“They don’t deserve to be there,” said Steven Navarrete, Ricardo’s older brother. “They’ve fought for everything they have in this country and they’re being unjustly detained.”</p><p>Federal immigration officials detained Ricardo and his mother on March 16 after they showed up for what they thought was a routine check-in for their asylum case, according to Kristy Morrow, who has helped connect the family with lawyers and has a son who plays club soccer with Ricardo. She also organized an online fundraiser to help with legal expenses.</p><p>Morrow said Ricardo and his mom received an email telling them to show up to immigration court to sign some documents. They arrived with their paperwork but were detained out in front of the building. Morrow called it a “trap.”</p><p>In a statement, an ICE spokesperson confirmed Ricardo and his mother were detained last month and said they were apprehended “for being unlawfully present in the United States.”</p><p>Lawyers for the family said Ricardo and Liliana had an active asylum application when they were detained and neither has a criminal record. The family sought to escape violence in Colombia, according to friends and family.</p><p>Immigration rights groups have accused federal immigration officials of ambushing immigrants when they appear at court hearings, including those with <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/asylum-seekers-pressured-leave-us-dhs-immigration-ice-detention-rcna259534" target="_blank" ><u>pending asylum applications</u></a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/03/26/nx-s1-5762691/doj-admits-ice-courthouse-arrests-relied-on-erroneous-information" target="_blank" ><u>Hundreds of migrants have been arrested</u></a> through the tactic.</p><p>Family and friends say it’s been difficult to communicate with Ricardo and his mother because officials have bounced them from one detention facility to another. Over the last month, Ricardo has been held in Oklahoma, Louisiana, Ohio and Indiana, they say. He and his mother are currently being held in separate facilities in Kentucky, according to an ICE database.</p><p>That movement also makes it difficult to obtain legal representation because the family needs to find lawyers licensed to practice in those states.</p><p>“Everytime he gets moved to a new place it's like starting over again,” Morrow said.</p><div class="Enhancement" Morrow said they’re hopeful court hearings with a judge could happen as soon as next week.</p><p>Ricardo has told friends and family that he's slept on the floor without a blanket and has spent time in solitary confinement.</p><p>“All ICE detention facilities operate in strict accordance with all applicable federal detention standards for safety, sanitation and humane treatment in accordance with national detention standards,” an ICE spokesperson wrote in a statement in response to questions from the Sun-Times about Ricardo’s claims. “In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens.”</p><p>Costel Serban, who coaches Ricardo’s soccer club, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/sports/2025/07/23/west-ridge-soccer-club-iproskills-academy-costel-catalin-serban-sports" target="_blank" ><u>iProSkills Academy</u></a>, said despite all that’s happened, Ricardo remains resilient and optimistic. He’s spoken with Ricardo several times since the teen was detained.</p><p>“Its incredible for me seeing such a young 18-year-old waking up every morning in a jail cell and he keeps telling me ‘Coach, don’t worry, I’m strong and I know my family is out there,’” Serban said.</p><p>Serban noticed that determination when the two first met, soon after Ricardo and his mother arrived in Chicago. Ricardo found Serban’s soccer club online and, because he didn’t have money for transportation, walked miles to their facility in the winter. Serban remembers it was a “crazy cold day” and being “shocked” by Ricardo’s maturity.</p><p>Though Serban didn’t know a lot of Spanish he learned about Ricardo’s family and their journey to America.</p><p>“His life was threatened in Colombia and he came here to start a new life, to start a career,” Serban said.</p><p>Ricardo’s new teammates rallied around his family, helping them pay for a motel, food and clothing while they searched for an apartment.</p><p>“He’s a great player, he’s so funny to be around, he’s a hilarious kid,” said Miles Morrow, Kristy’s son.</p><p>He said the bond they forged over the years “was like having a brother.” The team’s practices and games haven’t felt the same since Ricardo was detained.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Ricardo’s close friends at Mather, said the school’s hallways also feel different. Mateo said classmates wear shirts with Ricardo’s name to show their support.</p><p>“It’s been really hard in school, people really love him,” Mateo said. “It’s heartbreaking and it's been really tough to process.”</p><p>Teacher Eriq Vazquez, who runs the sanctuary committee at Mather, said Ricardo is in good academic standing and he is looking into getting Ricardo his diploma, despite missing classes while in detention.</p><p>“The Mather staff is going to do their best to amend the situation in the best way they can, to try to secure his future," he said.</p><p>Mateo, who is a senior like Ricardo, said his friend should be making end-of year plans with his classmates.</p><p>“Right now he should be focused on prom, on stuff like that for seniors, and it's unfair that he’s over there with ICE,” he said. “It’s not fair at all.”</p><p><i>Sarah Karp contributed reporting.</i></p>

title: ICE says 81% arrested in Operation Midway Blitz had no convictions, falsely asserts no citizens arrested
summary: <p>About 81% of those arrested in Chicago’s “Operation Midway Blitz” had no criminal convictions, despite federal immigration officials repeatedly claiming that the aggressive operation was intended to target “the worst of the worst.”</p><p>That’s according to answers given to Sen. Dick Durbin and the Illinois congressional delegation on April 13 — information sent nearly seven months after their request for details at the height of Operation Midway Blitz back in September. It comes as Todd Lyons, acting director of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, on Thursday tendered his resignation, effective May 31.</p><p>It marks the first concrete number of arrests that federal officials had previously declined to provide. </p><p>“The focus of Operation Midway Blitz was on arresting the worst criminal aliens and protecting the peace and dignity of Illinois’ communities,” Lyons wrote in the April 13 letter. “As a result of the efforts of the brave men and women of ICE, Illinois is safer than it was prior to Operation Midway Blitz.”</p><p>Despite that assertion, Lyons wrote that between Sept. 5 through Feb. 17, ICE conducted 4,570 “administrative arrests” in Illinois and said none of those arrests were U.S. citizens. Of those arrests, one person was identified as a DACA [Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals] recipient. </p><p>Asked how many people of those who were arrested had no criminal convictions, unrelated to immigration status, Lyons wrote that approximately 3,739 had no criminal convictions and instead had pending criminal charges or were “immigration violators.” Nine of those arrests were subject to expedited removal.</p><p>Federal agents targeted the Chicago area during Operation Midway Blitz between mid-September through mid-October. On Sept. 12, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González,</a> a father and cook originally from Mexico, was fatally shot at “close range” as he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop. Operation Midway Blitz slowed in mid-November.</p><p>In the letter, Lyons claims that no U.S. citizens were arrested by federal immigration officers during Operation Midway Blitz — despite documented reports of citizens being arrested. According to ProPublica, at least 170 citizens were detained in the first nine months of the Trump administration, and as of mid-October, about two dozen U.S. citizens had been held for more than a day without being able to contact anyone. Durbin’s staff has also documented the reported detention of at least 40 citizens in Illinois between late August and early November 2025.</p><p></p><p>The letter also says that DHS used several other federal agencies to help with immigration enforcement, including personnel from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Bureau of Prisons, the U.S. Marshals Service, and the State Department's Diplomatic Service. Even employees from the Internal Revenue Service “exercised their properly-delegated immigration authority and/or assisted ICE officers and special agents with immigration operations and actions,” Lyons wrote.</p><p>DHS did not track how many officers from other agencies worked with ICE, the letter says. Within DHS, 209 U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers worked with their ICE counterparts, and the Transportation Security Administration provided ICE about 100 federal air marshals on a rotating basis. Within DHS, TSA has a reimbursable agreement with ICE flight support up to $80 million.</p><p>Regarding use-of-force policies, Lyons wrote that DHS employees follow directives in their employee handbook — and wrote that “DHS does not have oversight of and does not direct how their federal law enforcement partners perform their duties.”</p><p>“All ICE officers are taught ICE’s Use of Force Continuum, which includes de-escalation training," Lyons wrote. "Furthermore, ICE officers are taught how to apply the reasonableness standard when using force. ICE officers may use only the amount of force which is objectively reasonable to gain control of a subject and the use of any level of force must discontinue immediately when the subject no longer presents a threat.”</p><p>Asked about social media influencers who tagged along to some of the most aggressive targeted operations, Lyons said those influencers were given prior approval and signed a waiver agreeing to abide by all ICE guidelines to participate in a ride-along. They declined to provide a list of which influencers were granted the access.</p><p></p><p>U.S. Rep Delia Ramirez, D-Illinois, railed against the letter, telling the Sun-Times in a statement that "every fascist in the administration responsible for the terror of Midway Blitz must be held accountable.</p><p>"Today, we have the data to prove what our communities knew all along: DHS is the biggest threat to our collective safety, and funding it only fuels our own destruction and human suffering," Ramirez said. </p>

Madison St.</b><br>Exclusive Record Store Day titles, plus a selection of $1 used vinyl.</p><p><b>Pinwheel Records, 1459 W. 18th St.</b><br>See live music from Macie Stewart, Flowering and Mail. title: Burdened by costs of an ICE facility in town, Broadview reckons with a spotlight it never wanted
summary: <p>In a lot of ways, what happened last fall to the small village of Broadview during President Donald Trump’s immigration “blitz” felt like a storm.</p><p>Broadview’s leaders and residents had no say in the scope or magnitude of the federal push that shuffled thousands of immigrants through the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility that’s long operated in their quiet town. They couldn’t control what was coming or predict the impact.</p><p>The 7,900 people living in the unassuming western suburb are still digging out.</p><p>Just as the village had gotten its financial house in order, it was hit with nearly $400,000 in unexpected costs as a result of last fall’s campaign — around 10% of the small municipality's discretionary budget. That’s in sharp contrast to local governments elsewhere in the country that have contracted with the federal government to have their costs covered — and more — for detaining immigrants in local jails.</p><p>Broadview’s mayor recently made an ambitious request for federal reimbursement — that the village’s budget is banking on — and announced grand plans to have the ICE facility shuttered to become a museum to help change Broadview’s image. But her requests are a long shot.</p><p>Regionally, Broadview is now synonymous with the federal immigration processing facility at 1930 Beach Street that last fall became a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/01/broadview-immigration-processing-center-detention-ice-dhs" target="_blank" ><u>de facto immigration detention site</u></a> and drew the area’s most contentious<b> </b>protests.</p><p>Reluctant to draw more attention to themselves or their village, many residents say they don’t want to publicly discuss the saga.</p><p>Broadview Mayor Katrina Thompson also canceled a scheduled interview with the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ after learning the village finance director answered a reporter’s budget questions without her knowledge. She sent word through spokesman David Ormsby who says, “There is currently no intent to reschedule.”</p><p>Still, after the Illinois legislature recently tried to restrict immigration enforcement facilities in residential areas, Thompson took to social media and wrote, “No community should have to experience what the Village of Broadview has endured.</p><p>“How do we ensure that no community is left to carry a burden it neither chose nor has the power to control?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a fiscal year that begins on May 1.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"It's costing us a ton,” finance director Thomas Hood told trustees this week. “So it's really led to a lot of expense for the village that we didn't count on. But we're hopeful that we're going to get reimbursed for some of that."</p><p>Justin Marlowe, Director of the Center for Municipal Finance at the University of Chicago, says, “that's a lot of money riding on something that's less than certain.”</p><p>The vast majority of Broadview’s budget — around 80% — is eaten up by police and fire department salaries and predetermined pension payments. That leaves around $4 million for discretionary spending on village programs. Last year, costs resulting from ICE facility activity ate up about 10% of this.</p><p>“If we weren't already in a great financial position, we'd be underwater now,” Hood told the Sun-Times. He calls the hundreds of thousands of dollars in unexpected spending a “huge deal.”</p><p>“It throws a wrench into your plans,” he says. “Plans that had been in place and going for maybe five years or even longer."</p><h3>Most other towns with ICE facilities, like in Indiana, don’t incur costs </h3><p>Nationally, Broadview stands out as one of only a few immigration centers that the federal government owns and operates. Most others are local jails<b> </b>that lease space to the federal government for a daily flat fee for each person detained there for alleged immigration violations.</p><p>One of the closest is in Clay County, Ind., a three-and-a-half-hour drive, where local taxpayers have at the very least been shielded from increases in related costs resulting from detaining more immigrants, such as a surge in ambulance runs to nearby hospitals.</p><p>That’s because Clay County collects $85 per day per immigrant, according to its contract with the U.S. Marshals Service. The deal has prompted lawsuits from immigrant-rights advocates accusing Clay County of profiting handsomely from increased detentions.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e50000" name="image-e50000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0cedc9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5173x2903+0+273/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3c%2Fc9%2F6fe2a9b2447f9ade4a926c42ee6c%2Fclay-county-jail-ext-03-h.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b93c327/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5173x2903+0+273/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3c%2Fc9%2F6fe2a9b2447f9ade4a926c42ee6c%2Fclay-county-jail-ext-03-h.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b2db943/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5173x2903+0+273/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F3c%2Fc9%2F6fe2a9b2447f9ade4a926c42ee6c%2Fclay-county-jail-ext-03-h.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Clay County Jail Ext 03 - </div><p>In her latest attempt to move Broadview out of an unwanted spotlight, Thompson has asked members of the Illinois congressional delegation for help securing reimbursement plus the closure of the ICE facility and its transformation into a museum.</p><p>Is that possible?</p><p>“If the federal government really wants to do that, they can find a way to do it, and they can find a way to do it including efforts to purchase commercial warehouses to open new detention centers. title: Marimar Martinez, Chicago woman shot 5 times by federal agent, to testify at Washington hearing
summary: <p>Marimar Martinez, the Chicago woman who survived being shot five times by a Border Patrol agent, will testify before the Homeland Security Committee in Washington next week — and committee Democrats are also requesting White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan appear.</p><p>Martinez, Miller and Homan's appearances are voluntary at the April 22 hearing and came at the request of minority Democrats on the committee — and Republican Chair Andrew Garbarino, R-NY, made sure to include some digs at Democrats in letters sent on Wednesday.</p><p>"The Committee does not believe this request to be in good faith and will be used, instead, as an attempt to politicize national security and gaslight the American public," he wrote.</p><p>Martinez's attorney Christopher Parente on Thursday confirmed her appearance at the second day of a hearing that is intended to discuss "the harmful impacts of the DHS Shutdown on Americans."</p><p>Republicans on the committee are using the hearing to blame Democrats for the shutdown that has stretched 61 days. Garbarino also criticized committee member Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Illinois, in the letters, writing that Ramirez on Feb. 10 "refused to let witnesses answer any questions," and stated, "DHS cannot be reformed; it must be dismantled."</p><p>The April 22 hearing will mark the first time Martinez will testify before an official committee. Martinez first appeared before Congress on Feb. 3 at a public forum organized in response to the deaths of two Minnesotans at the hands of federal immigration officers, telling lawmakers she wanted federal agents held accountable and to hear an apology. She also said she wanted the Trump administration to acknowledge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >she is “not a domestic terrorist.”</a></p><p>Martinez repeatedly called out Border Patrol agent Charles Exum, who shot her five times Oct. 4. She called him her “attempted executioner.”</p><p>Martinez attended a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing March 3, standing just five rows behind then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem as Noem was pushed by U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal to acknowledge Martinez's shooting was “wrong” during a testy hearing.</p><p>Despite comprehensive coverage of Martinez’s shooting and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >charges of impeding law enforcement that were later dropped</a> against her, Noem repeatedly claimed she didn’t know about the case.</p><p>“Sir, I don’t know the situation or the case,” Noem said. “I’ll look into it to ensure that all the procedures were followed properly.”</p><p>Noem was <a class="Link" href="https://www.google.com/search?q=noem+ousted+sun-times&oq=noem+ousted+sun-times&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIHCAEQABiABDIHCAIQABiABDIHCAMQABiABDIHCAQQABiABDIHCAUQABiABDIHCAYQABiABDIHCAcQABiABDIHCAgQABiABDIHCAkQABiABNIBCDE2OTRqMGo3qAIAsAIA&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8" target="_blank" >ousted from her post</a> two days later. There were rumblings of dissatisfaction from President Donald Trump after two straight days of testimony by Noem before Senate and House committees.</p><p>Ramirez on Thursday told the Chicago Sun-Times she sees Martinez's testimony as an opportunity for Republican members of the committee to look a U.S. citizen in the face "and have to wrestle with what they did to fail her." </p><p>"I think it's really important for her to come and confront the people that are responsible for allowing what happened to her, and to use her power to be able to speak up for the number of people that have been shot, that have been arrested, abducted and beat by this administration," Ramirez said. "I think it's also important for us, and people like me who represent Chicago, to give her added space and time to be able to set the record on so many of the things that I'm sure they're going to try to question, or, you know, lie about, that happened."</p><p>The Illinois congresswoman called the GOP digs in the committee letters "ridiculous."</p><p>"The majority wants to find any absolute excuse that they can in order to not have to be confronted by what they're doing, but also what they're complicit to," Ramirez said. "They don't want to see Stephen Miller and Tom Homan come before the committee. In some cases, it's because they know how bad things are."</p><p>Democrats on the committee have tried to subpoena both Miller and Homan, but they have been voted down by GOP members. Ramirez said they will continue to push for their appearances — and are also requesting that Markwayne Mullins, the new DHS head, appear. </p><p>"He should come before our committee to assure us that he is taking these policy reforms seriously," Ramirez said. "It would be smart of Garbarino to bring him before the committee to prove to us that he is not Kristi Noem, and that he takes his job and his oath seriously, especially if he wants funding."</p>
author: Tina Sfondeles

title: Autoridades en Chicago obtienen la primera declaración de culpabilidad en un caso del Operativo Midway Blitz
summary: <p>Los fiscales federales en Chicago aseguraron su primera declaración de culpabilidad relacionada con el Operativo Midway Blitz el miércoles, aunque no por el cargo de asalto que inicialmente se había presentado contra Anthony González Álvarez.</p><p>En su lugar, se declaró culpable de ocultar información sobre un crimen, admitiendo que reportó falsamente que su Ford F-250 había sido robada al Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD) después de chocar contra la parte trasera de un vehículo conducido por agentes de inmigración.</p><p>El cargo, oficialmente conocido como “encubrimiento de un delito grave”, es aparentemente lo suficientemente raro como para haber provocado una discusión en la corte sobre cómo pronunciar "encubrimiento".</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c80000" name="module-c80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Nunca había oído hablar de eso”, les dijo la jueza del distrito LaShonda Hunt a los abogados.</p><p>Se espera que Álvarez, de 27 años, pague $1,362 en restitución, pero evitará la prisión bajo los términos de un acuerdo alcanzado con los fiscales. Sin embargo, Hunt primero debe decidir si acepta o rechaza el acuerdo.</p><p>Ha pospuesto la decisión por ahora y fijó la sentencia para el 22 de julio.</p><p>Álvarez está entre los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >32 acusados conocidos</a> que enfrentan cargos por crímenes no relacionados con inmigración vinculados al Operativo Midway Blitz, la campaña de deportación que conmocionó el área de Chicago el año pasado. Veinte de los 32 han sido exonerados y otros tres están en camino a que se desestimen sus casos.</p><p>Cuatro de los ocho restantes son miembros del grupo originalmente conocido como los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/13/fiscalia-retira-los-cargos-de-conspiracion-contra-2-manifestantes-de-ice" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> y enfrentarán juicio el 26 de mayo. Otro hombre, Héctor Gómez, está programado para declararse culpable el 27 de abril tras ser acusado de cargos de armas relacionados con el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>La administración de Trump utilizó afirmaciones de violencia "aterradora" hacia agentes federales para justificar un esfuerzo por desplegar tropas de la Guardia Nacional en Chicago el otoño pasado. Inicialmente fueron bloqueados por la jueza del distrito April Perry y, finalmente, por la Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos.</p><p>A pesar de la declaración de culpabilidad de Álvarez, nadie en Chicago ha sido condenado en una corte federal por un acto de violencia hacia los agentes durante el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>Aún así, Álvarez admitió que a eso de las 10:30 a.m. del 3 de octubre, siguió a un vehículo de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) en el lado sur de la ciudad. Al girar a la derecha desde la 61th Street hacia Kedzie Avenue, chocó contra el lado trasero del vehículo de los agentes.</p><p>Más tarde ese día, Álvarez le dijo a CPD que su camioneta había sido robada, admitió.</p><p>Álvarez se declaró culpable a pesar de las preguntas planteadas anteriormente sobre el caso por su abogado defensor, Ricardo Meza. El abogado le dijo a Hunt en enero que "la camioneta que supuestamente fue golpeada ha sido reparada".</p><p>"Ni siquiera está en la condición en la que estaba cuando supuestamente fue golpeada por mi cliente, por lo que no podemos inspeccionarla", le dijo Meza a Hunt el 29 de enero. "Pero a pesar de eso, su Señoría, también queremos inspeccionarla porque queremos recuperar lo que se llama el registrador de datos de eventos".</p><p>Meza también dijo que solicitaría las notas de los agentes del Buró Federal de Investigaciones (FBI) porque "hay mucha confusión sobre lo que pasó, cuándo sucedió y cuántas veces fue golpeado un vehículo".</p><p>La asistente del fiscal estadounidense Stephanie Stern le dijo a la jueza que Meza tenía el poder de citar el vehículo él mismo, desde la compañía de alquiler de autos que estaba en posesión del vehículo.</p><p>"Está con Enterprise", dijo durante la audiencia de enero.</p><p>Cuestiones similares surgieron en el caso de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/04/marimar-martinez-baleada-por-agentes-de-migracion-se-pronuncia-contra-asesinatos" target="_blank" >Marimar Martínez</a>, la mujer a quien le disparó un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza el 4 de octubre. Poco después de que la acusaran de chocar contra el vehículo de ese agente, su abogado defensor reveló que el agente había llevado su vehículo a Maine antes de que el abogado pudiera inspeccionarlo. Los cargos en contra de Martínez fueron desestimados en noviembre.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
author: Jon Seidel

title: Cash-strapped DePaul closes the curtain on Downtown's historic Reskin Theatre
summary: <p>For nearly 120 years, the Merle Reskin Theatre has hosted everything from "Pygmalion" and "Life With Father" to "Mirror of Most Value: A Ms. Marvel Play," which opens mid-May for a two-week run.</p><p>What's playing after May? Darkness. And not the 2021 Andre Wright play with the same name, either.</p><p>DePaul University is closing the Reskin at the end of next month.</p><p>The university says it's the result of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/17/fewer-international-students-are-studying-at-some-illinois-universities" target="_blank" >budget crisis</a> that has been aggravated by the Trump administration's immigration policies that has reduced the amount of tuition-paying international students attending the school.</p><p>Also part of DePaul's budget troubles: The decision in February to close the respected <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/03/02/depaul-university-art-museum-closure-fullerton-lincoln-park-students-faculty-letter" target="_blank" >DePaul Art Museum</a> at 935 W. Fullerton Ave.</p><p>"The university is working to determine the future use of the Merle Reskin Theatre," a DePaul spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>But until that use is found, it's lights out for the Reskin, 60 E. Balbo Drive. The decision places in limbo a landmarked 1,400-seat Beaux Art playhouse designed by Benjamin H. Marshall, one of Chicago's preeminent architects.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" "I would pray and hope that some [theater] company would come along and claim it. But given the financial environment in general, I fear that it will be sitting there for a long time. It seems like it's really up for grabs for its future."</p><h3>Reskin ‘a wonderful asset’</h3><p>Built in 1910 as the Blackstone Theatre, the venue sits in the western shadow of the 21-story Blackstone Hotel, which was also designed by Marshall and completed in 1910.</p><p>Marshall and his firm Marshall & Fox designed scores of notable buildings around town, including the South Shore Cultural Center, 7059 S. South Shore Drive, and the Drake Hotel, 140 E. Walton St.</p><p>For much of the 20th century, Marshall's ornate Blackstone theater — with its columned entrances and mansard roof — and his elegant Second Empire-styled Blackstone Hotel were a swank brother-and-sister act that drew the best plays, conventions and events.</p><p>Legendary actors including John and Ethel Barrymore, Spencer Tracy and Helen Hayes performed at the Blackstone during the good years.</p><p>The venue closed in the mid-1980s and was bought by DePaul for its theater school.</p><p>A $2 million donation from businessman Harold Reskin and wife, Merle, who had been an actress, singer and dancer, helped refurbish what would open in 1992 as the Merle Reskin Theatre.</p><p>Merle Reskin died in 2023. class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The theater's French-inspired auditorium remained intact, although it has faded somewhat in recent decades. The Reskin is home to DePaul Theatre School's Chicago Playworks for Families and Young Audiences.</p><p>DePaul said the Chicago Playworks series will continue this fall at the Theatre School building in Lincoln Park.</p><p>"That DePaul, which is really such a great school and it's got a great theater department, will be bereft of this wonderful asset," Lepauw said of the Reskin, "l think it's just so sad."</p><h3>What’s next?</h3><p>Whatever the Reskin's fate, it won't be demolition. The theater is listed as a contributing structure in the landmark-protected 12-block long Historic Michigan Boulevard District.</p><p>For DePaul, money is tight. But tight is relative: The university managed to come up with enough scratch to start construction this year on a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/11/20/plan-commission-approves-depaul-practice-facility-morgan-park-commons" >$42 million</a> basketball and athletics center on its Lincoln Park campus.</p><p>It should be equally diligent in finding the funds to preserve, restore and reuse the Reskin. The city shouldn't lose a live entertainment venue anywhere, particularly Downtown.</p><p>And Chicago certainly doesn't need a dark, unused building glowering over Balbo Drive.</p><p>But suppose DePaul finds it no longer wants the Reskin. Then finding a new owner who can restore the theater and put it in league with Downtown's Chicago, Nederlander and Cadillac Palace theaters becomes paramount.</p><p>Rich Gamble, interim CEO of the Chicago Loop Alliance, said his group has been talking to DePaul about the Reskin. The university is a member of the downtown organization.</p><p>"I'm not in a position to explicitly state the nature of those conversations," Gamble said. "We're a supporter, an advocate and a promoter of what we would like to see happen, which is a vibrant district."</p>

title: Treasury says 53 million filers used new Trump tax breaks before the deadline
summary: <p>It's Tax Day on Wednesday — the deadline for most Americans to file taxes — and President Donald Trump's administration says millions of people have already used new breaks such as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/2026/02/19/no-tax-deductions-trump-irs-filing-season-hype-experts" >no tax on tips</a> and overtime, exemptions for interest on certain car loans, deductions for some seniors, and Trump Accounts for children’s savings.</p><p>More than 53 million filers claimed a deduction under one of those provisions from the administration's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/2026/02/22/congress-trump-obba-beautiful-bill-federal-irs-tax-returns" >massive tax and spending law</a>, a Treasury official told reporters Tuesday before the deadline, with 6 million people claiming no tax on tips, 21 million claiming the overtime deduction and 30 million <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/2026/02/20/older-adults-senior-tax-deduction-irs-obbba" >older Americans claiming the enhanced deduction</a>.</p><p>The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to preview the numbers, said the 2026 filing season was a success from the administration's perspective.</p><p>Still, the latest data comes as most Americans, or 7 in 10, still think their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes" >taxes</a> are too high, according to recent polling, despite the passage of the Republican tax law which promised big savings for taxpayers.</p><p>Illinois taxpayers who can't meet the April 15 deadline are automatically granted a six-month extension, according to the state's Department of Revenue. Those who file on a calendar-bases would have until Oct. 15.</p><p>But the department said in a news release that an extension doesn't extend the time to pay. "If taxes are owed, taxpayers must pay the amount due by April 15, 2026, to avoid penalties and interest," the department said.</p><p>As the tax season kicked off in January, the White House boasted that average refunds were projected to rise by at least $1,000. But currently, the average refund amount is $3,462, according to the latest IRS data, which is up 11% or about $350 from last tax year’s $3,116 average refund payment.</p><p>“People are getting refunds of $5,000, $8,000, $11,000 that they had no idea they were getting,” Trump said Wednesday on Fox Business News. “It’s turned out to be better — as good or better than I said it would be.”</p><p>The Treasury said tax refunds this season are up 24%, compared with the four-year average of refunds before Trump took office.</p><p>The White House has been trying to promote Trump's tax cuts as a way to get voters more enthusiastic about the way he's handling the economy before November's midterm elections, but the message has been overshadowed for weeks by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/03/25/iran-war-raising-chicago-gas-travel-medicine-food-oil-prices" >higher gas prices</a> caused by the war in Iran.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>The 2026 season comes as the IRS has gone through a leadership turnover and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/2026/02/19/irs-workforce-cuts-obba-tax-laws-delays-filers" >reduced its workforce</a> by 27% over the past year through cuts brought on by the Department of Government Efficiency.</p><p>IRS CEO Frank Bisignano testified to the Senate Finance Committee on Wednesday, extolling the IRS' implementation of the Trump administration's tax law. </p><p>However, Democratic lawmakers have been zeroing in on IRS disclosures of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/2026/02/26/irs-broke-law-confidential-information-ice-dhs-federal-judge" >confidential taxpayer information</a> to Immigration and Customs Enforcement as part of an agreement between ICE and the Department of Homeland Security to share information for the purpose of identifying and deporting people illegally in the U.S.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sun-Times</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div
