Working Group on Enforced and Involuntary Disappearances and <a class="Link" href="https://cjil.uchicago.edu/print-archive/latin-american-flavor-enforced-disappearances" target="_blank" ><u>wrote an article</u></a> summarizing enforced disappearances in Latin America, says that though happening at a smaller scale, he sees some similarities between those past regimes and present-day U.S.</p><p>“This is exactly what we saw in Latin America,” Dulitzky said. “It’s creating this terror that the authorities can come in the middle of the day, take you, don’t disclose where you are, don’t say why they are detaining you, don’t say who is detaining you —not only for you, but for everybody else to see that and to fear about what you are doing.”</p><p>Three elements define enforced disappearance: deprivation of liberty, government involvement and the government’s lack of acknowledgment of the detention or lack of transparency about the person’s whereabouts.</p><p>Dulitzky cautions that the situation in the U.S. is not nearly as dire as those Latin American countries decades ago. Forty-seven people have died while in ICE custody during Trump's second term, according to ICE <a class="Link" href="https://www.ice.gov/detain/detainee-death-reporting" target="_blank" >death reports</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.ice.gov/newsroom" target="_blank" >news releases</a>.</p><p>But he does believe that some recent examples of immigration arrests in the U.S. can be considered short-term enforced disappearances. Dulitzky said the ideological justification for the operations is the one “very, very similar” element between past Latin American regimes and the Trump administration.</p><p>“The way that the undocumented immigrants <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/watch-how-government-propaganda-techniques-portray-chicago-as-a-city-at-war-with-the-feds" title: Nearly 70 Chicago groups receive micro-grants after SNAP cuts, deportation campaign
summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson announced on Thursday that 67 organizations across Chicago are receiving $4,500 micro-grants each through the Greater Chicago Food Depository.</p><p>The money is being doled out to help offset the strain Chicago’s small businesses and community groups are feeling after the federal deportation campaign and cuts to food assistance under the Trump administration. </p><p>“I have to admit, I do know that sometimes government — we can move a little slow,” Johnson said at Malcolm X College Thursday. “So the $4,500 grants that are issued, we are not just investing in services that you provide, but the leadership that you provide and the trust that you have built with residents. You embody the spirit of our collective responsibility.”</p><p>In November 2025, Johnson signed an executive order directing city resources to the Food Depository to support local organizations and businesses affected by a lapse in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program funding during the 43-day government shutdown.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-740000" name="module-740000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Help for SNAP recipients </b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-59a96830-fb08-11f0-89d5-e38f58753511"><li><b>Update your SNAP information:</b> Illinois created a <a class="Link" href="https://aberp.illinois.gov/screener/ABAWD?lang=EN " target="_blank" >website</a> where you can see if you meet the new SNAP program requirements. You can update your information by calling 1-800-843-6154. <a class="Link" href="https://aberp.illinois.gov/screener/ABAWD?lang=EN" target="_blank" >https://aberp.illinois.gov/screener/ABAWD?lang=EN</a></li><li><b>Find a food pantry:</b> Here’s a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/10/29/where-to-find-chicago-area-food-pantries-if-snap-goes-away" target="_blank" >list of pantries</a> in the Chicago area </li><li><b>Where can I volunteer?</b> <br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-fa6424d3-1d8c-11f1-a5fc-4b8b8cb93c27"><li>The next Meals on Wheels Chicago pantry is March 24. <a class="Link" href="https://www.mealsonwheelschicago.org/volunteer-individuals-formstack" target="_blank" ><u>Visit</u> this website</a> to volunteer <br><a class="Link" href="https://www.mealsonwheelschicago.org/volunteer-individuals-formstack" target="_blank" ><u>https://www.mealsonwheelschicago.org/volunteer-individuals-formstack</u></a> </li><li>Volunteer shifts at Nourishing Hope’s pantries are available at their <a class="Link" href="https://nourishinghopechi.org/volunteer/" target="_blank" ><u>website</u></a><br><a class="Link" href="https://nourishinghopechi.org/volunteer/" target="_blank" ><u>https://nourishinghopechi.org/volunteer/</u></a></li><li>Care For Friends, 530 W. Fullerton Pkwy., can be reached at (773) 932-1010</li></ul></li></ul></div> </div><p>As part of that effort, the city launched the micro-grant program to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/15/mayor-brandon-johnson-snap-funding-food-insecurity" >help businesses</a> hit by both reduced SNAP purchasing power and drops in foot-traffic from federal immigration enforcement.</p><p>The SNAP funding pause was felt for many Chicagoans in early November, but small businesses and organizations were impacted months before due to increased immigration operations. In addition, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/13/older-chicagoans-high-risk-of-losing-snap-food-assistance-new-work-rules-kick-in-55-64-may" >expanded work requirements</a> for SNAP recipients that went into effect this spring are expected to push about 150,000 people out of the program starting in May, according to the latest estimates from state officials.</p><p>Working Family Solidarity lead organizer, Kevin Johnson Jr., 26, said more than half of his organization is Hispanic, and nearly 40% of members are undocumented.</p><p>“Directly after SNAP benefits were cut, it became kind of Armageddon for us a little bit,” he said.</p><p>The Pilsen-based community group provides support to Black and Latino communities across Chicago.</p><p>“One of our workers, who's a single mother of two children, had her benefits cut so this is something that is literally stopping individuals from being able to feed their children and feed themselves,” Johnson said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-670000" name="image-670000"></a> title: Migrantes de Chicago enfrentan estafas, rentas exorbitantes y condiciones peligrosas en su búsqueda de vivienda
summary: <p>En una ventosa tarde de jueves en febrero, Daniela y su familia, cuyas edades van de 9 a 35 años, no pensaban en la cena ni en las tareas escolares.</p><p>Estaban metiendo frenéticamente ropa, zapatos y otros artículos personales en bolsas, desesperados por desocupar su departamento de dos habitaciones en el vecindario de South Shore antes de que se metiera el sol.</p><p>El caos había comenzado más temprano esa semana con un golpe en la puerta. Una mujer que afirmaba representar a Atlas Asset Management, empresa que supervisa el edificio de tres pisos en el que vivían, estaba en la puerta, preguntando quiénes eran y a quién estaban pagando la renta.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-be0000" name="module-be0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Dijo que este departamento debía estar desocupado, que teníamos que irnos y que la policía estaba en camino”, dijo Daniela.</p><p>Daniela y su familia son de Venezuela y ya no tienen <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2025/03/04/fears-rise-for-venezuelan-chicagoans-after-trump-rescinds-temporary-protected-status" target="_blank" >un estatus legal temporal</a> en Estados Unidos. WBEZ no publica sus nombres completos porque la familia teme la deportación.</p><p>Sin que la familia lo supiera, eran ocupantes ilegales en un edificio que había cambiado de dueño recientemente, siendo víctimas de una estafa. Un agente de arrendamiento fraudulento había entrado a unidades vacías de un edificio en 79th Street y Paxton Avenue y las había alquilado a familias migrantes desesperadas como la de Daniela.</p><p>Cuando llegó el oficial de la policía, el mensaje fue directo: la familia tenía una semana para salir.</p><p>Encontrar una vivienda segura y adecuada se ha vuelto más complicado en Chicago, ya que los migrantes enfrentan estatus legal precario debido a los cambios en las políticas federales bajo la administración del presidente Donald Trump.</p><p>Su falta de ingresos estables y miedo a la deportación los han hecho más vulnerables a este tipo de estafas de vivienda. También deben lidiar con rentas exorbitantes y una escasez de viviendas asequibles.</p><p>Y una nueva ley estatal que entró en vigor en enero facilita a los dueños de propiedades llamar a la policía y desalojar a los ocupantes ilegales sin un proceso de desalojo prolongado, poniendo a familias migrantes como el de Daniela en riesgo de quedarse sin vivienda.</p><div class="Enhancement" Después de quedarse en un albergue para migrantes durante meses, recibieron un vale temporal de asistencia para la renta del estado y encontraron una casa que albergaba a los seis miembros por casi $2,000 al mes.</p><p>Pero la estabilidad fue efímera.</p><p>En seis meses, los pagos del vale temporal expiraron, y con solo uno de los adultos con un trabajo estable, no pudieron continuar pagando la renta.</p><p>“Durante esos seis meses, salí todos los días, recorriendo calle por calle buscando trabajo y no encontré nada”, dijo Pedro, el compañero de Daniela.</p><p>Sin empleo, Daniela comentó que estaban desesperados por dinero y mendigaban en las calles con su hijo de 4 años, incluso en fríos días de invierno.</p><p>Eventualmente, la familia tuvo que abandonar el espacioso hogar que pagaba con el vale. Se agruparon con amigos y conocidos en casas separadas hasta que la familia logró acomodar a seis personas en un departamento de una sola habitación.</p><p>“Mi mamá, su pareja y dos hijos compartían una habitación”, dijo Daniela. “Yo, mi pareja y mi hijo solíamos dormir en la sala, separados por una cortina”.</p><p>Estaban amontonados.</p><p>Así que en noviembre de 2025, cuando un hombre que hablaba español con fluidez les ofreció un departamento de dos habitaciones por $1,000 —solo un poco más de lo que estaban pagando por su departamento de una habitación— aprovecharon la oportunidad, ignorando varias señales de alerta.</p><p>El hombre, que decía ser el administrador del edificio, nunca les dio su nombre completo. Nunca recibieron un contrato de arrendamiento ni recibos al pagar la renta en efectivo. Todo lo que tenían era un acuerdo informal.</p><p>Además de todo, el departamento estaba plagado de peligros, entre ellos una puerta principal que no se cerraba con llave, la falta de calefacción central y la pintura pelada.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4b59fb" name="image-4b59fb"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3cdd03d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3995x2242+0+377/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F69%2F85c9ee5c4450b5dcb7a3d267f084%2Fimg-6677.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/91f7ed1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3995x2242+0+377/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F69%2F85c9ee5c4450b5dcb7a3d267f084%2Fimg-6677.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f8786da/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3995x2242+0+377/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F69%2F85c9ee5c4450b5dcb7a3d267f084%2Fimg-6677.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="El apartamento en 7900 S. Fue vendido a Osiris Chicago Portfolio LLC, que comparte dirección con Atlas, el 20 de noviembre de 2025, aproximadamente tres meses antes de que Daniela y su familia fueran desalojados.</p><p>Adam Walls, el jefe del anterior propietario 5812 Group, no respondió a una solicitud de entrevista.</p><p>A pesar de las condiciones del edificio, que reflejaban las de muchas propiedades en esa área, los migrantes desesperados se han asentado en South Shore, que ha llegado a ser conocida como la “capital de los desalojos de Chicago”.</p><p>El vecindario también es hogar del lugar de una redada federal de inmigración el año pasado. También hubo <a class="Link" href="https://www.propublica.org/article/chicago-venezuela-immigration-ice-raid-landlord-tren-de-aragua" target="_blank" >informes</a> de gerentes de propiedades que cobraron alquiler a migrantes desprevenidos en el edificio donde se llevó a cabo la redada.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c21fa4" name="image-c21fa4"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/11e0b48/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3704x2079+0+350/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F1f%2Fa35b357a410197c02a6a1ab1e840%2Fimg-6790.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b952bdf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3704x2079+0+350/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F1f%2Fa35b357a410197c02a6a1ab1e840%2Fimg-6790.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/86a80f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3704x2079+0+350/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F1f%2Fa35b357a410197c02a6a1ab1e840%2Fimg-6790.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chris Amatore, propietario de Manage Chicago, dijo que ha visto a muchos migrantes enfrentar desafíos de vivienda en los últimos años. También se solidariza con los administradores de propiedades y los propietarios, quienes enfrentan costos crecientes e impuestos más altos." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/86a80f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3704x2079+0+350/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F1f%2Fa35b357a410197c02a6a1ab1e840%2Fimg-6790.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1abaf1c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3704x2079+0+350/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F1f%2Fa35b357a410197c02a6a1ab1e840%2Fimg-6790.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/86a80f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3704x2079+0+350/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F1f%2Fa35b357a410197c02a6a1ab1e840%2Fimg-6790.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chris Amatore, propietario de Manage Chicago, dijo que ha visto a muchos migrantes enfrentar desafíos de vivienda en los últimos años. También se solidariza con los administradores de propiedades y los propietarios, quienes enfrentan costos crecientes e impuestos más altos.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>‘La compasión no es un sistema de alquiler’</h3><p>Como presidente de Manage Chicago, Chris Amatore supervisa miles de apartamentos para inquilinos de bajos ingresos. A finales de 2023, proporcionó apartamentos a cientos de migrantes en sus edificios tras experimentar un despertar espiritual.</p><p>Desde entonces, Amatore ha visto a muchos migrantes enfrentar desafíos de vivienda debido a la falta de oportunidades laborales, barreras lingüísticas y a “no saber a dónde acudir”, lo que los convierte en presas fáciles para estafas de apartamentos.</p><p>“Es realmente sólo matemáticas”, dijo Amatore. “No pueden pagar las rentas del mercado. Son de $2,000 a $2,700 por una unidad de tres habitaciones. Las rentas post-COVID han aumentado más rápido que el sueldo de un migrante”.</p><p>Destacó que los requisitos de puntaje de crédito y prueba de ingresos son también obstáculos para los migrantes que buscan alquilar apartamentos. El aumento de costos, los impuestos más altos y la inflación también han llevado a los propietarios a aumentar las rentas.</p><p>“Definitivamente simpatizo con los propietarios porque me ha pasado a mí y es muy frustrante”, dijo Amatore. “A nadie más le va a importar. A tu banco no le importa. Las empresas de servicios aún van a cortar el agua o el gas. Desafortunadamente, la compasión no es un sistema de alquiler”.</p><p>Aún así, Amatore dijo que hay una manera humana de trabajar con estas familias.</p><p>“Lo que haría es decir, ‘Está bien, yo soy el verdadero propietario, hagamos un trato’. [Los] pondría en un plan [de pago] y les daría una oportunidad”, señaló.</p><p>Recientemente, Amatore ha comenzado a notar que hay más migrantes durmiendo en las calles y en tiendas de campaña.</p><p>“Al principio, no veía muchos, pero ahora veo muchos más migrantes bajo el puente de Canalport y por 18th Street y Halsted, y en otras áreas”, dijo.</p><p>A medida que las rentas aumentan, la ayuda se agota y las opciones de vivienda disminuyen, dijo que cree que verá más migrantes en las calles y en carpas.</p><p>Daniela y su familia esperan que eso no les suceda.</p><p>Poco después de escapar del departamento de South Shore, encontraron uno nuevo, más caro, en el lado oeste por $1,400 al mes. Pero la mudanza, una vez más, desarraigó a la familia. Les tomó semanas inscribir a los niños en su nueva escuela. Y aunque ahora más adultos de la familia están empleados, aún luchan por reunir la renta cada mes.</p><p>Mientras tanto, de regreso en South Shore, el departamento donde vivían Daniela y su familia ha sido pintado y la cocina remodelada. A principios de abril, Atlas Asset Management había listado la unidad por $1,525.</p><p>El anuncio decía: “¡Bienvenidos a su nuevo hogar en el corazón de Chicago, Illinois! Este apartamento de dos habitaciones y un baño está disponible ahora y listo para impresionar”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

title: Michelada Fest announces full lineup with an added free day after last year’s cancellations
summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://www.michefest.live/" target="_blank" ><u>Michelada Fest</u></a> organizers announced Thursday that the weekend festival is returning to Chicago after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-culture/2025/05/06/michelada-fest-canceled-chicago-2025-oakwood-beach" target="_blank" ><u>last year’s event was </u></a>canceled amid fears around the “political climate” and issues with visas for foreign artists.</p><p>Happening June 26-28 at its new location Union Park, the lineup includes genre-blending Latin Mafia, Puerto Rican rapper and singer Jhayco, singer-songwriter Jessie Reyez and Jamaican rapper and singer Sean Paul. Michelada Fest, known simply as Miche Fest, celebrates Latin music, art, food and drink, especially the fest’s namesake Mexican cocktail: the michelada.</p><p>More than a dozen local and national artists will perform, including Mexican regional band Dareyes de la Sierra, producer Ovy on the Drums and singer Paloma Mami. Several local artists, such as DJ Eva Maria and Las Vibras de Chicago, will also take the stage that weekend. </p><p>Organizers are also expanding the festival to three days this year. The first day of the festival, on Friday, headlined by DannyLux and Herencia de Patrones, will be free to enter.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Latin artist Dannylux performs at Lollapalooza in 2022. The singer and songwriter is headlining the first day of Miche Fest.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kate Scott/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Fans will notice that there are fewer international artists on this year’s bill, and that was done intentionally, said Miche Fest founder Fernando Nieto.</p><p>Organizers cited problems with international artist visas, as well as the “rapidly changing political climate,” among the reasons for the cancellation last year.</p><p>Immigration enforcement is another concern for organizers. On Sept. 16, the Trump administration began its deportation campaign with Operation Midway Blitz, which put Chicago and the suburbs on high alert, especially in Latino and immigrant-majority neighborhoods.</p><p>“It's something that's at the top of our mind,” Nieto said. “We wanna not only protect our [fans] but also our staff and our vendors who might have undocumented workers. … We're really proud to take these additional necessary steps.”</p><p>Nieto added that Miche Fest volunteers and staff will be trained in de-escalation tactics if problems between law enforcement and artists, vendors or fans arise.</p><p>“We felt that our culture was under attack and they were targeting not only the community but artists and music in general,” Nieto said. “We had four to five artists lose their visas within two to three weeks of us canceling.”</p><p>For this year’s festival, Miche Fest organizers made the conscious decision to book artists whose visas are in good standing.</p><p>“Unfortunately, it did limit and change some of our approach, but we feel we have a really cool and strong lineup,” Nieto continued. “It was the safest path forward to building the festival lineup so that we wouldn't run into that issue for this year.”</p><p>After organizers canceled last year’s event, they focused on building a coalition of strong partnerships for the relaunch.</p><p>That includes working with Chicago artist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics/2022/1/28/22894092/sentrock-murals-chicago-fulton-market-joseph-perez" target="_blank" ><u>Sentrock</u></a>, who’s in charge of art installations and an “artist’s world” on the festival grounds, Nieto said. Chicago DJ collective <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/sentido.wav/" target="_blank" ><u>Sentido</u></a> is curating local artists to perform on an added second stage, and Chicago and Durango-based fashion brand Gente Fina is setting up an exclusive on-site merch pop-up.</p><p>The festival will feature 14 different michelada vendors, as well as plenty of local food options.</p><p>This year’s festival also has a new location: After years of the organizers working to move it to the West Side, Miche Fest will now be held at Union Park, 1501 W. Randolph St. The festival moved to Oakwood Beach from Pilsen in 2024<a class="Link" href="https://southsideweekly.com/5th-pilsen-michelada-festival/" target="_blank" ><u> after residents raised complaints</u></a> over the amount of foot traffic, noise and parking issues brought to the neighborhood.</p><p>“Transparently, we've been trying to get into Union Park for the last few years,” Nieto said. Logistically, he said, operating the festival at Oakwood Beach was a bit of a logistical “headache.”</p><p>Union Park’s proximity to the Green and Pink lines and several bus routes, plus the presence of several parking lots in the area, make it an ideal location, Nieto said.</p><p>“It is gonna make our lives a million times easier,” he said. While Miche Fest doesn’t have a multi-year deal with Union Park, a spokesperson said they intend to make it the festival’s home for years to come.</p><p>In a nod to its community-oriented roots, day one of the festival will be a free-entry day, Nieto said. Instead of tickets, attendees are encouraged to give a suggested donation of $10 to La Casa Norte, a not-for-profit organization for Chicagoans facing housing insecurity.</p><p>“We know that not everybody can afford to attend, so this is for them. This is for the community, this is for accessibility and inclusivity,” Nieto said.</p><p>Tickets are on sale now at <a class="Link" href="http://michefest.live" target="_blank" ><u>MicheFest.live</u></a> and start at $89 for Saturday and Sunday. Children under five years old get free admission with a ticketed adult.</p>

SNAP food benefits cutoff</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wijluyd-l-d/" target="_blank" >Elvia Malagón</a></h5><p><b>Policy problem</b>: Thousands of refugees, asylees and survivors of human trafficking are on the verge of losing food assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. President Donald Trump’s sweeping tax overhaul law, passed last year, limits which immigrants can access the SNAP food program, along with <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wijluyd-l-h/" target="_blank" >enacting expanded work requirements</a> for others. The changes for immigrants went into effect in Illinois on April 1 and are part of broader restrictions on the refugee resettlement program</p><p><b>New rules</b>: Under Trump's policy, refugees can only receive SNAP benefits once they become legal permanent residents. But the federal government isn’t processing refugee applications for green cards. As many as 16,000 people could lose SNAP benefits because of the change, according to the state health department. Historically, refugees have been given a legal form of immigration with a pathway to citizenship.</p><p><b>KQ's story</b>: K.Q. and her husband and four children are refugees who fled the civil war in Syria before they were accepted into the U.S. refugee resettlement program. After nearly three years in Chicago, they expect to lose the monthly $635 they receive in SNAP to supplement her husband’s income. "We came here because they chose us to come," she said. "Why now they [don’t] … help us to live here, because, here — it’s expensive."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wijluyd-l-k/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p> </p><h5>HOW TO HELP ✶</h5><p><b>Household items</b>: RefugeeOne, a Chicago resettlement nonprofit, is stocking up on toiletries, cleaning supplies and diapers to minimize expenses for families. Laura Fine and state Rep. Robyn Gabel, are proposing legislation to help Illinois better prepare for the sudden closure of safety net hospitals. The bills would require all hospitals to file plans with the state in case they close or scale back services, to make sure patients don’t fall through the cracks. For-profit hospitals owned by investors would have to give the state a deeper look into their finances, which now are largely shielded from the public.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: When West Suburban Medical Center abruptly closed its doors temporarily last month, saying it had run out of cash to pay staff, there was little warning for thousands of patients and hundreds of employees. Illinois regulators tasked with overseeing hospitals had little power to stop it.</p><p><b>The stakes</b>: Regulators might not be able to keep open some of the dozens of other safety net hospitals around the state that mostly treat low-income and immigrant communities, amid federal changes next year that could drastically reduce how much money medical centers get paid.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wijluyd-l-p/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p> </p><h4>LOCAL NEWS DAY ✍️</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/K5TeJPLAOd4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Local News Day with Chicago Journalists"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Today is national <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wijluyd-l-m/" target="_blank" >Local News Day</a>, which brings communities together around something we all rely on: Trusted, independent local news. title: Dear Trump supporters: How much more are you willing to ignore?
summary: <p>Tuesday morning, the president of the United States threatened genocide against another nation, all because he does not know how to get out of a war he started to distract Americans from his terrible economy, disastrous immigration headlines and attempts to bury the Epstein files.</p><p>“A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again,” he <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/116363336033995961" target="_blank" >wrote</a> on Truth Social, the social network he had to create so he can say deranged things like this without being deplatformed.</p><p>“I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will,” he continues flippantly, suggesting that he will “probably” nuke a nation that just a month ago he was insisting he wanted to liberate.</p><p>In case it needs pointing out, this threat of genocide would be a war crime, as are the many threats he’s made to strike Iranian infrastructure like water and bridges.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-850000" name="module-850000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>So as we sit on the precipice of what could be NUCLEAR WAR, my question to Donald Trump voters is this: What more are you willing to ignore?</p><p>What more are you willing to “compartmentalize” while you tell yourself this is all an acceptable bargain to get judges and tax cuts?</p><p>What indefensible, illiberal, un-American and inhumane garbage are you willing to defend in service of MAGA’s childish obsession with “owning the libs”?</p><p>How much more chaos, b.s., gaslighting, lying, grifting, incompetence and corruption are you willing to put up with?</p><p>And how much economic pain and destruction are you willing to suffer so that he can get rich and spend your taxpayer dollars bombing other countries, suing his political enemies and building monuments to himself?</p><p>Ten years ago, Trump told us exactly who he was, and he’s been revealing himself ever since.</p><p>He was a bad person then. During campaign rallies and his presidency, you watched as he made fun of people with disabilities, prisoners of war, women and children. You ignored it.</p><p>He was a bigot then. You watched as he defended neo-Nazis, called for travel bans against Muslims, called African countries “sh- -hole nations,” denigrated Black and Brown communities in American cities, called Mexican immigrants rapists and murderers, called himself a nationalist and welcomed white supremacists into the party. You ignored it.</p><p>He was a misogynist then. You watched as the “Access Hollywood” tape came out, as woman after woman told their stories of rape and sexual assault, as the Epstein rumors swirled for years, as porn stars revealed their affairs, as he made fun of women’s faces and biology. You ignored it.</p><p>He was a fraud then. You watched every story about the fraudulent Trump University and Trump Foundation, stories of tax fraud, licensing scams, real estate fraud, contractor nonpayment, election interference and now crypto corruption. You ignored it.</p><p>He was a terrible Christian then. You watched as he repeatedly broke nearly every Commandment, every tenet of Judeo-Christian faith, all while corrupting the religious right to sell Bibles with his name on them. You ignored it.</p><p>He was a terrible conservative then. You watched as he abandoned nearly every long-held conservative principle that Republicans had stood for, from lowering the debt and deficit, to anti-protectionism, to family values. You ignored it.</p><p>And he was a terrible leader then. You watched as he turned American against American, broke the trust of our allies, propped up our enemies, sent his own supporters down dangerous conspiracy theory rabbit holes, all while taking their hard-earned money to fight imaginary election fraud. You ignored it.</p><p>So what now? Does he need to nuke a nation to lose your trust and respect? Does he need to shoot someone in the middle of Fifth Avenue to test your moral compass? Does he need to bankrupt our country, destroy 250 years of American exceptionalism, undo 70-year-old international treaties and start World War III to get you to finally object to one more second of his unhinged lunacy?</p><p>If not now, when?</p><p>Sincerely,</p><p>Sane America</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. title: Refugee families are the latest group to face SNAP food benefit cutoff
summary: <p>K.Q. was sharing a hotel room with her husband and four children when she received a card loaded with funds from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.</p><p>The family had just arrived in Chicago, a city where they knew no one, after being accepted into the U.S. refugee resettlement program. They came from Lebanon, where they spent 12 years after fleeing Syria’s deadly civil war.</p><p>She took her four children to the grocery store, telling them they could buy anything they would like with the federal food assistance. It was a rare treat for the family that in Lebanon struggled to make ends meet.</p><p>“We are so happy because I can go buy everything for my children,” said K.Q., who asked not to be fully identified out of fear it could harm her application to become a legal permanent resident. “In Lebanon we had [a] hard time, and we don’t have enough money to buy anything the children need.”</p><p>But after less than three years here, they are on the verge of losing food assistance, along with thousands of other refugees, asylees and survivors of human trafficking. President Donald Trump’s sweeping tax overhaul law that passed last year limits which immigrants can access the SNAP food program, along with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/13/older-chicagoans-high-risk-of-losing-snap-food-assistance-new-work-rules-kick-in-55-64-may" >enacting expanded work requirements</a> for others. The changes for immigrants went into effect in Illinois on April 1 and are part of broader restrictions on the refugee resettlement program.</p><p>As many as 16,000 people could lose SNAP benefits because of the change in <a class="Link" href="https://www.dhs.state.il.us/?item=177780" target="_blank" ><u>eligibility for immigrants</u></a>, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services.</p><p>Trump’s policy changes put refugees in a Catch-22, resettlement agencies say. They can only receive SNAP benefits once they become legal permanent residents. But the federal government isn’t processing their green card applications. Historically, refugees have been given a legal form of immigration with a pathway to citizenship.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>K.Q. had hoped to get her GED diploma before trying to find a job but says she will now likely have to find work to make up for the expected loss in SNAP benefits for her family. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>For K.Q., this change has left her feeling confused and unsure how she will feed her family.</p><p>“We came here because they chose us to come,” she said. “Why now they [don’t] give us … help us to live here, because, here — it’s expensive.”</p><h3>Cloud of uncertainty for refugees </h3><p>For decades in the U.S., when refugees first arrived they could tap into SNAP and other safety-net programs, like Medicaid health insurance. That support was critical, people in refugee resettlement say, to provide stability because refugees' first jobs typically pay minimum wage. Most of their earnings go towards rent and other basic expenses.</p><p>“Refugees have counted on this vital part of the safety net to help them as they are trying to start over here in Chicago,” said Sally Schulze, communications manager for RefugeeOne, a Chicago resettlement nonprofit.</p><p>That was the case for K.Q. and her family, who lived in one hotel room for two months before they could move into an apartment in Chicago. The family initially received about $1,100 in monthly SNAP benefits, which was later reduced to $635 once her husband started working at an area airport. He is the sole breadwinner while K.Q. has focused on improving her English through classes with a community group.</p><p>The loss of SNAP is just one challenge refugees are facing. The Trump administration lowered the number of refugees allowed to 7,500 for the current fiscal year, the fewest since the program started in 1980, <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/10/30/g-s1-95823/trump-administration-sets-lowest-ever-cap-on-refugee-admissions" target="_blank" >NPR previously reported</a>. That’s down from 125,000 in 2025 under President Joe Biden.</p><p>Fears also persist in the community of being swept up in raids and ending up in an immigration detention center, advocates say.</p><p>World Relief Chicagoland, another local resettlement agency, has been meeting with families in anticipation of government plans to re-interview them, essentially serving as a second vetting of their refugee status, said Susan Sperry, executive director of World Relief Chicagoland.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9c0000" name="module-9c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>How to Help Refugee Families </b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-434fda32-3346-11f1-aa5e-5198da5caf11"><li><b>Household items</b>: RefugeeOne is stocking up on toiletries, cleaning supplies and diapers to minimize expenses for families. The group has an<a class="Link" href="https://www.amazon.com/registries/gl/guest-view/HW4ZYERO21XP?ref_=cm_sw_r_cp_ud_ggr-subnav-share_TF4S1M04JE8K96EAMR2Z" target="_blank" ><u> Amazon wish list</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://tinyurl.com/3kykf68s" target="_blank" ><u>https://tinyurl.com/3kykf68s</u></a></li><li><b>Grocery gift cards</b>: Resettlement agencies are collecting grocery gift cards to provide immediate assistance to refugee families. Those cards can be mailed to RefugeeOne at 6008 N. California Ave., Chicago, IL, 60659, or World Relief Chicagoland at 191 S. Gary Ave., Suite 130, Carol Stream, IL, 60188.</li><li><b>Support local pantries</b>: Groups are expecting more refugees to depend on local food pantries. For a list of pantries, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/10/29/where-to-find-chicago-area-food-pantries-if-snap-goes-away" target="_blank" ><u>visit https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/10/29/where-to-find-chicago-area-food-pantries-if-snap-goes-away</u></a>.</li></ul></div> </div><p>And last November, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in an internal memo said it was no longer processing refugee applications for green cards, according to the American Immigration Lawyers Association. It typically took about 13 months to receive a green card after applying.</p><p>In a statement, USCIS confirmed it paused adjudications for immigrants from countries deemed high risk by the Trump administration. It did not say when the pause would end.</p><p>“National security and the protection of every American must take precedence, even when weighed against potential challenges such as workforce shortages,” the agency stated in an email, adding that it believes the Biden’s administration did not properly vet immigrants.</p><p>Syria, where K.Q. and her family fled, is among the countries deemed high risk because it’s still emerging from civil unrest and “lacks an adequate central authority for issuing passports or civil documents,” according to the White House.</p><p>The family applied for legal permanent residency about a year ago, but like others, they’ve received no updates on their application.</p><p>“I hope everything could change because also here we need to be safe,” K.Q. said. “[If] we have [a] green card, we can stay here. I’m worried about, yes, about my children, about me.”</p><h3>‘The math just doesn’t add up’</h3><p>RefugeeOne anticipates 175 families, or 850 individuals they serve will lose SNAP benefits at some point this year, the majority of them children, Schulze said. World Relief Chicagoland expects more than 300 of their families will lose benefits.</p><p>The changes in green card applications adds to the uncertainty.</p><p>“Without a green card, that means they aren’t going to be able to get this food assistance that they desperately need for months, possibly even years, unless lawmakers make some changes,” Schulze said.</p><div class="Enhancement" She uses it to buy bread, cooking oil and Halal meat.</p><p>She hauls a black shopping cart to her English classes, where there’s also a weekly food pantry. During a recent trip, she grabbed two jugs of milk, lasagna pasta, eggs and a pineapple to supplement her family’s groceries. Although their rent has increased, they don’t want to risk moving and missing important letters about their immigration case.</p><p>“We do anything the government tells us,” she said.</p><p>She didn’t know anything about Chicago before living here, but she knew she needed to get her family out of Lebanon as Syria remained unstable. Her oldest son had to leave school in Lebanon to work and supplement her husband’s wages. K.Q. said Syrian children only received about four hours of schooling with limited subjects.</p><p>In Chicago, she has seen her children flourish in school. They have picked up English and are making friends. One of her sons, an 11th grader, is dreaming of going away to college to study computer science.</p><p>“He’s so excited about that, and I am so happy,” K.Q. said, lighting up. “He asked me before … ‘Mom, if I take a scholarship for college far from here, do you mind that?’ I told him, ‘No, this is your future, but I will miss you.’”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b90000" name="module-b90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>READ MORE</h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-9bf28172-1cac-11f1-b524-93678b2f15cd"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/13/older-chicagoans-high-risk-of-losing-snap-food-assistance-new-work-rules-kick-in-55-64-may" >Older Chicagoans at high risk of losing SNAP food assistance as new work rules kick in</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/26/new-snap-work-rules-leave-unemployed-englewood-man-thousands-of-others-at-risk-food-benefits-cut-off-trump" >New SNAP work rules leave unemployed Englewood man and thousands of others at risk</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/02/06/walmart-amazon-cps-top-employers-illinois-workers-still-need-snap-benefits-trump-work-requirements-lose-benefits" >Walmart, Amazon and CPS top list of employers where Illinois workers still need SNAP benefits</a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/21/new-snap-work-requirements-cook-county-warn-health-consequences-cut-off-congress-donald-trump-food-stamps" >As new SNAP rules loom, Cook County officials warn of health consequences for people cut off</a></li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

title: CPS Board calls on Gov. Pritzker to reject federal program that funds private school tuition
summary: <p>After a lively debate, the Chicago Board of Education approved a resolution Wednesday calling on Gov. JB Pritzker to reject a federal program championed by the Trump administration that can help cover private school tuition or offset public school costs.</p><p>Though the vote passed 15-0, three members abstained and one board member argued that the resolution was “politically motivated” and a vote should be postponed indefinitely, highlighting the contentious nature of an issue that has divided local and national lawmakers.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.cpsboe.org/content/documents/april_8__2026_arc_public_agenda_to_post.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>The resolution</u></a> calls on Pritzker and state lawmakers to reject any programs that would create, expand or “otherwise reintroduce school voucher programs in Illinois” because they would “undermine Illinois’ commitment to fully funded public schools.”</p><p>The resolution doesn’t mention a specific initiative by name, but it points to renewed efforts by the Trump administration at the federal level which seek to “expand and incentivize voucher or publicly funded scholarships for private schools.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/01/28/pritzker-still-deciding-if-illinois-will-join-federal-program-that-funds-private-school-scholarships" target="_blank" ><u>Pritzker is currently weighing whether to opt into</u></a> a new federal program that will allow donors to certain scholarship organizations to reduce how much they owe in federal income tax by up to $1,700. States have until Jan. 1, 2027 to join.</p><p>Those scholarships could fund private school tuition, or unlike other similar programs, they can <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2025/12/09/federal-tax-credit-scholarships-enacted-by-trump-start-to-take-shape/" target="_blank" ><u>support activities that cost money at public schools</u></a> like tutoring, after-school programs or school supplies. It was <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2025/07/03/how-trump-big-beautiful-bill-will-affect-children-and-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>created last year</u></a> as part of the president’s sweeping tax and spending law.</p><p>Families earning up to 300% of their area’s median income – in Chicago that would be about $230,000 or less – are eligible to receive scholarships. The tax credits won’t be available until next year.</p><p>Support for the program has mostly been divided along political lines. President Donald Trump’s administration and Republicans in Congress have lauded the program as a way to expand education options and make them more affordable.</p><p>Critics say it will undermine public schools by diverting taxpayer dollars. They also charge that public funds will go to schools with discriminatory policies. Private schools, for example, are not required to serve students with disabilities in the same way as public schools.</p><p>The resolution notes that private schools “are not held to the same transparency, accountability, civil rights, or governance standards as public schools.”</p><p>Ellen Rosenfeld, one of the three board members who abstained, led the effort to postpone the vote indefinitely. She said that though she wouldn’t support anything that divests funds from public schools, “politics don’t belong in the board room.”</p><p>Rosenfeld said the matter should instead be on the school board’s legislative agenda, which sets the district’s priorities in Springfield. She urged members to lobby the governor to oppose the program because it is ultimately his decision, and said the board should focus on matters that directly affect Chicago Public Schools students.</p><p>“I want to talk about learning, student voice, chronic absenteeism, student safety, that’s what I want to talk about here,” Rosenfeld said. “I will never support a resolution that is simply politically motivated, it is not our job.”</p><p>But member Debby Pope, who spearheaded the resolution, said it was important to take a stand against the program put forward by the Trump administration, given its moves to <a class="Link" href="https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/trump-again-proposes-major-education-cuts-in-new-budget-proposal/2026/04" target="_blank" ><u>undermine public education</u></a> and advance policies that have harmed CPS students, such as the president’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>mass deportation campaign</u></a>.</p><p>“How can we even consider the idea of not being opposed to a program that is being proposed by this president with his intentions to destroy the Department of Education?” Pope said.</p><p>Board member Che “Rhymefest” Smith, who also abstained, said the board spends too much time talking about politics and not enough time talking about how to improve student experiences.</p><p>“Fifty-four percent of our time is wasted on politics, and government things, and I’m not saying politics ain’t important, but what are we doing as a board when we only spend 14% of our time talking about student outcomes?” Smith said.</p><p>Member Jitu Brown said he disagreed with that line of thinking and argued “everything is about politics.”</p><p>Therese Boyle, the third board member who abstained, said she needed more time to research the “ins and outs” of the program.</p><p>Ahead of the vote, Chicago Teachers Union Vice President Jackson Potter called for the board to approve the resolution, likening the federal scholarship program to a “fox entering a hen house” that will lead to less accountability for public dollars.</p><p>“Vouchers do more to support wealthy families and children and undermine public services and schools,” Potter said. He pointed to states like Arizona, <a class="Link" href="https://www.propublica.org/article/arizona-school-vouchers-esa-private-schools" target="_blank" ><u>where reporting has found</u></a> students in richer ZIP codes are using vouchers more than those who live in low-income areas, and Florida, where <a class="Link" href="https://hechingerreport.org/universal-vouchers-have-public-schools-worried-about-something-new-market-share/" target="_blank" ><u>public schools have trimmed budgets</u></a> due to low enrollment partly because of the growing popularity of school vouchers.</p><p>Pritzker hasn’t been a strict opponent of similar programs in the past. When running for reelection in 2022 he said he supported the state’s now-defunct Invest in Kids program in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2022/10/18/23409566/19-questions-candidates-illinois-governor-pritzker-bailey-schluter-wbez-suntimes-issues" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times questionnaire.</u></a> Earlier this year, Pritzker told WBEZ he was evaluating the new federal program through a “lens focused on affordability for working families and what best supports Illinois, families and public schools.”</p><p>But he has also raised red flags about how the latest federal policy could be used, <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/03/23/pritzker-mendoza-split-school-tax-credit/" target="_blank" ><u>according to reporting by the Chicago Tribune</u></a>. Earlier this year Pritzker sent Comptroller Susana Mendoza a text message after <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/02/18/opinion-illinois-opt-in-federal-scholarship-program/" target="_blank" ><u>she wrote an opinion piece</u></a> in the Tribune calling for Illinois to opt in.</p><p>“State/federal tax credit dollars would go to support schools that teach children that gay people are evil, that ‘the KKK was fighting against the decline of morality,’ that white supremacy is God’s will — and other crazy notions,” Pritzker’s message said, according to texts obtained by the Tribune.</p><p>So far 29 states, mostly led by Republican governors, have opted into the federal program, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/federal-private-school-choice-which-states-are-opting-in/2025/08" target="_blank" ><u>tally kept by Education Week</u></a>. <a class="Link" href="https://www.the74million.org/article/colorado-gov-jared-polis-on-why-hes-taking-trumps-free-money/" target="_blank" ><u>Only two Democratic governors</u></a> have opted in, but a few others who initially said they were opposed to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/they-said-no-to-the-federal-school-choice-program-now-3-dems-are-reconsidering/2026/03" target="_blank" ><u>program are reconsidering</u></a>.</p><p>Illinois’ former Invest in Kids program allowed donors to authorized scholarship groups to reduce their state tax burden by as much as $1 million, but state lawmakers allowed that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/2/6/24063232/invest-in-kids-private-school-scholarship-program-sunset-illinois-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>program to sunset in 2023.</u></a></p><p>The Archdiocese of Chicago has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/01/26/archdiocese-catholic-school-closing-jerome-bruno-richard-francis-borgia-stanislaus-kostka" target="_blank" ><u>attributed declining enrollment and school closures</u></a> to the end of the program, though area Catholic schools have experienced a pattern of shutterings and dwindling student population for decades, due to a combination of factors.</p>

title: Illinois House advances bill restricting immigrant detention centers in neighborhoods
summary: <p>The Illinois House <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/25/broadview-ice-detention-center-illinois-legislation" >passed a bill </a>Wednesday restricting future immigration detention centers from being built near community buildings. </p><p>The bill would bar the placement of immigration detention centers within 1,500 feet of schools, churches, day care centers, cemeteries, public parks, forest preserves, private residences and public housing. Existing detention facilities like the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing center in Broadview would not be affected by the legislation.</p><p>After passing out of the House along partisan lines with support from Democrats and opposition from Republicans, the bill now goes toe the Illinois Senate. </p><p>House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, who sponsored the bill and represents areas in and around Broadview, said the legislation is the product of what residents in that community endured during Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>“What should be a place of peace and routine for that community has too often become a place of fear, disruption, trauma and instability,” Welch said during the bill’s debate. “This bill is not about politics, It's about people.”</p><p>“It's about the little kid at day care who should not grow up around chaos. It's about the family in their home who should not feel like they are living next to a crisis zone. It is about the church member walking into worship who should be met with peace, not tension. It is about saying that in Illinois, we will not place detention facilities in the heart of our neighborhoods and pretend there are no consequences.”</p><p>Republican House Floor Leader Patrick Windhorst, a lawmaker from Metropolis, raised concerns over the legislation's legality and compared it to a California law, struck down in a federal court, that would have phased out private, for-profit prisons and detention centers.</p><p>Welch argued his bill would not meet the same fate, saying the California law was a ban, while this is only a restriction.</p><p>“We are continually picking fights with the federal government,” Windhorst said. “The result of this effort to not work together with the federal government to resolve the issues, particularly related to immigration and enforcement of our laws, has resulted in huge problems in our state.”</p><p>Welch responded, “We're not picking a fight with the federal government, the federal government is picking a fight with us. We have states' rights, we know our rights, we know our power.”</p>

target="_blank" >Migrants face scams, sky-high rents and squalor in search for housing</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiydre-l-m/" target="_blank" >Esther Yoon-Ji Kang</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiydre-l-q/" target="_blank" >Adriana Cardona-Maguigad</a></h5><p><b>The challenges</b>: Finding safe and affordable housing has become more difficult in Chicago as migrants face a precarious legal status because of changing policies under President Trump’s administration. Lack of stable income and fear of deportation have also made many migrants more vulnerable to housing scams. Gleeson said he prosecuted criminals similar to Hoover, but that Hoover was different. He’s "grown up" and is remorseful, Gleeson told the Illinois Prisoner Review Board. The board is considering the 75-year-old ex-gang leader’s request for clemency from Gov. JB Pritzker.</p><p><b>The hearing</b>: Dozens of people, including Hoover’s wife, Winndye, attended a prisoner review board hearing downtown, where a panel heard testimony from Hoover’s supporters, along with prosecutors who oppose his freedom. Prosecutors said granting clemency would ignore the seriousness of the killing for which he’s locked up, would minimize crimes he later committed in prison and would put the public in danger.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Hoover and his supporters have increasing hope for his release despite decades of rejections in the state’s separate parole process. That’s because Hoover won a separate grant of clemency last year from President Trump for a federal drug conspiracy sentence.</p><p><a class="Link" content creator finds healing through the art of restoring vintage Coach bags</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiydre-l-tt/" target="_blank" >Esther Bergdahl</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiydre-l-ti/" target="_blank" >Minju Park</a></h5><p>Helena Kim's compact West Loop home studio, measuring about 12 by 12 feet, keeps a place for every tool. Her closets conceal an eye-popping variety of glues, dyes, conditioners, thread and other supplies. Floor-to-ceiling shelves boast the fruits of her labor: vintage Coach handbags, luxury purses rescued from thrift shops and restored to their original blues, greens, rich browns and chic blacks.</p><p>"I do have a very, very large collection at this point," Kim admitted. "It was nothing I set out to do. But every time I went thrifting, I’m like, 'I need to rescue her! She needs help!'"</p><p>On social media, Kim is known by her nickname, Yoonie, which is derived from her Korean name; she has more than 1.2 million followers. In her soothing videos, she explains how to hunt for and rehabilitate the saddest of bargain bin finds. She prefers distressed and abandoned small leather goods, which she revives with saddle soap, conditioners and a jaw-dropping assortment of trade skills.</p><p>When Kim stitches together loose panels, she’s gauging the tensile response of the leather. After she suds up her horsehair brush, she listens for the scrape of its bristles against the bag’s surface. As she massages a thirsty purse with lotion, her hands remember caring for her weary parents after work.</p><p>"When I do really resonate with a bag," Kim said, "I’m just emotionally connected to a bag, or I find this need to tell their story, or a story develops in my head." She loves finding clues about past lives in thrifted purses: A set of bridal hair clips, a magazine clipping to bring to a hairdresser.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiydre-l-td/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p> </p><h4>WATCH: CHICAGO’S COACH RESCUER ▶️</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/TM8No4SGtkk?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Restoring vintage Coach bags is more than Yoonie's hobby, it's like 'therapy'"></iframe> </div> </div></div><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wiydre-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>What’s a clear sign of spring in Chicago?</b></a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"Full tour boats." — <i>Sue Wynn</i></p><p>"Tulips come up on Michigan Avenue." — <i>Tara Goodwin</i></p><p>"Baseball fans complaining about the bullpen and lack of offense." — <i>Vince LiFonti</i></p><p>"Automobiles with tickets for not moving the vehicle during assigned street cleaning." — <i>Edward M. title: Chicago's migrants face scams, sky-high rents and squalor in search for housing
summary: <p>On a blustery Thursday afternoon in February, Daniela and her family — whose members range in age from 9 to 35 — weren’t thinking about dinner or homework.</p><p>They were frantically tossing clothes, shoes and other personal items into bags, desperate to clear out their two-bedroom South Shore apartment before the sun went down.</p><p>The chaos had started earlier that week with a knock at the door. A woman claiming to represent Atlas Asset Management, the company that oversees the three-story multifamily building, stood at the door, asking who they were and to whom they were paying rent.</p><p>“She said this apartment was [supposed to be] vacant … that we needed to leave and that the police were on their way,” Daniela said in Spanish.</p><p>Daniela and her family are from Venezuela and no longer have <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2025/03/04/fears-rise-for-venezuelan-chicagoans-after-trump-rescinds-temporary-protected-status" target="_blank" ><u>a temporary legal status</u></a> in the United States. WBEZ is not publishing their full names because the family fears deportation.</p><p>Unbeknownst to the family, they were squatters in a building that had recently changed ownership, having fallen victim to a scam. A fraudulent leasing agent had broken into vacant units at a building on 79th Street and Paxton Avenue and rented them out to desperate migrant families including Daniela’s.</p><p>When the police officer showed up, the message was blunt: The family had one week to get out.</p><p>Finding safe and suitable housing has become more difficult in Chicago as migrants face precarious legal statuses because of changing federal policies under President Donald Trump's administration.</p><p>Their lack of stable income and fear of deportation have made them more vulnerable to these types of housing scams. They also have to grapple with sky-high rents and an <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/race-class-communities/2024/02/06/chicago-migrants-search-for-housing-as-deadline-looms" target="_blank" ><u>affordable housing</u></a> shortage.</p><p>And a new state law that took effect in January makes it easier for landlords to call the police and vacate squatters without a lengthy eviction process, putting migrant households like Daniela’s at risk for homelessness.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul Chicago’s South Shore neighborhood.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Searching for a stable home</h3><p>Since arriving in Chicago in 2023, the family has moved more than five times. After staying at a migrant shelter for months, they got a temporary rent assistance voucher from the state and found a house that fit all six members for nearly $2,000 per month.</p><p>But the stability was short-lived.</p><p>Within six months, the temporary voucher payments expired, and with only one of the adults holding a steady job, they couldn’t keep up with rent.</p><p>“During those six months, I went out every day, walking street by street looking for work, and I didn't find anything,” said Daniela’s partner, Pedro, in Spanish.</p><p>Without employment, Daniela said they were <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2024/10/07/organizers-try-to-calm-chaos-at-a-south-side-home-depot-where-migrants-look-for-work" target="_blank" ><u>desperate for cash</u></a> and begged in the streets for money with her 4-year-old in tow, even on cold winter days.</p><p>Eventually the family had to leave the spacious home they paid for with the voucher. They doubled up with friends and acquaintances in separate homes until the family figured out how to fit six people in a one-bedroom apartment.</p><p>“My mom, her partner and two other kids usually shared one bedroom," Daniela said. “Me, my partner and child used to sleep in the living room divided by a curtain.”</p><p>They were crammed.</p><p>So in November 2025, when a man who spoke fluent Spanish offered them a two-bedroom apartment for $1,000 — just a little more than what they’ve been paying for their one-bedroom — they jumped at the chance, ignoring several red flags.</p><p>The man, who claimed to be the building manager, never gave them his full name. They never got a lease or receipts when they paid rent in cash. All they had was an informal agreement.</p><p>On top of it all, the apartment was riddled with hazards, including a front door that didn’t lock, no central heat and peeling paint.</p><div href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/PublicActs/View/104-0029" target="_blank" ><u>law</u></a> took effect in January, Gilbert said her organization has heard of cases in which police back off once tenants show rent receipts or leases. In those cases, landlords proceed with standard eviction procedures, in which a court hears the circumstances of both sides and decides whether the tenant has a right to stay. A legal process also could provide tenants with access to emergency rental assistance programs.</p><p>Gilbert said new property managers could misuse the squatter law by calling police on tenants they don’t recognize without finding out more information.</p><p>“You can't just buy a building and clear it out by calling the police,” she said.</p><p>Housing advocates also said forcing tenants out so quickly makes them worse off than they were before. In the case of Daniela’s family, they had to leave behind most of their belongings, all their furniture, and even a cart they used to sell empanadas — a source of sorely needed income.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b90000" name="image-b90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a6b0076/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3742x2100+0+353/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa9%2F4c%2F35771da24e2d9a5ced268a79f026%2Fimg-6775.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/156c0a9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3742x2100+0+353/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa9%2F4c%2F35771da24e2d9a5ced268a79f026%2Fimg-6775.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a786e3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3742x2100+0+353/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa9%2F4c%2F35771da24e2d9a5ced268a79f026%2Fimg-6775.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A building located at 7900 S. Paxton have recently undergone renovations.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A lawyer for Atlas Asset Management, the property management arm of the company that owns the building where Daniela’s family was living, said in a statement to WBEZ that upon taking over the building, “our team discovered complex and challenging conditions at the site” and vacated the units in order to “ensure the safety of residents. This included working to identify all authorized tenants with valid leases.”</p><p>Atlas did not answer multiple questions from WBEZ, including how management secured the building upon purchase, how it determined there were squatters, and whether the company worked with any area nonprofits to assist families with relocation.</p><p>A review of records obtained through a WBEZ public records request to the Chicago Police Department shows that officers were called to the building Feb. 2 by a property manager “regarding squatters in 3 or 4 of the vacant units of the building.”</p><p>Public records also show that the building, which had long been in disrepair, was previously owned by the 5812 Group, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/housing/2025/09/05/chicago-landlords-renters-property-management-llc?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>a limited liability company</u></a>. It was sold to Osiris Chicago Portfolio LLC, which shares an address with Atlas, on Nov. 20, 2025 — about three months before Daniela and her family were kicked out.</p><p>Adam Walls, the head of previous owner 5812 Group, did not respond to a request for an interview.</p><p>Despite the building’s conditions, which mirrored those of many properties in that area, desperate migrants have settled in South Shore, which has come to be known as the “eviction capital of Chicago.”</p><p>The neighborhood is also home to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/public-safety/2025/10/10/chicago-immigration-raid-south-shore-apartment-donald-trump-ice?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>site</u></a> of a federal immigration raid last year. There were also <a class="Link" href="https://www.propublica.org/article/chicago-venezuela-immigration-ice-raid-landlord-tren-de-aragua" target="_blank" ><u>reports</u></a> of fraudulent property managers collecting rent from unwitting migrants in the apartment building where the raid took place.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div He also sympathizes with property managers and landlords, who face rising costs and higher taxes.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>‘Compassion is not a rental system’ </h3><p>As president of Manage Chicago, Chris Amatore oversees thousands of apartments for low-income renters. In late 2023, he provided apartments for hundreds of migrants in his buildings after experiencing a spiritual awakening.</p><p>Since then, Amatore has seen many migrants face housing challenges due to a lack of job opportunities, a language barrier, and “just not knowing where to turn to,” making them easy prey for apartment scams.</p><p>“It’s really just math,” Amatore said. “They can't afford the market rents. It's $2,000 to $2,700 for a three-bed [unit]. Post-COVID rents have gone up faster than a migrant salary.”</p><p>He said credit score requirements and proof of income are also hurdles for migrants seeking to rent apartments. Rising costs, higher taxes and inflation have also made landlords hike rents.</p><p>“I definitely sympathize with landlords, because it's happened to me, and it sucks,” Amatore said. “No one else is going to care. Your bank doesn't care. The utility companies are still gonna turn off the water or gas. Unfortunately, compassion is not a rental system.”</p><p>Still, Amatore believes there’s a humane way to work with these families.</p><p>“What I would do is say, ‘OK, I'm the real landlord…. ‘Let's make a deal.’ [I’d] put them on a plan and give them an opportunity,” he said.</p><p>Lately, Amatore has started noticing there are more migrants sleeping on the streets and in tents.</p><p>“At first, I didn't see a lot, but I do see a lot more migrants under the Canalport bridge and by 18th and Halsted over there, and other areas,” he said.</p><p>As rents rise, aid has run out, and housing options dwindle, he thinks he’ll see more migrants out on the streets and in tents.</p><p>Daniela and her family hope that doesn’t happen to them.</p><p>Shortly after they fled the South Shore apartment they found a new, more expensive one on the West Side for $1,400 a month. But the move once again uprooted the family. It took weeks to enroll the children in their new school. And while more adults in the family are employed now, they still scramble to come up with rent each month.</p><p>Meanwhile, back in South Shore, the apartment Daniela and her family were living in has been repainted and the kitchen remodeled. As of early April, Atlas Asset Management had listed the unit for $1,525.</p><p>The listing read: “Welcome to your new home in the heart of Chicago, IL! This two-bedroom, one-bathroom unit is available now and ready to impress.”<br></p>

title: CPS students can now access books, tutoring, other library services with just a student ID
summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools students can now access books, tutors and other resources at city libraries with just their student ID number.</p><p>It's the latest effort by CPS and the Chicago Public Library to expand access to library materials through <a class="Link" href="https://www.chipublib.org/the-81-club/" target="_blank" ><u>The 81 Club</u></a>, an initiative that makes it easier for students to get books and other resources at all 81 public library branches.</p><p>All CPS students are automatically enrolled in the 81 Club, which launched in 2022, and they can now use their ID to check out library materials in person or online “with no application, paperwork or additional steps,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2026/april/81-club-expansion.html" target="_blank" ><u>according to CPS and CPL</u></a>. Students previously had to pick up 81 Club cards in person at a library. Still, some students may want to apply for a traditional library card, as that allows them to check out more than five physical items at a time.</p><p>Officials with the two agencies said this expansion is meant to help young people take advantage of what the library system has to offer, even if they lack stable housing or legal immigration status in the U.S. — barriers that could make it hard to get to the library in person or provide additional paperwork.</p><p>“We all know too well that talent is equally distributed across this large city in every single neighborhood, but opportunity access is not,” Michael Fassnacht, board chair of the Chicago Public Library Foundation, said during a Tuesday news conference at the Austin Branch Library.</p><p>Through the program, students have access to the library’s online databases and digital media and can request one-on-one tutoring services online or in person, among other services.</p><p>Last year, nearly 3,000 students from 390 different CPS schools activated their 81 Club accounts, <a class="Link" href="https://empowereverychicagoan.org/" target="_blank" ><u>according to the Chicago Library Foundation</u></a>, though that represents a small share of the district’s 316,000 students. It was not immediately clear how many CPS students are using the program now.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a It grants them access to research databases, instructional tools, as well as eBooks and audiobooks that they can use in the classroom.</p>
