title: 'Broadview 6' judge moves on from White House interference claims after feds' denial
summary: <p>The federal judge presiding over the conspiracy case against the remaining members of the “Broadview Six” largely closed the book Tuesday<b> </b>on a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >bid for White House communications</a> in the case, after prosecutors denied<b> </b>that any such correspondence exists.</p><p>The feds say “there are no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone” outside the U.S. attorney’s office, aside from local FBI investigators, and they’ve made clear that “includes anyone in the White House and all components and offices of Main Justice.”</p><p>That’s despite the fact that at least one defendant in the case, former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, had the attention of White House Deputy Press Secretary Abigail Jackson and far-right influencer Laura Loomer.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" >Remaining Broadview 6 defendants want records showing Trump administration’s influence on conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Defense attorneys wanted U.S. District Judge April Perry to order prosecutors<b> </b>to explain how they reached their conclusion, but she declined to do so Tuesday<b> </b>in the latest hearing in the case. She said the feds know how to do their job and that “their law licenses … are on the line.”</p><p>The judge ultimately denied as moot the defense bid for such communications, meaning the issue had already been resolved by the feds’ claims. She also denied other defense requests related to selective prosecution claims, noting that “being a politician is not a protected class.”</p><p>Being a member of a certain political party could qualify, but she told defense attorneys “you haven’t shown me any evidence that that was considered here.”</p><p>The defense recently disclosed a note<b> </b>sent by the federal agent at the center of the case, in which he identified the political positions held by some of the defendants. But, Perry noted, it did not mention their parties.</p><p>Besides, the agent also described one defendant as being an “Oak Park/Oakbrook Board of Trustees Member.”</p><p>“There’s a big difference between an Oak Park politician and an Oak Brook politician,” Perry remarked, prompting smiles among the defendants.</p><p>Point being, it was hard to make inferences from the note.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" >Selective prosecution claims in ‘Broadview Six’ case the result of ‘fevered paranoia,’ feds say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Charged in the case are four people involved in local Democratic politics. They are Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt and Andre Martin, a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff. The feds <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >also dropped charges</a><b> </b>against two others originally charged in the case.</p><p>The group is accused of a conspiracy<b> </b>to impede a federal agent. The case revolves around events on the morning of Sept. 26, outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview during protests against the Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>The defendants are accused of being part of a group that surrounded the agent’s vehicle<b> </b>and pushed, scratched and otherwise damaged it.</p><p>The case is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/28/broadview-six-conspiracy-case-involving-abughazaleh-could-go-to-trial-in-spring" target="_blank" >on track for trial</a> May 26, though a motion to dismiss the conspiracy charge on First Amendment grounds is still pending. Each defendant also faces a separate misdemeanor charge.</p><p>Defense attorneys said it’s another example of President Donald Trump’s administration using the Justice Department to target his “perceived political enemies.”<b> </b>Prosecutors said any claim of selective or vindictive prosecution is “the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >product of fevered paranoia</a> and delusional speculation.”</p><p>The note Perry referenced Tuesday was sent by the agent to three senior ICE officials the day the original six defendants were indicted, defense attorneys have said.</p><p>“Among the 6 defendants,” he wrote, “there is a US congressional candidate, a 45th ward Committee Person, and a Oak Park/Oakbrook Board of Trustees Member.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> title: After rocky first year, Chicago’s top federal prosecutor says he isn’t taking orders from Washington
summary: <p>When Chicago’s top federal prosecutor is asked if his office takes marching orders from Washington, he doesn’t mince words.</p><p>“You should write this down,” U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros recently told a Chicago Sun-Times reporter.</p><p>“[There is] not a single case, ok, involving politics in our decision making. Full stop. Period. Zero,” Boutros said. “And anyone who says otherwise is misstating reality. And anyone who says otherwise is an armchair expert who doesn’t know what they’re talking about. Period.”</p><p>He said he isn’t done with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >Operation Midway Blitz</a>. Nor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials" target="_blank" >public corruption</a> — he said people should “stay tuned.”<b> </b>And having reached the end of a volatile first year in office, in which President Donald Trump has been accused of weaponizing the Justice Department, Boutros said he has cases to bring “based on facts, law and the equities.”</p><p>But his first year also featured an “unprecedented exodus” of prosecutors from the office he leads, critics note. Most section chiefs left. And convictions have yet to emerge from the flurry of charges the office filed during Midway Blitz, the aggressive deportation campaign that hit the Chicago area last year.</p><p>It charged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, the woman shot by a Border Patrol agent and labeled a “domestic terrorist” before<b> </b>the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >charges were dropped</a>. And<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/juan-espinoza-martinez-cleared-of-bovino-murder-plot-still-in-detention-after-judge-denies-bail" target="_blank" >Juan<b> </b>Espinoza<b> </b>Martinez</a>, the man <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" target="_blank" >acquitted of putting a hit</a> on then-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration" target="_blank" >U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino</a>.</p><p>In his most extensive commentary to date about Midway Blitz, Boutros acknowledged all did not go according to plan. Especially when it came to working with an “out of town”<b> </b>group of agents.</p><p>But Boutros said repeatedly, “We want to get it right.”</p><p>He made his remarks in a wide-ranging conversation with the Sun-Times and Chicago Tribune to mark Tuesday’s<b> </b>one-year anniversary of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/28/former-prosecutor-andrew-boutros-named-chicagos-interim-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" >the day he took office</a>.</p><h3><b>Federal prosecutors under ‘unprecedented pressures’</b></h3><p>Boutros, the son of immigrants from Egypt, is the first person of color to hold the office. He’s overtly patriotic, calls Chicago his “adopted”<b> </b>home<b> </b>and often drops references to Al Capone and the 1985 Chicago Bears.</p><p>His office moved quickly last year to level a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/11/19/terrorism-charges-filed-after-woman-lit-on-fire-on-blue-line-in-loop" target="_blank" >terrorism charge</a> against the man accused of setting<b> </b>a woman on fire on the Blue Line, and a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/02/chicago-crime-sheridan-gorman-loyola" target="_blank" >weapons charge</a> this month against the man separately charged with the murder of Loyola University Chicago freshman<b> </b>Sheridan Gorman.</p><p>Christopher Amon, the special agent in charge of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in Chicago, said violent crime prosecutions “were not a priority”<b> </b>for the U.S. attorney’s office before Boutros’ arrival — and now that’s changed.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/30/andrew-boutros-interim-us-attorney-chicago-judges-role-pam-bondi" >Is Chicago’s interim U.S. attorney here to stay? Judges could play an unusual role in picking top prosecutor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Boutros had kind words for controversial Attorney General Pam Bondi, even after Trump fired her<b> </b>last week. Bondi<b> </b>first appointed Boutros to his post, and Boutros said “she was tremendously good to Chicago and to this office.” The city’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/07/25/chicagos-federal-judges-choose-andrew-boutros-as-top-prosecutor" target="_blank" >federal judges later chose Boutros</a> to serve in the role on a more permanent basis.</p><p>Still, Boutros knows he has his critics, having once referred to their “sneering disbelief.”<b> </b>He’s endured grand jurors refusing to hand up indictments against at least three people — considered a rare rebuke. And a magistrate judge in November <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/unusual-and-possibly-unprecedented-judge-calls-out-chicago-feds-as-midway-blitz-cases-fall-apart" target="_blank" >questioned the charging decisions of Boutros’ office</a> during Midway Blitz, noting that “these are not ordinary times”<b> </b>at Chicago’s federal courthouse.</p><p>Defense attorneys are also exploring whether the White House <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >involved itself in the conspiracy case</a> brought by Boutros’ office against a group of Midway Blitz protesters known as the “Broadview Six.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Prosecutors dropped charges against two others.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ron Safer, a former federal prosecutor in Chicago who left the U.S attorney’s office in 1999, told the Sun-Times that the “unprecedented exodus of experience, talent and leadership” under Boutros “diminishes the office in ways that are obvious and ways that are not so obvious.”</p><p>He said things might be different if Boutros’ office appeared to be “resisting”<b> </b>a Justice Department that Safer said has “sprinted from its founding principles.”</p><p>But another office alum, Joe Thompson, said “unprecedented pressures” have been placed on U.S. attorney’s offices across the country. Thompson is the former high-ranking federal prosecutor who left office in Minnesota after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/14/chicago-law-firm-representing-renee-nicole-goods-family-romanucci-blandin" target="_blank" >fatal shooting of Renee Good.</a></p><p>Now in private practice, Thompson’s clients include indicted journalist<b> </b>Don Lemon. He served in Chicago’s U.S. attorney’s office from 2009 until 2014, led Minnesota’s U.S. attorney’s office for several months in 2025 and served as second-in-command until shortly after Good was shot by an immigration officer.</p><p>“I think [Boutros] is in an incredibly difficult situation,” Thompson told the Sun-Times. “I think even [former U.S. Attorney] Patrick Fitzgerald would struggle to be U.S. attorney in the current environment, and Andrew certainly is having to navigate some rocky waters.”</p><h3><b>Blitz cases have collapsed — but more are coming</b></h3><p>There are “some very serious cases”<b> </b>still coming out of Midway Blitz, Boutros warned.</p><p>“You can’t commit a serious crime in this district and think that that’s OK,” he said. “There will be consequences.”</p><p>The handling of nonimmigration crimes tied to Midway Blitz is perhaps the most publicly prominent part of Boutros’ first year in office. Federal prosecutors charged<b> </b>32 known people with such crimes, but no one has been convicted. Twenty have already been cleared.</p><p>Federal prosecutors normally boast a conviction rate around 90%.<b> </b>They’re expected to bring charges only when they can prove them to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-250000" name="image-250000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8fa22e6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdf%2F59%2F4ebdcd7e4d92b49cb5a32e0b6638%2Fblitztoll-260301-14.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd52bd5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdf%2F59%2F4ebdcd7e4d92b49cb5a32e0b6638%2Fblitztoll-260301-14.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e65d438/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdf%2F59%2F4ebdcd7e4d92b49cb5a32e0b6638%2Fblitztoll-260301-14.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Jocelyne Robledo (left) and Ray Collins at their home in Englewood, Friday, Feb. 20, 2026. court, but the battles take a toll — ‘It’s about intimidation’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“We had a visiting law enforcement group that came from the border, came several hundred strong, and they were and other rights but that there was law and order that was happening, still, in the city,” Boutros said.</p><p>The result was “not perfect,”<b> </b>he said, but “not for lack of wanting to get it right.”<b> </b>He stressed that his team is willing to reconsider the cases it’s already charged based on “new video, new information, new facts, new equities.”</p><p>But there’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/chicago-ice-trump-bovino-marimar-martinez-crime-border-patrol-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >a cost to defendants who are charged</a> with federal crimes, even if those charges go away. A federal prosecution is intimidating. It carries the threat of prison time. Damaging news stories spread online.</p><p>Thompson said there’s “a real risk to the ongoing credibility of an office”<b> </b>when so many cases are dropped, abandoned or end in acquittals.</p><p>“It’s a significant red flag,”<b> </b>Thompson said.</p><h3><b>Resignations come with a cost</b></h3><p>Several veteran prosecutors left Boutros’ office in the last year, including nearly every criminal section chief. They took with them experience handling public corruption, violent crime and national security. Many of the section chiefs left later in Boutros' first year, after the start of Midway Blitz.</p><p>Boutros acknowledged it was a year of “transition.” But he touts the experience of a core team that includes First Assistant U.S. Attorney Jason Yonan, an 18-year veteran of the office; and criminal division chief Rick Young, a 24-year veteran.</p><p>Former prosecutors who left during Boutros’ first year either declined to comment for this article or did not respond to messages from the Sun-Times. Thompson, who left Minnesota’s U.S. attorney’s office in January, said everyone leaves “for his or her own reasons.”</p><p>“Some of those might be politics,” Thompson said. “Whether they disagree with the administration’s priority, or the U.S. attorney’s priorities. It could be more general: The type of case work they’re getting isn’t as professionally satisfying as they maybe had before.”</p><p>Regardless, he said it’s been happening around the country, in offices big and small.</p><p>Boutros explained that, “some people left because I told them I was going to demote them. Some people left because they came into my office and they said that they strongly dislike this administration and cannot work for this administration.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" >Marimar Martinez, shot by Border Patrol in Chicago, speaks out after Good, Pretti deaths: ‘I am their voice’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"Some of them came to me and told me they were leaving because of the Blitz,” Boutros said.</p><p>But there’s a price to pay when so many veterans walk out the door, Safer said. It goes beyond institutional knowledge. When prosecutors leave, cases are reassigned, and he said that “causes at least substantial delay because a new attorney has to come up to speed.”</p><p>“It’s hard to overstate the impact of having assistants who are handling long-term investigations leave the office and have to hand it off to somebody else,” Safer said. “It results not only in justice being delayed, but at times in justice He points to “historic lows”<b> </b>in “virtually every single metric that was tracked by the Department of Justice.” Statistics kept by the federal courts show cases were brought against 428 people here in 2024, down from 848 in 2020.</p><p>That number rose to 598 in 2025, most noticeably with a 115% increase in fraud cases. Boutros has also touted a large increase in cases brought with help from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/9/27/23891321/chicago-crime-guns-atf" target="_blank" >Crime Gun Intelligence Center</a> run by the ATF.</p><p>Safer said such numbers “are largely misleading and irrelevant.” The FBI investigation that snared Burke and Madigan took several years and involved massive resources. The impact and significance of such a case is not reflected in the data.</p><p>“We need to be prosecuting organizations — as only the U.S. attorney’s office can do — who present a danger to the people of the Northern District of Illinois,” Safer said.</p><p>Boutros insists “you can do both.”<b> </b>He said an emphasis on “big cases”<b> </b>doesn’t explain the numbers he saw when he took over.</p><p>There are now 88 assistant U.S. attorneys on the criminal side of Boutros’ office in Chicago, and 25 on the civil side. There are 123 total, including in Rockford. But Boutros said his office is “on a major hiring spree,”<b> </b>with hopes of picking up “close to 50 new people” by the end of the year.</p><p>He said he’s had no trouble finding experienced applicants, contradicting the claim that Justice Department jobs have lost their luster.</p><h3><b>Boutros focused on violent crime and corruption</b></h3><p>There’s plenty of work for Chicago’s federal prosecutors to do beyond Midway Blitz. Boutros said his office is focused on fraud, human trafficking, child exploitation, violence, cartels, drugs, guns and gangs.</p><p>It leveled a terrorism charge in November against Lawrence Reed,<b> </b>the man accused of approaching a 26-year-old woman on a CTA Blue Line train, dousing her with gasoline and setting her on fire.</p><p>And last week,<b> </b>it filed a weapons charge against Jose Medina, the Venezuelan immigrant separately accused of the March 19 murder of Gorman, the 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago freshman. Boutros said he was taking “no chances”<b> </b>that Medina might walk free.</p><p>There are other initiatives, too. title: U.S. welcomed us when we fled persecution for our Christian faith, but now it's closing doors
summary: <p>For each of us, choosing to follow Jesus was not a casual decision.</p><p>Growing up under the Soviet Union in what is now Russian-occupied Ukraine, Liza was often reminded of the cost when her parents smuggled the family to attend their Baptist church in secret and when her teachers mocked her faith in front of her peers. Later, when the Soviet Union collapsed, she attended Bible college and followed the call into ministry in India and Russia with Wycliffe Bible Translators.</p><p>In 2014, everything changed. Russia invaded Liza’s hometown in Ukraine, and suddenly, she was unsafe as a missionary in Russia and in her hometown. She was falsely accused of being a spy and narrowly escaped arrest. It was only through the <a class="Link" href="https://www.uscis.gov/green-card/green-card-eligibility/green-card-for-a-lautenberg-parolee" target="_blank" >Lautenberg program</a>, a provision within the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program created for religious minorities from the Soviet Union and <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/blog/celebrating-a-legislative-victory-for-refugees-and-religious-freedom/" target="_blank" >Iran</a>, that she was able to be resettled as a refugee in Illinois.</p><p>Growing up in Iran, Ara knew what happened to Muslim converts to Christianity: torture and death. Undeterred, he continued to share the good news of Jesus and began smuggling Bibles into the country. He was caught and lived for two years under house arrest. He fled and, like Liza, resettled in the United States.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e20000" name="module-e20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Now U.S. citizens, neither of us has stopped ministering to others in Jesus’ name. Liza works at World Relief, serving others who have fled persecution and arrived as refugees. And Ara is a pastor in Los Angeles, serving many in his congregation who fled persecution in Iran. It is a gift to have the freedom to share about Jesus, and we’re grateful for the support the U.S. has historically provided to believers.</p><p>Over the last year, though, doors have begun to close for others fleeing on account of their faith.</p><h3>Asylum requests denied</h3><p>In Ara’s own church, Iranian converts to Christianity who had arrived lawfully in the U.S. as asylum-seekers were violently arrested outside of their home in Los Angeles last summer and detained separately. Ara arrived on the scene and began filming the proceedings, which went viral on Facebook among U.S. and Iranian followers — and prompted authorities in Iran to search for Bibles in the couple’s parents’ home.</p><p>We watch fearfully as Iranian Christian converts are denied asylum and returned to Iran, praying that their lives might be spared upon arrival.</p><p>Others are swept up, too. Among others, Burmese Christians, many of whom were persecuted for their Baptist or Anglican beliefs and found safety in the U.S., were <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/voices/2026/01/25/ice-raids-minnesota-church-refugees/88304162007/" target="_blank" >detained and reinterviewed,</a> and families have been separated unnecessarily on U.S. soil.</p><p>This winter, <a class="Link" href="https://hias.org/statements/trump-administration-ends-refugee-pathway-persecuted-iranian-religious-minorities/" target="_blank" >the Resettlement Support Center in Vienna, Austria, was shuttered</a>. Little known to many Americans, this center has been a symbol of hope for Iranian Christians admitted through the Lautenberg program. Right now, more than 14,000 Iranians, who had been previously approved for resettlement with a credible fear of religious persecution, are trapped in limbo. They cannot return home, and they can’t move forward toward the friends and family who sponsored them to come to the U.S.</p><h3></h3><p>How did we get here?</p><p>On one hand, the legal mechanism that enabled our arrival in the U.S. as refugees, the Lautenberg Amendment, is still in effect, having recently been reauthorized by the U.S. Congress. We are grateful that there are members of Congress on both sides of the aisle who are passionate about protecting victims of religious persecution. It’s also an important issue for <a class="Link" href="https://worldrelief.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/FINAL-Letter-to-Admin-Afghan-Christians-May-2-2025-1.pdf" target="_blank" >many conservative Christian voters</a>.</p><p>In his <a class="Link" href="https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefings-statements/remarks-president-trump-united-nations-event-religious-freedom-new-york-ny/" target="_blank" >remarks</a> at the United Nations in 2019, President Donald Trump affirmed that “America will always be a voice for victims of religious persecution everywhere” and to those victims, “you have a place in the United States.” But behind the scenes, something has changed.</p><p>The U.S. Refugee Admissions Program is still a part of U.S. law. But beginning with the pause on the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program in January 2025, to the lowest refugee resettlement ceiling in history announced in October without options for those facing religious persecution, to the news of shuttered hubs serving persecuted Christians, the writing is on the wall. The U.S.' open doors to the persecuted are closing.</p><p>We urge President Trump to honor his own promises and reopen refugee resettlement for persecuted Christians. We also urge Congress to amend the Lautenberg program by setting a minimum threshold for resettlement for persecuted religious minorities from Iran, the former Soviet Union and those from other countries plagued by religious persecution.</p><p>We grieve on behalf of and alongside our brothers and sisters. </p><p><i>Liza Khalil is the director of case management for World Relief Chicagoland. The Rev. Ara Torosian is the pastor of Cornerstone West Los Angeles.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-650000" name="module-650000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

title: City Council and pope concur: Medicare for All is a common-sense solution
summary: <p>While it didn't make headlines, Chicago recently became the <a class="Link" href="https://www.medicare4allresolutions.org/" target="_blank" >largest city</a> in the U.S. to pass a <a class="Link" href="https://www.citizen.org/news/chicago-passes-medicare-for-all-resolution/" target="_blank" >resolution<u> </u></a>calling on Congress to support Medicare for All. The resolution was adopted the same day that Pope Leo XIV, a Chicago native, called upon nations to enact universal health care as a <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/pope-leo-calls-universal-healthcare-moral-imperative-2026-03-18/" target="_blank" >moral imperative</a>.</p><p>As physicians practicing in the Chicago area, this moral imperative couldn’t be clearer. Every day, we witness how our health care system prioritizes profits over patients. We see and live the gaps, inefficiencies and devastating consequences of this fragmented system.</p><p>While a city-level, nonbinding resolution might seem trivial, this unanimous vote supporting Medicare for All is a declaration that the status quo is no longer acceptable. It’s a rejection of small-scale reforms that force our patients to lose limbs because they chose paying rent over buying insulin. It’s a cry against systems that force us to stand by as women die prematurely of breast cancer because they can't afford a biopsy.</p><p>Chicago’s resolution reflects a growing recognition that incremental changes and new direct-to-consumer price reductions (such as <a class="Link" href="https://trumprx.gov/" target="_blank" >TrumpRx</a>) are simply not enough. It also signals an important shift: Medicare for All is no longer a fringe proposal but is now recognized as a common-sense solution. That recognition was echoed just one day prior to the City Council vote when Illinois Democratic primary voters chose <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-senate-illinois-primary-results" target="_blank" >Juliana Stratton</a>, who made Medicare for All central to her campaign for the U.S. Senate nomination.</p><p>There is a <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/12/10/most-americans-say-government-has-a-responsibility-to-ensure-health-care-coverage/" target="_blank" >growing consensus<u> </u></a>that the federal government should ensure all Americans have health care coverage. Medicare for All represents a solution to providing that coverage while building upon <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/05/delivering-most-favored-nation-prescription-drug-pricing-to-american-patients/" target="_blank" >ongoing efforts</a> to reduce health care costs and, per the <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/pope-leo-calls-universal-healthcare-moral-imperative-2026-03-18/" target="_blank" >words<u> </u>o</a>f Pope Leo XIV: "Universal health coverage is … a moral imperative for societies that wish to call themselves just.”</p><p>It is time to move beyond the complicated, inadequate reforms of the Affordable Care Act. There is a growing clarity, and now an increasingly prominent insistence, that a universal, national health program is the best next step. The rest of the Illinois Democratic coalition should take heed and find the courage to move in step with this rising public will.</p><p><i>Drs. Monica Maalouf, Winnie Lin and Alec Nicolas Angelo Jotte </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-730000" name="module-730000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Paying fair share of taxes benefits Americans </h3><p>At the parking garage near Grant Park, I entered the elevator with six other 70-somethings. As the door closed, I turned and asked, "Were you at the 1968 Democratic Convention too?" Same vibe at the "No Kings" rally, but no violence.</p><p>I was not there for myself, but for the others who have been more adversely impacted by the fascist movement that is now our government. I was there for my children, grandchildren and yet unborn great-grandchildren. I was also there to honor my parents and grandparents, whose generations fought against fascism in World War II.</p><p>I admire those who want to take action by protesting, but I could see on their faces that they did not know or understand how our democracy was taken away.</p><p>Simply put, following the Great Depression and World War II, our society transformed into a more perfect union. That <a class="Link" href="https://ncbudget.org/taxes-on-rich-people-helped-to-beat-inflation-and-hitler/" target="_blank" >growth was funded through taxes</a> — to pay for education, infrastructure, research, fighting poverty and so much more.</p><p>The new tax code was founded upon a principle born out of World War II, when illegal profiteering was "accepted" to facilitate the war effort. By the 1950s, the top-tier <a class="Link" href="https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2015/nov/15/bernie-sanders/income-tax-rates-were-90-percent-under-eisenhower-/" target="_blank" >tax bracket was 90%</a> to prevent excessive profits.</p><p>In turn, the taxes on those profits funded social services and a growing economy, as well as government.</p><p>The decline of the middle class can be linked with policies under the Nixon administration, including the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cato.org/commentary/remembering-nixons-wage-price-controls" target="_blank" >90-day freeze</a> on all prices and wages. Next was Ronald Reagan’s trickle-down tax plan, then <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbpp.org/research/the-legacy-of-the-2001-and-2003-bush-tax-cuts" target="_blank" >George W. Bush’s tax cuts</a>, followed by <a class="Link" href="https://time.com/5570679/trump-tax-cuts/" target="_blank" >not one</a> but <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/31/trump-tax-break-overtime-democrats-00848495" target="_blank" >two Donald Trump</a> tax cuts. In this time frame, the growth of American billionaires has grown exponentially, exceeding the robber barons of the 19th century Gilded Age. The post-World War II economy was designed to prevent having billionaires.</p><p>Republicans hate taxes. But taxes allow those people to make money and pay for the society they live in too. There is a great reversal taking place. But the problem remains that when we as a society forget our history, the door will once again be open to fascism.</p><p><i>Steve London, Edgewater</i> </p><h3>We’ve seen this war scenario before </h3><p>Once again, we are watching a war unfold with familiar justifications and predictable consequences.</p><p>It begins with certainty; claims are presented as urgent and undeniable. Soon, those claims shift. What was once about an imminent threat becomes a need for regime change and then something else altogether. The reasoning evolves, but the destruction does not.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/03/27/dozens-of-evanston-township-students-walk-out-of-school-to-protest-war-in-iran" target="_blank" >world hesitates</a>. Many nations step back. Yet a powerful few drag us into a conflict often influenced by allies with deep political clout in Washington, D.C. What follows is not strategy but suffering: Families displaced, lives shattered and<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/03/14/iran-children-school-bombing-u-s-israel-trump-negar-mortazavi-rummana-hussain" > futures erased</a>.</p><p>What is most troubling is how little seems to be learned. Humanity has witnessed immense tragedy in recent memory. The calls for restraint, diplomacy and basic decency are not new. Yet they are repeatedly ignored. Now we hope the war may come to an end, but what is ultimately driving us in that direction?</p><p>If we are honest, it often comes down to interests measured in barrels, markets and margins. How sad — oil prices are valued above faith teachings, humanity and even our own better judgment.</p><p><i>Irfan Sarwar, Wheeling</i></p><h3>Voting is an all-American right </h3><p>While passing out primary election materials, I saw a man intentionally shove a woman wearing a hijab as she approached the polling location, causing her to stumble. Fortunately, she sustained no injury.</p><p>I confronted the man for his inappropriate actions — a potential hate crime— until he agreed to leave the site. When the woman returned after voting with her two children in tow, she shared that such unpleasant interactions were not unusual for her, a Muslim woman living in Cook County.</p><p>The woman's commitment to our electoral process is exactly what makes democracy so powerful. Everyone's voice matters equally at the ballot box.</p><p>The fact that the Muslim woman was assaulted should not be surprising, considering the level of racist discourse coming from the president. The federal administration is doing everything it can to make people feel like their vote doesn't have an impact.</p><p>The so-called Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, or SAVE Act<i>, </i>which passed in the House and is now being debated in the Senate, will disenfranchise all voters and disproportionately impact minorities, the working class and women.</p><p>The requirement for in-person documented proof of citizenship is not easily implemented, which is on purpose. Over <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/millions-americans-dont-have-documents-proving-their-citizenship-readily" target="_blank" >21 million Americans</a> do not have documents readily accessible, and about <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/04/13/g-s1-59684/save-act-married-women-vote-rights-explained#:~:text=But%20for%20as%20many%20as,their%20proof%20of%20citizenship%20document." target="_blank" >69 million married</a> American women do not have a birth certificate with their married legal name on it.</p><p>Before the 2024 election, the percentage of Americans who registered to vote in person hovered <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/fact-checking-senate-minority-leader-chuck-schumer-on-the-effects-of-the-save-america-act" target="_blank" >around 11%</a>. In Cook County, we are expanding voting opportunities through same-day voter registration, a montlong early voting period, mail-in ballots and expansive polling locations. I led the effort to triple the number of languages in which our ballots are available (<a class="Link" href="https://www.commissionerscottbritton.com/vote" target="_blank" >the VOTE Ordinance</a>).</p><p>We must stand with those on the front lines fighting against voter suppression and civil rights violations, for history shows us that the suppression of rights eventually comes for us all.</p><p>Cook County United Against Hate supports communities pushing back against bigotry by leveraging County resources to investigate, educate and prosecute hate crimes. Our 90 partners are committed to building awareness and creating welcoming spaces. I invite all people of goodwill to join me in signing the pledge against hate at <a class="Link" href="http://www.cookcountyunitedagainsthate.com/" target="_blank" ><u>CookCountyUnitedAgainstHate.com</u></a><u>.</u></p><p><i>Scott Britton, Cook County commissioner, 14th District</i></p><h3>Holding parents accountable </h3><p>The so-called "teen takeovers" or "trends" are concerning. It is not simply the gathering of large numbers of youth, but the reality that, more often than not, a small group within the larger one damages property or, worse, engages in behavior that leads to a teenager being hurt or killed. We must protect our children.</p><p>Yes, we need programs for youth to be involved in, but few programs can be offered at 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. Months ago, I asked the city of Chicago to consider holding parents and guardians more responsible. The city failed to respond. I am now asking the City Council to pass an ordinance requiring police to issue a warning to parents the first time their children are detained. And if a youth is detained a second time, a fine between $300 to $500 should be imposed on the parents. The money generated by those fines should fund youth programming and preventive measures.</p><p>The teen "takeovers" or "trends" are not just a community program responsibility or a police responsibility. They are also a parental responsibility. The summer is about to begin. Let's be preemptive and not just reactive. Parents must step up. Property protection is definitely an issue, but the most important issue is our children's safety. That is our responsibility.</p><p>It's time for parents to step up or be held accountable.</p><p><i>Rev. Michael L. Pfleger</i>, <i>senior pastor, Faith Community of St. Sabina Church</i></p><h3>Weaponizing Loyola student’s murder to spread hate</h3><p>The tragic<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/27/sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-jose-medina" > murder</a> of Loyola University student Sheridan Gorman predictably has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" >weaponized by the far right</a> to attack all migrants to this country. Using this "logic," why don't the same people blame all white people for the crimes of Adolf Hitler?</p><p>Numerous studies from across the political spectrum, including the libertarian <a class="Link" href="https://www.cato.org/blog/immigrants-have-lower-lifetime-incarceration-rates-native-born-americans" target="_blank" >Cato Institute</a>, show that migrants are far less likely to commit crimes than people born in this country. This means nothing to the political vultures who promote hate against marginalized groups. Discrimination and more violence follow predictably in the wake of such campaigns.</p><p>For the record, many of the same people making political hay out of Gorman's murder found nothing illegal about the deaths caused by the 2020 storming of the U.S. Capitol and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol's murderous rampages. Oh, and many of their leaders, right on up to the White House, find no problem in palling around with Hitler-loving creeps like Nick Fuentes and David Duke.</p><p><i>Andy Thayer, Uptown</i> </p><h3>Paying for bad news</h3><p>As a loyal Sun-Times reader, I'm glad to pay a couple of bucks for the print edition. Also, I sometimes look forward to the more expensive Sunday edition because it usually includes a worthwhile supplement. But — and maybe you saw a "but" coming — last Sunday's supplement was too much to bear for a White Sox fan. The 2016 Cubs World Series victory was maybe the worst year for Sox fans, and don't forget, we recently had a year that set a record for most losses. So, thanks a lot for making us think about that terrible year once again and for charging an extra couple of bucks to do it.</p><p><i>Jim Bruton. Avondale</i></p><h3>Kennedy Space Center no more?</h3><p>Watch for the Trump Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida. You know it’s coming. </p><p><i>Alan Stoeck, Tinley Park</i></p><h3>Cheesy tidbit </h3><p>You wouldn’t know it from food writer Maggie Hennessy’s three <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/04/01/best-hamburgers-world-chicago-maggie-hennessy-burger-bible" >articles</a> in Wednesday’s Sun-Times, but it is possible to get a hamburger without cheese in Chicago. You just have to declare, in a firm voice, “No cheese.” And then repeat your statement.</p><p><i>Robert Cloud, Gold Coast</i><br></p>
author: Letters to the Editor

title: Illinois Accountability Commission requests testimony from Trump officials responsible for Midway Blitz
summary: <p>The Illinois Accountability Commission wants current and former officials responsible for Operation Midway Blitz to testify at two hearings as part of an ongoing probe of tactics used by federal agents.</p><p>The letters, sent Friday by the Commission’s Chair Judge Rubén Castillo, were to: Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff for policy; Tom Homan, White House “Border Czar;" Kristi Noem, former Secretary of Homeland Security; Gregory Bovino, former “Commander at Large” of Customs and Border Patrol and others, according to Gov. JB Pritzker's office. </p><p>“I established the Illinois Accountability Commission to preserve the truth and document how (President) Donald Trump and his accomplices violated the rights of Illinoisans and terrorized our communities during Operation Midway Blitz. These officials should answer directly to the people of Illinois for the chaos and violence they unleashed,” Pritzker said. “Regardless of whether these officials are still in their roles or not, the people of Illinois demand accountability from them all.”</p><p>Last October, Pritzker signed an executive order that established the commission to hold federal immigration agents accountable for their actions being in the Chicago area during Trump's administration's ongoing deportation campaign.</p><p>"The people of Illinois deserve to know how this operation was planned, authorized, and carried out — and to identify who was responsible for the decisions that led to its implementation in our state,” Castillo said. “The Commission’s work seeks to determine who authorized these actions, what safeguards were in place to protect Illinois residents, and what accountability mechanisms exist when federal operations harm communities.”<br></p>
author: Mohammad Samra

Seidel</a></h5><p><b>Fatal shooting</b>: It took hours for Loyola University Chicago students to get the first notification about the March 19 shooting death of Sheridan Gorman. The 18-year-old was with a group of friends taking pictures of the skyline at Tobey Prinz Beach Park when Jose Medina fatally shot her, officials said. Students say in the wake of the shooting, communication has been lacking.</p><p><b>Questions raised</b>: Many students are questioning why Loyola didn’t step up security or take other safety precautions as students grieved the loss of their classmate. Some students said they would like to see scaled-up campus police patrols at the beach where Gorman was killed and faster alerts when violent crimes happen near campus. The shooting has raised questions about Loyola's level of responsibility to protect its students.</p><p><b>Federal charges</b>: Chicago’s top federal prosecutor said he’s taking "no chances" that Medina will be released, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wirldo-l-p/" target="_blank" >filing an illegal gun possession charge for the 25-year-old</a> already charged with murdering Gorman. Medina, who immigrated from Venezuela, is now charged with possessing a gun while being unlawfully present in the U.S.</p><p><a class="Link" Illinois law and making arrests at Chicago-area courthouses, local officials alleged at a press conference Thursday. The Cook County Public Defender’s office said since late February, agents have been spotted entering the downtown Domestic Violence Courthouse or waiting directly outside. In at least two instances, someone was arrested. Agents had returned to the courthouse Thursday.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Gov. JB Pritzker signed a law in December banning federal agents from conducting civil immigration enforcement at state courthouses after the chief judge’s office barred civil arrests at county courthouses in October. Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle also signed an executive order prohibiting the feds from staging on county property as Chicago, Evanston and others did the same. The law doesn't carry criminal penalties; it requires a person, if detained, to file a civil lawsuit.</p><p><b>More on immigration</b>:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="line-height: inherit; margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px; margin-left: 24px; padding: 0px; list-style-type: disc;" id="rte-b7b5e382-2f61-11f1-bd48-95283f4c77e1"><li>Chicago police Supt. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wirldo-l-ti/" target="_blank" >Marshall High School boys basketball team’s state championship brings pride to West Side</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wirldo-l-td/" target="_blank" >Cindy Hernandez</a></h5><p>When the boys’ basketball team at John Marshall Metropolitan High School <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wirldo-l-th/" target="_blank" >took home the Class 1A state title</a> last month, it was bigger than just one school.</p><p>"This championship wasn’t just for us, it was for the West Side of Chicago," head coach Darrin Laye said Thursday, when the squad was honored with a celebration at the school.</p><p>Laye credited the victory, the school’s first basketball championship since 2008, to the players’ hard work and dedication. Marshall won the 3A title in 2008 and also captured state championships in 1958 and 1960.</p><p>"These kids deserve it," Laye said.</p><p>Students, faculty, parents and even alumni packed the auditorium of the East Garfield Park school, welcoming the team with applause and cheers.</p><p>"When that buzzer rang it was a great feeling," senior and team member Quinton Gibson said before the celebration. Gibson said his teammates kept each other motivated to continue to put in the work to succeed.</p><p>"We’re a family," Gibson said. "We all got each other. They’re like my brothers."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wirldo-l-tk/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Do you live near a vacant lot? title: Route 66-related news is music to my ears
summary: <p>Thanks to the Sun-Times for printing WBEZ's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/somer-van-benton" target="_blank" >Somer Van Benton</a>'s article on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/03/25/route-66-centennial-navy-pier-sign" >U.S. Route 66’s centennial celebration</a> and Navy Pier's new sign marking the legendary road's starting point<i> </i>connecting Chicago with Los Angeles.</p><p>While the article mentioned related historical tidbits only older readers are familiar with and Bobby Troup's famous song, it omitted mention of the song's most famous line, which is often cited as part of its title: "(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66." The song was covered by Chuck Berry and the Rolling Stones, but many of us older folks are familiar with Nat King Cole's original version that came out in 1946 — before the television age.</p><p>Last week's Route 66 celebration at Navy Pier brings back memories to us old-timers, who remember that song fondly. And what version of it is dearer to those who were around at the time than the Nat King Cole version? As many old-timers would say, "Back when music was music!"</p><p><i>Ted Z. Manuel, Hyde Park</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-980000" name="module-980000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Ivey needs Bible lessons </h3><p>Self-proclaimed Christian <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/03/30/league-source-says-bulls-working-exit-strategy-for-jaden-ivey" >Jaden Ivey</a> seems to have forgotten that all of us are God's children, and that regardless of whether a person is straight or gay or plays in the NBA, we are all equal in God's eyes.</p><p>Perhaps Mr. Ivey needs to spend some time contemplating <a class="Link" href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2022%3A39&version=NIV#:~:text=Matthew%2022:39%20NIV%20%2D%20And%20the%20second,like%20it:%20'Love%20your%20%2D%20Bible%20Gateway." target="_blank" >Matthew 22:39</a>, The Second Great Commandment of Jesus Christ: "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thy self," and <a class="Link" href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%207%3A3-4&version=NIV" target="_blank" >Matthew 7:3-4</a>, "Why do you look at the speck of sawdust in your neighbor's eye and pay no attention to the plank in your own eye?"</p><p><i>Chet Alexander, Alsip</i></p><h3>Ivey’s faith not problematic</h3><p>Joe Cowley's story about<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/03/31/jaden-ivey-fiasco-sheds-light-bulls-failing-front-office" > Jaden Ivey</a> disappointed me. A man's proclamation about Christ being in his life is not a red flag.</p><p><i>Michael Marsh, Chatham</i></p><h3>Inspired by ‘No Kings’ spirit </h3><p>On Saturday, my husband Tom and I joined our friends and neighbors in "Woke-Conda" — Wauconda — for the village's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/28/no-kings-rallies-kick-off-in-evanston-cicero-and-lincoln-square-as-hundreds-expected-to-protest-in-chicago" >“No Kings”</a> rally.</p><p>I couldn't help but think of my childhood in Rogers Park and the annual essay contest children entered titled "What Patriotism Means to Me." </p><p>At the rally, we met Beth, her best friend, her husband and their two fifth grade children who had signs that read "end war" and "I love democracy" and one that paraphrased Greta Thunberg: <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/policy/international/5342722-greta-thunberg-rips-trump-the-world-needs-a-lot-of-more-young-angry-women/" target="_blank" >“The world needs more angry women.” </a></p><p>It was uplifting to meet and witness civics lesson in action, as parents engaged with their children and instilled in them that democracy is for all Americans.</p><p>Beth's children chanted and cheered as motorists honked in support. They responded "we love you" to the few who disagreed. All good lessons.</p><p>My husband and I came home with a renewed sense of hope, knowing this family shared the real lesson of "What Patriotism Means to Me."</p><p><i>Eileen Gorrell Yacullo, retired Chicago Public Schools teacher, Wauconda</i></p><h3>Trump is a ‘mail’ man </h3><p>In response to Larry Craig, the gentleman from Wilmette who is against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/03/30/landlords-rental-inspections-trump-tsa-dhs-immigration-loyola-capitol-riots-mail-in-ballots" target="_blank" >mail-in voting</a>. I hope you are aware that the current president has <a class="Link" href="https://www.heraldmailmedia.com/story/opinion/columns/2026/03/29/trump-vote-by-mail-florida-election/89350654007/" target="_blank" >used mail-in voting</a> recently. So if he can, WE can.</p><p><i>Daniel Olsen, Naperville</i><br></p>

title: Some Loyola students call to improve off-campus safety and emergency alerts in wake of freshman’s murder
summary: <p>Like most Thursdays, Lilyana Halter was riding the Loyola University Chicago shuttle bus on March 19 when she got an email from the school that made her stomach drop.</p><p>Following an early-morning message from Loyola’s police force alerting students of a fatal shooting less than a mile from the Rogers Park campus, Loyola president Mark Reed informed students that an 18-year-old freshman, Sheridan Gorman, had been killed.</p><p>“Oh no,” Halter recalls thinking. “The homicide was one of us.”</p><p>That morning, students nudged each other in class, shocked, asking “Did you see the email?” Some professors began classes with tears in their eyes or a moment of silence honoring Gorman, students said.</p><p>“It’s so hard to explain the weird emotions I felt,” Halter said. She didn’t know Gorman personally, but she still felt a connection to her classmate. “She’s a Loyola Rambler.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" off-campus job in Rogers Park. It hasn’t felt safe. She’s noticed other students rethinking their decisions to walk around the neighborhood at night, too.</p><p>In campus-wide emails about the shooting, Loyola reminded students about its police patrols and mental health resources.</p><p>But Halter and other students question why Loyola didn’t step up security or take other safety precautions as students grieved the loss of their classmate. Some students said they would like to see beefed-up patrols at the beach where Gorman was killed and faster alerts when violent crimes happen near campus.</p><p>“Honestly, I just need to see something out of Loyola,” Halter said. “I can't have them just repeating the same things that we've always had, because it's not working.”</p><p>Gorman’s parents said they don’t fault Loyola for the shooting and said their daughter was happy and felt safe at school. Still, the shooting has raised fresh questions about the level of responsibility Loyola has to protect its students on and near campus. Its urban setting is one of Loyola’s biggest selling points, but it also means students, like other Chicago residents, aren’t insulated from crime.</p><p>A Loyola spokesperson didn’t respond to multiple requests to interview Reed or a list of questions about the school’s response to the shooting. But in a March 26 email obtained by the Sun-Times, Loyola officials told students: “Your safety and that of our entire community is always our top priority.”</p><h3>How students say Loyola could have done better in wake of Gorman’s death</h3><p>Gorman was with a group of friends taking pictures of the Chicago skyline at Tobey Prinz Beach Park when the shooting happened. Loyola’s private police force, Campus Safety, patrols the area surrounding campus, including the block on West Pratt Boulevard where Gorman was shot.</p><p>Gorman’s family has maintained Loyola is a safe place for students.</p><p>“We’ve also been asked whether students should feel safe there. The answer is yes,” Gorman’s parents said in a statement through their attorney, Thomas Tripodianos. “What happened to Sheridan was not a reflection of the Loyola community. was shot and killed.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Erin Hooley/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Still, current students say Loyola could inform students more quickly when violent crime happens and provide more information in follow-up communication.</p><p>In the case of Gorman’s killing, Loyola police sent a crime alert informing students and staff of the shooting at 4:41 a.m., more than three hours after the 1:30 a.m. shooting. Reed’s email identifying Gorman, sent at 9:10 that morning, told students there was “no ongoing threat to our campus community.” But no one was in police custody at the time, and some students worried that the suspect could still be armed near campus.</p><p>Some students, like junior Akanksha Bhanti, said students would have benefitted from getting the alert about Gorman’s shooting sooner.</p><p>“Who’s awake at 4:45 in the morning?” Bhanti said. “But it’s a very great chance that somebody’s awake at 1:30 or 2 in the morning, maybe walking around.”</p><p>Loyola officials announced a vigil in Gorman’s honor and reminded students of how to contact counselors through the school’s wellness center and campus ministry.</p><p>But several students wondered why classes weren’t canceled on the Rogers Park campus when the suspect was still at large — and wouldn’t be arrested for another three days.</p><p>“We all have class at 8 a.m. … That’s just hours later,” Bhanti said. “Nobody’s in custody, and you’re telling us that there’s no threat to the school.”</p><h3>Student concerns about violent crime near campus aren’t new</h3><p>Loyola and other urban colleges, including the University of Chicago, have long grappled with how to balance the safety of students while respecting the rights of residents who live in the surrounding neighborhood, especially when it comes to policing.</p><p>Loyola’s police force has jurisdiction over campus and roughly a half square mile of the surrounding neighborhood, including the beach where Gorman was shot and where students often spend time late at night.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-650000" name="html-embed-module-650000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/28340070"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/28340070/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>“It could have been any of us,” said sophomore Noah King, whose dorm is a seven-minute walk from the park.</p><p>Loyola’s communication about the shooting noted that it wasn’t on campus. But some students say that doesn’t absolve the school of its responsibility to protect students, especially if it’s within the limits of where campus police patrol.</p><p>“Obviously it’s not Loyola's fault that she got shot,” Bhanti said. “It kind of feels like Loyola is using the fact that it, geographically, wasn’t technically on campus to not have to do as much about it.”</p><p>Loyola deals with violent crime not infrequently. Rogers Park ranks in the middle among Chicago’s 77 community areas when it comes to the rate at which residents are shot or killed, according to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/crime/violence-tracker/" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by the Sun-Times</u></a>.</p><p>And this isn’t the first time a Loyola student has been shot and killed near campus. In 2014, a Loyola graduate student was the target of an attempted robbery on West Albion Avenue, steps from the Rogers Park campus. The student, Mutahir Rauf, didn’t believe the gun was real and tried to grab it, and the suspect fired, the Sun-Times reported at the time. Following that shooting, students expressed similar concerns about their safety.</p><p>“To know that someone was shot point blank so close to where I’m taking classes is not a very comfortable feeling,” Luigi Loizzo, then a Loyola junior, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2014/12/17/18579220/loyola-student-killed-in-robbery-was-bright-loyal-friends-say" target="_blank" ><u>told the Sun-Times at the time</u></a>.</p><p>In 2018, a student was brutally <a class="Link" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20180927165102/http://loyolaphoenix.com/2018/09/loyola-student-beaten-and-robbed-three-blocks-from-loyola-campus-cops-didnt-tell-students/" target="_blank" ><u>beaten and robbed blocks from the Rogers Park campus</u></a> and Loyola didn’t send an alert to students, according to reporting by the Loyola Phoenix, the school’s student newspaper.</p><p>In August and September that year, six violent crimes were reported near Loyola’s campuses <a class="Link" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20180927123819/http://loyolaphoenix.com/2018/09/campus-safety-hasnt-sent-a-crime-alert-this-semester-despite-violent-crime-near-campus/" target="_blank" ><u>without email alerts sent to students</u></a>, prompting the newspaper’s staff, which included this reporter at the time, to <a class="Link" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20180927121058/http://loyolaphoenix.com/2018/09/students-need-the-truth-campus-safety-must-notify-students-of-crimes-around-them/" target="_blank" ><u>pen an editorial</u></a> demanding the university alert students when violent crime happens on campus and where students are likely to be nearby.</p><p>Last October, three students reported being <a class="Link" href="https://loyolaphoenix.com/2023/10/three-students-robbed-at-gunpoint-outside-marquette-hall/" target="_blank" ><u>robbed at gunpoint</u></a> outside a Loyola residence hall. They told the Loyola Phoenix that the incident left them nervous to leave their dorms at night, even to go elsewhere on campus.</p><p>These kinds of incidents have prompted Loyola students to ask for faster and more reliable pickup times for the school’s free shared ride system, known as 8-RIDE, which some students have relied on more heavily since Gorman was killed, students say.</p><p>Loyola advises students to be patient and plan in advance when they need a ride, but students say the ride often takes more than 30 minutes to arrive and sometimes leaves them hanging after campus buildings close.</p><p>In 2018, following two fatal shootings police believed were carried out by the same man in Rogers Park, multiple students reported <a class="Link" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20181116155829/http://loyolaphoenix.com/2018/10/amid-safety-concerns-students-say-8-ride-vans-have-abandoned-them/" target="_blank" ><u>calling a ride that never showed</u></a>, the Loyola Phoenix reported.</p><p>Halter, who commutes to campus, said the 8-RIDE also has a limited pickup and dropoff zone. The shuttles don’t reach her home, for example, even though it’s in Rogers Park.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a title: Chicago's top cop stands by his officers interactions with ICE during Midway Blitz
summary: <p>Chicago police Supt. Larry Snelling is standing by his department’s actions during ramped-up immigration enforcement last year, telling residents his officers were “out there working to keep communities safe.”</p><p>Snelling joined the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability for a “special hearing” Thursday to discuss his department's interactions with federal immigration agents.</p><p>Dozens of people attended, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/08/residents-voice-frustrations-with-chicago-police-interactions-during-immigration-raids-who-protects-us" target="_blank" ><u>some accusing Chicago police of illegally coordinating with immigration agents</u></a> during President Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation campaign.</p><p>A similar meeting back in January also was packed, but this time around those attending heard responses from Snelling directly, leading to some tense moments in the crowd.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> "This is the response that I expected. … It’s easy to blame CPD when you’re looking for somebody to blame.”</p><p>The meeting ended to chants of “CPD, KKK, I-C-E, they’re all the same" as well as multiple people being escorted out of the building.</p><p>Though Snelling stood firmly by his department, he told commissioners if officers were found to be violating Chicago’s Welcoming City Ordinance they would be held accountable.</p><p>The commission voted Thursday to recommend the city’s Office of the Inspector General conduct an audit of possible violations. It’s common for Chicago police to work closely with federal agencies on criminal investigations.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9090e44/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcd%2F70%2F9263fe4e49cf926f091378e85005%2Fsnellingice-260403-34.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f5d42f2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcd%2F70%2F9263fe4e49cf926f091378e85005%2Fsnellingice-260403-34.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/42bfef9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcd%2F70%2F9263fe4e49cf926f091378e85005%2Fsnellingice-260403-34.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Public School security officials forcibly remove activists who disrupted a meeting of the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability on Thurdsay. This week, they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/02/chicago-ohare-ice-depaul-crime-oneill-burke-spit" >arrested a DePaul University student accused of spitting</a> on an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent at O’Hare airport, though the charges have been dropped.</p><p>But state and city law prohibit Chicago police from assisting with federal immigration enforcement. title: Venezuelan immigrant accused of killing Loyola freshman Sheridan Gorman now faces federal gun charge
summary: <p>Chicago’s top federal prosecutor said he’s taking “no chances”<b> </b>that Sheridan Gorman’s alleged killer will be released, filing an illegal gun possession charge<b> </b>Thursday<b> </b>against the Venezuelan immigrant already charged with the murder of the Loyola University Chicago freshman.</p><p>No federal court date has been scheduled for Jose Medina, 25,<b> </b>who was ordered detained Friday<b> </b>by a state court judge<b> </b>in connection with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/24/heres-what-to-know-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >Gorman’s slaying</a>. Medina’s attorney actually asked Cook County Circuit Court Judge D’Anthony Thedford<b> </b>to hold Medina in jail so he won’t be deported.</p><p>Now the feds have charged Medina with possessing<b> </b>a Smith & Wesson .40-caliber semiautomatic pistol while being unlawfully present in the United States, a charge carrying a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.</p><p>“Given the senseless, cold-blooded nature of the murder of a young student with a bright future ahead of her, the Chicago U.S. attorney’s office will take no chances that this illegal alien perpetrator will be released back into our community,” U.S. Attorney Andrew S. Boutros said in a statement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fe0000" complaint alleges Chicago police found the gun in a Sheridan Road residence that was searched after video captured “a male in black clothing, wearing a black mask, walking with a distinct limp and slow gait” entering shortly after the<b> </b>March 19 shooting.</p><p>Witnesses described the shooter similarly.</p><p>An ATF special agent at the Crime Gun Intelligence Center in Chicago wrote that the gun turned out to be a high-probability match for the one used in Gorman’s slaying.</p><p>The federal complaint lays out how Medina was born in Venezuela and has “no lawful status in the United States.”<b> </b>It says a Border Patrol agent “encountered”<b> </b>Medina<b> </b>in the El Paso border sector on May 9, 2023. Medina was allegedly unable to provide a valid U.S. address but said he planned to reside in New Rochelle, New York.</p><p>Medina was released on his own recognizance on May 24, 2023, and was scheduled to appear for a hearing before an immigration judge in New York on Oct. 13, 2023, according to the complaint.</p><p>However, it says there “is no indication of any record of any further immigration related proceedings or adjustments in status.”</p><p>Gorman’s killing reignited the national debate over immigration and even drew the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >attention of President Donald Trump</a>. Medina is accused of hiding at the end of a pier near Tobey Prinz Beach and shooting the 18-year-old Gorman<b> </b>in the back as she and her friends ran for cover.</p><p>Cook County Assistant Public Defender Julie Koehler has said that Medina <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/27/sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-jose-medina" target="_blank" >has a developmental disability</a> stemming from an earlier gunshot wound he suffered to his head during a robbery in Colombia. He can’t read or write, Koehler said.</p><p>Medina wound up in Chicago in 2023 after reaching the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas and being detained there, according to Koehler. Although he asked to be deported back to Colombia, officials in Texas purportedly bused him to Chicago.</p><p>With no family here, Medina stayed in a migrant shelter and contracted tuberculosis that went undiagnosed, his attorney said. title: Local officials warn of ICE arrests at domestic violence courthouse, decry feds violating state law
summary: <p>Federal immigration agents are violating Illinois law and making arrests at Chicago-area courthouses, several local officials alleged at a press conference Thursday.</p><p>The Cook County Public Defender’s office said since late February, federal immigration agents have been spotted entering the Domestic Violence Courthouse at 555 W. Harrison St., or waiting directly outside.</p><p>In at least two of those instances, someone was arrested, including that of a woman <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/groups/378158360786470/posts/1530031978932430/" target="_blank" ><u>followed out of the courthouse</u></a> and detained by federal agents March 10. The other occurred February 27, officials said. Still another person was detained on March 18 at a different location, the Maywood courthouse.</p><p>The press conference was held hours after federal agents returned to the courthouse with “the intent to take custody of a person who was scheduled to appear for a hearing today,” the Cook County Public Defender’s office said. Officials said they weren’t aware of any arrests being made Thursday, but noted they don’t always immediately know when someone is taken.</p><p></p><p>“Survivors should be able to walk into a courthouse without fear [that] doing the right thing will put a target on their backs,” State Rep. Graciela Guzmán <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/ICIRR/videos/1656661488801326" target="_blank" ><u>said at Thursday’s press conference</u></a>. “This is contempt for our laws, our courts and survivors.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fd0000" name="image-fd0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f02d21c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/43d4b8f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14c5806/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2Fe2%2F89870f11464797e4fab006a26450%2Ficepresser-260403-06.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Sen.
