title: Some airport bottlenecks ease as TSA says workers got their pay
summary: <p>After <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/airport-travel-delays-tsa-trump-a3452b3d6a212905fab23730bbe90138" target="_blank" >weeks of chaos in U.S. airports</a>, the Transportation Safety Administration said Monday that most of its officers received much of their backpay Monday for working during the shutdown.</p><p>Weary travelers hope the overdue paychecks will lead to the end of the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/airport-travel-delays-tsa-trump-a3452b3d6a212905fab23730bbe90138" target="_blank" >hours-long security lines</a> travelers experienced at several major U.S. airports in recent weeks.</p><p>Wait times at some TSA security bottlenecks, such as the airport checkpoints in Atlanta and Houston, already had improved significantly Monday morning.</p><p>But how long it will take for <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/shutdown-houston-airport-travel-impact-c46f4d6f49383bc9a457f3ebe001fbc1" target="_blank" >long security lines</a> to consistently return to normal — and how long federal immigration officers will maintain a visible presence in airport terminals — remains unknown as the busy spring break travel season continues.</p><p>“Working without pay forced more than 500 officers to leave TSA and thousands were forced to call out,” said Acting TSA Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/us-department-of-homeland-security" target="_blank" >DHS shutdown</a> resulted in not only <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/shutdown-houston-airport-travel-impact-c46f4d6f49383bc9a457f3ebe001fbc1" target="_blank" >travel delays</a> but also <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/airport-wait-times-shutdown-dhs-congress-tsa-391cbd731bed2e8433ab7f1a96ca9663" target="_blank" >warnings of airport closures</a> as TSA workers missing paychecks stopped going to work. Those workers were just recovering financially since last fall’s extended government shutdown.</p><p>Wait times still pushed beyond two hours at New York’s LaGuardia Airport Monday morning. Baltimore-Washington International Airport had minimal wait-times Monday morning, but continued to advise travelers to arrive three hours before their scheduled departure.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/donald-trump" target="_blank" >President Donald Trump</a> on Friday ordered the Department of Homeland Security <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/shutdown-tsa-executive-order-trump-c3c57b642efa1f29307e12e038c554d0" target="_blank" >to pay TSA officers immediately</a> to ease the lines plaguing airports. The move came after Trump rejected bipartisan congressional efforts to fund the TSA while negotiations continue with <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/congress-shutdown-johnson-thune-dhs-deal-unraveled-4ad4076c09705ca4bbebbdbcac7a0e75" target="_blank" >Democrats, who have refused</a> to approve more funding without restraints on Trump’s <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/immigration" target="_blank" >immigration enforcement and mass deportation operations</a>.</p><p>Democrats are demanding better identification for the officers, judicial warrants in some cases and for agents to refrain from conducting raids around schools, churches or other sensitive places. Republicans and the White House have been willing to negotiate on some points, but the sides have yet to reach a final agreement.</p><p>On Monday, there were few signs of progress on Capitol Hill, where the Senate held a short session without considering the House bill and resumed its two-week break. GOP Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota said afterward that Senate Republicans are talking with Democrats and also the House as they try to find a way to funding DHS.</p><p>TSA employees had gone without pay since DHS funding lapsed in February. The department’s shutdown reached 44 days on Sunday, eclipsing the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/government-shutdown-reopen-update-house-returns-5771f2befb15f4ab45e327369f2e98d9" target="_blank" >record 43-day shutdown</a> last fall that affected all of the federal government.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/us-department-of-homeland-security" target="_blank" >DHS shutdown</a> has resulted in not only <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/shutdown-houston-airport-travel-impact-c46f4d6f49383bc9a457f3ebe001fbc1" target="_blank" >travel delays</a> but also <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/airport-wait-times-shutdown-dhs-congress-tsa-391cbd731bed2e8433ab7f1a96ca9663" target="_blank" >warnings of airport closures</a> as TSA workers missing paychecks stopped going to work. Those workers had already endured the nation’s longest government shutdown last fall. Multiple airports experienced greater than 40% callout rates, and nearly 500 of the agency’s nearly 50,000 transportation security officers quit during the shutdown.</p><p>Trump <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/airport-screening-lines-ice-trump-shutdown-dhs-9c36ce9cc31647b59867fd2b62f9379d" target="_blank" >deployed Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents</a> to some airports a week ago to help with security as TSA callouts rose nationwide. How long they stay, White House border czar Tom Homan said, depends on how quickly TSA employees return to work. A TSA statement said the agency “has immediately begun the process of paying its workforce,” with paychecks arriving “as early as Monday.”</p><p>The overall absentee rate among TSA officers scheduled to work dipped slightly on Sunday, according to DHS. The highest were concentrated at major airports that have seen consistently elevated absences lately.</p><p>Those included BWI, both of Houston’s main airports; Louis Armstrong International Airport in New Orleans; Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport; and John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.</p>

title: There is no debate over the ongoing abuse of immigrants
summary: <p>Journalism is failing America.</p><p>At least mainstream media, newspapers and TV networks and such, the remnant still chugging away.</p><p>What's our job? To report the news, to convey what’s happening.</p><p>And what do we do? Describe fantasies, ghosts, processes that aren’t occurring.</p><p>Consider the recent murder of Loyola student Sheridan Gorman, out with a group of friends at a beach in Rogers Park when approached by a masked man, shot in the back and killed.</p><p>That was all too real.</p><p>But the moment the suspect was identified as a Venezuelan immigrant, the MAGA outrage machine started to whir. Led by President Donald Trump, who called him “an animal.” The murder was waved about as confirmation. Because one member of a minority group always represents everybody in that group. While white folks, naturally, are individuals, each unique in his or her own way, hardly responsible for their own actions, never mind stand-ins for anybody else.</p><p>And how did the media present this deceptive carnival? This acrobatic leap from one crime on the North Side of Chicago, one victim and one suspect, to the entire country and all immigrants everywhere?</p><p>A conversation. An argument. The Sun-Times called it “a national immigration debate.”</p><p>There is no conversation. No argument. Nobody is debating.</p><p>What is going on is dehumanization. The officially designated pariah group — nowadays, immigrants — is being stained with false rationales to justify their abuse: they are violent; they are diseased, they don't belong. If these rationals are contradictory — they are lazy and take all the good jobs — that doesn't matter. In the 1930s, the Jews were both dirty vermin crouched in the shadows and jewel-encrusted millionaires secretly running the world. Few Germans seemed bothered by the contradiction.</p><p>The nation is busily building ... let's call them “detention camps” ... for this despised group. Billions are being spent ramping up a paramilitary force to snatch people off the street. Don’t be fooled by the hesitation after Minneapolis. A temporary setback. The Democrats trying to get ICE under control is what the entire airport nightmare is about. Air travel in the United States is being throttled so we can deport more immigrants. A reminder that racism blows back on the racist. Trying to hurt others, they hurt themselves. Ask the Germans.</p><p>Why doesn't the media hit this point harder? Our error comes from a seventh grade civics class, how-a-bill-becomes-a-law mindset. It's our job to list the excuses given, noting, eventually, how inaccurate they are.</p><p>So we seek refuge recounting this Turning Point parody of debate. MAGA smugly states their premise: immigrants are violent murderers who add nothing to this country and must be forcibly expelled now. They grin condescendingly while some garble is offered in reply — in actuality, immigrants are 2 to 4 times more law-abiding, as a group, than native-born U.S. citizens. Then they twist that reply: “So now you're slandering American citizens...”</p><p>And away we go.</p><p>Words don't mean anything because they're not listening. They don’t care. As a Democrat, you’re nearly subhuman already. Maybe you’ll end up in those detention centers too. Gorman wasn’t a person, in their eyes, she’s a symbol, the latest in a list of sympathetic victims — always women — who can be performatively mourned while demanding faster deportations.</p><p>To argue is naive. It’s like the SAVE Act, the supposed election security bill. Talk all you like about the extreme rarity of voter fraud, they never reply, “Oh, right, point taken. Let’s address actual problems.” Because the bill isn’t designed to stop the fraud that isn’t there, it’s designed to constrain voting — not to help voting, but hurt it. The war against immigrants isn’t intended to stop crime; it’s intended to commit crime, against people whose lack of legal status makes them easy targets. Hurting them is called patriotism.</p><p>The ongoing horror is getting to seem so ... ordinary. Business as usual.</p><p>“Man is a creature that can get used to anything,” Dostoevsky writes in his semi-autobiographical novel, “The House of the Dead.” </p><p>That gets quoted often. Less noted is its context. The observation comes after a description of the low, stuffy room that was the narrator’s home for 10 years, sleeping on boards, amid “noise, uproar, laughter, swearing, the sound of chains, soot and fumes, shaven heads, branded faces, ragged clothes, all that is accursed and dishonored ... yes, man has great endurance.”</p><p>Is this endurance a good thing? Maybe Americans allow themselves to endure far too much. Yes, a third No Kings protest was held Saturday. Important? Sure. Maybe. Or maybe protest, like the media observing its rituals, is part of making something normal that should never be considered normal. This isn’t a debate. It’s madness. And we know where madness leads, or should.</p>

title: Small, independent landlords will need support if city mandates rental inspections
summary: <p>The city of Chicago’s move toward <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.councilmatic.org/legislation/o2025-0019991/" target="_blank" >mandatory pre-rental inspections</a> raises an obvious and unanswered question: Who will be expected to bear the cost?</p><p>If history is any guide, the answer will likely be small, independent landlords — the very people already navigating rising property taxes, insurance premiums, maintenance costs and increasingly complex regulatory burdens. This would be yet another in a long series of incremental pressures — the “thousand paper cuts”— that collectively make it harder to provide affordable housing at the neighborhood level.</p><p>At the <a class="Link" href="https://www.thecha.org/manage-properties-i-own/inspections" target="_blank" >Chicago Housing Authority</a>, inspections are funded by the agency itself. In those cases, the public entity requiring compliance also assumes the financial responsibility. Here, the city appears poised to mandate compliance while shifting the cost entirely onto property owners.</p><p>Let’s be candid: Policies like this don’t exist in a vacuum. When you increase the cost of operating small rental properties, those costs are inevitably passed along, whether through higher rents, reduced investment in maintenance or landlords exiting the market altogether. None of those outcomes benefits tenants or neighborhoods.</p><p>If the city insists on implementing a pre-rental inspection regime, it should at a minimum:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-cdf267a1-287b-11f1-8ac2-5bdd3a82ee6b" start="1"><li>Clearly disclose all associated costs and fees</li><li>Provide subsidies or waivers for small landlords</li><li>Ensure the program is about safety and habitability — not revenue generation.</li></ol><p>Absent those safeguards, this initiative could look less like sound housing policy and more like a thinly veiled revenue grab — one that risks doing more harm than good in the very communities it claims to protect.</p><p><i>Edward G. Irvin, landlord, Auburn Gresham</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-400000" name="module-400000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Pungent phrases</h3><p>Yeah, they said it.</p><p>"It’s hypocritical to say that these attacks harmed (Iranian) women and children when those women and children — the young girls that you reference — would live a life in a barbaric, unequal society behind a burqa, with no ability to make career choices" — <a class="Link" href="https://www.uscannenbergmedia.com/2026/03/09/international-womens-day-takes-on-new-significance-after-bombing-of-iranian-girls-school/" target="_blank" >Matt Schlapp</a>, chairman, American Conservative Union.</p><p>"I think it's worth to have a cost of, unfortunately, some gun deaths every single year so that we can have the Second Amendment to protect our other God-given rights." — <a class="Link" href="https://www.newsweek.com/charlie-kirk-says-gun-deaths-worth-it-2nd-amendment-1793113" target="_blank" >Charlie Kirk</a>.</p><p>"I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn't lose any voters, OK?" — <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2016/01/23/464129029/donald-trump-i-could-shoot-somebody-and-i-wouldnt-lose-any-voters" target="_blank" >Donald Trump</a>.</p><p>Remember President Richard Nixon’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/november-17/nixon-insists-that-he-is-not-a-crook" target="_blank" >“I’m not a crook”</a> quote? Such an innocent time.</p><p><i>Jim Newton, Itasca</i></p><h3>Privatize TSA tasks</h3><p>Amid all the teeth-gnashing, hand-wringing and political preening about Department of Homeland Security funding and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/travel/2026/03/24/what-we-know-and-dont-know-about-tsa-wait-times-at-ohare-and-midway-airports" >Transportation Security Administration</a> issues, one very important observation goes virtually without notice. The 20 U.S. airports that employ private security (e.g. <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/03/21/us/airports-without-tsa#:~:text=At%2020%20airports%20in%20the,uses%20contractors%20at%20the%20checkpoints." target="_blank" >San Francisco, Kansas City and Orlando</a>) have continued to function rather nicely during the partial government shutdown. Indeed, they were more effectively and efficiently run before the current TSA kerfuffle. That should come as no surprise, as private industry almost always outperforms the government.</p><p>If there is any good to come out of the current attention to airport security, the best thing would be to privatize that function.</p><p><i>William P. Gottschalk, Lake Forest</i></p><h3>No will to fix lapses</h3><p>Joe Biden may have let <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >Jose G. Medina</a>, Sheridan Gorman's alleged murderer, into the country, which was wrong. But what is currently being done to correct the problem? The Trump administration has had more than a year and millions of taxpayers' dollars to stop Medina and maybe could have.</p><p>Instead, there have been too many missteps along the way, and now Department of Homeland Security agents are in airports trying to learn Transportation Security Administration jobs. All of us want these criminals to be stopped, but is anything productive really being done?</p><p><i>Tom DeDore, Garfield Ridge</i></p><h3>Selective outrage</h3><p>President Donald Trump loves to throw shade at Democrats when people who shouldn't be in the country cause damage, like the undocumented migrant who allegedly gunned down Loyola University student<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" > Sheridan Gorman</a>.</p><p>But where is the outrage when someone pardoned by Trump causes great harm?</p><p>One example: Andrew Paul Johnson was convicted in August 2024 and sentenced to a year in prison for his role in the Jan. 6 “disturbance” at the U.S. Capitol. On Jan. 20, 2025, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/metro-state/2025/01/20/trumps-pardons-for-jan-6-riot-helps-more-than-50-defendants-from-illinois" >pardoned Johnson as well as everyone</a> else involved in that riot, no matter how violently they behaved.</p><p>On March 5, Johnson was convicted of two counts of child molestation, at least some of which occurred after he was released from prison, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/mar/05/capitol-rioter-life-sentence-molesting-children" target="_blank" >sentenced to life if prison</a>.</p><p>Does Trump feel any guilt or responsibility for the subsequent behavior of people he released back into society, or does his kind of outrage only apply to the other side?</p><p><i>Kevin Coughlin, Evanston</i></p><h3><b>Midterms will tell us a lot</b></h3><p>If there is voter's remorse for electing Donald Trump, we're not going to hear it from those voters. With all the political divisiveness in our country right now, who would admit to being on the losing end of his or her candidate selection?</p><p>We will find out in November's midterm elections.</p><p><i>John Petersen, Belmont Heights</i></p><h3>Limit mail-in ballot use </h3><p>Debating the constitutionality of accepting late <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/live/supreme-court-mail-in-ballots" target="_blank" >mail-in ballots</a> is a diversion from the real issue: whether mail-in voting should be accepted at all.</p><p>Why do we have polling places in the first place?</p><p>When people vote in person, we know who is voting and we know they are voting in secret, free from outside influences.</p><p>When people vote at home, we have no idea who is filling out the ballot or whether they were alone when they did.</p><p>Voting in person is a minimum safeguard for our elections. Mail-in voting may be allowed, perhaps only in the rarest of circumstances.</p><p><i>Larry Craig, Wilmette</i></p>

title: 2026 started as a renaissance year for composer Florence Price. Then came controversy
summary: <p>2026 looked to be a renaissance year for the composer <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/curious-city/2022/07/21/who-was-florence-price" target="_blank" >Florence Price,</a> a Black woman who made music in Chicago that is now being championed by the classical music world more than 70 years after her death.</p><p>Minnesota Opera premiered a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/classical/2026/02/05/florence-price-chicago-composer-minnesota-opera-arts-immigration-black-history-month" target="_blank" ><u>new work</u></a> in February about her life, and Cambridge University Press just released a scholarly companion to her music. Concerts featuring her compositions are scheduled everywhere from Baltimore to New York City this year.</p><p>But a New Year’s Concert in Vienna featuring her music — one of the most lauded events of the classical world in one of the genre’s most lauded venues, the Musikverein — has kicked up controversy for, arguably, not<i> </i>featuring her music at all.</p><div class="Enhancement" Illinois in 2009.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Special collections, University of Arkansas Library </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Her 1939 piece “Rainbow Waltz,” originally written for piano, was arranged for orchestra and conducted by Yannick Nézet-Séguin in the performance. But the piece that was played that day was so heavily stylized and reharmonized that online commentators erupted in criticism that has not <a class="Link" href="https://www.inquirer.com/arts/florence-price-yannick-nezet-seguin-philadelphia-orchestra-20260321.html" target="_blank" ><u>ebbed</u></a> in the months since <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/mar/19/vienna-philharmonic-re-orchestration-florence-price" target="_blank" ><u>the concert.</u></a></p><p>Scholar Alexandra Kori Hill, who<b> </b>co-edited the new <a class="Link" href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cambridge-companion-to-florence-b-price/3D58F23D2F563AD96D49382F9013627B" target="_blank" ><u>Cambridge companion</u></a> on Price’s music, describes “Rainbow Waltz” as rooted in 20th-century “Afro-American pastoralism.” That atmosphere, she says, is lost in the arrangement played in Vienna.</p><p>“In the classical tradition, there’s an expectation of performing the original of something, particularly with arrangements of music by a person whom we’re still starting to understand stylistically,” Hill said. “It becomes even more urgent when it is music by a person that comes from an underrepresented or systemically marginalized group of people.”</p><p>Price biographer Douglas Shadle says Price’s life was full of ambivalent victories. Her <a class="Link" href="https://cso.org/experience/article/8636/125-moments-072-prices-symphony-in-e-minor" target="_blank" ><u>1933 Chicago Symphony debut</u></a> is often hailed as a breakthrough for her and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/classical-music/2026/02/27/margaret-bonds-composer-gravestone-northwestern-university" target="_blank" ><u>Margaret Bonds</u></a>, another Black Chicago composer who soloed on the same program. Less mentioned is the overture by John Powell, an avowed white supremacist, which opened the program.</p><p>“It feels like a very Price situation,” Shadle said of the New Year’s episode. “The positive, again, has this strange counterweight to it.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" from her summer home outside Kankakee, Illinois in 2009.</p><p>Most of those rediscovered works were not registered with the United States Copyright Office prior to their discovery, meaning many — including “Rainbow Waltz" — are now public domain.</p><p>Price never heard her music performed abroad. She was planning a trip to Europe the year she died, in 1953. Posthumously, she became the first composer of color and, indeed, the first non-European composer ever featured in the Vienna Philharmonic’s New Year’s Concert, one of the biggest events in classical class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra, pictured here in January 2020, performs a traditional New Year’s concert at the golden hall of Vienna’s Musikverein, in Vienna, Austria, each year. The 2026 concert featured a controversial arrangement of Price’s music. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ronald Zak/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The concert reaches around 50 million viewers in more than 150 countries every year, via TV broadcasts, public radio and online streams.</p><p>This isn’t your average classical concert. Since the New Year’s Concert began in 1939 — as a Nazi-era fundraiser, as the Vienna Philharmonic has <a class="Link" href="https://www.wienerphilharmoniker.at/en/newyearsconcert/tradition-and-history" target="_blank" ><u>more openly acknowledged</u></a> in recent years — waltzes and other Viennese light music have been the evening fare. <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e7Yd-Jn1juc&list=RDe7Yd-Jn1juc&start_radio=1" target="_blank" ><u>“The Blue Danube,”</u></a> by “waltz king” Johann Strauss Jr. (1825–1899), is one such famous staple. So is the clapalong <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ztSI9DxsLyc&list=RDztSI9DxsLyc&start_radio=1" target="_blank" ><u>“Radetzky March”</u></a> by the composer’s father, Johann Strauss Sr. (1804–1849). Besides Price’s “Rainbow Waltz,” this year’s program featured works by exclusively Austrian composers, including both Strausses.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/rU5Id8LPDuQ?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Rainbow Waltz"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Both Price’s original and the Philharmonic’s version — by its favored arranger, Wolfgang Dörner — are in the same key: D-flat major, with a shared excursion to G-flat major. But as online commentators soon noted, what the Vienna Philharmonic performed was a world apart from Price’s “Rainbow Waltz."</p><p>Price’s version is introspective, with harmonic suspensions and bluesy modulations giving it a nostalgic twinge. By contrast, <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oz7hmV_boGU&list=RDOz7hmV_boGU&start_radio=1" target="_blank" ><u>Dörner’s arrangement</u></a> — the score to which the Vienna Philharmonic provided, upon request — turned the piece’s overall mood triumphant. He heavily stylized the main melody and reharmonized it so it resembled a textbook Viennese waltz. </p><p>The structure was different, too: An original introduction was added, as was a concluding coda that ratchets the key of the main melody up a half-step, to D major. (This is a popular trick in pop music, too: think of the middle of Whitney Houston’s <a class="Link" href="https://youtu.be/eH3giaIzONA?si=fWbRFuH-NG8L9uDw&t=210" target="_blank" ><u>“I Wanna Dance with Somebody.”</u></a>)</p><p>After hearing “Rainbow Waltz” on Austrian television<b>,</b> among those who joined <a class="Link" href="https://katherineneedlemanoboist.substack.com/p/a-musical-mystery" target="_blank" ><u>a chorus</u></a> <a class="Link" href="https://cooperm55.wixsite.com/jmc3/post/the-sincerest-form-of-insult" target="_blank" ><u>of prominent critical voices</u></a> was Johannes Glück, a Vienna-based musical theater composer and actor. At first, he didn’t know who Florence Price was. But when he sought out more information about “Rainbow Waltz” the following day, the music he found didn’t resemble what he’d heard.</p><p>“Whenever I have a feeling the work of a fellow composer is treated with disrespect, it makes me angry,” Glück said. “I feel this kind of solidarity.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Oz7hmV_boGU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Rainbow Waltz (Arr. for Orchestra by Wolfgang Dörner)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>In a video call from Vienna, Vienna Philharmonic chair and longtime violinist Daniel Froschauer, said he first learned about Price when Riccardo Muti and the CSO toured her Symphony No. 3 at the Musikverein in 2024.</p><p>He told WBEZ he was “surprised” by the backlash about the Dörner’s arrangement, particularly the accusation that it was meant to fool audiences. He claimed he specifically requested that Dörner “have in mind the sound of Johann Strauss Vater [Sr.] and the <i>ländler</i>” — another triple-time dance — “of Schubert.” From there, the piece was expanded so that it fit the conventional Viennese waltz formula: an introduction, a series of waltzes, then ending with an exuberant coda.</p><p>In other words, the discrepancy listeners noted was intentional.</p><p>“[‘Rainbow Waltz’] was written in 1939, and you will not get an exact sound of an 1800, 1900 waltz. But that's the setting of the New Year’s Concert,” Froschauer said. “The thought of having [Price] with us was more important than to say, ‘No, we can't use it, because there is no introduction.’”</p><p>This was not the first time Price’s music had been performed in Vienna. American bass-baritone Ryan Speedo Green included two of her songs on a 2015 recital at the Musikverein, the storied venue that also hosts the New Year’s Concert.</p><p>Mississippi-born, Chicago-educated conductor <a class="Link" href="https://www.williamgarfieldwalker.com/" target="_blank" ><u>William Garfield Walker</u></a> has also become an ambassador for Price’s music in Europe. His own <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t1OoLYJytc4" target="_blank" ><u>string orchestra arrangement</u></a> of her organ piece, “Adoration,” was live-streamed in 2020 as part of a G20 economic forum.</p><p>“After the first reading, the musicians fall in love with the music, and audiences have really enjoyed her works, as well,” said Walker, also a four-time award recipient from the Evanston-based Solti Foundation U.S.</p><p>But after the most widely viewed orchestral concert in the world put Price’s name — if not strictly her music — in front of countless audiences, some streams of Price recordings indeed went up, according to Walker, the conductor, and Michael Clark, a pianist who released a <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rU5Id8LPDuQ&list=RDrU5Id8LPDuQ&start_radio=1" target="_blank" ><u>studio recording</u></a> of “Rainbow Waltz” in 2024.</p><p>Through a representative, Nézet-Séguin declined an interview and follow-up questions. But in a written statement, the conductor touted his experience conducting Price’s music and said the arrangement intended to “introduce her music to a wider audience.”</p><p>“Different arrangements of her ‘Rainbow Waltz’ allow her music to reach different audiences and contexts: Wolfgang Dörner’s arrangement highlighted connections to the Viennese waltz tradition, and Valerie Coleman’s emphasizes an American sonority,” he wrote. “My hope is that these arrangements continue to promote the life and work of Price and bring her genius to audiences worldwide.”</p><p>Dörner also declined to comment for this story.</p><h3><b>Lessons learned? </b></h3><h3></h3><p>A musical “arrangement” can refer to vastly different treatments. Sometimes they match originals bar-to-bar. Other times, they are shuffled about, or extra stitching is added to piece them together.</p><p>And the same work can transform hugely in the hands of different arrangers. For example, Philadelphia audiences will hear another perspective on “Rainbow Waltz” in June, when Nézet-Séguin conducts a new arrangement of the work by award-winning composer and flutist <a class="Link" href="https://www.valeriecoleman.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Valerie Coleman</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-hangRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Rediscovered after her death, many of Florence Price’s works were not registered with the United States Copyright Office. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Special collections, University of Arkansas Library</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Price’s work was arranged in her own lifetime, too — but not always in ways she approved or appreciated. A <a class="Link" href="https://digitalcollections.uark.edu/digital/collection/p17212coll3/id/0/rec/50" target="_blank" ><u>partial, undated complaint letter</u></a> recovered from her summer home blasts a big-band arrangement that she felt wasn’t up to snuff.</p><p>“That really annoyed her,” said Samantha Ege, a scholar and pianist who co-edited the Cambridge companion with Hill. “We have her perspective on it, and we understand that this was something she encountered in her own time.”</p><p>Even the Strausses, whose music is at the heart of Vienna’s New Year’s Concert, may not be happy with how their music is being presented, were they alive today. Their descendant Eduard Strauss — who runs a <a class="Link" href="https://www.johann-strauss.at/en/" target="_blank" ><u>research institute</u></a> dedicated to his family’s music in Vienna — certainly isn’t. He says the New Year’s concert employs a far larger orchestra, and he objects to crowd-pleasing enhancements of some of his forebears’ music — like the bombastic percussion in the “Radetzky March.”</p><p>“I'm not invited, and I don't go there,” said Strauss of the New Year’s Concerts, which he says he hasn’t attended in decades. “I'm a purist. I want to have the music heard as it was composed.”</p><p>Froschauer, the Vienna Philharmonic chair, is conflicted over whether, in hindsight, the Philharmonic ought to have labeled Dörner’s creation as something other than an “arrangement.” </p><p>“Whatever we do seems to be at the center of attention. So, I'm just glad that Florence Price got to be the center of attention,” Froschauer said. “What I learned from this experience is to be, maybe, a little bit more careful.”</p><p>Today, Price has more advocates than ever. But as with any explosion of interest in a figure, Ege, the Price scholar and pianist, urges a deeper engagement from musicians and online commentators alike.</p><p>"I think that's how we ensure Price's legacy: by really spending time with her,” she says.<br></p>
author: Hannah Edgar | WBEZ

title: ‘No Kings’ rally draws thousands to Chicago’s Grant Park: ‘More and more people are horrified and activated’
summary: <p>For the third time in under a year, thousands of protesters across the Chicago area joined nationwide marches Saturday to make their voices heard regarding President Donald Trump and his policies.</p><p>An escalating conflict with Iran that has led to inflated gas prices and a lingering government shutdown that prompted Immigration and Customs Enforcement presence at various airports earlier this week are among the more recent developments drawing widespread criticism that brought protesters to the streets as part of the latest “No Kings” demonstrations. </p><p></p><p>The protest in Chicago’s Grant Park kicked off Saturday afternoon with a powerful rendition of “A Change Is Gonna Come,” and an original song called, “In This America,” by local artist Melody Angel.</p><div " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fbb5cf2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5177x2905+0+274/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2Fd0%2F5ebd4df849afbe1a73ff37dc202a%2Fnokings-260329-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/909411e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5177x2905+0+274/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2Fd0%2F5ebd4df849afbe1a73ff37dc202a%2Fnokings-260329-09.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fbb5cf2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5177x2905+0+274/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2Fd0%2F5ebd4df849afbe1a73ff37dc202a%2Fnokings-260329-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Thousands march through the Loop Saturday as part of the “No Kings” nationwide protest movement against the Trump administration.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She wrote the song in memory of Trayvon Martin, whose killing in 2012 galvanized the Black Lives Matter movement. She now dedicates the song to her niece and nephew.</p><p></p><p>"This is not the world I want for them, and I will change it," Angel said from the stage.</p><p></p><p>By 1:30 p.m., thousands gathered at Butler Field in Grant Park. Attendees held “Abolish Ice” and “No Kings Since 1776” signs as songs like “Fight the Power” and “I Will Survive” blared through the speakers. By 3 p.m., the crowd marched through the Loop holding large signs including, “ICE OUT,” before ending peacefully without any major incidents at 4:30 p.m.</p><p></p><p>The rally is part of a nationwide movement, dubbed “<a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/no-kings-protests-minnesota-trump-springsteen-2fab6b3a64e5275bcf111e8dd6d2e075" target="_blank" ><u>No Kings</u></a>,” to protest the Trump administration’s policies including mass deportations, the rollback of transgender rights and the war in Iran. The first No Kings protests, which took place last June, were planned to counter a military parade in Washington to mark the Army’s 250th anniversary and Trump’s 79th birthday.</p><p></p><p>The Loop rally was organized by the Hands Off Chicago Coalition, which includes Chicago Federation of Labor, Equality Illinois, Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, Indivisible Chicago Alliance and more, as well as the ACLU of Illinois. Volunteers said a crowd of 250,000 to 300,000 was expected, though the crowd appeared smaller than the one from last fall. </p><p></p><p>In October, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/live/2025/10/17/no-kings-protests-chicago-suburbs-trump" target="_blank" ><u>tens of thousands of people attended similar protests</u></a> across the Chicago region. Republicans had described protests as the “Hate America Rally.”</p><p></p><p>Reflecting on the progression of the “No Kings” protests over the last year, Laura Tanner, of Indivisible Chicago, said the resistance movement keeps growing.</p><p></p><p>“More and more people are horrified and activated, and just want to be a part of these mass demonstrations,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" nationwide protest movement against the Trump administration.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson, who took the stage in Grant Park briefly, called for an end to the endless “assault” on immigrants and working people. He also announced a forthcoming day of action on May 1 to pressure the “ultra-rich” to “pay their fair share in taxes.”</p><p></p><p>“Look around,” he said. “Our movement is bigger. Our resolve is stronger. And we’re sending a message: No kings in America.”</p><p></p><p>Natanael Hosen, of South Barrington, came to the United States from Argentina when he was 19 and “accomplished the American Dream.”</p><p></p><p>Hosen, 37, started his company and is raising five children, but he and his family have faced threats of deportation since the beginning of Trump’s immigration enforcement operations.</p><p></p><p>“I feel like I’m doing something wrong just by existing,” Hosen said. “I can’t go to airports. I can’t travel.”</p><p></p><p>Hosen, who feels “at risk” for the first time in his 18 years in the United States, said it was the bombing of Iran that was the “tipping point” for him to attend a rally.</p><p></p><p>“I have friends in the other countries, and they’re laughing at us,” Hosen said. “We just take whatever they give us, and this at some point has got to stop.”</p><p></p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>By 1:30 p.m. Saturday, thousands of people began gathering in Grant Park in Chicago to kick off the “No Kings” rally and march.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Linda Tucker, 70, of Kenwood, said she showed up to voice many grievances, including that a disproportionate number of <a class="Link" href="https://iwpr.org/iwpr-new-report-black-women-disproportionately-sidelined-in-year-one-of-trumps-second-term/" target="_blank" ><u>Black women were pushed out of the workforce</u></a> since Trump started his second term.</p><p></p><p>She said she was discouraged by the makeup of the crowd.</p><p></p><p>“There are so many people of my generation here and not enough young people,” she said. “My generation experienced assassinations, the Vietnam War, [Richard] Nixon and [Ronald] Reagan, and we know how hard it was to get what we had. There is no reason to take it for granted.”</p><p></p><p>Across the Chicago area Saturday, many participants took their children to the rallies, pointing to the importance of teaching them to speak out. Although many expressed frustration with Trump, some said they took comfort in the solidarity surrounding them.</p><p></p><p>Organizers said more than 3,100 events — 500 more than in October — were registered, in all 50 states, with protests also taking place in Europe, the AP reported. The Grant Park protest was expected to be the biggest in Chicago, but smaller ones took place in Lincoln Square and Irving Park. Outside of the city, other rallies took place in Cicero, Oak Park and Highland Park.</p><p></p><h3><b>‘We’ve been here before’</b></h3><p></p><p>As Joanne Bertalan sat in her wheelchair during Evanston’s “No Kings” rally Saturday morning, she thought back to the civil rights protests she attended as a college student at Bradley University in 1964.</p><p></p><p>“We’ve been here before,” said Bertalan, 77. “These people have all lived through a lot of stuff and wars. title: SAVE Act looks like racist laws of the past
summary: <p>When Kansas implemented its version of the Trump administration’s looming <a class="Link" href="https://campaignlegal.org/document/fact-sheet-save-act-threatens-all-voters" target="_blank" >voter-suppression law</a>, it denied at least <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/24/us/politics/proof-of-citizenship-voter-registration-kansas.html?unlocked_article_code=1.WFA.M6Rq.JGLPfJQF4PSr&smid=url-share" target="_blank" >31,000 eligible citizens</a> of their constitutional right to vote.</p><p>On the national level, it could block <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/new-save-act-bills-would-still-block-millions-americans-voting" target="_blank" >tens of millions</a> of Americans from casting a ballot.</p><p>That is, of course, exactly what the so-called Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, or SAVE Act<i>, </i>is intended to do.</p><p>Donald Trump himself is on record admitting his belief that allowing all eligible citizens to vote would <a class="Link" href="https://wapo.st/4rYIqMT" target="_blank" >hurt his party’s chances</a> of winning elections. Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DV84MHDFMuL/" target="_blank" >posted polling data </a>showing that his party is expected to lose control of the Senate this year and claimed the voter suppression bill could “turn this around.” </p><p>The president told his political allies earlier this month that his voter-suppression bill would <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/house/5776058-trump-republicans-save-america-act-midterms/#:~:text=Trump%20tells%20Republicans%20the%20SAVE,create%20new%20barriers%20to%20voting." target="_blank" >“guarantee” their success</a> not only in this year’s midterm elections but “every election for a long time.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c70000" name="module-c70000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>In fact, he is so desperate to keep American citizens from voting that he <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/03/23/homeland-security-tsa-shutdown-trump-airports/89285094007/" target="_blank" >blew up a deal</a> to end chaos at the nation’s airports, holding Transportation Security Administration funding hostage unless the voter suppression bill is passed.</p><h3>Millions would be sidelined</h3><p>The bill that passed the House last month and is currently before the Senate would prevent <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/anti-voter-save-act-must-be-stopped" target="_blank" >more eligible citizens from registering to vote</a> than any piece of legislation in American history and is more restrictive than the current law in any state except Ohio. Far from a simple “voter ID” bill, it would require specific proof of citizenship to register to vote. </p><p>For most Americans, that means either a U.S. passport or a certified birth certificate along with a government-issued photo ID. But more than 21 million Americans don’t have ready access to those documents, and about half of Americans don’t have a passport at all. Not all birth certificates<a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/1383/text#H704CC9D148E248EBB87A96421701221B" target="_blank" > meet the requirements</a> — about 69 million women and 4 million men do not have a birth certificate that matches their current legal name.</p><p>Already registered to vote and think the voter suppression law won’t apply to you? You could be in for a nasty surprise. The bill requires voter roll purges<i> every 30 days</i>, eliminating the 90-day protection from being mistakenly thrown off the rolls right before Election Day. Voters might not realize they’ve been purged until they show up at their polling place — and most of us will have to show up at a polling place. Even though eight states and the District of Columbia conduct <a class="Link" href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/report/mail-voting-is-safe-secure/" target="_blank" >safe and secure</a> elections entirely by mail, the bill prohibits universal <a class="Link" href="https://wapo.st/4rXx1gl" target="_blank" >mail voting</a>.</p><p>Anti-democracy activists have been invoking the <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/topics/voting-elections/vote-suppression/myth-voter-fraud" target="_blank" >myth of voter fraud</a> to justify voter suppression for <a class="Link" href="https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2019/01/the-200-year-history-of-using-voter-fraud-fears-to-block-access-to-the-ballot/" target="_blank" >nearly two centuries</a>, but have never been able to back up their claims with evidence. In 1883, Chicago party officials <a class="Link" href="https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2019/01/the-200-year-history-of-using-voter-fraud-fears-to-block-access-to-the-ballot/" target="_blank" >hired investigators</a> to monitor polling locations and offered a $300 reward to anyone who helped “in the apprehension and conviction of anyone who voted illegally.” No one was convicted.</p><p>An official who testified in defending the Kansas law admitted that over a span of 18 years, only 13 non-citizens had ended up on the voter rolls in Sedgwick County, none of which could be shown to be intentional rather than administrative errors. Only five noncitizens actually cast a ballot.</p><p>The secretary of state who unsuccessfully defended the Kansas voter suppression law, Kris Kobach, also <a class="Link" href="https://www.usnews.com/news/national-news/articles/2018-01-10/trump-commision-on-election-integrity-found-no-evidence-of-voter-fraud" target="_blank" >failed to unearth evidence of voter fraud</a> as vice-chair of the “Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity” established in 2017 to appease Trump’s embarrassment over losing the popular vote.</p><p>False claims of fraud were integral to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-J6-REPORT/html-submitted/ch3.html" target="_blank" >fake elector plot</a> that culminated in the Jan. 6 insurrection, but none of the <a class="Link" href="https://electioncases.osu.edu/case-tracker/?sortby=filing_date_desc&keywords=&status=all&state=all&topic=25" target="_blank" >more than 60 lawsuits</a> challenging the results of the election produced <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/3559758-conservative-group-finds-absolutely-no-evidence-of-widespread-fraud-in-2020-election/" target="_blank" >any credible evidence of fraud</a>, much less non-citizen voting.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2024/10/12/nx-s1-5147789/voting-election-2024-noncitizen-fact-check-trump" target="_blank" >rhetoric</a> that the Trump administration and its allies are using to promote the specter of noncitizen voting echoes the white nationalist <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-is-great-replacement-theory-and-how-does-it-fuel-racist-violence" target="_blank" >“Great Replacement</a>” conspiracy theory of a plot to diminish the influence of white people. </p><p>In 2024, then-Washington Post columnist Philip Bump called the voter suppression scheme the <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2024/07/09/save-act-republican-voting-immigration/" target="_blank" >Great Replacement theory in legislation form</a>. The legislation itself, which imposes <a class="Link" href="https://racism.org/articles/citizenship-rights/voting-rights/12869-the-save-america-act" target="_blank" >onerous financial burdens</a> on voters, is nothing short of a resurrection of the poll taxes of the Jim Crow era. And just like the racist Plessy v. Ferguson decision that gave rise to that dark period, the SAVE America Act belongs on the scrap heap of history.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a80000" name="module-a80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

title: How we photographed ICE agents working at O'Hare Airport
summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/anthony-vazquez" target="_blank" >Anthony Vazquez</a>. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/avazquezphoto?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet&igsh=ZDNlZDc0MzIxNw==" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>This image captures the recent usage of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in the role of TSA officers. Seeing ICE and TSA personnel side-by-side is a visual representation of how the transition has taken effect. Many lawmakers have pushed back on the use of ICE agents in airports — as have travelers — due to the agency's history of racial profiling and the wrongful detention of U.S. citizens. For many, their presence represents a move toward more aggressive policing in public spaces, turning a routine travel gate into a source of fear and anxiety.</p><h3><b>How did you get the photo?</b></h3><p>This photograph was captured during a trip to O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, following news reports of ICE agents being deployed to airports due to TSA shortages. Initially, the deployment to O'Hare was unconfirmed, leading to a "goose chase" between different terminals to verify the reports. The situation changed as ICE officers made their presence more visible. Their masks potentially contributed to their reduced concealment, making documentation easier. This particular image was obtained at a Terminal 1 exit where the agents were openly present, standing guard alongside TSA workers.</p><h3>Technical details:</h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" title: Inspired by Artemis II? Adler Planetarium can give you the moon
summary: <p>In 1969, humanity achieved one of its greatest milestones when astronauts first set foot on the moon. More than half a century later, we’re <a class="Link" href="https://www.floridatoday.com/story/tech/science/space/2026/03/24/artemis-ii-moon-mission-targets-april-1-launch-nasa-working-no-issues-kennedy-space-center/89298116007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=true&gca-epti=z113734p001350c001350v113734d--37--b--37--&gca-ft=63&gca-ds=sophi" target="_blank" >preparing to return</a>.</p><p>NASA’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/4/3/23668863/nasa-names-astronauts-to-next-moon-mission-first-crew-under-artemis" >Artemis</a> program, which followed the successful uncrewed Artemis I mission in 2022, is advancing towards Artemis II, the first crewed deep space lunar flyby of this new era. Soon, astronauts will once again travel beyond Earth’s orbit and around the moon.</p><p>This is an extraordinary moment in space exploration. But it is also a reminder of something deeply human: our enduring fascination with the moon and our desire to understand our place in the universe.</p><p>More than 50 years after Apollo, there is still much left to uncover. Humans returning to the moon is not about nostalgia. It is about discovery. It is about science. Studying the moon can help us better understand Earth, the solar system and what it will take for humans to venture further into space.</p><p>Chicago has a special role to play in this moment.</p><p>Space missions may launch far from Chicago, but the sense of discovery they inspire belongs to all of us. Institutions like the <a class="Link" href="https://www.adlerplanetarium.org/" target="_blank" >Adler Planetarium</a>, the oldest planetarium in the western hemisphere, connect the public to that story, translating complex space science into experiences that spark curiosity and understanding.</p><p>At a time when science is often misunderstood or dismissed, places like the Adler help people understand how scientific discovery works. Visitors can look through telescopes, experience immersive dome shows and meet the astronomers and educators working to interpret new discoveries about our cosmic neighborhood. When guests ask questions about Artemis or about what comes next in space exploration, they can hear directly from experts who study the universe every day.</p><p>That connection matters.</p><p>Space has a unique ability to inspire curiosity across generations. When a child asks why the Moon changes from night to night, or when a family gathers around a telescope to observe the sky together, they are participating in the same sense of discovery and connection that has driven human exploration since millennia.</p><p>As Artemis prepares to carry humanity back to the Moon, Chicagoans have an opportunity to reconnect with that exploration — and a front-row seat to the discoveries ahead.</p><p><i>Elizabeth C. Babcock, president and CEO, Adler Planetarium</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2a0000" name="module-2a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Pass on gas </h3><p>Should we allow ourselves to be led around by the nose by daily reports of the ups and downs of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/03/04/chicagoans-uneasy-gas-prices-iran-war-straight-hormuz-supply-chain-disruptions" >prices at the pump</a>, as though that is the one best gauge for the success or failure of the party in power?</p><p>What a trap — prices are up so we can gloat that a man most of us detest and the party that has elevated this monster for its own gain are failing in their promise to lower the cost of living. What happens when the price goes down? You want to laud Republicans then?</p><p>What hypocrisy for progressives (as I count myself) to shout ourselves hoarse about the real dangers of our warming planet, then complain about gasoline costing $4, or $5, or even $6 a gallon. To achieve the pressing goal of weaning ourselves from fossil fuels, gas should be $20 a gallon! Don't scoff at this.</p><p>The Republicans and their monster salesman have removed our great nation from the international climate agreement, rolled back federal initiatives to phase out coal and accepted hundreds of millions of dollars in bribes from oil producers to put their extraction back on the fast track while tearing down popular programs to promote renewable energy.</p><p>The sooner we, as citizens of a powerful and influential nation, join much of the rest of the world in grasping control of fossil fuel use, the better off the whole world will be.</p><p>If oil and natural gas were taxed to increase their price, intelligent Americans would drive less, stop sitting in idling cars, learn to use public transportation (which would then become better), use less heating and air conditioning and use fewer disposable goods.</p><p>If we put one-tenth of our military budget into achieving the goal of drawing down fossil fuel use, the future would look brighter for our children.</p><p>It starts in our everyday life, and that includes the gas pump. Don't get suckered into the short-sighted narrative of gas prices.</p><p><i>Kenneth Stein, Lombard</i></p><h3>Loyalty replaces thought</h3><p>George Orwell’s deepest warning in "1984" was not simply that those in power lie. Governments have always lied. His more unsettling point was that power can train people to accept each new lie as truth, even when it contradicts the lie that came before it. The goal is not merely deception. It is submission.</p><p>That is what made Ingsoc, the book's antagonists, so disturbing. The party did not just demand obedience in action — it demanded obedience of mind. It wanted people to accept each new version of events without insisting on consistency, memory or proof. The point was not honest persuasion. The point was to sever loyalty to reality and attach it instead to authority.</p><p>That part of Orwell’s vision feels painfully current. We live in a moment when many people no longer seem troubled by contradiction. An explanation is offered for some act of power, and days later the explanation changes. Yet those most committed absorb the new line and move on as if nothing happened.</p><p>This is not ordinary persuasion. It is the replacement of judgment by allegiance. What matters is not whether the explanation is true, but whether it came from the approved authority. That is why exposing a lie has become so difficult. When belief is rooted not in evidence but in devotion, facts lose much of their force. It was never accepted because it was proven — it was accepted because it came from the right source and served the right side.</p><p>I say that without innocence. I have seen good in political traditions that later disappointed me. The temptation to surrender judgment exists across political life. Belonging becomes dangerous when it asks us to stop thinking. That is why the problem is moral before it is partisan.</p><p>The real danger is not simply that falsehood spreads, but the habit of resisting falsehood disappears. Once people stop demanding consistency, proof and seriousness from those who seek power, they begin helping power erase reality itself.</p><p><i>Jodi Alain Weinstein, Naperville</i> </p><h3>Baffled by city’s hotel tax hike</h3><p>Am I the only Chicagoan confused after reading reporter Fran Spielman's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/18/hotel-tax-increase-tourism-improvement-district-choose-chicago" target="_blank" >story</a> last week headlined "To pay for tourism boost, Chicago ramps up hotel tax, making it nation's highest"?</p><p>The city of Chicago, prompted by the marketing group Choose Chicago, seeks to increase tourism by raising the city’s hotel tax to 19% — the highest in the nation. Simple logic and basic arithmetic together confirm that raising prices, and reducing any competitive advantages, reduces sales or tourist attraction to Chicago hotel rooms in 14 wards. This does not make sense.</p><p>Do they seek to make Chicago "the first city," rather than "the second city" in the wrong direction?</p><p>Last year, Choose Chicago adopted a new marketing slogan, "Never Done. Never Outdone." They unknowingly evoked arch-rival New York City, "the city that never sleeps."</p><p>I am confused. Can anyone help me?</p><p><i>Harvey J. Graff, Lincoln Park</i></p><h3>Mayor was right to veto wage hike freeze </h3><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson did the right thing by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/25/brandon-johnson-veto-freeze-subminimum-wage-phase-out-tipped-workers-restaurants" >vetoing the bill</a> that would freeze the minimum wage for tipped workers. Everyone knows tipping is customary, but it’s certainly not mandatory. A tip, whether it materializes or not, and its size, are completely at the whim of customers. Workers' livelihoods shouldn't be contingent on the whim of customers. And restaurateurs must figure out a way not to run their businesses on the backs of their hardest-working employees.</p><p><i>Joanne G. Murphy, West Ridge</i> </p><h3>Basking in strangers’ warmth while dining alone </h3><p>Just recently, a long-time friend and I made plans to meet at a restaurant for lunch. Unfortunately, my friend never showed up. She was OK and just needed to reschedule.</p><p>Early bird that I am, I had waited for some time for my friend in a comfortable enclosed area where diners entered and exited at a steady pace. It was the perfect place for observing people of all ages and backgrounds.</p><p>Three uniformed police officers were just leaving after enjoying their tasty breakfast. They held the door for four older adults, who all patted the officers on their forearms and told them, "God keep you safe" and "thank you for your service." The officers told the seniors that they truly appreciate their prayers and thoughts.</p><p>Eating alone, I witnessed many more acts of kindness, from a waiter carefully wiping up a rambunctious child's spill to a young woman helping her grandmother butter her toast. I heard the phrases, "Thank you," "God bless you," "have a wonderful day," "let's keep in touch," "so wonderful to see you" and "let's do this again sometime."</p><p>Did I feel left out? Not a bit, because I knew my friend and I would meet another day. Americans spend quite a bit of money at restaurants and maybe we sometimes regret that. But I dare say it is worth it, especially if we go back home satisfied, both physically and spiritually.</p><p><i>Kathleen Melia, Niles</i></p><h3>Unfortunate word choice</h3><p>I feel that it was extremely irresponsible journalism for the Sun-Times to echo the Donald Trump/Republican racist and jingoistic verbiage as it did with Monday’s large print screaming headline, "Venezuelan Migrant Charged With Murder Of Loyola Student." Neither the nationality, ethnicity or immigration status of the man who allgedly perpetrated this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" >horrible murder</a> is of any relevance, except to those for whom these categories determine the significance of events long before they occur. </p><p>In short, any crazed person might have done this, and deep down, most of us adults know this. Those at the Sun-Times taxed with creating the headlines, and even more so, those higher up in the newsroom who do the editing and revising, should take a long look at themselves in the mirror.</p><p><i>Steve Livingston, North Park</i></p><h3>Anti-immigrant rhetoric harmful and divisive </h3><h3></h3><p>Any time anyone in Chicago picks up and fires a gun at another person, it is a tragedy. As we mourn the death of Sheridan Gorman and try to make sense of a seemingly senseless act of violence, MAGA politicians from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" >Donald Trump</a> to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" >Darren Bailey</a> to 45th Ward <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DWR7pCAjX7d/?igsh=bzY5eXJleHRxdGFo" target="_blank" >Ald. Jim Gardiner</a> are politicizing her death to score points against their rivals and demonize immigrants. It’s the same tune they’ve sung for years: stoke fear against the most powerless groups to keep us divided and distracted. Shame on these men, and my condolences to the Gorman family, who must now grieve privately while politicians turn their sadness into a public spectacle.</p><p><i>S. Gronkiewicz-Doran, Jefferson Park</i></p><h3>Paydays for ICE — not TSA </h3><p>I fail to comprehend why U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel receive <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/why-do-ice-agents-get-paid-during-the-partial-government-shutdown-but-not-tsa" target="_blank" >government compensation</a> while Transportation Security Administration employees do not during the partial government shutdown.</p><p><i>Diane Blaszczyk, Norwood Park</i></p><h3>Expensing Trump’s trips </h3><p>Prior to the last election, Donald Trump wanted very much to get into the White House. Now that he is the president, instead of staying in the White House, he makes <a class="Link" href="https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/news/2025/05/03/trump-100-days-news-president-mar-a-lago-palm-beach-florida/83404838007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=false&gca-epti=z110301p000450c000450e007150v110301&gca-ft=35&gca-ds=sophi" target="_blank" >numerous trips</a> to Mar-a-Lago at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/mar/09/trump-golf-trips" target="_blank" >nation’s expense</a>. It's not only the cost of the flight but also the cost for the <a class="Link" href="https://gisme.georgetown.edu/publications/secret-service-costs-for-presidential-travel-continue-to-mount/" target="_blank" >Secret Service</a>, his entourage and other officials. Considering the nation's financial status, Trump should be made to reimburse the Treasury Department for these expenses. America cannot afford this extravagance.</p><p><i>Larry E. Nazimek, Logan Square</i></p><h3>Robotic moves </h3><p>The delivery robots that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/25/delivery-robot-smashes-into-old-town-bus-shelter-in-second-crash-of-the-week" >shattered the glass</a> at CTA bus shelters have been the object of misplaced derision. They deserve our praise for locating the most pristine, graffiti-free pane of glass in all of Chicago's CTA bus shelters. Perhaps a historical marker in their honor?</p><p><i>Judy Humphrys, Roscoe Village </i></p>

title: Macquline King, CPS grad and principal who led through mass school closures, rises to CEO
summary: <p>Macquline King was a young principal working hard at a small South Side elementary when she got word that her school was slated to close.</p><p>Teacher Claire Brandon remembers watching King fight to keep Dumas Technology Academy open “to the bitter end” alongside parents and staff.</p><p>“It was a hurtful time,” she says, remembering the many protests and hearings where King and parents begged school district officials for a reprieve, to no avail.</p><p>Not long after she hugged the students at Dumas goodbye, King was thrust into another tense situation. She became principal of Courtenay Language Arts Center on the North Side, which was designated to take in children grieving their own closed school.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div White/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>King says it was “horrible” watching one community lose its school and then difficult to bring together two schools that had different needs and demographics. At Courtenay, she says, she “began to really understand how policy played a large role in what happened in the day-to-day activities at a school.”</p><p>Those experiences propelled her to seek out a broader leadership position. It's also why some see her as uniquely qualified to lead the district as it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/09/25/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-restarts-decrease-migrant-students-latino-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>grapples with a big drop in enrollment</u></a> and current and future budget deficits.</p><p>She says the experiences taught her the importance of listening and not trying to tackle problems alone.</p><p>“I really believe in shared leadership,” she says. “Chicago is so big and it's so diverse, and so going around having round tables, having learning sessions, that's really important to me. Because I can't bring all of the families and the students into the building, but I can go out into the community to elevate their voices.”</p><p>The Chicago Teachers Union Vice President Jackson Potter says students need King to “meet the moment.” And he agrees she can’t do that solo.</p><p>“It will require her to lead a team in partnership with the mayor, board members, and educators who have been pushing to reconstruct and transform the district,” Potter said in a statement.</p><h3><b>King built leadership skills as Chicago principal</b></h3><p>After a nationwide search, it’s surprising in some ways that the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/26/cps-board-selects-macquline-king-as-permanent-ceo-will-vote-on-her-contract-monday" target="_blank" ><u>school board chose King</u></a>.</p><p>She originally <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/05/cps-ceo-search-macquline-king" target="_blank" ><u>wasn’t named a finalist for the permanent job</u></a>. Now the board is scheduled to vote to approve King as CEO on Monday, and will offer her a three-year contract.</p><p>Before becoming interim CEO 10 months ago, she’d never run a school district. She has not even run a Chicago Public Schools department or headed a network, which would have put her in charge of around 20 schools.</p><p>After spending 15 years as a principal of the two small elementary schools, she went to work on policy in former Mayor Lori Lightfoot's office and was kept on by Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div><p>King also doesn’t have a lot of experience lobbying for state policy or working with lawmakers at a time when CPS is about to have a fully elected board and is in desperate need of more state funding.</p><p>And she hasn’t created a budget for a big complex system like CPS. She and her staff are in the process of developing the spending plan for next school year.</p><p>However, the school board made <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/03/20/cps-school-board-votes-to-require-next-leader-be-an-educator-not-a-ceo" target="_blank" ><u>having a superintendent’s license a new requirement</u></a> for the CEO position, signaling that they wanted someone more steeped in teaching and learning than finance or bureaucracy.</p><p>In other ways, her background makes her ideal for the job. Teachers, parents and a former top Johnson aide all lauded King.</p><p>Tonda Lee, whose son transferred into Courtenay elementary from a school that closed, says she remembers King as a “lovely lady.” King won over several parents who carried their anger about their school closing into Courtenay.</p><p>“She's one that actually thinks about the parents and families. She has a way of bringing people together,” she says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>King spent 15 years as a principal in CPS, including at Courtenay Elementary in Uptown. She developed a reputation for being a caring leader who wanted to help staff improve.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lillian Mongeau Hughes/The Hechinger Report</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Brad Worrell, who taught under King for eight years, said he often left meetings held by King feeling “motivated and empowered” and that she had “tremendous” leadership skills.</p><p>“She is not afraid to roll up her sleeves and get into the dirty work,” said Worrell, who now teaches in Indiana. “She pushed us.”</p><p>Worrell says King also has a playful side. He still has a video of King competing against Courtenay students in a sack race, noting how she put her all into trying to get in front of the kids.</p><p>“She was in it to win it,” Worrell said.</p><p>Brandon, the Dumas elementary teacher, followed King to Courtenay. She says King sees “treasures” in people that they might not see in themselves. And, King knows how to provide criticism to her staff and then support them to improve, Brandon says.</p><p>Brandon says it is <a class="Link" href="https://hechingerreport.org/hire-black-principals/" target="_blank" ><u>rare as a Black woman to find a boss that looks like her</u></a> and is “caring, loving, supportive, and knows her stuff.”</p><h3><b>King’s time as CPS student and parent give her unique lens</b></h3><p>Like her two most recent predecessors, King is a homegrown talent.</p><p>She grew up on the South Side and in a twist that’s emblematic of CPS’ history, the schools she attended as a child and teen — Oakenwald North Elementary and a <a class="Link" href="http://www.metrohschicago.com/book.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>high school called Metropolitan School of Studies</u></a> — are now closed.</p><p>She earned a scholarship to attend Olive Harvey College, a City College of Chicago, and then went to the University of Illinois Chicago where she intended to become a pharmacist. But she says she fell in love with teaching while volunteering and changed course. She got her teaching and graduate degrees from National Louis University.</p><p>King is the mother of two grown sons who also attended and graduated from CPS. She says raising children in the city gave her another lens for seeing the system. She remembers how difficult it was to navigate the high school application process, and then her boys ended up on opposite ends of the city — one at Von Steuben in North Park on the North Side and the other at Kenwood on the South Side.</p><p>Getting to report card pickup at both schools from her teaching job was a struggle. “I had that battle,” she says.</p><h3><b>Lessons learned during time as interim CEO</b></h3><p>As interim CEO, King took some bold stances. But in other situations her response was tentative. Some criticize that hesitancy, while others say she was up against some unprecedented situations at a time when she didn’t have a secure leadership position.</p><p>Last June, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/06/26/interim-chicago-public-schools-ceo-pegs-deficit-at-730-million" target="_blank" ><u>she inherited a budget deficit</u></a> originally pegged at $734 million, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/08/14/majority-of-cps-board-demands-a-budget-with-pension-payment-and-loan-rebuffing-proposal-from-cps-leaders" target="_blank" ><u>got into a public disagreement</u></a> with the mayor’s office and school board allies over borrowing and then spent the fall <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/02/as-immigration-agents-swept-chicago-this-fall-communities-stepped-in-to-get-kids-to-school-safely" target="_blank" ><u>trying to protect students and families</u></a> from President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement operation.</p><p>More recently, she and her staff have had to figure out how to address a charter school network that ran out of money, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/19/former-aspira-students-try-to-adapt-after-troubled-charter-operator-closes-schools-midyear" target="_blank" ><u>forcing the unheard-of midyear displacement of nearly 600 high schoolers</u></a>.</p><p>Depending on where people sit, King gets different reviews.</p><p>She surprised many when she stood up to the mayor and his allies on the school board by refusing to draft a budget that could have put the district further into debt. The mayor’s people not only took issue with her decision, but they also said she didn’t communicate well with them. Initially, they did not see her as a contender for the permanent post.</p><p>Yet others applauded the stance, noting that CPS is already deep in debt and doesn’t need to take on more.</p><div
