pressure and really decide what was in the best interest, I believe, for CPS speaks volumes about her integrity, and so in that regard, I appreciate her leadership,” said 40th Ward Ald. Andre Vasquez, who represents parts of Edgewater and Lincoln Square on the North Side and is the chair of the Latino caucus.</p><p>That independence impresses Vasquez so much that he supports her, but he still wants to see Latinos in positions of power in CPS, where 46% of students are Latino. <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/18/chicago-public-schools-lacks-latino-ceo-finalists/" target="_blank" ><u>Some Latino leaders</u></a> criticized the school board for <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/13/cps-board-names-3-finalists-to-lead-district-interim-ceo-king-former-nyc-east-baton-rouge-schools-chiefs" target="_blank" ><u>not having any Latinos in the most recent finalist pool</u></a>.</p><p>Vasquez points to the school district’s fragmented response to the aggressive immigration enforcement this fall as evidence that CPS needs leadership who “understands the particular challenges faced by the Latino community and the undocumented Latino community.”</p><p>It took King and her team a month and a half to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>adjust protocols around when to lock down schools if federal agents were nearby</u></a> and to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/10/09/cps-ice-immigrant-student-families" target="_blank" ><u>create a 24-hour command center</u></a> that schools could go to for help.</p><p>King also insisted that the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/10/23/cps-school-board-remote-learning-immigration-ice-deportation-raids" target="_blank" ><u>state needed to give CPS permission</u></a> to put a remote learning option in place and, at least publicly, did not push Gov. JB Pritzker to allow it.</p><p>Vasquez says that a Latino leader might have pushed harder for virtual learning for families that were afraid to bring their children to school.</p><p>“I think those are pressures that if perhaps you've not experienced it or come from a community that's experienced it, you wouldn't have the appreciation for the dire need,” Vasquez said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/29/ctu-wants-to-bargain-with-cps-over-remote-learning-options" target="_blank" ><u>The Chicago Teachers Union has asked</u></a> King to bargain over issues related to protecting students and families should there be another surge of federal immigration agents coming into Chicago. So far, she has refused.</p><p>Still, Potter says he’s impressed with how King has kept her cool under pressure. CPS needs that as Trump continues to attack public education, immigrants, LGBTQ people and programs that support poor families, he says.</p><p>“We need someone who's going to go to bat for kids, and for school funding and take on the racist administration that is constantly attacking our city and our schools,” he said.</p><h3><b>Issues ahead: declining enrollment and troubled charter schools</b></h3><p>King typically reads prepared statements at board meetings, but at the October meeting her voice shook as she tried to address <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/10/23/cps-school-board-remote-learning-immigration-ice-deportation-raids" target="_blank" ><u>members’ concerns about the district’s response to immigration enforcement</u></a>.</p><p>She said she and her team were fielding calls at all hours about “every single detainee,” as well as other serious issues like gun violence.</p><p>“We have to carry that every day,” she said, pleading with board members to tap into their networks to help the school district.</p><p>As she <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/10/23/cps-school-board-remote-learning-immigration-ice-deportation-raids" target="_blank" ><u>gets ready to take the permanent position</u></a>, King says one of the biggest challenges is trying to keep students safe. In order to do that, she says the district has to work collaboratively with the city and other agencies.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In October 2025, King greeted students at Calmeca Academy of Fine Arts in Brighton Park as they studied math in Spanish.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It was humbling to understand just the power that a safe and trusted environment can have in the face of something so catastrophic as the federal activity,” she says. It reinforced “that this leadership role is not one that you can do on your own.”</p><p>Andrew Broy, president of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, said King also has been in a tough position as she’s had to deal with privately run public schools that are in trouble financially. That includes the Aspira charter school network, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/19/cps-revokes-aspiras-ability-to-operate-charter-schools-in-chicago-in-rare-move-board-of-education" target="_blank" ><u>which ran out of money and will officially close next week</u></a>.</p><p>Some board members are diametrically opposed to both charters and the idea of shutting down schools. That has resulted in “haphazard” decisions, he says.</p><p>When asked about charter schools, King doesn’t say whether or not she generally supports them. She says they are part of the CPS system and that she sees this moment as one where their role within the district “can be clarified.”</p><p>King also doesn’t rule out closing district-run schools.</p><p>There’s a growing buzz among fiscal conservatives and even some school board members and candidates that this needs to happen. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/chicagos-50-closed-schools" target="_blank" ><u>Since CPS closed 50 schools in 2013</u></a>, only a few additional district-run campuses have been shuttered. But CPS has about 85,000 fewer students than it did in 2014 and 44 district-run schools have dwindled to fewer than 200 students.</p><p>King, however, bristled at the idea that schools should be closed to save money.</p><p>“I do not want to reduce our students to dollars and numbers,” she said.</p><p>She says her time at Dumas and Courtenay taught her <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2018/05/22/study-2013-chicago-school-closings-failed-to-help-students" target="_blank" ><u>how much students and communities are impacted when their schools close</u></a>.</p><p>The focus, King says, must be on student experiences at really small schools that don’t have the budgets or students to host a variety of classes and clubs.</p><p>“Does the building itself or the programming or the funds set the conditions for us to fulfill our mission?” she says. “Are those students receiving the same experience as a student that’s in a school with a larger enrollment?”</p><p>While King acknowledges CPS is facing many complex issues, she says she’s looking forward to trying to set up the school system for the future. Artificial intelligence and other new technologies are reshaping the job market and she’s worried that if leaders don’t prepare students, they could be left behind.</p><p>“The landscape of education, the way we teach, hasn't really changed that much,” she says. “But society and the jobs that we're preparing students for are changing quite a bit.”</p>
author: Sarah Karp | WBEZ

title: Activists protest ICE agents at O'Hare Airport
summary: <p>Demonstrators gathered Friday evening at O’Hare International Airport to protest U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who have been called to assist with airport security amid a partial federal government shutdown.</p><p>ICE agents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >had been seen</a> at O’Hare since Monday after President Donald Trump directed them to help the Transportation Security Administration’s operations at airports nationwide amid the Department of Homeland Security funding lapse.</p><p>No ICE agents were seen Friday in Terminal 1, where the couple dozen protesters gathered, or Terminal 2.</p><p>“ICE out of O’Hare, ICE out of everywhere,” protesters shouted.</p><p>After an hour of standing outside at the departures area, the protesters walked inside Terminal 1, chanting, “ICE out now.” Many travelers and airline workers laughed and took videos of the protesters. One man pointed in protesters’ faces and shouted, “Get out now.”</p><p>Once demonstrators returned to their initial staging area outside, Chicago police officers issued a dispersal order for unlawful assembly, which was triggered when the protesters went inside. Police vehicles then blocked access to the Terminal 1 drop off area. No arrests were reported.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d20000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Earlier Friday, Trump signed an executive action that will pay TSA workers, who have gone without pay for weeks since the DHS shutdown began Feb. 14.</p><p>The TSA has faced staffing shortages during the shutdown as Democrats and Republicans in Congress quarrel over funding for DHS, which oversees the TSA, ICE and the U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Democrats have refused to fund DHS without changes to immigration enforcement practices.</p><p>The shortage has resulted in long lines for security checkpoints at airports across the country. Travelers at O’Hare have experienced lengthy lines during busy travel weekends, however, many travelers have recently reported wait times of less than half an hour.</p><p>About 75 ICE agents were expected to be stationed at O’Hare, Mayor Brandon Johnson said earlier this week. Agents were monitoring exit lanes and checkpoints, not performing security screenings. Agents were not deployed to Midway.</p><p>Friday’s protesters pointed to the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign last fall in the Chicago area, “Operation Midway Blitz,” that brought an influx of ICE and CBP agents who roved the streets and made thousands of arrests. The operation involved a seemingly indiscriminate use of tear gas and other chemical irritants, and the fatal shooting of Silverio Villegas Gonzalez and the shooting of Marimar Martinez at the hands of federal agents.</p><p>“I don’t like what’s going on in our country with ICE agents terrorizing our communities,” said Melissa Espinoza, 45, who calmly stood along protest-designated fencing holding title: Dozens of Evanston Township students walk out of school to protest war in Iran
summary: <p>Dozens of students walked out of Evanston Township High School Friday to protest the war in Iran as well as other moves made by President Donald Trump’s administration, including his mass deportation campaign.</p><p>Students from the north suburban school carried signs that read “war is costly, peace is priceless” and “Abolish ICE,” a slogan calling for the end of the U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency.</p><p>They walked to the school’s football field a few blocks away, where about 150 students gathered in the blue and orange stands. Speakers called for peace in Iran and other areas experiencing conflict, such as Gaza and Ukraine.</p><p>It’s the latest in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/02/02/hundreds-of-cps-students-walk-out-of-school-to-protest-trumps-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" ><u>string of student-led walkouts at high schools</u></a> nationally <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/13/immigration-ice-trump-administration-protest-students-walkouts" target="_blank" ><u>and in the Chicago area</u></a> but Friday’s walkout appears to be one of the few centered on the war in Iran. Students said they’ve discussed the conflict among themselves and in school. <a class="Link" href="https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/how-to-talk-to-students-about-the-u-s-iran-conflict/2026/03" target="_blank" ><u>Teachers have had to figure out the right way</u></a> to talk with students about the war.</p><p>Students at this school have walked out before. In January, they marched to protest ICE. Some students are planning on participating in <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/03/26/no-kings-protests-return-chicago-area-saturday-here-s-what-know" target="_blank" ><u>Saturday’s “No Kings” protests</u></a>.</p><p>Senior Lillian Roth has listened to a close friend who has family in Iran talk about the uncertainty she feels as the month-long war rages on.</p><p>“It’s really heartbreaking to know that there’s nothing she can even do about it, and there was really no reason for the war in the first place,” Lillian said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div who participated in a protest Friday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lillian is worried about the financial cost, too. The 17-year-old would rather the U.S. put <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/11/world/middleeast/iran-war-costs-pentagon.html" target="_blank" ><u>the billions it has spent on the war with Iran</u></a> toward other causes, like education, health care or improving infrastructure.</p><p>“There’s so many better things to put that money towards than war,” Lillian said. “My friends and I will talk about it outside of school, and it's a pressing issue to all of us.”</p><p>More than 1,900 people in Iran and nearly 1,100 people in Lebanon have been killed in the war. Millions have been displaced. Eighteen people have died in Israel, while four Israeli soldiers have also been killed in Lebanon. Thirteen U.S. military members have died.</p><p>“We’re all just scared of the death and the destruction that the major war powers are enacting, and it’s ridiculous, quite frankly,” said Kevin Watts, a junior. “I think the students here know that and they are fighting against it with this and with other protests.”</p><p>Kevin, a member of the school’s student union, which organized the protest, said while students are discussing these issues amongst each other in and out of school, the rally was also intended to raise awareness among those who aren’t as plugged in.</p><p>“People are definitely aware of what’s happening with immigration. They're aware about the war. Many of our students drive so they’re aware that the gas prices are going up,” Kevin said. “Some of them may be wondering why, which is why we have things like this.”</p><div class="Enhancement" Organizers handed out flyers with information about how to contact local representatives to share their concerns about the war, immigration policy or other issues affecting young people.</p><p>Freshman Valeria Miranda, 14, walked out of school to protest the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.</p><p>“My family is from Mexico and I feel awful about what’s happening,” Valeria said. “How people get deported straight off the streets. … I’m oftentimes scared that it could be my parents who are next.”</p><p>Valeria said more young people should be speaking out and was disappointed at the turnout for Friday’s protest which drew a fraction <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoisreportcard.com/school.aspx?source=studentcharacteristics&source2=enrollment&Schoolid=050162020170001" target="_blank" ><u>of the 3,400 students</u></a> who attend the school.</p><p>“The stands feel kind of empty and I wish that more people would have come out,” Valeria said. “Because right now things are awful.”</p><p>Contributing: AP</p>

title: Sheridan Gorman's suspected killer detained in Rogers Park ambush that stoked national immigration debate
summary: <p>In a case that has reignited a bitter national debate over immigration, and has even drawn <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >the attention of President Donald Trump</a>, a Venezuelan immigrant accused of killing a Loyola University Chicago freshman in Rogers Park made his first court appearance Friday.</p><p>Jose Medina, 25, is accused of hiding at the end of a pier near Tobey Prinz Beach and shooting 18-year-old Sheridan Gorman in the back as she and her friends ran for cover on March 19. Medina appeared in court virtually Friday because he's being treated for tuberculosis in the Cook County Jail's medical unit.</p><p>In an unusual move, Medina's attorney asked Judge D'Anthony Thedford to hold Medina in the jail out of fear that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement would act on a detainer issued after the shooting. "We fear if he's released, ICE will detain him and release him to a third country," said Medina's attorney, Cook County Assistant Public Defender Julie Koehler.</p><div class="Enhancement" midnight, the group left to see the skyline, Pekara said. They took photos outside the dorm, then made their way to the lakefront and took more photos.</p><p>As two members of the group left to find a bathroom, Gorman and the others continued walking down the beach toward the pier, Pekara said. Gorman reached the end of the pier first and was startled to find Medina behind a structure, whispering that there was someone there, Pekara said.</p><p>Then, Medina jumped out wearing a black ski mask and holding a gun, Pekara said. The group started running away as Medina allegedly fired one round, striking Gorman in her upper back.</p><p>Gorman collapsed as the others "continued running for their lives," Pekara said. The others found shelter in the grass or behind a concrete barrier. They waited as Medina allegedly walked slowly back and forth on the pier. After Medina walked away, one of the friends ran back to find Gorman bleeding and unresponsive, Pekara said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Gorman was taken to a hospital and pronounced dead.</p><p>Detectives eventually pinned the crime on Medina after analyzing video that led them to his apartment, Pekara said.</p><p>Video from the apartment building shows Medina left for the beach 20 minutes before the killing, Pekara said. The video allegedly shows him wearing a black ski mask and gloves, walking with a distinctive limp.</p><p>When police executed a search warrant on Medina's fourth-floor apartment, they found a gun wrapped in a ski mask near his bed and a leg brace with his name on it, Pekara said. Police also found clothes that match the ones seen in the video. </p><p>Medina was arrested during the search, Pekara said. He had an active warrant for an arrest in a 2023 shoplifting case. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >He is now charged</a> with first-degree murder, attempted murder and aggravated discharge of a firearm in Gorman's killing.</p><p>Medina's mother spoke with detectives and identified him in surveillance video, Pekara said. She said she remembered hearing him leave on the night of the shooting and noted that he walks with a limp from his gunshot injury.</p><p>Gorman's killing has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" target="_blank" >triggered widespread outrage</a>, especially among conservatives.</p><p>President Trump said Gorman’s killing was “devastating” and placed blame on the “open door policy” of his predecessor, Joe Biden. title: Trump says he’ll sign order to pay TSA agents as Congress struggles to reach funding deal
summary: <p>WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Thursday he would sign an order instructing the Homeland Security secretary to immediately pay Transportation Security Administration agents as Congress struggled to reach a deal to end a budget impasse that has jammed airports and left workers without paychecks.</p><p>Trump announced his decision in a social media post saying he wanted to quickly stop the “Chaos at the Airports.”</p><p>“It is not an easy thing to do, but I am going to do it!” the president posted.</p><p>With pressure mounting, the White House had floated the extraordinary move of invoking a national emergency to pay TSA agents, while senators were reviewing a “last and final” offer from Republicans to Democrats to end the funding impasse at the Department of Homeland Security.</p><p>Details of the president’s plan were not immediately available, but a national emergency declaration would be politically fraught and almost certain to face legal challenges. Instead, the president may simply be shifting money from other sources.</p><p>Democrats have been refusing to fund the Homeland Security as they demand changes to rein in Trump’s immigration enforcement operations. The Senate came to a standstill and senators, ready to leave town for their own spring break, had prepared to stay all night to reach a deal.</p><p>“The president is doing absolutely the right thing,” said Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., the GOP whip. “The TSA agents are going to be paid.”</p><p>Everett Kelley, national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, issued a statement saying that paying just TSA workers, while welcome, isn't enough. AFGE represents 47,000 TSA officers.</p><p>"We don’t yet know what this means for thousands of other DHS employees at FEMA, the Coast Guard, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, among others," Kelley said in his statement. </p><p>"These workers and their families cannot wait. All DHS workers must be paid immediately," he added. "Congress needs to continue working to pass a real, bipartisan appropriations deal that funds DHS, pays all DHS workers, and keeps these vital agencies running — even if that means canceling their upcoming vacation."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" >ICE agents deployed at O’Hare as partial government shutdown continues to impact travelers</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, the chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, has said there was funding elsewhere that can be legally used to pay TSA as well as the Coast Guard, without declaring a national emergency.</p><p>The funding shutdown, now in its 41st day, has resulted in travel delays, missed paychecks and even warnings of airport closures. TSA workers are coming up on their second missed payday Friday, with thousands refusing to show up for work.</p><p>Multiple airports are experiencing greater than 40% callout rates of TSA workers and nearly 500 of its nearly 50,000 transportation security officers have now quit during the shutdown. Nationwide on Wednesday, more than 11% of the TSA employees on the schedule missed work, according to DHS. That is more than 3,120 callouts.</p><p>Trump, who has largely left the issue to Congress to resolve, had warned he was ready to take action, even threatening to send the National Guard to airports, in addition to his deployment of ICE agents who are now checking travelers’ IDs — a development drawing concerns. The White House has been considering a menu of options.</p><p>“They need to end this shutdown immediately or we’ll have to take drastic measures,” Trump said during a morning Cabinet meeting at the White House.</p><p>At George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, Melissa Gates said she would not make her flight to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, after waiting more than 2½ hours and still not reaching the security checkpoint. She said no other flights were available until Friday.</p><p>“I should have just driven, right?” Gates said. “Five hours would have been hilarious next to this.”</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents stand guard at the exit point of the arrival area in Terminal 2 at O’Hare International Airport on Monday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>A ‘last and final’ offer on the table</h3><p>Earlier Thursday, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., announced he had given the final offer to the Democrats.</p><p>Thune did not disclose details of the new framework, but he said that it picked up on what had been the Republican offer over the weekend, before talks with the White House and Democrats had broken off.</p><p>“Enough is enough,” he said.</p><p>But as senators retreated to privately discuss the new plan, the action stalled out.</p><p>Democrats argue the GOP proposals have not gone far enough at putting guardrails on officers from ICE, Customs and Border Protection and other federal agencies who are engaged in the immigration sweeps, particularly after the deaths of two Americans protesting the actions in Minneapolis.</p><p>They want federal agents to wear identification, remove their face masks and refrain from conducting raids around schools, churches or other sensitive places. Democrats have also pushed for an end of administrative warrants, insisting that judges sign off before agents search people’s homes or private spaces.</p><p>Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said they needed to see real changes. “We’ve been talking about ICE reforms from day one,” he said.</p><p>Any deal will almost certainly need to involve a compromise as lawmakers on the left and right flanks revolt. Conservative Republicans have panned their own GOP proposals, demanding full funding for immigration operations and skeptical of the promise from leaders that they would address Trump’s proof-of-citizenship voting bill in a subsequent legislative package.</p><p>Republicans said after a private lunch meeting that there were other options to shift money than invoking the national emergency.</p><p>The GOP’s big tax cuts bill that Trump signed into law last year funneled billions to DHS, including $75 billion for ICE operations, ensuring the money is flowing for his immigration and deportation agenda even with the funding shutdown. ICE and other immigration officers are still being paid.</p><p>Republicans say the Trump administration has already made strides to meet Democrats’ demands, particularly after swearing in former Oklahoma Sen. Markwayne Mullin as the new homeland security secretary to replace Kristi Noem. He has given a nod to the need for the judicial warrants for searches.</p><h3>Airport lines grow as TSA workers endure hardships</h3><p>“This is a dire situation,” the acting TSA administrator, Ha Nguyen McNeill, testified at a House hearing Wednesday.</p><p>She described the multiple hardships facing unpaid TSA workers — piling up bills and eviction notices, even plasma donations to make ends meet — and warned of potential airport closures if more employees refuse to come to work.</p><p>“At this point, we have to look at all options on the table,” she said.</p><p>McNeil also said TSA officers working at the nation’s airports have experienced a more than 500% increase in the frequency of assaults since the shutdown began.</p><p>“This is unacceptable,” McNeill said.</p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press writers Joey Cappelletti, Kevin Freking, Rebecca Santana and Ben Finley in Washington, Lekan Oyekanmi in Houston, Wyatte Grantham-Philips in New York, Rio Yamat in Las Vegas, Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, and Gabriela Aoun Angueira in San Diego.</i></p>

title: Ex-federal prosecutors in Chicago taking on Trump's 'troubling' DOJ: ‘We feel compelled to speak and act'
summary: <p>Fearing President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice<b> </b>is “ignoring its founding principles,”<b> </b>a prominent group of former Chicago federal prosecutors invited<b> </b>more than 300<b> </b>fellow alums<b> </b>this week to join them in moving “from handwringing to action”<b> </b>to preserve the agency’s integrity.</p><p>The 14 signatories on the “Call to Action” email include three former Chicago U.S. attorneys: Dan Webb, Scott Lassar and Patrick Fitzgerald. They're calling for a non-partisan effort led by former department officials acting as “private citizens," according to a copy obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>“As lawyers who cherish the role DOJ should play in our criminal justice system, we feel compelled to speak and act against the troubling events underway at the Department,” the email states, “and we invite you to participate in those efforts.”</p><p>It appears to be the first Chicago-specific group of its kind, formed to push back against Trump’s Justice Department. But the group’s email acknowledges that “many like-minded non-partisan organizations”<b> </b>already exist that could serve as partners.</p><p>Their efforts could involve litigation aimed at protecting the “integrity of elections” and a push to ensure federal prosecutors can still be held accountable for misconduct, according to the email.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >Remaining Broadview 6 defendants want records showing Trump administration’s influence on conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a message from the Sun-Times seeking comment. But current U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros said in a statement that his office is "busy doing the people's business, which means prosecuting criminals who commit serious crimes."</p><p>"We recognize the immense power we wield over life, liberty, and reputation, and therefore, we strive every day to exercise that enormous responsibility with integrity, fairness, decency, and humility," Boutros said. "We are not interested in anything that distracts us from our mission."</p><p>The email follows more than a year of Justice Department controversies, including claims that Trump has used the agency to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >retaliate against political foes</a> like ex-FBI Director James Comey.</p><p>Fitzgerald represented Comey<b> </b>in court after Trump’s Justice Department secured an indictment<b> </b>against the former FBI boss. That indictment, in the Eastern District of Virginia, was tossed after a judge found the top prosecutor there acted as U.S. attorney without authorization.</p><p>Former federal prosecutor Ron Safer sent this week’s email and is among its 14 authors. They describe themselves as “Republicans, Independents, Democrats and everything in between.” Webb, Lassar and Fitzgerald were nominated to be U.S. attorney by Presidents Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton and George W. Bush, respectively.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-440000" Others have played prominent roles defending criminal defendants or in litigation against government agencies.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/11/10/superstar-prosecutor-convicted-madigan-burke-leaving-u-s-attorneys-office" target="_blank" >‘Superstar’ prosecutor who helped bring down Madigan, Burke parting ways with U.S. attorney’s office</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The new Chicago effort is also reminiscent of the <a class="Link" href="https://federaloverreach.org" target="_blank" >Fight Against Federal Overreach</a>, a national coalition of state court prosecutors who say they’ve come together “to ensure federal officials are held accountable when they exceed their lawful authority.”</p><p>But the authors of the Chicago email simply describe themselves as “a very informal group of former colleagues … who have chatted about whether we could move from handwringing to action.”<b> </b>They’re now at law firms of various sizes, and some are retired.</p><p>They say they’ve done “preliminary research”<b> </b>into three specific ways the group might push back against the Justice Department. title: Legisladores estatales avanzan ley para mantener los centros de detención de inmigrantes fuera de comunidades
summary: <p>Los legisladores estatales están tomando medidas para, en el futuro, mantener los centros de detención de inmigrantes fuera de las comunidades.</p><p>Bajo un proyecto de ley que salió de un comité de la Cámara de Illinois el miércoles, se prohibiría la construcción de nuevos centros de detención de inmigrantes dentro de un radio de 1,500 pies de escuelas, iglesias, centros de cuidado infantil, cementerios, parques públicos, reservas forestales, residencias privadas y vivienda pública</p><p>En apoyo a la legislación testificaron el presidente de la Cámara, Emanuel “Chris” Welch, y la alcaldesa de Broadview, Katrina Thompson, ambos representantes del área de Broadview, donde funciona un centro de procesamiento del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) que fue muy utilizado por ICE durante el Operativo Midway Blitz el otoño pasado.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ba0000" name="module-ba0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El proyecto de ley obtuvo un amplio apoyo de fue apoyado unánimemente por los demócratas, pero fue unánimemente rechazado por los republicanos.</p><p>“Este proyecto de ley dice algo muy simple y muy razonable: Las instalaciones de detención no pertenecen en medio de nuestros vecindarios”, dijo Welch. “No deberían estar al lado de escuelas, no deberían estar al lado de centros de cuidado infantil, no deberían estar al lado de parques, vivienda pública, lugares de culto o casas privadas como lo hace el centro de detención de Broadview”.</p><p>Welch destacó que a menos de 1,500 pies de la instalación de Broadview, hay dos centros de cuidado infantil, un parque, un lugar de culto y varias residencias privadas. El proyecto de ley no cerraría el actual centro de Broadview.</p><p>Broadview fue el epicentro de muchas protestas en contra de ICE durante la campaña de deportación. Seis manifestantes, apodados <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" target="_blank" >“Los Seis de Broadview”</a>, fueron acusados de conspiración, un delito federal, tras su participación en protestas en la instalación. Dos de los seis han tenido los cargos desestimados.</p><p>“Para una comunidad pequeña como la nuestra, esto no es solo un número, es una carga significativa para nuestros contribuyentes, y sin embargo, no ha habido reembolso”, dijo Thompson.</p><p>El representante Christopher Davidsmeyer, republicano de Jacksonville, votó en contra de la legislación, calificándola de “proyecto de ley política”. Espera que sea impugnada en las cortes si se aprueba.</p><p>“La realidad es que nuestras leyes han estado empujando las acciones de ICE en las direcciones que han estado tomando”, dijo Davidsmeyer. “Así que si simplemente trabajamos con ellos, las cosas podrían suceder pacíficamente y no tendríamos este problema”.</p><p>El proyecto de ley espera votos en la Cámara de Representantes y en el Senado. Varios miembros del comité pidieron ser añadidos como co-patrocinadores del proyecto de ley.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
author: Matt Trunfio

title: CPS Board selects Macquline King as permanent CEO, will vote on her contract Monday
summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education will vote on Monday to appoint Macquline King as the permanent leader of Chicago Public Schools, catapulting a Black woman with homegrown talent to the district’s top post 10 months after she was appointed to the interim role.</p><p>According to <a class="Link" href="https://www.cpsboe.org/content/documents/march_30_2026_special_board_meeting_public_agenda_to_post.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>documents posted on the CPS Board’s website</u></a> Thursday, the school board has offered King the job and she has accepted it.</p><p>The proposed contract would be effective July 1 through June 30, 2029 — meaning she would lead the district well past the transition to a fully elected school board. If approved, King’s salary will start at $380,000, more than former CEO Pedro Martinez was offered. He was granted a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2021/10/25/22744850/cps-ceo-pedro-martinez-salary-contract-public-school#:~:text=CPS%20CEO%20Pedro%20Martinez%20to,year%20contract%20%2D%20Chicago%20Sun%2DTimes" target="_blank" ><u>$340,000 annual salary on a five-year contract.</u></a></p><p>This brings to the end a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/13/cps-board-names-3-finalists-to-lead-district-interim-ceo-king-former-nyc-east-baton-rouge-schools-chiefs" target="_blank" ><u>protracted search</u></a> for a new leader of the school district. It started last year after <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2024/12/20/cps-ceo-pedro-martinez-threatens-to-sue-school-board-before-they-consider-firing-him-at-friday-meeting" target="_blank" ><u>Martinez was fired</u></a>.</p><p>Though the contract appoints her as CEO, King has a superintendent’s license, which the partly elected, partly appointed board <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/03/20/cps-school-board-votes-to-require-next-leader-be-an-educator-not-a-ceo" target="_blank" ><u>made a requirement for the position</u></a>. Those who have worked with King say she is an expert on teaching and learning, as well as building relationships and cultivating leadership.</p><p>Unlike some past CPS leaders, she does not have a background in accounting and will likely have to find a strong chief financial officer to help her navigate the district’s budget and debt. CPS is projected to face a $500 million deficit next school year, as well as future deficits.</p><p>King started as a teacher in CPS and became a principal of Dumas Elementary School on the South Side in 2007. She served there until CPS closed the school in 2013. She then became principal of a North Side elementary, which took in students from a nearby closed school.</p><p>She applied for the CEO position in 2021, but was passed over for Martinez. Mayor Lori Lightfoot hired King in 2022 to work in her office as the deputy education mayor.</p><p>Brandon Johnson kept King on when he became mayor. One of Johnson’s former top officials, who did not want to be named because they were not authorized to speak on the matter, called King a “wonderful person who was really well-liked.”</p><p>Though the school board is partially elected, Johnson still appoints the majority of its members.</p><p>As interim CEO, King immediately had to confront a budget deficit that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/06/26/interim-chicago-public-schools-ceo-pegs-deficit-at-730-million" target="_blank" ><u>she pegged at more than $700 million</u></a>. She gained the respect of some of Johnson’s opponents by <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/08/14/majority-of-cps-board-demands-a-budget-with-pension-payment-and-loan-rebuffing-proposal-from-cps-leaders" target="_blank" ><u>refusing to present a budget</u></a> that included borrowing, which was something that the mayor’s office argued the budget should allow for.</p><p>King <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/11/05/cps-ceo-search-macquline-king" target="_blank" ><u>wasn’t among the finalists in the fall</u></a>, which became a point of contention among some groups who supported her, such as the Westside Branch of the NAACP. But her standing among board members has risen over the last few months as she’s handled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2025/08/28/cps-board-denies-johnsons-preferred-budget-rejects-pension-payment-and-loan" target="_blank" ><u>tense budget discussions,</u></a> the closings of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/03/19/cps-revokes-aspiras-ability-to-operate-charter-schools-in-chicago-in-rare-move-board-of-education" target="_blank" ><u>privately managed public schools</u></a> and widespread <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>immigration enforcement that affected schools.</u></a> Board member Jitu Brown has said serving in the interim post has been like an “on the job interview” for King.</p><p>The board named three finalists earlier this month, but one of the candidates, Meisha Porter, the former leader of New York City’s school system, dropped out without offering a reason days later.</p><p>The other finalist was Sito Narcisse, the former head of Louisiana's second-largest school district, whose past job experience was somewhat polarizing. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/03/24/finalist-for-cps-ceo-sito-narcisse-courted-controversy-in-past-jobs-but-defenders-praise-his-vision" target="_blank" ><u>Some praised him as a “transformational leader”</u></a> but others criticized his leadership style.</p><p>There were some concerns among community members that the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/18/chicago-public-schools-lacks-latino-ceo-finalists/" target="_blank" ><u>finalists didn’t include a Latino candidate</u></a>. Chalkbeat Chicago reported that a fourth finalist dropped out, but board members wouldn’t say if that person was Latino.</p>
author: Emmanuel Camarillo

title: 49th Ward office closes temporarily after violent threats following killing of Loyola student in Rogers Park
summary: <p>The 49th Ward's office has closed for the rest of the week due to "threats of violence" to the alderperson and her staff following backlash to comments she made after the homicide of 18-year-old Loyola student Sheridan Gorman. </p><p>In a letter to constituents Wednesday, Ald. Maria Hadden (49th) announced her office was offering services remotely Wednesday and Thursday before closing entirely Friday due to "threats of violence against myself, my family, and my team."</p><p>Hadden said the threats involved "racist, misogynistic and homophobic language" and verbal abuse to her staff was "making it difficult to serve the constituents of the 49th Ward."</p><p>Hadden appeared on "Chicago Live" the same day Gorman was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/24/heres-what-to-know-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >shot and killed</a> for an interview that circulated in conservative news cycles and social media groups.</p><p>During the interview, Hadden was asked if members of the 49th Ward should be worried about their safety. </p><p>"They were just out, people go out to the beach all the time," Hadden responded as she described what she knew from police. "The kids were out doing normal things people do in the neighborhood, and it sounds like this might've been a wrong place, wrong time, running into a person who had a gun, they might've startled this person at the end of the pier unintentionally." </p><p>The fatal shooting garnered national attention, including from<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" target="_blank" > President Donald Trump</a>, after a Venezuelan migrant was charged with Gorman's murder. The shooting created an increased political discourse regarding immigration enforcement in Chicago, where elected officials have resisted enhanced enforcement tactics. </p><p>"Gun violence and immigration policy have been two of the most challenging issues facing our country and our city. Sheridan's murder has become a national story touching on these painful and difficult issues," Hadden said in her newsletter. "I know that people are in pain, and tensions will be high as we work to find solutions to keep everyone in our community safe."</p><p>Hadden declined to elaborate on the backlash when reached by a Sun-Times reporter Thursday. </p><p>Following the interview, Hadden said her office received "an overwhelming number" of calls and emails, mostly from people out-of-state "who are angry about my comments and Chicago's sanctuary city status."</p><p>"Our social media pages have also been inundated with negative reviews and hateful comments. The content of the phone messages and emails that my staff and I have been receiving is explicit and disturbing," Hadden wrote. </p><p>An anti-immigrant, anti-sanctuary city protest took place outside the Rogers Park office Tuesday and another was planned for Friday, according to Hadden. </p><p>The 49th Ward office was expected to fully reopen Monday. </p><p>"I ask that here, in the 49th Ward, we bring compassion, patience, and understanding to debates and discussions we have with our neighbors about this in the coming weeks," Hadden wrote. <br> </p>
author: Mohammad Samra

Washburn</a></h5><p><b>Medical emergency</b>: West Suburban Medical Center is temporarily shutting its doors and furloughing "many" employees as it struggles to pay staff, according to the Oak Park hospital’s owner, Manoj Prasad. He did not say when the safety net hospital, which has 234 beds, would reopen.</p><p><b>The scope</b>: The hospital’s emergency room, inpatient units and clinics are closing "effective immediately," Prasad said. He blamed the hospital’s year-old electronic medical record system "that has never functioned correctly" for the payroll issues. </p><p><b>Key context</b>: This comes seven months after Resilience Healthcare shuttered its other facility, Weiss Memorial Hospital in Uptown. Like Weiss, West Suburban serves a high percentage of patients who rely on Medicaid health insurance for people with low incomes or on Medicare for seniors, according to the most recent state data.</p><p><b>Big shock</b>: At the hospital Wednesday afternoon, some patients arriving for appointments were surprised to hear it was closing. Sanyaa Thomas, a hospital employee, said the news was a big shock to her and her co-workers. "It was still morning. And as we’re helping patients out, we just get an email that we were suspending patient care," she said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wthjiud-l-h/" But some of her most formative moments took place at the kitchen table in her grandmother’s South Side home.</p><p>Butler will honor that sacred space in her new work, "Her Table," which will premiere March 28 during La Femme Dance Festival at Harris Theater for Music and Dance. Presented by Red Clay Dance Company, the biennial event showcases diverse works by Black women, who are often underrepresented on large stages.</p><p>The work is inspired by "The Kitchen Table Series," a seminal 1990 photo project by artist Carrie Mae Weems, who is Black. The set of black-and-white images depicts Weems in different scenes around her kitchen table — embracing a lover, getting her hair brushed by her mother, applying makeup with her young daughter, conversing with friends, even sitting in solitude.</p><p>"I was seeing myself in a museum for the first time," Butler, 36, said of first encountering Weems' work. "I was looking back at myself and my grandmother and my mother and my auntie and my sisters. And it just encapsulated so much lineage and a breadth of differing women within the Black community."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wthjiud-l-jt/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's your defining memory of Opening Day in Chicago? ⚾</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Email us your answer.</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). title: Like Trump, DHS' Mullin will trash Republicans who don't toe the party line
summary: <p>Some Supreme Court justices are so eager to demonstrate their independence, President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/116236559151421767" target="_blank" >complained</a> last week, that they "openly disrespect the Presidents who nominate them." A few days later, Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R–Okla., who was <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/23/us/politics/mullins-confirmation-throwback-senate.html" target="_blank" >confirmed</a> this week as secretary of homeland security, explained why he had <a class="Link" href="https://www.wral.com/news/ap/8eaf5-the-latest-trump-fires-homeland-security-secretary-noem-amid-criticism-over-immigration-enforcement/" target="_blank" >called</a> Sen. Rand Paul, R–Ky., "a freaking snake": It "seems like you fight Republicans more than you work with us," Mullin <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/5789478-rand-paul-markwayne-mullin-dhs/" target="_blank" >told</a> Paul.</p><p>Trump and Mullin take it for granted that public officials should be prepared to sacrifice their principles on the altar of party loyalty. But those officials, whether they serve on the Supreme Court or in the U.S. Senate, have higher duties that may require them to take stands that invite misguided rebukes like these.</p><p>The specific targets of Trump's ire were Justices Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett, who last month had the temerity to <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/02/20/the-supreme-court-just-struck-down-trumps-emergency-tariffs/" target="_blank" >reject</a> his claim of essentially unlimited authority to impose "emergency" tariffs. In Trump's view, their defiance of his will was unforgivable because he is the guy who gave them their jobs.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3a0000" name="module-3a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Contrary to Trump's take, the tariff case, which <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/02/25/the-scotus-tariff-decision-vindicates-the-rule-of-law-and-the-separation-of-powers/" target="_blank" >hinged</a> on statutory interpretation informed by the separation of powers, was not a test of personal or party loyalty. If Gorsuch and Barrett had automatically agreed with the president who appointed them, they would have <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/03/17/kavanaugh-should-be-embarrassed-by-trumps-praise-for-his-tariffs-dissent/" target="_blank" >forsaken</a> their obligation to reach conclusions based on their honest assessment of the facts and the law.</p><p>Trump is not oblivious to that obligation. In fact, he <a class="Link" href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/116236559151421767" target="_blank" >faulted</a> "the Democrats on the Court" for ignoring it, complaining that they "always 'stick together,' no matter how strong a case is put before them." Trump <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/03/20/judges-and-justices-should-be-independent-trump-says-as-long-as-they-side-with-him/" target="_blank" >thinks</a> justices should be independent, as long as they side with him.</p><p>Mullin seems similarly dismayed by Paul's periodic failures to toe the party line. But like Gorsuch and Barrett, Paul has what he takes to be good reasons for antagonizing the president and <a class="Link" href="https://www.ms.now/opinion/markwayne-mullin-cabinet-project-47-newsletter" target="_blank" >lapdog loyalists</a> like Mullin.</p><p>Paul, for instance, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/10/08/the-constitution-does-not-allow-the-president-to-unilaterally-blow-suspected-drug-smugglers-to-smithereens/" target="_blank" >objects</a> to Trump's policy of <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/12/10/trumps-word-games-cant-conceal-the-murderous-reality-of-his-anti-drug-strategy/" target="_blank" >summarily executing</a> suspected cocaine smugglers without statutory authorization or any semblance of due process. Mullin, by contrast, <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4M9ox2_dL3o" target="_blank" >has</a> "zero problems with sending them to the bottom of the ocean."</p><p>Mullin likewise seemed untroubled when immigration agents <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/25/the-trump-administration-is-lying-about-gun-rights-and-the-death-of-alex-pretti/" target="_blank" >fatally shot</a> Minneapolis protester Alex Pretti on Jan. 24, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/Acyn/status/2015245390082343176" target="_blank" >saying</a> they had defended themselves against a "deranged individual" who "came in to cause max damage." Paul, by contrast, called for an independent investigation and <a class="Link" href="https://www.c-span.org/clip/news-conference/senator-rand-paul-calls-for-independent-investigation-into-alex-pretti-killing/5191081" target="_blank" >questioned</a> the initial account of the shooting, noting that it was <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/25/dhs-again-promises-a-thorough-investigation-of-a-fatal-shooting-after-prejudging-the-outcome/" target="_blank" >immediately contradicted</a> by video evidence.</p><p>Paul <a class="Link" href="https://www.foxnews.com/opinion/sen-rand-paul-america-war-but-americans-didnt-vote" target="_blank" >thinks</a> Trump should have sought congressional approval for his war with Iran, since the Constitution gives the legislative branch the sole authority to "declare war." Mullin, by contrast, <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/Acyn/status/2028952215290036261" target="_blank" >can’t even seem to decide</a> whether the extensive U.S. attacks on Iran qualify as "war."</p><p>Mullin played similar word games when he parroted Trump's defense of the steep, wide-ranging, ever-changing tariffs that the Supreme Court later ruled illegal. "This isn't a trade war," Mullin <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/04/06/mullin-coons-trump-tariffs-message-00274485" target="_blank" >said</a> on Fox News last year. "This is balancing our economy with countries that have taken advantage of us."</p><p>Here, too, Paul takes a decidedly different view. The argument that "we're being ripped off" is "a fallacy," he noted in an <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QzTQd_RR1jc" target="_blank" >interview</a> with Reason's Nick Gillespie last November, because voluntary trade always entails mutual benefits.</p><p>"The farm state senators will all privately tell you, 'We are [for] free trade, and this is killing our farmers,'" Paul said. "But they will not stand up, and they will not vote with me to end the emergencies" that Trump declared to justify his tariffs.</p><p>That reticence, Paul said, reflected a broader problem. "What Founding Father would ever have imagined a Congress with no ambition?" he asked.</p><p>Most Republican legislators, Paul complained, are "feckless," "completely without principles," "afraid of their own shadow," "afraid of their own president," and "unable to even squeak." You can start to see why Mullin, who fits that description pretty well, was so mad at Paul.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-940000" name="module-940000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
author: Jacob Sullum

title: Hegseth, Bondi and Gabbard may soon get the boot by 'blame-shifting' boss
summary: <p>If I were Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, I might start packing up my office at the Pentagon.</p><p>While President Donald Trump is boasting about the so-called success of a war with Iran that has no clear mission nor end in sight, Americans are souring on it. Big time.</p><p>New polling from <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/opinion-poll-iran-war-regime-2028-03-22/" target="_blank" >CBS News/YouGov</a> shows an increasingly bearish public when it comes to the war, with 57% saying it’s going somewhat or very badly. Sixty-three percent believe the war will make the U.S. economy weaker in the short term, while a whopping 92% say the most important thing the U.S. should do with regard to Iran right now is “end the conflict as quickly as possible.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-df0000" name="module-df0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Hardly a rousing endorsement. We know Trump closely monitors the polls, which is perhaps why he said what he did on Monday while at a roundtable in Memphis.</p><p>While discussing crime, Trump oddly <a class="Link" href="https://www.mediaite.com/media/tv/trump-goes-out-of-his-way-to-say-hegseth-was-the-first-to-advocate-iran-war-you-said-lets-do-it/" target="_blank" >detoured</a> to brag about his decision to go to war with Iran and then pointed to Hegseth, who was in the room, and said: “And Pete, I think you were the first one to speak up. And you said, ‘Let’s do it, because you can’t let them have a nuclear weapon.’ ”</p><p>Now, any other time and any other president and you’d call this a compliment. But seasoned Trump-watchers’ eyebrows raised at the subtle but discernible sign of what may be to come.</p><p>It would be, after all, a very Trumpian and convenient blame-shift to make the war all Pete’s idea when it’s slumping in the polls, and it doesn’t help Hegseth that <a class="Link" href="https://www.tarapalmeri.com/p/exclusive-theres-zero-confidence" target="_blank" >reports</a> are swirling around D.C. that Republicans on the Hill and inside the administration have “zero confidence” in him.</p><p>As former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem knows all too well, Trump only loves you until he doesn’t. When U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in Minneapolis turned deadly and the sordid headlines around her spending and personal life got too unbearable, Trump dumped the glammed-up grifter with an unceremonious thanks and a move to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/noem-thanks-trump-new-shield-americas-special-envoy-role-after-dhs-ouster" target="_blank" >made-up new post</a>.</p><p>Former Kennedy Center head Ric Grenell had also been one of Trump’s longtime favorites, but he too lost his job this month after overseeing plummeting ticket sales, a mass exodus of artists, and scathing headlines. And that’s after he put Trump’s name on the building!</p><p>A couple other Trump cabinet members may want to prepare for early exits, while we’re at it.</p><p>Attorney General Pam Bondi’s Department of Justice has been rightfully dragged through the mud for its incompetence and political hackery, overseeing multiple failed attempts at indicting Trump’s political opponents, an obvious cover-up of the Epstein files, and losing so much talent it now has to recruit prosecutors straight out of law school. Maybe that’s why Bondi recently hung the North Korea-coded banner of Trump on DOJ headquarters.</p><p>Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard might not be long for this world either. She’s been excluded from high-level meetings at the White House, so much so that the joke <a class="Link" href="https://katv.com/news/nation-world/tulsi-gabbard-excluded-from-the-plan-to-oust-maduro-report-venezuela-donald-trump-director-of-national-intelligence-civil-war" target="_blank" >among aides</a> is that DNI stands for “Do Not Invite.” Even Trump has <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/06/17/politics/video/trump-gabbard-iran-nuclear-weapons-collins-digvid" target="_blank" >publicly dismissed</a> her advice.</p><p>If you’re wondering why these folks continue to work for a guy who humiliates them, sidelines them, and then dumps them, that’s easy — they have no principles, integrity or self-respect! And when you’re solely motivated by naked power grabs and money, you can put up with a lot.</p><p>Only time will tell if Hegseth, Bondi and Gabbard can survive what will only become worse and worse headlines. But in the meantime, Pete might want to put a Trump banner up on the Pentagon — just in case.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7a0000" name="module-7a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
author: S. E. Cupp

title: State lawmakers advance bill to keep immigration detention centers out of communities like suburban Broadview
summary: <p>State lawmakers are taking steps to, in the future, keep immigration detention centers out of communities. </p><p>Under a bill that moved out of an Illinois House committee Wednesday, new immigration detention centers would be prohibited within 1,500 feet of schools, churches, day care centers, cemeteries, public parks, forest preserves, private residences and public housing. </p><p>Testifying in support of the legislation was House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch and Broadview Mayor Katrina Thompson, both of whom represent the Broadview area, where a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing center played a major role in Operation Midway Blitz last fall. The bill got broad support from Democrats, but was unanimously opposed by Republicans.</p><p>“This bill says something very simple and very reasonable: Detention facilities do not belong in the middle of our neighborhoods,” Welch said. “They should not be next to schools, they should not be next to day care centers, they should not sit beside parks, public housing, places of worship, or private homes like the Broadview detention center does.”</p><p>Welch noted that within 1,500 feet of the Broadview facility, there are two day care centers, a park, a place of worship and several private residences. The bill would not close the current Broadview center. </p><p>That facility became a flashpoint for anti-ICE protests during the deportation campaign. Six protesters, nicknamed<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" > the Broadview Six, </a>were charged with conspiracy, a federal felony, following their participation in protests at the facility. Two of the six have had charges dropped. </p><p>Thompson testified about the financial strain of housing the Broadview center put on her community, which amounted to more than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/broadview-mayor-demands-closure-of-ice-facility-reimbursement-of-village-costs-business-losses-police-fire-congress-trump-detention" target="_blank" ><u>$700,000</u></a>, according to village officials.</p><p>“For a small community like ours this is not just a number, that is a significant burden on our taxpayers, and yet there has been no reimbursement,” Thompson said.</p><p>Rep. Christopher Davidsmeyer, a Republican from Jacksonville, voted against the legislation, calling it just a "political bill." He expects it to be challenged in the courts if it passes.</p><p>“The reality is our laws have actually been pushing ICE’s actions in the directions they have been going,” Davidsmeyer said. “So if we would just work with them, things could happen peacefully and we wouldn't have this problem.”</p><p>The bill awaits votes in both the House and Senate. Several committee members asked to be added as co-sponsors to the bill. </p>
author: Matt Trunfio

title: Mayor Johnson unveils 'Abolish ICE' snowplow
summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson and city officials unveiled Wednesday the “Abolish ICE” snowplow, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/02/23/abolish-ice-among-winners-in-chicagos-you-name-a-snowplow-contest" target="_blank" >the winner of this year’s snowplow naming contest</a>, which drew a record number of submissions.</p><p>The mayor said the winning snowplow name is a message to the federal government that U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement isn’t welcome in Chicago.</p><p>But the unveiling in West Town came as Chicago has again become a focal point of America’s debate over immigration policies following last week’s fatal shooting of an 18-year-old college student.</p><p>Loyola University Chicago freshman Sheridan Gorman was shot and killed near the Rogers Park campus. The alleged gunman, Jose G. Medina, is a Venezuelan immigrant who had been taken into custody by U.S. Border Patrol in May 2023, released, then arrested again months later on shoplifting charges.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-crime-trump-pritzker-bovino-immigration-midway-blitz-deport-immigration" >Sheridan Gorman’s killing puts Chicago back at the center of America’s bitter fight over immigration</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/24/heres-what-to-know-killing-sheridan-gorman" >What to know about the killing of Sheridan Gorman</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>One heckler at Wednesday’s event called out the mayor for unveiling the snowplow less than a week after Gorman’s death.</p><p>"You're making a joke out of Sheridan Gorman!" the heckler shouted. "Shame on you!"</p><p>“My condolences to the family of Sheridan. This is a terrible tragedy,” Johnson said. “And what I’ve said from the very beginning, I’m going to continue to use every single tool that’s available to me to protect the residents of the city of Chicago. And this tragedy is not going to deter us from our work. In fact, it’s going to challenge us all to double down on our efforts to ensure that we are protecting every single individual across neighborhoods.”</p><p>The fourth annual “You Name a Snowplow” contest returned in December and yielded 13,300 submissions. The slogan “Abolish ICE,” taking aim at the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, was submitted around 9,300 times, or about 70% of entries.</p><p>The flood of “Abolish ICE” entries followed several tense months in Chicago during which federal immigration agents caravanned around the city making arrests and deploying tear gas and other chemical irritants at protesters. Federal agents fatally shot one man, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas Gonzalez</a>, and wounded a woman, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, in separate incidents.</p><p>Protests occurred regularly around the city and at the ICE processing facility in suburban Broadview.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >ICE agents were also deployed</a> to airports across the country, including to O'Hare Airport, on Monday amid a partial government shutdown that has left TSA officers working without pay for weeks.</p><p>“This name derives from our city’s legacy of standing up for justice, dignity and the rights of all people no matter where they come from,” Johnson said. “I want to take this moment to reiterate that Chicago does not want ICE on our streets, in our airports nor in our city. Chicago believes in abolishing ICE.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Zubaer Khan</i></p>
author: Kade Heather

title: Alcaldesa de Broadview exige cierre de instalación de ICE y el reembolso de pérdidas económicas del suburbio
summary: <p>La alcaldesade Broadview, suburbio al oeste de Chicago, está pidiendo al gobierno federal que cierre un centro de detención de inmigrantes “de facto” que fue el epicentro de protestas —y respuestas violentas por parte de agentes federales— que envolvieron al pequeño suburbio el otoño pasado.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/10/04/broadview-mayor-katrina-thompson-ice-detention-center-arrests-kristi-noem-gregory-bovino" target="_blank" >La alcaldesa Katrina Thompson</a> también está solicitando a las autoridades federales un reembolso de más de $700,000 para cubrir los costos operativos incurridos por la Municipalidad y las pérdidas económicas sufridas por dos negocios adyacentes a las instalaciones del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, la intensa campaña de deportación que alcanzó su punto máximo de septiembre a noviembre.</p><p>Thompson presentó las solicitudes durante una visita a Washington, D.C., a principios de este mes y en una carta dirigida a varios miembros de la delegación congresional de Illinois.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2b0000" name="module-2b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Broadview no pidió este operativo, y nuestros residentes, nuestros oficiales de policía, nuestros bomberos, nuestros dueños de negocios no deberían ser quienes paguen por ello”, dijo Thompson en un comunicado de prensa el martes. “Abogué por el reembolso federal para comunidades como la nuestra afectadas por operativos de ICE, enfatizando que los contribuyentes locales no deberían asumir el costo de responsabilidades federales. También insistí en el cierre del Centro de Procesamiento de ICE en Broadview, centrándonos en la dignidad, la seguridad y una visión más fuerte para nuestra comunidad”.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Archivo Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Los costos municipales asociados con la respuesta a la actividad cerca de la instalación de ICE ascendieron a $361,536, según funcionarios de Broadview.</p><p>Registros obtenidos por el Chicago Sun-Times a través de una solicitud de la ley de Libertad de Información (FOIA) muestran que $71,185 de esa suma se pagaron en horas extras para la policía, con más de $3,000 destinados a equipos de protección personal adicionales para los oficiales. El suburbio gastó aproximadamente $41,000 en costos legales, incluido un juicio federal para retirar una cerca erigida alrededor de la instalación de ICE. Las transferencias en ambulancia desde la dirección de la instalación de ICE costaron casi $250,000. Y las horas extras para el personal de ambulancias y bomberos costaron cerca de $12,100.</p><p>Incluso antes del reembolso federal solicitado, aún no estaba claro si el poblado recuperaría alguna parte de ese dinero, como los transportes de paramédicos que podrían ser pagados a través del seguro de Medicaid.</p><p>Los funcionarios de Broadview también señalaron pérdidas de $353,813 para dos negocios locales dentro de dos cuadras de la instalación de ICE: Reynolds Advanced Materials y Wagner Brass Foundry, Inc. Ninguno de los negocios hizo comentarios de inmediato el martes.</p><p>La agitación que sacudió el suburbio, que tiene aproximadamente 8,000 residentes, en otoño se trasladó a los jardines frontales y patios traseros de muchos vecinos. Cientos de personas se presentaron casi a diario para protestar frente a la instalación donde la gran mayoría de los inmigrantes arrestados durante el Operativo Midway Blitz fueron llevados para su procesamiento antes de ser trasladados a centros de detención en el Medio Oeste.</p><p>Las condiciones descritas por los detenidos y los defensores como “inhumanas” se agravaron en el edificio sobrepoblado, donde las personas dormían en el suelo con acceso limitado a comida o agua.</p><p>Los manifestantes, incluidos miembros del clero, fueron recibidos con la fuerza de agentes federales de ICE y de la Protección de Aduanas y Fronteras (CBP) que a menudo perseguían a los manifestantes por los vecindarios y disparaban bolas de goma y gas lacrimógeno contra las multitudes.</p><p>En su carta a los legisladores, Thompson solicitó ayuda para cerrar la instalación y transferir su propiedad del gobierno federal al suburbio para desarrollarlo como un museo. El “Broadview Justice Corridor”, como llamó al proyecto, convertiría la instalación de ICE en un “centro nacional dedicado a la historia de la inmigración, la educación en derechos civiles, el liderazgo cívico y el turismo cultural”.</p><p>“Esta transformación convertiría un sitio asociado con el miedo, las protestas y la división en uno que promueve la educación, la reconciliación y el diálogo nacional”, escribió Thompson en la carta, estimando que la propuesta podría atraer hasta 250,000 visitantes anuales y generar hasta $31 millones en actividad económica.</p><p>Un portavoz de Broadview dijo que Thompson aún no ha recibido respuesta a su apelación a los dos senadores y seis representantes, todos demócratas.</p><p>Pero es poco probable que influya en la administración de línea dura del presidente Donald Trump, que ha buscado abrir nuevos centros de detención de inmigrantes en el último año en lugar de cerrar cualquier instalación de ICE. Algunos de los legisladores que recibieron la apelación de Thompson fueron criticados por funcionarios de la administración y se les negó la entrada a la instalación de Broadview el año pasado cuando intentaron inspeccionar las condiciones.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

in Chicago, the city and its sanctuary policies have landed back into the national spotlight following the fatal shooting of Loyola University student Sheridan Gorman, 18. Her death has become a rallying cry for politicians demanding stricter immigration enforcement, as alleged gunman Jose G. Medina is a Venezuelan immigrant.</p><p><b>Trading blame</b>: Trump called Gorman’s killing "devastating" and blamed the "open door policy" of President Joe Biden. Other Republicans have directed their anger at Gov. JB Pritzker and Mayor Brandon Johnson. But Pritzker said failures within the system "extend beyond the borders of Illinois." At a Tuesday news conference, he said, "They’re national failures — a failure to have comprehensive immigration reform, a failure of the president to follow his own edict to go after the worst of the worst."</p><p><b>Politicizing murders</b>: Gorman’s death is quickly becoming as symbolic to Republicans as the murder of Laken Riley, a Georgia nursing student slain in 2024 by Jose Antonio Ibarra, a Venezuelan native who was in the U.S. without legal status. The Trump administration often invokes Riley’s name to justify mass deportations. But research including a <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-wtdhldy-l-u/" target="_blank" >Northwestern University study</a> from 2024 shows immigrants are consistently less and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-wtdhldy-l-p/" target="_blank" >Dan Mihalopoulos</a></h5><p><b>Fraud investigation</b>: When Debra Parker was appointed to the Chicago Housing Authority board in 2018, she was touted as the first person with a housing voucher to serve as a board member. Eight years later, she’s fighting to keep her seat and the voucher itself, after an internal investigation by the CHA revealed that she committed fraud, according to a copy of the hearing officer’s decision reviewed by the Sun-Times and WBEZ.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The 62-page decision became public Tuesday, in response to a court motion filed on behalf of WBEZ and the Sun-Times. Parker currently receives a subsidy to rent a four-bedroom home on the city’s South Side, according to records. However, the document indicates Parker and her son — who both are supposed to be living at the South Side home — have actually been residing with her fiancé, Charles Bell, in a luxury high-rise in River North.</p><p><b>Key quote</b>: CHA Board Chair and interim Operating Chairman Matthew Brewer told Mayor Johnson he should consider removing Parker. Records show Parker sued the CHA and Brewer in Cook County Circuit Court, seeking an emergency hearing to prevent the housing subsidy from being taken away. Asked for comment Tuesday, Parker said, "Y’all so obsessed with me. Do what you do," and hung up the phone. She then called back and said she "never committed any kind of fraud in my life. I’m 59 years old and never ever been involved in anything like that."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-wtdhldy-l-b/" target="_blank" ><b>READ
