Narcisse has been linked to controversies in previous roles, leading some to question how he became a finalist.</p><p><b>Controversy and lawsuit</b>: When Narcisse was superintendent of Louisiana’s East Baton Rouge Parish Schools in 2023, families sued him and the school board, alleging the district misled parents when it promoted a career fair that included overt religious messaging. Plaintiffs claim organizers split high schoolers by gender and had boys compete in physical contests while girls were "graphically lectured by pastors and other religious figures about virginity, rape, abuse, and suicide and were told to 'forgive' their rapists and abusers." Narcisse has said he was "not aware of any religious components."</p><p><b>Critics and supporters</b>: Some teachers and ex-school board members who worked alongside Narcisse have criticized his leadership style, saying he has a bold vision for education but sometimes overlooks community concerns. But supporters say his initiatives focus on what’s best for students and that the pushback stems from resistance to altering the status quo.</p><p><a class="Link" This got a Curious City listener wondering: What was the city’s first art gallery?</p><p><b>It depends</b>: Naming Chicago’s first art gallery depends on what one considers a gallery at all. In the 1840s, exclusive spaces opened, many of which called themselves galleries. These were often places for patrons to see expensive art for sale, such as an auction house or an art dealer, according to Anne Helmreich, director of the Archives of American Art at the Smithsonian Institution. It wasn’t until 1865 that Chicago saw the modern idea of a commercial art gallery: Crosby’s Opera House and Art Gallery. The space was immense in size and scope, complete with 18-foot ceilings and a skylight.</p><p><b>Lack of representation</b>: Most 19th-century art in commercial galleries was created by wealthy white men with access to art supplies and education. Native artists in the Great Lakes region made intricate beadwork and wove other designs, but these works were often displayed at fairs as artifacts. And the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition had the potential to exhibit achievements of Black people nearly 30 years after the end of slavery, but fair organizers refused to allow them a title: Suburbs also home to affordable housing shortage
summary: <p>In <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/06/chicago-225-000-affordable-rental-units-poorest-residents-nlihc-report" >“Chicago area short nearly 225,000 affordable rental units for its poorest residents, report finds,</a>" Sun-Times reporter Abby Miller highlights a staggering reality: Our region is failing to meet the housing needs of its most vulnerable residents.</p><p>While the data often centers on the city of Chicago, this crisis extends far beyond city limits. In the suburbs, where the <a class="Link" href="https://hodc.org/" target="_blank" >Housing Opportunity Development Corporatio</a>n does most of its work, the need is just as real, even if it is less visible.</p><p>Poverty exists in every community, including those often perceived as stable or well-resourced. But in suburban areas, it can be harder to see and even harder to address. Each municipality has its own zoning rules, political dynamics and levels of investment in affordable housing. This patchwork approach makes it more difficult to create the scale of housing our region truly needs.</p><p>Behind every statistic is a person. It is the parent who can finally afford both rent and groceries when housing is within reach. It is the senior who no longer has to choose between medication and staying in their home. It is the individual with a disability who can live with dignity in a safe, stable community.</p><p>When we talk about a shortage of 225,000 homes, we are really talking about thousands of people forced into impossible choices every day. It is this issue that we work to address every day.</p><p>Affordable housing is not just about the buildings we develop and manage; it is about stability, health, and opportunity. When people have a home they can afford, they are better able to work, care for their families, and actively contribute to their communities.</p><p>We know what solutions are needed: deeper investment in affordable housing, expanded rental assistance and stronger regional collaboration that includes both the city and the suburbs. What we need now is the collective will to act.</p><p>Because everyone — no matter their income or ZIP code — deserves a place to call home.</p><p><i>Richard Koenig, executive director, Housing Opportunity Development Corporation</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-470000" name="module-470000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Republican policies failed slain Loyola student </h3><p>My deepest sympathies to the Gorman family for the unimaginable horror of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" >Sheridan’s </a>murder.</p><p>I agree with the Gorman family that the fatal shooting resulted from "the policies and failures that allowed this individual to remain in a position to commit this crime."</p><p>But let's be clear that this tragedy is the result of Republican policies — not because of Illinois sanctuary policies. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott shouldn't have sent migrants to Illinois at taxpayers' expense. Republicans should have had policies in place to integrate the migrants into the U.S. immigration system.</p><p>A bipartisan border bill was crafted in 2024, but Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2024/03/13/chaos-and-cruelty-at-the-border-suit-republicans-agenda" >urged Republicans to oppose it</a>, so he could make it an election issue.</p><p>It was U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection officers who failed. While they were terrorizing children, assaulting and murdering people — American citizens and noncitizens — they didn't find Jose Medina before he could shoot Sheridan.</p><p><i>Beth Najberg</i>, <i>Near North Side</i></p><h3>Sanctuary laws led to student’s killing </h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" >Jose Medina</a> is NOT a "migrant" ("Venezuelan migrant charged with murder of Loyola student"). He is what I call an "illegal." Giant difference. </p><p>The Sun-Times print edition headline that called him a migrant insults people who came here legally, followed our laws and all due process to gain entry and citizenship.</p><p>Sheridan Gorman's murder is on the sanctuary state and cities' policies of Joe Biden, JB Pritzker and Brandon Johnson. Again, it's innocent Americans who pay.</p><p><i>Jim Lanham, Joliet</i></p><h3>Protecting alleged abusers like Chávez is damaging </h3><p>César Chávez allegedly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/03/18/allegations-of-abuse-by-cesar-chavez-sadden-shock-chicagos-latino-community" >sexually assaulted</a> children and young female volunteers within his organization, recent reports show. But during his lifetime, he enjoyed his international status as a revered labor leader.</p><p>The women who have come forward to speak about the vile abuse they suffered are still hurting. Some of the abuse was revealed when Chávez was alive. But, it seems, no one wanted to taint the image of an icon. No one wanted the farmworker rights movement to suffer.</p><p>So, at this juncture, what must be done in light of the allegations? Many <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/03/20/leaders-at-southwest-side-elementary-school-named-for-cesar-chavez-moving-to-potentially-rename-school" >schools and streets</a> have been named after Chávez. His birthday, March 31, was honored in California for years. It won't happen next week, though.</p><p>The character of people is largely defined by the life they lead when no one is watching and doors are locked. What character do they truly represent? Sexual abuse that children and young adults experience alters the course of their lives. Glorifying the abuser doesn't help the abused. What lesson is being taught when the abuser is continually exalted?</p><p>Keeping quiet only helps the abuser, as the abuse will continue with others. The farmworker rights movement has consisted of volunteers across the country who push for and implement the change that is needed. The movement wasn't and isn't César Chávez. He took advantage of his position as a leader and used it to sexually abuse children and others. What now?</p><p><i>Harriette Dawson, Glencoe</i></p><h3>Penny for Trump voters’ thoughts </h3><p>We are at the point at which it is hardly worth commenting on Donald Trump's vicious response to the death of former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/21/robert-mueller-former-fbi-director-who-probed-trump-ties-to-russia-dies-at-81" >FBI Director Robert Mueller</a>, as such outrages by him have become as common as the sun rising. Trump's shamelessness and delight in inflicting pain are such well-established facts that the editor reading this is likely to be thinking, "That's obvious" and reaching for the "delete" button.</p><p>What is not obvious, and what I will always wonder about, is: What portion of 2024 Trump voters, despite ample evidence, did not grasp these facts? How might their lives be negatively affected by having such a president? And what portion actually regarded these antisocial characteristics as selling points?</p><p><i>Curt Fredrikson, Mokena</i></p><p></p><h3></h3>

title: Sheridan Gorman’s killing puts Chicago back at the center of America's bitter fight over immigration
summary: <p>Months after President Donald Trump ended a pummeling deportation blitz in Chicago, the city and its “sanctuary” policies have been thrust back into the national spotlight following the fatal shooting of an 18-year-old college student.</p><p>As loved ones and fellow Loyola University Chicago students mourn freshman Sheridan Gorman, her death has become a rallying cry for politicians demanding stricter immigration enforcement. The alleged gunman, Jose G. Medina, is a Venezuelan immigrant.</p><p>Trump said Gorman’s killing was “devastating” and placed blame on the “open door policy” of his predecessor, Joe Biden. Other Republicans have directed their anger at Gov. JB Pritzker and Mayor Brandon Johnson. </p><p>“JB Pritzker’s soft on crime policies must come to an end,” Darren Bailey, the Republican challenging the governor in the November election, said in a statement Tuesday calling on Trump and Pritzker to work together. “Illinois families deserve accountability.”</p><p>But Pritzker said the “failures” within the immigration system “extend beyond the borders of Illinois.”</p><p>“They’re national failures — a failure to have comprehensive immigration reform, a failure of the president to follow his own edict to go after the worst of the worst,” Pritzker said at a Tuesday news conference in Springfield. “And in my view, we have a lot of work that we need to continue to do.”</p><h3><b>A tragic killing</b></h3><p>Gorman’s family has said they’re “gravely disappointed by the policies and failures that allowed this individual to remain in a position to commit this crime.”</p><p>“When systems fail — whether through release decisions, lack of coordination, or unwillingness to act — the consequences are not abstract. They are real,” the family said in a statement.</p><p>Gorman was walking with friends along the lakefront early Thursday when she spotted a masked gunman hiding in the shadows, prosecutors said. He fired one shot as the group tried to run away, striking Gorman in the back and killing her.</p><p>Medina has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >charged with first-degree murder</a>, attempted murder, aggravated discharge He had an active warrant in the theft case at the time of the killing, court records show.</p><p>Mayor Johnson on Tuesday said anyone who commits a crime in Chicago “regardless of their status,” will be held accountable. </p><p>“The proof is in how our Chicago Police Department swiftly interacted and was able to identify, establish the case and submit to the state’s attorney,” he told reporters, referring to the investigation of Gorman’s slaying.</p><p>Johnson said the purpose of the Welcoming City Ordinance and Illinois Trust Act — policies that prohibit local police from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement — are to ensure “undocumented individuals do not feel intimidated when they reach out to law enforcement.”</p><p>“We know that this President has not taken this situation and this challenge in our country seriously,” said Johnson. “Because my question would be: Isn’t it time for the President of the United States of America and congress to actually act and pass comprehensive immigration reform?” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1a0000" with the Gorman family. </p><p>“When something like this happens — a tragedy where a young person is gunned down — you automatically think about your own children. You just do,” Johnson said. “There’s no words that one could express that could properly console a family that lost their baby. My condolences to the Gorman family. I’m gonna continue to pray for their strength.” </p><p>When the Trump administration launched Operation Midway Blitz last September, officials said the immigration enforcement campaign was targeting “criminal illegal aliens” who’d flocked to Chicago and Illinois because of sanctuary policies. In the two and a half months that followed, scores of masked agents arrested thousands of people — though the majority had no criminal records. </p><p>Agents, primarily led by outgoing U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, used extreme force throughout the campaign. They frequently deployed tear gas and pepper balls on residential streets. And immigration agents shot two people, seriously wounding Marimar Martinez and killing Silverio Villegas González in separate incidents.</p><p>After Chicago, Trump sent a surge of agents to Minneapolis. The campaign there turned out to be a breaking point for the administration, which struggled to justify the shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.</p><p>Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem was fired, and Bovino was sent back to his normal post in southern California. He is now retiring.</p><h3><b>‘Demand accountability’</b></h3><p>Gorman’s death is quickly becoming as symbolic to Republicans as the murder of Laken Riley, a Georgia nursing student slain in 2024 by Jose Antonio Ibarra, a Venezuelan native who was in the U.S. without legal status.</p><p>The Trump administration often invokes Riley’s name to justify mass deportations. The talking point remains that “open border” policies by the Biden administration led to such tragic deaths.</p><p>But research, including a <a class="Link" href="https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2024/03/immigrants-are-significantly-less-likely-to-commit-crimes-than-the-us-born" target="_blank" >Northwestern University study</a> from 2024, shows immigrants were consistently less likely to commit crimes than those born in the U.S.</p><p>Riley’s family in March 2024 told <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/laken-riley-dad-today-interview-rcna143742" target="_blank" >NBC News</a> they did not want her name to be used in public debates about immigration.</p><p>Last year, DHS dedicated Operation Midway Blitz to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/09/08/operation-midway-blitz-katie-abraham-illinois-dhs-kristi-noem-donald-trump" target="_blank" >Katie Abraham</a>, one of two women killed in an Urbana drunken driving crash in 2025, allegedly by an undocumented Guatemalan man who fled the scene.</p><p>Trump and other Republicans had previously highlighted the case and called Abraham’s family target="_blank" >testimony by Pritzker</a>, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul.</p><p>Joe Abraham, Katie Abraham’s father, has become a vocal proponent of Trump’s immigration policies, including heaping praise on the Chicago deportation operation, which he said was about creating an immigration system that was “humane and secure.”</p><p>“It would be unjust and unreasonable to separate my family’s loss from the policies that failed us,” Abraham said in an October 2025 Chicago Tribune op-ed.</p><p>“We did everything right. We worked hard, obeyed the law, paid our taxes, and trusted that government would protect us in return. That trust was broken. Our leaders — from the governor’s office on down — have treated immigration as a numbers game, not as a matter of public safety or national security.”</p><p>Joe Abraham this week wrote on social media that Gorman’s death marked “another young life lost to preventable violence in Illinois.”</p><p>“How many more? Enough is enough.”</p><p>Denise Lorence, Katie Abraham’s mother, has <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/10/21/opinion-katie-abraham-operation-midway-blitz/" target="_blank" >countered his views</a>, writing in October that her daughter would not want to be associated with Trump’s deportation efforts.</p><p>“Katie would not want to be associated with an operation in which kids witness their parents being taken into custody on their way to or from school,” she wrote. “She wouldn’t support scaring kids with the use of military efforts in their neighborhoods or in their apartment.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/24/heres-what-to-know-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >What to know about the killing of Sheridan Gorman</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" target="_blank" >Trump decries Loyola student’s killing while pushing deportations; suspect’s court date postponed</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >Man charged with murder of Loyola student Sheridan Gorman</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Finalist for CPS CEO courted controversy in past jobs, but defenders praise his bold vision
summary: <p>When Meisha Porter, the former leader of New York City’s school system, withdrew her name from consideration to become the CEO of Chicago Public Schools last week, the district suddenly found itself with just two candidates for the job.</p><p>One of them is Macquline King, who has been serving as CPS’ interim leader since June. The former CPS principal did not make the cut to be a finalist back in the fall. But some board members have recently warmed up to her, citing how she’s handled contentious issues, such as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/08/14/majority-of-cps-board-demands-a-budget-with-pension-payment-and-loan-rebuffing-proposal-from-cps-leaders" target="_blank" ><u>the budget process</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>responding to aggressive immigration enforcement</u></a> that impacted schools.</p><p>Given the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/20/meisha-porter-withdraws-from-chicago-public-schools-ceo-search/" target="_blank" ><u>dwindling field</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/13/cps-board-names-3-finalists-to-lead-district-interim-ceo-king-former-nyc-east-baton-rouge-schools-chiefs" target="_blank" ><u>protracted search</u></a>, King’s standing appears to be rising.</p><p>The other is Sito Narcisse, a former leader of Louisiana’s second-largest school district who has been linked to controversies in his previous roles, leading some to question how he made it to be a finalist to lead the third-largest school district in the country with many red flags.</p><p>His work at times has been polarizing. In Baton Rouge, families sued him and the district over a controversial event he promoted. Early in his career in Boston, Narcisse was criticized for making sweeping changes at the school he led with little or no community input, a concern that would follow him.</p><p>Supporters say Narcisse has been a victim of local politics that have stymied his vision, calling him a “transformational leader” who moves fast to drive change and increase positive outcomes for students.</p><p>For his part, Narcisse says that while not everyone has supported all his moves, he’s made decisions with the best interests of students in mind.</p><p>“In every place I have been, outcomes for students and culture for staff have improved,” Narcisse wrote in an email to the Sun-Times/WBEZ.</p><h3>Lawsuit and ties to ousted leader </h3><p>One of the most notable controversies happened when Narcisse was superintendent of Louisiana’s East Baton Rouge Parish Schools, which he led from 2021 to 2024. It was the only time he’s served as the top leader of a school district.</p><p>Families filed a lawsuit against Narcisse and the school board in 2023 <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/parents-students-complain-east-baton-rouge-schools-field-trip-was-more-like-church-service/article_97dc38c2-3a0d-11ed-a388-3f7b65892ceb.html" target="_blank" ><u>alleging the district misled parents </u></a>when it promoted a career fair for seniors hosted at a local church that included overt religious messaging.</p><p>The families allege that organizers split high schoolers into groups by gender and had the boys compete in physical contests while girls were “graphically lectured by pastors and other religious figures about virginity, rape, abuse, and suicide and were told to ‘forgive’ their rapists and abusers,” according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Narcisse <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93PB0iA_Uiw&t=116s" target="_blank" ><u>appeared on local television</u></a> to promote the “Day of Hope” alongside one of the co-founders of the organizers, 29:11 Academy, whose name is a reference to the Bible, <a class="Link" href="https://www.2911mentor.com/" target="_blank" ><u>according to its website</u></a>. They talked about how the event could help students find careers and make good choices, but didn’t mention any religious components.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/judge-keeps-baton-rouge-school-board-in-day-of-hope-suit/article_397de226-8b23-11ef-8a4e-432f40734807.html" target="_blank" ><u>Board members have said</u> t</a>hat they were out of the loop because the district allows the superintendent to award contracts worth less than $10,000 without board approval. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbrz.com/news/day-of-hope-cost-school-system-only-200-less-than-amount-required-for-school-board-approval/" target="_blank" ><u>This contract totaled $9,800.</u></a></p><p>Narcisse has denied the allegations in the lawsuit, which is ongoing, and the case is heading to a possible trial, according to court records.</p><p>In response to questions about the event, Narcisse wrote in an email that the “Day of Hope” was established 10 years before he became superintendent and he was “not aware of any religious components.” He said “the focus was on motivating students to stay in school, explore their futures, and think about next steps.”</p><p>Michael Gaudet, who was on the East Baton Rouge school board at the time, and is still a member, defended Narcisse, saying the situation was “drummed up” by an attorney “who is a publicity hound.” <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/participants-defend-controversial-day-of-hope-event-to-school-board-we-all-enjoyed-it/article_e3fd0e5a-45b8-11ed-bc0d-c7a6b674f638.html" target="_blank" ><u>Some participants said they enjoyed the event.</u></a></p><p>“We could have probably done a better job of monitoring that, but none of the allegations have ever been proven true,” Gaudet said.</p><p>He pointed to the school board’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/no-evidence-for-day-of-hope-controversy-school-leader-says-board-could-seek-investigation/article_c20ac41a-45b6-11ed-9962-4f58e489f0d1.html" target="_blank" ><u>internal investigation</u></a> which “found no evidential proof” of the claims, though several students and parents spoke to local news outlets to express concerns. Some board members introduced a resolution calling for an independent investigation, but <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbrz.com/news/ebr-schools-superintendent-says-criticism-of-day-of-hope-has-been-unfair/" target="_blank" ><u>that was voted down</u></a>.</p><p>Gaudet said the situation was like “a tempest in a teapot… There was nothing to it.”</p><p>In 2023 the school board <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/narcisse-rejected-next-baton-rouge-schools-leader-unclear/article_afc3b158-9539-11ee-84e6-bb9fa648edc7.html" target="_blank" ><u>narrowly voted not to renew Narcisse’s contract</u></a> amid a debate about a pay raise. He agreed to a voluntary buyout and stepped down after three years in charge. <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/narcisse-supporters-rally-to-keep-baton-rouge-schools-chief/article_d7191668-9dee-11ee-bc28-0b3178838957.html" target="_blank" ><u>A group of supporters rallied to keep him. </u></a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a00000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Michael Gaudet, a school board member in East Baton Rouge Parish, says his school district parted ways with Narcisse for reasons unrelated to performance.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>East Baton Rouge Parish School Board</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gaudet said the decision not to renew Narcisse’s contract wasn’t due to his performance. He said that six new board members were voted onto the nine-member body during Narcisse’s tenure, and most wanted to move in a different direction.</p><p>A few years earlier, Narcisse faced a turbulent tenure as the chief of schools at Metro Nashville Public Schools, where he was second-in-command to director of schools Shawn Joseph. Joseph hired Narcisse after the two worked together at Prince George’s County Public Schools in suburban Maryland.</p><p>Joseph’s three-year tenure in Nashville was <a class="Link" href="https://www.newschannel5.com/news/newschannel-5-investigates/what-you-need-to-know-about-shawn-josephs-controversies" target="_blank" ><u>marked by a string of controversies</u></a>, including claims that he mishandled allegations of sexual harassment against a principal and complaints that he attempted to award no-bid contracts. A veteran administrator also accused the district of pay discrimination between men and women in high-level positions and said Narcisse, her boss at the time, <a class="Link" href="https://www.newschannel5.com/news/newschannel-5-investigates/metro-schools/administrator-accuses-mnps-of-pay-discrimination-retaliation" target="_blank" ><u>questioned her performance</u></a> when she dug into the district’s salary data.</p><p>In response to questions from the Sun-Times/WBEZ, Narcisse said he did not make salary decisions when he worked in Nashville.</p><p>The board eventually <a class="Link" href="https://wpln.org/post/shawn-josephs-contract-is-terminated-during-heated-school-board-meeting/" target="_blank" ><u>decided to buy out Joseph’s contract.</u></a> Narcisse voluntarily left the district shortly after.</p><p>Amy Frogge, who was on the school board in Nashville at the time and was among Joseph’s most outspoken critics, said that while Joseph was the face of the controversies, Narcisse likely knew what the superintendent was up to as his No. 2.</p><p>"They were extremely close, they were friends,” Frogge said. "It was a painful few years in Nashville when they were there.”</p><h3>Some bristle at leadership style, while others celebrate it</h3><p>Some teachers and former school board members who worked alongside Narcisse have criticized his leadership style, saying he has a bold vision for education but has sometimes overlooked community concerns.</p><p>Dawn Chanet Collins, who served on the East Baton Rouge Parish School Board when Narcisse was superintendent, said his ideas sometimes clashed with those of longtime staff and community members who felt he needed to better understand the makeup of the district before making changes.</p><p>“Each instance where he made decisions that resulted in public chaos he was advised otherwise by staff who would explain the possible consequences of various decisions,” said Collins, who was often vocal when she disagreed with his decisions. “He appeared to not either hear or not care about the potential issues that were being raised.”</p><p>For example, when Narcisse wanted to equitably deal with staffing shortages ahead of the 2022-2023 school year, he <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/as-parents-teachers-protest-baton-rouge-school-re-staffing-school-board-seeks-explanation/article_a1886f92-d619-11ec-b975-874bd1939115.html" target="_blank" ><u>decided to reassign teachers and other staff</u></a> to schools that were understaffed. Hundreds of employees were told their positions were eliminated and they could apply for the vacant positions at other schools or be reassigned.</p><p>It’s the kind of shakeup that would be hard to pull off without criticism. <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/superintendent-faces-protest-loads-of-questions-on-re-staffing-of-baton-rouge-schools/article_7509cdf4-d7a8-11ec-aa1e-ab8f10afd905.html" target="_blank" ><u>Some community members supported the initiative</u></a>, saying those speaking out against it mostly came from schools that already had plenty of resources.</p><p>But employees who were happy with their roles were upset, saying it disrupted school communities and programs and took away principal autonomy. Parents protested at board meetings. Several board members criticized Narcisse for not working with them on the changes. One said his <a class="Link" href="https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/education/superintendent-faces-protest-loads-of-questions-on-re-staffing-of-baton-rouge-schools/article_7509cdf4-d7a8-11ec-aa1e-ab8f10afd905.html" target="_blank" ><u>top-down management was “breeding mistrust.”</u></a></p><p>Narcisse’s supporters say his initiatives focus on what’s best for students and the pushback stems from resistance to altering the status quo.</p><p>“When you talk about change, that can sometimes be uncomfortable but it’s for the better good of students,” said Dadrius Lanus, who served as school board president in East Baton Rouge Parish when Narcisse was superintendent and is still on the board.</p><p>“Every superintendent is going to have some pushback from the community, but the question is, the moves that he was able to make, did it better our district? And I would say absolutely,” Lanus said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ac0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dadrius Lanus of the East Baton Rouge Parish School Board credited Narcisse with helping to expand kindergarten access and get more high schoolers college credit or career credentials during his time in the district.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>East Baton Rouge Parish School Board</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lanus pointed to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cgcs.org/resources/newsroom/urban-educator/digital-urban-educator-junejuly-2025/class-of-2025-graduate-stories/east-baton-rouge-students-make-history" target="_blank" ><u>“Pathways to Bright Futures” program</u></a> that Narcisse spearheaded as an example. The program helps high schoolers earn college credits or career credentials. Lanus also said Narcisse was responsible for expanding kindergarten access in the district, among other accomplishments.</p><p>But to Ursula Parkerson, a teacher in East Baton Rouge Parish, Narcisse “came in like a wrecking ball” and pushed forward with his plans despite concerns from the community. That dynamic led to low morale among educators, said Parkerson, a member of the East Baton Rouge Parish Association of Educators, a local teachers union.</p><p>“He was wanting to make big changes and not really caring, it felt like to us, about who got railroaded in the process,” Parkerson said.</p><p>Narcisse faced similar criticisms early in his career, too. As the leader of a struggling public high school in Boston, he tried several controversial turnaround strategies including eliminating the grade “D,” establishing single-sex classrooms and getting rid of many staffers. Three-quarters of the school’s teachers and administrators left, <a class="Link" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20141017071730/https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2012/06/24/troubled-english-high-school-showing-little-improvement-after-three-tumultuous-years-under-untested-headmaster-sito-narcisse/XNwPoz4RLD02uCdWePvEfK/story.html" target="_blank" ><u>according to The Boston Globe</u></a>, and while test scores ticked up slightly, the dropout rate, failure rate and absentee rate all rose, as well.</p><p>Gaudet pushed back on critics who said Narcisse didn’t take input from others into account, though he conceded that Narcisse might have moved too quickly at times in Baton Rouge.</p><p>“I would say his philosophy towards leadership is always what’s best for the kids and his leadership style is very collaborative,” Gaudet said. “I think maybe he tried to do a little too much too fast, but it was in a desire to move the needle.”</p><p>Lanus said he wished East Baton Rouge Parish had kept Narcisse on.</p><p>“If Chicago Public Schools were to select him, they are literally selecting somebody who can take the district to the next level,” Lanus said. “They’re going to get a transformational leader.”</p>

title: What to know about the killing of Sheridan Gorman
summary: <p>The fatal shooting of Loyola student Sheridan Gorman has rocked the school’s community and attracted national attention.</p><p>Here’s what to know about the incident and where things currently stand in the alleged killer's criminal case.</p><h3>Who was Sheridan Gorman? </h3><p>Gorman was an 18-year-old freshman at Loyola University Chicago from Yorktown, New York. She was a member of the campus Christian organization Cru and was studying business.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" target="_blank" >Friends and family describe her</a> as a kind and positive person who always had a smile on her face.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-230000" </div><p>“She was full of life, full of kindness, and full of a love that she gave freely to everyone around her,” Gorman’s parents wrote in a statement. “She made people feel seen. She made people feel valued. Whether it was her friends, her family, or someone she had just met, Sheridan had a way of leaving people better than she found them.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/support-for-the-gorman-family-cz6ns" target="_blank" >A fundraiser is gathering donations</a> for Gorman’s memorial and a scholarship in her honor. Over $150,000 was raised as of Tuesday.</p><h3>What happened to her? </h3><p>Gorman and her friends took an early morning stroll around 1:30 a.m. on March 19 to the pier at Tobey Prinz Beach — just north of the Rogers Park campus. They were hoping to capture photos of the city skyline and potentially the Northern Lights, her parents said in a statement.</p><p>Gorman was the first to reach the end of the pier when she spotted a masked gunman. He fired a single shot as Gorman and her friends fled, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" target="_blank" >according to prosecutors</a>.</p><div </figure> </div> </div><p>The friends ran for cover when the shot rang out. But then they saw Gorman on the ground and went to her aid. She had been shot in the back, prosecutors said — not in the head as police initially reported. She was pronounced dead at the scene, according to authorities.</p><p>One of Gorman’s friends who witnessed the shooting told the Sun-Times that “it didn’t seem like it was intentionally targeted toward any of us.”</p><p>“It seemed like he was there for a reason, and we were just [in the] wrong place, wrong time. I’m guessing, because there was not another shot after that. It was just one,” the friend said.</p><h3>Who is the suspect? </h3><p>Jose Medina, 25, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >was arrested and charged in Gorman’s murder</a>. He faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted murder and aggravated discharge of a firearm.</p><p>He has yet to make his first appearance in court because he is currently hospitalized with tuberculosis. A full detention hearing was postponed until Friday, but <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration " target="_blank" >prosecutors provided a brief accounting</a> of the shooting in court on Monday.</p><p>Video captured Medina walking from the beach into a building in the 6800 block of North Sheridan Road, according to an arrest report. He wore all black clothing and a mask and had a “distinct gait.”</p><p>Police recovered black clothing and a .40 caliber handgun inside Medina’s apartment, prosecutors said. The gun matched the shell casing found at the shooting scene.</p><p>The arrest report shows police worked closely with U.S. Customs and Border Protection during the investigation. CBP used facial recognition to identify the man in the video as Medina, according to the report.</p><p>Records show Medina was born in Venezuela and at one point lived in a temporary migrant shelter at the Leone Beach Park Field House.</p><p>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement issued an arrest detainer on March 22 naming Medina before police announced the charges. The Department of Homeland Security claims Medina entered the U.S. illegally. </p><p>Chicago police have not commented on his immigration status. Prosecutors also did not share that information in court Monday.</p><p>In May 2023, federal officials say he came into contact with Border Patrol agents and was released.</p><p>About a month later, he faced a single misdemeanor charge for shoplifting $132.50 of merchandise from the State Street Macy’s in June 2023. A judge issued a warrant for him in that case after he failed to appear for a court date. Records show the outstanding warrant is still active.</p><h3>How has Gorman’s death become politicized? </h3><p>President Donald Trump and his administration have used Gorman’s death to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" target="_blank" >justify his push for mass deportations</a>.</p><p>Acting Assistant DHS Secretary Lauren Bis claimed in a statement Gorman was “failed by open border policies and sanctuary politicians.”</p><p>This isn't the first time the Trump administration has used a young woman's death to make the case that undocumented immigrants put Americans in danger. However, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/23/chicago-crime-trump-sheridan-gorman-loyola-murder-shooting-deportation-immigration" target="_blank" >numerous studies have found</a> that immigrants without legal status are less likely to commit serious crimes than U.S.-born citizens.</p><p>The killing of Laken Riley, a nursing student in Georgia who was fatally attacked in 2024 by an immigrant, spurred federal legislation that mandates detention of undocumented immigrants accused of theft, burglary, assaulting a law enforcement officer and any crime that causes death or serious injury.</p><p>Operation Midway Blitz was dedicated to Katie Abraham, an Illinois native killed in 2025 by a drunken driver who allegedly lacked legal status. Notably, Abraham's mother <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/10/21/opinion-katie-abraham-operation-midway-blitz/" target="_blank" >wrote an op-ed</a> last fall decrying the administration's use of her daughter's name in immigration enforcement operations.</p><p>“Sheridan Gorman’s life was allegedly taken from her at the hands of a criminal alien shielded by the anti-American sanctuary policies of the city of Chicago and the state of Illinois,” U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said on social media Monday.</p><p>Legislation signed by former Illinois Gov. Bruce Rauner, a Republican, limits cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities. The Illinois TRUST Act generally bars police from sharing information with immigration agents or handing over people in custody unless a federal criminal warrant is issued.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker issued a response saying, “Violent crime has no place in our streets.”</p><p>“We expect the alleged perpetrator to be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law,” Pritzker said in a statement. “The Trump Administration needs to stop politicizing heinous tragedies and instead focus on real solutions, like reinstating federal funds to prevent violence that support our public safety efforts.”</p><p>Panas in Chicago, a group that works with Venezuelan migrants, <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/panasenchicago" target="_blank" >said in a statement</a> the organization stands with Gorman’s family.</p><p>“Violence does not represent us,” the statement reads. “The Venezuelan community is made up of hardworking individuals with values, faith and a genuine commitment to contributing positively to the society that has welcomed us. We categorically reject any act of violence, regardless of who commits it. One individual’s actions, no matter how serious, do not define an entire community.”</p><h3><b>What’s next in the case? </b></h3><p>Medina, who remains hospitalized with tuberculosis, is scheduled to make his first full court appearance on Friday for a pretrial detention hearing. Judge Luciano Panici ordered he remain in custody pending the full hearing.</p><p>A community vigil and a private service will be held for Gorman on March 28 in Yorktown, New York.</p>
author: Sun-Times staff

title: Broadview mayor demands closure of ICE facility, reimbursement of village, business losses
summary: <p>The mayor of west suburban Broadview is calling on the federal government to shut down a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/01/broadview-immigration-processing-center-detention-ice-dhs" target="_blank" ><u>de facto immigration detention cente</u></a><u>r</u> that was the epicenter of protests — and violent responses from federal agents — that engulfed the small village last fall.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/10/04/broadview-mayor-katrina-thompson-ice-detention-center-arrests-kristi-noem-gregory-bovino" target="_blank" ><u>Mayor Katrina Thompson</u></a> is also asking the feds for a more than $700,000 reimbursement to make up for operational costs incurred by the village and economic losses suffered by two businesses adjacent to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility during Operation Midway Blitz, the intense deportation campaign that peaked from September through November.</p><p>She made the requests during a visit to Washington, D.C., earlier this month and in a letter to several members of the Illinois congressional delegation.</p><p>“Broadview did not ask for this operation, and our residents, our police officers, our firefighters, our business owners should not be the ones paying for it,” Thompson was quoted as saying in a news release. “I advocated for federal reimbursement for communities like ours impacted by ICE operations, emphasizing that local taxpayers should not bear the cost of federal responsibilities. I also pushed for the closure of the Broadview ICE Processing Center, centering dignity, safety, and a stronger vision for our community.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mayor Katrina Thompson is looking to push Broadview past the trouble surrounding the ICE facility in the western suburb.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The municipal costs associated with responding to activity around the ICE facility amounted to $361,536, according to Broadview officials.</p><p>Records obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times through a freedom of information request show $71,185 of that sum was paid as police overtime, with more than $3,000 for additional personal protective equipment for officers. The village spent about $41,000 on legal costs, including for a federal lawsuit to remove a fence erected around the ICE facility. Ambulance transfers from the ICE facility’s address cost another nearly $250,000. And overtime for fire and ambulance personnel cost about $12,100.</p><p>Even before the requested federal reimbursement, it was still unclear whether the village would otherwise recoup any of that money, such as EMT transports that might be paid through Medicaid insurance.</p><p>Broadview officials also noted $353,813 in losses for two local businesses within two blocks of the ICE facility: Reynolds Advanced Materials and Wagner Brass Foundry, Inc.</p><p>The turmoil that roiled the village of about 8,000 residents in the fall spilled onto the front lawns and backyards of many neighbors. Hundreds of people showed up for near daily protests outside the facility where the vast majority of immigrants arrested during Operation Midway Blitz were taken for processing before being moved to detention facilities in the Midwest. Conditions described by detainees and advocates as “inhumane” festered in the overcrowded building, where people slept on floors with limited access to food or water.</p><p>Demonstrators, including clergy, were met with force from federal agents with ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection who often chased protesters through neighborhoods and shot rubber bullets and tear gas into the crowds.</p><p>In her letter to lawmakers, Thompson asked for help to close the facility and transfer its ownership from the federal government to the village for redevelopment as a museum. The “Broadview Justice Corridor,” as she called the project, would turn the ICE facility into a “national center dedicated to immigration history, civil rights education, civic leadership, and cultural tourism.</p><p>“This transformation would convert a site associated with fear, protest, and division into one that promotes education, reconciliation, and national dialogue,” Thompson wrote in the letter, estimating the proposal would draw up to 250,000 visitors annually and generate up to $31 million in economic activity.</p><p>Thompson’s appeal to the two senators and six representatives, all Democrats, is unlikely to sway President Donald Trump’s hard-line administration, which has looked to open new immigration detention centers in the past year rather than close any ICE facilities. Some of the lawmakers who received Thompson’s appeal were criticized by administration officials and denied entry to the Broadview facility last year as they sought to inspect the conditions.</p>

title: Trump condena el asesinato de estudiante de Loyola mientras promueve deportaciones
summary: <p>A medida que el presidente Donald Trump utilizó el “devastador” asesinato de la estudiante de la Universidad Loyola de Chicago, Sheridan Gorman, para justificar su impulso hacia las deportaciones masivas, el presunto hombre armado permanecía hospitalizado y se perdió su audiencia judicial inicial en la tarde del lunes.</p><p>José G. Medina, un inmigrante venezolano, fue <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/23/migrante-venezolano-acusado-de-asesinato-de-la-estudiante-de-la-universidad-loyola" target="_blank" >acusado de asesinato en primer grado</a>, intento de asesinato, descarga agravada de un arma de fuego y posesión ilegal de un arma en relación con el ataque del jueves cerca de la playa Tobey Prinz, según los registros judiciales del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Trump les dijo a los periodistas el lunes que había sido informado sobre el asesinato de Gorman, argumentando que el tiroteo mortal mostró la necesidad de intensificar los esfuerzos de aplicación de la ley de inmigración.</p><p>“Esta persona entró por la política de puerta abierta de [el expresidente] Joe Biden y tenemos otros”, dijo Trump. “Los estamos sacando por decenas de miles. Estamos haciendo un gran trabajo, pero es una pena”.</p><p>Medina, de 25 años, era buscado con una orden de arresto en un caso local de robo en tiendas en el momento de su último arresto.</p><p>La familia de Gorman dijo que estaban “profundamente decepcionados por las políticas y fracasos que permitieron que este individuo permaneciera en una posición para cometer este crimen”.</p><p>“Cuando los sistemas fallan —ya sea por decisiones de liberación, falta de coordinación o falta de voluntad para actuar— las consecuencias no son abstractas. Son reales”, dijo la familia en un comunicado.</p><p>“Y en nuestro caso, son permanentes. Este caso debe ser presentado en la máxima medida de la ley estatal y federal. No puede haber vacíos, no puede haber atajos, y no puede haber segundas oportunidades que pongan a otros en riesgo. La responsabilidad debe ser completa”.</p><p>Una <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/support-for-the-gorman-family-cz6ns" target="_blank" >recaudación de fondos en línea</a> que busca reunir dinero para un fondo memorial y de becas en honor a Gorman casi había alcanzado los $150,000 la tarde del lunes. La meta subió a $180,000.</p><p>Los fiscales proporcionaron pocos detalles adicionales sobre el caso criminal de Medina durante la breve audiencia del lunes.</p><p>Medina se perdió la corte porque actualmente está hospitalizado con tuberculosis, dijeron los funcionarios. El juez Luciano Panici ordenó que permaneciera "bajo custodia" a la espera de una audiencia completa el viernes.</p><p>Gorman, de 18 años, salió a caminar hacia la costa, justo al norte del campus de Loyola, temprano el jueves para tomar fotos del horizonte, dijeron los fiscales. Fue la primera en llegar al final del muelle cerca de la playa Tobey Prinz cuando vio al tirador enmascarado escondido cerca del faro.</p><p>Disparó un tiro mientras Gorman y sus amigos huían, dijeron los fiscales. Gorman fue alcanzada por un tiro en la espalda, no en la cabeza, como informó inicialmente la policía.</p><p>Una de las amigas de Gorman que presenció el tiroteo <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" target="_blank" >dijo al Chicago Sun-Times</a> que "no parecía que estuviera dirigido intencionadamente hacia ninguno de nosotros".</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Los oficiales del Departamento de Policía de Chicago investigan en el muelle de la playa Tobey Prinz después de que la estudiante de 18 años de la Universidad Loyola, Sheridan Gorman, fuera asesinada a tiros el jueves.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Un video captó a Medina caminando desde la escena hacia un edificio en la cuadra 6800 al norte de Sheridan Road, según un informe de arresto. Llevaba ropa completamente negra y una máscara y tenía una “caminata distintiva”.</p><p>La policía recuperó ropa negra y una pistola calibre .40 dentro del apartamento de Medina, dijeron los fiscales. El arma coincidía con el casquillo encontrado en la escena del tiroteo.</p><p>El informe de arresto muestra que la policía trabajó en estrecha colaboración con la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) durante la investigación. La CBP, que fue fundamental en la agresiva campaña de deportación en Chicago el año pasado, utilizó el reconocimiento facial para identificar al hombre en el video como Medina, según el informe.</p><p>CBP es parte del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) que identificó públicamente a Medina como el sospechoso antes de que los fiscales del Condado de Cook aprobaran los cargos. El departamento también anunció que había emitido una orden de detención para Medina.</p><p>DHS dijo que Medina había sido detenido por la Patrulla Fronteriza en mayo de 2023, liberado y luego arrestado nuevamente dos meses después por robo en tiendas. Tenía una orden activa en el caso de robo, según los registros judiciales.</p><p>La administración de Trump ha utilizado las muertes de otras jóvenes para argumentar que la inmigración indocumentada pone en peligro a los estadounidenses. Sin embargo, los esfuerzos por enmarcar el crimen como la fuerza motriz detrás de su misión de deportación han sido subvertidos en ocasiones por datos e investigaciones.</p><p>El asesinato de Laken Riley, una estudiante de enfermería en Georgia que fue fatalmente atacada por un inmigrante, impulsó una legislación que exige la detención y fortalece la aplicación de la ley contra inmigrantes indocumentados acusados de ciertos delitos.</p><p>El Operativo Midway Blitz, la campaña de deportación desenfrenada que azotó el área de Chicago el otoño pasado, fue dedicada a Katie Abraham, originaria de Illinois asesinada por un conductor ebrio que supuestamente carecía de estatus legal.</p><p>“La vida de Sheridan Gorman fue supuestamente arrebatada por un extranjero criminal protegido por las políticas de santuario antiamericanas de la Ciudad de Chicago y del estado de Illinois”, dijo el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) en las redes sociales el lunes.</p><p>El gobernador JB Pritzker emitió una respuesta el lunes, diciendo, "El crimen violento no tiene lugar en nuestras calles".</p><p>"Esperamos que el presunto perpetrador sea responsabilizado en la máxima medida de la ley", dijo Pritzker en un comunicado. "La administración de Trump necesita dejar de politizar tragedias atroces y en su lugar enfocarse en soluciones reales, como restablecer los fondos federales para prevenir la violencia que apoyen nuestros esfuerzos de seguridad pública".</p><p>Hablando después de la corte el lunes, el concejal Ray López (15º) instó a la Municipalidad y al estado a enmendar sus leyes "de una manera que tenga sentido", mientras aún se da la bienvenida a "aquellos que quieren estar aquí".</p><p>“Cuando tienes individuos que eligen involucrarse en comportamientos criminales peligrosos aquí en este país, si no son ciudadanos, no deberíamos darles la bienvenida”, dijo López. “No deberíamos darles refugio”.</p><p>Numerosos estudios han revelado que los inmigrantes sin estatus legal son menos propensos a cometer delitos graves que los ciudadanos nacidos en Estados Unidos.</p><p>Un estudio de 2024 financiado por el Instituto Nacional de Justicia que examina datos del Departamento de Seguridad Pública de Texas reveló que los inmigrantes indocumentados son arrestados a menos de la mitad de la tasa de ciudadanos nacidos en Estados Unidos por delitos violentos y de drogas, y a una cuarta parte de la tasa de ciudadanos nacidos en Estados Unidos por delitos contra la propiedad.</p><p>Y según el <a class="Link" href="https://www.migrationpolicy.org/content/immigrants-and-crime" target="_blank" >Instituto de Políticas Migratorias</a>, los estudios han demostrado que los inmigrantes no aumentan las tasas de criminalidad en las comunidades locales donde se establecen. El instituto cita un estudio de la <a class="Link" href="https://www.umass.edu/preferen/You%20Must%20Read%20This/Lee%20Immigration%20and%20Crime.pdf" target="_blank" >Universidad de Massachusetts</a> que conecta la menor actividad delictiva, incluidos los crímenes violentos, con comunidades que tienen políticas de inmigración inclusivas.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

title: Despliegan a agentes de ICE en O'Hare mientras continúa el cierre parcial del gobierno que afecta a viajeros
summary: <p>Los agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) estuvieron presentes en el Aeropuerto O'Hare el lunes, luego de que la administración de Trump anunciara que los agentes ayudarían en la escasez de personal de seguridad del aeropuerto en todo el país en medio de la actual paralización parcial del gobierno.</p><p>Al menos una docena de agentes con ropa de ICE fueron vistos en las Terminales 1, 2 y 3 a finales de la mañana del lunes.</p><p>El presidente Donald Trump dejó claro el domingo que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/22/union-tsa-workers-push-back-demand-pay-after-trump-admin-deploys-ice-agents-in-airports-monday" target="_blank" >desplegaría agentes de ICE en los aeropuertos</a> de todo el país para asistir en las operaciones de seguridad de la Administración de Seguridad en el Transporte (TSA). Trump culpó a los problemas de personal de la TSA, que han provocado largas filas de seguridad en ocasiones, a los demócratas por no llegar a un acuerdo sobre un proyecto de ley para financiar el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS).</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e60000" name="module-e60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>O'Hare fue uno de los 14 aeropuertos donde se preveía el despliegue de agentes de ICE, según CNN.</p><p>Se esperaba que cerca de 75 agentes de ICE estuvieran asignados en O'Hare, según fuentes familiarizadas con el plan. Estaban monitoreando los carriles de salida y puntos de control, no realizando inspecciones de seguridad.</p><p>Los agentes vistos en O'Hare el lunes por un reportero del Sun-Times llevaban en su mayoría mascarillas, en contra de los deseos de Trump, quien dijo que prefiere que no las usen.</p><p>"Soy un GRAN defensor de que los agentes de ICE usen mascarillas mientras buscan y se ven obligados a lidiar con criminales peligrosos", escribió Trump el lunes en las redes sociales, y agregó, "Sin embargo, agradecería enormemente que NO USEN MASCARILLAS cuando ayuden a nuestro país a salir del CAOS causado por los demócratas en los aeropuertos, etc.".</p><p>El gobernador JB Pritzker dijo que el despliegue de agentes de ICE en los aeropuertos está "causando caos e infundiendo miedo".</p><p>“Es hora de que los aeropuertos de nuestra nación vuelvan a la normalidad”, comentó Pritzker en una publicación en redes sociales.</p><p>El alcalde Brandon Johnson declaró el lunes en un comunicado que su oficina está utilizando "todas las herramientas que tenemos para asegurar que las personas, sin importar su estatus migratorio, puedan viajar a y de Chicago de manera segura y sin acoso por parte del gobierno federal".</p><p>El representante Jesús "Chuy" García dijo que la presencia de agentes de ICE en los aeropuertos "no está haciendo que los viajeros estén más seguros ni abordando las largas filas de seguridad".</p><p>"En cambio, esta acción sin precedentes está haciendo que la gente tenga miedo de ir al aeropuerto y causando confusión y violencia, como el incidente anoche en San Francisco", dijo García, refiriéndose a la detención de una mujer y su hija por parte de agentes de ICE el domingo en el Aeropuerto de San Francisco.</p><p>Algunos viajeros de O'Hare dicen que ICE no debería estar en el aeropuerto</p><p>Luke Hoover y Mary Dickey, de North Center, se prepararon para largas filas de seguridad y llegaron tres horas antes de su vuelo a Nueva Zelanda para su luna de miel.</p><p>La pareja, al igual que varias personas que hablaron con el Sun-Times y WBEZ el lunes, dijo que la presencia de agentes de ICE les hizo dudar.</p><p>"No somos grandes fanáticos de esto”, dijo Hoover.</p><p>"Sólo [el] proceso de la TSA, tener personas que no están capacitadas en el proceso tratando de... agilizar el proceso, simplemente no tiene sentido para mí", dijo Dickey.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0e34f0" name="image-0e34f0"></a> <picture Karimi, un conductor de camión que estaba en la ciudad por trabajo, dijo que tiene amigos con tarjeta de residencia que fueron detenidos en Omaha.</p><p>Aunque los agentes no hicieron que Karimi se sintiera menos seguro, dijo que aún prefiere que estén alejados de los aeropuertos.</p><p>"No deberían estar aquí porque el aeropuerto tiene su propia seguridad, su propia policía", destacó Karimi.</p><p>Trump menciona posible despliegue de la Guardia Nacional en aeropuertos</p><p>Trump dijo el lunes que consideraría llamar a la Guardia Nacional para ayudar con la seguridad en los aeropuertos.</p><p>“Quiero agradecer a ICE porque intervinieron de manera muy, muy contundente. Harán un gran trabajo. Y si eso no es suficiente, traeré a la Guardia Nacional”, dijo Trump.</p><p>La Guardia Nacional no respondió de inmediato a una petición de comentarios.</p><p>Mientras tanto, el “zar de la frontera” de la Casa Blanca, Tom Homan, dijo el lunes que esperaba que los agentes fueran recibidos con protestas.</p><p>“Primero [los] vamos a enviar a los aeropuertos más grandes con las mayores filas de espera”, comentó Homan en el programa de Chris Cuomo en SiriusXM.</p><p>Cuando se le preguntó si eso significaba que ya se estaba preparando para protestas, Homan respondió, “Estoy seguro de que las habrá. Pero cuando revisó la aplicación de la TSA para ver cuánto tiempo era la fila de seguridad, la aplicación no estaba actualizando el tiempo de espera.</p><p>"Estoy aquí tres horas antes, por suerte las filas no son largas en este momento", dijo Castro. "Normalmente llegamos dos horas antes, pero cuando escuché que tienes que estar aquí de cuatro a cinco horas antes, me asusté".</p><p>Castro dijo que le preocupaba que los agentes de ICE estuvieran en los aeropuertos.</p><p>"Son agentes de ICE. Es diferente de la TSA, así que te asusta un poco", comentó Castro. “Soy inmigrante, así que es aterrador”.</p><p>El domingo, los funcionarios del sindicato de la TSA dijeron al Sun-Times que están preocupados acerca de la presencia de agentes de ICE en los aeropuertos. Uno de ellos dijo que hay peligro debido a la falta de capacitación de ICE en seguridad aérea.</p><p>Lori Houzer, siguiendo las instrucciones, llegó a Midway más de tres horas antes de su vuelo a Canadá el lunes. Pero llegó tan temprano que no había personal para registrar su equipaje.</p><p>"Hubiera llegado, como máximo, dos horas antes si estoy registrando maletas, que es más que suficiente, a veces una hora y media", dijo. "Ahora son al menos dos horas más. title: O'Neill Burke rejects bid for special prosecutor to target ICE, says it threatens to 'thwart' justice
summary: <p>Cook County's top prosecutor argued Tuesday that a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" target="_blank" >bid to name a special prosecutor</a> to investigate the federal agents behind last fall’s Operation Midway Blitz amounts to a “frivolous”<b> </b>and “heavy handed”<b> </b>attempt to usurp her authority — and could come at a cost.</p><p>State’s Attorney Eileen<b> </b>O’Neill Burke<b> </b>denied that any conflict exists to warrant the move. She said she’s not intimidated by “vague”<b> </b>threats of political retaliation. And she said a broad coalition’s argument to the contrary actually threatens to “thwart”<b> </b>justice.</p><p>“Acting outside the bounds of the law comes with a price,” O’Neill Burke argued. “And that price here would be compromising the prosecution’s ability to obtain justice for victims and the community.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" >Seeking special prosecutor to target ICE, coalition says O’Neill Burke turned ‘blind eye’ to feds’ violence</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The commentary came in a 24-page response to the high-profile bid<b> </b>for a special prosecutor, launched earlier this month<b> </b>by a coalition of more than 200 elected officials, clergy, journalists and attorneys. They say O’Neill Burke has turned a “blind eye”<b> </b>to myriad crimes committed by federal agents during the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation blitz last fall.</p><p>The alleged crimes include murder, assault, perjury and even conspiracy. The coalition’s March 12 petition<b> </b>seeking a special prosecutor prominently cited the September killing of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" >Silverio<b> </b>Villegas<b> </b>Gonzalez</a><b> </b>and the October<b> </b>shooting of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, both at the hands of federal agents.</p><p>Now O’Neill Burke has submitted the most substantive response to her critics to date. She insisted any investigation must be conducted by law enforcement, but also noted that any prosecutor “should be loath to provide information on any ongoing investigation.”</p><p>“Petitioners are claiming that the state’s attorney has an actual conflict because she is not abdicating her prosecutorial discretion to elected officials and the public or succumbing to political pressure,” she argued in her filing.</p><p>O’Neill Burke again pointed to a 2017 <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoiscourts.gov/resources/bb31d7b0-e90c-4843-8486-c740ae2624ef/file" target="_blank" >Illinois Supreme Court decision</a> she says limits her ability to investigate the agents. But coalition attorney Steve Art insisted that every special prosecutor “takes on the role of an elected state’s attorney and investigates and prosecutes” a crime.</p><p>Art said O’Neill Burke’s argument is “exactly”<b> </b>why a special prosecutor is needed. The coalition he represents has been “asking for justice for months,”<b> </b>he said.</p><p>“Instead of getting any commitment to do justice — to investigate, to prosecute — all we get from the state’s attorney is legal obstacles,” Art told reporters Tuesday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" >How can Chicago’s top prosecutor hold ICE accountable?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>O’Neill Burke’s deputies filed her response to the petition during a brief hearing Tuesday before Cook County Circuit Judge Erica<b> </b>Reddick, the presiding judge of the criminal division. Lawyers are due back April 10<b> </b>in Reddick’s courtroom<b> </b>at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse.</p><p>The coalition includes the Chicago News Guild, which represents journalists at the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Prosecuting federal agents in state court would require <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/can-state-officials-prosecute-the-feds-calls-grow-after-minneapolis-shooting" target="_blank" >showing they acted unreasonably</a> while fulfilling their duties. Meanwhile, prosecutors like O’Neill Burke are entrusted with discretion to choose which cases to pursue. The coalition argued O’Neill Burke’s impartiality “has been irrevocably tainted” by her failure to respond to public demands<b> </b>for an investigation, though.</p><p>In her filing Tuesday, O’Neill Burke repeatedly cited the Illinois Supreme Court ruling addressing the power of a state’s attorney to investigate alleged crimes.</p><p>The court found the duty is “limited to circumstances where other law enforcement agencies inadequately deal with such investigation … or where a law enforcement agency asks the state’s attorney for assistance.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“Petitioners make no allegation that the state’s attorney has been presented with any credible evidence from law enforcement which she refused to charge,” O’Neill Burke wrote Tuesday, “but instead fault her with not investigating criminal conduct, where they have not established it is her duty to investigate.”</p><p>She said the coalition failed to find any “specific personal interest”<b> </b>creating a conflict. She rejected the idea that she’s susceptible to intimidation by President Donald Trump’s Justice Department. And in any event, she said no specific threat of retaliation has been made.</p><p>“It is common for people to threaten the state’s attorney or her assistants,” O’Neill Burke wrote, “and those threats generally do not engender any concern from outside parties or prompt the filing of a petition to appoint a special prosecutor.”</p><p>O’Neill Burke criticized the coalition for “boldly”<b> </b>seeking input in the process of selecting a special prosecutor. She also took a shot at the law firm leading the charge, Loevy and Loevy, for its handling of separate litigation in federal court last fall.</p><p>The firm helped <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >secure an order</a> from U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis restricting the feds’ use of force during Midway Blitz. But later, after the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals signaled the feds<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/19/federal-appeals-court-halts-ruling-that-curbed-use-of-force-during-immigration-campaign" target="_blank" >were likely to prevail</a> in the end, the firm <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/02/lawyers-who-secured-bovino-testimony-body-cam-video-move-to-end-case-that-challenged-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >sought to dismiss the case</a> voluntarily.</p><p>The appeals court formally vacated Ellis’ order<b> </b>earlier this month, citing in part the voluntary dismissal.</p><p>“These times call for serious people,” O’Neill Burke wrote Tuesday. “Not those who cut and run ‘at the first sign of trouble.’”</p><p><i>Neither the reporter nor editors who worked on this story — including some represented by the News Guild — have been involved in the litigation described in this article.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/70/0f/0d9f739b4ad8909f116f7deb173c/eobresponse.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

title: What we know and don't know about TSA wait times at O'Hare and Midway airports
summary: <p>The stalemate in Congress over funding the Department of Homeland Security has left airports understaffed, causing unpredictable wait times in security lines that have at times lasted hours.</p><p>Workers for the Transportation Security Administration, which operates under DHS, have gone unpaid for weeks during the partial federal government shutdown.</p><p>Wait times at Chicago’s O’Hare and Midway airports have not been as long as what has been reported at other airports countrywide, but they have occasionally in recent weeks built up to lengthy waits.</p><p>Here’s what we know so far about how the partial government shutdown is impacting air travel in Chicago:</p><h3><b>How long are wait times at O’Hare and Midway?</b></h3><p>The wait times at both airports have been relatively short, with many travelers this week <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/realtalkstruth/status/2036441969870655909" target="_blank" >reporting on social media</a> less than half-hour waits for security.</p><p>Up-to-date wait times have been mostly unclear because the MyTSA app, which usually shows live wait times, is not being managed during the partial government shutdown.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Aviation also does not track wait times for O'Hare and Midway, </p><p>Security lines at O’Hare on March 16, the day after St. Patrick’s Day weekend — which attracts thousands of travelers — were bottlenecked in the morning, but travelers haven’t experienced such extreme gridlocks since then.</p><h3><b>How many TSA employees are calling out of work?</b></h3><p>The number of TSA workers who have called off at O’Hare and Midway airports wasn’t available.</p><p>Nationally, at least 450 TSA workers have quit altogether since the shutdown began Feb. 14 and thousands have been calling off work, according to DHS.</p><p>Almost 11% of TSA workers — more than 3,200 — missed work Monday, DHS said.</p><p>Sunday’s call out rate of 11.75% at airports nationwide was the highest yet of the government shutdown, according to DHS.</p><h3><b>What is ICE doing at airports?</b></h3><p>President Donald Trump’s administration <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/23/ice-agents-ohare-airport-partial-government-shutdown" target="_blank" >deployed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents</a> to airports across the country, including O’Hare, Monday in an effort to assist the short-staffed airport security personnel.</p><p>About 75 ICE agents were expected to be stationed at O’Hare, according to Mayor Brandon Johnson. Agents were monitoring exit lanes and checkpoints, not performing security screenings. Agents were not deployed to Midway.</p><p>White House border czar Tom Homan said Sunday that ICE agents could potentially cover exits currently monitored by TSA agents, freeing them to work screening lines.</p><p>It’s unclear if any updated guidance was provided to ICE agents, including whether they would be directed to not wear masks while working at airports.</p><p>Agents spotted at O’Hare on Monday by a Sun-Times reporter were mostly wearing face masks, against the wishes of Trump, who said he prefers them to not wear masks.</p><h3><b>Will the National Guard be deployed? </b></h3><p>Trump told reporters Monday that if bringing ICE agents to airports doesn’t help alleviate long wait times, he would consider also deploying the National Guard to help.</p><p>The National Guard did not say whether it has received communication from the Trump administration about potential deployment.</p><h3><b>When will this all be over?</b></h3><p>Senators raced Tuesday to clinch an emerging proposal to end the DHS shutdown by funding much of the department, including the TSA airport workers going without pay, but excluding the ICE enforcement operations that have been core to the dispute.</p><p>While the Trump administration has blamed Democrats over the DHS funding lapse, Democrats have blamed the Trump administration and Republicans for not agreeing to their offer to fund all of the DHS except for ICE. </p><p>"There is one solution that immediately solves the problem at our airports: pay the people who are already trained to protect us — today," Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., said Monday on the Senate floor. </p><p>Next steps in Congress could move quickly, if lawmakers can reach a deal, or sputter out just as fast.</p><h3><b>What does this mean for me?</b></h3><p>Travelers have been urged to arrive at airports early in anticipation of long wait times due to staffing shortages and an influx of spring break travelers.</p><p>The TSA and airlines recommend arriving at least two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international flight — even for people who are enrolled in expedited screening programs like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR.</p><p><i>Associated Press contributed.</i></p>
