In a few hours, Gerstein would be on a plane headed for New York City, where she was due for a rehearsal with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and its music director, Klaus Mäkelä, at Carnegie Hall. Gerstein was at the start of a weeklong tour that would also go to Boston and Bethesda, Maryland. All the while she had her baby in tow.</p><p><b>Touring while parenting</b>: Mäkelä is ramping up events with Chicago’s orchestra as he prepares to take the podium in 2027. Gerstein, the orchestra's second flute, wanted to be there for his first tour with the symphony. But she also wanted to keep breastfeeding her son, who is her second child.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Women in the arts who perform in highly visible, prestigious roles have often privately discussed how to balance work and parenthood: Backstage, in locker rooms, over the rhythmic whir of breast pumps. Even at the symphony, which music directors have helped make more welcoming for families, there remains a fear that motherhood can be a career killer. On tour, Gerstein kept a diary for WBEZ, offering a rare window into a working mom’s perennial balancing act.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wtdeld-l-s/" city’s new co-ed baseball team that will offer up a brand of ball made popular by the Savannah Bananas in recent years — is to be goofy and entertain. Think baseball’s version of the Harlem Globetrotters.</p><p>The Banana League offers a variety of exhibition baseball known as Banana Ball, which has filled the country’s biggest stadiums with family friendly two-hour games featuring hurlers on stilts, flaming bats, backflipping catches, singing, dancing and the occasional crawling-baby race between innings.</p><p>The Snowballs, which have no affiliation with the Banana League, will take the field for their first game in front of paying customers on May 2 at Kerry Wood Cubs Field in Roscoe Village. Snowballs CEO Cherie Travis likens them to a traveling circus, with about 10 games a month scheduled through September at ballparks in the Chicago area and around the Midwest.</p><p>"Everything that coaches have been telling them their whole lives: 'Don’t mess around. Don’t be a show off.' We told them we are encouraging that. That is what we want to see," said Snowballs Project Manager Kristen Adamiak. "As soon as we gave them that freedom they were instantly like, 'OK. Let’s go.'"</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wtdeld-l-jr/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE CHICAGO 📸</h4><div class="Enhancement" title: Migrante venezolano acusado de asesinato de la estudiante de la Universidad Loyola
summary: <p>Un migrante venezolano ha sido acusado del asesinato de Sheridan Gorman, estudiante de la Universidad Loyola de Chicago, anunciaron las autoridades policiales el domingo, lo que provocó la indignación de funcionarios de la administración de Trump, quienes calificaron su asesinato como el resultado de las políticas de santuario en Illinois.</p><p>José Medina, de 25 años, enfrenta cargos de asesinato en primer grado, intento de asesinato y descarga agravada de un arma de fuego por el ataque del 19 de marzo cerca de un muelle en la playa Tobey Prinz, según la Policía de Chicago.</p><p>Gorman, de 18 años, y sus amigos dieron un paseo el jueves por la mañana justo al norte del campus de Rogers Park, con la esperanza de tomar algunas fotos con vista al horizonte y potencialmente a las Auroras Boreales, dijo su familia en un comunicado.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6c0000" name="module-6c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Cuando llegaron, un hombre enmascarado “emergió de las sombras” y disparó un solo tiro mientras ellos huían, según un informe de la Policía de Chicago. Uno de los amigos de Gorman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" target="_blank" >que fue testigo del tiroteo</a> le contó al Chicago Sun-Times que “no parecía que estuviera dirigido intencionalmente hacia ninguno de nosotros”.</p><p>Los amigos corrieron en diferentes direcciones cuando se disparó, pero volvieron al ver a Gorman en el suelo. Ella había recibido un tiro en el torso y fue <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/19/woman-18-shot-to-death-in-predawn-rogers-park-attack" target="_blank" >declarada muerta en la escena</a>, informaron las autoridades.</p><p>Las autoridades federales de inmigración informaron que el Servicio de Inmigración y Aduanas (ICE) emitió un aviso de detención que nombraba a Medina horas antes de que la policía anunciara los cargos.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" </div><p>El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) indicó que Medina fue detenido por la Patrulla Fronteriza en mayo de 2023, liberado y luego nuevamente detenido dos meses después por robo. Se le acusó de robo menor en ese caso, acusado de robar $132.50 en mercancía de Macy's en State Street, según los registros de la corte del condado. Una orden de arresto pendiente de ese caso está activa.</p><p>Los registros muestran que Medina nació en Venezuela y en un momento vivió en un refugio temporal para migrantes en el edificio del Leone Beach Park, que cerró en 2024. Formó parte de miles de migrantes que llegaron a Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2024/02/15/busing-migrants-chicago-texas-origins-start-donald-trump-tucker-carlson-ted-cruz" target="_blank" >muchos de ellos enviados a la ciudad por el gobernador republicano de Texas, Greg Abbott</a>, en protesta por las políticas fronterizas del expresidente Joe Biden.</p><p>La oficina de Pritzker no emitió comentarios inmediatos.</p><p>La legislación firmada por el exgobernador republicano de Illinois, Bruce Rauner, limita la cooperación entre la policía local y las autoridades federales de inmigración. La ley Illinois TRUST Act generalmente prohíbe a la policía compartir información con agentes de inmigración o entregar a personas en custodia a menos que se emita una orden de arresto criminal federal, una política criticada durante mucho tiempo por el presidente Donald Trump y otros críticos conservadores.</p><p>La secretaria interina de DHS, Lauren Bis, afirmó en un comunicado que a Gorman le "fallaron las políticas de fronteras abiertas y políticos de santuario" y exhortó al gobernador JB Pritzker a no liberar a Medina, quien estaba programado para hacer su primera aparición en la corte el lunes.</p><p>En un comunicado, la familia de Gorman expresó su "profunda decepción por las políticas y fracasos que permitieron que este individuo permaneciera en una posición para cometer este crimen.</p><p>“Cuando los sistemas fallan —ya sea por decisiones de liberación, falta de coordinación o falta de voluntad para actuar— las consecuencias no son abstractas. Son reales. Y en nuestro caso, son permanentes”, dijo la familia de Gorman. “Este caso debe ser presentado en la máxima medida de la ley estatal y federal. No puede haber vacíos, no puede haber atajos, y no puede haber segundas oportunidades que pongan a otros en riesgo. La responsabilidad debe ser completa”.</p><p>La familia insistió, “no permitiremos que esto se desestime como ‘el lugar y el momento equivocados’. Esto no fue una desgracia aleatoria. Esto fue un acto violento y prevenible”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

title: ICE agents spotted at O’Hare Airport as partial government shutdown continues to impact travelers
summary: <p>U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers were present at O'Hare International Airport Monday, after the Trump administration said agents would be deployed to airports nationwide to help amid the ongoing partial government shutdown.</p><p>At least three agents in ICE gear were seen at Terminal 3 around 10 a.m. Monday morning.</p><p>A day after saying he would use immigration officers for <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/government-shutdown-tsa-workers-920577c153ffd1877f59dfb8f8efed39" target="_blank" ><u>airport security</u></a> starting Monday unless Democrats agreed on a bill to fund the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/us-department-of-homeland-security" target="_blank" ><u>Department of Homeland Security</u></a>, Trump made clear Sunday that he was going ahead with the plan to assist the Transportation Security Administration.</p><p>O’Hare was among 13 airports included in a list of where ICE agents would be present to assist, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/us/live-news/tsa-wait-times-ice-airports-03-23-26?post-id=cmn37qf65000q3b6rfo32wpep" target="_blank" >according to CNN</a>. Department of Homeland Security acting assistant secretary Lauren Bis said in a statement, “For operational security reasons, we are not going to confirm the locations of our officers," but flagged nine major airports, including Baltimore/Washington International Airport in Maryland and John F. Kennedy Airport International in New York as having high TSA worker callout rates on Sunday. O'Hare and Midway Airports were not on that list.</p><p>Luke Hoover and Mary Dickey, of North Center, were on their way to New Zealand for their honeymoon and got to O'Hare three hours early for their flight after bracing for possible delays stemming from the partial government shutdown. </p><p>"It gives us pause, [we're] not a big fan of it," Hoover said of ICE agents at O'Hare. "We figured with that plus TSA just being a bit of a mess lately, we'd get here early and ready to go." </p><p>"Just [the] TSA process alone, having people who aren’t trained in the process trying to, you know, expedite the process, just doesn’t make sense to me," Dickey added. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Homan told the program’s executive producer, Alexandra “Dusty” Cohen.</p><p>When asked if that meant he was already preparing for protests, Homan responded, "I'm sure there will be. impacted.</p><p>Anayeli Castro, who was waiting for her husband by the security check point with her two young kids, had heard online that they should arrive at least four hours early. She tried checking the TSA app to see how long the security line was but the app was not updating the wait time.</p><p>“I'm here three hours before, luckily the lines are not long right now,” Castro said. “We normally arrive two hours early but I when heard you have to be here 4 to 5 hours early, I was freaking out.”</p><p>She also saw on social media that ICE agents could be deployed to Chicago airports.</p><p>“They're ICE agents. It's different from TSA, so it does kind of freak you out a little bit," Castro said. “I am an immigrant, so it's scary but it seems pretty calm right now.”</p><p>Lori Houzer found a place to sit at Midway Airport while she waited to check her bags for her flight to Canada. She said she followed recommended instructions to arrive three to four hours beforehand but despite the early arrival there are no staff to check in passengers.</p><p>“I would have arrived max two hours early if I'm checking luggage, which is more than enough time, sometimes an hour and a half,” she said. “Now it's at least two hours more, and that's if things go well,” she said.</p><p>Houzer said she kept up with the news and knew TSA agents were not getting paid due to the government shutdown.</p><p>“People should get paid because not only is it incorrect to ask people who already aren't earning very much money to get no money, but also what is their motivation for doing their job really well?” she said. “It's a security job. I would like people to take it seriously.”</p><p>She isn’t worried about ICE agents being at airports, but she does think it’s a bad use of funds.</p><p>“They're gonna pay ICE but they're not gonna pay regular people?” she questioned. “I'm also Canadian. I don't really understand it very well.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/22/union-tsa-workers-push-back-demand-pay-after-trump-admin-deploys-ice-agents-in-airports-monday" target="_blank" >TSA union officials raised concerns</a> over passenger security with ICE agents present.</p><p>“Our members at TSA have been showing up every day, without a paycheck, because they believe in the mission of keeping the flying public safe,” Everett Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, said in a statement Sunday. “They deserve to be paid, not replaced by untrained, armed agents who have shown how dangerous they can be.”</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p><p><i>Contributing Violet Miller</i></p>

title: Trump decries Loyola student's killing while pushing deportations; suspect will likely miss court
summary: <p>As President Donald Trump used the “devastating” killing of Loyola University Chicago student Sheridan Gorman to justify his push for mass deportations on Monday, the alleged gunman remained hospitalized and was expected to miss his initial court hearing later in the day.</p><p>Jose G. Medina, a Venezuelan immigrant, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >charged with first-degree murder</a>, attempted murder, aggravated discharge of a firearm, and illegal gun possession in connection to the March 19 attack near Tobey Prinz Beach, Cook County court records show.</p><p>Trump told reporters Monday that he had been briefed on Gorman’s killing, arguing that the fatal shooting showed there was a need for ramped up immigration enforcement efforts.</p><p>“This person came in through the open door policy of [former President] Joe Biden and we have others,” Trump said. “ We’re taking them out by the tens of thousands. We’re doing a great job, but it’s a shame.”</p><p>Medina, 25, was wanted on a warrant in a local shoplifting case at the time of his latest arrest.</p><p>Gorman’s family said they were “gravely disappointed by the policies and failures that allowed this individual to remain in a position to commit this crime."</p><p>“When systems fail — whether through release decisions, lack of coordination, or unwillingness to act — the consequences are not abstract. They are real,” the family said in a statement.</p><p>“And in our case, they are permanent. This case must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of both state and federal law. There can be no gaps, no shortcuts, and no second chances that put others at risk. Accountability must be complete.”</p><p>Gorman, 18, and her friends took an early morning walk Thursday to the beach just north of Loyola’s campus to take pictures of the skyline, according to her family.</p><p>When they arrived, a masked gunman “emerged from the shadows” and fired a single shot as they fled, according to police records. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/19/woman-18-shot-to-death-in-predawn-rogers-park-attack" target="_blank" >Gorman was struck in the back</a> as she attempted to flee. Police initially reported she’d been struck in the head. </p><p>One of Gorman’s friends who witnessed the shooting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" target="_blank" >told the Chicago Sun-Times</a> that “it didn’t seem like it was intentionally targeted toward any of us.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f80000" from the scene into a building in the 6800 block of West Sheridan Road, according to the arrest report. He wore all black clothing and a mask and had a “distinct gait.”</p><p>The report shows the police department worked closely with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to identify the suspect. CBP, which was integral to the aggressive deportation campaign in Chicago last year, reportedly used facial recognition to identify the man in the video as Medina.</p><p>CBP is a part of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which publicly identified Medina as the suspect before charges were approved by Cook County prosecutors. The department also announced that it had issued an arrest detainer for Medina.</p><p>DHS said Medina had been taken into custody by U.S. Border Patrol in May 2023, released and then arrested again two months later for shoplifting. He had an active warrant in the theft case, court records show.</p><p>The Trump administration has used the deaths of other young women to make a case that undocumented immigration puts Americans in danger. However, the efforts to frame crime as the driving force behind its deportation mission have at times been undercut by data and research.</p><p>The killing of Laken Riley, a nursing student in Georgia who was fatally attacked by an immigrant, spurred legislation that mandates detention and strengthens enforcement against undocumented immigrants charged with certain crimes.</p><p>Operation Midway Blitz, the pummeling deportation campaign that tore through the Chicago area last fall, was dedicated to Katie Abraham, an Illinois native killed by a drunken driver who allegedly lacked legal status.</p><p>“Sheridan Gorman's life was allegedly taken from her at the hands of a criminal alien shielded by the anti-American sanctuary policies of the city of Chicago and the state of Illinois,” U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said on social media Monday.</p><p>Numerous studies have found that immigrants without legal status are less likely to commit serious crimes than U.S.-born citizens.</p><p>A 2024 National Institute of Justice-funded study examining data from the Texas Department of Public Safety found that undocumented immigrants are arrested at less than half the rate of native-born U.S. citizens for violent and drug crimes and a quarter the rate of native-born citizens for property crimes.<a class="Link" href="https://docs.house.gov/meetings/JU/JU01/20250122/117827/HHRG-119-JU01-20250122-SD004.pdf" target="_blank" > </a></p><p>And according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.migrationpolicy.org/content/immigrants-and-crime" target="_blank" >Migration and Policy Institute</a>, studies have shown that immigrants do not raise crime rates in the local communities where they settle. The institute cites a study by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.umass.edu/preferen/You%20Must%20Read%20This/Lee%20Immigration%20and%20Crime.pdf" target="_blank" >University of Massachusetts</a> that connects lower crime activity, including violent crime, with communities that have inclusive immigration policies.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/19/woman-18-shot-to-death-in-predawn-rogers-park-attack" target="_blank" >Loyola University student, 18, shot to death in predawn attack at Rogers Park beach</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" target="_blank" >Friend of slain Loyola student Sheridan Gorman says Rogers Park shooting didn’t feel ‘targeted’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/ice-detainer-loyola-student-killing-sheridan-gorman" target="_blank" >Venezuelan migrant charged with murder of Loyola student Sheridan Gorman</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

battle between Chance The Rapper, real name Chancelor Bennett, and his former manager, Pat Corcoran, ended Friday. A Cook County jury found Corcoran had failed to prove he was owed the $3.8 million in unpaid commissions and royalties he sought in his lawsuit against his former friend and business partner.</p><p><b>$35 in damages</b>: Jurors also ruled in Bennett's countersuit, which was combined with Corcoran’s lawsuit for purposes of the trial. Bennett had originally sought $1 million in damages. The jury decided Corcoran must pay him $35, and recommended that Corcoran turn over the internet domain name ChanceRaps.com, which Corcoran used to sell Chance the Rapper merchandise.</p><p><b>Fraught relationship</b>: Over their eight-year working relationship, Bennett and Corcoran had been the industry model for a successful, independent artist-manager partnership without record label interference. But as both parties rested their cases, a different narrative emerged. Corcoran’s legal team described a hardworking manager who deserved to be paid for contributing to the ascent of the Grammy-winning rapper. Bennett’s attorneys tried to portray him as an opportunistic ex-employee who was fired for a reason.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-wtitkiy-l-m/" target="_blank" Calbert Wright, who’s been working at Ford’s Chicago Heights plant since 1963</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-wtitkiy-l-ji/" target="_blank" >Neil Steinberg</a></h5><p>He didn't think he'd stick around. When Calbert Wright began work at the Ford Motor Company’s Chicago Stamping Plant in Chicago Heights in 1963, the factory was a noisy, smelly, smoky hellscape with a leaky roof. Plus Black workers, such as himself, were given the hardest duties. But stay he did.</p><p>When Wright, at the age of 23, began work at Ford, John F. Kennedy was president. Henry Ford II, grandson of the man who founded the automobile manufacturer in 1903, still ran the business. That means Wright, who walks the floor today, has worked for Ford for more than half the 123 years since the company sold its first car, a two-cylinder, two-passenger Model A, in red, for $850 to Ernest Pfennig, a dentist on Clybourn Avenue.</p><p>Why did he stay?</p><p>“There weren’t jobs paying like this,” he said, laughing: $1.40 an hour. “Big money.” He had a wife, Thelma — now married 65 years — and an infant son to consider. And things were changing. "[Martin Luther] King, plus the union, made everybody be classified,” Wright said. Conditions improved. He moved up from stacking steel. “That’s why I stayed so long.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-i-wtitkiy-l-jt/" target="_blank" ><b>READ title: Venezuelan migrant charged with murder of Loyola student Sheridan Gorman
summary: <p>A Venezuelan migrant has been charged with the murder of Loyola University Chicago student Sheridan Gorman, police announced Sunday, prompting outrage from Trump administration officials who branded her killing as the result of sanctuary policies in Illinois. </p><p>Jose Medina, 25, faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted murder and aggravated discharge of a firearm for the March 19 attack near a pier at Tobey Prinz Beach, according to Chicago police. </p><p>Federal immigration authorities said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement issued an arrest detainer naming Medina hours before police announced the charges. </p><p>The Department of Homeland Security said Medina was taken into custody by the U.S. Border Patrol in May 2023, released and then taken into custody again two months later for shoplifting. He was charged with misdemeanor retail theft in that case, accused of stealing $132.50 of merchandise from the State Street Macy's, county court records show. An outstanding warrant from that case is active.</p><p>Records show Medina was born in Venezuela and at one point lived in a temporary migrant shelter at the Leone Beach Park Field House, which closed in 2024. He was among thousands of migrants who arrived in Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2024/02/15/busing-migrants-chicago-texas-origins-start-donald-trump-tucker-carlson-ted-cruz" >many of them bused to the city by GOP Texas Gov. Greg Abbott</a> in protest of former President Joe Biden's border policies. </p><p>Acting Assistant DHS Secretary Lauren Bis claimed in a statement that Gorman was "failed by open border policies and sanctuary politicians" and urged Gov. JB Pritzker to not release Medina, who was scheduled to make his first court appearance Monday. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure </div><p>Pritzker's office did not have any immediate comment. </p><p>Legislation signed by Republican former Illinois Gov. Bruce Rauner limits cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities. The Illinois TRUST Act generally bars police from sharing information with immigration agents or handing over people in custody unless a federal criminal warrant is issued, a policy long denigrated by President Donald Trump and other conservative critics.</p><p>Gorman, 18, and her friends took an early morning stroll Thursday just north of the Rogers Park campus, hoping to capture some photos with a view of the skyline and potentially the Northern Lights, her family said in a statement.</p><p>When they arrived, a masked gunman “emerged from the shadows” and fired a single shot as they fled, according to a Chicago police report. One of Gorman’s friends <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" target="_blank" ><u>who witnessed the shooting</u></a> told the Chicago Sun-Times that “it didn’t seem like it was intentionally targeted toward any of us.”</p><p>The friends ran in different directions when the shot was fired, but returned when they saw Gorman on the ground. She had been shot in her torso and was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/19/woman-18-shot-to-death-in-predawn-rogers-park-attack" target="_blank" ><u>pronounced dead at the scene</u></a>, officials said.</p><p>In a statement, Gorman's family said they were "gravely disappointed by the policies and failures that allowed this individual to remain in a position to commit this crime. </p><p>"When systems fail — whether through release decisions, lack of coordination, or unwillingness to act — the consequences are not abstract. They are real. And in our case, they are permanent," Gorman's family said. “This case must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of both state and federal law. There can be no gaps, no shortcuts, and no second chances that put others at risk. Accountability must be complete.”</p><p>The family insisted "we will not allow this to be dismissed as ‘wrong place, wrong time.’ This was not random misfortune. This was a violent and preventable act.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/20/chicago-loyola-sheridan-gorman-rogers-park-crime-shooting-murder" >Friend of slain Loyola student Sheridan Gorman says Rogers Park shooting didn’t feel ‘targeted’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/21/police-questioning-person-of-interest-in-fatal-shooting-of-18-year-old-loyola-student" >Police questioning person of interest in fatal shooting of 18-year-old Loyola student</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/19/woman-18-shot-to-death-in-predawn-rogers-park-attack" >Loyola University student, 18, shot to death in predawn attack at Rogers Park beach</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Judge rules Broadview protest curfew violates First Amendment
summary: <p>A federal Judge on Sunday struck down the village of Broadview’s curfew on protests, ruling that restrictions set by suburban leaders have violated demonstrators' First Amendments rights. </p><p>Chicago attorney Robert Held filed for a preliminary injunction <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/13/lawyer-seeking-preliminary-injunction-in-lawsuit-against-broadview-over-protest-hours-appears-outside-ice-facility" >last fall</a> as part of a federal lawsuit against Broadview to overturn Mayor Katrina Thompson’s executive order establishing time limits and designated areas for protests outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Edmond Chang granted the preliminary injunction, writing in his decision that Broadview’s “current restrictions cannot stand under the First Amendment.”</p><p>Held called the ruling a “heartwarming victory.”</p><p>“The judge looked at the facts and the law and slapped down mayor,” Held told the Sun-Times. “This is a victory not just for the protesters, but anyone in this country who cares about the First Amendment and Constitution.”</p><p>The ICE property became the site <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/11/14/scuffles-erupt-during-broadview-protest-several-arrested" >for major protests</a> against “Operation Midway Blitz,” the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign in Chicago and its suburbs last year.</p><p>In response, Thompson issued several executive orders restricting where and when people can protest at the facility, which included establishing “free speech zones” and a daily curfew for demonstrations from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.</p><p>Held filed the federal complaint in October against Thompson and Broadview Chief of Police Thomas Mills in an effort to overturn the village’s protest restrictions.</p><p>In granting the preliminary injunction, Chang said the ongoing daily limits on protests “fail to survive First Amendment scrutiny.” But the village is allowed to keep the protest zones and enact “more specific limits for specific protests on specific days.”</p><p>A Broadview spokesperson did not immediately respond a request for comment.</p><p><i>Contributing: Violet Miller</i> </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/6d/90/bf9520534073a8b9fdcd01ee8bdc/broadviewpiopinion.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

title: Union TSA workers push back, demand pay as Trump admin floats plan to deploy ICE agents in airports Monday
summary: <p>After President Donald Trump threatened to deploy federal immigration agents to airports amid a Department of Homeland Security funding fight in Congress, union members in the Midwest are expressing concern about agents' lack of training and their own lack of pay.</p><p>A day after saying he would use immigration officers for <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/government-shutdown-tsa-workers-920577c153ffd1877f59dfb8f8efed39" target="_blank" >airport security</a> starting Monday unless Democrats agreed on a bill to fund the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/us-department-of-homeland-security" target="_blank" >Department of Homeland Security</a>, Trump made clear Sunday that he was going ahead with the plan to assist the Transportation Security Administration.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/tsa-lines-airport-wait-times-shutdown-5b1abfe9f0ec32475fe2bdad88dd9174" target="_blank" >Hundreds of thousands of homeland security workers</a>, including from the TSA, U.S. Secret Service and Coast Guard, have <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/tsa-lines-airport-shutdown-food-banks-a1e52ca10557f4f70c1360e878567b4b" target="_blank" >worked without pay</a> since <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/tsa-airports-immigration-homeland-security-570088e5f8cb5f53233d5fea3322e86c" target="_blank" >Congress failed to renew DHS funding</a> last month. Democrats are demanding major changes in the conduct of federal immigration agents.</p><p>White House border czar Tom Homan said in Sunday news show interviews that the increased role of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement at airports was subject to discussions with the leadership of TSA and ICE “to find out where we can fit in.” Immigration officers, as an example, could cover exits currently monitored by TSA agents, freeing them to work screening lines, or have ICE agents check identification before people enter screenings areas.</p><p>Homan promised “a plan by the end of today, where we’re sending — what airports we’re starting with and where we’re sending them."</p><p>DHS and ICE officials issued statements blaming Democrats for the "pointless, reckless" shutdown, and saying the Trump administration was trying to shorten security wait times in airports. Neither agency responded to questions about the timing of the deployment or role agents would take on.</p><p>The city of Chicago and its Department of Aviation didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-570000" name="image-570000"></a> <picture 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Everett Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, which represents TSA agents and other federal workers in Illinois and Wisconsin, said with the agents’ deployment raises security concerns for passengers.</p><p>“Our members at TSA have been showing up every day, without a paycheck, because they believe in the mission of keeping the flying public safe,” Kelley said in a statement. “They deserve to be paid, not replaced by untrained, armed agents who have shown how dangerous they can be.”</p><p>Darrell English, president of AFGE Local 777, said the danger also extends to the agents’ lack of training regarding aviation security. Adding ICE agents to the mix could slow the screening process for travelers, since they lack the seven months of training TSA agents go through before screening solo, according to English.</p><p>“It’s always concerning when you hear language like that in terms of changing the security that’s being implemented,” English said. “It leaves a hole... TSA understands the threat to aviation and the flying public, and it also takes years of understanding that to be efficient and secure.”</p><p>Responding to similar criticism, Homan said “certainly, a highly trained ICE law enforcement officer can cover an exit... Stuff like that relieves that TSA officer to go to screening and to reduce those lines.”</p><p>“ICE agents are assigned at many airports across the country already," Homan said "[But] I don’t see an ICE agent looking at an X-ray machine, because we’re not trained in that."</p><p>The vast majority of TSA employees are considered essential and have continued to work without pay during the funding lapse. Call-out rates have started to increase at some airports, and DHS said at least 376 have quit since the partial shutdown began Feb. 14.</p><p>The Senate rejected a motion by Democrats Saturday to take up legislation to fund the TSA. Republicans argue that they need to fund all parts of DHS.</p><p>If the funding fight doesn’t wrap up by Friday, it will make for the second missed paycheck for impacted federal workers. English said he was aware of several officers within Local 777 who left during the prolonged shutdown last year as well as during the most recent, though he didn’t have a specific count.</p><p>“If they can't take care of their family because of the financial issues with TSA, they're going to look for different avenues," English said, urging others to reach out to their federal elected officials about it. "These are years of training you’re losing when these veterans leave.”</p><p></p><p>It comes just about a year after the Trump administration first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2025/03/10/tsa-contract-cancel-labor-federal-government-trump-administration" target="_blank" ><u>attempted to throw out the contract for the union’s</u></a><u>,</u> which covers 47,000 workers. The administration tried <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/homeland-security-tsa-union-b754702c295fdec5900bc04baaff3fa4" target="_blank" ><u>again</u></a> in December.</p><p>It stemmed from a September memo from former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, issued months after a federal judge blocked her earlier directive, saying TSA screeners “have a primary function of national security” and therefore should not engage in <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/collective-bargaining-agreement-tsa-homeland-security-e3eb1d5e0ae8e1b4a6fdb87cd7f6bd39" target="_blank" ><u>collective bargaining</u></a> or be represented by a union.</p><p>That fight continues as the union awaits a court date on the second challenge to their contract, English said.</p><p>“This is the worst I've seen the conditions with TSA,” English said. “Not only have they not been paid and their collective bargaining rights challenged, but now they have to worry about other individuals that may be coming in to assist or replace them… If they get paid, they can do their job and there won’t be a need for outside assistance.”</p><p><i>Contributing: AP</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/21/ice-officers-will-help-with-airport-security-unless-dhs-funding-bill-is-passed-trump-says" >ICE officers will help with airport security unless DHS funding bill is passed, Trump says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2025/03/10/tsa-contract-cancel-labor-federal-government-trump-administration" >Midwest TSA agents left with questions amid attempted contract cancellation</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: ICE officers will help with airport security unless DHS funding bill is passed, Trump says
summary: <p>President Donald Trump said Saturday he will order federal immigration officers to take a role in airport security starting Monday unless Democrats agree on a bill to fund the Department of Homeland Security.</p><p>In a pair of social media posts, Trump first threatened and then said he had made plans to put officers from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in airports if the congressional standoff continues. He made the announcement as a partial shutdown contributes to long lines to pass through screening at some of the nation's largest airports.</p><p>The Republican president suggested ICE agents would bring the administration’s immigration crackdown into the nation’s airports, promising to arrest “all Illegal Immigrants."</p><p>“I look forward to moving ICE in on Monday, and have already told them to, “GET READY.” NO MORE WAITING, NO MORE GAMES!” Trump wrote while spending the weekend in Florida.</p><p>The move appears to be a pointed effort to expand the type of immigration enforcement that has become a sticking point in Congress. Democrats pledged to oppose funding for DHS unless changes were made in the wake of a crackdown in Minnesota that led to the fatal shootings of two protesters. Democrats are asking for better identification for federal law enforcement officers, a new code of conduct for those agencies and more use of judicial warrants, among other measures.</p><p>The Minnesota operation was tied in part to allegations of fraud involving Somali residents. On Saturday, Trump said ICE officers sent to airports would focus on arresting immigrants from Somalia who are in the United States illegally. Repeating his criticism on Somalis, he said they “totally destroyed” Minnesota.</p><p>“If the Democrats do not allow for Just and Proper Security at our Airports, and elsewhere throughout our Country, ICE will do the job far better than ever done before,” Trump said.</p><p>Trump’s posts did not offer additional detail on how ICE would take a role in airport security and what it meant for the Transportation Security Administration, which screens passengers and luggage for hazardous items.</p><p>The vast majority of TSA employees are considered essential and continue to work during the funding lapse, but they are doing so without pay. Call-out rates have started to increase at some airports, and DHS said at least 376 have quit since the partial shutdown began Feb. 14.</p><p>On Saturday, in a rare weekend session, the Senate rejected a motion by Democrats to take up legislation to reopen TSA and pay workers who are now going without paychecks. Republicans argue that they need to fund all parts of the DHS, not just certain ones. A bill to fund the Cabinet department failed to advance in the Senate on Friday.</p><p>There were signs of progress, though, with the restarting in recent days of stalled talks between Democrats and the White House. On Saturday, Republican and Democratic senators were set to meet for a third consecutive day with White House officials behind closed doors as Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York spoke of “productive conversations.”</p><p>Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., urged the bipartisan group to act quickly. He has said repeatedly that Democrats and the White House need to find compromise as lines at airports have grown.</p><p>“If that group that’s meeting can’t come up with a solution really quickly, things are going to get worse and worse,” Thune said Saturday.</p>

title: Iran war carried out to boost Trump's ego and soothe his 'psychic wounds'
summary: <p>Two weeks after the start of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/03/01/chicagoans-iran-middle-east-ties-worry-united-states-israel-continue-bombing" >Iran war,</a> the picture is coming into focus. Why would a president who promised countless times not to start new wars have leapt into this conflict? </p><p>As always in the age of Donald Trump, it's necessary to separate the president's motives and mindset from the old ways we used to decide questions of war and peace, tariffs, sanctions, immigration, taxes and other matters. Before venturing into Trump's mind, let's consider the shape of the discussion.</p><p>Those who imagine that we are still operating in a normal world are making arguments in favor of military action as if we were engaged in a national debate. </p><p>Where is the acknowledgment, they demand, of what a vicious regime the mullahs in Iran run? The Islamic Republic has been at war with us since 1979, they stress, and if you doubt their murderous intent, you're forgetting the 444 days our diplomats were held hostage, the attack on our Beirut Embassy and on Marines stationed at the Beirut airport, the Khobar Towers bombing and countless improvised explosive devices and other attacks by Iranian proxies during the Iraq War, to say nothing of their unofficial national slogan "Death to America/Death to Israel."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9d0000" name="module-9d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Iran's internal repression is nearly as brutal as its external support for terrorism, with women in particular bearing the brunt. The population loathes the regime, as we've witnessed many times, but most recently in January when they thronged the streets in their tens of thousands — only to be <a class="Link" href="https://time.com/7357635/more-than-30000-killed-in-iran-say-senior-officials/" target="_blank" >gunned down en masse</a>.</p><h3>Where was the risk analysis?</h3><h3></h3><p>If we had a normal administration and a normal decision-making process, those factors would have been considered. We would have weighed the risks of war against the opportunity to strike a fatal blow to a terrible regime. The fact of Iran being a nasty piece of work is not dispositive on the matter of going to war. A poorly planned or executed war can make things worse.</p><p>Now we turn to the juvenile, facts-optional world of Trump, where the president commits the U.S. to war without planning, without consultation with allies, without congressional authorization and without a clue about how badly things could go.</p><p>Thrilled by U.S. firepower in last summer's attack on Iran's nuclear facilities, and giddy from the perceived success of removing Nicolás Maduro, Trump came to believe that the military was a magic wand that he could wave according to his whim. Of course, he was aware of his vows to keep us out of wars, but wars are boots on the ground, not beautiful strikes from the skies. </p><p>Disregarding warnings from wiser heads about the risks to the Strait of Hormuz, Trump dove in.</p><p>My best understanding of his motive harks back to the hostage crisis of 1979. Trump lives in the past more than most people, and due to his exceptional sensitivity to humiliation, I think he carries the shame of that episode in his heart. In a 1980 interview that is believed to be his first public statement on foreign policy, he said, "That this country sits back and allows a country such as Iran to hold our hostages, to my way of thinking, is a horror."</p><h3>Surviving equals victory for Iranian regime</h3><p>In addition to wounded pride, we must add vainglory. The Lindsey Graham/Benjamin Netanyahu tag team played upon Trump's lust for glory by convincing him that while Iran had been a thorn in our side for half a century and previous presidents had vowed not to permit it to become a nuclear power, no other president had the cojones to do the job.</p><p>Trump obviously thought he could achieve regime change with an air campaign alone. He invited the Iranian people in the early hours of the attacks to take back their country. Perhaps both he and Netanyahu misread the lesson of January, believing that the people would seize power. But the real lesson of January was that the regime would do anything, including massacring thousands of its own citizens, to maintain its grip on power. The brutality worked. Only the regime has guns. The demonstrations subsided.</p><p>Iran has inflicted pain on its people for decades, and it is more than happy to intensify it now. They can bear shortages, blackouts, misery and death because they have no choice. All the mullahs have to do to "win" this conflict is survive. Meanwhile, an American public that was never consulted and certainly not convinced to undertake a risky war will be intolerant of even higher inflation or a recession. The advantage in a contest of wills goes to the mullahs.</p><p>The Iranian regime is one of the worst on the planet, and we must still hope for the sake of the Iranian people and the world that it does not survive. But this war is being conducted to heal psychic wounds and to boost the ego of our dangerous commander-in-chief, who is now obliged to plead for help opening the Strait of Hormuz from (former?) allies and enemies alike. If the Iranian regime survives, even in a weakened condition, it may be more dangerous than ever, having shown the world that it can withstand simultaneous assault from the "big and little Satans."</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of The Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1b0000" name="module-1b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

title: Inmates warn people are being wrongfully detained despite no-cash bail under SAFE-T Act
summary: <p>As a longtime advocate for criminal justice reform and chairman of the West Side Heroin/Opioid Task Force, I have dedicated years to promoting policies that treat addiction as a public health issue while enhancing public safety. That is why I was concerned during a recent visit to the Cook County Jail, where I met with more than 100 detainees to hear firsthand about their experiences under Illinois’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/02/20/naysayers-pretrial-fairness-act-would-worsen-crime-homicides-robberies-down-rep-lisa-davis" >no-cash bail</a> system. </p><p>Many expressed concerns that prosecutors are seeking detention in cases that do not seem to involve violent offenses or clear public safety risks, raising serious questions about whether the law is being implemented as intended.</p><p>Illinois adopted a no-bail system to end the injustice of keeping people in jail just because they cannot afford to pay for their release. The goal was never to detain more people; it was to detain the right people: those who genuinely threaten public safety. When implementation appears inconsistent or overly harsh, it undermines trust in the reform and increases public mistrust.</p><p>We also must recognize that individuals struggling with substance use disorder should not be confined in jail cells. Addiction is a public health issue, not a moral failing. People battling substance use disorder should be directed to treatment, recovery services and mental health support, not incarceration. When people are jailed instead of receiving help, they lose jobs, fall behind on rent and child support and sink further into a system that destabilizes families and harms businesses dependent on a stable workforce.</p><p>Taxpayers deserve better. They deserve a justice system that is fair, consistent and uses public resources efficiently. Detaining individuals unnecessarily costs millions of dollars, strains county budgets and does nothing to improve community safety. Fairness is both a moral obligation and a fiscal responsibility.</p><p>For these reasons, I am urging the Cook County state’s attorney’s office to ensure transparency and accountability regarding detention practices, including data on who prosecutors seek to detain and why. Prosecutorial discretion must never happen without public oversight.</p><p>Given the serious concerns raised by the detainees, I also urge the Illinois attorney general to review and investigate detention decisions in Cook County to ensure they comply with the law and are enforced fairly and without bias.</p><p>Reform must be effective in practice, not just in theory. Victims deserve protection, communities deserve trust, defendants deserve fairness, families deserve stability and taxpayers deserve a justice system that maintains integrity.</p><p><i>State Rep. La Shawn K. Ford, D-Chicago, chairman, West Side Heroin/Opioid Task Force, and </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-house-illinois-7th-congressional-district-primary-results" ><i>Democratic nominee,</i></a> <i>Illinois’ 7th Congressional District</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2e0000" name="module-2e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Good luck, Maddie Lee, but not to the Dodgers</h3><p>I am writing to express gratitude to longtime Cubs beat writer Maddie Lee, who I was sad to hear is <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/maddie_m_lee/status/2031876043263656339?s=20" target="_blank" >moving to the Los Angeles Times</a> to cover the Dodgers.</p><p>Ms. Lee’s writing about the Cubs was nothing less than outstanding. She has a deep understanding of contemporary analytics and statistics, a grasp of the emotional connections Cubs fans feel toward the team, as well as the franchise’s complicated history. She also had a graceful and engaging prose style; her stories were always a pleasure to read, even if they dealt with Cubs losses far too often.</p><p>No knock on whoever takes over the Cubs beat for the Sun-Times, but Ms. Lee will be missed. I just hope she will be OK when the Cubs beat the Dodgers in the National League Championship Series this October.</p><p><i>Bill Savage, Rogers Park</i></p><h3>People are the same everywhere </h3><p>President Donald Trump has been making cruel, divisive ethnic comments for years, but recently he has targeted a tiny minority of American immigrants from Somalia. It’s unlikely he has ever personally known a Somali, and he admits he’s never visited the country. But that doesn’t stop him from labeling Somalia a <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/12/05/nx-s1-5632602/trumps-garbage-comment-met-with-disappointment-in-somalia" target="_blank" >garbage country</a> and its people not worthy of being accepted into the fabric of America.</p><p>In 1967 I began Peace Corps service in Somalia as a middle school teacher, and it was as different from life in the Chicago suburb where I grew up as you could imagine. And while there were many things that were hard to adjust to, the kids that I taught were not among them. They were 11 and 12 years old, and I found them <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2025/12/19/somalia-immigrant-minnesota-trump-ice-detention-nicu-postpartum-baby" >easy to get to know and love</a>. It turned out that they delighted in a good prank and were quick to laugh. But they were also sensitive and feelings were easily hurt. Some were impressively smart, some struggled, and all wanted to do well.</p><p>Upon returning home in 1969 I taught sixth grade at a modern school in Northbrook with air conditioning, carpeted classrooms and all the teaching aids I could ask for. It could not have been more different from my school in Somalia, except that the kids were exactly the same. Their insecurities were identical.</p><p>They all wanted to be accepted by their peers, and they all wanted to be seen as successful. The things that made them laugh or cry were no different from my Somali students.</p><p>In 1979 I started an air freight company in Chicago that 33 years later grew into a global company with thousands of employees across the United States and dozens of other countries around the world. Our employees dressed differently, had their own music, language and religion, but they all had important things in common. They appreciated being respected, thanked and working in an organization that was honest and supportive. Our company culture bridged all their local cultures, and that culture was our most valuable asset. What I learned in Somalia is that people are the same everywhere in the ways that truly matter. Every leader should understand that, especially the U.S. president.</p><p><i>Bill McInerney, retired founder/CEO, Phoenix International Freight Services Ltd., Park Ridge</i></p><h3><b>Chicago’s antisemitism report demands action</b></h3><p>The Chicago Commission on Human Relations’ <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/content/dam/city/depts/cchr/general/MBJ%20Anti-Jewish%20Hate%20Crimes%20Report%202.11.26.pdf" target="_blank" >recent report</a> on rising antisemitism, covered in the Sun-Times, should be a wake-up call for the city. Will it stand against antisemitism or stand back and do nothing?</p><p>The commission has done what history demands and issued a report on rising antisemitism in Chicago. Under the leadership of Chair Nancy Andrade, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2025/09/08/anti-semitism-hate-crimes-chicago-commission-on-human-relations" >commission undertook the difficult</a> but necessary work of gathering testimony and confronting uncomfortable truths. This report is not just a collection of data points. It reflects the experiences of Jewish Chicagoans who have seen old hatreds resurface in new forms.</p><p>Days ago, a group of Jewish students attending a campus meetup at a cafe near DePaul University were harassed and intimidated simply for being Jewish. This was not an isolated misunderstanding. It reflects a broader and troubling pattern. Antisemitism is no longer confined to rhetoric online. It is surfacing in classrooms, public spaces and neighborhoods across Chicago.</p><p>Now it’s up to Mayor Brandon Johnson. Will he stand with those who spoke up, or allow their warnings to be lost in the noise of city politics?</p><p>This should not be a partisan question. It is about whether city leaders will act when residents raise serious concerns about hate.</p><p>The commission’s recommendations are not radical. They are the basic tools every city should use to protect its residents: clear ways to report hate, stronger coordination and a commitment to confront antisemitism wherever it appears.</p><p>The City Council has already taken an important step by unanimously adopting and codifying the <a class="Link" href="https://chicagomaroon.com/51005/news/chicago-codifies-ihra-definition-of-antisemitism-after-uchicago-student-lobbying/" target="_blank" >International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s</a> working definition of antisemitism into law. The commission’s report builds on that foundation by translating principles into policy.</p><p>Turning away from these findings would deepen the sense of abandonment many already feel.</p><p>At the Simon Wiesenthal Center, where I serve as director of social action and partnerships for the Midwest and South, we work to confront antisemitism and hate through education, accountability, and civic engagement.</p><p>Chicago prides itself on being a city of inclusion. Supporting the commission’s recommendations is a chance to prove it.</p><p>The commission has done its work. Now Chicago’s leadership must do theirs.</p><p><i>Alison Pure-Slovin, Midwest director of social action and partnerships, Simon Wiesenthal Center</i></p><h3>PAC attack</h3><p>Thank you for your reporting on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/13/super-pacs-influence-2026-illinois-primary-races-glossary" target="_blank" >various PACs</a> that tried to influence Tuesday's primary elections. One might think that the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision has made us helpless against this onslaught of dark money, but it did not. Every state has the right to decide what powers it grants to corporations doing business in that state — and which powers it does not. The <a class="Link" href="https://transparentelection.org/" target="_blank" >Transparent Election Initiative</a>, which began in Montana but is spreading to other states, including Illinois, aims to deny corporations the power to meddle in politics. This can be done through legislation or by changing the state constitution.</p><p>State Rep. <a class="Link" href="https://ilhousedems.com/2026/03/11/chung-introduces-bill-preventing-corporate-interference-with-elections/" target="_blank" >Sharon Chung</a>, D-Bloomington, has introduced <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=18&DocNum=4435&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=165138&SessionID=114" target="_blank" >House Bill 4435</a>, which would clarify that corporations do not have the power "to engage in activities related to the nomination or election of candidates for public office or the initiation, submission, or consideration of questions of public policy."</p><p>We should all urge our state representative to support this bill.</p><p><i>Tom McDougal, South Kenwood</i></p><h3>When youngsters are old enough to vote</h3><p>What a great idea to have students run an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/03/13/cook-county-high-school-early-voting-program-alternative-energy" >early voting program</a> in Cook County. Allowing students to vote, however, is another matter. Science has shown, the prefrontal cortex of the human brain, which, among other functions, controls decision-making, does not mature until age 24 or 25. That fact, along with the limited amount of education high-school students receive in civics and history classes — sometimes from teachers who don't conceal their political preferences — dictates that young adult students should not be entrusted with the important task of voting on issues that will affect thousands of people. Karma, however, just might come back at them when those students become older adults and have to live with the consequences of decisions made by their 18-year-old immature and inexperienced selves.</p><p><i>Sherry Szilage Stoffel, North Aurora</i></p><h3>Back to regular programming</h3><p>I’m so grateful the primary election is over because I was so tired of seeing the same commercials over and over on who praised U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, who wants to abolish ICE and who got money from an<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/08/raja-krishnamoorthi-us-senate-candidate-acceptance-trump-maga-contributions-shyam-sankar-ice-contractor" > ICE contractor</a>. I now look forward to all the personal injury attorney commercials where I just have to dial one number to contact them.</p><p><i>Richard Barber, Mount Greenwood</i></p><h3>With Iran war, MAGA could go bust</h3><p>Most of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/us-iran-war-israel-how-other-countries-view-middle-east-conflict/" target="_blank" >entire world</a> seems to be opposed to the war in Iran. Other than Israel, which is attacking Iran with the U.S., very few countries are willing to step up to help. American support <a class="Link" href="https://criticalissues.umd.edu/feature/do-americans-favor-attacking-iran-under-current-circumstances-latest-critical-issues-poll-0" target="_blank" >dwindles</a> with every <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/03/04/chicagoans-uneasy-gas-prices-iran-war-straight-hormuz-supply-chain-disruptions" >gasoline price hike</a>. By the time the midterms roll around, our economy will be in tatters. I suppose the bright side is that Trump's MAGA will be "completely obliterated".</p><p><i>Tony Galati, Lemont</i> </p><h3>Trump should help with gas money</h3><p>With oil around <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/stocks-markets-oil-iran-trump-1abeddf7c4bf19d1dc96b3f23c1de402" target="_blank" >$100 to $115 a barrel</a>, U.S. oil producers are charging higher prices for gasoline at the pump. The cost to extract oil with the U.S. has not increased. The producers are reaping a <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/mar/17/democrats-windfall-tax-fossil-fuel-companies-iran-war" target="_blank" >windfall gain</a> due to rising global prices due to Donald's Trump's war.</p><p>If Trump cared about working families, he could tax the windfall gain and send us all a check to help pay for our gas fill-ups.</p><p><i>Don Wedd, Hyde Park</i></p><h3>Going to bat for Venezuela?</h3><p>Now that President Donald Trump has become Venezuela's self-appointed leader, do we congratulate him on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/mlb/2026/03/17/venezuela-beats-us-to-win-its-first-world-baseball-classic-title" >Venezuela winning</a> the World Baseball Classic by defeating the United States 3-2?</p><p><i>John Farrell, DeKalb</i><br></p>

title: Chicago young voter turnout jumped from previous midterm primary, but it’s no ‘systemic rise’
summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/18/illinois-primary-super-pac-spending-aipac-cryptocurrency-ai-sports-betting" >more than $50 million</a> from super PACs, dark money and special interest groups that poured into this week's primary races across the Chicago area proved to be a significant motivator for young people to vote.</p><p>Finding out who was funding which campaigns was among the first topics Alan Cervantes, 24, researched when deciding for whom he would cast his votes. He was mostly moved to vote against candidates who received money from groups that support U.S. military aid to Israel amid the deadly conflicts in the Middle East.</p><p>“I cannot feel comfortable with our tax money going to atrocities over there, especially because we have so many people at home who need that money and instead it’s going to war,” said Cervantes, a Hoffman Estates resident who voted in suburban Cook County and helped mobilize his peers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to vote.</p><p>Preliminary voter turnout data showed the number of voters aged 17 to 34 notably increased in the 2026 primary election compared to the 2022 midterm primary, according to the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners. Residents who are 17, but will be 18 years old by the November general election, are allowed to vote in the primary.</p><p>According to the Board of Elections, about 85,000 people between 17 and 34 voted in Tuesday’s primary, with more mail-in votes still to be counted until March 31. That’s up from the close to 62,000 voters in that age group in the 2022 primary, but it’s similar to the 86,000 in the 2018 primary.</p><p>An age breakdown of voter turnout in suburban Cook County was not immediately available.</p><p>“Money in our politics was a really big one this year,” said Stevie Valles, CEO of Chicago Votes, which collaborated with Chicago Public Schools and Noble Network of Charter Schools to help thousands of students vote. “We saw a lot of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/18/illinois-primary-super-pac-spending-aipac-cryptocurrency-ai-sports-betting" target="_blank" ><u>spending</u></a> from different sources — this election season more than many others, that came up amongst young people more often.”</p><p>But other issues also drove young voters to the polls, like affordability, federal immigration enforcement, health care access, education funding and racial justice, Valles said. </p><p>Latrice Johnson, 29, from South Shore, was especially interested in judicial races in her district because “judges make a lot of decisions.” Among her most passionate votes was for Radiance Ward, a Cook County assistant public defender who won the Democratic primary race for judge in the 1st subcircuit.</p><p>Simply exercising her right to vote was most important to Johnson, though.</p><p>“It’s a valuable thing to be able to go out to vote because there were so many people that have gone before me, gone before us as a Black community who fought really hard [for the right to vote],” Johnson said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Primary elections tend to be driven by voters aged 55 and older, said Max Bever, the Chicago Board of Elections director of public information.</p><p>The plurality of voters in this year's primary were between 65 and 74 years old, making up almost 40% of the ballots cast. The 17 to 24 age group made up nearly 17% of votes and ages 25 to 34 were about 18% — the two lowest of all age groups, according to Chicago Board of Elections data as of Tuesday night. </p><p>The latter numbers are a significant jump from the previous primary, which saw about 10% turnout from voters 17 to 24 years old and 14% turnout in ages 25 to 34, according Board of Elections data.</p><p>Despite this year’s increase in young voter turnout, Bever said he hasn’t necessarily seen a “systemic rise in younger voters," because they still make up a smaller portion of overall turnout.</p><p>“I think [primary elections are] tougher for all voters, but especially for younger voters who are asked to choose a political party and only vote that political party ballot,” Bever said. “I think it’s also somewhat of a question for campaigns and for candidates. Are they reaching out to younger voters? Are they connecting with them? Are they getting them to the polls?”</p><p>Kayla Pilgrim, 20, of Berwyn, wanted to be a number in the voter turnout figures.</p><p>“I didn’t want my voice left out of that data,” Pilgrim said.</p><p>She said young voters should show up for elections — especially primaries when voters can choose which type of candidate they want in the general election — because it will show future candidates how to shape their platforms to attract the youth vote.</p><p>“It’s important to be collected so that when other people look at [which] platforms garnered support, it then encourages other political leaders to make sure that when they run in the future, that their positions actually are in line with what young people care about,” Pilgrim said. “And you can show that in the primaries.”</p>

title: Government shutdowns, long airport lines have become the new normal
summary: <p>If you’ve ever traveled to France, chances are you’ve come up against this all-too-common phenomenon. You get to the train station and, without warning, your train is out of service. Or a restaurant is oddly closed during regular business hours.</p><p>"C’est la grève," you may hear from a local, accompanied by a shrug. It’s the strike.</p><p>There’s a joke in France about its time-honored tradition of labor protests: A tourist asks a waiter what the signs are about at a protest across the street. The waiter hardly looks up and simply says, "Thursday."</p><p>Strikes, protests, work stoppages and closures are so frequent in France, there are multiple apps and websites devoted to letting locals and tourists alike know what will be open and what will be closed, and those in the know check daily.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d80000" name="module-d80000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Columnist</div> </div><p>A strike today at schools in Dijon, Lyon and Rennes; an ongoing transport strike in Rouen; closures at the Louvre. <a class="Link" href="https://www.cestlagreve.fr/" target="_blank" >One site</a> promises: "Thanks to our service, unexpected problems are a thing of the past. You’ll no longer be stuck waiting for your train, and you can plan a backup solution!"</p><p>Americans may hear this and smugly scoff at a society that’s turned such dysfunction into a revered art form. But our pride is increasingly undeserved.</p><p>Last week I flew between Newark and Austin. As you may have seen on the news, the security lines were hours long and, in some cases, snaked out the airport doors and onto the street.</p><p>This wasn’t because of a protest or a strike, however, but yet another government shutdown, the third in just six months.</p><p>Starting in October last year and lasting for 43 days, we endured the longest shutdown in U.S. history due to an impasse over Affordable Care Act subsidies. Then, earlier this year, a partial shutdown over delays in a funding package linked to immigration. And now, going on more than a month, we’re in another partial shutdown over Department of Homeland Security funding.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/16/travel/tsa-airport-delays-shutdown.html" target="_blank" >shutdown</a> has meant about 50,000 Transportation Security Administration officers have been working without pay. Many have picked up second jobs, while others are calling in sick and more than 300 have simply quit.</p><p>Acting Deputy TSA Administrator Adam Stahl says we’re rapidly approaching a breaking point:</p><p>“If the call rate does climb," <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/tsa-airports-could-shut-down-officer-call-out-rate-climbs/" target="_blank" >he said</a> of agents calling out of work, "there could be scenarios where we may have to shut down airports. This is a serious situation."</p><p>You’d think Congress would want to fix this quickly in an election year, but all evidence points to the contrary. Republicans and Democrats remain in a stalemate over DHS funding, with both parties blaming each other and using strikingly similar language to do so.</p><p>"Democrats need to end their political posturing, stop using our TSA agents as political pawns, and fully fund DHS," <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/03/19/us/tsa-political-impacts" target="_blank" >said</a> Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala.</p><p>Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/nClkqs020bw" target="_blank" >said</a>, "I think it’s simply wrong for my Republican colleagues to use these hard-working Americans as leverage, as pawns, in what they are presenting as a false choice to the American people."</p><p>But while both parties finger-point, all the average American sees is a dysfunctional government getting more dysfunctional by the day, with basic pursuits — like air travel — feeling more like capricious and unreliable luxuries.</p><p>While inching through security in Austin, someone asked me what the lines were about. "The shutdown," I said. He didn’t even know we were in one again.</p><p>We deserve better from our government. But if this is just our new normal — where on any given day we’re left wondering what parts of our government are open and running — we may, like the French, need to get ourselves an app for that.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8f0000" name="module-8f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. title: 'Broadview Six' ICE protesters can see White House communications about their case — if they exist
summary: <p>If the White House encouraged<b> </b>Chicago’s U.S. attorney's office in writing to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >bring a conspiracy<b> </b>indictment</a> against six<b> </b>immigration protesters last fall, defense attorneys should be allowed to see it, a prosecutor agreed Thursday.</p><p>But Assistant U.S. Attorney William<b> </b>Hogan<b> </b>said he didn’t expect to find anything related to the case against the so-called “Broadview Six.” Hogan made the comment while speaking to U.S. District Judge<b> </b>April Perry about recent defense motions in the case.</p><p>“To my knowledge — I’m not saying that I know for sure — but my understanding is there is no such communication,” Hogan said. “Certainly, [there] was none before the indictment.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/16/chicago-broadview-six-kat-abughazaleh-midway-blitz-trump-ice" >Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants want conspiracy charge tossed, argue protesting isn’t a crime</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Hogan also confirmed for the judge that prosecutors still expect to take four of the original six defendants to trial. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >The feds last week dropped charges</a> against musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and former Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp.</p><p>Still charged are<b> </b>former congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt and Andre Martin,<b> </b>a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff. They’re all set for trial May 26.</p><p>Straw was the only defendant to attend Thursday’s hearing.<b> </b>Each of the four remaining defendants are involved in local Democratic politics.<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/us-house-illinois-9th-congressional-district-primary-results" target="_blank" >Abughazaleh placed second</a> in Tuesday’s primary for the Democratic nomination for Illinois’ 9th Congressional District seat, won by Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"
