title: Federal judge extends order blocking Trump cuts to Illinois public health funding
summary: <p>A federal judge in Chicago extended an order blocking the Trump administration from cutting $600 million in public heath grants to Illinois and three other Democratic-led states.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Manish S. Shah issued a preliminary injunction Friday in the Northern District of Illinois Court, extending <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/02/12/federal-judge-temporarily-blocks-trump-cuts-to-hiv-lead-poisoning-prevention-funds" target="_blank" >a temporary restraining order he issued last month</a> that was set to expire.</p><p>The four targeted states — Illinois, Minnesota, Colorado and California — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/02/11/federal-cuts-hiv-lead-poisoning-prevention-grants-raoul" target="_blank" >filed a federal lawsuit </a>in February.</p><p>The funding cuts would have targeted HIV tracking, lead-poisoning prevention, family planning and other public health initiatives across the four states. In Illinois, the planned cuts targeted at least $29 million in grants funding the American Medical Association in Illinois, which supports gender-affirming care, and various HIV prevention programs.</p><p>In the injunction, Shah said the cuts could have led to “irreparable harm” and that the public interest favored preserving the funding. Any actions taken to halt payments to the targeted states from the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention should be considered “null, void, and rescinded,” Shah wrote.</p><p>The judge set another hearing in the case for March 23.</p><p>In a statement, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said the grants were cut because they "do not reflect agency priorities."</p><p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul previously said the cuts would lead to the loss of 100 jobs at the Illinois Department of Public Health and the end of lead-poisoning prevention grants in 25 local health departments.</p><p>“Targeting four Democrat-run states that are standing up to his completely unrelated immigration policies is a transparent attempt to bully us into compliance,” Raoul said in a statement after Shah issued the temporary restraining order. “We remain unflinching in our commitment to defending against the Trump administration’s continued unlawful directives intended to force us to implement immigration and other unrelated policies.”</p><p>Raoul did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the preliminary injunction.</p>
author: Mary Norkol

title: Pritzker taunts Bovino amid reports of Border Patrol chief’s retirement: 'No one is above the law'
summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker on Monday celebrated the reported retirement of U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, who led President Donald Trump’s aggressive — and at times deadly — deportation campaigns in Chicago and other cities.</p><p>“Greg Bovino won’t just get to walk away — he will be held accountable and responsible for the damage he’s done to our nation,” Pritzker said on the social media platform X. “We won’t forget, and neither should you. No one is above the law.”</p><p>Bovino reportedly told <a class="Link" href="“The greatest honor of my entire life was to work alongside Border Patrol agents on the border and in the interior of the United States in some of the most challenging conditions the agency has ever faced.” Bovino went on to add, “Watching these agents out there giving it their all in some of the most dangerous of environments we have ever faced was humbling.”" target="_blank" >Breitbart</a> he plans to retire at the end of the month, and other outlets have since reported the news. The Sun-Times hasn’t independently verified those reports. A DHS spokesperson said, “Chief Bovino has not submitted any retirement paperwork.”</p><p>Bovino became <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration" target="_blank" >the face of the Trump administration’s controversial immigration enforcement efforts</a>, using social media to tout arrests and take on critics, including Pritzker. Agents under his command in Chicago made allegedly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2025/10/17/gregory-bovino-border-customs-enforcement-deportation-trump-california-chicago" target="_blank" >race-based stops</a>, used <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/14/ice-bovino-border-patrol-homeland-security-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" >risky tactics and pummeling force</a> and often deployed chemical irritants against protesters.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >restricted the feds’ use of force</a> under Bovino’s watch in an order that was formally vacated earlier this month by a federal appeals court. Ellis notably accused Bovino about lying under oath about his justification for the use of tear gas in Little Village.</p><p>Bovino was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/26/border-patrol-gregory-bovino-tom-homan-immigration-alex-pretti" target="_blank" >sent back to the El Centro Sector</a> in Southern California following the killing of Alex Pretti on Jan. 24 in Minneapolis. Pretti, a nurse for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, was fatally shot by two Customs and Border Protection agents.</p><p>After the shooting, Bovino said Pretti “approached law enforcement with a weapon” and sought to “massacre” them — a claim that was quickly undercut by video evidence, though Pretti was legally carrying a weapon.</p><p>Bovino was hired before July 6, 2008, making him <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbp.gov/employee-resources/retirement/leo-cbpo/cbpo-retirement" target="_blank" >exempt from the agency’s mandatory retirement</a> — which is the last day of the month in which a CBP employee both turns 57 and reaches 20 years of service. He turns 56 later this month.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/12/gregory-bovino-border-patrol-deportation-elcentro-california-blowing-rock-boone-north-carolina-migrants-immigration" target="_blank" >Greg Bovino’s the star of Trump’s deportation show. We trace his roots.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’" target="_blank" >Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/14/ice-bovino-border-patrol-homeland-security-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" >Tear gas, car crashes, chokeholds: Risky tactics have driven Trump’s Chicago deportation ‘blitz’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Mayor Johnson signals support for letting CPS students take a day off to push for school funding
summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Monday hinted strongly that he supports the Chicago Teachers Union’s call to officially sanction a one-day strike on May 1 that would allow students at Chicago Public Schools to miss a day of classes to make their case for increased school funding.</p><p>Johnson is a former middle school teacher and paid organizer for the CTU — whose mayoral campaign was buoyed by $5.6 million in campaign contributions and hundreds of foot soldiers provided by the CTU and its affiliates.</p><p>His decision to declare a record $1 billion tax increment financing surplus helped to rescue CPS and bankroll the new teachers contract.</p><p>Now the teachers union wants the mayor and CPS's hybrid school board still narrowly controlled by Johnson’s appointees to essentially sanction May 1 as a school holiday, which would allow students to participate in a “no school, no work, no shopping” day.</p><p>Appearing Monday on WBEZ-FM Radio’s “Ask the Mayor” program, Johnson said his longstanding push to tax major corporations and the wealthy Chicagoans to bolster school funding has so far gone nowhere — and it’s time to push the envelope by turning talk into protest action.</p><p>"People all over the country are tired. Working people have had to bear the weight of a sluggish economy while the ultra-rich continue to get richer. Our schools are woefully underfunded… People want more investment in our public transportation system,” the mayor said. “All of that requires a push from working people to challenge elected leaders.”</p><p>WBEZ host Sasha-Ann Simons noted that CPS students already will be off Tuesday and Wednesday this week, and will be off all next week for spring break and again on April 3.</p><p>Johnson said he's aware of that, but argued that CPS parents also "want their schools to be fully-funded." </p><p>“If we just believe that we can just sit on our hands and just hope and wish, that clearly has not worked. I’ve called for taxing corporations and I’ve had other elected leaders fight me who are also Democrats," he said.</p><p>Johnson said Rev. Jesse Jackson, the civil rights icon who died last month at the age of 84, would never have achieved all that he did without “direct action and organizing.” He “literally had to protest to ensure that we have a right to vote,” a right that is now under threat, the mayor said.</p><p>“We are experiencing unprecedented levels of attack [on] the gains that our ancestors made. And if we believe for one minute that the way in which we’re gonna receive our God-given rights our is by just simply asking questions or having town halls — absent taking it to the streets — we are missing the moment,” the mayor said. “We have to push… government to do right by working people. And that will require protest.”</p><p>Ald. Jeanette Taylor (20th), Johnson’s handpicked chair of the City Council’s Education Committee, has two grandchildren who attend Chicago Public Schools. Taylor said she does not believe the mayor should sanction students to skip classes, unless they learn something from it.</p><p>“Are they going down to Springfield? Are they coming down to City Hall? What work is gonna be done? There needs to be something else other than just taking a day off. I want young people to understand them taking the day off. Are we teaching them about May Day? Are we teaching them about workers rights? Are we teaching them to advocate in Springfield for themselves? What comes with it?” Taylor said.</p><p>"It has to be a day of action. Don’t ask me to let my kids take a day off of school so they can sit at home, because we know what they’re gonna do at home. They’re gonna be on the internet. They’re gonna be doing everything but what they’re supposed to be doing.”</p><p>The resolution approved by the CTU’s 730-member House of Delegates last week calls for CPS to join a national movement embracing <a class="Link" href="https://maydaystrong.org/" target="_blank" >a day of “no school, no work, no shopping</a>.” Participants plan to call for higher taxes on the wealthy, better-funded schools, protections for immigrants and other reforms.</p><p>Union leaders cited several reasons for participating, including to demand that ICE gets “out of our cities,” referring to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and to push to “tax the rich to support our schools and vital services,” according to the resolution. It also says public education is facing attacks from “MAGA politicians” who support the policies of President Donald Trump and “corporate interests."</p><p>The union wants members and students to use the day to take part in “age-appropriate” civic education, labor history programming, voter registration and know-your-rights training, as well as rallies and marches.</p>

title: Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants want conspiracy charge tossed, argue protesting isn’t a crime
summary: <p>Arguing that federal prosecutors have made a “crime out of what under the Constitution cannot be a crime,” the group of protesters<b> </b>originally known as the "Broadview Six" asked a judge Monday to toss the conspiracy charge<b> </b>filed against them because it runs afoul of the First Amendment’s freedom of assembly.</p><p>It’s the latest attempt to challenge the indictment brought against the group<b> </b>— and one that a defendant in the case had an active role in drafting. The prosecution is one of several to result from the Trump administration's Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>The group is now down to four, after prosecutors<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped<b> </b>the charges against<b> </b>two</a> of the defendants last week. Those who remain say the government’s allegations of conspiracy — a felony that could lead to a prison sentence of up to six years — enhances a misdemeanor charge based on the defendants’ “exercise of their First Amendment rights of assembly and association.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" >Broadview 4? </div><p>“That a misdemeanor … can be escalated to a felony conspiracy charge simply because it occurred in the midst of an otherwise peaceable assembly creates a substantial risk of chilling the public’s willingness to exercise their First Amendment rights of freedom of assembly and freedom of speech,” defense attorneys wrote in an 18-page motion<b> </b>filed Monday.</p><p>The motion was filed on behalf of all the remaining defendants. But one of them, Oak Park village trustee and lawyer Brian Straw, played an active role in drafting it. That's according to Straw attorney Christopher Parente, who said Straw invested "a lot of his blood, sweat and tears."</p><p>"I think the bigger issue for Brian is the right for people to peacefully assemble and to protest their government, regardless of what the issue is," Parente told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Charged along with Straw are 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh,<b> </b>and a senior member of Abughazaleh's campaign staff, Andre Martin. Abughazaleh is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/02/25/congressional-9th-district-15-democrats-march-17-primary-jan-schakowsky-seat" target="_blank" >seeking the Democratic nomination</a><b> </b>in Tuesday’s primary for Illinois’ 9th District<b> </b>congressional seat.</p><p>Prosecutors last week dropped charges against Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh, a musician, and Catherine “Cat” Sharp, a Democrat who dropped her bid for Cook County Board to focus on her legal defense. The feds also recently narrowed<b> </b>their theory of the case.</p><p>Challenges have followed in recent days from the four defendants who still face trial May 26. They sought records Friday<b> </b>that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >might show an improper influence</a> on the case<b> </b>by the Trump administration.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/13/chicago-trump-abughazaleh-justice-department-broadview-midway-blitz-ice" >Remaining Broadview 6 defendants want records showing Trump administration’s influence on conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now they’ve asked U.S. District Judge April Perry<b> </b>to toss the conspiracy charge on First Amendment grounds, arguing that the feds' theory "puts any protester at risk of being charged with a felony on account of being in the wrong place at the wrong time with others." The lawyers are due back in Perry’s courtroom March 31. Each of the four also face a misdemeanor charge alleging they impeded an officer.</p><p>The conspiracy charge revolves around events on the morning of Sept. 26 outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility<b> </b>in Broadview. It became a hotbed for protests during Midway Blitz.</p><p>The indictment alleges that, while a federal agent drove a vehicle<b> </b>toward the ICE facility, the defendants and others surrounded it. Members of the larger crowd allegedly<b> </b>banged on the vehicle, pushed against it, scratched it and even etched the word “PIG”<b> </b>into it.</p><p>The crowd allegedly broke a side mirror<b> </b>and a rear windshield wiper<b> </b>and forced the agent “to drive at an extremely slow rate of speed.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Rather, the indictment generally accuses the four of bracing themselves with their hands and bodies against the vehicle,<b> </b>hindering its progress.</p><p>They did so after exercising their First Amendment rights “in a location specified for such protests by the Village of Broadview,” and after the agent decided to slowly drive<b> </b>into the crowd, according to the defense attorneys.</p><p>The agent did not wait for police to clear a path, did not identify himself and did not order the crowd to move aside, the attorneys argued.</p><p>“Their only actions — aside from bracing themselves against a vehicle that drove into a crowd of protesters — was being in that crowd of protesters,” the defense attorneys wrote. “Their actions are inseparable from the exercise of their constitutional right to assemble — in the exact location where Broadview police had allowed them to do so all morning."</p><p>Evan<b> </b>Bernick, an associate professor<b> </b>at Northern Illinois University<b> </b>College of Law, said he spoke with Straw<b> </b>and his attorneys<b> </b>about the motion filed Monday. He said the allegations in the case could have a chilling effect on protests beyond those against Midway Blitz. That's because of the concern that lawful protesters could be on the hook for the illegal actions of others through a conspiracy charge.</p><p>"This prosecution is not just about this prosecution," Bernick said. "It's about the prosecution of anybody who might go into public and engage in an assembly with peaceful purposes, with lawful purposes, and then decide not to on the belief that they might get targeted and successfully indicted, even though they have done nothing wrong."</p>

title: Mayor Brandon Johnson meets with men in prison working toward Northwestern University degrees
summary: <p>For the past three weeks, Northwestern University student Anthony Ehlers has been painting a portrait of Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>Ehlers has been working on the painting, which depicts the mayor signing an executive order concerning the National Guard, in anticipation of Johnson’s visit on Sunday to Sheridan Correctional Center, where Ehlers is incarcerated.</p><p>“He’s here on a Sunday when he usually is at church with his family; that’s pretty meaningful,” Ehlers said. “He knows we can’t vote, so he’s not stumping for votes; He’s really talking about issues that affect us.”</p><p>More than 100 people gathered in Sheridan’s gymnasium, about 70 miles southwest of Chicago. Students of the Northwestern Prison Education Program, which offers undergraduate degrees to men incarcerated at Sheridan, their families and professors had the opportunity to speak with the mayor.</p><p>In 2023, <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2023/11/21/history-making-ceremony-men-prison-earn-degrees-northwestern-university-we-want-show-what" target="_blank" ><u>their initial graduating class</u></a> became the first group of incarcerated students to earn a bachelor’s degree from a top university. Northwestern also offers a bachelor’s degree program at the largest women’s prison in the state, Logan Correctional Center.</p><p>“I'm here to learn and ensure that my responsibility as a leader of the city in Chicago, that you all know that you will always be front and center in all of the decisions that I make,” Johnson said to the crowd.</p><p>In a fireside chat-style program, student Nikolas Gacho spoke about how he was expelled three times with little support from the five different schools he attended. Giovanni Rios told Johnson how every day he had had to split two loaves of bread with numerous family members for a meal. Hugo Ocon raised concerns over federal immigration raids across the city.</p><p>Following their personal statements, the students, now all graduates or graduates-to-be of Northwestern University, moved on to questions. They asked what Johnson’s administration is doing to strengthen public schools, enact compassionate immigration policy and support incarcerated people, as about 40% of people in Illinois prisons are sentenced in Cook County.</p><p>In his response, Johnson discussed his family’s own experience with the prison system, the necessity of educational investments, and the city’s Director of Reentry Joseph Mapp, who is tasked with providing Chicagoans leaving prison with access to housing, mental health support and job training.</p><p>“People who are closest to the danger, are closest to the solutions. We have to center our work around the people who have experienced these failed systems,” Johnson said.</p><p>For student Darvin Henderson, the mayor’s visit was “magical.”</p><p>“I didn’t come from a place where we meet people like that, like the mayor. … I didn’t even grow up around that,” Henderson said. “Those opportunities never even was available. And look, I’m in prison. People would think I’m at the bottom. And yet I’m meeting – rubbing elbows with people that’s at the top!”</p><p>As student Taki Peacock hopes to make his eventual release as easy as possible, he was interested to learn about the Office of Reentry.</p><p>“Leaving incarceration, where basically you’ve been taken care of your whole incarceration whether it be family members or the system itself taking care of you to having to go into society and provide for yourself completely, that’s a frightening perspective,” Peacock said.</p><p>Ian Valencia, a Northwestern senior incarcerated at Sheridan, has been locked up half his life, since he was 17.</p><p>The visit of a sitting Chicago mayor to a state prison – perhaps the first of its kind, according to Northwestern students – is symbolically important, Valencia said.</p><p>“It’s helping give me a more hopeful look on what’s possible, if more people get involved in trying to change what prison is supposed to be like,” he said.</p><p>Earlier in the week, students found out their family members could join the event.</p><p>It gave Rob Cunningham the opportunity to see her son Demetrius Cunningham play the keyboard for the first time. Cunningham bought Demetrius keyboard instructional books, who while in prison taught himself how to play using only<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/written-inside/2017/03/21/ep-1-a-silent-piano" target="_blank" ><u> a piece of cardboard</u></a>. Cunningham said it was amazing to see Demetrius playing for the crowd.</p><p>Student Anthony Harris Jr.’s father drove eight hours from Memphis with less than a week’s notice to attend the event. It had been about a year and a half since father and son had seen each other. Anthony Harris Sr. said seeing the changes NPEP brings to students’ lives is a “blessing.”</p><p>William Shafiq Peeples, formerly on death row before Illinois abolished capital punishment, is serving a life sentence for murder. Peeples said he hopes the visit helped the mayor understand the value of educating people in prison – even those, like himself, who will never be released.</p><p>“So I understand when some people hear about the program and they say, ‘You’re giving all this education to a murderer.’ I think talking to him today will help him be able to explain to them why this is necessary,” Peeples said. “Education transforms human beings.”</p><p><i>This story is a collaboration between WBEZ and WTTW News.</i></p>

title: Mayor Brandon Johnson answers your questions on In The Loop with Sasha-Ann Simons
summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson returns to WBEZ 91.5 at 9 a.m. Monday to answer your questions live on the morning talk show “In the Loop” with host Sasha-Ann Simons. Call 866-915-WBEZ to ask the mayor a question.</p><p>Last month, Johnson talked about an executive order aiming to create new ways to hold U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents accountable for alleged wrongdoing.</p><p>"The state’s attorney has made it clear she would prosecute criminal behavior if there was evidence brought to her," Johnson said. "So now there is a clear directive that I’ve provided to my police department to ensure that evidence is not just collected, but it’s preserved."</p><p>Amy in the Jefferson Park neighborhood was worried Johnson’s rhetoric would encourage the Trump administration to send ICE agents back to Chicago. Johnson responded by saying, "This is everything about what this president is determined to do, which is undermine our democracy. ...This is not a challenge to the president; this is a challenge to us as people who define this country through a very fundamental value, the ability to have free and fair elections and to be able to have communities and cities that are safe and vibrant. We should not be afraid of our own government."</p><p>Johnson has previously answered listener questions about community resources for kids, job opportunities for Black Chicagoans, teen curfew concerns and locking horns with City Council over the city budget.</p><p><i>WBEZ’s “In the Loop” connects you with the people behind the stories: experts, neighbors and newsmakers who shape the city we share. For more on “In the Loop” and to listen to their segments, visit their website. You can also listen to the show on Spotify or the WBEZ app.</i></p>
author: Sasha-Ann Simons | WBEZ

title: Chicago and suburban Democratic voters more likely to vote for candidates who fought ICE, poll finds
summary: <p>Democratic and independent voters still see immigration enforcement as a top issue in Chicago and the surrounding suburbs — and are more likely to support a candidate who protested President Donald Trump’s "Operation Midway Blitz," a new poll commissioned by a progressive coalition found.</p><p>Several candidates in congressional and state races have made their anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement stance a focal point of their campaigns, including the top U.S. Senate Democratic candidates. Tuesday’s primary elections will serve as a test of whether campaign messaging about fighting ICE worked — and how views on immigration have changed during Trump’s second term.</p><p>When voters were asked about ICE, 63% had an unfavorable view, while 31% had a favorable view. That broke down sharply by political parties, with 90% of Democrats viewing ICE unfavorably compared to 9% of Republicans. Among independents, the number was 62%. </p><p>In Chicago, 75% of those polled overall had an unfavorable view of ICE. In the rest of Cook County, 62% of those polled viewed ICE unfavorably, and in surrounding counties, 56% had an unfavorable view of ICE. </p><p>About 70% of likely Democratic primary voters who participated in the poll said a candidate’s position on ICE was the most important issue or very important to how they’d cast their vote. Nearly two-thirds of respondents said they’d be more likely to support a candidate who has been active in anti-ICE protests.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/voter-guide-primary-election-illinois/" >2026 Illinois Primary Elections Voter Guide</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>About 14% of participants said they resisted ICE actions themselves, and about a quarter of the others said they wished they could have done more. Those who took action were more likely to be younger Chicago residents who consider themselves liberal voters.</p><p>Those actions included signing anti-ICE petitions (32%), contacting local officials (27%), joining vigils or protests (24%), tracking ICE locally (16%) and blowing whistles to alert their neighbors to ICE presence (11%).</p><p>The survey of 800 registered voters in the Chicago media market, including Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Kane, Kankakee, Kendall, McHenry and Will counties, was taken March 1-4. Interviews were conducted by live phone calls and text-to-web responses. According to the pollster, self-described Democrats outnumbered Republicans in the sample 44% to 22%. Another 33% identifying as independent voters.</p><p>Of those polled, 33% approved of the job Trump is doing as president, while 64% disapproved. On Trump's handling of immigration, 35% approved, while 63% said they disapproved.</p><p>The poll was commissioned by Hands Off Chicago, a coalition of progressive community groups including the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, Equality Illinois and the Chicago Federation of Labor. The group also conducted four in-person focus groups — two with white progressives and liberals, one with Latinas and another with Black men. They also conducted an online focus group with swing voters.</p><p>Exposure to ICE played a role in voters’ reaction to the agency, with 73% of those who saw raids in their neighborhoods holding an unfavorable view of the agency. The number declined for those who didn’t have raids in their neighborhood, with 51% of those voters viewing ICE unfavorably.</p><p>The poll also found that 29% of Latinos said they saw ICE agents in their communities personally, more than twice the rate of Black or white voters.</p><p>About 75% of poll respondents said immigration is good for the country, with 83% saying they support providing a path to citizenship for people in the U.S. without documentation.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/31/brandon-johnson-investigate-ice-prosecution-executive-order-chicago" >Mayor Brandon Johnson orders CPD to investigate federal immigration agents for potential prosecution</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>At least 2,800 people were arrested in Illinois during "Operation Midway Blitz" between mid-September through mid-October, primarily in the Chicago area, according to ICE data obtained by the Data Deportation Project and statements about Border Patrol arrests made by the Justice Department in court. On Sept. 12, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González,</a> a father and cook originally from Mexico, was fatally shot at “close range” as he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop. Operation Midway Blitz slowed in mid-November.</p>
author: Mitchell Armentrout

title: CPS Board names 3 finalists to lead district: Interim CEO King, former NYC, East Baton Rouge schools chiefs
summary: <p>The Chicago Board of Education announced three finalists to run the school district Friday.</p><p>One surprising name on the list: Macquline King, who has been serving as interim leader of Chicago Public Schools since June, after originally being told she was not in the running for the permanent position.</p><p>She joins Meisha Porter, the first Black woman to lead New York City’s school system, and Sito Narcisse, the son of Haitian immigrants who led Louisiana’s second-largest school district and oversaw secondary schools in the District of Columbia.</p><p>Next week, the finalists will meet with Mayor Brandon Johnson and will be interviewed by a 15-member panel that includes students, parents, teachers and community members.</p><p>It’s unclear what role the mayor will play in picking the school district’s permanent leader, but the school board says on its website that the mayor will be part of the “decision making process” and that they will work “closely together to find a leader that can champion our district into its next chapter.”</p><p>The Chicago Teachers Union, which is allied with Johnson, believes that until there’s a fully elected board, state law gives the mayor authority to appoint CPS’ leader. CTU Vice President Jackson Potter argued that’s a good thing, given Johnson’s teaching experience.</p><p>“For so long, we've had these people chosen by the Broad Foundation and billionaires, like the Waltons and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, people who were more responsible for financial oversight, such as Pedro Martinez, than learning and instruction,” Potter said. “So having someone who understands the education world granularly is really an advantage.”</p><p>Norma Rios-Sierra, a board member who represents the North Side, said the finalists were leaders who had all worked in large cities, like Chicago.</p><p>“We wanted someone who understood the city and understood the challenges and could really jump in and do the work,” she said. She said she is looking forward to having someone in place who can create the type of stability CPS needs.</p><p>The announcement comes after a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/02/13/is-cps-superintendent-search-on-track-or-stalled-depends-who-you-ask-on-school-board" target="_blank" ><u>months-long search process</u></a> that encountered several hiccups.</p><p>Originally, school board members <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2025/11/07/cps-school-board-signs-ndas-faces-criticism-about-transparency-in-ceo-search" target="_blank" ><u>did not plan to make the names of the finalists public</u></a> because the search firm they hired said that would discourage candidates from applying. In November, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/07/school-leaders-from-new-york-city-and-denver-finalists-cps-top-job-ceo-superintendent" target="_blank" ><u>Porter and another candidate’s name became public</u></a>, and that candidate dropped out of contention.</p><p>At that point, the search was re-opened and board members conducted a new round of interviews.</p><h3>King makes a comeback as a candidate</h3><p>The fact that King was not a finalist in November <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/05/cps-ceo-search-macquline-king" target="_blank" ><u>became a point of contention</u></a>. The West Side NAACP and some school board members suggested that she be kept on until at least January 2027 — when the board will go from being partially appointed by the mayor to being fully elected by voters.</p><p>King, a former CPS principal who previously served in the mayor’s office, had irked some board members during last summer's contentious budget discussions. Though the mayor’s appointees put her in the role, she presented a budget that did not include borrowing, which the mayor’s office wanted to shore up any potential shortfalls.</p><p>This past fall she had the challenging task of figuring out how the school district should address the aggressive immigration enforcement that sent waves of fear through communities. Though some community activists have complained that the school district was slow to respond, CPS eventually stood up a 24-hour command center to help schools.</p><p>At one board meeting, King became emotional as she talked about having to support families who were directly impacted by immigration enforcement.</p><p>School board member Jitu Brown, who represents a West Side district, said the last few months have been an “on the job interview” for King. He points to the way she has handled the closings of privately managed public schools. He said she has been attentive to parents and teachers at The Chicago Academy for the Arts, which the district is taking over, and Aspira Charter Schools, which is abruptly closing two high schools mid-year.</p><p>“You just saw her dealing with crisis situations, being responsive in a way that was different,” he said.</p><h3>Notable absence of Latino candidates in finalist pool</h3><p>Almost half of CPS students are Latino and many community members wanted to see a Latino candidate for CEO. But there are none among the finalists.</p><p>Chalkbeat Chicago reported that a fourth finalist dropped out. Board members would not say whether that person was Latino. They tell WBEZ and the Sun-Times that they were focused on finding someone who represented their values.</p><p>When former CEO Pedro Martinez and Mayor Brandon Johnson clashed in 2024 — ultimately leading to Martinez's ouster — Latino organizations, elected officials and civic leaders <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RkxhTMjJE3Y" target="_blank" ><u>came to Martinez’s defense</u></a>. Among them was Juan Rangel, a former charter school operator who is now CEO of The Urban Center, a nonprofit that advocates for quality schools.</p><p>On Friday, Rangel said it was “unfortunate” that no Latinos were among the final list of candidates and said it showed that the community continues to be an “afterthought” for CPS.</p><p>“It's about having leaders that look like the communities that they serve,” Rangel said. “Apparently not at CPS.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://alumni.mercy.edu/meisha-ross-porter" target="_blank" ><u>Porter was born and raised</u></a> in New York City and attended public schools there. She holds a degree in English from Hunter College, where she concentrated on cross-cultural literature and Black and Puerto Rican studies.</p><p>Porter worked for the New York City school system for more than 20 years, rising from teacher to principal to executive superintendent of schools in the Bronx, New York City’s largest borough. She was named the first Black woman chancellor of New York City schools in February 2021, but her term was short. She was replaced by newly elected Mayor Eric Adams in January 2022.</p><p>She did a short stint as the leader of a community foundation in New York and is currently a fellow for The Center for Educational Innovation, a nonprofit organization that focuses on “building high performing schools in underserved communities.”</p><p>Narcisse served as the superintendent of East Baton Rouge Parish schools in Louisiana from 2021 through 2024, according to his LinkedIn profile. He’s also held leadership roles in Metro Nashville Public Schools and Montgomery County Public Schools in Maryland.</p><p>He currently works with SJ Apple Group, a consulting agency that helps K-12 school districts develop “data-driven solutions that improve student outcomes.” The consulting group <a class="Link" href="https://www.sjapple.com/team" target="_blank" ><u>lists him as its founder</u></a>.</p><p>Narcisse grew up speaking Creole and French in New York. He went through the public school system there while learning English. He graduated from Kennesaw State University in Georgia with a degree in French and went on to earn a master’s of education from Vanderbilt University and a doctorate in education administration from the University of Pittsburgh.</p><p>In an interview with an <a class="Link" href="https://dmj.dmgroupk12.com/articles/taking-on-the-challenges-of-urban-education" target="_blank" ><u>education management group</u></a>, he said that to him, public education has “always been about impact, specifically on Black and Brown kids, because I’m a product of that growing up in New York.”</p>
author: Emmanuel Camarillo

title: Remaining Broadview 6 defendants want records showing Trump administration's influence on conspiracy case
summary: <p>Four demonstrators who say they’ve been targeted for conspiracy charges because they spoke out against the Trump administration want a judge<b> </b>to force prosecutors<b> </b>to hand over records that could show the White House<b> </b>improperly influenced their<b> </b>indictment.</p><p>A new 26-page motion<b> </b>lays out a case<b> </b>that the charges leveled against the group, including congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, is another example of President Donald Trump's administration using the Justice Department to target his “perceived political enemies.”</p><p>“The record readily shows how the Trump administration and its allies have expressly targeted Ms. Abughazaleh on numerous occasions in response to her public criticisms of it and its aggressive immigration enforcement tactics,” the defense attorneys wrote.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" >Broadview 4? Feds drop conspiracy charges against 2 ICE protesters, including Dem who ended campaign</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Abughazaleh is running in Tuesday’s primary for the Democratic nomination<b> </b>for Illinois’ 9th Congressional District.</p><p>But the new motion also points to the activism of Abughazaleh’s co-defendants. They include Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt and Andre Martin, a senior member of Abughazaleh’s campaign.</p><p>The motion comes one day after prosecutors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped<b> </b>charges against two</a> of the original six defendants in the case: Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh, a musician, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/06/cook-county-board-candidate-suspends-campaign-to-fight-indictment" target="_blank" >Catherine “Cat” Sharp</a>, a Democrat who dropped her bid for Cook County Board<b> </b>in Tuesday’s primary<b> </b>to fight the charges.</p><p>The conspiracy case is set for trial May 26. The charges revolve around events on the morning of Sept. 26<b> </b>outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement<b> </b>facility<b> </b>in Broadview. Prosecutors on Friday said they intend to narrow the case to claims that the group conspired to prevent, "by force and intimidation," a federal agent from discharging his duties.</p><div title: Fiscalía retira los cargos de conspiración contra 2 manifestantes de ICE
summary: <p>El jueves, los fiscales federales desestimaron los cargos de conspiración que habían presentado contra dos de las seis personas que protestaron el otoño pasado frente a la instalación de detención de inmigrantes en los suburbios, incluyendo a una ex candidata a la Junta del Condado de Cook que suspendió su campaña para las elecciones primarias del martes para luchar contra los cargos.</p><p>El grupo de acusados, conocido como los “Broadview Six”, quedará reducido a cuatro si la jueza del distrito April Perry concede la moción presentada por los fiscales federales. Esta busca desestimar los cargos contra <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/06/cook-county-board-candidate-suspends-campaign-to-fight-indictment" target="_blank" >Catherine “Cat” Sharp</a> y la artista Joselyn Walsh.</p><p>Sharp expresó que la decisión "prueba lo que siempre hemos sabido, que la acusación en este caso fue defectuosa desde el principio.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-5f0000" name="module-5f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz </div><p>"Aunque estoy, por supuesto, emocionada por este resultado, el abuso del [Servicio de Inmigración y Aduanas (ICE)] contra inmigrantes y refugiados en nuestras comunidades continúa", dijo.</p><p>Walsh comentó que la desestimación de la acusación "no cambia la interrupción que causó en mi vida durante los últimos seis meses”.</p><p>"También no cambia que fui víctima de la violencia de ICE cuando le dispararon a mi guitarra y que muchos siguen experimentando violencia a manos de agentes federales", añadió.</p><p>El fiscal adjunto William Hogan escribió en la moción del jueves que, "como hace la oficina del fiscal en cada caso, el gobierno ha seguido evaluando nuevos hechos, pruebas e información para asegurarse de que se sirvan los intereses de la justicia”.</p><p>“Por lo tanto, el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos solicita desestimar con prejuicio la acusación contra Catherine Sharp y Joselyn Walsh, en interés de la justicia”, añadió.</p><div class="Enhancement" Congreso, Kat Abughazaleh, el concejal de Oak Park Brian Straw, el miembro del comité demócrata del 45° distrito Michael Rabbitt y Andre Martin. Se les acusa de un complot para obstaculizar a un oficial federal.</p><p>Abughazaleh busca la nominación demócrata para el escaño del Distrito 9 de Illinois en las primarias del martes.</p><p>La noticia llega después de que los fiscales dijeran que planeaban reducir y revisar el caso de conspiración contra el grupo. Esto significa que Sharp y Walsh <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >se unirán a una lista cada vez mayor</a> de personas que han sido exoneradas después de ser acusadas de delitos no relacionados con la inmigración vinculados al Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>También es un golpe significativo para una acusación de alto perfil relacionada con la campaña de cumplimiento de inmigración.</p><p>Los fiscales federales en Chicago acusaron a 32 personas de delitos no relacionados con la inmigración conectados al Operativo Midway Blitz. Una vez que Perry conceda la nueva moción relacionada con Sharp y Walsh, 19 de los 32 habrán sido exonerados. Hasta ahora, ninguno de los 32 ha sido condenado.</p><p>Los acusados exonerados incluyen a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/04/marimar-martinez-baleada-por-agentes-de-migracion-se-pronuncia-contra-asesinatoshttps://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/04/marimar-martinez-baleada-por-agentes-de-migracion-se-pronuncia-contra-asesinatos" target="_blank" >Marimar Martínez</a>, la mujer a la que un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza le disparó cinco veces en octubre pasado en el lado suroeste. Los fiscales abandonaron el caso en su contra en noviembre.</p><p>Un jurado también exoneró a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/01/23/jurado-rechaza-complot-de-asesinato-de-greg-bovino-y-absuelve-a-hombre-de-chicago" target="_blank" >Juan Espinoza Martinez</a> en enero después de haber sido acusado de ofrecer $10,000 por el asesinato del comandante de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Gregory Bovino. Las autoridades de inmigración detuvieron a Espinoza Martinez después de su absolución y lo han mantenido en custodia desde entonces.</p><p>Sin embargo, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/02/los-manifestantes-anti-ice-golpean-a-trump-en-la-corte-de-chicago-pero-todo-sigue-teniendo-un-costo" target="_blank" >el enjuiciamiento federal aún tiene un costo</a>, incluso cuando los cargos son finalmente abandonados. En el caso de Sharp, esto incluye la suspensión de su campaña para la Junta del Condado de Cook para que pudiera concentrarse en su defensa legal.</p><p>Los acusados de conspiración restantes de Broadview están programados para juicio el 26 de mayo. Los cargos giran en torno a eventos de la mañana del 26 de septiembre frente a la instalación de ICE en Broadview.</p><p>Una acusación alega que, mientras un agente conducía un vehículo hacia la instalación, los acusados y otros lo rodearon. Se alega que los miembros de la multitud golpearon el vehículo, lo empujaron, lo rayaron e incluso grabaron la palabra “PIG” (“puerco”) en él.</p><p>La multitud supuestamente rompió un espejo lateral y un limpiaparabrisas trasero y obligó al agente “a conducir a una velocidad extremadamente lenta”. Sin embargo, los fiscales acordaron recientemente eliminar cierto lenguaje de la acusación. También reconocieron durante una audiencia reciente que el período de la supuesta conspiración se limita al 26 de septiembre, que fue “espontánea” sin evidencia de un acuerdo explícito, y que todos los posibles co-conspiradores estaban presentes en Broadview en ese momento.</p><p>Los abogados defensores han señalado que un tema clave en el juicio podría ser la “decisión y motivación del agente para conducir su vehículo hacia una multitud de más de 50 individuos que protestaban pacíficamente por las atrocidades documentadas que ocurrían dentro de la instalación de Broadview”.</p><p>Han afirmado que sus clientes y otros estaban participando en una “Caminata de Jericó” supervisada por la policía local, que ayudó a que el tráfico pasara de manera segura a través de la manifestación.</p><p>Finalmente, un vehículo Ford Expedition conducido por un agente de ICE se volvió “directamente” hacia la multitud, según los documentos de defensa. No hay evidencia de que el agente de ICE esperara asistencia policial, sino que optó por “girar directamente hacia donde estaba reunida la multitud”, dicen los abogados defensores.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

target="_blank" >How Quinn Chapel AME put its faith in action</a></h3><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wtriuhd-tlkjhhnv-q/" target="_blank" >Nicole Jeanine Johnson</a></h5><p><b>Community heart</b>: By the 1840s, free Blacks flocked to Chicago to steer clear of slavery. Some of them started Quinn Chapel AME, the city’s first Black church, and its physical building served as a beacon for freedom seekers. As the law closed free Blacks off from public society, the church became the center of the community. It was where people learned to read, engaged in debate club, and had women’s Bible study and singing classes.</p><p><b>Underground Railroad station</b>: Those who led Quinn Chapel’s emancipation work were among the city’s Black elite — leaders in the business community and in politics. But the veil of class, wealth and mixed ancestry didn't fool church members into thinking they couldn’t be returned to slavery or taken into bondage for the first time. The chapel's location along the Chicago River, with close proximity to Lake Michigan, made it a strategic station on the Underground Railroad.</p><p><b>Living history</b>: Inside the church is a massive organ purchased from the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition German pavilion. Members at the time held the first ever June Rose benefit concert to pay for the instrument. Since then, Quinn Chapel has hosted the concerts for more than 130 years. "It’s kind of a homecoming for everybody," Senior Pastor Troy Venning said.</p><p><a class="Link" title: President Trump's economy is a failure of his own making
summary: <p>As a candidate, President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/editorial-photos-videos/detail?itemid=cf9f6cb9fad145bfa6626afc0f2deb33&mediatype=video" target="_blank" >promised</a> to "create millions and millions of jobs, massively raise wages for American workers, and make the United States into a manufacturing powerhouse like it used to be many years ago."</p><p>More than a year in, the Trump economy is an explicit failure, with conditions ominously reminiscent of the months leading up to the Great Recession of 2008. The difference is that the Great Recession was precipitated by a global financial crisis. The current downturn is the result of the administration’s own policy decisions, including tariffs, immigration restrictions and government workforce reductions.</p><p>From day one, the second Trump administration began destabilizing the labor market, presiding over a stunning collapse in federal employment. </p><p>The Department of Government Efficiency — charged with shrinking the federal workforce — oversaw the elimination of more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.hcamag.com/ca/specialization/payroll/us-job-cuts-surge-in-february-amid-federal-workforce-reductions/527698#:~:text=Industries%20facing%20biggest%20layoffs,job%20cuts%20through%20February%202024." target="_blank" >62,530 federal jobs</a> in just the first two months of 2025, a staggering 41,311%<b></b> increase in federal layoffs compared with the previous year, according to the website Human Resources Director, which looks at hiring trends. These cuts didn’t simply trim bureaucracy — they decimated entire agencies, hollowed out public services and sent shock waves through communities dependent on federal employment.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Columnist</div> </div><p>The job losses did not stop in Washington, D.C. Federal contract cancellations and funding freezes created collateral damage, prompting layoffs across the private sector. Technology firms, nonprofits and service providers found themselves suddenly cut off from long-standing federal contracts and grants. Private employers cited the "DOGE impact" as the reason for 63,583 layoffs, showing clearly how reckless cuts spilled into the broader economy.</p><h3>Where’s the hiring boom?</h3><p>Rather than ushering in a hiring boom, the U.S. economy has racked up months of job losses. The nation lost a <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/u-s-lost-92000-jobs-last-month-and-unemployment-rate-rises-to-4-4#:~:text=to%2D4%2D4-,U.S.%20lost%2092%2C000%20jobs%20last%20month%20and%20unemployment%20rate%20rises,could%20add%20to%20that%20uncertainty" target="_blank" >stunning 92,000 jobs </a>in February, while the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.4%, with the increase entirely at the expense of Americans of color. </p><h3></h3><p>While the white unemployment rate remained unchanged at 3.7%, the Black, Latino and Asian rates all rose — with the Black rate more than double the white rate at 7.7%. With revisions showing a loss of 17,000 jobs in December, total job growth over the last 14 months has been <a class="Link" href="https://www.ms.now/rachel-maddow-show/maddowblog/team-trump-struggles-to-spin-on-the-worst-job-numbers-since-the-great-recession" target="_blank" >just 150,000</a> — a sharp contrast to the 1.74 million jobs added in the 14 months prior.</p><p>This is not the record of a president creating "millions and millions" of new jobs — it is the record of a labor market stifled by federal decisions.</p><p>Trump also promised to "massively raise wages," but here again, the results fall far short. To be sure, wages have risen — but only modestly. </p><p>Average hourly earnings increased<a class="Link" href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/03/06/february-2026-jobs-report.html" target="_blank" > 3.8% year‑over‑year by this February</a>, and weekly wages rose 4.3% year‑over‑year. These gains are not insignificant, but they are nowhere near the sweeping wage transformation Trump promised. In fact, much of the improvement in real wages owes to falling inflation — down from 3% when Trump took office to 2.4% by January — rather than to rapid wage acceleration. That wage growth, such as it is, is largely offset by soaring costs: Electricity is up <a class="Link" href="https://www.foxbusiness.com/economy/americans-hit-soaring-electricity-bills-price-hikes-outpace-inflation-nationwide" target="_blank" >6.3%,</a> medical care is up <a class="Link" href="https://press.spglobal.com/2014-01-09-Healthcare-Expenditures-for-Commercial-Plans-up-3-2-in-the-Year-to-August-2013-S-P-Healthcare-Claims-Indices" target="_blank" >3.2%</a>, and housing <a class="Link" href="https://www.nerdwallet.com/finance/learn/rental-market-trends" target="_blank" >continues to rise</a>.</p><p>Nowhere is the distance between promise and performance greater than in manufacturing. Far from restoring America’s industrial might, manufacturing employment instead has declined. The sector lost 12,000 jobs in February alone, defying economists’ expectations of gains. Manufacturers shed <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/trumps-trade-war-squeezes-middle-class-manufacturing-employment/#:~:text=Manufacturing%20employment%20has%20been%20falling,by%2076%2C000%20and%2018%2C000%2C%20respectively." target="_blank" >42,000 jobs</a> between April 2025 and August 2025, and total manufacturing employment fell by 33,000 jobs in 2025 — hardly the profile of a “manufacturing powerhouse.”</p><h3>Tariff strategy misfires</h3><p>The administration’s tariffs strategy has massively backfired. John Deere reported <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/04/business/john-deere-tractor-sales-down-farmers-struggle.html" target="_blank" >$300 million in tariff‑related costs</a> before laying off hundreds of workers. Tariff uncertainty prompted companies to pause investment and reduce hiring, while retaliatory trade actions weakened U.S. export competitiveness. Rather than strengthening manufacturing, a reckless and unstable environment is eating away at profits and <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/29/business/trump-tariffs-small-businesses.html#:~:text=While%20many%20larger%20companies%20have,has%20been%20reducing%20other%20costs." target="_blank" >crushing small businesses.</a></p><p>The broader economic picture is equally concerning. Gross domestic product growth fell from 4.4% in the third quarter of 2025 to just 1.4% in the fourth quarter, dragged down by federal spending cuts, shutdowns and trade disruptions. For the full year, GDP <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/20/business/economy/us-economy-gdp.html" target="_blank" >grew only 2.2%</a>, down from 2.8% in 2024, representing the weakest annual expansion in nine years, excluding the pandemic. This slowdown is the result of a federal policy environment that works against economic expansion, not in service of it.</p><p>Instead of a jobs boom, the country has seen policy‑driven layoffs. Instead of massive wage growth, workers have experienced modest gains overshadowed by inflation in essential categories. Instead of a manufacturing renaissance, factory jobs have plummeted.</p><p>Campaign rhetoric is easy. Governing is harder. But when a president pledges an economic transformation and delivers chaos and catastrophe instead, voters and workers deserve to see the truth plainly: The administration’s policies have not only fallen short — they have actively undermined the economic agenda Trump promised to build.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/marc-h-morial" target="_blank" ><i>Marc H. Morial</i></a><i> is president and CEO of the National Urban League</i> <i>and</i> <i>was mayor of New Orleans from 1994 to 2002.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1f0000" name="module-1f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

title: Libertyville troubadour Ike Reilly is more vocal than ever
summary: <p>Ike Reilly has made a career of speaking truth to power. But his blue-collar ballads, outsider anthems and punk rock poetry about the American Dream deferred have never felt more urgent than right now, a time when the Libertyville troubadour also feels more galvanized than ever.</p><p>Ahead of his live band, The Ike Reilly Assassination, taking over Schubas Tavern March 14, 15 and 17, he's been guesting at politically charged shows with his fellow L-ville pal Tom Morello.</p><p>Last November, Reilly was part of the guitarist’s “and friends” ensemble at the Vic Theater along with his son/frequent collaborator Shane and Rise Against frontman Tim McIlrath where they contributed to covers of Woody Guthrie and John Lennon. In February, a similar lineup assembled for Morello’s “resistance and solidarity” benefit concert in Minneapolis to support the families of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, who were fatally shot this year by federal immigration agents during a protest and an immigration enforcement incident, respectively.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure As he watched friends like Morello leave Libertyville and prosper, and even as the New York Times and Stephen King sang his praises, the 62-year-old commercially floundered, losing the family’s beloved log home at one of the lowest points. “I've always put more effort into the songs and the creative end of it than the business out of it. I think I’ve got the lawsuits and credit rating to prove it,” Reilly joked. “But I’m straightforward with the level of obscurity that I inhabit.”</p><p>Reilly’s hard-knocks story is the subject of the acclaimed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2024/08/13/ike-reilly-documentary-dont-turn-your-back-libertyville-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>2024 documentary, “Don’t Turn Your Back on Friday Night”</u></a> (executive produced by Morello), which paints him as a George Bailey type while espousing the merits of his “wonderful life.”</p><p>Reilly comes full circle with the new album “Blind and Surrounded” (out June 12) as the album’s title pays homage to his “Salesmen and Racists” debut. Except this time, the two men featured on the cover are not a pair of New York racketeers coming out of court with their faces covered, but rather Reilly and his son Shane staring deadpan at the camera. It comes as a new generation of family talent emerges: Shane wrote half the songs on the album while brothers Kevin and Mickey are part of the Ike Reilly Assassination band.</p><p>“I'm really proud of the record. There are some introspective ballads and some ferocious rock and roll songs,” Reilly previewed. “Someone said to me it sounds like one guy has a glimmer of hope, and the other guy sounds like he’s taking a beating and I kind of like that.”</p><p>Like all of Reilly’s material, it speaks to how many, including himself, are feeling now in light of the sociopolitical issues Reilly and Morello have been vocal about onstage.</p><p>“What I will never understand is, why wouldn't we want everybody to do well? … I've been poor. I've been desperate. And I may be again. But the currency that I hope I have is the ability to sing and play and speak my mind and make people feel part of something bigger than themselves.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-400000" name="module-400000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>The Ike Reilly Assassination</h3><br><b>When:</b> March 14, 15 and 17<br><b>Where:</b> Schubas Tavern, 3159 N. author: Selena Fragassi

title: Chicago police, other agencies take in millions by seizing cars, cash even without an arrest or conviction
summary: <p>Courtroom 1707 at the Daley Center. People steadily stream in, hoping they'll end up able to hold onto what's often their most valuable possession: a car.</p><p>Most are Black or Latino. Most don’t have lawyers. And many are trying to stop the government from taking their vehicles for good.</p><p>Every year, the Chicago Police Department and other law enforcement agencies across Illinois seize thousands of cars, along with piles of cash and other property. Prosecutors say the seized assets are tied to crimes that range from drug offenses to traffic violations — and occasionally violent acts.</p><p>The seizures bring in millions of dollars for law enforcement.</p><p>But critics say the Illinois civil asset forfeiture system flips on its head a foundational rule of American justice: You're innocent until proven guilty.</p><p>Under Illinois law, though, the police can seize property based on suspicion alone — even if the owner is never arrested, never charged with any crime, never convicted.</p><p>A 2023 report from the Chicago Appleseed Center for Fair Courts, an advocacy group, called for Illinois to scrap civil asset forfeitures, arguing that the system is fundamentally unfair.</p><p>U.S. Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch has questioned the constitutionality of civil asset forfeiture, saying, "Even innocent owners can wait for months or years for forfeiture proceedings to play out.”</p><p>State lawmakers have passed modest reforms over the past decade, shifting the burden onto the government to prove that property seized is tied to crime and requiring agencies to provide some details on what they seize and how they spend it.</p><p>Supporters, though, say the system works and should be kept in place.</p><p>“I am 100% for this,” says Tom Weitzel, retired chief of the Riverside police department. “Activists are taking a handful of cases and exploiting them for political gain as if they represent the whole system. They don’t.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-dd0000" name="image-dd0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Inside ‘forfeiture court’</b></h3><p>To get a closeup look at how the system works, we went to the Daley Center, where Courtroom 1707 is Ground Zero for forfeitures in Cook County.</p><p>On Mondays and Wednesdays, dozens of people — most of them appearing on screen via Zoom — respond to lawsuits filed by prosecutors seeking to keep their property. Tuesdays and Thursdays, the trials that stem from these cases are held.</p><p>There are a lot of them. Last year, more than 3,100 forfeiture cases were filed in Cook County.</p><p>In court, the judges walk people through the maze of legal steps. You file a claim, enter an appearance, submit an answer.</p><p>For those without lawyers, though, the paperwork can be overwhelming.</p><p>Supporters of a bill being considered in Springfield say they're aiming to streamline the system by allowing prosecutors to send forfeiture notices by email instead of regular mail.</p><p>Some defense lawyers say they worry that those emailed notices could wind up buried in spam folders.</p><p>Missing one can be devastating. If people fail to respond within 45 days, a judge can order their property forfeited by default.</p><p>Even people who don’t technically own their cars — they bought them but are still paying off their car loans — can see their credit take a big hit if a vehicle is taken.</p><p>Sometimes, judges return cars temporarily when the owners argue that a seizure is causing hardship because they can’t get to work or school.</p><p>Others file what’s known as an “innocent owner” defense, claiming that someone else — often a relative — was driving their vehicle.</p><p>For many people navigating the system alone, it’s a lot to absorb and often confusing.</p><h3><b>Waiting a year for $5,000</b></h3><p>Two men appeared in court recently trying to recover about $5,000 each that Chicago police officers took from them after a traffic stop in which officers found a small amount of cannabis. The men say they’re auto dealers and were carrying the cash to buy a vehicle. They told a judge the misdemeanor drug charges against them were dismissed.</p><p>But their forfeiture case is still dragging on.</p><p>In early March, the officer involved failed to appear in court. That prompted a delay until late April.</p><p>The men — who said they couldn’t afford a lawyer because his fee would be more than what they're trying to get back — have now been waiting nearly a year.</p><p>“This thing just keeps dragging on with no end in sight,” says one, speaking on the condition of not being named.</p><h3><b>One man’s win</b></h3><p>Every once in a while, someone scores a victory.</p><p>Wynton Kyle Dozier, 40, got his 2014 Ford Fusion back on March 5 when prosecutors dropped his forfeiture case.</p><p>Chicago police officers had arrested Dozier the day after Christmas in 2024 after stopping him for failing to use a turn signal. Officers said they found drugs in the car.</p><p>In August, a judge threw out the criminal case, ruling the search was illegal.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div It took more than eight months to recover his car, which prosecutors valued at $4,150.</p><p>“They just want you to give up and take your things for free,” Dozier says.</p><p>He says he never understood why he had to fight two legal battles — one for his freedom and another for his car.</p><p>“It doesn’t make sense,” he says.</p><p>Another man, Maurice Walker, 63, decided to make a deal. His 2013 Cadillac, valued at $2,800, was seized in Markham after police in the suburb stopped him last April for running a red light. He was arrested for driving on a license suspended because of a DUI, a charge prosecutors dropped last July<b>.</b></p><p>Complicating his case, prosecutors had released his Cadillac CTS to a woman who said she needed the car, claiming a hardship.</p><p>At a recent forfeiture hearing, Walker was confused why he still needed to fight to get his car back.</p><p>“My case was dismissed,” he told the judge. “How do I owe you anything? The only thing left is them trying to take my car.”</p><p>A prosecutor responded: “The criminal case don’t mean nothing.”</p><p>The judge explained the legal differences between a criminal case and a civil forfeiture case.</p><p>After huddling with the prosecutor, Walker agreed to give the police $1,050 for fees for towing and storing his car.</p><p>The judge told Walker he wouldn’t have to go to trial to fight for his car as long as he pays up by May.</p><p>“I’m OK with that,” Walker replied. “Thank you, judge.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/02/20/dea-cash-forfeitures-trump-biden-gold-miner-civil-rights " target="_blank" >DEA didn’t arrest gold miner stopped at Union Station but seized his $115K and kept it for 7 years</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3><b>Millions to Chicago police</b></h3><p>How often property owners win or lose isn't clear. Those numbers aren't reported to the Illinois State Police.</p><p>The money involved is easier to trace. Under state law, proceeds from seized cash and auctioned property are distributed by the state police. The seizing agency gets 65%, the local state’s attorney’s office 12.5%, appellate prosecutors 12.5%, and the state police 10% for administering the program.</p><p>According to the latest report from the state police, reflecting 2024 seizures, the Chicago Police Department took in $9.4 million in assets that year — including 962 vehicles worth more than $7.7 million, plus cash. Every other law enforcement agency in Illinois combined reported seizing 595 vehicles.</p><p>A Chicago police spokesman says civil asset forfeiture "plays an important role in disrupting organized criminal networks," saying the money goes toward “strengthening public safety."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-570000" name="module-570000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>CHICAGO POLICE FORFEITURES</h3><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-78d3ea20-1e10-11f1-a08f-7df7c31be9ee" data-pm-slice="3 3 []"><li>In 2024, the Chicago Police Department collected $1.3 million from the Illinois State Police through the process of various agencies sharing the money from civil asset forfeitures.</li><li>The department spent $1.4 million, including $1.2 million for operating expenses, $77,000 for informants and undercover drug buys and $67,000 for travel, meals and training. </li><li>In recent years, the department also spent forfeiture funds on car leases, phone service, vehicle repairs, lab equipment — and hundreds of thousands of dollars that went to a company that supplies surveillance technology to law enforcement agencies, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, records show.</li><li>Those records also show that, in April 2025, roughly $4.5 million was sitting in the Chicago Police Department’s drug forfeiture fund along with $409,000 in a forfeiture fund tied to money-laundering seizures. That was nearly 40% less than the department held in 2020 — a drop sources say is tied to a sharp decline in search warrants following reforms prompted by wrongful police raids.</li></ul></div> </div><p>Under a law that took effect Jan. 1, the state police will collect even more information from police agencies, including the property owner's race, sex, age and ZIP code as well as more data about the spending of forfeiture money, including purchases of surveillance technology.</p><h3>A tool — or abuse?</h3><p>Despite the big money involved, Weitzel, the former Riverside police chief, rejects the idea that civil asset forfeiture is a money grab.</p><p>Forfeiture is “one of the few tools that weakens criminal networks financially, not just through arrests,” Weitzel says.</p><p>He says strict controls governed how his department seized and spent forfeiture funds.</p><p>But critics say the system needs changes. Some point to Michigan, where Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signed bipartisan legislation in 2019 largely banning police from forfeiting property worth $50,000 or less without a criminal conviction. Lawmakers later modified the law to allow forfeitures over $20,000 at airports without a conviction.</p><p>If that law applied in Illinois, lots of the civil asset forfeiture cases that now go through Courtroom 1707 would never be filed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-660000"
