title: Another Trump administration deportation blitz hasn’t materialized in Chicago
summary: <p>When U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b>left town last fall, Chicago’s reprieve came with a warning: The tear gas, chaos and fear associated with Operation Midway Blitz could return to the city’s streets<b> </b>fourfold<b> </b>in March.</p><p>Now March is here. And President Donald Trump has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/05/trump-fires-noem-dhs-ice-border-patrol-markwayne-mullin" target="_blank" >fired Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem</a>, instead.</p><p>Bovino’s out too. The White House put him on the sidelines in January after the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal officers<b> </b>in Minneapolis. Even Tricia<b> </b>McLaughlin<b>, </b>the assistant secretary who once fiercely defended Homeland Security, has moved on.</p><p>All told, there’s little on the horizon to suggest Operation Midway Blitz 2.0 is about to materialize.</p><p>Much has changed since a source told the Chicago Sun-Times<b> </b>in November<b> </b>that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/11/u-s-border-patrol-boss-greg-bovino-fellow-agents-expected-to-soon-leave-chicago" target="_blank" >1,000 agents could return</a><b> </b>this month.<b> </b>The enforcement surge in Minnesota that followed the earlier Chicago campaign<b> </b>turned out to be a breaking point, leaving the Trump administration struggling to justify the shooting deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.</p><p>Calls to reform immigration enforcement<b> </b>have led to a partial government shutdown. Senate Democrats last week blocked<b> </b>Homeland Security funding<b> </b>for a third time,<b> </b>refusing to approve a spending bill without<b> </b>stricter use-of-force policies and a ban on officers wearing masks.</p><p>Steve Art, an attorney<b> </b>who challenged the feds’ tactics<b> </b>in court last fall, said the Minneapolis campaign gave the American people<b> </b>"a look at what we saw in Chicago throughout Operation Midway Blitz."</p><p>And, he said,<b> </b>"the American people didn’t like it."</p><p>The Chicago operation featured roving bands of masked agents, thousands of arrests, the seemingly indiscriminate use of tear gas and pepper balls, and two shootings, one of which claimed the life of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/12/ice-officer-fatally-shoots-man-during-traffic-stop-in-chicago-suburb-authorities-say" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González</a>. </p><p>"Bovino being gone and Noem being gone within six months of the start of Operation Midway Blitz really shows you how politically untenable it is to engage in that kind of operation in the United States," Art said. "And that should give everybody a lot of hope."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ac0000" name="html-embed-module-ac0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27969115"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27969115/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>A Homeland Security spokesperson said officials in the department "do not discuss future or potential operations."</p><p>"Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country including in Chicago," the spokesperson added.</p><p>Immigration enforcement remains a key pillar of Trump’s second term. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has a mountain of funding and continues to hire and increase its capacity<b> </b>to remove immigrants from the country, according to a former Homeland Security official.</p><p>The feds are still fighting a court order that would govern the treatment of people held<b> </b>in an immigration processing facility<b> </b>in Broadview. Last fall, a judge heard<b> </b>that<b> </b>people were crammed<b> </b>100 at a time<b> </b>into a cell there, with nowhere to sleep<b> </b>but a dirty floor<b> </b>near an open toilet.</p><p>Art said it’s good to be prepared for another surge in enforcement. But he also warned of future issues "relating to the election and to polling places." </p><p>Meanwhile, in the nation’s capital, U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez<b> </b>said Democrats<b> </b>"can’t keep sabotaging ourselves." She took Noem to task<b> </b>in a fiery meeting<b> </b>last month<b> </b>and told her, "your days may be numbered."</p><p>That was eight days before<b> </b>Trump showed Noem the door.</p><p>Now, with Homeland Security on its heels, Ramirez told the Sun-Times "this is our moment."</p><p>"Our strategy has to be, delay as far as you possibly can," the Illinois Democrat said. "Delay till November, if you can. Maybe January. And then let us get into the majority."</p><h3><b>Changing tactics</b></h3><p>The public outcry<b> </b>that stifled the feds’ immigration operation<b> </b>in Minneapolis<b> </b>led to<b> </b>new<b> </b>ICE directives<b> </b>that were relayed during<b> </b>recent<b> </b>agency-wide leadership meetings, the former Homeland Security official<b> </b>told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Leaders were told to prioritize<b> </b>"targeted enforcement,"<b> </b>instead of the "street sweeps" and large-scale campaigns like Midway Blitz, the official said. That would mean a return to ICE’s traditional, but still aggressive, enforcement tactics.</p><p>It would also mean setting aside the hallmark, but controversial, tactics of Midway Blitz: Roaming Chicago’s neighborhoods and stopping anyone whose legal status appeared to be in doubt. Those tactics came roaring back Dec. 16, when Bovino led Border Patrol agents on a brief trip to the Chicago area.</p><p>ICE still has vast financial resources and access to vital information from other government agencies that helps agents identify and target people.</p><p>“Does the Chicago field office just really try to do a lot of enforcement without supplemental folks from other areas and other federal agencies?” the former official said. “Do they look at different ways of arresting people, like worksites?”</p><p>“It doesn’t appear that they’re going to stop doing immigration enforcement because they’re ramping up all the other parts of the system.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>There’s no obvious sign of another Chicago surge within Homeland Security spending, though. Last summer,<b> </b>the agency stocked up on office supplies and ammunition to be used<b> </b>here, while also investing in relocation services for agents, according to federal data.</p><p>Similar purchases were made in Minnesota and North Carolina in the months leading up to increased immigration enforcement<b> </b>in those states.</p><p>The department has continued buying supplies and security equipment in Minnesota over the past month, as large swaths of agents remain in the area.</p><p>But the department<b> </b>hasn’t made any major purchases<b> </b>for use<b> </b>here<b> </b>since the withdrawal<b> </b>of Bovino and many of his agents<b> </b>in November.</p><p>The last contract<b> </b>the department signed<b> </b>related to the Broadview holding facility<b> </b>was a $349,000<b> </b>purchase<b> </b>for box lunch services<b> </b>on Dec. 8.</p><p>Those services are set to expire in early April.</p><h3><b>Plans for polling places?</b></h3><p>The spending impasse in Washington leaves immigration enforcement largely unaffected. That’s because the agencies at the crux of the argument are considered essential under a shutdown.</p><p>That includes ICE, which received<b> </b>$75 billion<b> </b>in Trump’s major tax and spending bill, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That also allows the agency to ride out the funding lapse while other departments under Homeland Security will be forced to furlough workers and cut operations.</p><p>Chicago Democrats<b> </b>like Ramirez<b> </b>hope the impasse — and Noem’s firing — will delay any plans to target Chicago in another sweeping immigration operation. Trump said he would nominate U.S. Sen. Markwayne<b> </b>Mullin, R-Oklahoma, as his next Homeland Security secretary.</p><p>But Ramirez said Mullin<b> </b>is unlikely to be confirmed by the Senate until some time in April.</p><p>“Frankly, it wouldn't work well with them if they end up continuing these big operations without a leader at the helm,” Ramirez said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" U.S. Sen. Chris<b> </b>Coons<b> </b>asked Noem last week, before she was fired, whether she would rule out<b> </b>deploying agents<b> </b>to polling places.</p><p>“There are no plans to have ICE officers at our polling locations,” Noem told the Delaware<b> </b>Democrat.</p><p>Coons cited a law<b> </b>forbidding troops at the polls<b> </b>and continued to press Noem on whether she would “rule it out.”<b> </b>Noem retorted, “do you plan on illegal aliens voting in our elections, senator?”</p><p>Others share Coons’ concern. Art said plans are in the works<b> </b>to litigate<b> </b>“whether there’s ever a reason to have federal forces, like we saw during Operation Midway Blitz, anywhere near a polling place.”</p><p>“We think the obvious answer to that, under the law, is no,” Art said.<b> </b>“But it’s our intention to litigate that issue far in advance.”</p><p>Art helped win<b> </b>last fall’s<b> </b>order<b> </b>from U.S. District Judge<b> </b>Sara Ellis<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >restricting<b> </b>the feds’ use of force</a> during<b> </b>Midway Blitz — an order <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b3/26/ced883424be7b53aa5b8d9586922/chc7thorderuse.pdf" target="_blank" >formally vacated<b> </b>last week</a> by the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. Art's team also secured<b> </b>an under-oath deposition<b> </b>from Bovino, during which Ellis said<b> </b>he lied<b> </b>about his justification<b> </b>for the use of tear gas<b> </b>in Little Village.</p><h3><b>‘They say they’re coming back’</b></h3><p>The ICE holding facility in Broadview became a focal point of Midway Blitz. Not only did many of the feds’ detainees find themselves held there at some point, but it became the site of near-daily protests.</p><p>Designed as a short-term holding facility, U.S. District Judge Robert<b> </b>Gettleman<b> </b>remarked last November that it had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/04/claims-of-unsanitary-black-hole-conditions-at-broadviews-ice-facility-to-be-heard-by-federal-judge" target="_blank" >“really become a prison.”</a><b> </b>He did so while presiding over a lawsuit that alleges the feds were “warehousing people at Broadview for days on end.”</p><p>Gettleman handed down a temporary restraining order<b> </b>that month<b> </b>aimed at improving conditions inside the facility.<b> </b>He required<b> </b>a clean mat<b> </b>and bedding<b> </b>for everyone<b> </b>held there overnight,<b> </b>and that cells<b> </b>be cleaned<b> </b>twice daily.</p><p>The order is still in effect. A two-day<b> </b>hearing<b> </b>over whether Gettleman should enter a more permanent order<b> </b>is set to begin April 21.</p><p>But in mid-December, a month after Bovino and his agents first left town, the Justice Department seemed to have an opportunity to bring the case to an end. DOJ lawyer Jana<b> </b>Brady<b> </b>told the judge that “Broadview is back to being just a processing center.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" reason to keep arguing about it. The controversy was over.</p><p>But Gettleman pressed her on the question on many Chicagoans’ minds. He said he would consider whether the case had become irrelevant<b> </b>if Brady would only “stipulate”<b> </b>that a second surge in immigration enforcement was not in the works.</p><p>“If the government learns that we’re not going to have a surge again, and is able to give assurances about that, then I would be open to some sort of resolution,” Gettleman told her.</p><p>“What you’re asking for is law-enforcement-sensitive information,” Brady replied. She said it could lead to the “thwarting”<b> </b>of a mission or “safety issues for all involved.”</p><p>So the case is still ongoing, three months later.</p><p>Gettleman told Brady he was simply taking her client at its word.</p><p>“They say they’re coming back here in force,” he told her.</p><p><i>Contributing: Tom Schuba</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/05/trump-fires-noem-dhs-ice-border-patrol-markwayne-mullin" target="_blank" >Trump ousts Kristi Noem, Pritzker says ‘don’t let the door hit you on the way out’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/03/dhs-kristi-noem-senate-judiciary-committee-testimony-marimar-martinez-dick-durbin" target="_blank" >DHS head Noem claims she doesn’t know about Marimar Martinez, Chicago woman shot 5 times by federal agent</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/04/claims-of-unsanitary-black-hole-conditions-at-broadviews-ice-facility-to-be-heard-by-federal-judge" target="_blank" >Federal judge likely to intervene at Broadview’s ICE facility: ‘It has really become a prison’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

So it's a great, positive message, and it's very heartfelt.”</p><p>Interviewing people on opening night, the message that America is a country powered by immigrants (“Immigrants, we get the job done!”) within the performance landed with many audience members.</p><p>A.D. title: Chicago law firm leading push to appoint special prosecutor to target ICE, Border Patrol agents
summary: <p>A high-powered Chicago law firm that fought Operation Midway Blitz in federal court announced a plan Monday to push for the appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate and potentially charge the law enforcement officials who carried out the aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area.</p><p>The firm, Loevy and Loevy, said 200 individuals and organizations are supporting a petition to install an outsider in the office of Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, who has spent weeks saying her staff can only go so far to target the feds.</p><p>The coalition plans to hold a news conference Thursday afternoon at Federal Plaza downtown, Loevy and Loevy said in a statement.</p><p>O’Neill Burke rebuked the call for a special prosecutor, slamming any petition as “frivolous [and] contrary to centuries of legal precedent and court rulings.”</p><p>“The reported plan to petition for a special prosecutor will make it more difficult for the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office to prosecute and win convictions against [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] agents who break the law and secure justice for victims harmed by their conduct,” O’Neill Burke wrote in a statement.</p><p>“The stakes are too high for us to get this wrong, and I will strenuously oppose this petition.”</p><p>In its statement, Loevy and Loevy highlighted the extreme force used by federal immigration officials during the monthslong deportation campaign, referring to the on-duty actions as “crimes.” They cited widespread tear-gassing, attacks against “peaceful civilians” and shootings that wounded <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/evidence-shows-feds-lied-about-marimar-martinezs-shooting-in-chicago-attorney-says" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a> and killed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González</a>.</p><p>“Yet there has been no federal or state investigation or prosecution of any [of] the individuals who perpetrated these offenses,” the firm said. “An independent, special prosecutor is essential to ensure that there is accountability in Cook County.”</p><p>The demands for O'Neill Burke’s office to target federal agents are nothing new. In fact, another lawyer already filed a lawsuit earlier this year seeking to install a special prosecutor to handle such cases in county court. </p><p>O'Neill Burke has maintained that her office is limited in its ability to prosecute and secure convictions against on-duty federal agents. Still, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >she released guidance</a> last month showing how she could pursue charges if a case were brought to her office. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> which includes elected officials, community organizations, journalists and other attorneys.</p><p>Loevy and Loevy was involved in a case last year in which U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis took the extraordinary step of issuing a preliminary injunction to rein in the feds’ aggressive actions. The injunction was <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/b3/26/ced883424be7b53aa5b8d9586922/chc7thorderuse.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>formally vacated</u><b><u> </u></b><u>last week</u></a> by the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.</p><p>Loevy and Loevy noted that sworn statements were submitted and hundreds of hours of video footage was compiled as part of federal court proceedings tied to Midway Blitz, indicating there’s already a pile of evidence waiting for a possible special prosecutor.</p><p>O’Neill Burke previously criticized Mayor Brandon Johnson's executive order directing the Chicago Police Department to go after federal agents, calling it "wholly inappropriate" because it instructed officers to make referrals to prosecutors "at the direction of the mayor's office." O'Neill Burke later released her own guidance last month. </p><p>Under the guidance, law enforcement agencies would lead criminal investigations by collecting and preserving evidence. Then, prosecutors would conduct an independent review of all evidence and make charging decisions, as they do in all felony cases. Her office said local law enforcement agencies haven't sought charges against any on-duty immigration officials.</p><p>O’Neill Burke noted on Monday that cases against the feds would be difficult to pursue, citing protections offered to on-duty agents and “challenges in acquiring evidence from federal law enforcement under this current administration.”</p><p>"My office’s goal is not to merely charge, but to successfully prosecute and convict criminal ICE agents,” O’Neill Burke said. “We are obligated to follow the law, evaluate evidence that is presented to us, and make a charging decision based on the facts.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" target="_blank" >Veteran attorneys have been skeptical</a> about a judge’s ability to install a special prosecutor to investigate federal agents. Traditionally, special prosecutors are put in place when there is a conflict of interest or allegation of misconduct within the state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>The earlier petition for a special prosecutor, filed by attorney Sheryl Weikal, remains pending.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" target="_blank" >How can Chicago’s top prosecutor hold ICE accountable?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/06/eileen-oneill-burke-brandon-johnson-immigration-ice-law" target="_blank" >County’s top prosecutor calls Mayor Brandon Johnson’s ICE executive order ‘wholly inappropriate’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjuiidy-tlkjhhnv-q/" target="_blank" >Frank Main</a></h5><p><b>A way out</b>: Decades of undiagnosed mental illness beginning when Lottie Elliott was 15 led her to homelessness, her children being taken away and repeated arrests. In 2022, Elliott was offered a way to stop that damaging cycle through Bridges of Colorado, which places mental health liaisons in courtrooms across the state to help defendants whose persistent mental illness has contributed to repeated arrests.</p><p><b>Results</b>: Elliott says people from the Bridges program worked with her in jail until she was found to be competent to face criminal charges. The liaisons helped get her into a residential sober-living program with intensive therapy under the monitoring of a judge, who granted her probation. She’s now in her own apartment, has reunited with her son, is taking regular mental health medication and is helping others as a peer counselor.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: An Illinois task force of legislators, law enforcement, judiciary officials and mental health professionals is looking at Bridges of Colorado as a potential model for Illinois. They've been working to figure out how to improve the handling of criminal defendants with severe, persistent mental illness.</p><p><b>Chance to thrive</b>: "My life is incredibly humbling," Elliott says. "I want to share with people who were like me, who believed there was no hope and it was not possible. It is. We can recover."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/06/mentally-ill-downtown-killings-chicago-police-department-mental-health-care-bridges-colorado" title: U.S. citizen from Skokie stopped at O'Hare, detained by immigration officials for nearly 30 hours
summary: <p>A U.S. citizen from Skokie spent nearly 30 hours in custody by federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration" >immigration</a> officials after she was detained at O'Hare Airport following a work trip Thursday, drawing rebukes from family, friends and politicians. </p><p>Sundas "Sunny" Naqvi and five colleagues, including two other U.S. citizens and three individuals with green cards, were all detained at the airport by federal immigration agents for their "recent travel history" after returning from Istanbul, Cook County commissioner and family friend Kevin Morrison told reporters outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement center in Broadview Sunday. </p><p>Naqvi, 28, and the others were taken to the Broadview facility where they were then transferred to a facility in Dodge County, Wisconsin, sometime Friday evening, according to Morrison. She was then released around 5 a.m. Saturday after nearly 30 hours and a woman gave her a ride to a hotel where she reunited with family who followed her phone's location until service died. </p><p>"All she was told was that there was some curious travel history, but they had no cause to detain her for those 30 hours," Morrison said, adding that federal agents "lied to" local law enforcement and elected officials by saying Naqvi was never detained. </p><p>Immigration officials didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>"We need transparency, we need accountability and we need to make sure that we are incredibly mindful of the steps we must take as a nation to protect all of our civil rights and civil liberties," said Morrison. "The fact that this could happen to any U.S. citizen should terrify us all." </p><p>Naqvi's sister, Sarah Afzal, said she almost filed a missing persons report when she couldn’t get answers from local or federal police. </p><p>"She was right here and then she was in Wisconsin," Afzal said. "It was terrifying." </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/08/deportation-francisco-gonzalez-jasso-panchito-gang-latin-kings-deported-ice-mexico-midway-blitz-little-village" >Labeled a gang member and deported, longtime Chicagoan tries to restart in his Mexican hometown</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>A number of candidates running for Congress were on hand at Broadview to talk to news media, including 7th District candidate Reed Showalter and 9th District candidates Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss, Kat Abughazaleh, Bushra Amiwala and Illinois state Sen. Laura Fine.</p><p>"They were only brought home after their families and our community refused to back down and kept asking for answers," Abughazaleh said. "This is going to be the new normal if we don't stand up against it." </p><p>Fine called the arrests "completely unconscionable" and emphasized the importance of continued congressional oversight. </p><p>"We are not getting the full story, we are not getting all of the facts and it is up to Congress to dig deep into what's going on so we understand as citizens and as residents what is happening and [so] that we could get down to the truth," Fine said. </p><p>Amiwala, who knows Naqvi, praised the efforts by family and friends to seek the woman's release.</p><p>"For her to have a community that she does — that was able to rally this many people on such short span — is a testament and reflection to her and her family," Amiwala said. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/chicago-ice-trump-bovino-marimar-martinez-crime-border-patrol-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >ICE protesters keep beating Trump in Chicago court, but the battles take a toll — ‘It’s about intimidation’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/19/chicago-ice-crime-border-patrol-trump-midway-blitz-alex-pretti-renee-good-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" >Cook County’s top prosecutor outlines plan to charge ICE agents with crimes</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/12/chicago-area-resident-lawsuit-facebook-ice-tracking-app" target="_blank" >Chicago-area resident sues Trump officials over Facebook shutting down popular ICE sighting page</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Labeled a gang member and deported, longtime Chicagoan tries to restart in his Mexican hometown
summary: <p>Francisco Gonzalez-Jasso, a longtime Little Village resident, didn't know exactly how to make his way back to his childhood home in Torreón, a city in Mexico's northern state of Cahuila. He hadn’t been there in 33 years.</p><p>“I kept asking people on the bus, 'Is Torreón next?' ” Gonzalez-Jasso, 55, says in his native Spanish.</p><p>In Torreón, he took a cab to his old block. But the years had erased his memory of the house. He paced the street, checking the addresses on every door. When he found the right one, he says, the house looked different. It was really small.</p><p>“I started yelling out my brother’s name: Cesar, Cesar,” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “Once I saw his face, I told the taxi driver to leave. Then, I embraced my brother.</p><p>“I was broken.".</p><p>The last time they were together, Cesar, now 50, was 17.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso is trying to rebuild his life in Mexico after he was arrested by Border Patrol agents last October in Little Village in front of friends and neighbors. He was deported a few days later. WBEZ has been keeping up with Gonzalez-Jasso after visiting him in Mexico in December, not long after he arrived there.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" He has a large extended family in his hometown but the adjustment back home has been a struggle.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Duilio Rodríguez/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The tall man with a sturdy build was a well-known presence in his Chicago neighborhood for more than three decades. Still, despite not having a criminal record, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security branded him a member of the Latin Kings gang — a tag that has followed him to Mexico.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso is among hundreds of people swept up during Operation Midway Blitz, the aggressive Trump administration deportation campaign aimed at clearing “violent criminals” off Chicago-area streets. He also is among immigrants who say they were wrongly accused of being a criminal or having ties to gangs.</p><p>“It’s humiliating for me,” Gonzalez-Jasso says. “I’m not a criminal. I never harmed anyone.”</p><h3>‘This was his home’ </h3><p>Gonzalez-Jasso was known on 26th Street in Little Village as Panchito. His arrest and deportation last fall were a gut punch to neighbors who remember him as a friendly face always ready to lend a hand.</p><p>“I cried, honestly, I cried when I learned that Panchito was arrested,” Carlos Macías, the owner of Carniceria y Taqueria Aguas Calientes on 26th street, said in Spanish. The two have been friends for more than 20 years.</p><p>Also speaking Spanish, Ana Guerrero, a waitress at the <i>taqueria</i> who often served Gonzalez-Jasso, said: “He was like your daily coffee, always here in the mornings before heading to work. He was always very respectful. deportation, Gonzalez-Jasso is living on a modest pension from his construction work. He shipped his clothes from Chicago and gave away the furniture he left behind. He is trying to get someone to haul his two cars.</p><p>He’s keeping busy remodeling his parents’ home, doing a complete overhaul of the kitchen and the bedrooms.</p><p>But he worries about the violence in Mexico. One of his brothers disappeared years ago and was never found.</p><p>Once in a while, he replays the video of his arrest. It’s painful to hear the sounds — the whistles, a woman yelling <i>“la migra”</i> — and to see himself surrounded by Border Patrol agents.</p><p>Gonzalez-Jasso wants to clear his name so everyone knows he’s not a gang member. But he doesn’t know where to start.</p><p>And he misses his Little Village friends and neighbors. Some of them recently traveled to Mexico to see him for a few days. They aren't his blood relatives. But they were his family.</p><p>In Chicago, he says, his voice cracking, “There are many people who love me. And I miss them.”</p>

title: Illinois arts funding shouldn't be treated as an afterthought
summary: <p>In Illinois, lawmakers debate tax freezes for a state-of-the-art stadium. In Indiana, legislation advances to create the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/26/bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-hammong-senate-passes-bill-27-arlington-heights-george-mccaaskey-kevin-warren-nfl" >Northwest Indiana Stadium Authority </a>to lure the Bears across state lines. Public officials in both states are assembling incentive packages and long-term financing strategies, with estimates suggesting up to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/02/26/chicago-bears-property-tax-incentives-illinois-house-city-opposition-arlington-heights-proposed-stadium" >$855 million</a> in indirect public support.</p><p>When a professional team signals movement, government responds with urgency.</p><p>Across Chicago, a different negotiation is unfolding — quieter but no less important. Small and midsized arts organizations are negotiating leases, absorbing rising costs and operating without permanent infrastructure or predictable public investment.</p><p>For years, the Chicago Latino Theater Alliance has convened and supported Latino theater companies across the city. Many operate itinerantly, rehearsing in borrowed or rented spaces. Sets are built to be struck quickly. Seasons are shaped as much by space availability as by artistic intention.</p><p>These are professional artists producing year-round work without long-term stability. They employ actors, designers and administrators and serve audiences across neighborhoods — yet they do so without consistent growth in public funding.</p><p>The aspiration is not a billion-dollar complex. It is stability: a permanent cultural home where companies can rehearse without watching the clock and productions are not dictated by rental calendars.</p><p>There is no interstate bidding war for that vision.</p><p>Each year, the Chicago Latino Theater Alliance provides grants ranging from $3,500 to $10,000 to small Latino theater companies participating in Destinos: Chicago International Latino Theater Festival. That support helps cover stipends, rehearsal space and production expenses, stabilizing investments that ensure productions move forward.</p><p>But philanthropy cannot carry this alone.</p><p>In Gov. JB Pritzker’s proposed 2026–2027 state budget, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/02/23/pritzker-budget-arts-funding-flat-illinois-2026-2027-grants-trump" >arts funding remains flat</a>. In an inflationary environment, flat funding amounts to a reduction in real support, as rent, labor and production costs rise. At the federal level, National Endowment for the Arts <a class="Link" href="https://glasstire.com/2026/01/21/u-s-congress-passes-bill-fully-funding-nea-and-neh-through-2026/" target="_blank" >funding</a> remains modest and politically uncertain.</p><p>Decades of <a class="Link" href="https://www.brookings.edu/books/sports-jobs-and-taxes/" target="_blank" >economic research</a> suggest publicly financed stadiums rarely deliver the transformative growth often promised. Meanwhile, arts and cultural production contributes <a class="Link" href="https://www.arts.gov/news/press-releases/2025/arts-and-cultural-industries-grew-twice-rate-us-economy-adding-12-trillion" target="_blank" >more than $1 trillion</a> annually to the U.S. economy — over 4% of gross domestic product, according to federal data.</p><p>If public officials can mobilize with such fierce dedication around a stadium, they can do the same for cultural institutions that operate year-round, employ local workers and strengthen neighborhoods.</p><p>Culture, too, is infrastructure.</p><p><i>Jorge Valdivia, executive director, Chicago Latino Theater Alliance</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bf0000" name="module-bf0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Volunteering isn’t a fleeting activity</h3><p>I didn’t like Jane at first. She was blunt, sarcastic, openly irritated by anyone who approached her with practiced concern. The first time I spoke to her, she didn’t look up. She just said, loud enough for others to hear, "Oh great. Another one."</p><p>When I sat beside her, she sighed. "What do you want?" Not, "Can you help me?" Just, "What do you want?"</p><p>I was working in a shelter for the unhoused, still new to outreach and still believing that kindness and effort were enough. I thought people pushed help away because they didn’t really want it.</p><p>Jane used sarcasm as armor. She had learned how to expose fake compassion and deflate people who came believing they were different. So she tested me.</p><p>"Why are you talking to me?" "What makes you think you can help?" "Oh, please — spare me."</p><p>Every sentence dared me to leave. What I didn’t understand then was that Jane wasn’t trying to push me away. She was trying to find out if I would stay.</p><p>At the time, I still believed helping meant fixing. I thought kindness would be enough. I didn’t yet understand what it meant to sit with someone whose life had taught them not to trust anything that came easily.</p><p>One day, after an especially biting comment about "rookies who think they’re saviors," something in me shifted. I didn’t defend myself. I didn’t walk away.</p><p>I stayed. Quietly. Steadily.</p><p>She looked at me — real eye contact, for the first time — and said, "Huh. Interesting."</p><p>From that day on, pieces of Jane surfaced through the cracks: a memory here, a fear she didn’t name, clarity tangled with confusion. She knew when her thoughts weren’t trustworthy. That awareness didn’t empower her — it haunted her.</p><p>One day, she told me, "You’re not listening like the others. You’re actually here. You might be good at this ... if you don’t quit."</p><p>It wasn’t praise. It was a warning. Jane didn’t soften for me. She didn’t change because of me.</p><p>I changed because of her. She taught me that helping isn’t about being liked. It’s about returning the next day after being pushed away the day before. About letting someone challenge your patience without taking it personally. Before you can help, you have to be willing to stay.</p><p><i>Donna Lomelino, Springfield</i></p><h3>A ‘special relationship’</h3><p>The phrase <a class="Link" href="https://www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/explainer/us-uk-special-relationship" target="_blank" >“special relationship” </a>has often been used to describe the relationship between the U.S. and the United Kingdom.</p><p>Actually, it is a better fit to describe the relationship between the U.S and Israel.</p><p>The U.S. gives <a class="Link" href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/us-aid-israel-four-charts" target="_blank" >more military aid to Israel </a>than any other country. As set by law, annual appropriations amount to $3.8 billion per year. In addition, emergency funds have been allocated far exceeding this amount.</p><p>As the military action against Iran illustrates, intelligence-sharing and military cooperation dramatically reveal how closely aligned each country is to each other.</p><p>Also, while the Trump administration says it opposes Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank, it <a class="Link" href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/24/us-to-provide-consular-services-in-illegal-israeli-settlement" target="_blank" >hasn’t take any steps to curb</a> these incursions that violate international law. </p><p>While Trump has often championed the notion of making <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-remarks-on-canada-becoming-the-51st-state-raise-a-lot-of-questions" target="_blank" >Canada the 51st state</a>, the “special relationship” between the U.S. and Israel and the fact that the U.S. has been more supportive of Israel than any other country, actually illustrate that Israel is as close to being a state as you can possibly get without a formal process being advocated and implemented.</p><p><i>Larry Vigon, Jefferson Park</i></p><h3>Neighborhoods aren’t ‘saved’ with less housing</h3><p>Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2025/11/06/wall-street-ratings-agency-sounds-alarm-about-chicago-s-finances" target="_blank" >dire</a> financial position will keep getting worse without drastic action. Making it easier to build homes and expand the city’s tax base is critical to addressing this budget gap. As housing costs continue <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/residential-real-estate/housing-affordability-improves-big-cities-not-chicago" target="_blank" >rising</a>, Chicago must make more homes. Failing to build new homes steals opportunities from families and pushes higher costs of living onto current and future Chicagoans.</p><p>The problem is exacerbated by <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoyimby.com/2025/01/a-breakdown-of-aldermanic-prerogative-as-old-town-canvas-is-blocked.html" target="_blank" >aldermanic prerogative</a> and deference to community groups that <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2025/10/29/former-sheffield-neighborhood-group-members-say-its-process-favors-insiders/" target="_blank" >rarely reflect</a> the neighborhood’s actual composition. Frustratingly, even when solutions are approved, another issue exists: neighbors filing lawsuits.</p><p>On the North Side, two different groups are suing to overturn city zoning decisions. An old adage about litigation says that "If you can’t win on merit, then you try to win on procedure." This fits the lawsuits from the 1660 LaSalle Condominium Association in Old Town and the Edgewater Residents for Responsible Development.</p><p>In July, the 1660 LaSalle Condominium Association <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/07/15/old-town-condo-association-lawsuit-developer-fern-hill-36-story-residential-tower" target="_blank" >filed suit</a> against the city and the developer of Old Town Canvas, a 349-home <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.urbanize.city/post/city-council-approves-old-town-canvas-1600-n-lasalle" target="_blank" >development</a> near multiple CTA stops. Despite three years of community engagement, the lawsuit claims that the city "usurped the community engagement process" — although <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoyimby.com/2025/04/old-town-canvas-approved-by-city-council-after-years-of-reviews.html" target="_blank" >nearly a dozen</a> public meetings took place and remain <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/@fernhillcompany/videos" target="_blank" >viewable<u> </u></a>online.</p><p>In October, the City Council <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/chicago-city-council-vote-taller-buildings-more-housing-broadway-edgewater-uptown/" target="_blank" >approved</a> the Broadway Land Use Framework, permitting more housing along a busy commercial corridor in Uptown. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/content/dam/city/sites/broadway-land-use-planning/webinar_presentation_13125.pdf" target="_blank" >plan</a> aims to spur new development nesr four recently <a class="Link" href="https://www.transitchicago.com/rpm/whatsnew/" target="_blank" >modernized</a> CTA stations. During the yearlong community engagement <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/sites/broadway-land-use-planning/home.html" target="_blank" >process</a>, Edgewater Residents for Responsible Development formed as opposition to the land use plan, <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2025/09/18/broadway-rezoning-fight-intensifies-in-edgewater-with-some-neighbors-taking-out-billboards/" target="_blank" >purchased billboards</a> decrying the proposed changes and filed a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/01/13/edgewater-residents-businesses-sue-chicago-broadway-zoning-changes" >lawsuit</a> in January, claiming the city “failed to give proper notice” of the zoning changes.</p><p>In these cases, each group claims to be "saving" their neighborhoods: Both include the word "save" in their website domains. If Chicago’s recent budget <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2025/12/20/city-council-votes-30-18-approve-final-part-2026-budget-will-mayor-veto-it" target="_blank" >fiasco</a> were any indication, saving our city means growing our tax base.</p><p>The plaintiffs may believe they are "saving" their neighborhoods, but their litigation harms Chicago by denying new housing and raising the cost of living. To truly save our neighborhoods, the first step should be dismissing these lawsuits with prejudice. When community groups litigate to block housing, it is a form of generational theft against current and future residents.</p><p><i>Josh Chodor,</i> <i>Urban Planning and Policy graduate student, University of Illinois Chicago</i></p><h3>Desk decor</h3><p>Harry Truman had a sign on his desk that read <a class="Link" href="https://www.trumanlibrary.gov/education/trivia/buck-stops-here-sign" target="_blank" >“The Buck Stops Here.”</a> Donald Trump needs one that reads "The Bull— Starts Here".</p><p><i>Don Kolodziey, Richton Park</i></p><h3>Trump’s logic to start war</h3><p>Wow, my approval rating is way down. What to do? Americans support a wartime president. Who can I invade? Iran looks good. Preapproval by Congress ? Hah! That's a laugh. My people will follow me lock-step. What comes after? I don't care. I can't worry about worldwide chaos. I think I could use a Big Mac.</p><p><i>Philip S. Witt, Northbrook</i></p><h3>Tired of Trump</h3><p>I am tired of waking up every morning wondering what new damage and/or embarrassing action and/or words will come from our president. It is exhausting!</p><p><i>Carole Harrington, Bartlett</i></p><h3>Know-nothing Noem </h3><p>Kristi Noem testified that she <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/03/dhs-kristi-noem-senate-judiciary-committee-testimony-marimar-martinez-dick-durbin" >knows nothing</a> about Marimar Martinez, the Chicago woman who was shot five times by gun-happy Border Patrol thugs.</p><p>Does she read the newspapers? Does she watch television news — even Fox "Phony News?" Is she on the internet? Does she listen to her subordinates?</p><p>This is the woman who shot her dog because she was unable to train it. And she was our Homeland Security secretary?!</p><p><i>Dan McGuire, Bensenville</i></p><h3>Tips for Ticketmaster </h3><p>It was 11:30 a.m. on Feb. 20. I was seated at my desk on my computer waiting for <a class="Link" href="https://www.ticketmaster.com/bruce-springsteen-and-the-e-street-tickets/artist/860453?landing=c&awtrc=true&c=SEM_TMMCONCERTS_ggl_23581234228_192116752303_bruce%20springsteen%20ticketmaster&GCID=0&gclsrcshybbb=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23581234228&gbraid=0AAAAAD_KsMIloamz2NacAz2l79yiPsSP9&gclid=CjwKCAiAqprNBhB6EiwAMe3yhk2WzM3Y-lAVJXQthXP02Hy-2nFOxZi5fn5rX2eeTWzR-NEv08DYjBoCaXsQAvD_BwE" target="_blank" >Bruce Springsteen</a> tickets at the United Center to go on sale at noon. I was ready. I was quickly notified that I was in a "virtual waiting room." I got excited, hoping to get two, possibly four seats.</p><p>The clock struck noon. I was informed that I was number 27,312 in line. The "bots" have won again. Do Ticketmaster officials care? I think not. They also sell after-market tickets from "scalpers" on the Ticketmaster website — another way to pick your pocket.</p><p>If they were serious about thwarting bots, here's what they could do, although I am not naive, and I know that they will never do this: <br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-1219bda1-1334-11f1-b6c9-693938b9c72a" start="1"><li>Offer a maximum of two tickets per order.</li><li>Require ticket purchasers to attend the show with a photo ID.</li><li>Require the purchaser to send ID information of the second person attending the performance during the purchase procedure.</li><li>Require that second person to bring the same ID to gain entrance to the concerts.</li></ol><p>These actions would solve many problems. This would frustrate ticket brokers while selling tickets to fans who actually want to go to the concert. </p><p>Shame on the performers for not demanding changes. Sadly, it appears as if they don't care who attends their show either.</p><p><i>Jerry Bernacchi, Rolling Meadows</i> </p><h3>Sun-Times’ Rev. Jesse Jackson coverage informative </h3><p>Thank you for the daily and extensive coverage of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/02/17/rev-jesse-jackson-civil-rights-leader-rainbow-push-obituary" >Rev. Jesse Jackson’s</a> life and impact. I am a Sun-Times newspaper subscriber, so I saved the special Feb. 18 section and have savored every additional article.</p><p>Although I am of Jackson's generation and have admired him from the beginning, your <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/02/18/lights-camera-jesse-jackson-civil-rights-leader-pop-culture-presence" >coverage</a> helped me learn so much more. I carry an exuberant memory of his speech at the 1984 Democratic National Convention. Thank you. He was somebody!</p><p><i>Kay Whitlock, Lake View East</i></p><h3>Chicago institution proves pivotal </h3><p>Many years ago, I attended a performance by the late 12-string guitarist and vocalist Glen Campbell at Old Town School of Folk Music. It changed my life. </p><p><i>Scott Schada, Glenview</i><br></p>

title: Chicago short nearly 225,000 affordable rental units for its poorest residents, report finds
summary: <p>Chicago's affordable housing shortage is placing severe financial strain on low-income renters, according to a report released Thursday by Housing Action Illinois and the National Low Income Housing Coalition. </p><p>The study found only 31 affordable homes are available for rent for every 100 extremely low-income renter households in Chicago. In Illinois, it's 34 available homes for every 100 extremely low-income renter household.</p><p>Extremely low-income renters are those who have annual incomes at or below 30% of the area median income. In Chicago, that’s $35,970 for a family of four and $25,200 for an individual. Most households considered extremely low-income are because they're either working low-wage jobs, are seniors or have a disability, according to the report. </p><p>The annual <a class="Link" href="file:///Users/s.h./Downloads/gap-report_2026_english.pdf" target="_blank" >study</a> estimates the availability of affordable homes for renters at different income levels, with a focus on extremely low-income households. It also provides estimates of affordable housing needs for the U.S. and the 50 largest metropolitan areas, including Chicago. It's based on data from the 2024 American Community Survey Public Use Microdata Sample, a nationwide survey of about 3.5 million addresses.</p><p>Extremely low-income renters are most likely to be impacted by the housing shortage. And that’s especially true in Chicago, Bob Palmer, policy director at Housing Action Illinois, said. </p><p>He said Chicago’s figures don’t vary much from last year, but the data shows the region’s lack of affordable housing is persistent — especially for the lowest-income renters.</p><p>“It's a chronic problem that everyone knows about, but there hasn't been the political will to deal with it in a way that fundamentally changes the current problems,” Palmer said.</p><p>The report found no major city, or state, with an adequate supply of available affordable homes for extremely low-income renters. And Chicago, typically seen as more affordable than its coastal counterparts, was no exception.</p><p>Housing Action Illinois and the National Low Income Housing Coalition found the Chicago metro area was short 224,445 units of affordable housing for its poorest residents. It means 76% of extremely low-income renters in Chicago are spending more than half of their household income on rent. Experts say renters should typically spend no more than 30% of their monthly income on housing in order to budget for other necessities, like health care and groceries.</p><p>“You have neighborhoods that are gentrifying, where there's a lot of housing pressure,” Palmer said. “You have neighborhoods mostly on the South or West Side where there's a declining housing stock because of disinvestment in the housing [and] housing being torn down.”</p><p>The lack of affordable housing contributes to homelessness and evictions, Palmer said, as well as population loss. Illinois’ population has been growing for the last three years, according to the Illinois Policy Institute, but it was on a nine-year decline before then.</p><p>The state's growth in recent years has largely been attributed to an influx in immigration. Without immigration, Illinois’ population would have declined, according to the institute. More than 40,000 residents left Illinois last year to live in another state.</p><p>“Housing is an issue or a factor that very, very much influences the future of our state,” Palmer said.</p><p>Housing affordability remains an issue because of constraints in the private market. Much of the recent apartment development in Chicago is considered luxury or high-end because developers can't afford to build lower-rate units without government subsidies, Palmer said. </p><p>The report also found Illinois needs nearly 290,000 more homes for extremely low-income households. Expanding access to rental assistance and building deeply affordable rental homes could help ease the shortage, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition.</p>

title: Reality is immaterial in today's politics
summary: <p>Unless you’ve been under a rock, you likely know that former President Bill Clinton seemed to say that he flew on Jeffrey Epstein’s private jet with JB Pritzker and his spouse — after saying that it was likely that Epstein as well as his notorious co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell were passengers on every flight he took on that plane.</p><p>Clinton made his remarks during a deposition taken by the U.S. House Oversight Committee last month. He was asked during the deposition about whether Epstein and Maxwell were on “every flight” he took on the jet. Clinton said "I think he was" about Epstein’s presence and "I think she was" about Maxwell’s.</p><p>The former Democratic president then went on to say, "I think it was on one of these trips, I think that I had my first trip for the man who’s now the governor of Illinois, JB Pritzker and his wife, they gave me, they helped me get started." The video snippet was released online by the "rapid response" unit of the Republican National Committee.</p><p>The story has no <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/03/03/jb-pritzker-bill-clinton-erroneous-testimony-jeffrey-epstein-aircraft" >factual support</a>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-040000" name="module-040000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Columnist</div> </div><p>Clinton and Epstein went separate ways in the early 2000s and the Clinton flights with the Pritzkers were in 2008 and 2013.</p><p>Pritzker has never shown up on flight logs for Epstein’s plane.</p><p>A top Clinton aide issued a correction to his boss’ comments that very night, and the Pritzker campaign issued a flat-out denial.</p><p>KSDK TV in St. Louis checked the flight logs for both the 2008 and 2013 Clinton/Pritzker trips and <a class="Link" href="https://www.ksdk.com/article/news/local/flight-records-court-records-contradict-claims-illinois-gov-pritzker-flew-on-jeffrey-epsteins-plane/63-15809848-1862-4bf4-8f47-695be87e36f0" target="_blank" >confirmed no Epstein connections</a> whatsoever.</p><p>But this is 2026. Reality matters less to more people than possibly ever before in politics. Both major parties have succumbed to fantasy worlds of their own making.</p><p>As just one example, a quick glance at Democratic primaries in this state at almost every level shows that some "true blue" Democrats are now regularly accused of being "MAGA supporters" on the flimsiest of pretenses.</p><p>Pritzker himself is funding a multi-million-dollar moral panic U.S. Senate campaign on behalf of his Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton and against one of her rivals Democratic U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, which basically calls an immigrant a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement cheerleader who literally "sold us out."</p><p>State Sen. Willie Preston, D-Chicago, and his congressional campaign have been intensely pushing an insanely false story about how one of his congressional rivals sought out the support of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Sen. Robert Peters, D-Chicago, is Jewish, so maybe that’s why, but there is no way on this planet that the progressive senator wanted AIPAC’s support. It’s laughable on its face.</p><p>Thankfully, no mass media outlets have taken that seriously and neither should you. After we took a pass on the story, Preston’s spokesperson accused us of not treating his candidate fairly. In the real world, it ranked right up there as the dumbest story pitch of the campaign season.</p><p>Incumbent state Rep. Jaime Andrade, D-Chicago, is trying to fend off a progressive primary challenger who’s backed by the Chicago Teachers Union by attempting to paint his leftie Latino activist and community leader rival as a supporter of… wait for it… ICE. Yes, ICE. Miguel Alvelo-Rivera may be a lot of things, but an ICE supporter he most definitely ain’t.</p><p>And this is how Andrade justified the claims he’s made repeatedly in advertising to the Chicago Tribune: "Congresswoman [Delia] Ramirez supports Alvelo-Rivera; Ramirez has received campaign contributions from two California Democrats, U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia and House Democratic Chair Pete Aguilar; and those California lawmakers voted in 2024 for a resolution that included funding increases for parts of ICE."</p><p>Gimme a break.</p><p>This crud isn’t new, of course. We’ve had a problem in this country and in this state with hallucinatory campaigns that go beyond the normal campaign fibs for a very long time.</p><p>And connecting political rivals with pedophiles is also hardly new at the state level. Republican state legislative candidates who advocated for reducing state government mandates on school districts were regularly accused by Illinois House Democrats of opening the door for pedophiles and other dregs of society into children’s classrooms.</p><p>But a video of a former president saying he thinks he flew on Epstein’s jet with Pritzker and likely Epstein himself? Clinton did say what he said. The video is on the internet, and the internet is forever and quite strange. The fact that Pritzker’s wealthy cousin had close ties to Epstein will likely only fuel the fire.</p><p>It is undoubtedly false, but I doubt it’ll ever totally go away.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b50000" name="module-b50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjkjhjt-tlkjhhnv-jr/" target="_blank" >Reginald Ponder</a></h5><p>A cold night with temperatures plunging below zero in Chicago can’t stop Buddy Guy. A standing-room-only crowd packed into his Legends club on a frigid January night, waiting in anticipation for not just the master of the blues, but the genre’s protector and champion.</p><p>"I’m a lucky guy, because I got a chance to play with all of them [blues legends] before they passed away, and they told me, 'Buddy if you can do me a favor, just keep the blues alive,' and that’s all I’m trying to do," he told the crowd.</p><p>When Guy finally took the stage, silence fell over the audience. The next sound was not a musical note, but Guy being the color commentator of his own performance. He proceeded to weave in and out of being musical master and master storyteller.</p><p>"I know y’all don’t want me to talk, but I like to explain some s--- that I’ve experienced by being a guitar player well enough to be invited around the world," he said. Guy then opened with "Damn Right, I’ve Got the Blues."</p><p>It’s his approach to the blues that fills a room. Writer and director Ryan Coogler uses that to anchor the film "Sinners" and pay tribute to the music as well as the culture. title: Don't punish TSA agents for Homeland Security's transgressions
summary: <p>A friend of mine is a Transportation Security Administration agent. We had a very interesting conversation when I called him to check on how he was doing. He is OK, he said. </p><p>But his heart breaks for some of his co-workers: the single mom who just bought a house and now can’t meet her mortgage payment; the co-worker who may be evicted; the co-worker whose transmission went out and now cannot come to work because repairs are too expensive; co-workers who have medical issues; people who wonder if they can afford gas or food and are now looking at food pantries as an option.</p><p>Yes, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's actions are abhorrent, and we need to take a strong stand, raise our voices, vote, protest and expect Congress to stand up to the Department of Homeland Security for the inhumane treatment of undocumented immigrants.</p><p>But don't forget the plight of <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/5759740-government-shutdown-tsa-funding/" target="_blank" >TSA agents</a>, who've also being unjustly targeted by the partial government shutdown due to an impasse over funding DHS. These TSA agents have nothing to do with ICE, and yet they are being penalized. We need to find a better solution. These American citizens do not deserve to be the scapegoat in this showdown.</p><p><i>Elizabeth Butler Marren, Beverly</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-220000" name="module-220000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>More election guidance, please</h3><p>Thank you for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/voter-guide-primary-election-illinois/" target="_blank" >2026 Illinois Primary Elections Voters Guide</a> in Sunday's Sun-Times. It’s a great summary of our choices in this primary election. However, I want more. One suggestion is that you could publish in-depth interviews with the candidates. </p><p>Also, when I lived in San Francisco, for every election, primary or general, I would get a thick paper booklet in the mail with statements from each candidate. As long as the candidate submitted the statement on time, within the word limits and without vulgarity, the Board of Elections would print their statement verbatim. This made it so much easier to research candidates. Because it was not produced by a specific party or candidate, it was comprehensive and helpful. Perhaps the Sun-Times could coordinate such a publication for future elections?</p><p><i>Barry Charles Saiff, South Loop</i></p><h3>Good news</h3><p>Saturday's Sun-Times made my day with its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/02/25/buddy-guy-sinners-movie-ryan-coogler-blues-music" >front page cover</a> of blues man Buddy Guy. Then, I turned to Page 9 to read an incredible story about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/02/25/john-sharkey-renowned-naperville-karate-instructor-whose-students-have-gone-on-to-hollywood-dies-at-69" >John Sharkey</a>, a karate teacher, who was taken too young. He devoted his life to karate with the help of his father. It is good to read heartwarming stories instead of those about war and hate, both downers. Thank you Sun-Times.</p><p><i>Virginia Dare McGraw, Naperville</i></p><h3>Foreign fiasco</h3><p>Donald Trump has opened a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/02/28/iran-trump-israel" >global can of worms</a> without a clue about what comes next. Trump doesn't plan past his next Diet Coke. This is what happens when you elect a repugnant, ignoramus president. Thanks, America. </p><p><i>Michael Shepherd, Bellwood</i></p><h3></h3>

title: Aspira will soon have no teachers or money. CPS is still struggling to close it
summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools finds itself stuck in a quagmire as it tries to transfer students out of a charter school network that has, thus far, refused to officially close, even though it will run out of money next month.</p><p>The unprecedented situation is <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/02/26/cps-to-shut-down-financially-distressed-aspira-campuses-scattering-students-to-new-schools" target="_blank" ><u>creating confusion for some 545 students</u></a> as they face the prospect of finding a new school just months before the end of the year. It’s also fueled an ongoing debate about the adequacy of charter school funding and raised questions about charter school accountability.</p><p>Aspira Charter School Network sent out layoff notices on Wednesday to about 60 teachers and staff, acknowledging that CPS is transitioning students out of their two Northwest Side high schools and that the district “will not provide any further funding for the operation of these schools.”</p><p>But in those notices Aspira leaders also say they hope the school closures are “temporary.” CEO Edgar Lopez tells WBEZ that legally he had to send out the layoff notices, pointing out that he even got one. He said he is still working to keep the schools open through June.</p><p>In another sign that Aspira has not yet given up: the charter network launched a crowdsourcing campaign to try to raise money so that students can “finish out the school year in a stable and uninterrupted environment.” But it has raised only $2,000 in the six days since it launched — <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/02/11/cps-charter-school-cant-make-payroll-insolvent-closed-march-aspira-chiarts-cpsboard" target="_blank" ><u>well short of the millions that Aspira has said it needs</u></a> to continue paying teachers for the next few months.</p><p>CPS officials finally made it clear last week that they think students should abandon Aspira. They sent letters to families saying that students will be offered a seat at a nearby school for the remainder of the school year. CPS also met with families Thursday afternoon.</p><p>Still, they noted that Aspira’s charter, which allows it to operate schools within CPS, is not being revoked “at this time.”</p><h3><b>CPS says state law makes it difficult to close Aspira outright</b></h3><p>School board members approved Aspira’s most recent contract back in May. It runs from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2027. But Aspira hasn’t signed a written agreement yet and CPS says they are still in negotiations with the charter operator, as well as several others approved in May.</p><p>Yet CPS says they can’t just close Aspira, regardless of whether there’s a signed written agreement.</p><p>“The Illinois Charter School Law explicitly states that, ‘no local school board may arbitrarily or capriciously revoke or not renew a charter” and “revocation shall take place at the end of a school year,’” a CPS spokesperson told WBEZ in an email.</p><p>Earlier this week, CPS interim CEO/Superintendent Macquline King said those terms put the school district in a tricky position.</p><p>“They have to elect to self-close or CPS will be in violation of their contract,” King said. “We are walking a very fine line to respond in a way that is humane and acceptable and shows that we hear all of the community members that come before us each day, while honoring the contract.”</p><p>The Chicago Teachers Union, though, which represents Aspira teachers, clinicians and classroom aides, thinks the school district should be taking more definitive action. Union officials say the school district should be more focused on the “crisis facing students” rather than the “district’s desire to avoid the possibility of litigation.”</p><p>The union called on CPS to allow students to transfer together in cohorts, to designate specific “welcoming” schools that will take in Aspira students and to allow some Aspira teachers and other staff to follow their students so they see familiar faces.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, which advocates for charter schools, said CPS should have done more to prevent Aspira from running out of money.</p><p>The group said that CPS’ inaction was “political and not in the best interest of CPS families,” noting that many Aspira students and families were <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/02/as-immigration-agents-swept-chicago-this-fall-communities-stepped-in-to-get-kids-to-school-safely" target="_blank" ><u>affected by ramped up federal immigration enforcement in their neighborhoods</u></a>.</p><p>“Stability matters right now,” INCS officials said in a statement. “Keeping both campuses open through the end of the academic year should be the focus — and would avoid the obvious negative consequences of moving high schoolers to an unfamiliar school just weeks ahead of graduation.”</p><p>INCS and Aspira also say CPS has made it harder for charter schools to operate by providing too little funding per student and changing how it assigns students to schools. CPS has said it is providing charters as much funding as it can, while complying with state law.</p><p>CPS is increasingly finding it is limited in how it can address troubled charter schools.</p><p>When school districts started giving contracts to private organizations to run public schools 30 years ago, a selling point was that their contracts could simply be canceled and it would be easier to close a charter school than one run by the district.</p><p>But school board members have hesitated to close charters or let them voluntarily close as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2018/05/22/study-2013-chicago-school-closings-failed-to-help-students" target="_blank" ><u>research has shown that school closings often harm students</u></a>. Over the last two years, Chicago’s school board has voted to take over six privately run charter schools after their operators no longer wanted to run them.</p><p>The district also has had to contend with legal challenges. In 2022, a judge prevented CPS from revoking its contract with the charter network Urban Prep, which the district sought to cancel due to Urban Prep’s financial troubles and allegations of sexual misconduct by its then-CEO.</p><p>Urban Prep contended that a state moratorium on school closures applied to charter schools and, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2024/06/07/cps-decision-not-renew-urban-prep-charter-ok-appellate-judge-rules" target="_blank" ><u>after a protracted legal fight</u></a>, was allowed to stay open. That moratorium is no longer in place, but Urban Prep still holds a contract to run schools in CPS.<br></p>
author: Sarah Karp | WBEZ

title: After trades, Blackhawks motivated to make this the last time they sell at deadline
summary: <p>Just two weeks ago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> forwards Connor Bedard, Ryan Greene and Colton Dach were vacationing together in Mexico during the Olympics.</p><p>"We were talking about, 'After we win the [Stanley] Cup, we're going to go back,'" Bedard recalled Thursday.</p><p>Now, Dach is no longer a Hawk, having been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/03/04/blackhawks-oilers-trade-jason-dickinson-colton-dach-draft-pick" target="_blank" >traded to the Oilers</a> alongside Jason Dickinson — joining Connor Murphy — as the organization goes through the familiar dance of converting pending free agents and on-the-outs players into draft picks ahead of the NHL deadline at 2 p.m. CT Friday.</p><p>Bedard and the rest of the Hawks understand why that's smart and necessary from a managerial standpoint. But that doesn't make losing friends sting any less.</p><p>"It's motivating that this is the last year that we're in a spot where we're moving guys that help us win," Bedard added. "That's a [expletive] feeling. [We'll] just try to not let that happen [again]."</p><p>Hawks captain Nick Foligno, who might no longer be the captain very soon, has heard that same sentiment throughout the locker room. </p><p>He called it a "wake-up call to a lot of guys" that the Hawks need to finally be in the playoff race next season to avoid going through this dance yet again.</p><p>"This is the tough part of the season, right?" Foligno said. "These are the emotions and feelings you have when you lose some really good people. You don't want to be in this spot too many times. </p><p>"That's probably the message that's been heard the loudest the last few days here from the group. I think they're getting tired of being in this spot. So hopefully it's a motivating factor for years to come."</p><p>Foligno spoke in past tense throughout his interview Thursday. There's a sizable chance the pending free agent will move Friday and finish out elsewhere what might be the last season of his career.</p><p>The Blue Jackets, whom Foligno formerly captained and who have enough salary-cap space to absorb Foligno's $4.5 million cap hit easily (despite the Hawks' lack of available salary-retention slots), would make sense. They're in the East playoff race, and Foligno owns a home in Columbus.</p><p>"It's been an absolute honor to be the captain here, so I'm still fully committed to that until told otherwise," he said. "But there's a competitor inside you, too, that wants to be playing meaningful games."</p><p>If he does move, the Hawks will have traded their entire leadership group — their captain and both alternate captains — in the span of a week, which would be unprecedented.</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill said his staff is working on deciding who besides Bedard, who had already filled in as alternate when Foligno was injured in November, will inherit those letters and leadership roles.</p><p>But it's clear they'll be distributed within the group of youngsters that compose an increasingly large percentage of the Hawks' roster. Alex Vlasic and Frank Nazar have to be strong candidates at the least.</p><p>"I've had it in my career where you wonder, 'What's it going to be like to lose this guy?'" Foligno said. "And then you realize, 'Well, there's more that I can give.' That's the message that these guys have to understand: 'There's more of yourself to give.' </p><p>"[Murphy, Dickinson and I] were once in your position and had to figure out how to be good pros, how to be the guys that people look to. That's the journey these guys are going to go on now."</p><h3><b>Notes</b></h3><p>Andrew Mangiapane, a salary dump from the Oilers, will "get an opportunity to be a good player" for the Hawks after his U.S. immigration paperwork clears, Blashill said.</p><p>Oliver Moore slid into the third-line center role vacated by Dickinson, and Wyatt Kaiser (knee injury) fully participated in practice and should play Friday against the Canucks. Kevin Korchinski was sent down to Rockford.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="sl" dir="ltr">Blackhawks lines in practice today:<br><br>Greene-Bedard-Burakovsky <br>Donato-Nazar-Teravainen<br>Bertuzzi-Moore-Mikheyev <br>Slaggert-Foligno-Lafferty<br><br>Vlasic-Crevier<br>Kaiser-Rinzel<br>Grzelcyk-Levshunov<br>Del Mastro-Korchinski</p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://twitter.com/BenPopeCST/status/2029607036925677737?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>
