title: Who is Markwayne Mullin, Trump choice to replace Noem at DHS
summary: <p>Sen. Markwayne Mullin, President Trump's pick to replace Kristi Noem as head of the Department of Homeland Security, is, like Noem, a vocal advocate for the president's immigration policies.</p><p>Mullin, who served in the House for years before being elected to the Senate in November 2022, is one of Trump’s closest allies on Capitol Hill and has been a frequent intermediary between the White House and congressional Republicans.</p><p>He has often leaned on his longstanding House ties, working with his former colleagues there as the GOP hashed out the party’s sweeping tax and border security law last year.</p><p>His selection still must be approved by the Senate, but under a federal law governing executive branch vacancies, he would be allowed to serve as an acting Homeland Security secretary as long as his nomination is formally pending.</p><p>Voting in the Senate just after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/05/trump-fires-noem-dhs-ice-border-patrol-markwayne-mullin" >Trump announced he had fired Noem,</a> DHS announcement, Mullin said he has “no idea” how quickly his nomination will move. He also said that he spoke to Trump just before the announcement went out.</p><p>“The president and I are good friends. So we look forward to working closer with the White House, and obviously I’m gonna be over there a lot more,” he said.</p><p>Mullin would take over the third-largest department in government that has responsibility for carrying out Trump’s hardline immigration agenda.</p><p>And he takes the office at a pivotal time for that agenda. Immigration enforcement during the first year of Trump’s administration was largely defined by high-profile, made-for-social-media operations with flashy names that were often led by Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, who reported directly to Noem.</p><p>Noem herself often went out on those operations, riding along with officers when they went out to make arrests.</p><p>Mullin told reporters at the Capitol he would get DHS “focused on protecting the homeland.”</p><p>“Whether you support me or don’t support me, I’m going to be laser-focused on getting that done,” he added.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/05/trump-fires-noem-dhs-ice-border-patrol-markwayne-mullin" >Trump fires Kristi Noem, Pritzker says ‘don’t let the door hit you on the way out’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
author: AP

title: Trump fires Kristi Noem, Pritzker says 'don’t let the door hit you on the way out'
summary: <p>Illinois Democrats are welcoming the exit of controversial Department of Homeland Security head Kristi Noem – months after she led aggressive immigration operations in the Chicago area that left one person dead and another surviving being shot five times by a federal immigration agent. </p><p>"Don't let the door hit you on the way out, Kristi Noem," Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker wrote on social media. U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, who last week met with Noem and reminded her that her days were numbered, wrote on X, "Good riddance! We still have to impeach her, Melt ICE and dismantle DHS."</p><p>There were rumblings of dissatisfaction from President Donald Trump following two consecutive days of testimony by Noem before Senate and House committees, which featured grilling from both Democrats and Republicans. Trump on Truth Social said he will instead nominate Oklahoma Republican Sen. Markwayne Mullin to replace her. Trump says he’ll make Noem a “Special Envoy for The Shield of the Americas,” a new security initiative that he said would focus on the Western Hemisphere.</p><p>Noem is the first Cabinet secretary to leave during Trump’s second term. </p><p>Sen. Dick Durbin reacted to Noem's exit by saying she was "unfit for the job" and accusing her of lying under oath before Congress. </p><p>“Kristi Noem was the face of an unpopular, illegal, and outright dangerous mass deportation campaign that claimed the lives of innocent Americans and terrorized many more. Our country expressed outrage, she repeatedly lied before Congress, and even the President finally conceded she was unfit for the job," Durbin said. “Kristi Noem slipped on the outrages of ICE. Will this Oklahoma Senator be any better? We will find out as the Senate exercises its authority under the Constitution to provide advice and consent on this appointment."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good</a> in Minneapolis, as well as Marimar Martinez, the Chicago woman who survived being shot five times by a federal agent in October. In each case, DHS labeled the victims “domestic terrorists.”</p><p>“We have ample video evidence and eyewitness testimony proving you are wrong. Your statements caused immeasurable pain to these families,” Durbin told Noem. “Let me give you an opportunity to do the right thing. Do you retract these statements identifying these individuals as domestic terrorists?”</p><p>Noem called the shootings “tragic situations” and said “we always offer our condolences to those families.” The DHS head said she was “relying on reports from the ground and from agents that are there and working to be transparent.”</p><p>Durbin on Thursday also accused Noem of lying under oath during Tuesday's Senate Judiciary Committee, including stating that DHS is following court orders, despite a sworn declaration that ICE has violated over 50 court orders in the state of New Jersey. She also denied that DHS had detained American citizens, which is also false, Durbin said. And she denied that aide Corey Lewandowski had any role in approving DHS contracts. </p><p>“I have served on this Committee for more than 25 years … and I’ve never been through a hearing like our DHS oversight hearing with Secretary Noem [on] Tuesday," Durbin said. "The Secretary took an oath to tell the truth. But instead, she repeatedly failed to do so," Durbin said. "...This should concern every member of this Committee — Republican and Democrat alike. This Committee has an obligation to hold the Secretary accountable. I look forward to discussing this with you and other members of the Committee [about] what our recourse is.”</p><p>On Wednesday, Noem faced questions before the House Judiciary Committee about an advertising contract — glitzy ads starring Noem discussing Trump's ongoing immigration campaign. Under questioning, Noem said the president had signed off on the $220 million ad campaign. </p><p>But Trump on Thursday contradicted that claim, according to Reuters: “I never knew anything about it,” Trump said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/25/rep-delia-ramirez-homeland-security-secretary-kristi-noem-meeting-dhs-actions-impeachment-plans" target="_blank" >Ramirez met with Noem last week</a> and came equipped with specific requests, including barring federal agents from churches, schools and hospitals — and revoking a controversial policy that allows U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to enter homes without judicial warrants. </p><p>She also told her in no uncertain terms — twice — that she’ll work to impeach her. She also told her she recognized that her "days may be numbered."</p><p>Silverio Villegas González, a father and cook originally from Mexico, was shot at “close range” as he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop Sept. 12, just days after the Trump administration announced Operation Midway Blitz, an aggressive deportation campaign targeting the Chicago area.<br></p>

title: Chicago Symphony Orchestra’s 2026-27 season to feature Yo-Yo Ma, a lot of Beethoven and imprint of Klaus Mäkelä
summary: <p>The Chicago Symphony Orchestra announced its 2026-27 lineup Thursday, featuring everyone from <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/classical/2025/08/25/yo-yo-ma-chicago-angelique-kidjo-concert" target="_blank" ><u>Yo-Yo Ma</u></a> to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/02/24/andrew-bird-debut-chicago-symphony-orchestra" target="_blank" ><u>Andrew Bird</u></a>. The lineup also includes a world premiere from composer Mason Bates, a season-long deep dive into Beethoven and a healthy showing of Finnish music.</p><p>That last part is thanks to CSO’s incoming music director, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/classical/2026/02/26/klaus-makela-conductor-cso-chicago-art-institute-tour" target="_blank" ><u>Klaus Mäkelä</u></a>. Although the 30-year-old Finnish conductor and cellist will not officially be in the role until <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/2024/04/02/chicago-symphony-orchestra-names-klaus-makela-music-director" target="_blank" ><u>the following season</u></a>, Mäkelä’s is already helping shape what gets played inside Orchestra Hall.</p><p>“I have lots of music that I really want to bring to the orchestra. and this is just a couple pieces,” Mäkelä said from his backstage office this week. “I bring music that I think the orchestra should play. I also bring music that I think the audience should hear, and some things that I really just think are fun.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> During one of those appearances, Mäkelä will conduct Gustav Mahler’s Ninth Symphony in October, a nod to the CSO’s long history with the piece. The orchestra has won <a class="Link" href="https://cso.org/experience/article/23522/the-chicago-symphony-orchestra-and-mahlers-ni" target="_blank" ><u>multiple Grammy Awards</u></a> for its recordings of the work.</p><p>Now, the new maestro will look to put his spin on it. “One of the great things about it, is that as long as your interpretation has deep logic and coherence, it can take really lots of different treatments,” he said.</p><p>Then, next spring he will return to conduct the U.S. premiere of a new work co-commissioned by the CSO from Finnish composer Magnus Lindberg. The season also includes a U.S. premiere from another Finnish composer, Esa-Pekka Salonen. Chicago’s orchestra will also premiere “The Escapist Symphony” from Bates, a former CSO composer in residence, which Manfred Honeck will conduct in February.</p><p>Together, the 2026-27 season represents an era of new music, which Mäkelä has championed. </div><p>“I think it's important to keep playing new music, because orchestras have always played new music,” Mäkelä said. “But it's also important to play old music and to put things in context.”</p><p>That context arrives, in part, with the season-long exploration of Ludwig van Beethoven, timed to the 200th anniversary of his death. There will be performances of each of Beethoven’s five piano concertos by acclaimed Chinese pianist Lang Lang, spread across a three-concert residency in March. It all builds to Mäkelä conducting Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony (which concludes with “Ode to Joy”) to close out the season in June 2027.</p><p>That performance is one of several on the lineup that include a collaboration with the Chicago Symphony Chorus under director <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-culture/2025/06/03/donald-palumbo-named-director-of-the-chicago-symphony-orchestra-chorus" target="_blank" ><u>Donald Palumbo</u></a>. Lang.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Sonja Mueller</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The CSO will also go the road in January with an eight-city, 12-concert European tour under Mäkelä’s baton. That follows the maestro’s first tour with the orchestra last month to the East Coast. For him, tours are essential to artistic growth. “I've never been on tour with an orchestra that hasn't come home as a better orchestra,” he said.</p><p>As Mäkelä prepares to become the orchestra’s 11th director, he faces a series of challenges: There are multiple vacancies on stage that need permanent filling, and global politics have affected <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/classical/2026/02/18/venezuela-classical-musicians-el-sistema-pipeline-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>classical music’s talent pipeline</u></a>. Plus, not all musicians want to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/05/14/canceled-tetzlaff-chicago-visa-musicians-recital-trump-era-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>perform in the United States</u></a> right now.</p><p>“We are not searching for the best players, we are searching for the most suitable players who make our orchestra a better orchestra,” Mäkelä said. “Unless we choose the right people and the best people, our orchestra doesn't stay the world's best, so it's a wonderful challenge.”</p><h3><b>Other highlights of the 2026-27 CSO season include: </b></h3><p></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-f2863410-1814-11f1-a985-cfcf01f83549"><li>French pianist Jean-Yves Thibaudet will make three appearances next season — Oct. 18, Feb. 11-13 and May 24 — as the CSO’s artist in residence. </li><li>The season will open Sept. 17-19 with an appearance from former CSO artist-in-residence Hilary Hahn. The program conducted by Petr Popelka will feature Felix Mendelssohn’s Violin Concerto, Robert Schumann’s Overture to Manfred and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 5.</li><li>The superstar Canadian pianist and 2021 International Chopin Piano Competition winner Bruce Liu is returning to Chicago on Nov. 1. Last summer, Liu helped the CSO open its annual residency at Ravinia. His performance this fall will feature a wide range of music, including Chopin.</li><li>Fan-favorite Yo-Yo Ma returns to the CSO on Nov. 11 with one of the first concertos he ever recorded, Dmitri Shostakovich’s First Cello Concerto.</li><li>CSO’s annual movie series that pairs films with live orchestra performance,  kicks off with “How to Train Your Dragon 2” (Nov. 27-29). The series will also include “Elf” (Dec. 11-13), “West Side Story” (Jan. 29-30) and “Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back” (June 25-27, 2027).</li><li>The holiday season will include performances of George Frideric Handel’s “Messiah” Dec. 17-19.</li><li>On April 4, 2027, Mexican singer-songwriter Lila Downs will bring her program, “Cambias mi mundo” to town. It’s a soulful blend of songs about identity and justice.</li><li>The Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra will return for a two-day residency in April 2027, during what will be the final season with legendary trumpeter Wynton Marsalis as artistic director.</li><li>Tan Dun, the Oscar-winning Chinese composer and conductor, who will make his CSO debut with a program of his own works May 20-22. The program will also feature percussionist Yuri Yamashita in her CSO debut. Composers Masaaki Suzuki and Maxim Emelyanychev will also take the podium in Chicago for the first time. </li></ul><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ. </i></p>

title: Ojala Islamic Center, the first Latino-led mosque in the Midwest, opens in Berwyn
summary: <p>In the basement of one of the Chicago area's newest places of worship, all the fixings of a traditional Mexican meal were laid out to enjoy.</p><p>“We have mole, birria, spaghetti verde, arroz. We even have flautas,” Cesar Cortina, 39, said Sunday evening at the space. </p><p>It’s a spread one might find following services at any of Chicago’s many predominately Mexican Roman Catholic churches.</p><p>But this was not at a church.</p><p>It was at the first mosque in the Midwest geared toward Latino Muslims, and one of only a handful nationwide. Ojala Islamic Center opened Feb. 17, the first day of Ramadan. The center is in a former church in a quiet neighborhood in west suburban Berwyn.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-150000" name="image-150000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/eb34423/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6208x3484+0+328/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2F5e%2F51aadd1e46ddb138082a8982b8d9%2Flatino-muslims-260304-022.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5092dcc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6208x3484+0+328/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2F5e%2F51aadd1e46ddb138082a8982b8d9%2Flatino-muslims-260304-022.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/923a5a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6208x3484+0+328/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2F5e%2F51aadd1e46ddb138082a8982b8d9%2Flatino-muslims-260304-022.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Members and guests enjoy an iftar spread at Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn, Sunday, March 1, 2026. Ojala is the first Latino mosque in the Midwest." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/923a5a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6208x3484+0+328/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2F5e%2F51aadd1e46ddb138082a8982b8d9%2Flatino-muslims-260304-022.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a747c4c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6208x3484+0+328/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2F5e%2F51aadd1e46ddb138082a8982b8d9%2Flatino-muslims-260304-022.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/923a5a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6208x3484+0+328/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F89%2F5e%2F51aadd1e46ddb138082a8982b8d9%2Flatino-muslims-260304-022.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Members and guests enjoy an iftar spread at Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn on Sunday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It just feels more and more like home to me,” said Cortina, who became a Muslim a year ago. “I love it.”</p><p>“This is needed now because our community is growing at numbers that we've never seen before,” said Imam Christopher AbdulKareem Pavlicek, 48, the center's director.</p><p>“We knew eight years ago when we started this work that there was a need," Pavlicek said. "As we continue to do work in the community, the community just started growing at such a rapid rate. We didn’t necessarily have places to meet on our own. Having this place, it was a perfect time for us.”</p><p>Latinos make up a small but growing part of the Muslim population in the U.S., with Pew Research <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2011/08/30/section-1-a-demographic-portrait-of-muslim-americans/" target="_blank" >polls</a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2017/07/26/demographic-portrait-of-muslim-americans" target="_blank" >showing</a> practicing members of the faith rose from 6% to 8% between 2011 and 2017.</p><p>The effort that eventually led to the mosque opening last month started more than a decade ago when there wasn't much for Latino Muslims in the Chicago area and no space of their own.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fc0000" name="image-fc0000"></a> <picture Pavlicek is a co-founder of the foundation. </p><p>Foundation members have spent time serving to the needs of those less fortunate, including providing food to the homeless in Chicago’s Latino neighborhoods, including Little Village, Pilsen, Humboldt Park and Marquette Park.</p><p>After eight years of raising funds, the Ojala Foundation took possession of the church structure on May 5 of last year. Soon after, it began removing all the symbols and wooden benches you’d typically find in a Christian church. </p><p>Just a few weeks ago, workers completed installing carpet in the main prayer space.</p><p>“I've been in this work for over 20-plus years. When we started doing all of this work, it was because there was a very sincere need from our side, as new converts to the faith, not being able to find anyone that was like us,” said Alma Campos, who sits on the Ojala Foundation board and was a co-founder. </p><p>Campos converted to Islam nearly three decades ago after being brought up Catholic. Nearly 80% of Mexicans are Roman Catholic, according to a 2020 <a class="Link" href="https://www.state.gov/reports/2022-report-on-international-religious-freedom/mexico" target="_blank" ><u>survey</u></a> by the Mexican government.</p><p>Her best friend introduced the religion to her.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-420000" name="image-420000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/19fbb06/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7868x4416+0+416/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F84%2F00%2Fd1c957224648ae724f4136e99a80%2Flatino-muslims-260304-012.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f23990f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7868x4416+0+416/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F84%2F00%2Fd1c957224648ae724f4136e99a80%2Flatino-muslims-260304-012.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f28e791/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7868x4416+0+416/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F84%2F00%2Fd1c957224648ae724f4136e99a80%2Flatino-muslims-260304-012.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Men perform prayer at Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn, Sunday, March 1, 2026. Ojala is the first Latino mosque in the Midwest.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It’s been an ongoing effort for a very long time," she said. "Seeing it culminate in this, and us being able to purchase our own space where we could have all of the things that we were not able to have and provide that for the community — it's an amazing feeling."</p><p>Ojala member Christopher Nevarez-Azdar’s family is from Mexico and also grew up in a Roman Catholic household.</p><p>Nevarez-Azdar converted in 2018, the first in his family, as an undergraduate student at University of Illinois Chicago.</p><p>He said part of the mission of the mosque is to reach out to the Latino community and to help those who wish to convert to Islam. But non-Latinos are welcomed as well, he said.</p><p>“The idea of Ojala is to be a space where people who become Muslim feel comfortable. Most of us happen to be Latino, but a lot of them are not Latino," said Nevarez-Azdar, 28, an assistant public defender in Cook County. </p><p>"We also have folks that are part of our community, that aren't Muslim but may be interested in Islam. You have people from our community. We have South Asian representation, Arab representation, West African, North African."</p><p>Nevarez-Azdar sees a lot of similarities between Islam and the Catholic faiths.</p><p>“You have a lot of family values that are very universal to both religions. The importance of women and respecting women and respecting one's mother. It's truly very important," he said.</p><p>Ojala Islamic Center, he said, allows Latino Muslims to practice their faith in a language they understand by offering sermons, lectures and classes in Spanish. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-930000" name="image-930000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a22982/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F99%2F061863374596826f53d6c2df0fe4%2Flatino-muslims-260304-001.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/aa6bd07/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F99%2F061863374596826f53d6c2df0fe4%2Flatino-muslims-260304-001.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ce87fad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F99%2F061863374596826f53d6c2df0fe4%2Flatino-muslims-260304-001.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ven Howard-Paez (center) prepares food for iftar at Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn, Sunday, March 1, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ce87fad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F99%2F061863374596826f53d6c2df0fe4%2Flatino-muslims-260304-001.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/906b872/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F99%2F061863374596826f53d6c2df0fe4%2Flatino-muslims-260304-001.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ce87fad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F22%2F99%2F061863374596826f53d6c2df0fe4%2Flatino-muslims-260304-001.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ven Howard-Paez prepares food for iftar at Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn on Sunday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“The way that we present Islam to people, it's a universal message. But it's presented in a way that we would understand it. That's why we think that there was that need for a Latino mosque, especially in a super Latino area," he said.</p><p>For Ojala’s 200 or so members, the opening of the mosque comes at a perilous time.</p><p>Since last fall, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement have targeted Latinos nationwide and in Chicago in President Trump’s aggressive deportation initiative.</p><p>And, over the weekend, Trump partnered with Israel in ordering an attack on Iran.</p><p>Those who are Muslim and Latino could feel they’re being targeted on two fronts.</p><p>Pavlicek said he’s heard hurtful comments from people targeting Ojala’s members for being both Latino and Muslim.</p><p>“There were people making comments like, 'Double deport. Deport them for both reasons,'” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-710000" name="image-710000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cfc1f5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8089x4540+0+428/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fa0%2Ffab8028c4fc99345382d459afb8b%2Flatino-muslims-260304-009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6dcc93b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8089x4540+0+428/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fa0%2Ffab8028c4fc99345382d459afb8b%2Flatino-muslims-260304-009.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/311e5cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8089x4540+0+428/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fa0%2Ffab8028c4fc99345382d459afb8b%2Flatino-muslims-260304-009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Board Member Alma Campos (far right) prays at Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn, Sunday, March 1, 2026. Ojala is the first Latino mosque in the Midwest. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/311e5cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8089x4540+0+428/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fa0%2Ffab8028c4fc99345382d459afb8b%2Flatino-muslims-260304-009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c36096c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8089x4540+0+428/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fa0%2Ffab8028c4fc99345382d459afb8b%2Flatino-muslims-260304-009.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/311e5cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8089x4540+0+428/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2Fa0%2Ffab8028c4fc99345382d459afb8b%2Flatino-muslims-260304-009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Board Member Alma Campos (far right) prays at Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn on Sunday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It impacted fundraising for the new center. Some events had to be done virtually for the safety of Ojala’s members in September, he said.</p><p>"We have a lot of people in our community that are undocumented, and other people that are here completely legal. But they're getting picked up too," Pavlicek said. "People were really hesitant to come out and come be a part of things. It greatly affected us."</p><p>Alma Campos said it’s a challenging time, but that's no different than any other time.</p><p>“Being a Latina that is first generation born and raised here, I never thought that I would see the day that I would hear the stories of earlier generations when ICE was really ‘la migra.' I never thought that I would see the day where I would be able to see that for myself," she said. "It's something that definitely weighs heavy on us because, at the end of the day, these are our brothers and sisters in humanity. So we are here for our Latino people. We are from the Latino people.”</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and weekend anchor for WBEZ. Reach him at </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:mpuente@wbez.org" target="_blank" ><i><u>mpuente@wbez.org</u></i></a><i>. </i></p>

title: Former Notre Dame football coach Lou Holtz dies at age 89
summary: <p>Lou Holtz, the College Football Hall of Fame coach who led Notre Dame to its last national title in 1988, died Wednesday. He was 89.</p><p>Holtz spent parts of five decades as a college football head coach, leading four programs to Top 25 finishes and six schools to bowl games, an NCAA record. While he didn’t last a full season in his lone stint in the NFL with the New York Jets in 1976 and he was dogged by controversy at times, Holtz’s 11-year run at Notre Dame cemented his status as one of the game’s great coaches.</p><p>“Notre Dame mourns the loss of Lou Holtz, a legendary football coach, a beloved member of the Notre Dame family and devoted husband, father and grandfather,” Notre Dame President Rev. Robert A. Dowd said in a news release.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">From the family of Lou Holtz <a href="https://t.co/aYWiXYVnLq">pic.twitter.com/aYWiXYVnLq</a></p>— The Fighting Irish (@FightingIrish) <a href="https://twitter.com/FightingIrish/status/2029308530398724260?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“Among his many accomplishments, we will remember him above all as a teacher, leader and mentor who brought out the very best in his players, on and off the field, earning their respect and admiration for a lifetime. ... Whenever Notre Dame called to ask for his help, Lou answered with his characteristic generosity, and he will be sorely missed."</p><p>Coming off years of mediocrity, Notre Dame hired Holtz before the 1986 season and by 1988 he had built the Fighting Irish back into a title-contending team. Led by quarterback Tony Rice, running backs Mark Green and Ricky Watters along with receiver/kick returner Raghib Ismail, the Fighting Irish beat four ranked teams and finished 12-0.</p><p>“Everyone told me why we couldn't win,” Holtz wrote. “The academic standards, the tough schedule, the no-redshirting policy, the lack of an athletic dormitory — all those were reasons people gave me why Notre Dame would never be great again.”</p><p>The biggest test that season came on Oct. 15, 1988, when Notre Dame faced Miami, which was ranked No. 1 and coached by Jimmy Johnson at the time. Billed as “Catholics vs. Convicts,” Notre Dame won 31-30 to end the Hurricanes' 36-game regular-season win.</p><p>Notre Dame finished atop the AP and coaches poll after a 34-21 victory against the third-ranked West Virginia Mountaineers at the Fiesta Bowl. Holtz coached Notre Dome to one-loss seasons in 1989 and 1993, finishing second in the polls each season.</p><p>He stepped down in 1996 after compiling a 100-30-2 record at the school.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Remembering the life and legacy of Lou Holtz <a href="https://t.co/8WiEtVr6fT">pic.twitter.com/8WiEtVr6fT</a></p>— Notre Dame Football (@NDFootball) <a href="https://twitter.com/NDFootball/status/2029309958412447938?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">March 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>After two years working for CBS Sports, Holtz returned to the sideline with South Carolina. He was selected as the 2000 SEC Coach of the Year and led the Gamecocks to consecutive postseason bowls for the first time in school history. But his six-season tenure ended after his team and Clemson were involved a 10-minute brawl in November 2004, which led both schools to forgo bowl bids.</p><p>His final career record was 249-132-7.</p><p>South Carolina was put on probation after Holtz’s departure, the third such Holtz-led program to be sanctioned by the NCAA.</p><p>Holtz returned to television, this time for ESPN where he spent a decade as a college football analyst.</p><p>A staunch Republican, Holtz drew heavy criticism a few times in his 31 years as a head college football coach and afterward. He backed Republican Jesse Helms, a longtime opponent to civil rights legislation, in a reelection bid while Holtz was a coach at Arkansas in the early 1980s.</p><p>Holtz endorsed Donald Trump during the 2016 presidential campaign and his comments on immigration cost him speaking engagements. He called the immigrants coming to the U.S. an “invasion” and criticized immigrants for not assimilating.</p><p>“I don’t want to become you,” Holtz said at a Republican pro-life luncheon in July 2016. “I don’t want to speak your language. I don’t want to celebrate your holidays. I sure as hell don’t want to cheer for your soccer team.”</p><p>Holtz flirted with the idea of running for Congress in 2009, although he decided not to enter the race for a Florida seat.</p><p></p><p><i>Read more at </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com" target="_blank" ><i>usatoday.com</i></a></p>

title: Durante audiencia, Kristi Noem dijo no conocer a Marimar Martínez, la mujer de Chicago a la que un agente de ICE le disparó
summary: <p>Marimar Martínez, la mujer de Chicago que sobrevivió a haber sido baleada cinco veces por agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza el año pasado, se encontraba a sólo cinco filas detrás de la secretaria del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS), Kristi Noem durante una tensa audiencia del Comité Judicial del Senado el martes mientras era presionada por el senador Richard Blumenthal para que reconociera que el tiroteo fue “incorrecto”.</p><p>Con Blumenthal describiendo el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >tiroteo de octubre que dejó a Martínez con daños</a> a los nervios de su mano derecha, el demócrata de Connecticut le preguntó a Noem si el tiroteo de Martínez fue “incorrecto” y también destacó —a través de grandes letreros— imágenes de mensajes de texto que mostraban al agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/11/agentes-dijeron-es-hora-de-ser-agresivos-en-video-que-contradice-las-afirmaciones-contra-marimar-martinez" target="_blank" >Charles Exum presumiendo del tiroteo</a> y alegando haber escrito en inglés: “Le disparé 5 balas y ella tenía 7 agujeros. Tomen nota, muchachos”.</p><p>A pesar de la amplia cobertura del tiroteo de Martínez y de las <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/11/21/desestiman-el-caso-contra-mujer-a-la-que-le-disparo-agente-de-la-patrulla-fronteriza-en-brighton-park" target="_blank" >acusaciones de obstruir la justicia que luego fueron desestimadas</a> en su contra, Noem afirmó repetidamente que no conocía el caso.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-aa0000" name="module-aa0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Señor, no conozco la situación ni el caso”, dijo Noem. “Lo investigaré para asegurarme de que todos los procedimientos se hayan seguido correctamente”.</p><p>Noem tampoco proporcionó detalles sobre si Exum, el agente que le disparó a Martínez, sigue en su puesto, “portando un arma”. Un portavoz de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) dijo el mes pasado al Chicago Sun-Times que a Exum lo habían descansado. El portavoz no respondió a un correo electrónico de seguimiento que preguntaba cuándo comenzó la licencia administrativa o si todavía está en efecto. Noem dijo que no conocía los detalles, pero que “averiguará y enviaré esa información”.</p><p>“Creo que a los estadounidenses les parecería absolutamente aterrador que ese agente siga en el trabajo, portando un arma”, dijo Blumenthal. “Y el hecho de que no puedes decirme que lo quitarás de su puesto”.</p><p>El testimonio de Noem en Washington ante el Congreso ocurre mientras el financiamiento de DHS permanece detenido durante un cierre parcial del gobierno, con el Congreso en un punto muerto por las políticas de inmigración. A pesar del cierre, los senadores se centraron principalmente en la aplicación de la ley del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) en las principales ciudades y los tiroteos fatales de Alex Pretti y Renee Good por agentes federales en Minnesota.</p><p>Martínez emitió un comunicado el martes diciendo que las afirmaciones de Noem sobre no conocer su caso vienen a ser “lo contrario a la evidencia que publicamos en mi caso”. Dijo que los mensajes de texto prueban que Exum contó con el apoyo de Noem después del tiroteo y quiere que Noem investigue a Exum “por su intento de ejecución”.</p><p>“Francamente, creo que es aún peor si la secretaria Noem no conoce los hechos de mi caso”, agregó Martínez. “Ella es la líder de DHS y uno de sus agentes intentó matarme, a una ciudadana estadounidense, en las calles de Chicago. Se informó en todos los medios nacionales durante meses. ¿No lee el periódico? ¿No le informan sobre los tiroteos de ciudadanos estadounidenses por agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza? Que la líder del DHS no sepa sobre el tiroteo de una ciudadana estadounidense, en nuestro propio país, por uno de sus agentes es más alarmante que la negativa de su agencia a investigar estas acciones ilegales”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-14d75d" name="image-14d75d"></a> <picture Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Fiscalía de los Estados Unidos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>El senador Dick Durbin también le preguntó a Noem sobre los asesinatos de Pretti y Good en Minneapolis, así como el tiroteo de Martínez en Chicago. En cada caso, DHS etiquetó a las víctimas como “terroristas domésticos”.</p><p>“Tenemos amplias pruebas en video y testimonios de testigos que demuestran que estás equivocada. Tus declaraciones causaron un dolor inconmensurable a estas familias”, le dijo Durbin a Noem. “Déjame darte la oportunidad de hacer lo correcto. ¿Retirarás estas declaraciones identificando a estos individuos como terroristas domésticos?”.</p><p>Noem calificó los tiroteos como “situaciones trágicas” y dijo que “siempre ofrecemos nuestras condolencias a esas familias”. La jefa del DHS afirmó que se estaba “basando en informes desde el terreno y de los agentes que están allí y trabajan para ser transparentes”.</p><p>Durbin le preguntó a Noem cómo el apodarles “terroristas domésticos en el lugar de los hechos iba a calmar la situación”.</p><p>“Estamos trabajando en esas situaciones donde hay una pérdida trágica de vida y en las que nuestros agentes están involucrados, de las que seguimos brindando información”, aseguró Noem.</p><p>“¿Es tan difícil decir que te equivocaste?”, interrumpió Durbin.</p><p>“... Me esfuerzo absolutamente por proporcionar información factual y continuaremos haciéndolo”, dijo Noem.</p><p>“Y cuando fallas, ¿lo admites públicamente?”, preguntó Durbin. Noem respondió, “Absolutamente. Siempre sabemos que hay espacio para mejorar”.</p><p>Noem también fue cuestionada repetidamente sobre el aliado de Trump y exasesor Steve Bannon, quien expresó su apoyo a la iniciativa de Trump de nacionalizar las elecciones, incluyendo el despliegue de funcionarios de ICE en los lugares de votación.</p><p>“No hay planes para tener oficiales de ICE en nuestros lugares de votación”, aseguró Noem.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" >La Voz Chicago</a></p>

target="_blank" >Noem says she doesn’t know about case of Chicago woman shot by Border Patrol</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-k/" target="_blank" >Tina Sfondeles</a></h5><p><b>Tuesday hearing</b>: Marimar Martinez, the Chicago woman who survived being shot five times by Border Patrol agents last year, stood just five rows behind U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem as she was pushed by U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal to acknowledge the shooting was "wrong" during a testy Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday.</p><p><b>What happened</b>: With Blumenthal describing the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-u/" target="_blank" >October shooting that left Martinez with nerve damage</a> to her right hand, the Connecticut Democrat asked Noem whether Martinez’s shooting was "wrong" and also highlighted — via large posters — images of text messages that showed Border Patrol agent <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-o/" target="_blank" >Charles Exum bragging about the shooting</a> and allegedly writing, "I fired 5 rounds and she had 7 holes. Put that in your book boys."</p><p><b>Noem's response</b>: Despite comprehensive coverage of Martinez’s shooting and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-b/" target="_blank" >charges of impeding law enforcement that were later dropped</a>, Noem repeatedly claimed she didn’t know about it. "Sir, I don’t know the situation or the case," Noem said. "I’ll look into it to ensure that all the procedures were followed properly." She also would not provide details on whether Exum, the agent who shot Martinez, is still on the job "carrying a gun."</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Noem’s testimony in Washington comes as DHS funding remains halted during a partial government shutdown — with Congress at an impasse over immigration policies. Despite the shutdown, senators largely focused on ICE enforcement in major cities and the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good by federal agents in Minnesota.</p><p><a class="Link" races to save the Midwest’s native seeds</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-x/" target="_blank" >Juanpablo Ramirez-Franco</a></h5><p><b>The need for seed</b>: As climate change intensifies wildfires and other extreme weather events, demand for native seeds is surging. In 2024, the Chicago Botanic Garden helped launch the Midwest Native Seed Network, a first step in improving the region’s fragile seed supply.</p><p><b>Program's growth</b>: The coalition now includes roughly 300 restoration ecologists, land managers and seed growers across 150 institutions in 11 states. Together, they are researching which species are most in demand, where they are likely to thrive, and what it will take to produce them at scale and get them in the ground.</p><p><b>The goal</b>: The collaborative is compiling information on seed collection, processing, germination and propagation while identifying regional research gaps and planning collaborative projects to address them. Ultimately, the goal is to connect people who need seeds with those who know how to grow them, the Chicago Botanic Garden said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-m/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>ARCHITECTURE AND DESIGN 📐</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-160000" name="image-160000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c005ab/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F75%2Fa2%2Fa7d408704c5dba875afe79478b88%2Fmetro-260225-20.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6c681ed/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F75%2Fa2%2Fa7d408704c5dba875afe79478b88%2Fmetro-260225-20.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1e01a0a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F75%2Fa2%2Fa7d408704c5dba875afe79478b88%2Fmetro-260225-20.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Metropolitan Missionary Baptist Church located at 2151 W. >Monday Night Foodball showcases city’s rising dining stars</a></h3><h3></h3><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-il/" target="_blank" >Jennifer Tanaka</a></h5><p>In late August 2021, the Delta variant of COVID-19 was kicking the pandemic into a terrifying new phase of unknowns. Here in Chicago, the city reinstated an indoor mask mandate for stores, restaurants, gyms and other places where humans gathered in public. Into this dismal scene, local food writer Mike Sula launched a tiny, hopeful project.</p><p>The idea was simple: Invite an up-and-coming chef to offer a special menu at a local bar for one night only, pop-up style.</p><p>"All these unknown restaurant workers — bartenders, servers, line cooks — that had been furloughed or laid off started cooking out of their apartments or out of a shared kitchen and doing preorder deliveries or drop-offs," Sula said. So he started writing about these interesting, emergent cooking projects for the Reader and, eventually, the two things merged.</p><p>On Aug. 23, 2021, chefs Jeanette Tran-Dean and David Hollinger brought their Vietnamese-Guatemalan mashup cuisine to Kedzie Inn, a since-shuttered dive bar in Irving Park, and Monday Night Foodball was born. <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-ir/" target="_blank" >Next Monday will mark Foodball’s 201st event</a>. Originally offered as a seven-week series, Foodball just kept rolling.</p><p>The economics of a Foodball are meant to boost everyone’s fortunes. Held on Mondays, when traffic can be so slow that many restaurants close anyway, the event brings in new business. Chefs pay for ingredients and labor and, correspondingly, take 100% of food sales. The host venue loans the use of its kitchen and space for free and pockets all beverage sales, including any special menu of drinks it creates.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjhykkd-l-iy/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's the best Chicago-themed gift you've ever received — or given? title: DHS head Noem claims she doesn't know about Marimar Martinez, Chicago woman shot 5 times by federal agent
summary: <p>Marimar Martinez, the Chicago woman who survived being shot five times by Border Patrol agents last year, stood just five rows behind Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem as she was pushed by U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal to acknowledge the shooting was "wrong" during a testy Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday.</p><p>With Blumenthal describing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >October shooting that left Martinez with nerve damage</a> to her right hand, the Connecticut Democrat asked Noem whether Martinez's shooting was "wrong" and also highlighted — via large posters — images of text messages which showed Border Patrol agent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/10/marimar-martinez-the-chicago-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-expected-to-file-lawsuit-release-evidence" target="_blank" >Charles Exum bragging about the shooting</a> and allegedly writing, “I fired 5 rounds and she had 7 holes. Put that in your book boys.” </p><p>Despite comprehensive coverage of Martinez's shooting and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >charges of impeding law enforcement that were later dropped</a> against her, Noem repeatedly claimed she didn't know about the case.</p><p>"Sir, I don't know the situation or the case," Noem said. "I'll look into it to ensure that all the procedures were followed properly."</p><p>Noem also would not provide details on whether Exum, the agent who shot Martinez, is still on the job, "carrying a gun." A U.S. Customs and Border Protection spokesperson last month told the Chicago Sun-Times Exum <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/11/evidence-shows-feds-lied-about-marimar-martinezs-shooting-in-chicago-attorney-says" target="_blank" >“was placed on administrative leave.”</a> The spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up email asking when the leave began, or if it’s still in effect. Noem said she didn't know the details, but "will find out and get that information to you." </p><p>"I think Americans would find it absolutely terrifying that that agent is still on the job, carrying a gun," Blumenthal said. "And the fact that you can't tell me that you will take him off."</p><p>Noem's testimony in Washington before Congress comes as DHS funding remains halted during a partial government shutdown — with Congress at an impasse over immigration policies. Despite the shutdown, senators largely focused on ICE enforcement in major cities and the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good by federal agents in Minnesota. </p><p>Martinez released a statement Tuesday saying Noem's claims of not knowing her case comes as "the evidence we released in my case demonstrates otherwise." She said the text messages prove Exum had Noem's support after the shooting — and she wants Noem to investigate Exum "for his attempted execution." </p><p>"Frankly, I think it is even worse if Secretary Noem does not know about the facts of my case," Martinez said. "She is the leader of DHS and one of her agents attempted to kill me, a U.S. citizen on the streets of Chicago. It was reported in every national news outlet for months. Does she not read the newspaper? Is she not briefed on shootings of U.S. citizens by border patrol agents? For the leader of DHS to not know about the shooting of a U.S. citizen, in our own country, by one of her agents is more alarming than her agency's refusal to investigate these unlawful actions." Dick Durbin also asked Noem about the killings of Pretti and Good in Minneapolis, as well as Martinez's shooting in Chicago. In each case, DHS labeled the victims "domestic terrorists."</p><p>"We have ample video evidence and eyewitness testimony proving you are wrong. Your statements caused immeasurable pain to these families," Durbin told Noem. "Let me give you an opportunity to do the right thing. Do you retract these statements identifying these individuals domestic terrorists?"</p><p>Noem called the shootings "tragic situations" and said "we always offer our condolences to those families." The DHS head said she was "relying on reports from the ground and from agents that are there and working to be transparent." </p><p>Durbin asked Noem how dubbing them "domestic terrorists at the scene was somehow going to calm the situation."</p><p>"We are working in those situations where there's a tragic loss of life and that there is something that our agents are involved in, that we continue to deliver information," Noem said. </p><p>"Is it so hard to say you were wrong?" Durbin interjected.</p><p>"...I absolutely strive to provide factual information and we'll continue to do that," Noem said. </p><p>"And when you fail, do you admit it publicly?" Durbin asked. Noem replied, "Absolutely. We always know that there's room for improvement." </p><p>Noem was also repeatedly asked about Trump ally and former adviser Steve Bannon voicing support for Trump's push to nationalize elections, including deploying ICE officials to polling sites. </p><p>"There are no plans to have ICE officers at our polling locations," Noem said. </p>

title: Juez ordena liberar a 32 detenidos del centro de detención de Broadview, pero algunos ya han sido deportados
summary: <p>Un juez federal ordenó el viernes la liberación de 32 personas arrestadas durante el Operativo Midway Blitz debido a violaciones de un decreto de consentimiento de mucho tiempo, incluyendo a dos personas atrapadas en la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/10/02/gran-redada-de-inmigracion-en-edificio-de-apartamentos-de-chicago-deja-a-residentes-aturdidos" target="_blank" >redada de estilo militar</a> en un complejo de apartamentos de South Shore el otoño pasado.</p><p>Sin embargo, muchas de las 32 personas ya han sido liberadas o deportadas. De todos modos, el juez del distrito Jeffrey Cummings dijo que quiere que el gobierno federal libere a las personas que aún están bajo su custodia antes del mediodía del jueves. Se ofreció a permitir que los funcionarios federales argumenten por una extensión de tiempo “razonable”, si es necesario.</p><p>También les dijo,“no hay necesidad de mantenerlos hasta el 5 de marzo si pueden ser liberados más rápidamente”. El juez dijo que sigue considerando cómo fallar en los casos de cinco personas adicionales, lo que significa que su orden escrita final podría aplicarse a hasta 37 individuos. Dio el fallo desde el banquillo el viernes durante una audiencia en la Corte Federal Dirksen.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-470000" name="module-470000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Cummings dijo que las personas deberían ser liberadas “bajo su propia responsabilidad, sin condiciones y sin fianza”. Consideró las circunstancias de aproximadamente 50 personas, siguiendo la orientación y las restricciones recientes emitidas por un tribunal de apelaciones federal.</p><p>El juez encontró que muchas de las personas ahora programadas para ser liberadas fueron arrestadas sin una orden, y que los agentes carecían de causa probable para creer que se escaparían.</p><div class="Enhancement"
