title: Pro-Israel group's interest in Chicago-area Democratic congressional fights puts candidates on the defensive
summary: <p>When the American Israel Public Affairs Committee reached out to Democratic congressional candidate Jeff Cohen in November, he was open to talking about the group’s potential support in his run for retiring U.S. Rep. Jan Schakowsky’s seat.</p><p>Cohen, an economist from Evanston, says he staunchly supports the U.S.-Israel alliance and was interested in hearing from the group that has championed that cause for decades. At the same time, he does not believe U.S. military aid to Israel should be a blank check.</p><p>The meeting was at a coffee shop and lasted an hour. Cohen says he expressed support for Israel but “probably sounded like someone who was going to take a very hard look” at the country’s “behavior” in Gaza.</p><p>Cohen never heard back from AIPAC. Then he noticed a deluge of donations from around the country for another candidate — a state senator who had not called for stricter conditions on aid to Israel.</p><p>Cohen is among several Democrats in four wide-open Chicago-area congressional primaries to have met with AIPAC and learned the group has drawn a hard line on one thing: unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel. The topic has become a flashpoint for candidates and voters as more Democrats call for improving human rights in Gaza.</p><p>AIPAC donors and affiliates have spent more than $10.6 million on the group’s preferred candidates in the four races, a WBEZ analysis of federal campaign disclosures found. Those candidates, meantime, have evaded most questions, or favored Israel, in a WBEZ survey about U.S. support for Israel and the war in Gaza.</p><p>WBEZ surveyed the 46 candidates in the Chicago area’s four hard-fought Democratic congressional primaries about whether there should be strict U.S. conditions on military aid to Israel, whether that country has committed genocide in Gaza, and whether AIPAC funding should be off-limits in these races.</p><p>Most of the respondents said yes to those questions, but the four AIPAC-aligned candidates would not answer yes or no.<b> </b></p><p>Big campaign spending isn’t new for AIPAC, which has been around for 72 years. But the group is operating more covertly than ever, Democratic strategists say. AIPAC is working through newly formed political action committees that are hard to trace and that bankroll campaign mailers, phone calls and TV commercials. So far, that publicity hasn’t mentioned the Middle East, focusing instead on things like immigration and affordability.</p><p>AIPAC has not responded to WBEZ questions about its candidate selection criteria or Chicago-area tactics.</p><p>“They’re trying to influence these elections … by invoking other issues that have nothing to do with Israel,” says veteran political consultant David Axelrod, who was chief strategist and senior advisor to President Barack Obama.</p><p>“This isn’t unusual in American politics,” he adds. “But given the volatility of issues involving Israel now, it’s conspicuous in this case that they’re working so hard to submerge their own participation.”</p><h3>Secretive spending</h3><p>The AIPAC-linked candidates — all Democrats — include Cook County Commissioner Donna Miller in the 2nd District, Chicago City Treasurer Melissa Conyears-Ervin in the 7th, former U.S. Rep. Melissa Bean in the 8th and state Sen. Laura Fine in the 9th.</p><p>AIPAC is supporting them in two main ways. The first is steering AIPAC donors to the candidates through online fundraisers, in-person events and email solicitations.</p><p>In all, 1,726 donors to AIPAC or its main super PAC had contributed to at least one of the four candidates by the start of the year, according to the WBEZ analysis. Of those donors, 1,524 (88.3%) lived outside Illinois and nearly a third contributed to more than one of the candidates. The AIPAC-linked donations totaled nearly $2.9 million.</p><p>Candidates receiving those donations have depicted the link to AIPAC as a coincidence.</p><p>The second way AIPAC has propelled the Chicago-area candidates is through super PACs, which cannot donate directly to candidates or coordinate with them but can raise and spend unlimited sums on their behalf.</p><p>AIPAC-tied super PACs have spent more than $7.7 million on TV ads, phone outreach and mailers for the four candidates, according to federal filings.</p><p>AIPAC, a national lobbying organization with more than 6 million members, tries to ensure U.S. policies and public perception favor Israel. The group spends big on Republican and Democratic candidates alike and aggressively targets Israel critics.</p><p>But AIPAC over the years has fallen out of favor with some Democrats and Jewish progressives who have recoiled from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s tactics in Gaza and from AIPAC’s backing of Republicans who <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/mar/23/aipac-pro-israel-group-backs-insurrectionist-republicans" target="_blank" ><u>voted to overturn</u></a> the 2020 presidential election.</p><p>Illinois’ two-term Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, believes AIPAC has “abandoned their principles.” Pritzker, the state’s third Jewish governor, was a driving force behind construction of the Illinois Holocaust Museum.</p><p>“Just because they donate to certain Democrats doesn’t change the fact that they are heeding the words and direction of Jared Kushner and other Trump acolytes,” Pritzker campaign spokesman Alex Gough said in a statement.</p><p>Pritzker is not alone with that sentiment.</p><p>“There’s no question they’re right-wing,” says Steve Sheffey, who writes the Jewish newsletter The Fine Print and was an AIPAC member for 25 years. “They wouldn’t think of themselves as that, but they are right-wing on the issue that they advocate for, and also right-wing in who they support.”</p><p>Axelrod says that reputation has pushed AIPAC to operate “under the cloak of darkness.”</p><p>“Younger Jews who aren’t as steeped in [Israeli] history may have been horrified by what happened on Oct. 7 but then were horrified by what followed,” Axelrod says.</p><p>Hamas killed more than 1,200 people during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack in Israel, according to Israeli officials. More than 72,000 Palestinians have been killed since, according to Gaza health officials. Some died during a food shortage that a U.N. panel declared was a famine. A slew of human rights groups have concluded Israel has committed genocide in Gaza — a finding that Israel denies.</p><p>AIPAC has shown interest in Chicago-area Democratic congressional primaries that seem to be wide open after the retirement of longtime incumbents.</p><p>“With these four districts, where it can be anybody’s game, they’re heavily invested,” says Nick Sous, an organizer with the U.S. Palestinian Community Network, which is critical of AIPAC.</p><p>AIPAC has a chance in three of the races to replace incumbents increasingly critical of weapons sales to Israel.</p><p>Rep. Robin Kelly, who is stepping down to run for retiring U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin’s seat, and retiring Reps. Danny Davis and Schakowsky signed onto the “Block the Bombs” bill last year. The measure would place more stringent human rights conditions on the sale of certain weapons — like bunker-busting bombs that can tear through concrete.</p><p>“They’re trying to force a power shift,” says Sous, whose group has pushed Illinois politicians to sign onto the bill.</p><h3>Shell PACs</h3><p>Newly formed super PACs with ties to AIPAC cropped up in January, joining the United Democracy Project, which has been active for four years and is throwing its weight behind Conyears-Ervin in the race for the 7th District, which stretches from the western suburbs to some Downtown and South Side areas.</p><p>The websites of <a class="Link" href="https://affordablechicagonow.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Affordable Chicago Now</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://electchicagowomen.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Elect Chicago Women</u></a> include no information about Bean, Fine or Miller and no mention of Israel.</p><p>The committees’ ties to AIPAC and UDP aren’t obvious. But a WBEZ review of federal and state disclosures found the groups identifying shared registered agents and vendors</p><p>Their TV commercials and mailers have contained no reference to Israel. They have focused on domestic issues such as health care and immigration enforcement.</p><p>Neither ACN nor ECW responded to WBEZ questions on why the groups have poured millions of dollars into Fine, Miller and Beans’ candidacies.</p><p>In the 2nd Congressional District, which covers part of the South Side and some nearby suburbs and rural areas, Miller is among 11 Democratic candidates vying to replace Kelly.</p><p>In addition to nearly $1.5 million in super PAC spending, Miller has received a huge amount directly from AIPAC donors. They accounted for more than 72% of her $1.3 million in total receipts at the start of the year, according to the WBEZ analysis.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-100000" name="html-embed-module-100000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27812440"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27812440/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>At least 578, or 65%, of her individual donors had contributed to AIPAC or UDP, the analysis shows. Of those, 515 (89%) lived outside Illinois. Since 2021, those donors and their immediate family members had given more than $28.5 million to the two PACs.</p><p>Still, Miller leans into a technical truth: “AIPAC has not given me any campaign contributions,” she told WBEZ.</p><p>At a forum this month, Miller said she had received funds from a “broad base.”</p><p>“I don’t think that money coming into your campaign decides how you’re going to legislate, how you’re going to effectuate change in your district,” Miller said.</p><p>Miller’s campaign this week circulated a letter from Jewish leaders, including U.S. Rep. Brad Schneider and Chicago Ald. Debra Silverstein, that paints AIPAC’s role in the race as “Jewish engagement” and warns that criticizing the engagement “risks reinforcing harmful narratives at a time when antisemitism is rising.”</p><p>But Miller’s AIPAC support led to her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/02/19/rep-jan-schakowsky-withdrawal-donna-miller-endorsement-2nd-congressional-district-aipac-support" target="_blank" ><u>losing Schakowsky’s endorsement</u></a> this month. The longtime congresswoman, who is Jewish, said Illinois “deserves leaders who put voters first, not AIPAC.”</p><h3>Ground skirmishes</h3><p>AIPAC’s role is drawing fire from progressive candidates, especially in the 9th Congressional District, which stretches from the North Side to several northern and northwestern suburbs. The district is home to many Israelis and Palestinians, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, which doesn’t track religion.</p><p>In that primary, federal campaign finance records show, Elect Chicago Women has shelled out $1.4 million for Fine, the state senator.</p><p>Fine has also landed huge sums of AIPAC-tied cash. At least 987, or 67%, of her individual donors by the start of this year had contributed to AIPAC or UDP, the WBEZ analysis shows. Of those, 851 (86%) lived outside Illinois. The AIPAC-linked donors accounted for 73% of her $1.9 million in total receipts. Since 2021, the donors and their immediate family members have given more than $46 million to those pro-Israel committees.</p><p>This has become an issue for Fine in recent weeks. At a <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/DanielBiss/status/2024672880714301700?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>forum</u></a>, candidates were handed signs with “yes” on one side and “no” on the other and asked a series of single-answer questions. When the moderator queried the group about whether they accepted money from AIPAC or its supporters, Fine was the only candidate among six on-stage to hold up a “yes” sign.</p><p>Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss posted video of the moment on his X account and drew nearly 22,000 views.</p><p>“She supports a blank check of military aid for Israel,” said Biss, who is Jewish and frequently talks up his ties to Israel but increasingly criticizes its actions. “That is a right-wing policy that is bad for Palestinians, Jews, Israelis, America and the world.”</p><p>Fine, also Jewish, hit back, saying Biss himself took AIPAC-connected money in 2024.</p><p>Elect Chicago Women last weekend unveiled its first negative TV ad against Biss, accusing him of “saying anything to get elected.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-810000" name="html-embed-module-810000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27815367"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27815367/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>In the 8th Congressional District, which covers some western and northwestern suburbs, Bean is among candidates hoping to replace Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who is running for Durbin’s Senate seat. She has benefited from $2.6 million in AIPAC-linked super PAC spending and, by the start of the year, her campaign had received more than a half-million dollars from AIPAC donors.</p><p>At least 314, or 57%, of Bean’s individual donors have also contributed to AIPAC or UDP since 2021, the WBEZ analysis shows. Of those, 272 (87%) lived outside Illinois. Those donors accounted for more than 39% of her $1.3 million in total receipts by the start of the year.</p><p>At a news conference focused on AIPAC spending, Bean rival Junaid Ahmed accused her of selling her candidacy.</p><p>“Melissa Bean will take their millions and then rubber stamp billions in unchecked military aid to Israel. Melissa Bean will look the other way as Israel commits a genocide,” said Ahmed, a director at a cloud computing firm.</p><p>In response to WBEZ’s survey, Bean declined to provide yes-or-no answers but added, “I support a two-state solution in the Middle East that allows both Israelis and Palestinians to live in peace, safety and dignity.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-f50000" name="html-embed-module-f50000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27815247"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27815247/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>AIPAC has also been accused of parachuting into majority-Black areas where, candidates say, U.S.-Israel relations are not a top concern.</p><p>“They’re not investing in our schools. They’re not supporting the marginalized," said Anthony Driver, who is running to replace Davis. “The 7th District is not for sale. My community is not for sale.”</p><p>Peters, a 2nd District candidate, stood with Driver at the AIPAC-focused news conference.</p><p>“I’m Black and Jewish and … AIPAC is not my friend,” Petershe said. “[I]t gets conflated that AIPAC is about Jewish safety. I want to dissuade that. It is about Israel. Jewish safety comes through solidarity.”</p><h3>Choosing favorites</h3><p>A whopping 46 Democrats are running across the four congressional primaries. Most respondents to the WBEZ survey showed support for Palestinian rights.</p><p>More than two-thirds of respondents answered they would denounce AIPAC funding if offered. Two-thirds said they support strict human rights conditions on aid to Israel. More than half said they believe Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.</p><p>The four AIPAC-linked candidates were among a minority of respondents who declined to provide yes-or-no answers to a majority of questions. Conyears-Ervin did answer one question with a straightforward answer, saying she would not oppose sending U.S. military aid to Israel today.</p><p>Some primary contenders say AIPAC has a litmus test for choosing whom to back: Does the candidate support unconditional U.S. aid to Israel?</p><p>A “no” answer is disqualifying, according to candidates in the 2nd, 8th and 9th districts who took meetings with either AIPAC or the United Democracy Project, the group’s super PAC.</p><p>State Rep. La Shawn Ford, D-Chicago, another candidate running to replace Davis, met with AIPAC late last year at a community graduation in his district. The AIPAC representative stressed the effect of Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack in southern Israel, telling Ford, “You have to remember that date,” the candidate recalled.</p><p>Ford’s impression was that AIPAC would support candidates only if they oppose the “Block the Bombs” bill.</p><p>The AIPAC contact, whom Ford would not identify, eventually called him with news that the group would instead support Conyears-Ervin “and that they’re going to come out hard for her,” Ford recalled.</p><p>AIPAC’s spending has been most transparent in that race, where it is supporting Conyears-Ervin to the tune of $1.5 million through the UDP, whose donors through December have been disclosed. AIPAC’s role in that district, the 7th, has also evolved. At first, its donors were showering hundreds of thousands of dollars on River North developer Jason Friedman.</p><p>In a message to WBEZ, Conyears-Ervin responded to accusations that AIPAC’s support would influence her voting in Congress: “The idea that a Black woman’s vote is for sale is insulting and racist.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-900000" name="html-embed-module-900000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27813578"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27813578/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>State Sen. Willie Preston, D-Chicago, running to replace Kelly in the 2nd, also spoke with AIPAC but says it seemed the group sought “100% control.”</p><p>“The problem with AIPAC is that they are looking for slaves,” says Preston, chair of the Illinois Senate Black Caucus.</p><p>Neither AIPAC nor UDP responded to requests for comment about the alleged litmus test, but UDP spokesperson Patrick Dorton described it to the Jewish Telegraph this month.</p><p>“We are going to have a focus on stopping candidates who are detractors of Israel or who want to put conditions on aid,” Dorton said.</p>
author: Mawa Iqbal | WBEZ

title: ICE protesters keep beating Trump in Chicago court, but the battles take a toll. 'It’s about intimidation'
summary: <p>Photographs of Ray Collins and Jocelyne Robledo in federal custody are just a Google search away, as easy to find as the social media posts calling them<b> </b>“armed rioters” and “deranged individuals."</p><p>Authorities arrested the Englewood couple five months ago outside of an immigration processing center<b> </b>in Broadview, just weeks after President Donald Trump launched a pummeling deportation campaign across the Chicago area last September.</p><p>Their assault cases quickly fell apart when a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/08/feds-dropping-charges-against-couple-who-lawfully-carried-guns-outside-ice-facility" target="_blank" >grand jury refused to indict</a>. Collins still found himself being called “everything from a thug to a predator.” And he now has a warning for potential employers who might try to look him up: “I was arrested for a felony.”</p><p>“It’s almost embarrassing,” he told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>But he’s resilient.</p><p>“I know myself and my character, that those things would never stick,” Collins said. “They can’t tarnish what I’ve done in my community. They can’t tarnish who I am as a person.”</p><p>Collins and Robledo are among a growing number of protesters who have been left to pick up the pieces after taking on the Trump administration in court — and winning.</p><p>Prosecutions for nonimmigration crimes tied to Operation Midway Blitz have disintegrated at an alarming rate at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse since October. Cases against 17<b> </b>of 32 known defendants <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >have already collapsed</a>, including the ones against Collins and Robledo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8d2e831/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2Ff3%2F78dc2ce04265a3e22c5276e8b7f7%2Fbroadview-092825-0096.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8eb54c5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fde%2Ff3%2F78dc2ce04265a3e22c5276e8b7f7%2Fbroadview-092825-0096.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection man the gate at the Broadview processing facility on Sept. 27, 2025, the day Ray Collins and Jocelyne Robledo were arrested.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But they still come at a cost. A federal prosecution is intimidating. It carries the threat of prison time. Damaging news stories spread online. Freedoms are often restricted, even in minor cases. Lawyers are needed, though federal defenders have saved people from big legal bills.</p><p>Then there’s jail.</p><p>The 17 cleared defendants spent a combined 150 days in federal custody, records show. That doesn’t include 35 days, and counting, that Juan Espinoza Martinez has been held by immigration authorities <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" target="_blank" >since he was acquitted</a> for allegedly placing a hit on Gregory Bovino, the Border Patrol official who became the face of the deportation operation.</p><p>That’s to say nothing of the flesh-and-blood cost borne by Marimar Martinez, the woman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >shot five times by a Border Patrol agent</a> on the Southwest Side in early October.</p><p>The stakes aren’t so high in every case. Jackie Guataquira, whose four-month old misdemeanor case was recently dropped, said she never spent a night in jail and didn’t have to physically appear in court. But the prosecution kept her from visiting family in Mexico, Guataquira said.</p><p>It just shows “they want to come for people at every single level,” she told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“They’re really just trying to take people’s lives away, deport them out of this country, or at the … more minor level, paint people who are righteously protesting and standing up to this as ‘terrorists,’” she said. “They’re slapping these people’s photos all over social media for this, just to get people away from being able to protest.”</p><h3>‘Your life gets turned upside down’</h3><p>Federal prosecutors are expected to bring charges only when they can prove them to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt. Normally, they boast <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/06/14/fewer-than-1-of-defendants-in-federal-criminal-cases-were-acquitted-in-2022/#:~:text=This%20analysis%20is%20based%20on,Office%20of%20the%20U.S.%20Courts" target="_blank" >a conviction rate of around 90%</a>. But Trump’s Justice Department has suffered a string of high-profile losses tied to its national immigration campaign, including in a recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-02-06/federal-public-defenders-winning" target="_blank" >six-case losing streak</a> in Los Angeles.</p><p>In Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/30/andrew-boutros-interim-us-attorney-chicago-judges-role-pam-bondi" target="_blank" >U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’</a> office is looking at a best-case conviction rate of around 47% in such cases. That’s assuming it secures a conviction against each of the remaining 15 defendants, and no additional charges are brought.</p><p>Boutros said many of the cases were brought as a result of “reactive arrests” in the field. Some of them were better suited for state court, he said. Others were dropped out of concern that jurors would reject charges even when they’re proven, or for mitigating factors like mental health.</p><p>“Our grace should not be confused as a reflection of the strength of any particular case or whether a charge should have been filed,” Boutros said in a statement. “It is a testament to our view that the role of the prosecutor is to seek justice and not just convict.</p><p>“We decide cases based on facts, law, and equities without regard to the attitude of sneering disbelief held by a certain group of critics.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6e0000" name="html-embed-module-6e0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-table" data-src="visualisation/27349648"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27349648/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="table visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Attorney General Pam Bondi <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/28/former-prosecutor-andrew-boutros-named-chicagos-interim-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" >initially appointed Boutros</a> to his job on a temporary basis in early 2025. Chicago’s U.S. District Court judges then <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/07/25/chicagos-federal-judges-choose-andrew-boutros-as-top-prosecutor" target="_blank" >picked him to serve</a> on a more permanent basis once Bondi’s appointment expired.</p><p>Laurie Levenson, a professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said there are “enormous consequences” when someone is charged with a federal crime. That’s true even if the prosecution is abandoned, Levenson said.</p><p>“Your life gets turned upside down when you’re charged with a federal case,” Levenson said.</p><p>But<b> </b>the greater cost, she said, is to “the credibility of the justice system.”</p><h3>Charges dropped — but damage is done </h3><p>Authorities arrested Collins, 32, and Robledo, 30, on Sept. 27 outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview, which became a hub for fierce protests.</p><p>Three days earlier, a shooter opened fire on an ICE facility<b> </b>in Dallas. Emotions ran high. Without naming the couple, Bovino referred to Collins and Robledo online as “two deranged individuals, armed with pistols.” Users on X shared <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/CMDROpAtLargeCA/status/1972684789028171930" target="_blank" >his social media post</a> 278 times.</p><p>“Don’t find out the hard way,” Bovino wrote.</p><p>Collins and Robledo never faced any charges related to the guns,<b> </b>which they were lawfully carrying and never brandished.</p><p>Instead, a criminal complaint alleged that Robledo ignored commands and pushed back when law enforcement told people to move.</p><p>Once officers began to struggle with Robledo, Collins allegedly yelled at them to get away and charged toward them. The feds said Collins resisted agents — and injured one agent’s thumb. Collins told the Sun-Times he "did not start"<b> </b>the altercation and "did not assault anyone."</p><p>Prosecutors later sought to have the couple detained. U.S. Magistrate Judge Gabriel Fuentes ruled that Robledo didn’t qualify<b> </b>for detention. Collins did, because of the agent’s injury, and Collins’ attorney insisted on an immediate hearing.</p><p>The judge ordered Collins detained. He questioned Collins’ judgment in bringing a gun to an ICE protest, “particularly given ICE’s recent history of aggressive enforcement tactics while heavily armed.”</p><p>Robledo said Collins, who is Black, was seemingly held in jail longer “simply because of the color of his skin.”<b> </b>Collins said he suspects the judge “subconsciously” assumed “I carried and I was a dangerous individual because of my presentation in court, my looks, and the area that I’m from.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ADy5XJc9b-Y?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="This Chicago couple fought charges brought by the Trump administration — and won"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>In his written order, Fuentes said the defense request for an immediate hearing left him without a report that might have addressed Collins’ employment and lack of criminal history, as well as his personal background. The decision “was an extremely close call,” the judge wrote.</p><p>Fuentes predicted that a reviewing judge could take advantage of “a more fulsome record.”</p><p>Three days later, U.S. District Judge Sunil Harjani<b> </b>ordered Collins’ release with that additional information in hand.</p><p>Then, on Oct. 8, the feds dropped the charges. A grand jury had refused to indict, in a rare rebuke of federal prosecutors.</p><p>The time spent in jail was “nerve-wracking,” Collins said.</p><p>“Not because I was scared that I was in federal prison,” he explained. “But just the stress of knowing that I can’t take care of my pets, my family. That the justice system does not work even when you haven’t done anything wrong.”</p><p>Robledo has been hesitant to join protests in Broadview ever since. As someone who has been involved in demonstrations since the age of 13, Robledo said that’s “life changing”<b> </b>— but insisted it’s not “life ruining.”</p><p>“It makes it harder for you to do anything,” Robledo said of the prosecution. “That’s the point, right?</p><p>“But I decided a long time ago that that wasn’t going to happen to me.”</p><p>Fuentes has since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/unusual-and-possibly-unprecedented-judge-calls-out-chicago-feds-as-midway-blitz-cases-fall-apart" target="_blank" >questioned some of the charges</a> brought amid Operation Midway Blitz, including against Collins and Robledo. He did so in an opinion<b> </b>issued in late November, after a series of cases before him<b> </b>fell apart.</p><p>The judge wrote that he’d “obtained sworn confirmation that video backed up”<b> </b>the feds’ claims against Collins and Robledo. Still, he wrote, “the grand jury refused to find probable cause.”</p><p>“That is a sobering event for a magistrate judge,” Fuentes wrote.</p><p>He added: “Any responsible federal prosecutor knows that federal charges, or any actions by the United States attorney directed at the citizenry, must be undertaken with the utmost care.”</p><h3>‘Levels of repression’</h3><p>Martinez has become the most prominent of the 17 cleared Midway Blitz defendants in Chicago. She testified recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-goes-to-washington-wants-trump-officials-to-admit-not-a-domestic-terrorist" target="_blank" >before Democratic members of Congress</a>. She also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/05/marimar-martinez-shot-5-times-by-border-patrol-in-chicago-plans-to-attend-trumps-state-of-the-union" target="_blank" >attended Trump’s State of the Union</a> address Tuesday as a guest of U.S. Rep. Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, an Illinois Democrat.</p><p>But in early October, she found herself recovering from her bullet wounds for one night in the Metropolitan Correctional Center. The 30-year-old Montessori school teacher’s assistant said it was “everything you see in the movies.”</p><p>She said she learned not to trust anyone there,<b> </b>including the guards.</p><p>“I remember, I used to hear the inmates above banging, making beats on the walls,” Martinez said in a recent interview. “It was surreal.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Then, on Nov. 20, federal prosecutors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >abruptly dropped the charges</a> against her and another man, Anthony Ian Santos Ruiz.</p><p>Homeland Security officials labeled Martinez a “domestic terrorist” and have refused to rescind the claim, even though a social media post about Collins and Robledo seems to have disappeared.</p><p>ICE officials did not respond to a request for comment about Collins and Robledo.</p><p>Only one Midway Blitz case <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/21/bovino-murder-for-hire-trial-moving-fast-at-federal-courthouse-where-itll-soon-be-in-jurors-hands" target="_blank" >has gone to trial</a>, so far. The feds accused Espinoza Martinez, 37, of offering $10,000 for Bovino’s murder. Espinoza Martinez spent 109 days in jail — far more than any other Midway Blitz defendant who's been cleared.</p><p>His prosecution revolved around a Snapchat message he sent to an acquaintance<b> </b>that purportedly offered $2,000 for Bovino’s capture and $10,000 for his head. title: Caught in the middle: More than 500 students to be displaced by CPS shutdown of Aspira schools
summary: <p>Arichely Medina should be spending the last months of high school making sure she has enough financial aid and scholarships to pay for college and preparing for prom and all the other exciting activities that come with graduation.</p><p>Instead she is preparing to transfer to a new high school, just a few months before graduation. Arichely is one of about 545 students who attend two high schools run by the financially-distressed Aspira Charter School Network. More than 90% of students at the two schools are Latino, more than two-thirds are low income and more than half are English Language Learners.</p><p>After months of back-and-forth, Chicago Public Schools officials are telling students that the network does not have the money to make it through the school year and that they should transfer before the start of the last quarter “to safeguard their education stability." While there’s debate about whether it is CPS’ fault or Aspira’s, such a mid-year school closing is virtually unheard of.</p><p>Arichely, like other students, has a long list of concerns and questions about credits, grades, senior events and graduation. But she also has a more emotional worry. She lives far from her current school, Aspira Business and Finance Academy in Avondale, and, if she’s sent to her neighborhood school, she doesn’t think many of her friends will go there.</p><p>She describes herself as shy and wonders what it will be like to walk into a new school three-quarters of the way into the year.</p><p>“I think my biggest issue is that I'm going to have to reintroduce myself to people that I don't know,” she said. “Now I'm gonna be all alone, and I'm not gonna have the people that I'm used to having.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Milwaukee Ave., in Chicago’s Avondale neighborhood.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>CPS points to missing audit</b></p><p>News broke Thursday that CPS officials were making the call to transition students out of the two Northwest Side high schools run by Aspira Charter School Network. At the Chicago Board of Education meeting Thursday, CPS officials addressed the students before explaining their decision.</p><p>“This is not the outcome that anyone hoped for,” said Zabrina Evans, CPS executive director of Innovation and Incubation. “We understand the stress and difficulty of today's news. We understand the uncertainty and disruption that comes with changing schools in the middle of the current school year.” </p><p>Evans then explained that getting to this point has been “long and complicated,” but that essentially Aspira, like all charter organizations, agreed to operate a school with the money provided by CPS and that Aspira has not been able to do that.</p><p>“CPS provides funding and support, and charter operators deliver educational services to students,” she said. Not only has Aspira been unable to prove to the district that it can provide those educational services through June, but the charter operator has failed to turn over an audit and other required financial documents, she said.</p><p>She also noted that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/25/cps-to-help-aspira-make-payroll-but-charter-operators-financial-woes-remain" target="_blank" ><u>CPS has given Aspira $2.25 million in cash advances</u></a> and yet the network still says it needs millions more to pay teachers and staff.</p><p>CPS is “moving forward with this student transition process… due to the dire situation created by the failure of Aspira to demonstrate financial stability, which places the education of Aspira students at risk,” she said.</p><p>Up until Wednesday night, Aspira Chief Executive Director Edgar Lopez seemed hopeful that he could save the schools. He told CPS that he was meeting with a bank to get a bridge loan and looking at fundraising, even a crowdfunding campaign.</p><p>But speaking at the board meeting, Lopez blamed CPS for the charter schools’ financial problems. He said charters get 83% of what district-run CPS schools receive, though school district officials refute that figure.</p><p>“I feel like charters are stepchildren to CPS,” he said. “Our families pay taxes just like all the rest of the families pay taxes. ”</p><p>Lopez has also accused CPS of undermining charter schools through its high school application process by prioritizing sending students to district-run schools. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Aspira’s executive director, Edgar Lopez, spoke with students at Aspira Business & Finance High School on Wednesday. Lopez says the charter network’s financial troubles stem from chronic underfunding by Chicago Public Schools. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Charter schools’ budgets are closely tied to student enrollment and, with an overall <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/09/25/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-restarts-decrease-migrant-students-latino-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>decline in the CPS student population</u></a>, charters are having trouble filling their seats. This year Aspira’s high schools started out with less than 600 students, some 200 less than five years ago. Charter school operators also cite other issues that have added to their financial troubles, including rising labor costs.</p><p>Lopez told the board no “irregularities” will be found in Aspira’s finances and that it has had clean audits, but the one for last year is not yet complete.</p><p>He pleaded with the board to keep the school intact, even if they remove Aspira management, at least until the end of the school year.</p><p>“If this is for the kids, then worry about the kids,” he said.</p><h3><b>‘We should be celebrating our future’</b></h3><p>Arichely and dozens of other students and teachers attended Thursday’s meeting. Some of them assigned blame to Aspira and Lopez, while others said CPS is responsible and should do more.</p><p>But more than anything, they lamented the fact that they were caught in the middle.</p><p>Brian Walsh, who teaches math at the Business and Finance Academy, cited a study that showed students are more likely to drop out of school, face violence and suffer from depression after a mid-year school closing.</p><p>He said teachers like him will figure out how to make it through, but they are worried about the students.</p><p>“We need assurances that the students will be looked after and they will face as little fracture as possible,” he said. “CPS needs to give them the dignity of an actionable plan that does not repeat history. This is your responsibility, unless you are resigned to make them another statistic.” </p><p>Students expressed frustration, but they also wanted to know what was going to happen next.</p><p>Senior Lavelle Turner said he was looking forward to his last season playing on the Aspira baseball team and getting ready to take tests to see if he could get college credit for advanced placement classes. He wanted to know whether he would even be able to play baseball and complete his AP classes. </p><p>“We should not have to pay and sacrifice our future,” he said. “We should be celebrating our future.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d80000" name="image-d80000"></a> <picture But now she is wondering if she will graduate on time and whether the transition will affect her ability to get scholarships.</p><p>“How would a teacher that doesn't really know who we are write a recommendation letter,” she said. </p><p>Arichely and other seniors said they were dismayed by the idea that they won’t get to go to senior luncheon, Six Flags and prom with each other.</p><p>Arichely said she’s built a large group of friends and she looked forward to having fun with them, but if they aren’t at these events, she won’t go. </p><p>“I think I'd feel a bit left out because I don't know anyone, and then I wouldn't feel comfortable going to a place or … participating in an activity without my friends,” she said. </p><p>Senior Emilo Zurita said he is concerned that some students won’t even go to a new school, at least for the rest of this year.</p><p>“I've heard them say if Aspira closes, they feel like dropping out because they don't feel safe in another school,” he said. “They'd rather drop out than be in a school where they could get shot or something could happen to them.”</p><h3>A warning for other charter schools</h3><p>Conrad Timbers-Ausar, CPS’ acting chief portfolio officer, said he is working on a transition plan including a list of high schools near Aspira that will guarantee a seat to the displaced students. He said these schools will have a designated transition coordinator who will do check-ins with students.</p><p>They also will be provided “wraparound services tailored to students needs including mentoring, tutoring, mental health services and more,” he told board members. “They will also be prepared to provide additional items like technology, uniforms and school gear that students may need to be successful in the school. Students will receive CPS bus cards to get safely to and from school.”</p><p>The district will make sure that credits transfer and that students are able to complete classes, he said. Students will be given a letter to send to colleges explaining the transfer.</p><p>Karen Zaccor, a school board member who represents the North Side, said she wants to make sure students can play on spring sports teams. She also instructed CPS officials to look into arranging senior events, like prom and graduation, exclusively for Aspira students, even if they are no longer together.</p><p>“I think we need to think outside the box and make sure that those things happen,” she said. </p><p>Debby Pope, who represents a different North Side district, called the situation a “terrible experience” and “unfair.”</p><p>But she said she hopes this sends a warning to other charters.</p><p>“You have to behave responsibly,” she said. “You have to have your finances in order. You have to be transparent. You have to turn in your audits. We cannot do this to our children. It is just not okay.”</p>

title: En reunión, la representante Delia Ramírez exige demandas y amenaza con destituir a la jefa de DHS
summary: <p>La representante Delia Ramírez se reunió cara a cara con la secretaria de Seguridad Nacional (DHS), Kristi Noem, el miércoles en una reunión combativa a puerta cerrada en Washington, D.C. y le dijo sin rodeos —dos veces— que trabajará para destituirla.</p><p>Ramírez, miembro del Comité de Seguridad Nacional de la Cámara de Representantes, pasó aproximadamente 35 minutos con Noem, quien también llevó a su hijo a la reunión y se sentó detrás de la secretaria. Noem le había dicho a Ramírez en diciembre durante una audiencia del comité que se reuniría con ella tras repetidas solicitudes, a pesar de que Ramírez acusaba a la jefa de la agencia de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/12/12/en-washington-la-representante-ramirez-llama-mentirosa-a-noem-y-duckworth-cuestiona-despliegues-de-trump" target="_blank" >violar órdenes judiciales y mentirle al público.</a></p><p>La reunión comenzó y terminó con la demócrata de Illinois advirtiéndole a Noem que sus días en la administración podrían estar contados.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-170000" name="module-170000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Le dije, ‘Quiero ser bastante clara contigo a medida que comenzamos. Voy a decirte todo lo que te he dicho en público, y es importante que escuches esto directamente de mí. Primero, sigo pidiendo tu destitución’”, dijo Ramírez al Sun-Times. “‘Espero que renuncies. Si no renuncias o te destituyen, también reconozco que tus días pueden estar contados’, y creo que así es. Sin embargo, ella sigue siendo la secretaria. Ella claramente ocupa esa posición y, como tal, espero que cumpla su juramento y se atenga a las leyes de los Estados Unidos”.</p><p>Al preguntarle sobre la reunión, DHS dijo en un comunicado que Noem se reúne regularmente con miembros del Congreso, independientemente de su partido. Pero un portavoz también culpó a los demócratas por el último cierre gubernamental.</p><p>“Esperamos que la congresista ponga la misma cantidad de energía en financiar a DHS para que podamos hacer nuestro trabajo de proteger a los estadounidenses de amenazas de terroristas, criminales y peligros a la seguridad pública, así como lo ha hecho escribiendo cartas a la secretaria pidiendo su renuncia”, dijo un portavoz. “Cada día que este cierre continúa, a los miembros demócratas se les sigue pagando mientras ponen nuestra seguridad nacional en segundo plazo después de la política”.</p><p>Ramírez llegó equipada con lo que ella llamó “acciones mínimas”. Incluyeron pedirle a Noem que restableciera áreas protegidas, incluyendo iglesias, escuelas y hospitales, de acuerdo con la solicitud de Noem para reinstaurar un memorando de 2021 del ex secretario de DHS, Alejandro Mayorkas.</p><p>También le pidió a Noem que estableciera y codificara estándares sobre el uso de la fuerza, argumentando que el departamento ha sido empoderado a través de la falta de supervisión y ha tenido demasiado margen para violar derechos bajo el pretexto de la seguridad. Ramírez lidera un esfuerzo para que se mantenga por ley la política de uso de fuerza del DHS. Según Ramírez, Noem le dijo que el departamento tiene un procedimiento para informes de uso de la fuerza y dijo que esto está cubierto en la capacitación.</p><p>Otra solicitud fue que Noem revocara un memorando de entrar a domicilios sin orden judicial, una política controversial que ha permitido a los agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) entrar en hogares sin una orden de un juez y pidió que el DHS respetara las leyes y regulaciones, incluyendo las leyes de registro de vehículos que prohíben intercambiar o cambiar placas.</p><p>A raíz de informes sobre oficiales de inmigración federales conduciendo vehículos sin placas adecuadas o con placas modificadas, en octubre el secretario de Estado, Alexi Giannoulias, creó una línea de denuncias para recoger e investigar violaciones de placas. El anuncio ocurrió dos semanas después de que el Sun-Times le enviara pruebas de oficiales de DHS conduciendo en calles públicas <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/09/federal-immigration-officers-ice-dhs-license-plates-immigration" target="_blank" >sin una o ambas placas de Illinois</a>.</p><p>Ramírez también le dijo a Noem que los agentes federales deben cumplir con las órdenes judiciales, pero según Ramírez, Noem insistió en que los agentes efectivamente están siguiendo las órdenes. Cuando Ramírez insistió, Noem pidió más detalles sobre órdenes judiciales específicas que están violando. Ramírez mencionó que agentes del DHS utilizaron armas químicas al menos cuatro veces, a pesar de las órdenes de la jueza de distrito Sara Ellis.</p><p>En una discusión sobre los centros de detención, Ramírez mencionó informes de todo el país sobre personas que no recibieron atención médica oportuna mientras estaban detenidas y sobre algunos de sus electores que detallaron escasez de alimentos en las instalaciones. Noem negó ante Ramírez que las personas no estén recibiendo atención médica y pidió una lista específica de personas que han presentado quejas.</p><p>Noem también le dijo a Ramírez que hay planes de “consolidar” algunos de los 225 centros de detención del país. No se refirió específicamente a Illinois.</p><p>Ramírez detalló incidentes en Chicago en los que las personas fueron rociadas con gas lacrimógeno al entrar en una tienda de comestibles a solo una cuadra de una escuela, niños siendo apresurados afuera de los patios de las escuelas y agentes químicos siendo rociados cerca de niños. También habló sobre visitas no anunciadas de agentes de inmigración federales en hospitales de la zona.</p><p>“Le dije, ‘Continúas negando lo que tus agentes están haciendo en el terreno, pero te voy a contar lo que he visto con mis propios ojos que hacen tus agentes’”, dijo Ramírez. “Ella actuó como si no tuviera idea de lo que estaba hablando, como si no supiera que tenía agentes en el hospital durante días esperando a uno de mis electores, que había sido herido mientras intentaban detenerlo”.</p><p>Ramírez también le habló a Noem sobre <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/10/22/tras-ser-esposada-por-agentes-de-ice-concejal-jessie-fuentes-los-demanda-por-100k" target="_blank" >la concejal Jessie Fuentes siendo esposada por agentes en un hospital de Humboldt Park</a> cuando fue a revisar a ese elector en octubre. Fuentes les preguntó a los agentes si habían firmado una orden judicial y luego fue empujada por un agente, quien estaba completamente enmascarado y no llevaba identificación, según un video publicado en las redes sociales. Después de su tercera pregunta sobre una orden judicial, la concejal fue esposada. Fuentes fue liberada finalmente, pero desde entonces ha presentado un reclamo federal buscando $100,000 en daños.</p><p>Ramírez dijo que Noem le dijo repetidamente que le hiciera saber “cuando estas cosas están ocurriendo”.</p><p>“Tú y yo sabemos que ella sabe lo que está sucediendo, y ha elegido ignorarlo”, dijo Ramírez. “Así que ella es la responsable”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

title: Federal prosecutors agree to clarify, narrow 'Broadview Six' protest conspiracy case
summary: <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago are narrowing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/12/kat-abughazaleh-operation-midway-blitz-donald-trump-jb-pritzker-brandon-johnson-other-candidates-face-arraignment-in-broadview-conspiracy-case" target="_blank" >controversial conspiracy case</a> they brought against six people, including four Democratic politicians, who were involved in protests last fall outside the suburban immigration facility<b> </b>central to Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>The feds also offered clarity about the allegations Thursday in the first hearing before U.S. District Judge April Perry since the lead prosecutor in the case left for a new assignment in the U.S. Senate.</p><p>Kat Abughazaleh, who is running in next month’s primary for the Democratic nomination for Illinois’ 9th District congressional seat, is among the six defendants. So is Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw and former Cook County Board candidate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/06/cook-county-board-candidate-suspends-campaign-to-fight-indictment" target="_blank" >Catherine “Cat” Sharp</a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/02/05/federal-prosecutors-fear-tainted-jury-pool-if-public-sees-evidence-in-broadview-six-conspiracy-case" >Federal prosecutors fear tainted jury pool if public sees evidence in Broadview Six conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Also charged are 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, Andre Martin and musician Joselyn Walsh.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney William Hogan told the judge his team plans to<b> </b>remove language in the indictment alleging the six conspired to injure an agent who drove an SUV toward the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview on Sept. 26.</p><p>Other language in the indictment refers to a conspiracy to prevent the agent from discharging his duties and to injure his property. Hogan said it’s unlikely the first of those two clauses would also be removed, but added, “we’re going to take a look at everything.”</p><p>The indictment alleges that the six and others surrounded the SUV, banged and pushed against it,<b> </b>scratched it and even etched the word "PIG" onto it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure A defense attorney even told a judge Thursday that one member of that group has had “a change of heart” after discussing a pretrial diversion agreement — and now “wishes to proceed to trial.”</p><p>Prosecutors also acknowledged during Thursday's hearing that the timeframe of the alleged conspiracy is limited to Sept. 26, that it was “spontaneous” with no evidence of an explicit agreement, and that all potential co-conspirators were present at Broadview at the time.</p><p>Those acknowledgments came in response to a bid for a so-called bill of particulars, through which defense attorneys hoped to force prosecutors<b> </b>to identify all alleged conspirators,<b> </b>the timeframe of the conspiracy, and under which theory the feds planned to proceed.</p><p>Perry did not grant their request, but she told them “we’ve gotten you quite a bit of the way there.” She said their real problem was that they “fundamentally do not believe the evidence supports a charge or a conviction.”</p><p>“A bill of particulars is not going to solve that problem,” Perry said. “A jury will.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s immigration blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Only one such case has gone to trial so far, and it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" target="_blank" >ended with an acquittal</a> last month. The Broadview conspiracy case is set for trial May 26.</p><p>The former lead prosecutor in the Broadview case, Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri Mecklenburg, withdrew Feb. 13. She’s now serving as counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee, according to a source.</p><p>A spokesperson for Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said Mecklenburg has not been detailed to his staff. A spokesperson for Ranking Member Dick Durbin, D-Illinois, would not comment.</p><p>Joseph Fitzpatrick, a spokesman for U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros, called Mecklenburg "an experienced prosecutor who applied for and received a temporary detail." He said, "we wish her the best and look forward to her returning to our office."</p><p>Defense attorneys for the six Broadview defendants say newly produced body-worn camera footage contradicts the feds’ claims about the case.<b> </b>The attorneys detailed the events of Sept. 26 in their recent court filings.</p><p>They wrote that the defendants and others<b> </b>engaged in a “Jericho Walk” near the Broadview facility, walking back and forth across a public crosswalk at Harvard Street and 25th Avenue.</p><p>Broadview police officers supervised the Jericho Walk and helped control traffic, including by stopping the demonstration “and parting the crowd of protesters when vehicles sought to pass through,” the attorneys wrote.</p><p>A Ford Expedition driven by an ICE agent turned “directly” into the crowd around 7:45 a.m., according to the defense filings. The attorneys said they’d seen no evidence of the ICE agent waiting for police assistance, but rather that he opted instead to<b> </b>“drive directly into where the crowd was gathered.”</p><div title: The IRS broke the law by disclosing confidential information to ICE 42,695 times, judge says
summary: <p>A federal judge said Thursday that the IRS broke the law by disclosing confidential taxpayer information “approximately 42,695 times" to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly found that the IRS had erroneously shared the taxpayer information of thousands of people with the Department of Homeland Security as part of the agencies’ controversial agreement to share information on immigrants for the purpose of identifying and deporting people illegally in the U.S.</p><p>Her finding was based off a declaration filed earlier this month by Dottie Romo, IRS’ chief risk and control officer, which revealed that the IRS had provided DHS with information on 47,000 of the 1.28 million people that ICE requested — and, in most of those cases, gave ICE additional address information in violation of privacy rules created to protect taxpayer data.</p><p>Kollar-Kotelly said in her Thursday decision that the agency violated IRS Code 6103, one of the strictest confidentiality laws in federal statute, “approximately 42,695 times by disclosing last known taxpayer addresses to ICE.” She called the Romo declaration “a significant development in this case.”</p><p>“The IRS not only failed to ensure that ICE’s request for confidential taxpayer address information met the statutory requirements, but this failure led the IRS to disclose confidential taxpayer addresses to ICE in situations where ICE’s request for that information was patently deficient," she wrote.</p><p>The government is appealing the case, but the Thursday ruling is significant because Romo's declaration supports the decision on appeal.</p><p>Nina Olson, founder of the Center for Taxpayer Rights, which has sued the government over the disclosure, says “this confirms what we’ve been saying all along: that the IRS has an unlawful policy that violates the Internal Revenue Code’s protections by releasing these addresses in a way that violates the law’s requirements.”</p><p>Representatives from the IRS and Treasury Department didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><p>A data-sharing agreement signed last April by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem allows ICE to submit names and addresses of immigrants inside the U.S. illegally to the IRS for cross-verification against tax records. The deal led the then-acting commissioner of the IRS to resign.</p><p>There are several ongoing cases that challenge the IRS-DHS agreement.</p><p>Earlier this week, a three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit declined to issue a preliminary injunction for the immigrants’ rights group, Centro de Trabajadores Unidos, and other nonprofits that are suing the federal government to stop implementation of the agreement.</p><p>In declining the preliminary injunction request, Judge Harry T. Edwards wrote that the nonprofit groups “are unlikely to succeed on the merits of their claim,” since the information the agencies are sharing isn’t covered by the IRS privacy statute.</p><p>Still, two separate court orders have blocked the agencies from massive transfers of taxpayer information and blocked ICE from acting upon any IRS data in its possession. Those preliminary injunctions are still in place.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/2026/02/22/congress-trump-obba-beautiful-bill-federal-irs-tax-returns" >Congress passed Trump’s sweeping tax bill. Here’s how it’ll affect your returns</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/2026/02/22/charitable-donations-gifts-irs-obbba-tax-rules" >New tax rules are changing charitable deductions — here’s how to make the most of them</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjthitk-l-t/" target="_blank" >Leak and Sons prepares for Jesse Jackson’s funeral and to play ‘small part’ in history</a></h3><h3></h3><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjthitk-l-i/" target="_blank" >Mariah Rush</a></h5><p><b>Family business</b>: Leak and Sons Funeral Home has been tasked with planning and executing funeral services for civil rights activist Rev. Jesse Jackson — who died Feb. 17 at age 84 —  including scouting service locations in South Carolina and Washington and handling Jackson's remains. But the death also hits close to home. For decades, Spencer Leak Jr. said, his family and the Jacksons were "intertwined." Leak’s grandfather, Andrew, welcomed Jackson and his family into his home, where they stayed upon first moving to Chicago in 1964.</p><p><b>Business history</b>: Andrew Leak started the business in 1933 with a $500 loan from his wife, Dottie, and $500 that he saved from working as a bathroom attendant at the Chicago World’s Fair. Leak wanted Black Chicagoans to be able to bury their loved ones respectfully. The couple ran the business with their three sons. The funeral home has handled services and burials for prominent Black figures including Sam Cooke, Bernie Mac and Juice WRLD — and is known for not turning anyone away despite financial status.</p><p><b>Civil rights legacy</b>: Jackson went on to work with Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. Andrew Leak — who became friends with King and provided limousine services to him when he was in town — was also an advocate of social justice. In 1964, Leak led a march with his son Spencer Leak and 10,000 people that led to the desegregation of Oak Woods Cemetery.</p><p><b>Services begin</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjthitk-l-d/" target="_blank" >Jackson will lie in repose Thursday and Friday</a> at Rainbow PUSH’s Kenwood headquarters. services planned there.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjthitk-l-h/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>CITY HALL 🏛️</h4><div >Fran Spielman</a></h5><p><b>Mayor's pick</b>: Mayor Johnson is rallying behind Susan Cappello, his permanent choice to lead Chicago’s Commission on Animal Care and Control, amid concerns about high euthanasia rates and shelter conditions that allegedly neglect and endanger dogs, cats and volunteers. >Waymo takes step toward deploying autonomous vehicles in Chicago</a></h3><h3></h3><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wjthitk-l-n/" target="_blank" >Violet Miller</a></h5><p><b>Robotaxis arrive</b>: Waymo’s self-driving vehicles are hitting Chicago streets — but with human drivers, for now. The company, a subsidiary of Google’s parent Alphabet, said that human drivers began driving its vehicles Wednesday to help the company map the city. The cars will be used east of the Kennedy and Dan Ryan expressways, from the South Loop to Wrigleyville. </p><p><b>Not authorized</b>: Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office says the city was given a heads up, but that "as of now, autonomous vehicles have not been authorized within the City of A California cyclist suing the company alleges a passenger opened a door when the vehicle was parked in a bike lane, hitting the cyclist and throwing her off her bike, only for the cyclist to be hit by another Waymo pulling over. title: In ruling blasting ICE agents wearing masks, W. Va. judge points to case involving Chicago police officers
summary: <p>A federal judge in West Virginia has invoked a more than decade-old lawsuit against Chicago police officers to underscore what he called a constitutional failing in the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement tactics: the use of masked agents.</p><p>In a sharply worded order last week, Judge Joseph Goodwin directed the release of an El Salvadoran man from federal custody and condemned masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents for concealing their identities during a Jan. 7 traffic stop they conducted because there was a plastic cover on the man’s license plate. The man said he was in the U.S. legally with a pending asylum case, a work permit and a driver’s license.</p><p>“An anonymous government is no government at all,” Goodwin wrote. “It cannot be held accountable. A masked agent freely uses force without justifying his actions and the public cannot name him to challenge his conduct. A regime of secret policing has no place in our society.”</p><p>He said the traffic stop violated the Fourth and Fifth amendments of the constitution. The ruling, issued Feb. 19, doesn’t bind courts in Chicago, which sit in a different federal appeals circuit. Still, lawyers said the opinion could serve as persuasive authority in cases challenging arrests by ICE or the Border Patrol in Illinois and elsewhere.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> the 7400 block of North Oconto Avenue.<b> </b></p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>To bolster his reasoning, Goodwin pointed to a case that began in Chicago on a cold February night in 2013. Joseph Doornbos, then 35, stepped off a Red Line train at the Wilson Avenue station in Uptown after his work day at a Loop law firm where he was a customer service manager. He was headed to a friend’s house to watch a Blackhawks game when three plainclothes Chicago police officers approached him outside the station.</p><p>According to court records, Doornbos said one of the cops, whom he described as disheveled, ordered him to stop but didn't identify himself as a police officer. Believing he was about to be robbed, he shouted for help, prompting bystanders to call 911. When Doornbos tried to flee, one officer tackled him and two others joined the struggle.</p><p>The officers contended that they stopped Doornbos because he was carrying an open beer can in a paper bag, an allegation he denied. During the arrest, police recovered $5 worth of marijuana from his coat pocket. Doornbos was charged with drug possession and resisting arrest but was acquitted after a Cook County trial.</p><p>He sued the officers in federal court. He lost that lawsuit, but the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overturned the verdict in 2016, finding the trial judge had improperly instructed jurors.</p><p>“The jury asked the judge whether plainclothes officers are required to identify themselves when they conduct a stop,” the appeals court wrote. “The judge said no. We conclude that the answer is yes.”</p><p>With limited exceptions, the court held, officers in plain clothes must identify themselves when initiating a stop.</p><p>In 2018, Chicago officials agreed to pay $100,000 to settle the case.</p><p>The question of identification has since taken on new urgency as immigration enforcement has intensified in several cities, including Chicago and Minneapolis. During a series of deportation operations here last year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/14/ice-bovino-border-patrol-homeland-security-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" ><u>masked agents deployed tear gas and other crowd-control munitions against protesters</u></a>. In two separate episodes last fall, masked officers shot people in vehicles: An immigrant driver was killed in Franklin Park, and a woman who’s a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" ><u>U.S. citizen was wounded in Brighton Park.</u></a></p><p>In Washington earlier this month, House Democrats moved to partially withhold funding from the Department of Homeland Security, demanding changes to immigration enforcement practices, including a prohibition on masks. Congress remains at a stalemate on the issue.</p><p>In his ruling, Goodwin said there’s a key difference between the Chicago case and what’s going on with DHS agents wearing masks.</p><p>“Immigration enforcement is distinguishable from the <i>Doornbos </i>officer in a material way: We are not merely dealing with a plainclothes officer who fails to self-identify — we are dealing with groups of masked individuals arriving in unmarked vehicles, without badges or a means of discerning who they are. They are the problem that the court in <i>Doornbos </i>foreshadowed: a presence indistinguishable from lawbreakers,” he wrote.</p><p>Goodwin rejected the government’s position that masks are necessary to ensure the safety of the federal agents.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li </div> </div><p>Torreya Hamilton, one of Doornbos’s<b> </b>attorneys in the 2013 lawsuit and a former Cook County prosecutor, said Goodwin’s reliance on the case reflects the novelty of the issue.</p><p>“These judges are having to scour all over the country to find legal opinions to cite because until recently our law enforcement officers have not worn masks and driven around in rental cars without license plates,” Hamilton said. “The reason the West Virginia judge is citing to our Chicago case is because there is not a lot of law out there on this topic. It has long been a forbidden practice for an officer to hide his identity while acting on behalf of the government.”</p><p>She added that the principle at stake is a basic one. </p><p>“Like the police officers in my case, these ICE and border patrol agents are government employees and therefore we are their employers," Hamilton said. “And we have every right to hold them accountable for their conduct, which we can’t do unless we know who they are.”</p>

title: Senate race to replace Dick Durbin heats up with 10 Democrats on the ballot
summary: <p>Two members of Congress, a lieutenant governor and seven other Democrats are seeking to succeed Dick Durbin in a contentious open U.S. Senate race.</p><p>Durbin’s announcement last year <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/senator-dick-durbin-reelection" target="_blank" ><u>not to seek a sixth term</u></a> was anticipated, but it led to a game of political music chairs, with a long roster of Democrats who had been quietly jockeying for his position free to jump into the spotlight.</p><p>U.S. Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly and Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton have consistently ranked in the top three in several recent polls, according to a New York Times analysis.</p><p>Rounding out the list are Steve Botsford Jr., Sean Brown, Awisi A. Bustos, Jonathan Dean, Bryan Maxwell, Kevin Ryan and Christopher Swann. In the Republican primary, candidates include R. Cary Capparelli, Casey Chlebek, Jeannie Evans, Pamela Denise Long, Jimmie Lee Tillman II and Don Tracy.</p><h3>Top Dems have key differences</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/01/26/senate-debate-illinois-krishnamoorthi-stratton-kelly" >In debates,</a> Krishnamoorthi, Kelly and Stratton have shown voters some of their key policy differences. They include differing opinions on future nominations made by President Donald Trump, the minimum wage, age limits for members of Congress and how to handle the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation campaign.</p><p>Stratton supports a $25 an hour minimum wage plan, while Krishnamoorthi and Kelly support a $17 an hour plan, which they said would have a more realistic chance of passing in the Senate.</p><p>When it comes to a retirement age for members of Congress, Krishnamoorthi said he supports a limit, while Kelly and Stratton reject the idea.</p><p>“We need fighters at any age,” Stratton said during a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/01/29/us-senate-democratic-primary-abc7-debate-krishnamoorthi-kelly-stratton" >Jan. 29 debate.</a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fa0000" name="image-fa0000"></a> <picture
