title: As Stratton airs ad with anti-Trump expletive, Krishnamoorthi launches first negative TV ad attacking her
summary: <p>As Juliana Stratton runs a campaign ad uttering the words "F*** Trump, her U.S. Senate rival U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi is airing the first negative TV ad targeting the lieutenant governor.</p><p>The final weeks of a heated U.S. Senate race have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/01/26/senate-debate-illinois-krishnamoorthi-stratton-kelly" target="_blank" >proven to be feisty during live forums and debates,</a> but a bit tamer on television — until now. Krishnamoorthi's foray into an attack ad is the first to go negative on television in the statewide race to replace retiring U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin. And it comes as Stratton airs her first TV ad — and a pro-Stratton super PAC with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/01/31/juliana-stratton-jb-pritzker-campaign-contribution-5-million" target="_blank" >$5 million of Gov. JB Pritzker’s dollars</a> being used to run pro-Stratton ads.</p><p>Krishnamoorthi's campaign framed it as a response to "six months of repeated attacks from Juliana Stratton."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XhaGqq4ToO0" target="_blank" >The 30-second ad</a> cites a Sun-Times story that shows Stratton's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/21/juliana-stratton-us-senate-bid-march-primary-corporate-pac-money" target="_blank" >history of receiving money from corporate owners and directors</a> into her state campaign funds, despite her Senate campaign disavowing corporate PAC money. It claims Stratton took MAGA donor money, citing research from Krishnamoorthi's campaign. The Sun-Times reported Stratton received a $2,500 contribution from Union Pacific in September 2024 into her state campaign fund, which can’t be used for her Senate run. The corporate PAC helped fund the White House ballroom. U.S. Rep. Robin Kelly, another contender in the Democratic primary race for Durbin’s seat, also received contributions from PACs affiliated with the fund.</p><p>The ad also cites a CBS story that reported a Stratton super PAC received a six-figure donation from ICE contractor CoreCivic. That was in reference to the Democratic Lieutenant Governor's Association PAC, which has said they'll donate money to the National Immigration Law Center. It also mentions an error on the part of Illinois Future PAC, a super PAC created to support Stratton, which had to update an ad after Krishnamoorthi’s campaign noted it appeared to violate federal campaign finance law by failing to disclose that it was not authorized by Stratton or her campaign. The PAC quickly updated the ad. </p><p>"Juliana Stratton. Corporate and MAGA donations, ICE contractor money, accused of breaking federal laws," the ad's narrator says. "Hypocrisy we can't trust."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DU8q15METdr/" target="_blank" >Stratton aired her first TV ad on Feb. 19</a>, which features five people blankly stating, "F*** Trump," and details her support for abolishing ICE and to "hold Trump accountable for the crimes he's committed." Others join in on the expletive, including U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who has endorsed Stratton. Pritzker is also featured in the ad, but does not swear.</p><p>"Vote Juliana," Pritzker says. </p><p>The expletives are bleeped on television, but not online. </p><p>Stratton's campaign has aired negative digital ads targeting Krishnamoorthi since August, but not on television. Krishnamoorthi has raised more than $28 million in the race and has been <a class="Link" href="https://www.google.com/search?q=raja+krishnamoorthi+first+tv+ad&sca_esv=2df5d5c022344074&biw=1435&bih=713&tbm=nws&sxsrf=ANbL-n5AKKvwQZKEZEeiHTzWbcmbKHwWcw%3A1771632461897&ei=TfeYaYq9NpXAp84Pxtu8mA4&ved=0ahUKEwjKl8GcpemSAxUV4MkDHcYtD-MQ4dUDCBA&uact=5&oq=raja+krishnamoorthi+first+tv+ad&gs_lp=Egxnd3Mtd2l6LW5ld3MiH3JhamEga3Jpc2huYW1vb3J0aGkgZmlyc3QgdHYgYWRIhhFQ3wVYjhBwAXgAkAEAmAF3oAHVCqoBBDEyLjO4AQPIAQD4AQGYAgWgAvIDwgIFECEYoAHCAgsQABiABBiRAhiKBcICBhAAGBYYHsICCxAAGIAEGLEDGIMBwgIFEAAYgASYAwCIBgGSBwMzLjKgB9EasgcDMy4yuAfyA8IHBTEuMS4zyAcQgAgA&sclient=gws-wiz-news" target="_blank" >airing ads since July</a>. He had $15.2 million cash on hand at the end of December, according to the Federal Election Commission. Stratton had $1.1 million for the same time period, and Kelly had $1.59 million. Kelly is also airing TV ads for the final four weeks of the campaign. </p><p>Other Democrats vying for the race are Steve Botsford Jr., Sean Brown, Awisi A. Bustos, Jonathan Dean, Bryan Maxwell, Kevin Ryan and Christopher Swann.</p>

title: Rev. Jackson's message of hope resonates well beyond Chicago
summary: <p>To really appreciate the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/obituary/2026/02/17/jesse-jackson-embodied-era-civil-rights-leadership-natalie-moore?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=02172026%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=02172026%20Morning%20Edition+CID_18ae33b9ac0c6725278bbe9fb4d34c16&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Rev%20Jackson%20was%20a%20symbol%20of%20Black%20politics%20and%20Black%20America&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >Rev. Jesse Jackson</a> Sr. I think you have to step outside the Chicago lens, where media familiarity does not always result in the full measure of the man.</p><p>I first met him when our anti-apartheid organization hosted a visitor from the African National Congress. I ended up bringing my infant daughter with me because I was a working nursing mother. He did not bat an eye. In fact, he and the great Rev. Willie Barrow invited me to join in for the announcement of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/1986/12/05/business/apartheid-pullout-by-revlon.html" target="_blank" >Revlon makeup boycott</a>. This led to a lifelong collaboration and friendship. </p><p>Rev. Jackson was incredibly media literate and a skilled speaker. He hosted numerous radio and television iterations of "Keep Hope Alive," his public affairs program. Over the years, he found brilliant representatives from academia, politics and culture. He could break down complex issues and concepts, such as <a class="Link" href="https://www.tulsalibrary.org/black-wall-street" target="_blank" >Black Wall Street</a>, the 2008 housing bubble and Black farming. He could smack-talk. He could pray. </p><p>When I served as an occasional fill-in host on his national radio show or traveled to Detroit to work on his daughter Santita‘s TV program, I learned that members of the Rainbow PUSH Coalition were effective, committed and everywhere.  </p><p>As a producer for "Chicago Tonight," I watched a group of Humboldt Park protesters gain strength as they shouted, "Jesse is here,” when he appeared at their Puerto Rican protest, and cameras came too. Jesse was able to uplift voices and issues to serve others. </p><p>Watching him celebrate his daughter surrounded by children and grandchildren, he was quiet, loving and, yes, humble. </p><p>In a world that is quick to cannibalize Black culture and diminish our history, what can we do in this moment? Let’s show compassion and care, not only to his family but also to the contemporaries he leaves behind who are suffering on a personal level. Let’s get the story right and pass it on to our children with all the lessons and complexity that his life has to offer. Let’s "Keep Hope Alive," with an added dose of resilience!</p><p><i>Sylvia Ewing, vice president</i> <i>of</i> <i>journalism and media engagement, Public Narrative</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2c0000" name="module-2c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Sun-Times captured Jackson’s legacy </h3><p>Congratulations, Sun-Times, with much gratitude, for your extraordinary journalistic homage to the Rev. Jesse Jackson — an American political giant who diligently built, for multiple generations, a sturdy and reliable bridge between the 1960s Civil Rights Movement and today's fight against social and racial injustice.</p><p>Your 20-page special section honoring the multiple legacies of Rev. Jackson eloquently surpassed the journalistic coverage of other outstanding newspapers such as the New York Times, USA Today and the Chicago Tribune.</p><p>Your historically robust visual archive of Rev. Jackson's political journey through the decades reminded me of when I saw him run for president in the 1980s when I was still a young Mexican immigrant college student. That moment made me realize that the names of Americans of color, both within and outside my community, could actually get prominent national recognition in the world of politics.</p><p>In my view, Rev. Jackson broke the presidential race ceiling in the late 20th century for our own 21st century President Barack Obama.</p><p>Perhaps even more importantly, Rev. Jackson's moral vision for a better society, including his ongoing belief in a "rainbow coalition" that truly captures the multicultural American society that we have always been, offers a compelling map for how to nurture a better America for the new generations.</p><p>May Rev. Jesse Jackson rest in peace and power.</p><p><i>Alejandro Lugo, Park Forest</i></p><h3>Latino heritage rooted in Chicago </h3><p>In the first week of January, I traveled to Chicago to meet with historic preservation partners — from established practitioners to grassroots neighborhood leaders. In La Villita — Little Village — community leaders spoke about what it now takes to remain in place: keeping businesses open, families together and neighborhoods intact amid federal immigration enforcement pressure and ongoing uncertainty.</p><p>What is unfolding here reflects a national moment that is redefining how American history is interpreted and preserved.</p><p>As the United States nears its 250th anniversary, public attention is turning toward questions of origin, belonging and national memory. Chicago has long influenced how the country understands culture, civic life and preservation. Latino communities are part of that continuum, visible across neighborhoods, institutions and public space, even when their presence is treated as recent or temporary.</p><p>In historic neighborhoods like Little Village and Pilsen, the past is lived daily through family-owned businesses, housing stability and community networks that allow residents to remain rooted.</p><p>Actions such as Operation Midway Blitz, which separated thousands of families, continue to affect how residents move through their neighborhoods, how businesses operate and how communities organize for safety and mutual support.</p><p>That context is why, in August, Latinos in Heritage Conservation will bring its national historic preservation conference, Congreso, to Chicago.</p><p>This region is a living archive of migration, labor, resistance and reinvention. Afro Latino, Indigenous, Mexican, Central American, Caribbean and working-class communities have shaped its cultural landscape for generations. Decisions about community safety, displacement and who is able to remain are happening now, and preservation must be part of them.</p><p>It is also a place where Latino communities have carried that legacy forward through everyday stewardship, sustaining family-owned businesses, organizing for housing stability and protecting cultural spaces that anchor community life. This year, we will gather not to observe this history, but to stand within it and to affirm clearly and publicly that we are here, and we have always been here.</p><p><i>Sehila Mota Casper, executive director, Latinos in Heritage Conservation</i></p><h3>Funding parity for charter students is not a bailout</h3><p>Recent coverage of financial distress facing some <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/11/cps-charter-school-cant-make-payroll-insolvent-closed-march-aspira-chiarts-cpsboard" >charter schools</a> has focused on whether Chicago Public Schools should provide short-term financial support. The coverage mischaracterizes these payments as "bailouts," when in actuality they are the foreseeable consequence of many years of structural underfunding.</p><p>CPS is required by law to provide charter schools at least 97% of the state’s per capita tuition charge. Yet after deducting pension, debt service, management fees and other districtwide costs, charter schools receive, on average, roughly 83% of that amount. That means thousands of dollars less per student, even when charter and district-run schools serve similar student populations in the same neighborhoods.</p><p>In one example reported by <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/02/11/chicago-public-schools-charter-financial-problems/#:~:text=Does%20CPS%20fund%20charters%20equitably,the%20entire%20district%20is%20facing." target="_blank" >Chalkbeat Chicago</a>, two high schools with fewer than 300 students share a building on the Far South Side. Noble’s Baker College Prep, a charter public school, received $15,800 per student this year, while the district-run Bowen High School received $25,150 per student, according to CPS data. The building is the same. The students are similar. The funding is not.</p><p>CPS data also shows that 287 of 498 school buildings are categorized as underutilized. Some schools have fewer than 200 students. Douglass High School has just 28 students in a building built for 912. District-run schools receive guaranteed staffing positions regardless of enrollment and are subsidized to remain open. Charter schools, by contrast, are funded largely based on enrollment alone, even though 87% of charter students live in poverty compared with 69% in district-run schools.</p><p>Charter schools are concentrated on the South and West sides of the city, where population decline has been steepest, but the need for high-quality public schools remains urgent. These students deserve stability and equitable funding.</p><p>When district-run schools receive additional support to remain open, we call it equity and investment<b>. </b>When charter students seek parity with their district-run peers, it should be viewed through the same lens. Every public school student in Chicago deserves fair treatment under the law and a funding system that supports their success.</p><p><i>Andrew Broy, president, Illinois Network of Charter Schools</i></p><h3>School choice is misguided choice</h3><p>It’s a shame the Archdiocese of Chicago has to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/01/26/archdiocese-catholic-school-closing-jerome-bruno-richard-francis-borgia-stanislaus-kostka" >close more schools </a>due to lack of funding, but saving them with taxpayer funds or vouchers is not the answer.</p><p>As education historian Dianne Ravitch <a class="Link" href="https://dianeravitch.net/2023/04/12/school-choice-will-destroy-public-schools/" target="_blank" >states</a>, “Choice is a means to defund what should be our common good.” Redirecting funds means fewer dollars for the neediest students. Any choice model that diverts public funds to private interests destroys the social contract that is meant to strengthen public schools for the common good.</p><p>The answer isn’t to increase the <a class="Link" href="https://tax.illinois.gov/questionsandanswers/answer.28.html" target="_blank" >Illinois K-12 education expense credit</a> for private education, as some suggest. That would further enable taxpayers to opt out of public education. The results would be catastrophic: more school closings due to lack of funding, lower property values and a higher likelihood of becoming the subject of a watchdog task force.</p><p>The archdiocese is taking the necessary steps to ease its financial burden. To grow, it may want to consider a different approach to attract students to certain parochial schools: classical education.</p><p>Depending on the parish's progressiveness, the faith community might embrace a classical education model for their children. Teachers need to work hard to ensure the school maintains state accreditation, but it has worked.</p><p>For example, over time, <a class="Link" href="https://stjeromeacademy.org/" target="_blank" >St. Jerome Academy</a> in Hyattsville, Maryland, shifted from a traditional curriculum to a classical Catholic education, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.sjaclassical.org/classical-vs-progressive-education" target="_blank" >“consists in cultivating virtuous dispositions in students.”</a> Today, the school is at total capacity with <a class="Link" href="https://streetcarsuburbs.news/st-jerome-academy-announces-major-expansion/" target="_blank" >waitlists</a>.</p><p>St. Jerome's goal was to reimagine education. It is infinitely more effective than reshuffling funds like a shell game.</p><p><i>Mary Dooms, Hoffman Estates</i></p><h3>Bon voyage, Bears </h3><p>If the Chicago Bears want to build a new home in the Chicago suburbs, that's fine with me.<br>If they want to profit more by moving to Indiana — a location less accessible to Chicago area fans, so be it. But they won't be the Chicago Bears to me anymore, and I won't follow their exploits. Nor, I expect, will they get the Chicago media coverage they currently enjoy. Their past glories will fade into memory like any deceased relative. Hammond Hawks, anyone?</p><p><i>Charles Berg,</i> <i>Hyde Park/Kenwood</i></p><h3>Suburban sprawl</h3><p>Now that it's very possible that the Bears will leave <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/02/19/chicago-bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-move" target="_blank" >Illinois and become the Hammond Bears or the Indiana Bears</a>, there will be a large vacant parcel of land in the northwest suburbs. I have a radical suggestion for the new owners of the property. They can build a racetrack there and name it Arlington Park!</p><p><i>Craig Jacobson, Skokie</i></p><h3><b>Bears move: quarterback sneak</b></h3><p>I don't have a stake in this potential relocation, but I hate the secrecy behind the process.</p><p>We saw it with the New York Giants and Jets moving to the New Jersey Meadowlands Sports Complex. By the time these funding bills get passed and news releases floated, it's often a fait accompli. Negotiations typically have already taken place, between stakeholders and local elected officials and the team ownership, long before we see it in the headlines. Unfortunately, the taxpayers who fund the new stadiums are the last to know.</p><p>But everyone wants to be an NFL town, right? So they don't complain too much.</p><p>Then again, a Bears move to Indiana (or to Iowa, as also rumored) could fall through — like the supposed Washington Commanders move to northern Virginia a couple years ago, which never materialized.</p><p><i>Adam Silbert, New York City</i></p><h3>Baseball prayers </h3><p>Watching the recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.ncronline.org/news/music-and-multicultural-witness-ronald-hicks-begins-his-new-york-ministry" target="_blank" >installation</a> of Bishop Ronald Hicks, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2025/12/18/pope-leo-appoints-ronald-hicks-archbishop-new-york-replacing-cardinal-timothy-dolan" >a Chicago area native</a>, as archbishop of New York at St. Patrick's Cathedral, I remembered his recent comment that he will remain a <a class="Link" href="https://longisland.news12.com/pope-names-fellow-chicagoan-bishop-ronald-hicks-as-new-archbishop-of-new-york" target="_blank" >Cubs fan</a>.</p><p>As a Mets fan for over 60 years, I have no problem with that.</p><p>But if Archbishop Hicks decides to replace the traditional recessional hymn after Mass with "Go Cubs Go," and if the Cubs meet <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv" target="_blank" >Pope Leo XIV</a>'s White Sox in this year's World Series, I'll start going to Mass daily. </p><p>God bless New York AND Chicago. (God knows we both need it.)</p><p><i>Jim Vespe, Mamaroneck, New York</i> <br></p>

title: How we photographed the impact of Rev. Jesse Jackson's death
summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from visual journalist intern Giacomo Cain. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/gcain.photo" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><p></p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>U.S. Rep. Jonathan Jackson is one of six children to survive their father, civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson. All except one of Rev. Jackson’s children were present for a news conference Wednesday in front of the family's South Shore home. They spoke about their father’s legacy and his global impact. Rev. Jackson had been battling with progressive supranuclear palsy and died Tuesday. He was a groundbreaking icon who fought alongside Martin Luther King Jr. and founded Operation PUSH. His children told emotional stories of who he was as a father and a civil rights leader, describing him as dedicated to his pursuit of social justice. Jonathan Jackson is the second oldest of the siblings, and serves in Congress as a representative of the 1st District of Illinois.</p><h3>How did you get the photo?</h3><p>There are only so many different angles you can photograph people standing behind a mic, so once the press conference was finished, I documented interactions between Rev. Jackson's children, supporters, friends and family. With my telephoto lens, I stood on a mound of dirt to see above people’s heads. Given the emotional atmosphere, I was waiting for people to hug, which this photo shows. I try to capture emotion, because it shows real human nature and helps the viewer connect to the story. </p><p>While looking around for Rev. Jackson's children, Jonathan walked in my direction and approached a supporter. I raised my camera to my eye and snapped away. This is where my telephoto lens came in handy; I zoomed into Jonathan's face, excluding unnecessary elements and focusing on his expression. I really like his expression in this photo, because at first glance you see anguish, but if you look longer, you might see a hint of a smile. Whatever you see, for me, it makes me think of his love for his father and his passion for continuing his legacy.</p><h3>Technical details:</h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" title: Measles cases are rising, and RFK Jr. is only making it worse
summary: <p>The number of <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html" target="_blank" >measles cases </a>in the U.S. has soared over the past two years. In 2024, there were 285 reported cases, while in 2025, there were 2,280 cases. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html" target="_blank" >number of cases</a> reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of Feb. 19 is 982 and growing. The U.S. is on track this year to have the <a class="Link" href="https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-measles-cases" target="_blank" >most measles cases</a> since 1990. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://dph.sc.gov/diseases-conditions/infectious-diseases/measles-rubeola/measles-dashboard" target="_blank" >South Carolina</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/5736370-map-which-states-have-the-most-measles-cases-in-2026/" target="_blank" >Utah</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.floridahealth.gov/diseases-and-conditions/disease/measles/" target="_blank" >Florida</a> are the states with the most cases so far this year. Illinois now has <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/diseases-and-conditions/measles.html" target="_blank" >two cases</a>, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health.</p><p>This surge in cases places the U.S. at risk of losing its <a class="Link" href="https://www.astho.org/communications/blog/2026/understanding-current-us-measles-outbreaks-elimination-status/" target="_blank" >measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000</a>, largely driven by effective measles vaccination uptake.</p><p>Some may argue that measles is a <a class="Link" href="http://www.bowdish.ca/lab/2024/03/07/measles-is-not-a-harmless-childhood-infection-dr-bowdish-explains/" target="_blank" >harmless infectious disease</a>, so children having measles is more of an inconvenience than a risk. This is simply not true.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Measles can cause an <a class="Link" href="https://www.uchicagomedicine.org/forefront/pediatrics-articles/measles-is-still-a-very-dangerous-disease" target="_blank" >acute encephalitis</a>, or swelling of the brain, as well as death.</p><p>On a practical note, when children are infected with measles, they must be kept out of school, forcing parents and their caregivers to miss time from <a class="Link" href="https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/28-fmla" target="_blank" >work</a> to care for them. In 2025, of the 2,267 measles cases, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html" target="_blank" >11%</a> resulted in hospitalizations, and three of these patients died. Moreover, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html" target="_blank" >18% of children under 5</a> who were infected had to be hospitalized. All such data demonstrates that measles is more than just a benign infection.</p><p>Cases of measles are now surfacing at <a class="Link" href="https://www.ice.gov/" target="_blank" >Immigration and Customs Enforcement</a> (ICE) detention facilities in <a class="Link" href="https://www.powershealth.org/about-us/newsroom/health-library/2026/02/02/arizona-confirms-measles-case-in-ice-custody-as-state-total-rises" target="_blank" >Arizona</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ice-dilley-center-texas-measles-cases/" target="_blank" >Texas</a>. Given measles’ high <a class="Link" href="https://www.gideononline.com/blogs/understanding-the-basic-reproduction-number-r0-the-key-to-tracking-disease-spread/" target="_blank" >basic reproduction number</a>, R0, which measures the average number of new infections that a single infected person can spread in a completely susceptible population, dozens more cases are certain to be reported in the coming weeks.</p><p>What makes the uptick in measles cases so concerning is that it serves as the “<a class="Link" href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/what-happened-canary-coal-mine-story-how-real-life-animal-helper-became-just-metaphor-180961570/" target="_blank" >canary in the mine shaft</a>” for other vaccine-preventable infectious diseases. <a class="Link" href="https://www.gavi.org/vaccineswork/contagion-scale-which-diseases-spread-fastest" target="_blank" >Measles is the most transmissible infectious disease that children contract</a>, with its R0 value <a class="Link" href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28757186/" target="_blank" >between 12 and 18</a>. Other infectious diseases with high R0 value include <a class="Link" href="https://www.gavi.org/vaccineswork/contagion-scale-which-diseases-spread-fastest" target="_blank" >polio (12 to 17) and rubella (10-12)</a>.</p><p></p><h3>RFK Jr. fuels vaccine hesitancy</h3><h3></h3><p>People attribute this surge in measles cases to <a class="Link" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3906279/" target="_blank" >vaccine hesitancy</a>, which has been exacerbated and fanned by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.hhs.gov/" target="_blank" >Health and Human Services</a> secretary, <a class="Link" href="https://www.hhs.gov/about/leadership/robert-kennedy.html" target="_blank" >Robert F. Kennedy Jr.,</a> who has a long <a class="Link" href="https://dcimmunized.org/rfk-jr-says-hes-not-anti-vaccine/" target="_blank" >history of marginalizing</a> the use of vaccines to prevent diseases. He has continued to promulgate his personal beliefs and agenda by revamping the <a class="Link" href="https://cdc.gov/" target="_blank" >CDC</a> and its <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/acip/index.html" target="_blank" >Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices</a>. Though vaccine hesitancy is certainly part of the risk calculus driving higher numbers of infections, the number of people <a class="Link" href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/ivac/2025/across-the-us-childhood-vaccination-rates-continue-to-decline" target="_blank" >who continue to get vaccinated</a> and support vaccination for their children remains high, albeit not as high as it was six years ago.</p><p>The advisory committee also recently revamped the <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/other-health/the-new-federal-vaccine-schedule-what-changed/" target="_blank" >childhood immunization schedule</a>, aligning it more closely with <a class="Link" href="https://vaccine-schedule.ecdc.europa.eu/Scheduler/ByCountry?SelectedCountryId=58&IncludeChildAgeGroup=true&IncludeChildAgeGroup=false&IncludeAdultAgeGroup=true&IncludeAdultAgeGroup=false" target="_blank" >Denmark’s schedule</a>. This resulted in six fewer diseases covered on the <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/other-health/the-new-federal-vaccine-schedule-what-changed/" target="_blank" >U.S. schedule.</a> The change instituted by the advisory committee that impacted measles was the change at 12 months through 3 years, that the varicella vaccine should be given separately from the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/vaccines/index.html" target="_blank" >measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine</a>.</p><p>Much of the changed attitudes towards childhood vaccines appear to be driven by <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/kindergarten-routine-vaccination-rates-continue-to-decline/" target="_blank" >circulating misinformation about vaccines and a decline in trust in health authorities</a>. <a class="Link" href="https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/156/2/e2025072714/202656/Medical-vs-Nonmedical-Immunization-Exemptions-for?autologincheck=redirected" target="_blank" >Non-medical vaccine exemptions </a>for school attendance have been <a class="Link" href="https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/quality/public-health/nonmedical-vaccine-exemptions-on-the-rise-4-things-to-know/" target="_blank" >on the rise</a>, creating <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/01/14/health/vaccine-exemptions-county-risk-measles-vis" target="_blank" >pockets of disease outbreaks</a> and making it more difficult for school districts to achieve <a class="Link" href="https://historyofvaccines.org/vaccines-101/what-do-vaccines-do/how-herd-immunity-works" target="_blank" >herd immunity</a>.</p><p>Multiple decades of success with pediatric vaccines to protect against the plethora of childhood infectious diseases have confirmed their effectiveness and safety. <a class="Link" href="https://immunizationevidence.org/summary/vaccines-have-a-high-return-on-investment-every-1-spent-on-vaccine-programs-returns-up-to-44/" target="_blank" >Studies</a> have shown that money invested in childhood immunization has a positive return. Unfortunately, falsehoods and hesitancy about the COVID-19 vaccines fueled vaccine hesitancy against all vaccines, even those that have been well accepted for many decades.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.aap.org/" target="_blank" >American Academy of Pediatrics</a> took it upon itself to issue its own recommended childhood <a class="Link" href="https://downloads.aap.org/AAP/PDF/AAP-Immunization-Schedule.pdf" target="_blank" >immunization schedule</a>, closely aligning with the schedule that was eliminated by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/acip/index.html" target="_blank" >Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices</a>. In addition, the American College of Physicians <a class="Link" href="https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/ANNALS-25-01576?_gl=1*13dhed3*_gcl_aw*R0NMLjE3Njk2MzUxMTkuRUFJYUlRb2JDaE1JdGZTRTk4U0dfUUlWTU9iakJ4Mjl3d3dzRUFBWUFTQUFFZ0lNRF9EX0J3RQ..*_gcl_dc*R0NMLjE3Njk2MzUxMTkuRUFJYUlRb2JDaE1JdGZTRTk4U0dfUUlWTU9iakJ4Mjl3d3dzRUFBWUFTQUFFZ0lNRF9EX0J3RQ..*_gcl_au*MTM2MTAzNzA3MC4xNzY3MDI4NDk5*_ga*ODAzOTk2OTI5LjE3NTgxMzEwNDM.*_ga_PM4F5HBGFQ*czE3Njk2MzUxMDEkbzI4JGcxJHQxNzY5NjM1MTcyJGo2MCRsMCRoMA..&_ga=2.148120436.2107346431.1769616888-803996929.1758131043&_gac=1.49611410.1769635102.EAIaIQobChMItfSE98SG_QIVMObjBx29wwwsEAAYASAAEgIMD_D_BwE" target="_blank" >supports</a> the previous 2025 advisory committee recommendations.</p><p>These are no ordinary times when it comes to immunization. <a class="Link" href="https://www.immunize.org/vaccines/vaccine-timeline/" target="_blank" >Vaccines developed over the past 70 years</a> have prevented numerous infections and saved countless lives. Returning to <a class="Link" href="https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/immunizations/Pages/Vaccination-Protects-Against-These-Diseases.aspx" target="_blank" >earlier times</a> when children routinely were infected with numerous childhood diseases is not a formula for healthy living. The best advice that parents can take is to look to professional medical societies that have an established record of supporting health and healthy living and allow them to become the beacon of guidance for protecting your children and yourself. Indeed, the lights of reliable guidance and recommendations that once shone from the CDC have tragically gone dark.</p><p><i>Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a computer science professor in the Grainger College of Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. As a data scientist, he uses his expertise in risk-based analytics to address issues impacting public policy and public health.</i></p><p><i> Janet A. Jokela, M.D., is an infectious disease and public health physician, and clinical professor at Carle Illinois College of Medicine at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.  She serves as a member of the Illinois Immunization Advisory Committee. </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-300000" name="module-300000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. title: How changes to the child tax credit and other policies will impact parents
summary: <p>Parents looking for tax breaks in the 2025 tax year will find many options available to them, while undocumented and mixed-status families are at risk of losing certain federal tax benefits.</p><p>As President Donald Trump’s administration seeks to curb immigration, it’s also going after benefits that have historically been available to immigrant families.</p><p>Last year’s passage of the "One Big Beautiful Bill," included tax provisions that permanently increased the federal child tax credit from $2,000 to $2,200 per child under age 17, with annual adjustments for inflation starting in 2026. The credit phases out for single filers with a modified adjusted gross income of $200,000, or $400,000 for those married filing jointly.</p><p>But undocumented individuals or mixed status families may no longer be able to claim the credit, due to changes in the filing requirements.</p><p>That’s because the law now requires a parent, or spouse if filing jointly, to have a Social Security number, as well as the qualifying child. The change could impact around 176,000 children, who are U.S. citizens with undocumented parents, according to data from the Migration Policy Institute.</p><p>Before the bill passed last year, taxpayers could file with a taxpayer identification number, or TIN, which is commonly used among the immigrant community and for those without a Social Security number.</p><p>If a parent has little to no income tax liability, they could qualify for the additional child tax credit that provides up to $1,700 per qualifying child. The additional child tax credit allows low-income families to receive a cash payment, compared to the child tax credit that reduces a family’s tax liability.</p><p>In order to receive the additional credit, taxpayers are required to have earned income of at least $2,500.</p><p>This could impact veteran families, particularly those who are transitioning into the civilian workforce and may not yet have an income, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. The center estimates 21,000 veteran families in Illinois could be affected by the income threshold.</p><p>Veteran and immigrant families with at least one child under 12 may still be eligible for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/taxes/illinois-eitc-earned-income-tax-credit-claimed" >Illinois child tax credit</a>, which is 40% of a taxpayer’s state earned income tax credit, for tax year 2025. The benefit would be $300 to $600 per family, double the amount available last year.</p><h3>Dependent care credits</h3><p>There’s also a federal credit for other dependents, available to families with dependents who don’t meet the criteria to claim the child tax credit or additional child tax credit.</p><p>Filers can claim the $500 credit for a dependent child over age 16 or another dependent relative. The credit was available under the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and was made permanent with the passage of the new tax and spending bill, with the same income-based phaseouts as the child tax credit.</p><p>Another valuable tax credit for families is the child and dependent care credit, which covers a percentage of child care expenses for children under 13 or dependents who can’t care for themselves.</p><p>Trump’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act allows taxpayers to claim up to 50% of eligible expenses, starting this year. But the amount of expenses used to calculate the credit remains the same at $3,000 for one person, or $6,000 for two or more people, according to H&R Block.</p><p>The credit also phases down at higher income levels compared to previous years.</p><p>The 2025 federal tax bill expanded the annual contribution limit on dependent care accounts as well. Administered through certain employers, dependent care accounts — also known as flexible spending accounts — can now receive pretax contributions of up to $7,500 (up from $5,000) to be used for work-related child care expenses, including summer day camp.</p><h3>Adoption tax credit</h3><p>Adopting a child can be expensive, but some parents will see a significant tax relief to help offset some of the costs. Parents can claim the credit if the child is under age 18, or physically or mentally incapable of self-care.</p><p>For 2025, the maximum credit for qualified adoption expenses increases to $17,820 per child, up from $16,810 in 2024.</p><p>But one significant change started in 2025: Taxpayers who adopt can receive a refundable credit of up to $5,000. Prior to the bill’s passing, the federal credit was nonrefundable, so it could reduce the taxes owed to zero, but it couldn’t provide a tax refund.</p><p>Income limits were also adjusted under the massive bill. For the 2025 tax year, the full credit is available to filers with a modified adjusted gross income of up to $259,190. The credit phases out and becomes unavailable to those whose MAGI equals or exceeds $299,190.</p><h3>Child savings accounts</h3><p>Also new this year: Trump Accounts.</p><p>For American citizens who have a baby between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, the federal government will contribute $1,000 into a 530A account, also known as a Trump Account, on the child’s behalf. The account is similar to an individual retirement account and is expected to be available starting July.</p><p>Families can make annual after-tax contributions of up to $5,000. Employers and charitable organizations may also make contributions into the child’s account.</p><p>From ages 18 to 30, the child can withdraw the funds tax-free as long as it’s used for qualifying expenses such as higher education, job training, a first-time home purchase, starting a small business or certain workforce expenses. After age 30, the money is taxed as ordinary income.</p><p>Parents can fill out the new Form 4547 or elect to wait for an online portal that is expected to open in mid-2026.</p><p>Amanda Paton, partner and owner of Deerfield-based Clover CPAs and Consultants, said Trump Accounts are “not this overwhelming advantage, but it is something.”</p><p>She said the help is more limited given that Trump’s bill also cut funding for Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.</p><p>Meanwhile, the bill expanded how 529 plans can be used. The tax-advantaged accounts are an option for families who want to save for their child’s educational expenses.</p><p>The bill expanded qualifying expenses for K-12 costs to include tutoring, standardized test fees, books and more. And as of Jan. 1, parents can withdraw $20,000 per year to pay for K-12 expenses, up from $10,000.</p>

title: Funeral held for Chicago teen who battled cancer while fighting for father's release from ICE detention
summary: <p>The blue Ford Mustang that Ofelia Giselle Torres Hidalgo’s father gifted her helped escort the 16-year-old’s ivory coffin to St. William Parish on Friday morning in the Northwest Side's Montclare neighborhood. </p><p>Dozens of mourners hugged as they left the private funeral Mass on the cold, cloudy morning as church bells rang.</p><p>The Rev. Ryszard Gron, who delivered the funeral homily, told reporters outside the church that their community was “lucky to be accompanying the family of Ofelia.”</p><p>“Our future life will [always be based] on what we do here,” Gron said. “She will be happy now, and she is happy now in the hands of God.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel title: Review: “American Icons” showcases the exceptional melting pot that is the Joffrey and American dance
summary: <p>The Joffrey Ballet’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/dance/2024/09/18/joffrey-ballet-archives-exhibit-new-york-public-library" target="_blank" >early years</a> have been enshrined in American legend, as the small troupe toured the country in a station wagon full of entrepreneurial postwar spirit and youthful enthusiasm.</p><p>Founded in 1956 by Robert Joffrey, son of a Pashtun father and an Italian mother, and second-generation Italian immigrant Gerald Arpino, the 70-year-old company continues to draw exceptional dancers from around the world to Chicago. </p><p>The Joffrey is, quintessentially, a company of immigrants in an American city powered by immigration.</p><p>The Joffrey’s<a class="Link" href="https://joffrey.org/performances-and-tickets/25-26-season/american-icons/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=pmax&utm_campaign=americanicons26&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23482247753&gbraid=0AAAAADnc7R_3h1iG2VZahjlbnFjlJv6Eo&gclid=Cj0KCQiAqeDMBhDcARIsAJEbU9T3z-2I2sYEFUmW3UNLXFBUdN8Nfsjlywtqgafa6N_ziCNeP8-f6SIaAr_kEALw_wcB" target="_blank" > “American Icons” </a>program, running through March 1 at the Lyric, is, appropriately, a melting pot, too. Showcasing work by Joffrey and Arpino, plus dances by founding company dancer Glen Tetley and iconic modern choreographer Martha Graham, the evening’s collection evokes Old Vienna, Ancient Greece, Belle Époque Paris and the Catholic Church.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> Joffrey Ballet's "American Icons" </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c80000" name="module-c80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Where:</b> Lyric Opera of Chicago, 20 N. Wacker Drive<br><b>When:</b> Through March 1<br><b>Tickets:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://joffrey.org/performances-and-tickets/25-26-season/american-icons/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=pmax&utm_campaign=americanicons26&gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23482247753&gbraid=0AAAAADnc7R_3h1iG2VZahjlbnFjlJv6Eo&gclid=Cj0KCQiAqeDMBhDcARIsAJEbU9T3z-2I2sYEFUmW3UNLXFBUdN8Nfsjlywtqgafa6N_ziCNeP8-f6SIaAr_kEALw_wcB" target="_blank" >From $45</a><br></div> </div><p>Collectively, the works communicate a modern American perspective on the Old World, and they represent an essential Americanness even while expressing the statelessness of dance.</p><p>Arpino’s “Kettentanz” (1971), set to a suite of waltzes, polkas and galops by Johann Strauss Sr. and Johann Mayer, establishes the frisky tone that defines much of the program. Across eight variations the dancers prance and flirt, partnering with a light touch through at times impossibly brisk footwork.</p><p>Gayeon Jung and Evan Boersma (on opening night) share a waltzing duet marked by astonishing lifts, as Jung alternately leaps into Boersma’s arms and then seems to almost fly away. Elsewhere, the men aim to outdo each other with bravura tours and cabrioles, and a vivacious Ao Wang practically levitates as she bounces through a rapid-fire duet with Jung.</p><p>With Jack Mehler’s giant tree looming upstage, it’s as though the balls of Vienna are removed from the drawing room and restaged as a frolic in the bracing country air.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Martha Graham’s 1962 piece “Secular Games” features a loose and playful energy felt throughout the Joffrey’s “American Icons” program.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Cheryl Mann</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Graham’s 1962 piece “Secular Games” continues this loose and playful energy. Ostensibly set on a Greek island beach, the piece draws less explicitly from myth than Graham’s early work (no minotaurs, no Medea). Still, her modernist hallmarks endure.</p><p>Here six men, barechested, preen, stretch, arc, and contract like a clutch of peacocks, jousting their way through sets of stag leaps and other Graham angularities. As their torsos flex and ripple in courtship and competition, they manipulate their female partners into gloriously off-kilter shapes, arabesques askew and elbows akimbo.</p><p>But while all in all, this is a showcase of athletic masculine virility, a pas de deux for Boersma and Olivia Duryea pulls the work in a classical direction, as the pair moves together in fluid unity.</p><p>An excerpt from Joffrey’s “Postcards” (1980) is similarly lighthearted, enriched by the surprise appearance of mezzo-soprano Camille Robles. Clad in white, Anais Bueno and Stefan Gonçalvez execute a sinuous and youthful pas de deux. Bueno’s port de bras are exquisitely expressive, and the brief work feels both romantic and fresh. Robles’s rendition of a Satie chanson evokes the Parisian café setting and leaves the audience longing for more.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Cheryl Mann </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The mood shifts dramatically with the final work: Glen Tetley’s “Voluntaries,” created in 1973 for the Stuttgart Ballet as a memorial for his friend John Cranko. If the rest of “American Icons” channels America’s youthful exuberance, “Voluntaries” is a move into maturity, alternately elegiac and hopeful, grappling with mortality and meaning.</p><p>“Voluntaries” begins in silence and stillness, Joffrey principals Victoria Jaiani and Dylan Gutierrez in white unitards center stage against the backdrop of a glowing orb. They move forward and, as Jaiani extends her endless leg, the first chord of Poulenc’s “Concerto for Organ, Strings and Timpani” crashes down, breaking the spell, and she is lifted, spiraling toward the sky.</p><p>With the full company on stage, the work is a perpetual motion machine, the dancers moving in unison and in canon through motifs surely grueling in their technical demands. Tetley’s choreography is classical in essence but requires the dancers to twist and contract along unexpected meridians as they breathe through the endlessly iterating arabesques and sidelong tilts of modern dance.</p><p>The men eat up the stage with liquid leaps; the women are swept into daring lifts, piking overhead, diving to their partners’ ankles, and repeatedly borne aloft in narrow X’s reminiscent of the Crucifixion — an image later made explicit as the dancers repeatedly extend their arms, birdlike, into a downturned cross.</p><p>The religious, or spiritual, overtones are clear, with the organ blasts contributing to the air of majesty. As an exploration of grief, “Voluntaries” is emotional and expansive. With a purity of movement and intent, there is nothing coy happening here, just pain, joy and transcendence. The whole evening delivers, but in the stunning hands — and legs — of the Joffrey dancers, “Voluntaries” lifts the program to the heavens.<br></p>

title: Fiscal principal del Condado de Cook presenta plan para acusar a agentes de ICE de delitos
summary: <p>La fiscal estatal del Condado de Cook, Eileen O’Neill Burke, presentó nuevas directrices el jueves para procesar los presuntos delitos de los agentes federales de inmigración, después de desaprobar de un plan propuesto por el alcalde Brandon Johnson y enfrentar una creciente presión para hacer más frente a las tácticas a veces agresivas y violentas de los federales.</p><p>Esta medida representa el paso más tangible que la oficina de O’Neill Burke ha tomado para reprimir a los agentes federales que llevan a cabo la agresiva campaña de deportación del presidente Donald Trump.</p><p>“Nadie está por encima de la ley, incluidos los agentes de ICE y los fiscales”, dijo O'Neill Burke en un comunicado. “Si un agente de la ley federal comete un delito, mi oficina no dudará en actuar de acuerdo con la ley estatal. Este protocolo establece pautas claras y legalmente sólidas para garantizar que tengamos un camino responsable y efectivo para buscar responsabilidad”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ba0000" name="module-ba0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Según las directrices, las agencias de aplicación de la ley dirigirán las investigaciones criminales recolectando y preservando evidencias. Si las autoridades necesitan asistencia para obtener testimonios jurados o evidencias adicionales que no se ofrezcan de manera voluntaria, la oficina de la fiscal estatal puede intervenir y constituir un gran jurado.</p><p>Los fiscales llevarán a cabo una revisión independiente de todas las evidencias y tomarán decisiones sobre las acusaciones, tal como lo hacen en todos los casos de delitos graves.</p><p>Sin embargo, en estos casos, la oficina de O’Neill Burke también tendrá que considerar las protecciones específicas que se ofrecen a los agentes federales en servicio, lo que demuestra que el oficial no tiene inmunidad bajo la Cláusula de Supremacía. Esto protege a los oficiales federales de la prosecución estatal mientras actúan en su capacidad oficial, siempre que “no hicieran más de lo necesario y correcto”.</p><p>El protocolo para presentar cargos, desarrollado en colaboración con el fiscal general de Illinois, Kwame Raoul, y la Asociación de Fiscales del Estado de Illinois, fue elogiado por el alcalde Johnson, cuyo decreto ejecutivo “ICE sobre aviso” recibió fuertes críticas de la oficina de O’Neill Burke a principios de este mes.</p><p>La objeción se basaba en la decisión de Johnson de ordenar a la Policía de Chicago que hiciera referencias penales a los fiscales “bajo la dirección de la Oficina del Alcalde”. La oficina de O’Neill Burke calificó la orden de “totalmente inapropiada”, diciendo que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/06/eileen-oneill-burke-brandon-johnson-immigration-ice-law" target="_blank" >plantea problemas de interferencia política</a> que podrían poner en peligro los casos criminales. Pero el jueves, Johnson emitió un comunicado diciendo que su orden y las nuevas directrices de O’Neill Burke son “aspectos alineados del mismo marco de seguridad pública”.</p><p>“El Protocolo de la Fiscal Estatal establece el proceso de enjuiciamiento que sigue a esas referencias, asegurando que los casos sean evaluados bajo los mismos estándares legales que se aplican a cualquier otra persona”, destacó Johnson. “Juntos, refuerzan un principio simple: los agentes federales que operan en Chicago siguen sujetos a la ley, y cuando ocurren incidentes graves, debe haber un camino claro y coordinado hacia la responsabilidad”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fbccfd" Larry Snelling walks past Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson before a press conference at the Chicago Police Headquarters, Tuesday, Oct. 31, 2023." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/69e5cf7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6041x3390+0+318/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F0d%2F4532124df4d3ada2b0471abb0034%2Fshoot-110123-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/389b0b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6041x3390+0+318/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F0d%2F4532124df4d3ada2b0471abb0034%2Fshoot-110123-7.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/69e5cf7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6041x3390+0+318/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F65%2F0d%2F4532124df4d3ada2b0471abb0034%2Fshoot-110123-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>El superintendente de la Policía de Chicago, Larry Snelling, pasa junto al alcalde Brandon Johnson antes de una conferencia de prensa en la sede de la policía en octubre de 2023.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>‘Por lo menos hay una política establecida’ </b></h3><p>Durante el último mes, funcionarios electos han instado a O’Neill Burke a actuar con la misma agresividad que sus contrapartes en Minnesota, en respuesta a los tiroteos fatales por parte de agentes federales. O’Neill Burke ha mantenido que su oficina está <a class="Link" href="http://limited in its ability to actually prosecute" target="_blank" >limitada en su capacidad de realmente procesar</a> y condenar a agentes federales en servicio.</p><p>Mientras tanto, su oficina ha estado trabajando para desarrollar un sistema que aclare los roles que los policías y los fiscales jugarán en la investigación y en la presentación de cargos contra los agentes federales acusados de delitos, incluidos los tiroteos y otros actos de violencia.</p><p>El fiscal general Kwame Raoul enfatizó la importancia de tener “un entendimiento común de cuál es la ley en estas situaciones y qué protocolo debería implementarse para hacer cumplir la ley”.</p><p>“No se trata sólo de si crees o no que alguien hizo algo mal, se trata de si, con las evidencias que tienes disponibles, has llegado a un punto donde puedes proceder, donde estás seguro de que puedes probar el caso más allá de una duda razonable”, dijo Raoul en una entrevista.</p><p>Raoul afirmó que comprende las frustraciones de los funcionarios electos y los miembros de la comunidad que han visto videos virales de personas siendo asesinadas por agentes federales. Pero dijo que es crucial que los fiscales sigan las nuevas directrices y advirtió contra el riesgo de sobrepasar su autoridad.</p><p>“Una de las cosas de las que debemos tener cuidado es no caer en lo mismo por lo que criticamos al actual presidente”, dijo. “El presidente Trump ha, en muchas ocasiones, dado directivas muy públicas al Departamento de Justicia y a otras fuerzas del orden para perseguir a individuos específicos”.</p><p>En los últimos seis meses, los agentes federales han arrasado ciudades en todo el país, llevando a cabo el audaz operativo de aplicación de Trump. Los agentes han desatado niveles sin precedentes de fuerza, utilizando gas lacrimógeno, bolas de gas pimienta y disparando fatalmente a personas en Minneapolis y Chicago en los últimos meses.</p><p>Hasta ahora, ningún agente federal ha sido acusado de cometer un delito mientras estaba en el trabajo.</p><p>El abogado de Marimar Martínez, la mujer de Chicago que fue baleada por un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza el otoño pasado en el vecindario de Brighton Park, dijo que es optimista de que el protocolo actuará como “un poco de disuasión”, especialmente si los federales regresan con fuerza.</p><p>“Por lo menos hay una política establecida en el Condado de Cook de que si actúan ilegalmente, al menos podrían estar potencialmente sujetos a algún tipo de investigación”, dijo el abogado Chris Parente. “Creo que eso es mejor que nada”.</p><p>Parente ha sido informado de que hay una investigación activa sobre la conducta del agente Charles Exum por parte de la oficina del fiscal en South Bend, Indiana. Pero si esa investigación no avanza, Parente dijo que recurrirá a los fiscales estatales.</p><p>Las autoridades en Minneapolis han iniciado una investigación sobre los tiroteos fatales de Renee Good y Alex Pretti, pero no han presentado cargos y están encontrando obstáculos para obtener pruebas del gobierno federal.</p><p>En el Condado de Cook, un oficial del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) ha sido <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/23/ice-officer-charged-with-attacking-immigrant-rights-activist-in-chicago-suburbs" target="_blank" >acusado de atacar a un manifestante</a> mientras estaba fuera de servicio en Brookfield.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
author: Sophie Sherry

title: Marked decline in homicides, robberies proves critics wrong about Pretrial Fairness Act
summary: <p>Beginning two years ago, crime began plummeting across the country — including here in Chicago. The decrease we’ve seen since the high-water mark during the pandemic is astounding. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/criminal-justice/2025/04/16/chicagos-robbery-surge-is-over" target="_blank" >Starting in July 2024</a>, Chicago began experiencing a double-digit drop in robberies compared to the year prior. At the end of 2025, they had <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2025/12/30/chicago-set-end-2025-fewest-homicides-years-after-30-drop" target="_blank" >dropped 35%</a>. </p><p>Murders likewise began <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/cpd/2025/05/01/chicago-hasnt-seen-an-april-with-fewer-murders-since-1962" target="_blank" >dramatically declining in 2023</a>, and last year, Chicago had its <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/2025-chicago-had-fewest-murders-recorded-1960s-violent-crime-down-preliminary-cpd-data/18338816/?userab=abcn_du_cat_topic_feature_holdout-474*variant_b_redesign-1939,abcn_news_for_you_exp-528*variant_b_bptt-2204" target="_blank" >lowest murder rate in 60 years</a>.</p><p>We should be celebrating this data, which represents real human lives saved and injuries avoided, while also exploring what caused the drop in violent crime and then modeling those practices. Fortunately, experts are fairly uniform in their assessment: We invested in communities.</p><p>Wesley Skogan, a professor emeritus at Northwestern University who analyzes crime numbers, attributed the drop to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/criminal-justice/2025/04/16/chicagos-robbery-surge-is-over" target="_blank" >the more frequent use of violence interruption programs and fully functional youth and recreational services</a>. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cc0000" name="module-cc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Nationally recognized crime data analyst Jeff Asher likewise <a class="Link" href="https://jasher.substack.com/p/why-i-think-murder-is-plunging" target="_blank" >theorizes that</a>, “a strong investment in communities from private and public sources after the shock of the pandemic stands out as a major cause” of the decrease in homicides." </p><p>That includes money spent on infrastructure, violence intervention, job support and supporting communities. Some of the money came from state and local investments, and some from the federal government. Unfortunately, President Donald Trump is now rolling back many of these investments and using U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Border Patrol and the threat of the National Guard to destabilize our communities.</p><p>We cannot forget that we now have a blueprint for community safety that is worth pursuing. Unlike jail and prison, these community investments actually address the root causes of crime.</p><p>Even as our investments are working, some want to return to the failed “lock 'em up” policies that created mass incarceration but didn’t create safety. Trump has made a concerted effort to take credit for our success in Illinois, saying that decreases in crime — which significantly predate the federal government's invasion — are due to its reign of terror and kidnapping residents off the street.</p><p>Just as decreases in crime started long before Trump’s invasion, decreases in crime started long before the new Cook County state’s attorney took office. Crime started falling in 2023 from its COVID-19 high, and the trends in Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://jasher.substack.com/p/why-i-think-murder-is-plunging" target="_blank" >mirror those we see across the country</a>. This, of course, suggests that the professors and data analysts are right: Something else is afoot.</p><p>We also know that increased jailing actually leads to negative public safety consequences long term. Studies have repeatedly shown that even <a class="Link" href="https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/security=policy:eyJleHBpcnkiOjQwNzg3NjQwMDAsImNhbGwiOlsicGljayIsInJlYWQiLCJ3cml0ZSIsIndyaXRlVXJsIiwic3RvcmUiLCJjb252ZXJ0IiwicmVtb3ZlIiwicnVuV29ya2Zsb3ciXX0=,signature:9df63ee50143fbd862145c8fb4ed2fcc17d068183103740b1212c4c9bc858f63/NPfbpQtCQzyQFam13VLU" target="_blank" >short periods of pretrial jailing increase the likelihood that someone will be arrested again</a>.</p><p>It is no coincidence that the decrease in crime has coincided with the number of people jailed awaiting trial decreasing over the last decade. It’s because ensuring as many people as possible are home awaiting trial has long-term, positive consequences. People are able to keep their jobs, family and community connections and housing while awaiting their day in court.</p><p>When implemented, the Pretrial Fairness Act ended the use of money bond in 2023. We ensured that families would no longer have to choose between paying the rent or paying ransom to secure the constitutional right to the presumption of innocence. </p><p>Judges are now receiving more information and spending more time on decisions regarding pretrial release and detention. And most importantly, the law is working. In Cook County, the vast majority of people on pretrial release are succeeding. In the two years since the Pretrial Fairness Act took effect, <a class="Link" href="https://ocj-web-files.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/documents/2025-12-27_OCJ_PFA_Dashboard_New_Layout_25.12.15_FINAL.pdf?VersionId=SB34JEQ_HSHWWp197pKXbqCLujcAOTng" target="_blank" >94% of the more than 130,000 people released pretrial have not been charged with new offenses against a person</a>, according to summary data compiled by staff at the Cook County chief judge's office.</p><p>We must not lose sight of what works. In 2023, in addition to ending money bond, opening back up our schools, recreation centers and public gathering spaces, we started investing in programs that have been shown to actually protect safety: <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2025/april/20-Mil-Violence-Intervention-Grant.html" target="_blank" >community violence interruption programs</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/06/illinois-opioid-drug-overdose-deaths" target="_blank" >substance use disorder treatment and harm reduction programs</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicagohealthonline.com/change-makers/" target="_blank" >hospital-based violence intervention programs</a> that support the people most affected by gun violence.</p><p>These investments and reforms to our criminal legal system are working. It would be a mistake to allow politicians who are focused on advancing their careers at the expense of our communities to allow us to return to the failed “public safety” policies of the past. It takes a long time for root-cause solutions to show results, and we are finally seeing the effect here in Chicago and nationally.</p><p><i>Illinois state Rep. Lisa Davis, D-Chicago, represents the 32nd District.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-600000" name="module-600000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
author: Lisa Davis

title: Operation Midway Blitz fallout lingers in Latino neighborhoods
summary: <p>The ground shifted under Chicago last fall. What's normal in the city's majority-Latino communities today isn't what it was before Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>The Southeast Side, long defined by steel mills and working-class communities, was one of the first places Mexicans came to Chicago more than a century ago. On the Lower West Side, Pilsen stands out for its colorful murals, rich arts and culinary scene and lively Mexican American culture. Farther southwest, Little Village, also known as La Villita, has a vibrant commercial corridor and community celebrations like the Mexican Independence Day parade that are among the oldest and largest in the Midwest.</p><p>These neighborhoods carved separate paths to becoming majority-Latino and cultural centers for Mexican communities in Chicago. But they shared a common experience last fall: the Trump administration's Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/live/2025/09/16/cbp-raids-ice-chicago-elgin-operation-at-large" >The immigration enforcement campaign began Sept. 16,</a> Mexican Independence Day.</p><p>Federal officials said the operation targeted violent criminals without legal status, though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/03/28/tren-de-aragua-venezuela-gang-trump-tom-homan-terrorism-violence-crime-chicago-colombia-honduras-ecuador-nicolas-maduro-salvador" >this proved largely untrue</a>. As enforcement increased, fear spread across Chicago and its suburbs. Latino and immigrant-majority neighborhoods, including Pilsen, Little Village and the Southeast Side, went on high alert.</p><p>These communities developed their Latino identities over generations, shaped by migration, labor and displacement. Trump’s targeted immigration operations created a shared moment in their histories — a moment filled with fear, uncertainty and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/02/13/shop-local-campaign-brighton-park-immigration-raids-local-businesses" >community pride</a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> century</h3><h4>Southeast Side </h4><p>Chicago’s Mexican American population first took root in the early 1900s. Many arrived in 1919, when they were recruited during a national steel mill strike. These communities became part of the backbone of heavily industrial South Chicago and the East Side, creating an identity that endures today.</p><p>In 1923, the community established Our Lady of Guadalupe Church, the first Mexican American parish in the city.</p><p>As of 2023, Latinos on the East Side and South Chicago made up half of the neighborhoods’ 52,000 residents, according to the Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning. The East Side alone is nearly 90% Latino.</p><p><b>Stories from South Chicago and the Southeast Side</b>: <a class="Link" href="#sc-masa" >Cecy’s Molino de Masa</a> | <a class="Link" href="#sc-maria" Pilsen became known for its Mexican and Mexican American identity — its streets lined with colorful murals, Mexican stores and restaurants — the neighborhood was home to waves of European immigrants. Named after Plzeň in what is now the Czech Republic, Pilsen began to change in the mid-20th century as Mexican and Puerto Rican families moved in, many displaced from the Near West Side by expressway construction and the expansion of the University of Illinois Chicago campus.</p><p>By the 1960s, Pilsen had become predominantly Latino, shaped by social activism, civic engagement and artistic expression. Today, Pilsen is 68% Latino and Hispanic, according to U.S. Census data. In recent years, rising housing costs and new development have raised concerns about gentrification and the displacement of longtime residents.</p><p><b>Stories from Pilsen and the Southwest Side</b>: This plan was met with resistance from the Chicago Board of Education.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h4>Little Village</h4><p>Located in South Lawndale, Little Village was once known as “Czech California,” reflecting its strong Czech, Slovak and other Eastern European communities and their businesses along 26th Street.</p><p>In the mid-1960s, as Black people moved to neighboring North Lawndale, the white business owners and leaders of South Lawndale began calling that area “Little Village” to highlight the European ethnic community and differentiate it from North Lawndale, according to a city report on the neighborhood’s history. But Little Village’s white residents still moved to the suburbs, leaving room for Mexican families, many of whom were pushed west from Pilsen.</p><p>By 1980, Latinos made up nearly half of Little Village’s population, with Mexicans as the dominant group. In 1990, the Mexican government donated the Little Village arch, cementing the neighborhood's identity. It reads “Bienvenidos a Little Village.”</p><p>The neighborhood was proud of its roots. Many began to call Little Village the “Mexico of the Midwest.” The latest U.S. Census data shows South Lawndale, still the area’s official name, is 81% Latino and Hispanic.</p><p>The Pilsen and Little Village corridor now has the largest concentration of Latinos in the Midwest. Little Village’s 26th Street commercial corridor generates millions in annual revenue and is the city's second highest tax-generating district, after the Magnificent Mile.</p><p><b>Stories from Little The funeral service was at St. Pius Catholic Church, 1919 S. Ashland Ave., and the procession went down 26th Street in Pilsen. Washington attended the funeral.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Operation Midway Blitz’s disruption of communities</h3><p>The feds’ targeting of Latino and immigrant-majority neighborhoods wasn’t surprising, but the agents’ aggression, detention of nonviolent immigrants and blatant contempt for people of color became flash points.</p><p>Early during Operation Midway Blitz, in September, Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino told a WBEZ reporter that some people are arrested based partly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/28/ice-agents-spotted-downtown-on-michigan-avenue-along-chicago-river" >on “how they look.”</a></p><p>Toward the end of the operation, on Nov. 10, dozens of Border Patrol agents posed Downtown in front of The Bean. As they prepared to take the picture, an agent reportedly said, “Everyone say ‘Little Village!” According to media reports, the agents shouted back “Little Village!”</p><p>In between, federal agents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/05/daycare-teacher-taken-by-ice-north-side-immigration" >disrupted daily life</a>, particularly in places like Little Village, Pilsen and the Southeast Side. Immigrants and other Chicagoans feared detention while walking outside, waiting for the bus or taking children to school.</p><p>In some neighborhoods, the streets were empty. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/07/chicago-business-civic-leaders-ice-economy" >Business owners saw drastic declines in sales.</a> Some feared having to close. Community events and parades were canceled.</p><p>Neighborhoods known for their vibrancy and close-knit community life were quiet.</p><p>Families feared separation, and parents worried about the long-term impact on their children.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" >Critics of the immigration operations pointed to violent tactics</a>, performative operations and unconstitutional detentions. Supporters said the federal government was targeting violent and dangerous immigrants.</p><p>According to U.S. Department of Justice documents, 97% of those detained during Operation Midway Blitz had no criminal records.</p><p>The Trump administration continued to push the narrative that it was taking murders and rapists off the streets.</p><p>After the agents posed at The Bean, they began leaving Chicago. The federal influx of some 300 agents for Operation Midway Blitz ended. But ICE enforcement — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — continues. And while that enforcement has remained at pre-Blitz levels, the communities the feds swarmed are changed. href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wbez-staff" >WBEZ Staff </a></strong> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div> </div><p>Before Operation Midway Blitz, the captains and runners of Viento, the Little Village run club, would message each other only to cancel a run. Now they message to check if there have been sightings of federal agents and then decide when they’ll run and their route.</p><p>“I'm usually checking in, ‘How are you all personally?’ but also, ‘What do you think about running today? What's something that we should keep an eye on?’” says Jess Vergara, 37, who was part of the group that created the club 13 years ago. “So we are prepared when things kind of pop up.”</p><p>The club has a new rule: No one can run by themselves. Vergara says runners will slow down or run back to make sure no one is too far behind.</p><p>Viento means "wind" in Spanish. The club is mostly Latino and runs three times a week, meeting at 26th Street and South Central Park Avenue, as they have for 13 years.</p><p>Residents recognize them. Business owners wave as they pass, and members often gather after runs at restaurants for coffee.</p><p>Federal immigration agents arrived in September, about a month before the Chicago Marathon. For many runners, not running wasn’t an option after weeks of training.</p><p>Vergara and the other captains wanted to keep the runners safe. They mapped out routes and water stops; they identified safe havens in case agents targeted them. Members provided emergency contacts in case any runners were detained. The club held Know Your Rights training for runners and their families.</p><p>Now, Vergara says, they are trying to keep the runners motivated, but they are also preparing, in case the feds come back.</p><p>“We are constantly checking the news, what other organizations are doing in La Villita and around Chicago,” she says. “We keep in touch with the rapid response teams and see what they're saying.”</p><p>“It's such a different feeling. It's this constant vigilance and heightened anxiety."</p><p><a class="Link" href="#lv-top" ><i>Return to top</i></a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a
