title: Democrats have a chance to pounce
summary: <p>President Donald Trump's approval rating is sinking and gasping for air. His average net approval stands at negative 13.7, which is lower than Joe Biden's was at this point in his term. This matters beyond cosmic justice: The president's approval rating is the best predictor of midterm election outcomes. When it falls below 50%, his party tends to lose seats, as in the 1982, 1994, 2006, 2010, 2014 and 2018 elections.</p><p>So the Democratic Party, written off as dead by some a few months ago, stands poised for victory in November. That's good, but not good enough.</p><p>The stakes are so high that a win isn't sufficient to meet the moment. We need a crushing repudiation of this fascistic horror show.</p><p>The easiest issue, perhaps surprisingly, is immigration. Since 2024, Democrats have been snakebit on the subject, afraid that their instinctive pro-immigrant positions were unpopular enough to lead voters to select a snarling villain vowing mass deportations. They can exhale. What the polls over the last year suggest is that most Americans are not white-supremacist goons like Stephen Miller, ready to trash the Constitution in the name of purifying <i>die Volk</i>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d10000" name="module-d10000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Columnist</div> </div><p>Instead, voters actually believed that Trump would only deport "the worst of the worst." As they watched the inhuman treatment of gardeners, veterans, children and American citizen protesters, they soured fast. After the shooting of Alex Pretti, fully 60% of respondents told NBC they disapproved of Trump's immigration policies, 49% strongly so.</p><p>If Democrats present themselves as opposing the brutal tactics of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection and favoring firm border controls, they should find themselves in the sweet spot. Messages like Billie Eilish's "No one is illegal on stolen land" are unhelpful. By all means, get angry about the savagery; stress that law and order means that first and foremost the state cannot be the lawbreaker. But also add that borders are not notional, and chaos cannot be permitted to prevail along the Rio Grande.</p><p>The other big issue on voters' minds is inflation, or "affordability." The reality is that politicians cannot actually bring prices down, as Trump promised to do in 2024, except by crashing the economy. Still, some voters presumably believed him, and they are disillusioned now. Some Democrats may be tempted to run on taxing the rich. This is a comfortable old shoe for Democrats, but as a political strategy it hasn't been terribly successful. Middle-class voters often fear that they will be labeled as rich.</p><p>On the other hand, voters have already concluded that tariffs are making life more expensive. The issue is a layup — if Democrats can get out of their own way. Nearly 60% of Americans blame Trump for rising prices, and 65% disapprove of his tariffs. Fifty-nine percent of independent voters say the tariffs have hurt the economy and their personal finances. Voters are rarely able to connect policy to outcomes, but they have done so in the case of tariffs. Back in 2024, Americans were about equally divided on the question of trade, with some favoring higher tariffs and roughly similar numbers opting for lower tariffs. Experience has changed their views.</p><p>The progressive wing of the party has long favored tariffs as a way to protect American workers from competition from low-wage nations. This muddies the waters.</p><p>Cutting tariffs is one of the only levers governments can pull that will actually reduce prices, and since price sensitivity is very much on voters' minds, does it make sense to temper that message at all? All House Democrats voted in favor of a resolution that would end the national emergency excuse for tariffs, and three Republicans joined them. This is the moment. Tariffs are bad — full stop.</p><p>Finally, a vulnerability that Democrats must overcome is seeming to be soft on crime. Here again the Trump administration has handed them a golden opportunity. MAGA is so fixated on ethnic cleansing that it is pulling Justice Department officials off crime-fighting to pursue immigration cases. A memo from acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed officers who had been working on transnational organized crime, money-laundering and major drug trafficking networks to focus instead on assisting ICE. Ditto for the FBI Joint Terrorism Task Forces. In fact, about 25% of FBI agents (and 40% in larger field offices) have been diverted from fighting financial crimes, public corruption, cybercrime and complex corporate investigations and pulled into immigration enforcement. Most maddening are the thousands of FBI and Homeland Security agents who've been pulled from investigations of child sex abuse to assist with deportations — as if the administration needed more ways of signaling that it's OK with child sex trafficking.</p><p>Democrats should stress that the funds appropriated for ICE would be far better deployed to local police departments. Bill Clinton's promise to hire 100,000 police officers was very popular in the '90s and cut against the Democrats' soft-on-crime image. The slogans write themselves: More Cops, Less ICE.</p><p>The voters are the last redoubt in the fight to reclaim American democracy and decency, and the Democratic Party, the world's oldest political party since the advent of universal suffrage, is the only entity that can carry the burden. If it can win a resounding victory in the House and Senate in nine months, there is hope for us.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of The Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6d0000" name="module-6d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
author: Mona Charen

title: Longtime incumbent Preckwinkle faces stiff challenge from Ald. Reilly in Cook County board president primary
summary: <p>Chicago Ald. Brendan Reilly, one of the most conservative members of the City Council, who bills himself as an independent voice, wants a new gig: to run Cook County government.</p><p>He’s looking to unseat longtime County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, who doubles as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2024/03/14/toni-preckwinkle-political-muscle-democrats-march-primary-election" ><u>powerful leader</u> </a>of the Cook County Democratic Party, in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/how-to-vote-illinois-primary" ><u>general primary</u> </a>on March 17, Preckwinkle’s 79th birthday.</p><p>She oversees one of the biggest counties in the U.S., including the county’s jail, vast court system and large public health system that has a mission to treat patients <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2025/05/23/how-medicaid-cuts-from-congress-could-affect-every-cook-county-resident" target="_blank" ><u>no matter if they can pay</u></a>. The county employs more than 20,000 people and has a roughly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/11/20/cook-county-board-toni-preckwinkle-10-billion-2026-budget" target="_blank" ><u>$10 billion annual budget</u></a> that must be approved by a 17-member board of separately elected commissioners. Preckwinkle also oversees the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2024/04/27/palos-preserves-gets-10-million-makeover" target="_blank" ><u>Forest Preserves</u></a> of Cook County.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8e0000" name="image-8e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/48521c8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7392x4149+0+391/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fac%2Fc44b3d5b4d9894dcc51cdafbc2b5%2Fmayorbudget-101725-50.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bc1a541/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7392x4149+0+391/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fac%2Fc44b3d5b4d9894dcc51cdafbc2b5%2Fmayorbudget-101725-50.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8864ddb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7392x4149+0+391/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fac%2Fc44b3d5b4d9894dcc51cdafbc2b5%2Fmayorbudget-101725-50.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) speaks with reporters after Mayor Brandon Johnson presented his proposed 2026 budget during a Chicago City Council meeting Oct. 16, 2025." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8864ddb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7392x4149+0+391/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fac%2Fc44b3d5b4d9894dcc51cdafbc2b5%2Fmayorbudget-101725-50.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3bdf7cf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7392x4149+0+391/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fac%2Fc44b3d5b4d9894dcc51cdafbc2b5%2Fmayorbudget-101725-50.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8864ddb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7392x4149+0+391/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff3%2Fac%2Fc44b3d5b4d9894dcc51cdafbc2b5%2Fmayorbudget-101725-50.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) speaks with reporters after Mayor Brandon Johnson presented his proposed 2026 budget during a Chicago City Council meeting Oct. 16, 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Reilly, 54, who has represented downtown Chicago for roughly 19 years, is hammering Preckwinkle over a property tax system upgrade that, according to the Chicago Tribune and Injustice Watch, has been plagued by delays. Property tax bills have gone out late, causing school districts across the region to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/19/property-tax-payment-delay-costs-chicago-public-schools-almost-a-quarter-million-dollars-a-day" target="_blank" ><u>take out loans</u></a> with interest, as they waited to collect their share of property taxes.</p><p>“While my opponent has had a great career in public service, she’s stayed a bit too long,” Reilly said. “Cook County government is broken in a number of areas that are making it a lot less affordable to be able to live here.”</p><p>Reilly said he would terminate the county’s contract with Tyler Technologies, which has been working to upgrade the technology behind the property tax system for years, if needed.</p><p>Preckwinkle countered she’s one of several separately elected officials who oversee a complicated tax system. Other elected officials, such as the county assessor and treasurer, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/02/06/what-to-know-democratic-primary-cook-county-assessor-fritz-kaegi-pat-hynes" target="_blank" ><u>determine property values</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/18/cook-county-treasurer-maria-pappas-mayoral-campaign-chicago-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>mail tax bills</u></a>.</p><p>“My view has been to try to get people to work together to solve the problems,” Preckwinkle said. “You can’t do that if you point fingers and throw people under the bus.”</p><div class="Enhancement" JB Pritzker speak after signing the Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act during a ceremony at Union Station Dec. 16, 2025. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Preckwinkle is known for running a tight financial ship. She hasn’t raised the county’s portion of property taxes during her 16-year tenure, though a <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2017/10/16/toni-preckwinkle-soda-tax-repeal-county-budget-shortfall" target="_blank" ><u>soda tax she supported years ago was repealed</u></a> after a huge backlash. The county’s pension fund is funded around 66%, <a class="Link" href="https://www.civicfed.org/dashboard/localgovtpensions" target="_blank" ><u>more than double</u></a> some of the city’s pension funds. The county has received four bond rating upgrades since 2021, while Chicago is mired in debt.</p><p>Preckwinkle underscores that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/12/19/chicago-city-council-approves-alternate-revenue-plan-minus-mayor-brandon-johnsons-corporate-head-tax" target="_blank" ><u>Reilly and a group</u></a> of conservative and moderate alders recently muscled through a Chicago budget that includes a host of tax hikes, including a property tax increase for Chicago public libraries. While the budget avoided a new tax on the city’s largest corporations, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2025/12/12/corporate-head-tax-brandon-johnson-2026-proposed-budget-job-killer-claim" target="_blank" ><u>detested by Chicago’s business community</u></a>, it “puts the burden entirely on taxpayers while exempting labor from any shared burden,” and included “only a handful of efficiencies and cost savings,” the Civic Federation, a non-partisan government watchdog, <a class="Link" href="https://civicfed.org/chicagos-fy2026-adopted-budget" target="_blank" ><u>wrote in an analysis</u></a>.</p><p>Roughly $5 billion of the city’s $16.6 billion budget this year will go toward pension and debt payments, after decades of mismanagement. That burden contributed to a nearly $1.2 billion gap between revenue and expenses in 2026, as the city has limited avenues to raise money aside from property tax and fee hikes.</p><p>Preckwinkle is a former history teacher and longtime Chicago alderperson representing the South Side before she was elected county board president in 2010. She uses her political power and progressive values to shape how the county spends money. She has championed <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/cook-county/2025/04/08/cook-county-leaders-are-touting-the-success-of-their-guaranteed-income-pilot-program" target="_blank" ><u>guaranteed income </u></a>for low to moderate income residents, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2025/06/05/cook-county-erases-nearly-665-million-in-medical-debt-for-more-than-a-half-million-residents" target="_blank" ><u>erased more than $600 million of medical debt</u></a>, and helped <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/the-end-of-cash-bail-in-illinois" target="_blank" ><u>eliminate cash bail</u></a> in Illinois. She has mentored many into higher office.</p><p>Reilly got his start in public service in the 1990s and worked as an aide to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2025/02/13/what-former-illinois-house-speaker-michael-madigans-conviction-means-for-his-legacy" target="_blank" ><u>now-convicted </u></a>former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan. He left for the private sector and worked as an AT&T executive before defeating long-serving City Council incumbent, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2020/6/11/21288690/former-downtown-ald-burt-natarus-dies-council-obituary-carriages-valet-street-musicians" target="_blank" ><u>Burt Natarus</u></a>, in 2007.</p><p>Reilly hasn’t faced an opponent since. In 2020, he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2020/10/27/21537277/alderman-brendan-reilly-states-attorney-kim-foxx-republican-pat-obrien-cook-county" target="_blank" ><u>broke with the Democratic Party</u></a> to endorse Republican Patrick O’Brien over Kim Foxx, Preckwinkle’s former chief of staff, for Cook County state’s attorney.</p><h3>Preckwinkle runs again because of Trump</h3><p>Preckwinkle said she was inspired to run for a fifth, four-year term to guard against Republican President Donald Trump. His One Big Beautiful Bill calls for <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/medicaid/allocating-cbos-estimates-of-federal-medicaid-spending-reductions-across-the-states-enacted-reconciliation-package/" target="_blank" ><u>sweeping cuts</u></a> to public programs that support thousands of county residents, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2025/05/23/how-medicaid-cuts-from-congress-could-affect-every-cook-county-resident" target="_blank" ><u>could put a big dent</u></a> in the overall county budget.</p><p>As immigration agents detained people off the streets and fired <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/21/judge-hands-down-critical-review-of-federal-immigration-agents-unprecedented-use-of-force" target="_blank" ><u>pepper balls and tear gas</u></a> at protesters throughout Chicago and the suburbs, she issued an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/16/preckwinkle-issues-executive-order-to-create-ice-free-zones-in-cook-county" target="_blank" ><u>executive order</u></a> to create “ICE-free zones” in Cook County.</p><p>“Trump’s declared war on us,” Preckwinkle said. “We need somebody who’s going to stand up to him and stand for our residents and the rule of law. He’s not that man,” she said of Reilly.</p><p>She points to his support for a measure aimed at creating carveouts in Chicago’s sanctuary law that prohibit police from helping with civil immigration enforcement. Reilly was one of 11 Council members who pushed for a vote on the now-stalled measure, after a chorus of advocacy organizations <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/01/10/donald-trump-deportation-plan-ice-immigration-advocates-chicago-police" target="_blank" ><u>warned it</u></a> would open the door to constitutional rights violations and legal challenges.</p><p>In a statement, Reilly said he supports abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and returning the agency to its “core functions during the Obama administration.” He said he would defend the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountyil.gov/news/president-preckwinkle-signs-executive-order-banning-use-cook-county-owned-property-and" target="_blank" ><u>county’s restrictions</u></a> on using local resources for certain federal immigration enforcement. But he supports carveouts for people arrested or convicted for felonies such as sex crimes involving children or gang-related violence.</p><p>One of the biggest challenges the county faces is bracing for an estimated almost $300 million in losses per year, largely due to people losing their health insurance. Low-income residents who have public Medicaid health insurance will have <a class="Link" href="https://hfs.illinois.gov/info/fedresctr/medicaidfedpolicychfs.html" target="_blank" ><u>new work requirements</u></a> next year and more frequent checks to make sure they qualify, while others might drop insurance they bought on the government exchanges because <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/health-subsidies-expire-launching-millions-of-americans-into-2026-with-steep-insurance-hikes" target="_blank" ><u>subsidies are gone</u></a>.</p><p>People might still show up for medical care at Cook County Health’s two hospitals and several clinics, but might not be able to afford to pay what could be big bills. That means less money flowing to the county. The majority of the county’s patients have Medicaid or no insurance, records show. Dr. Erik Mikaitis, CEO of CCH, said the amount of uninsured patients is already swelling.</p><p>Reilly said the county should have planned for Medicaid losses earlier.</p><p>“You don’t wait for federal cuts to happen,” Reilly said. “You build a firewall before they hit.”</p><p>County leaders say they have been preparing. The health system started tightening its belt last year, with 10% cuts across all departments that will continue through 2026. They froze about 200 vacant positions. The county has set aside around $320 million in reserves, partly in case federal grants for everything from transportation to public health get cut, and nearly $70 million for potential Medicaid losses, a county spokesman said.</p><p>Reilly suggests pre-ranking medical services to keep or cut, prioritizing the ER and trauma care. He declined to say what he would cut, deferring to the health system.</p><p>Mikaitis said there are contingency plans — not cutting services but potentially consolidating them, such as offering a service in three clinics instead of five.</p><h3>Reilly suggests a Cook County ID</h3><p>In a statement, Reilly said he wants to make sure “Cook County services are for Cook County residents,” and that the county isn’t absorbing costs from other counties. He points to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2020/03/12/treating-uninsured-patients-is-wreaking-havoc-on-cook-county-finances" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ reporting</u></a> that underscores the impact on county finances for providing the most charity care, or discounted care, of any hospital in Illinois — around $217 million at the county’s John H. Stroger Jr. Hospital in 2024, a WBEZ analysis of the most recent <a class="Link" href="https://hfsrb.illinois.gov/inventories-data.html" target="_blank" ><u>state records</u></a> shows. In some cases, private hospitals stabilize patients, then refer them to the county for follow-up care.</p><p>“Verified residency and referral data would allow the county and the Attorney General to audit community benefit reports, enforce state discount laws, and hold private systems accountable when costs are shifted onto the public safety net,” Reilly said.</p><p>A health system spokeswoman said only about 4% of patients live outside the county. The county’s financial assistance program, CareLink, is only for county residents, and <a class="Link" href="https://healthcarereportcard.illinois.gov/hospital-uninsured-patient-discount-act" target="_blank" ><u>an Illinois law</u></a> caps how much any hospital can collect from uninsured patients who live in the state. Patients who live outside of Illinois and pay out of pocket could qualify for a discount.</p><p>Reilly said a countywide ID, which county commissioners have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/7/5/18342498/two-cook-county-commissioners-proposing-county-i-d-card" target="_blank" ><u>floated before</u></a>, would help people prove residency for county services, such as medical care. The idea is not to restrict care or duplicate existing ID programs, like Chicago’s CityKey, Reilly said. The county ID would be for suburban residents, he suggests.</p><p>Whoever wins the Democratic primary would likely win in the November general election. There is <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountyclerkil.gov/elections/results-and-election-data/election-results/candidate-filing" target="_blank" ><u>no Republican candidate</u></a> for county board president. Michael Murphy is running as a Libertarian. Preckwinkle last won with about 69% of the vote in 2022 against Bob Fioretti.</p><p>Should she win, Preckwinkle said it would be her last term as county board president. She said she also plans to run for just one more, two-year term this spring to lead the Democratic Party.</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch and Mariah Woelfel cover government for WBEZ. </i><br></p>
author: Mariah Woelfel | WBEZ

title: Grocery prices in Chicago have climbed double digits over the last year. Here's how we know
summary: <p>It’s been more than a year since the Chicago Sun-Times started tracking the monthly price of 35 common grocery items at Jewel-Osco, Mariano's, Target and Walmart.</p><p>The verdict? What went up, mostly didn’t come down.</p><p>At Chicago’s largest grocery chain Jewel-Osco, 18 items went up in price, 15 stayed the same and two — Land O’ Lakes butter and Doritos nacho cheese chips — dropped by 50 cents and 80 cents, respectively, over the past 13 months.</p><p>With most items going up in price, it meant our shopping cart at Jewel went up by a total of $21.80 — from $263.15 on Jan. 7, 2025, to $284.95 on Feb. 3, 2026.</p><p>President Donald Trump famously said during his 2024 campaign he’d get prices down “starting on Day One” of his presidency. And high grocery prices played an out-sized role in the presidential election, with many voters saying they were “very concerned” about food costs, according to a 2024 survey by the Associated Press.</p><p>Edgewater resident Lena Howard, 30, said she doesn’t need hard data to know that groceries are expensive.</p><p>“Everything is expensive — the milk, the eggs, the cereal,” Howard, a mother of two boys, aged 10 and 8, said as she loaded groceries into her car at a North Side Jewel. “For a box of cereal, they want damn near $10.”</p><p>Howard said she spends about $250 a week on food and household items. To stretch her budget, she cooks at home, except on Fridays, and makes big batches of spaghetti and chicken Alfredo that can be repurposed for lunches or kept in the freezer.</p><p>She usually shops at Jewel because it’s close to her home but sometimes she makes the half-hour drive to a Walmart in Skokie, where prices are lower.</p><p>At Walmart, many of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/07/18/supermarket-super-pain-trump-campaign-food-prices-inflation-tariffs" >35 items on our list</a> dropped in price more often than they rose, compared to one year ago. Seventeen items went down totaling $9.60 in savings, seven items increased totaling $5.81, seven stayed the same and four didn’t have enough data to be tracked.</p><p>The prices of our items at Mariano’s and Target mostly increased or stayed flat. A grand total for the baskets couldn’t be made because not every item was available each month.</p><p>At Mariano’s, 14 items stayed the same in price, 13 went up, six went down and two did not have enough data. At Target, 19 items went up, 10 went down, five stayed the same and one didn’t have enough data.</p><p>Grocery expert Phil Lempert, known as the “Supermarket Guru,” said the truth is price increases that slammed consumers beginning in mid-2022 are mostly not going away.</p><p>Climate change is affecting crops and cattle, tariffs are hitting imports and messing up farming forecasts and immigration enforcement is impacting labor, Lempert said. And the large publicly-owned food and consumer product companies are under pressure to deliver growth for their stockholders.</p><p>“It puts the consumer in a really difficult position because there’s not a lot we can do,” Lempert said.</p><p>Jewel and Mariano’s, as well as their parent companies Albertsons and Kroger, respectively, didn’t respond to requests for comment. A Target spokeswoman declined to comment.</p><p>Some of the products whose prices rose from January 2025 to February 2026 include:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f7a844a2-084d-11f1-99ee-413f9fa0de1f"><li><b>Folgers ground coffee:</b> Jumped in price at all four stores. At Jewel and Mariano’s, prices rose 38.5%, from $6.49 in January 2025 to $8.99 in February 2026. At Target, it increased from $6.29 to $8.49, up 35%, and at Walmart, the price increased 20.6%,from $5.78 to $6.97. Coffee prices are up nationwide due to poor harvests globally, as well as lingering effects from tariffs.</li><li><b>Nathan’s Famous bun-length hot dogs:</b> Increased in price at all four stores. At Jewel, the price climbed from $6.49 to $8.49, a 30.8% increase. The price at Mariano’s went from $6.49 to $7.99.</li><li><b>Ground beef:</b> Over the past year, prices rose 25% at Jewel and Walmart. Price increases nationwide are blamed on drought, smaller herd sizes and increased costs for cattle feed.</li><li><b>M&M’s peanut candy:</b> An 18.08-ounce bag cost more at Jewel, Mariano’s and Target, with the price at Jewel hitting a whopping $13.99, up 27.3% from $10.99 in January 2025.</li><li><b>Oreo:</b> Prices for an 18.12-ounce package also increased at Jewel, Mariano’s and Target. It reached $7.49 this month at Jewel, up from $6.99 in January 2025. At Mariano’s, it was $7.39, up from $6.49.</li><li><b>Coke:</b> A 12-pack cost more at all four stores. The price was $9.99 in January 2025 at Jewel and Mariano’s, and increased 20% to $11.99 this month.</li><li><b>Always:</b> A package of the feminine product rose at all four stores. At Jewel, a 46-count box jumped from $9.49 in January 2025 to $11.99 this month, a 26.3% increase.</li><li><b>Pampers Swaddlers:</b> A box of 84 size 2 diapers went up Jewel, Mariano’s and Target, with the biggest increase at Mariano’s, up 9.4% from $31.99 to $34.99.</li></ul><p>Egg prices hit a breaking point for many consumers early last year, when avian flu decimated farms and caused prices to skyrocket. </p><p>The Sun-Times tracked Eggland's Best grade-A large white eggs, as well as individual store brands and recorded a peak in March 2025, when a dozen eggs of Eggland’s Best hit $9.49 at Mariano’s.</p><p>Those super-high prices have largely dropped now that the bird flu crisis is less of a threat.</p><p>This month, Eggland’s Best eggs were $5.99 at Jewel; $5.49 at Mariano’s for a dozen large eggs; and $3.96 for extra-large eggs at Walmart.</p><p>Store brand eggs were as low as $1.99 at Target and $1.97 at Walmart.</p><h3>Shrinkflation’s double-whammy</h3><p>Tide original liquid laundry detergent rose in price at two of the four stores we checked. It also shrunk in size by 4 ounces over the course of 13 months to 80 ounces.</p><p>Henry Molski, spokesperson for Procter & Gamble, manufacturer of Tide, said the amount is less but the detergent is still able to clean the same 64 loads of laundry advertised on the label — assuming loads of 6 pounds — because it was reformulated at a higher concentration.</p><p>“Tide continues to concentrate to provide a superior cleaning experience. In fact, Tide made its biggest upgrade in liquid in over 20 years with the Tide boosted formula in the fall of ‘25,” Molski said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Tide was $14.99 at Jewel in January 2025, and it's now $15.99. At Target, it went from $12.99 for an 84-ounce bottle to $13.69 for 80 ounces.</p><p>Edgar Dworsky, founder of <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumerworld.org/" target="_blank" >ConsumerWorld.org</a> and a former assistant attorney general for Massachusetts, was one of the first to spot the smaller size of Tide and said many consumers won’t realize they need to use less detergent per load to get the same 64 loads.</p><p>He said shrinking products pop up everywhere from toilet paper rolls, with a few less sheets, to a cereal box that stays the same height but gets narrower and bottles that get tapered or dimpled so they hold less liquid.</p><div class="ActionBox Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="ActionBox-content"> <div class="ActionBox-title">What are you seeing at the grocery store? </div> <div class="ActionBox-description">Tell your story to reporter Stephanie Zimmermann.</div> </div> <div class="ActionBox-cta"> <a class="Button" href="mailto:szimmermann@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email me</a> </div> </div><p>When the price stays the same on a shrinking product, the consumer loses money. When the price increases on a smaller version, it’s a double-whammy.</p><p>Shrinking products were more prevalent a few years ago, when inflation was higher, Dworsky said. Inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, as the world emerged from the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>“Shrinkflation, downsizing has been around forever, and it’s not going anywhere, but we see it in waves,” he said. “At the moment, it’s fairly even.”</p><p>Consumers can guard against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2025/11/15/paying-more-smaller-restaurant-grocery-portions-shrinkflation" >shrinkflation</a> by paying attention to what's in the package, whether it's by weight or by count, of the products they regularly purchase, Dworsky said.</p><p>Because he tracks the prices of items he regularly buys, it helps him recognize when a sale is worth it. </p><p>“When you recognize a good deal, load up on that item,” he said.</p><h3>Tracking sales</h3><p>The Sun-Times tracked shelf prices, but also the sale prices when the deal was for a single item that didn’t require a mobile app or loyalty program.</p><p>Some sales were significant. For example, those eye-popping $13.99 bag of peanut M&M’s at Jewel were on sale in February for $8.99 — no coupon required.</p><p>But with some items we followed, the cost climbed so high that the promotional price exceeded the old shelf price.</p><p>For example, a 1-pound package of 85% lean ground beef at Jewel was on sale for $6.99 this month, $1 more than the shelf price from January 2025. The sale price this month for Folgers coffee was $8.49, which was $2 more than its shelf price of $6.49 in January 2025. We also saw this trend with Oreo cookies, Tropicana orange juice and Always pads.</p><p>A New York Times/Siena poll released last month found that while a majority of Americans said they’re able to afford basics like rent, gas and groceries, close to 60% are concerned about rising costs and only 14% said they’re able to get ahead financially.</p><p>Art Friedson, of Lake View, caught a glimpse of consumers' anxiety in November. While in line at the supermarket, he saw an older couple and an “unbelievably patient” cashier spend several minutes leafing through the store’s flyer and checking its mobile app to find a coupon for one of the handful of items they were purchasing.</p><p>The couple's grand total was only $7.01. “You don’t do that unless you really, really need those extra couple of pennies,” Friedson said. “That’s how things are in a supermarket these days. It’s heartbreaking.”</p><p>Many consumers treat sales and coupons as an integral part of their shopping.</p><p>Daniel Serafini, of Grayslake, said he won’t set foot in Jewel without checking the store’s ads and downloading digital coupons off Jewel’s mobile app.</p><p>The retired computer programmer said he’s found some decent deals, like four boxes of cereal for $8, though he always checks his receipt to make sure the digital coupons were applied and tells customer service if they weren’t.</p><p>But his real savings strategy is going to Woodman’s Markets, where the prices are often lower. He’ll also go to Menards, which despite being known for selling home improvement and hardware items also stocks many grocery products.</p><p>At Menards, Serafini shops during the store’s rebate periods then mails his receipts to get an in-store rebate coupon, equal to 11% of what he spent. He then uses those coupons to buy more items on his shopping list. He recently got close to $40 in free groceries.</p><p>“It’s worth it,” Serafini said. ”To me, it’s a no brainer.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-480000" name="module-480000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Ways to save</h3><ul id="rte-67c528e2-0856-11f1-8b6f-937da1d85873"><li>Plan ahead by creating weekly meal plans and batch-cook foods that can be frozen or eaten as leftovers and lunches.</li><li>Always shop with a list.</li><li>Check for store sales in advance. If your go-to store has an app, consider downloading it to clip digital coupons.</li><li>Stock up, if you can, when sales are good. But if you see a sale that requires you to buy multiples of a product, compare the unit price to make sure it’s truly a great deal.</li><li>Choose a store’s private label brand, which is often just as good as the brand-name product but often 25% cheaper. Aldi and Trader Joe’s are two grocers known for selling products under their own brands at lower prices.</li><li>Eat less meat and add more beans, lentils and other legumes to your diet.</li></ul></div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-af0000" name="module-af0000"></a> <div file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><h3>How we’re tracking grocery prices</h3><br>The Chicago Sun-Times has been tracking the shelf and sale prices for 35 items, from staples like milk, bread and eggs to fresh produce, meats and frozen food as well as coffee, cookies and candy. We’ve also tracked products like shampoo, diapers, detergent and toilet paper.<br><br>We decided to choose packaged items from well-known manufacturers such as Procter & Gamble, Kraft Heinz, Tyson Foods, Hormel, Smithfield Foods, Nestle, Mars, Mondelez, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, General Mills and Unilever.<br><br>Prices skyrocketed in mid-2022, under former President Joe Biden’s administration and following the COVID-19 pandemic. The high cost of groceries played a large role in the 2024 presidential campaign, in which then-candidate Donald Trump repeatedly promised to lower grocery prices.<br><br>Our price data is from the first Tuesday of each month and was tracked in person and online at Jewel, as well as online at Mariano’s, Target and Walmart, using the same store locations each time. title: Chicago resistance to ICE abuses echoes opposition to Fugitive Slave Act 175 years ago
summary: <p>Jim Gray arrived in chains.</p><p>At the railroad station in Ottawa, Illinois, about 80 miles southwest of Chicago.</p><p>Gray wore leg irons, his arms bound to his sides, and was led by a rope.</p><p>It was Oct 19, 1859.</p><p>The month before he had escaped from slavery in New Madrid, Missouri. Caught by an Illinois sheriff "in sympathy with the slave owners," Gray was being returned to bondage. A crowd awaited him, including a local merchant named John Hossack, an immigrant from Scotland.</p><p>"What crime has he committed?" Hossack shouted. "Has he done anything but want to be free?"</p><p>A question that echoes through the years and across the country today. With federal immigration agents this past year prowling Democratic cities — Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis — kidnapping Latino individuals and dragging them off to exile, and billions being pumped into immigration enforcement, gearing up to grab more people and confine them to enormous facilities now being constructed nationwide, it's impossible not to think of the Fugitive Slave Act, the 1850 law that also created a federal force tasked with snaring people for the crime of wanting to live in freedom.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-460000" name="module-460000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>There was already a law, the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793, empowering owners to retrieve their chattel from the North. But Southerners were upset that California was being admitted to the union as a free state. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 was a sop to them, meting out punishment to anyone helping Blacks escape slavery, and creating monetary incentives for agents bringing escapees back. The law gave bite to the slave drivers' bark.</p><p>Then as now, local communities fiercely resisted this federal intrusion into their constitutional rights. Then as now, street clashes erupted as national law and human decency faced off against each other. This being February — Black History Month — and with the Trump administration waging war on Black History, scrubbing it from the Smithsonian, from college campuses and federal websites in an attempt to declare the civil rights struggle an unmentionable blot upon enforced patriotic zeal, it seemed important to explore the subject in depth, while we still enjoy the right to do so.</p><p>"All historical analogies are the same," said Matthew Pinsker, a history professor and director of the House Divided Project at Dickinson College. "There's always some similarities and plenty of differences. This is a battle between the national administration and blue state governments. In the Fugitive Slave days, it was a battle between Washington and Northern states, which passed laws called 'personal liberty laws' that were like the sanctuary city laws that Trump is trying to overturn."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/photography/2025/12/18/midway-blitz-chicago-immigration-raids-photography-photos" >The most pivotal moments of Operation Midway Blitz, captured by Sun-Times photographers</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Hundreds of Ottawa residents showed up for Gray's hearing the next day in the courtroom of Justice Dean Caton, who ruled that while Gray had broken no Illinois law, the Fugitive Slave Act demanded he go to Springfield to face charges.</p><p>Gray never got there.</p><p>As a marshal began to lead Gray from the courthouse, local men sprang into action. The officer was restrained, while Hossack grabbed Gray by the elbow.</p><p>"If you want liberty, run!" Hossack urged, dragging Gray from the courthouse. They jumped a fence, climbed into a waiting carriage, and were sped out of town.</p><p>Gray escaped north to Canada. But Hossack was arrested and sent to stand trial in federal court in Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Scouting Heritage Museum.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Chicago’s resistance. Strong then, strong now</h3><p>Resistance to the Fugitive Slave Act was particularly strong in Chicago, the city "a sinkhole of abolition" in the words of one downstate editor. A hub of actual railroads, it was also a center for the Underground Railroad, an informal confederation hurrying those escaping slavery north to Canada. When a slave catcher arrived at Chicago in October, 1850, he was informed that his safety could not be guaranteed, and the enslaved servant he had brought with him was helped to escape.</p><p>The same month, the Chicago Common Council — predecessor of the City Council — passed a law condemning the Fugitive Slave Act as "cruel and unjust" and ordering the police force — nine men at the time — "not to render any assistance for the arrest of fugitive slaves."</p><p>Uncannily similar to the challenge Mayor Brandon Johnson would face 175 years later: how much cooperation must local government give to federal authorities enforcing a despised and unjust law? The council in 1850 minced no words, damning any free state representatives supporting the bill as "fit only to be ranked with the traitors, Benedict Arnold, and Judas Iscariot who betrayed his Lord and master for thirty pieces of silver."</p><p>Last October, the City Council passed a similar, if less florid, resolution, focused on trying to protect children from traumatic seizure by ICE agents and urging citizens to report the misconduct they witness.</p><p>What was motivating Chicago to push back against the Fugitive Slave Act? While its tempting to just superimpose Chicago's current sanctuary city liberalism onto the mid-19th century city, that wasn't the case. There were only 323 Black people living in Chicago in 1850 — about 1% of the population. Illinois had passed its own "Black Laws" in 1848, forbidding the immigration of free Blacks into the state and, as amended in 1853, forbidding Black visitors from spending more than 10 nights in the city.</p><p>"These protectors of fugitive slaves raised no objection to the exclusion of Negro testimony against a white person in the courts of law," historian Bessie Louise Pierce noted in 1940. "They seemed to see no inconsistencies in providing a separate section in the theaters for Negroes, and in segregating the races in the common schools."</p><p>To whites, this was more about protecting their own rights than the rights of Black Chicagoans.</p><p>"In a state like Illinois, there were people who cared about free Black residents, but there were an awful lot of white people who cared mostly about personal liberty and state and local rights," said Pinsker, whose newly published book "Boss Lincoln" examines the 16th president's mastery of grassroots politics "They didn't want the federal government or Southern slave owners telling them how to run their own lives... you can see a similar emotion rising in a place like Minneapolis, when they feel like masked federal agents [are] roving around the city, picking up people regardless of whether they are criminals or illegal, but just because of the color of their skin."</p><h3>‘A federalism battle’</h3><p>The issue has already been settled, legally.</p><p>"It's a federalism battle," said Pinsker. "Can states be forced to enforce federal law? That's something the Supreme Court has weighed in on multiple times, and they said no. The sanctuary city advocates are probably going to win in court on the same principles that draw all the way back to Fugitive Slave days."</p><p>If history is a guide, ICE loses.</p><p>"Frankly, this is a historical analogy that should concern the Trump administration," said Pinsker. "Despite all the talk of the Fugitive Slave law being draconian, it was an abject failure. The moral revulsion of Northerners against it stopped it from being enforced... the decade from its passage and the Civil War, there were very few and scattered successful episodes. Most Southerners felt it was a complete failure."</p><p>History is made by individuals standing up to be counted. Renee Good and Alex Pretti now, John Hossack back then.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c30000" name="image-c30000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/69d1ba1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5028x2822+0+265/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fec%2F28%2Fc70cfedd425baf83934aee8fa734%2F2257497538.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/733b00f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5028x2822+0+265/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fec%2F28%2Fc70cfedd425baf83934aee8fa734%2F2257497538.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/231e4b5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5028x2822+0+265/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fec%2F28%2Fc70cfedd425baf83934aee8fa734%2F2257497538.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A photograph of 37-year-old Alex Pretti can be seen at a makeshift memorial in the area where he was shot dead by federal immigration agents earlier in the day in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on January 24, 2026. The death came less than three weeks after US citizen Renee Good was shot and killed by an ICE officer. Testimony began with Richard Phillipps, Gray's former owner.</p><p>"That boy belonged to me," he testified. "I bought him and paid for him."</p><p>The cost? One thousand dollars.</p><p>Hossack was found guilty. He had the right to make a statement before sentencing and didn't let the opportunity go to waste.</p><h3>Hossack addresses the court</h3><p>"It may appear strange to your Honor that I have no sense of guilt," he began, explaining he came "from the tyranny of the Old World" finding himself "a stranger in a strange land."</p><p>He came over to dig the canal, then went into business.</p><p>"I am one of the men who have made Chicago what it is today, having shipped some of the first grain that was exported from this city." Hossack said. "I am, Sir, one of the pioneers of Illinois, who have gone through the many hardships of the settlement of a new country. I have spent upon it my best days, the strength of my manhood. I have eleven children, who are natives of this my adopted country. No living man, Sir, has greater interest in its welfare; and it is because I am opposed to carrying out wicked and ungodly laws, and love the freedom of my country, that I stand before you today."</p><p>Like those opposing ICE today, he knew what his freedom was based upon.</p><p>"Sir, I place myself upon the Constitution, in the presence of a nation who have the Declaration of Independence read to them every Fourth of July, and profess to believe it. In the presence of civilized man, I hold up the Constitution of my adopted country as clear from the blood of men, and from a tyranny that would make crowned heads blush. The parties who prostitute the Constitution to the support of slavery are traitors — traitors not only to the liberties of millions of enslaved countrymen, but traitors to the Constitution itself which they have sworn to support. A foreigner upon your soil, I go not to the platforms of contending parties to find truth. I go, Sir, to the Constitution of my country: the word slave is not to be found."</p><p>He quoted the prosecutor claiming it was ungrateful of Hossack to find protection under American law, yet disobey it:</p><p>"Surely, I have been protected. The fish in the rivers, the quail in the stubble, the deer in the forest, have been protected. Shall I join hands with those who make wicked laws, in crushing out the poor Black man, for whom there is no protection but in the grave, where the wicked cease from troubling, and the weary are at rest?... As a man who had fled from the crushing aristocracy of my native land, how could I support a worse aristocracy in this land?"</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div><p>He quoted the Fugitive Slave Act, mandating that reaching free soil did not end a person's slavery.</p><p>"That is the provision that is claimed transforms the government into a monster of iniquity," Hossack said. "How these three or four lines can transform this government, ordained to secure justice, into a mean tool to aid the plunderers of cradles, the destroyers of home, the ravishers of women, and the oppressors of men, to carry on their hellish work — how it can do this thing, I cannot see."</p><p>At times, Hossack seemed to speak across the years to our present administration and its masked agents.</p><p>"Sir, no law can be enacted so bad but that it will find men deluded or base enough to execute it. The law of Egypt that consigned the new-born babe to the slaughter found tools for its execution. The bloody decree of Herod found men ready to obey the law of the country, though it commanded the slaughter of the innocents of a province, Sir, tell me not of men ready and willing to execute the law! My Redeemer, whose name I am hardly worthy to speak, and yet whose name is all my trust, although he knew no sin, yet he was crucified by law."</p><p>He continued.</p><p>"This law so plainly tramples upon the divine law, that it cannot be binding upon any human being under any circumstances to obey it. The law that bids me do to other men as I would have other men do to me, is too plain, too simple to be misunderstood."</p><p>Hossack asks a question that rings today:</p><p>"What country is this? Can it be that I live in a land boasting of freedom, of morality, of Christianity? How long, O, how long, shall the people bow down and worship this great image set up in this nation?"</p><p>And he ends by noting, presciently:</p><p>"When the history of the great struggle shall be candidly written, the rescuers of Jim Gray will be considered as having done honor to God, to humanity, and to themselves."</p><p>Hossack faced a $1,000 fine and six months in jail. Judge Drummond gave him 10 days and fined him $100, which citizens of Chicago promptly paid. Chicago feted him as a hero during his captivity — Mayor John Wentworth sprung him, temporarily, to go for a carriage ride and invited him to his home to dinner. Abolitionists turned Hossack's speech into a handbill and distributed it nationwide, and it <a class="Link" href="https://readingroo.ms/1/3/9/8/13987/13987-h/13987-h.htm" target="_blank" >lives online today.</a> Sadly, the speech still makes for relevant reading.</p>

title: Federal judge temporarily blocks Trump cuts to HIV, lead poisoning prevention funds
summary: <p>A federal judge has temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's administration from cutting more than $600 million in public health grants for Illinois and three other Democratic-led states, a day after Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul joined a coalition of states in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/02/11/federal-cuts-hiv-lead-poisoning-prevention-grants-raoul" target="_blank" >federal lawsuit</a> to challenge the cuts. </p><p>Judge Manish S. Shah, who issued <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisattorneygeneral.gov/News-Room/Current-News/2022%2002%2012%20TRO%20CDC%20grants.pdf?language_id=1" target="_blank" ><u>the temporary restraining order</u></a> in the Northern District Court of Illinois, said the attorneys general were “likely to succeed” in their argument because the Trump administration’s cuts were based on “arbitrary, capricious or unconstitutional” reasons, according to court documents.</p><p>Raoul said Trump was “playing politics with critical public health funding" by cutting millions of dollars from HIV tracking and lead poisoning prevention from California, Colorado, Illinois and Minnesota. He said the order ensures funding from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention along with other funds will continue flowing to Illinois while the case plays out.</p><p>“Targeting four Democrat-run states that are standing up to his completely unrelated immigration policies is a transparent attempt to bully us into compliance,” Raoul said in a statement. “We remain unflinching in our commitment to defending against the Trump administration’s continued unlawful directives intended to force us to implement immigration and other unrelated policies.”</p><p>The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>In total, at least <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/02/10/trump-administration-cuts-illinois-hiv-prevention-grants" target="_blank" ><u>$29 million in Illinois grants</u></a> are on the “hit list” being held up by the judge’s order, which include city, state and other health centers’ family planning and HIV prevention programs, according to a list of grants obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><p>They also included $7.2 million in grant cuts to the American Medical Association in Illinois, which supports gender-affirming care, as well as $5.2 million slashed from an HIV prevention program at Lurie Children’s Hospital — which recently was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/20/lurie-childrens-pauses-gender-affirming-meds-under-18" target="_blank" ><u>threatened with another federal investigation</u></a> over its gender-affirming care for youth.</p><p>Additionally, Raoul said the cuts would force the Illinois Department of Public Health to cut nearly 100 employees, end lead poisoning prevention grants to 25 local health departments and wipe out the state’s HIV surveillance system that tracks the spread of outbreaks.</p><p>It’s the latest legal win for Raoul and other attorneys general across the country suing the federal government.</p><p>In September, Raoul was part of a large coalition of legal officials that won a suit for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/24/illinois-wins-suit-on-disaster-relief-funding-held-by-dhs-over-sanctuary-laws" target="_blank" ><u>release of $2 billion in federal disaster relief funding</u></a> held up by the White House over sanctuary city policies. Two months later, a separate federal judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/11/04/judge-blocks-trump-administration-transportation-funds" target="_blank" ><u>released federal transportation funding</u></a> in response to another suit after the Trump administration attempted to block that money over immigration enforcement.</p>
author: Violet Miller

title: Underdog U.S. Senate candidates call for new voices in Washington at UChicago debate
summary: <p>Seven underdog candidates seeking retiring U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin’s coveted seat tried capturing voters’ attention Thursday night during a debate at the University of Chicago.</p><p>Fewer fireworks flew at this discussion compared to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/01/26/senate-debate-illinois-krishnamoorthi-stratton-kelly" target="_blank" ><u>last month’s U.S. Senate debate</u></a> between front-runner contenders Lt. Gov. Julianna Stratton and U.S. Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly.</p><p>The lesser-known candidates mostly recognized the long-shot chance at winning the primary election, with the exception of the lone Republican candidate in attendance who will likely face one other contender in that primary. Instead, they largely shared their campaign priorities and laid bare the reasoning why they were relegated to a separate debate.</p><p>“I think it’s telling that there are multiple aspects of our democratic process that are broken because… we only look to money as the only metric of viability. This debate is a great example,” said Democratic primary challenger Kevin Ryan, a Chicago Public Schools teacher and U.S. Marine veteran.</p><p>The University of Chicago’s Institute of Politics and International House hosted and moderated the event. It also hosted last month’s debate between Stratton, Krishnamoorthi and Kelly, which was also sponsored by the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div title: Preckwinkle calls on top Cook County prosecutor to investigate ICE, feds involved in Chicago area shootings
summary: <p>Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, along with more than half of the county’s commissioners, have called on Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neil Burke to file charges against federal immigration agents involved in shootings that took place last year in the Chicago area — though Burke says her office has no jurisdiction.</p><p>The statement points to the fatal shooting of Silverio Villegas González, who was shot by federal immigration agents last September in suburban Franklin Park. The statement also points to the shooting that wounded Marimar Martinez, who survived after being shot multiple times by a federal agent last year. It asks the state’s attorney to investigate any and “all available charges” and “use of excessive force” in the shootings.</p><p>They also point to the historic disproportionate use of force by law enforcement against Black residents, and said justice must be applied evenly because, “No officer and no agency is above the law.”</p><p>“The Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement agenda has produced a clear and alarming pattern of violence,” the statement said. “We support thorough law enforcement investigations wherever federal agents have violated the law. We urge the Cook County State’s Attorney to act swiftly, proactively and transparently to ensure accountability and deliver justice for the families and communities who have been harmed.”</p><p>It comes just over a week after Illinois House Democrats <a class="Link" href="https://ilhousedems.com/2026/02/03/elected-officials-call-on-cook-county-states-attorney-eileen-oneil-burke-to-investigate-the-fatal-shooting-of-silverio-villegas-gonzalez-and-the-near-fatal-shooting-of-marimar-martin/" target="_blank" ><u>released a similar call to action</u></a> aimed at the state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>The Cook County State’s Attorney’s office said though Burke is “deeply concerned” about the “abhorrent behavior” of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents nationwide, her office “does not conduct independent investigations into criminal conduct and lacks jurisdiction over federal agencies, except in extremely narrow and limited circumstances.”</p><p>Burke said her team has drafted a protocol for how local legal systems can respond to federal agents in a way that’s “clear and grounded in law,” which the office said has been shared with local and state law enforcement, as well as other prosecutors for feedback.</p><p>“We are committed to doing all we can under the law to support and review law enforcement investigations of that conduct and prosecute when appropriate,” Burke's office said in a statement.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/06/eileen-oneill-burke-brandon-johnson-immigration-ice-law" >County’s top prosecutor calls Mayor Brandon Johnson’s ICE executive order ‘wholly inappropriate’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/02/03/mayor-brandon-johnson-executive-order-accountability-ice-agents-operation-midway-blitz-states-attorney-eileen-oneill-burke" >Mayor Johnson defends executive order aimed at holding ICE accountable for alleged abuses</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Burke has found herself between local leaders grasping at ways to hold federal agents accountable for wounding and killing residents, federal laws that often block those actions, and President Donald Trump's administration which has blocked use of force investigations. </p><p>Last week, Burke told her staff that Mayor Brandon Johnson’s recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/02/03/mayor-brandon-johnson-executive-order-accountability-ice-agents-operation-midway-blitz-states-attorney-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" ><u>executive order</u></a> — which orders CPD to document potential crimes committed by federal agents — is inappropriate and could jeopardize criminal prosecutions.</p><p>Johnson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/02/03/mayor-brandon-johnson-executive-order-accountability-ice-agents-operation-midway-blitz-states-attorney-eileen-oneill-burke" target="_blank" ><u>defended the move</u></a>, and said he was trying to help Burke by providing evidence for prosecutions of federal agents, which he claimed she has spoken about publicly.</p><p>It’s one of many moves state, county and local officials have taken in attempts to curb federal agents in the Chicago area, though many have faced legal uncertainty, and experts have cast doubt on one executive order Johnson signed in August that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/30/mayor-johnson-protecting-chicago-initiative-executive-order" target="_blank" ><u>threatened lawsuits against federal agents</u></a>.</p><p>In November, now former Cook County Circuit Chief Judge Timothy Evans <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/14/top-cook-county-judge-bars-civil-arrests-at-courthouses-citing-chilling-effect" target="_blank" ><u>signed an order</u></a> barring civil arrests, or those without a warrant signed by a judge, at county courts, though federal officials vowed to violate it anyways.</p>
author: Violet Miller

title: Chicago-area resident sues Trump officials over Facebook shutting down popular ICE sighting page
summary: <p>The founder of one of the largest Facebook pages to track and report federal immigration activity activity in the Chicago area during the Trump administration's Operation Midway Blitz is fighting back after Facebook disabled the page in October.</p><p>In a <a class="Link" href="https://www.thefire.org/sites/default/files/2026/02/Verified%20Complaint%20-%20Rosado%20v.%20Bondi.pdf " target="_blank" >lawsuit filed Wednesday</a>, Cicero small business owner Kassandra "Kae" Rosado alleged U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi and U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem coerced Facebook into removing the popular "ICE Sighting-Chicagoland" page, violating Rosado's First Amendment rights. </p><p>"Defendants retaliated against Rosado's Facebook group for the simple reason that the government disfavors the speech being shared. But the government has no legitimate interest in 'stopping private actors from speaking as they wish' to 'tilt public debate in a preferred direction,'" the lawsuit reads.</p><p>Rosado started the page in January 2025 to keep individuals and small businesses informed about where U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was operating in Chicago, according to the lawsuit. The page was initially made up of fellow business owners and Rosado's friends and family. Group membership increased in September as ICE enforcement surged in the city and surrounding suburbs. </p><p>The page had almost 100,000 members by October, with thousands of posts and comments per day from members sharing information about violent encounters and arrests across the city, according to the lawsuit.</p><p>But on Oct. 12, right-wing activist and Trump ally Laura Loomer <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/LauraLoomer/status/1977345952718438707" target="_blank" >tagged Noem and Bondi in a post</a> claiming that the Facebook page and others like it "are getting people killed." The next day, Loomer <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/LauraLoomer/status/1977812771799461893?s=20" target="_blank" >said in a post</a> that a Department of Justice source told her that they had contacted executives at Meta, Facebook's parent company, "to tell them they need to remove these ICE tracking pages from the platform." </p><p>Noem and Bondi announced the removal of the Facebook page on their social media accounts on Oct. 14. "Anti-ICE radicals are using social media apps to dox, threaten, and terrorize the brave men and women of ICE and their families," Noem <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/Sec_Noem/status/1978182132414448008?s=20 " target="_blank" >said in the post. </a></p><p>According to the suit, Rosado was notified by Facebook that the page was disabled because it "went against the Community Standards multiple times." </p><p>While the page was active, the suit said Facebook moderators had removed five posts in the group that were not created or approved by Rosado or her moderators. Additionally, the suit said Facebook had previously advised Rosado that "it had only identified this handful of 'participant violations' of its rules, which 'don't hurt your group.'"</p><p>"By censoring our group, the government continues to erode our trust," Rosado said in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.thefire.org/news/fire-sues-bondi-noem-censoring-facebook-group-and-app-reporting-ice-activity" target="_blank" >statement</a>. "They silenced not only my voice, but the voices of nearly 100,000 other community members."</p><p>Rosado filed the suit with Mark Hodges, an Indiana resident who created the app Eyes Up, which allowed users to record, securely store and view videos of ICE officers committing potential civil rights violations. According to the suit, Apple removed the app from the App Store in October, allegedly after pressure from the federal government and violating Hodges' First Amendment-protected right to record law enforcement in public.</p><p>The Department of Justice, Apple and Meta did not respond immediately to requests for comment.</p><p>In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security's Assistant Secretary Tricia McLaughlin said, "ICE tracking apps put the lives of the men and women of law enforcement in danger as they go after terrorists, vicious gangs and violent criminal rings."</p><p>"But, of course, FIRE spins this correct decision for Apple to remove these apps as them caving to pressure instead of helping prevent further harm to federal officers," she added.</p><p>The lawsuit asks the court to declare that Bondi and Noem's coercion of Facebook and Apple suppressed disfavored speech, which violates the First Amendment.</p><p>"Plaintiffs bring this case to preserve our country's fundamental character as a free nation, asking this Court to protect the basic First Amendment right to share information about our government and its activities," the suit said.</p>

title: Hombre de Chicago absuelto del complot de asesinato de Bovino sigue detenido tras que juez le negó la fianza
summary: <p>Un juez de inmigración negó la fianza a un hombre de Chicago, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" target="_blank" >absuelto el mes pasado</a> de orquestar un complot de asesinato por encargo contra el comandante de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Gregory Bovino, y lo calificó de “potencial” peligro para la comunidad a pesar del veredicto.</p><p>En una audiencia de fianza el miércoles, el juez Matthew Beese dijo que los abogados del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) presentaron evidencia “sustancial” del juicio criminal para respaldar su afirmación de que él representaba un peligro.</p><p>Los fiscales en ese juicio no lograron probar su caso más allá de una duda razonable, según lo determinó un jurado. Pero Beese enfatizó que su decisión se basaba en los estándares de la corte de inmigración, los cuales difieren de aquellos en la corte criminal.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-030000" name="module-030000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los abogados del DHS pasaron una parte significativa de la audiencia presentando evidencia que había sido rechazada por el jurado durante el juicio criminal o prohibida por el juez que lo supervisó.</p><p>Los abogados citaron el miércoles un informe de Investigaciones de DHS que incluía registros telefónicos que alegaban que Espinoza Martínez, de 37 años de edad, estaba afiliado a los Latin Kings y tenía acceso a armas de fuego.</p><p>También señalaron un mensaje de Snapchat que Espinoza Martínez envió a principios de octubre, que seguía a una foto de Bovino. El mensaje decía: “2k en info cuando lo agarren,” “10k si lo derribas,” y “LK … sobre él”.</p><p>Bovino fue la cara del Operativo Midway Blitz, la agresiva campaña de deportación de la administración de Trump en el área de Chicago el año pasado.</p><p>Los fiscales en el caso penal no se propusieron probar la afiliación de Espinoza Martínez con los Latin Kings. Sin esa afirmación, la jueza del distrito Joan Lefkow <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/01/09/fiscales-ya-no-intentaran-comprobar-que-hombre-acusado-de-poner-recompensa-por-greg-bovino-era-pandillero" target="_blank" >prohibió la evidencia relacionada con pandillas</a> en su juicio.</p><p>Espinoza Martínez ha estado en custodia federal durante más de cuatro meses desde su arresto por cargos de asesinato por encargo a principios de octubre, según muestran los registros.</p><p>El jurado absolvió a Espinoza Martínez el 22 de enero después de un breve juicio en la Corte de Justicia Federal Dirksen. Fue <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/01/26/hombre-absuelto-del-complot-de-asesinato-de-gregory-bovino-es-detenido-por-ice" target="_blank" >rápidamente llevado a la custodia</a> del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><p>Los funcionarios del DHS han acusado a Espinoza Martínez de estar en el país ilegalmente.</p><p>Sussethe Rentería, abogada de inmigración que representa a Espinoza Martínez, dijo que ingresó al país a los 5 años y que Chicago era “el único hogar que conoce”.</p><p>Rentería rechazó las afirmaciones de que Espinoza Martínez representara un peligro para la comunidad o un riesgo de fuga, diciendo que Seguridad Nacional estaba “intentos de revivir el caso criminal” a pesar de su absolución.</p><p>Destacó que Espinoza Martínez no tenía antecedentes penales aparte de infracciones menores de tránsito y negó que tuviera alguna implicación con una pandilla.</p><p>“Aunque respetamos la decisión de la corte, estamos decepcionados con el resultado”, dijo Rentería después de la audiencia. “Él cuenta con el apoyo inquebrantable de su comunidad y su familia, y tiene tres hijos y una esposa desesperada por que regrese a casa. Estamos seguros de que se hará justicia”.</p><p>Rentería comentó que estaba considerando apelar la decisión de la corte.</p><p>Durante la audiencia, Rentería también presentó una declaración del concejal Michael Rodriguez (22°) que afirmaba que Espinoza Martínez, que vive en el vecindario de La Villita, “no tenía conexión con actividades de pandillas”. Enfatizó que simplemente vivir en un vecindario con presencia de pandillas no convierte a alguien en miembro de una pandilla.</p><p>La semana pasada, un juez federal en Indiana <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/04/juez-federal-ordena-no-deportar-a-hombre-de-chicago-exonerado-del-complot-de-asesinato-de-bovino" target="_blank" >bloqueó temporalmente</a> a la administración de Trump de deportar a Espinoza Martínez, quien estaba detenido en el Centro de Justicia del Condado de Clay en Brazil, Indiana. Su abogado, Michael Adler, presentó una petición el 2 de febrero en el Distrito Sur de Indiana para impugnar su detención.</p><p>El juez ordenó a la administración de Trump que no moviera a Espinoza Martínez “fuera de la jurisdicción de los Estados Unidos”, o fuera del 7° Circuito —que incluye Illinois, Indiana y Wisconsin— mientras se avanza en el litigio.</p><p>Se programó una audiencia de expulsión para el 25 de febrero. Rentería dijo que presentará una solicitud para cancelar la expulsión.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Jon Seidel </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

title: Voters cast ballots at Loop Supersite as early voting kicks off
summary: <p>Voters looking to avoid long lines cast their ballots Thursday morning in the Loop as early voting opened for the Illinois primary election.</p><p>Kamilah Banks-Word didn’t want to wait to vote, so she stopped by the new voting supersite at 137 S. State St. on her way to work.</p><p>“Voting makes a difference in terms of how our society runs,” said Banks-Word, 47. “I think a lot of us are not aware of how important the primary and midterm elections are. Most people just vote for the presidency, and we see how that turned out.”</p><p>Banks-Word, of the South Loop, said she was voting to protect people’s rights across the country and wanted everyone to feel safe wherever they are.</p><p>“Everything's at stake at this point,” she said. “We've seen how everything has been going downhill, how people are being harassed by different political groups and law enforcement agents.”</p><p>Banks-Word wasn’t the only one encouraged to vote because of the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement campaign, which has sent hundreds of federal agents into cities across the country — including Chicago.</p><p>In early December, the Department of Homeland Security said at least 4,400 people had been detained during Operation Midway Blitz, the Chicago area campaign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2e0000"
