in the Loop.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Don’t wait until the last second,” Chicago Board of Elections Chair Marisel Hernandez said at a morning media briefing at the supersite.</p><p>Hernandez also said the board would ensure that all voters feel safe casting their ballots after a former White House aide said federal agents should be at polling sites.</p><p>“Every voter has the right to register to vote and then vote free of intimidation, threats and coercion,” Hernandez said. “We have federal and state laws that prohibit any type of intimidation of voters during elections, and in fact, these laws specifically prohibit the presence of federal officers at any polling place.”</p><p>White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said last week that she <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/live/donald-trump-news-updates-2-5-2026" target="_blank" >“can’t guarantee”</a> a federal agent wouldn’t be near a polling location.</p><p>“I mean, that’s, frankly, a very silly hypothetical question,” said Leavitt. “But what I can tell you is, I haven’t heard the president discuss any formal plans to put ICE outside of polling locations. It’s a disingenuous question.”</p><p>Hernandez said all election judges know to call the board and 911 if they see any unusual activity near voting sites.</p><p>Officials also reminded voters casting ballots by mail to return them quickly after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/02/04/usps-postmark-change-could-threaten-mail-in-voters-cook-county-officials-warn" target="_blank" >U.S. Postal Service announced</a> that it could not guarantee ballots would be postmarked before Election Day.</p><p>Under the new policy, mail will be postmarked, then date-stamped, on the day it is processed at the post office, rather than the day it is dropped in a mailbox.</p><p>Because mail is often processed days after it is dropped off, if ballots are postmarked after Election Day it could jeopardize whether votes are counted. Mail-in ballots must be postmarked by Election Day and received within 14 days to be counted.</p><p>“Don't risk a late postmark on your ballot,” said Hernandez. “Your vote needs to be counted.”</p>

Karp</a></h5><p><b>ICE and education</b>: As President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign surged in Chicago last fall, Chicago Public Schools officials fielded an influx of calls for support from schools due to immigration enforcement activity near their buildings, records show.</p><p><b>The impact</b>: The presence of federal agents forced students inside during recess and after-school activities, disrupted learning, and at times created chaos. Students, both those from immigrant families and their peers, say the heightened environment left them looking over their shoulders and unable to concentrate, frequently glancing at classroom doors or worrying about family members.</p><p><b>CPS' role</b>: It also placed an unprecedented burden on school principals and district officials, who had to ensure timely communication with families without sowing fear or spreading rumors. Community members say coordination with CPS was difficult at first and eventually improved, but the district still faces a big challenge if widespread enforcement returns.</p><p><b>Key quote</b>: Educators say they've tried not to let the situation affect their classrooms, but it's difficult to ignore. "Every time we would look at the Bill of Rights, there was a question mark, saying, 'Well, but do I really have these rights?'" said Mary Urban, a special education teacher in Humboldt Park. "There was this sense of sadness, of trauma, but also injustice because young people understand what’s happening in the world around them."</p><p><a class="Link" The two friends decided they “had to do something” after a longtime Polish restaurant closed in 2018 and opened Polish Pączki Cafe.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wykdtyd-l-tl/" target="_blank" >At Polish Pączki Cafe, tradition is the secret ingredient</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wykdtyd-l-tr/" target="_blank" >Joanna Marszałek</a></h5><p>It is 10 a.m. on a recent Saturday, and at Polish Pączki Cafe on the Northwest Side, a line starts to form at the counter. Customers just say "10," "six," "12," and there’s no need for explanation. Although the unassuming place, located in a strip mall, serves a variety of savory dishes, the namesake pączki are the star.</p><p>Poles in Chicago and in Poland eat pączki throughout the year, with many bakeries, delis and supermarkets offering a variety of fillings and glazes. But the real celebration is on Tłusty Czwartek (Fat Thursday), which precedes America’s Pączki Day (Fat Tuesday), and is traditionally a time to consume all fats and sugar before Lent.</p><p>At Polish Pączki Cafe, 7210 W. Foster Ave., every now and then a customer unfamiliar with the classic Polish delicacy walks in, lured by the activity inside and the boxes others carry out. If co-owner Anna Niziołek is around, she will educate newcomers on the pronunciation ("two PAWNCH-key but one PAWN-chek"), the origins and the process of making pączki.</p><p>She will gently correct those who call her pączki "doughnuts" and is quick to explain that they don’t sell them with custard, chocolate or other fillings. The original filling — a mix of plum, rose and raspberry marmalades imported from Poland — is hand-folded into the dough before frying, rather than injected afterward.</p><p>"Our pączki are special because we make them fresh every day from scratch by hand, using a very old Polish recipe," Niziołek said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wykdtyd-l-ty/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's the best way to spend Valentine's Day in Chicago if you're single? ❤️</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Email us</i></a><i> with your answer (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><p>Yesterday, we asked you: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wykdtyd-l-tt/" target="_blank" >What’s your favorite work of art that you’ve seen at Chicago’s museums?</a></p><p>Here’s some of what you said…</p><p>"Edward Hopper’s 'Nighthawks.' A few lonely people late at night in a diner — it makes me wonder how many of us who’ve been that lonely at some point have seen ourselves in that Art Institute masterwork." — <i>Paul Lockwood</i></p><p>"'Paris Street on a Rainy Day,' 1877, by the French artist Gustave Caillebotte, [which] hangs in the Art Institute collection. It’s so lifelike, it feels as if you could reach out and shake hands with the couple in the foreground." — <i>Russell Bath</i></p><p>"The Marc Chagall stained glass windows [at the Art Intitute] has always been one of my favorites." — <i>Laura Pergola</i></p><p>"My favorite exhibited work is 'Judith Slaying Holofernes' by Artemisia Gentileschi. The painting shows a Biblical scene, unusual for a woman at this time, and unusual in showing the strength and determination of Judith and her maid. But we can also see it as a working out of her rage at being raped by one of her father's students at the age of 18." — <i>Ed Walker</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Eydie Cubarrubia</p><hr><p><i>The Chicago Sun-Times is a nonprofit supported by readers like you. administration issued the executive order titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History,” which criticizes the Smithsonian for promoting what it calls “divisive race-centered ideology.” The order puts the museum campus under federal scrutiny by authorizing reviews of exhibitions and programming. The goal, it reads, is to emphasize "American exceptionalism" and remove what the Trump administration calls "partisan narratives."</p><p>Officials have warned federal funding could be withheld if the museums don't comply. But the directive has prompted resignations and high-profile artist cancellations, such as by painter Amy Sherald.</p><p>In a moment of “incredible upheaval,” says Sarah Newman, the James Dicke Curator of Contemporary Art and acting head curator at SAAM, “Nick is proposing a way to navigate through that change, a way to look at our environment and our heritage, take solace in it, honor and learn from it, and look toward creativity as a way to locate your place in the world.”</p><p>At 67, Cave is best known for <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2022/05/19/artist-nick-cave-and-his-soundsuits-take-over-chicago-mca-dusable" target="_blank" ><u>his Soundsuits,</u></a> folkloric, futuristic sculptural forms that blur the line between costume and armor. Sometimes glittering, other times spectral, the suits evoke both Maurice Sendak’s “wild things” and the heightened drama of Schiaparelli couture.</p><p>Cave began making the Soundsuits in 1991 in response to the brutal Los Angeles Police Department beating of Rodney King, a Black man whose assault ignited the 1992 L.A. riots, and national outrage, over police brutality. Here the Soundsuits are pictured in an exhibition at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago in 2022.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A former dancer who trained at the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, Cave has long straddled the worlds of fashion, performance and art. He is a professor of fashion studies at the School of the Art Institute and has exhibited widely across the United States, including major solo exhibitions at the Guggenheim, MASS MoCA, and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago.</p><p>In Chicago, one of Cave’s Soundsuits is currently on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago as part of the show, “City in a Garden: Queer Art and Activism in Chicago.” Two additional pieces hang in the Art Institute of Chicago exhibition “On Loss and Absence.” On the South Side, Cave designed the floral-inspired mosaic ceiling at the Washington Park Green Line stop and will unveil a new commission for the Obama Presidential Center later this spring.</p><p>Cave and his partner in life and art, Bob Faust, also run a gallery from their expansive live-work space, Facility, in Old Irving Park.</p><p>While Cave’s work seems to dance, often literally. around overt political declarations, the artist doesn't shy from pointed critique. “Is the work somewhat political?” Cave asks, rhetorically. “Oh yeah, it’s in there.”</p><p>All of Cave’s creations hold grief and celebration, agony and ecstasy, in equal measure.</p><h3><b>A legacy of craftmaking and meticulous handiwork</b></h3><p>For Cave, the Smithsonian show began with a personal excavation. “I started thinking, how was I made?” says Cave. “How did I become who I am?”</p><p>Cave grew up one of seven brothers in Missouri. Many of his favorite memories were shaped on his grandparents’ farm where he was surrounded by aunts and uncles who made things with their hands. “They were all just making stuff anyway, but didn’t call it art,” recalls Cave. “It was really just hobbies, craftsmanship. Things they did on Saturdays and Sundays.”</p><p>As a boy, Cave especially loved watching his grandmother work. “At seven o’clock, she would say, ‘Knick Knack, go pull my quilt out of the chest,’” he recalls, “and she would sit down and just start to quilt.” He also remembers how his grandmother would cut clothing patterns from brown paper bags, pin them directly onto one of her many grandchildren, and assemble garments in a matter of hours.</p><p>But the making was only part of it. Pageantry mattered, too. When a quilt or painting was finished, “there would be this big reveal,” says Cave. “Something about it was magical.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-fullBleed> <div class="Enhancement-item" He incorporates beadwork into his new exhibition.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Cave’s memories weave through exhibition, which includes “Roam;” a series of five towering lifeguard chairs; figurative bronze sculptures molded from Cave’s own body; and a 60-foot beaded curtain that hangs over a mural designed by Cave’s partner, Faust, inspired by the Missouri farm. Cave’s mammoths also appear throughout the gallery spaces, some in full form, others reduced to skulls or tusks.</p><p>The show’s most intimate work, however, sprawls across a 70-foot light table. Titled “A Lit History,” the massive assemblage is created from thousands of objects — pie pans, nails, trivets, bingo ball cages, thimbles, crocheted doilies, metal coils — that Cave has collected over the last three decades, many of them from his grandparents’ house. Those unadorned, everyday items sit alongside elaborate pieces of Cave’s own invention: veils fashioned from plastic ties and price tags, hats assembled from knobbed keychain rings, and garments stitched from tens of thousands of buttons.</p><p>It registers in two ways at once. From a distance, “A Lit History” provokes sheer bewilderment and wonder; up close, the display reveals intricate and meticulous craftsmanship.</p><p>“Nick has this unique ability to see beauty and art in things that people would otherwise be so quick to discard or not value,” says Michelle Boone, the president of the Poetry Foundation and former cultural commissioner, who has known Cave for years.</p><p>Boone recalls a visit to the Randolph Street Market that revealed Cave’s way of seeing. She remembers passing a long wooden slab — “I think it was an African bed,” she says — and wondering aloud what anyone would ever do with it. An hour later, she saw Cave walking through the antique market with the piece tucked under his arm. When she later visited his home, the bed had become the centerpiece of his dining table. “It never would have occurred to me to see that as an art piece. The way Nick views the world is very, very different from most people.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e80000" name="image-e80000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5cce36f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8256x4633+0+435/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F22%2Fee1a998e489bbdab59b9a2a485a3%2F240430-5830-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cba893f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8256x4633+0+435/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F22%2Fee1a998e489bbdab59b9a2a485a3%2F240430-5830-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a661045/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8256x4633+0+435/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F22%2Fee1a998e489bbdab59b9a2a485a3%2F240430-5830-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Nick Cave constructing one of his Woolly mammoths. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a661045/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8256x4633+0+435/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F22%2Fee1a998e489bbdab59b9a2a485a3%2F240430-5830-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ef4be10/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8256x4633+0+435/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F22%2Fee1a998e489bbdab59b9a2a485a3%2F240430-5830-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a661045/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8256x4633+0+435/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F22%2Fee1a998e489bbdab59b9a2a485a3%2F240430-5830-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cave stands inside an early, spectral prototype of one of his mammoths. He originally imagined them fully skinned.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of James Prinz Photography</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Cave is perhaps more like a bowerbird, collecting artifacts of daily life and assembling them into a world of his own making.</p><p>And like the forest bird’s elaborate nests, no object in Cave’s “Mammoth” is incidental. One, though, stands apart as a particular talisman: a walking cane that belonged to Cave’s youngest brother, Stacy, who died at 20. In the museum gallery, “it’s the first object you encounter,” explains Cave, who placed the cane in the show without altering it. “It was his cane. I didn’t need to do anything. It was everything it needed to be.”</p><p>The fact that his family’s relics are now on display at the Smithsonian simply amazes Cave. “My grandmother’s thimbles are in the Smithsonian,” he smiles. “That is American history.”</p><h3><b>An artist seizes the moment </b></h3><p>A week before “Mammoth” is set to open, Cave has just returned from Washington, D.C., where he finished installing the exhibition. A handful of studio assistants work studiously at their stations nearby. Cave employs ten full-time assistants, several of whom wore the mammoths for “Roam,” but that number can climb as high as 30 at the height of a project.</p><p>Today, the studio is quieter than it has been in months. Not only does “Mammoth” open as the Smithsonian sits at the center of the Trump administration’s anti-diversity campaign, but it also appears in a moment when stories of state violence dominate the headlines. That includes the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis, news that carries a grim echo of the early days of Cave’s career when he created his first Soundsuit.</p><p>Walking the studio floor, Cave pauses at a few mammoth heads that rest in a corner. He will eventually make a total of 13 mammoths — enough to form a herd — for a performance at the museum later this year. Looking at the pieces, Cave recalls the moment when the animal’s final form first came into focus.</p><p>Cave, who made the mammoths with the Chicago metal fabrication studio, Manifold, originally imagined the creatures fully skinned. But once he saw people standing beneath an early prototype, visible through the ribs, Cave changed his mind. “Something about that just revealed the state of the world today,” he says.</p><div We will not change the show.”</p><p>The exhibition may have been nearly a decade in the making, but Cave believes the work is arriving in the world exactly when it’s meant to. “I believe I’m not ever given anything that I’m not supposed to have at any given moment,” reflects Cave. “So,” he adds, “I have a job to do.”</p><p><i>Elly Fishman’s reporting on news and culture has appeared in The New York Times, Rolling Stone, GQ, Fast Company, Chicago, and WBEZ, among others. title: No recess, lockdowns, less learning: How immigration agents disrupted CPS schools this fall
summary: <p>Alma’s 11-year-old boys had difficult questions for her after their school, Jungman Elementary in Pilsen, went on lockdown because federal immigration agents were nearby.</p><p>Her fifth graders remember being rushed back into their classrooms during dismissal on a day in late October as teachers ran out of the building to make sure no one was left outside. Afterwards, they wanted to know if it was safe to go back to school.</p><p>“I didn’t know what to say,” said Alma, who asked to be identified by only her first name because she is an immigrant and fears being targeted. “I told them that they are going to be safe inside the school, and they just have to be ready if it happens again.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div mass deportation campaign surged in Chicago last fall, Chicago Public Schools officials fielded an influx of calls for support from schools due to immigration enforcement activity near their class="Figure-content"><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Eric White/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The presence of federal agents forced students inside during recess, canceled some after-school activities, disrupted learning and at times created chaos. Students, both from immigrant families and their peers, say the heightened environment left them looking over their shoulders and unable to concentrate on schoolwork, frequently glancing at classroom doors or worrying about family members.</p><p>It also placed an unprecedented burden on school principals and district officials, who had to ensure timely communication with families without sowing fear or spreading rumors. Community members say coordination with CPS was difficult at first and eventually improved, but the district still faces a big challenge if widespread enforcement returns.</p><p>“I don’t think we are where we need to be,” said Patrick Brosnan, executive director of the Brighton Park Neighborhood Council, a nonprofit on the Southwest Side that works closely with schools. He credits the school district for making adjustments to confront what he calls a “bananas” situation. At the same time, he said the school district and the city still needs to share information more freely and promptly.</p><p>“There is no blueprint for this, but we are going through it,” added Yesenia Lopez, a CPS board member whose heavily Latino district on the city’s Southwest Side has been a hotspot for enforcement operations. “Things keep escalating based on what we’ve seen out in other states and we're going to have to continue to act quickly as a district.”</p><h3>Widespread disruption when federal agents came near Chicago schools</h3><p>When Trump’s Chicago-area deportation campaign was at its peak last fall, schools reported federal immigration agents staging in school parking lots, showing up at elementary school soccer games, and detaining people on school grounds or where students could see them.</p><p>On Oct. 3, students had to stay inside when federal agents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/09/funston-elementary-logan-square-school-tear-gas-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>threw tear gas on the street near Funston Elementary</u></a> in Logan Square.</p><p>Though the exact number of times federal activity disrupted schools isn’t known, it’s clear the effect was widespread. The Sun-Times and WBEZ compiled the most comprehensive accounting to date by reviewing district briefings for school board members and records of letters CPS sent to families informing them about federal activity near their schools.</p><p>CPS received nearly 200 calls for support from 109 schools between Oct. 20, when it opened a command center to centralize calls for assistance, through mid-December, according to CPS documents obtained through an open records request.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-190000" name="html-embed-module-190000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27483195"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27483195/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>That’s likely an underestimate of how often agents came near schools, as principals often acted without reaching out to the central office and the command center launched more than a month into the deportation campaign.</p><p>CPS officials did not agree to an interview, but said in a statement that federal activity on school grounds is extremely rare and the district has mostly responded to reports of activity near school buildings. Over the last year, there have been no known instances of enforcement activity inside a CPS school.</p><p>Still, schools called the command center for help nearly every day in October and early November. On some days, CPS fielded dozens of calls.</p><p>For example, when federal agents flooded the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/10/24/immigration-agents-arrest-lake-view-protest-tear-gas-west-town" target="_blank" ><u>North and Northwest sides on Oct. 24,</u></a> the command center got 37 calls from schools seeking help — the most recorded by the district this fall.</p><p>At least 10 schools thought the situation this fall posed enough of a safety risk to staff and students that they went on lockdown, according to a log of messages the district sent to parents. That means they kept students indoors and secured the doors.</p><p>North-Grand High School in Humboldt Park went on lockdown in early September after receiving reports of several suspected law enforcement vehicles in the parking lot of an adjacent shopping center. CPS officials couldn’t verify who the vehicles belonged to, but students assumed federal immigration agents were using them.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>When suspected law enforcement vehicles showed up in a parking lot near North-Grand High School in Humboldt Park, the school went on lockdown. Some students are glad their schools take measures like this to keep them safe, but they can put children and teens in a state of high alert.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“A lot of kids were freaked out,” said Carrie, a 16-year-old student at North-Grand. We’re not using her real name because some of her family members are immigrants without legal status in the U.S.</p><p>That day the North-Grand junior sent panicked texts to her relatives, telling them to avoid the school. She started to cry when she didn’t get a response, worried that she’d sent the warning too late.</p><p>“I was texting my mother that I loved her so much,” she said.</p><p>After the lockdown, Carrie decided to stay home from school for a few days. Coming back meant working through her anxieties.</p><p>But the experience left a mark. She’s still on high alert while she’s in class.</p><p>“I look more at the door, I pay attention to who is at the doorway, who is leaving, who is in my classroom and who could be walking the halls,” Carrie said. “I memorized some of my friend’s footstep patterns.”</p><p>It’s not uncommon for fears about the presence of immigration agents to weigh heavily on children’s minds, psychologists say. They may become more emotional, distrust authority and have trouble sleeping.</p><p>“We may be asking them to take their history exam during the ninth period when their mind is worried about the commute home,” said Claudio Rivera, a pediatric psychologist and an assistant professor at the University of Chicago. “That’s not allowing them to focus on the learning opportunities that’s in front of them.”</p><p>The exact number of schools that went on lockdown during the fall is likely higher as the district doesn’t comprehensively track them.</p><p>In October, for example, Brosnan told Chalkbeat Chicago that <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/10/23/chicago-public-schools-board-members-want-virtual-learning-immigration/" target="_blank" ><u>about 30 schools on the Southwest Side</u></a> alone went on lockdown because of enforcement activity. Lopez, whose district includes Brighton Park, said that’s partly because federal agents frequently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/27/tamale-vendor-arrested-back-of-the-yards-ice-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>stalked the Home Depot in neighboring Back of the Yards</u></a>, which is surrounded by several schools.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-900000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Julia Markut, a junior at Lane Tech High School, saw how the presence of federal immigration agents near her school affected her classmates’ mental health and made some students afraid to leave the building for lunch.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>At Lane Tech High School in the North Center neighborhood, junior Julia Markut said her peers were surprised when in October a loudspeaker message alerted them of federal immigration enforcement activity nearby. She watched in shock as one of her friends broke down in tears.</p><p>Her friend said: “I don’t know how I'll be able to get home, I have to call my parents,” Markut said. “It was sort of dehumanizing to see her experiencing that.”</p><p>Soon the loudspeaker alerts were coming multiple times a week, making the situation almost “normalized,” Markut said. The school started encouraging students, many of whom like to go out for lunch, to stay inside. It opened classrooms where students who are afraid to leave can find refuge.</p><p>But Julia thinks it shouldn't have to be this way.</p><p>“This fear shouldn't be incorporated into our routines,” she said.</p><p>The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to multiple requests to answer specific questions about federal activity around Chicago schools. The agency has said <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/09/19/suburban-parents-sound-alarm-on-immigration-enforcement-around-schools" target="_blank" ><u>its agents do not target schools</u></a>.</p><h3>Schools had to develop communications playbook around federal activity <b> </b></h3><p>The unpredictability of immigration enforcement actions made it difficult for CPS to figure out how and when to tell families about activity near schools.</p><p>Kia Banks, president of the Chicago Principals & Administrators Association, the union that represents CPS principals, said in the past schools initiated lockdowns following a set protocol, usually in response to something like a shooting, and coordinated with the Chicago Police Department and the school district.</p><p>But that protocol was turned on its head when federal agents repeatedly came near schools. Community organizations and schools were alerting CPS, rather than the other way around, and coordinating with the district to get communication out to parents could take hours. So, especially in the early days of the federal immigration operation, many Chicago principals made their own calls.</p><p>“There is no playbook for how to manage this level of an emergency,” Banks said. “You are burdened with the responsibility of protecting your school community and you do that any way you know how.”</p><p>Chris Graves, principal at Jordan Elementary School in Rogers Park, knows how that felt.</p><p>In his community, parents were finding out about immigration enforcement through their own networks or by listening to the whistles from neighborhood spotters. Waiting two hours to get permission from CPS to notify families about federal immigration agents in the area was too long, he said. He learned families preferred if the school acknowledged the situation in real time, even if it was to say that the sighting of agents was not confirmed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-e00000" name="html-embed-module-e00000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-map" data-src="visualisation/27482980"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27482980/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="map visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>“That helped create a lot of sense of calm, because families saw that we were constantly messaging something,” Graves said.</p><p>The district eventually gave school leaders clearer guidance about how to handle immigration enforcement activity near their buildings. <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/78/b0/f53090534ffba3c272f450ff45e5/october-2025-cps-guidance.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Introduced in October</u></a>, it instructs school leaders to bring students and staff inside and secure doors if federal activity is happening on the same block. If it's further away, they should monitor the activity. That’s something community members and rapid response teams can help with, Lopez noted.</p><p>School board members and principals say communication improved once schools had a single hotline to call and the district gave school leaders the go-ahead to use their own judgment to act quickly.</p><p>Steps like this have helped students like eighth grader Dennise Marioni at Gunsaulus Scholastic Academy. Parents said the Brighton Park school kept students indoors multiple times last fall, but Marioni said clear communication from the school kept her calm. In addition, staff often set up a perimeter around the school during dismissal or arrival to monitor for federal agents.</p><p>“They’re keeping us safe,” Marioni said.</p><p>CPS noted in a statement that <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/services-and-supports/new-presidential-administration-guidance/immigration-resources" target="_blank" ><u>district staff and school leaders worked</u></a> to “make rapid, real-time decisions in response to evolving conditions outside school campuses.” The district trained staff on how to respond to enforcement campaigns in the spring of 2025, and repeated the training in the fall when actions ramped up. CPS has also provided guidance to staff on what to do if a student’s parent or guardian is detained during the school day.</p><p>“The District acknowledges that these circumstances placed extraordinary demands on principals and central office staff, who worked diligently to keep students safe while also communicating accurately and responsibly with families,” a CPS spokesperson wrote in an email.</p><p>Lopez said while CPS did make great strides during an unprecedented event, the district could be more proactive in preparing for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/04/doj-lawyer-warns-midway-blitz-is-not-over-as-judge-considers-lawsuits-dismissal" target="_blank" ><u>possible return of widespread enforcement</u></a> in the spring.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cd0000" </div><p>She and Brosnan would like to see the district temporarily expand the Safe Passage program, which helps students get to and from school safely, and make sure its command center hotline won’t crash if it receives more calls than in the fall.</p><p>Lopez would also like the district to seriously consider offering remote learning to students who are afraid to attend school during enforcement operations — something the district has said it would need <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/29/ctu-wants-to-bargain-with-cps-over-remote-learning-options" target="_blank" ><u>state approval to do</u></a>.</p><p>There is a renewed sense of urgency to make sure schools feel prepared after escalating events in Minnesota last month. There, federal agents detained a 5-year-old boy <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/us/valley-view-elementary-minnesota-children-ice-detention.html" target="_blank" ><u>on the way home from school</u></a> and deployed chemical irritants and tackled several people <a class="Link" href="https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/01/08/after-border-patrol-clash-at-roosevelt-minneapolis-schools-cancel-classes" target="_blank" ><u>at a high school</u></a> in south Minneapolis. Closer to home, masked federal agents scanned the face of a 16-year-old outside an Aurora high school, <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisattorneygeneral.gov/News-Room/Current-News/001%20-%20Complaint%201.12.26.pdf?language_id=1" target="_blank" ><u>according to court records</u></a>, which can give agents access to sensitive personal information.</p><p>The Trump administration also has told federal agents that they have broad powers to arrest people without warrants and <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/us/politics/ice-expands-power-agents-warrants.html" target="_blank" ><u>enter homes with a warrant that hasn’t been signed by a judge.</u></a> That’s left Chicago principals wanting more guidance from the district if federal agents apply that logic to schools.</p><p>Mary Urban, a special education teacher at North-Grand High School, said teachers have tried not to let the situation affect their classrooms, but it’s been difficult to ignore. Urban was teaching a unit on the U.S. Constitution in the fall when immigration enforcement ramped up.</p><p>“Every time we would look at the Bill of Rights, there was a question mark, saying, ‘Well, but do I really have these rights?’” Urban said. “There was this sense of sadness, of trauma, but also injustice because young people understand what's happening in the world around them.”</p><bsp-list-loadmore data-module class="PageListD" data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-hide-reading-time="true" ><a title: DHS says Border Patrol agent was 'placed on administrative leave' after shooting Chicago woman 5 times
summary: <p>The Border Patrol agent who shot Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a> once wrote that his superiors had been supportive of him, “big time.”</p><p>U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino praised him after the shooting. The support continued up the chain, he said, from Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem up to someone known as “El Jefe himself” — who might even be President Donald Trump.</p><p>But Martinez and her attorneys say <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/10/marimar-martinez-the-chicago-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-expected-to-file-lawsuit-release-evidence" target="_blank" >newly released evidence</a> shows Border Patrol agent Charles Exum lied to justify her shooting. And Wednesday, a U.S. Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said Exum “was placed on administrative leave.”</p><p>The spokesperson, who made the comment in an email to the Chicago Sun-Times, did not respond to a follow-up email asking when the leave began, or if it’s still in effect.</p><p>While incremental, it’s a notable development that comes after a weekslong campaign by Martinez, who was shot five times by Exum on Oct. 4 on the Southwest Side. Martinez decided to speak out last month after immigration officers in Minneapolis<b> </b>fatally shot Renee Macklin Good and Alex Pretti.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Greg Bovino to Border Patrol agent Charles Exum after the Oct. 4 shooting of Marimar Martinez in Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>U.S. Attorney’s Office</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Hours after Martinez’s shooting last fall, Bovino told Exum in an email he wanted to extend Exum’s retirement “beyond age 57.”</p><p>“In light of your excellent service in Chicago,” Bovino wrote, “you have much yet left to do!!”</p><p>Exum also testified in November that he’d “never” been suspended by Border Patrol.</p><p>Now the CBP spokesperson says “all significant use-of-force incidents are thoroughly investigated, reviewed, and presented to the National Use of Force Review Board.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" >Marimar Martinez, shot by Border Patrol in Chicago, speaks out after Good, Pretti deaths: ‘I am their voice’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Federal prosecutors in Chicago filed assault charges against Martinez after her encounter with Exum. They <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >dropped the case Nov. 20</a>, but Homeland Security officials have refused to rescind previous claims that she is a “domestic terrorist.”</p><p>Martinez’s attorneys held a press conference Wednesday to explain how recently released evidence showed that Exum and others lied to justify her shooting. They pointed to a diagram drawn by an agent of the shooting scene.</p><p>The drawing depicts three vehicles ahead of Exum’s Chevrolet Tahoe, in addition to Martinez’s Nissan Rogue and a GMC Envoy driven by another man who faced criminal charges.</p><p>Video shows the three cars depicted ahead of Exum’s Tahoe “don’t exist,” attorney Christopher Parente said.</p><div class="Enhancement" </div> </div><p>He also disputed Exum’s claim to the FBI that Exum fired all five shots at Martinez through her front windshield. Parente said three were fired into the passenger side of her Rogue, a fourth “kicks out the rear passenger window,” and a fifth went from the back of her car through the front passenger seat.</p><p>Parente said he’s been told there’s an ongoing investigation into Exum’s conduct by the U.S. Attorney’s office in South Bend, Indiana. But it’s unclear where that investigation stands.</p><p>He and other members of Martinez’s legal team said they plan to pursue a Federal Tort Claim Act complaint against Homeland Security and Exum.</p><p>“This is a time where you just cannot trust the words of our federal officials,” Parente said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/10/marimar-martinez-the-chicago-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-expected-to-file-lawsuit-release-evidence" >Border Patrol agents say ‘time to get aggressive’ in footage that contradicts claims against Marimar Martinez</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Evidence in Martinez’s case was released Tuesday by Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office. It released the records even though it had previously objected to the disclosure of certain evidence, including text messages.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Georgia Alexakis on Friday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/02/06/federal-judge-will-let-marimar-martinez-release-text-messages-sent-by-border-patrol-agent-who-shot-her" target="_blank" >gave Martinez permission</a> to release the evidence, anyway. By releasing it Tuesday, prosecutors preempted Martinez’s news conference Wednesday.</p><p>Parente said they released it “at the eleventh hour in a misguided attempt to take the sting out of just how damaging it is for the government.”</p><p>Martinez followed the Tahoe driven by Exum on Oct. 4. She honked her horn, yelled “la migra” and tried to warn people about the agents.</p><p>She said she pulled her Rogue beside the Tahoe near 39th and Kedzie, where she said Exum swerved toward her Rogue and their vehicles swiped each other.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/nXGuQ7FrC38?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Border Patrol footage contradicts claims against Marimar Martinez"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>In body-worn camera footage from the incident, agents riding in the Tahoe are heard saying “it’s time to get aggressive” and “we’re going to make contact, we’re boxed in.”</p><p>Exum appears to turn his steering wheel to the left,<b> </b>toward Martinez’s car, as his Tahoe collided with the Rogue. Exum told the FBI he “veered his vehicle to the left” after the collision “in an attempt to create space.”</p><p>However, that undermines the initial claim by Homeland Security that Martinez “rammed” Exum’s Tahoe with her Rogue.</p><p>After the collision, an agent can be heard saying “we’ve been struck, we’ve been struck.” Exum also gets out of the vehicle, and five gunshots are heard off-camera.</p><p>Martinez said she stopped her Rogue but feared being “manhandled” by the agents, so she drove away. She said she drove to her “farthest left” to avoid the agents climbing out of their vehicle on her right. But as she passed, she said Exum opened fire.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-110000" title: Illinois sues feds over $600M in cuts to HIV, lead poisoning prevention grants
summary: <p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul joined a coalition of legal officials suing the Trump administration over its attempts to withhold $600 million in public health grants for Illinois and three other Democratic-led states, according to Raoul’s office.</p><p>The attorneys general of California, Colorado and Minnesota, representing the other states targeted by the federal directive, also signed onto the suit.</p><p>They say the “lawless” cuts are based on “arbitrary political animus” and that the move violates the Administrative Procedure Act — which dictates how federal agencies make regulations and decisions — as well as the Constitution.</p><p>In total, at least <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/02/10/trump-administration-cuts-illinois-hiv-prevention-grants" target="_blank" ><u>$29 million in Illinois grants</u></a> are on the “hit list,” including city, state and other health centers’ family planning and HIV prevention programs, according to a list of grants reported by the Sun-Times Tuesday.</p><p>They also included $7.2 million in grant cuts to the American Medical Association in Illinois, which supports gender-affirming care, as well as $5.2 million slashed from an HIV prevention program at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital — which recently was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/20/lurie-childrens-pauses-gender-affirming-meds-under-18" target="_blank" ><u>threatened with another federal investigation</u></a> over its gender affirming care for youth.</p><p>“The president is blatantly targeting states that are disfavored for political reasons, and our residents are the ones who will suffer,” Raoul said in a statement. </p><p>Additionally, Raoul said the cuts would force the Illinois Department of Public Health to cut nearly 100 employees, end Lead Poisoning Prevention grants to 25 local health departments and wipe out the state’s HIV surveillance system that tracks the spread of outbreaks.</p><p>“These grants are being terminated because they do not reflect agency priorities,” a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson told the Sun-Times on Tuesday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module ‘agency priorities’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/20/lurie-childrens-pauses-gender-affirming-meds-under-18" >Lurie Children’s Hospital pauses gender-affirming meds for new patients under 18 after feds threaten probe</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Raoul said more than $100 million in grants received by Illinois could be in jeopardy if U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention grant funding is terminated entirely.</p><p>The lawsuit also says the Trump administration has made “numerous attempts to strip funds from programs in States whose policies it disagrees with” and deployed National Guard troops in some of the same states, ultimately losing several legal challenges to those actions.</p><p>In September, Raoul was part of a large coalition of legal officials that won a suit for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/24/illinois-wins-suit-on-disaster-relief-funding-held-by-dhs-over-sanctuary-laws" target="_blank" ><u>release of $2 billion in federal disaster relief funding</u></a> held up by the White House over sanctuary city policies. Two months later, a separate federal judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/11/04/judge-blocks-trump-administration-transportation-funds" target="_blank" ><u>released federal transportation funding</u></a> in response to another suit after the Trump administration attempted to block that money over immigration enforcement.</p><p>Last month, in response to another suit from Raoul and other legal officials, a federal appeals court <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/06/appeals-court-kwame-raoul-trump-administration-medical-research" target="_blank" ><u>ruled to restore medical research funding</u></a> cut by the Trump administration.</p><p>“Sanctuary cities are a disaster, so I put out an order, anybody that does a sanctuary city is not getting any money,” Trump said on a podcast last month, according to the suit. “Let’s see what happens, you know, it’ll get wiped out by these liberal courts.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div title: How many Chicagoans are from the countries Bad Bunny named in his Super Bowl halftime show?
summary: <p>There’s a lot to unpack in musician Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl halftime show, which lovingly paid homage to his <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2026/02/03/bad-bunnys-hottest-local-super-bowl-pregame-is-at-the-chicago-public-library" target="_blank" ><u>native Puerto Rico</u></a> in rich detail.</p><p>But one part near the end of his 13-minute set, performed predominantly in Spanish, stood out because it was one of the few times he spoke in English.</p><p>Bad Bunny proclaimed “God Bless América,” in English, before listing off dozens of countries and territories in the Western Hemisphere, starting from Chile in South America all the way up to Canada in North America and ending with Puerto Rico. He then spiked a football painted with the English words “Together, we are America.”</p><p>Local academics say his message was clear: The Puerto Rican musician was reframing what it means to be an “American” beyond just the 50 states of the United States.</p><p>“Most Americans, when we talk about the U.S., we call it America as if the U.S. is the only nation that’s America, but for people in Latin America and the Caribbean, América refers to the entire hemisphere,” said Lilia Fernández, a history professor at the University of Illinois at Chicago.</p><p>Fernández says Bad Bunny’s unifying message likely <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/02/08/humboldt-park-benito-bowl-bad-bunny-superbowl" target="_blank" ><u>resonated with many in Chicago</u></a> who themselves are from the countries or territories he named or are descendents of relatives who were born there.</p><p>A WBEZ analysis of census data from the most recent American Community Survey estimates finds roughly 1 in every 8 Chicagoans was born outside of the 50 U.S. states but in one of the countries or territories that make up the Western Hemisphere spanning from South to Central to North America.</p><p>Mexico is by far the most common place of origin for Chicagoans born outside of the 50 U.S. states, followed by Puerto Rico, Ecuador, Guatemala and Venezuela, in that order.</p><p>Of course, the number of Chicagoans who identify as the children or grandchildren of people born in those places is likely much larger.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-3a0000" name="html-embed-module-3a0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/27595327"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/27595327/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Bad Bunny’s closing message builds on a centuries-old critique of the United States as the sole “America,” said Mérida M. Rúa, a Latino and Latina studies professor at Northwestern University.</p><p>Rúa says artists like Latin musician and politician Rubén Blades, in his 1984 album “Buscando América,” have explicitly called out the idea of America as a continent. Hundreds of years before Blades, the pan-American vision of Simón Bolívar, who led the charge against Spanish colonial rule in South America, was carried on by scholars like Cuban poet José Martí in his 1891 essay “Nuestra América.”</p><p>While Bad Bunny is the latest in a long lineage of people who have reframed the meaning of “America,” he’s the first to do it on a stage as large as the NFL Super Bowl halftime show.</p><p>It’s also a powerful statement to make in the current political environment, said Fernández. Just last month, U.S. military forces <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/01/03/chicago-venezuelans-applaud-maduro-ouster-trump-attack-motives" target="_blank" ><u>captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro</u></a>. Meanwhile, the Trump administration continues its immigration enforcement campaigns across the country. On Sunday, President Donald Trump called the Super Bowl halftime show “absolutely terrible” and “an affront to the Greatness of America” in a post on Truth Social.</p><p>“It seemed to be a message of inclusion and an alternative vision to the politics we're seeing right now in the United States, particularly from coming out of the White House and supporters of the president and his enforcement policies,” Fernández said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/02/08/humboldt-park-benito-bowl-bad-bunny-superbowl" >Joy fills Humboldt Park during ‘Benito Bowl’ halftime show watch party: ‘It’s a good day to be Puerto Rican’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/02/10/super-bowl-lx-averages-124-9-million-viewers-bad-bunny-gets-128-2-million-for-halftime-show" >Super Bowl LX most-watched program in NBC history; Bad Bunny gets 128.2 million viewers</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/02/09/bad-bunny-superbowl-halftime-chicago-conductor-giancarlo-guerrero-lady-gaga-ricky-martin-music" >Bad Bunny taps Chicago conductor to lead surprise orchestra in Super Bowl halftime show</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/12/immigrant-population-chicago-ice-immigration-enforcement-trump" >A portrait of immigrants in Chicago: Immigrant population reaches its highest point in nearly two decades</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Chicago man cleared of Bovino murder plot still in detention after judge denies bail
summary: <p>An immigration judge denied bail to a Chicago man <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/22/federal-jury-rejects-bovino-murder-plot-after-called-upon-stand-up-overreaching-government" target="_blank" >acquitted last month</a> of orchestrating a murder-for-hire plot against U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, calling him a “potential” danger to the community despite the verdict.</p><p>At a bond hearing Wednesday, Judge Matthew Beese said lawyers for the Department of Homeland Security presented “substantial” evidence from the criminal trial to support their claim that he posed a danger.</p><p>Prosecutors in that trial failed to prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt, a jury found. But Beese emphasized that his decision was based on immigration court standards, which differ from those in criminal court.</p><p>Homeland Security lawyers spent a significant portion of the hearing presenting evidence that had either been rejected by jurors during the criminal trial, or barred by the judge who oversaw it.</p><p>Lawyers on Wednesday cited a Homeland Security Investigations report that included phone records alleging Espinoza Martinez, 37, was affiliated with the Latin Kings and had access to firearms.</p><p>They also pointed to a Snapchat message Espinoza Martinez sent in early October that followed a photo of Bovino. The message read, “2k on info cuando lo agarren,” “10k if u take him down,” and “LK … on him.”</p><p>Bovino served as the face of Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area last year.</p><p>Prosecutors in the criminal case did not set out to prove Espinoza Martinez’s affiliation with the Latin Kings. Without that claim, U.S. District Judge Joan Lefkow <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/15/federal-judge-bars-gang-evidence-from-bovino-murder-for-hire-trial" target="_blank" ><u>barred gang-related evidence</u></a> from his trial.</p><p>Espinoza Martinez has been in federal custody for more than four months since his arrest on murder-for-hire charges in early October, records show.</p><p>The jury acquitted Espinoza Martinez on Jan. 22 after a brief trial at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. He was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/24/juan-espinoza-martinez-bovino-murder-plot-ice-custody" target="_blank" >quickly taken into the custody</a> of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.</p><p>Homeland Security officials have accused Espinoza Martinez of being in the country illegally.</p><p>Sussethe Renteria, an immigration attorney representing Espinoza Martinez, said he entered the country at age 5 and Chicago was “the only home he knows.”</p><p>Renteria rejected claims that Espinoza Martinez posed a danger to the community or a flight risk, saying Homeland Security was “attempting to relitigate the criminal case” despite his acquittal.</p><p>She said Espinoza Martinez had no criminal record aside from minor traffic violations and denied that he had any involvement with a gang.</p><p>“While we respect the court's decision, we are disappointed with the outcome,” Renteria said after the hearing. “He has the unwavering support of his community and his family, and has three children and a wife desperate for him to come home. We are confident that justice will be served.”</p><p>Renteria said she was considering appealing the court’s decision.</p><p>During the hearing, Renteria also presented a statement from Ald. Michael Rodriguez (22nd) stating that Espinoza Martinez, who lives in the Little Village neighborhood, had “no connection to gang activity.” She stressed that merely living in a neighborhood with gang presence does not make someone a gang member.</p><p>Last week, a federal judge in Indiana <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/04/federal-judge-orders-trump-administration-not-to-deport-chicago-man-cleared-of-bovino-murder-plot" target="_blank" >temporarily blocked</a> the Trump administration from deporting Espinoza Marinez who was being held in the Clay County Justice Center in Brazil, Indiana. His attorney, Michael Adler, filed a petition Feb. 2 in the Southern District of Indiana challenging his detention.</p><p>The judge ordered the Trump administration not to move Espinoza Martinez “outside the jurisdiction of the United States,” or outside the 7th U.S. Circuit — which includes Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin — while the litigation proceeds.</p><p>A removal hearing was scheduled for Feb. 25. Renteria said she would file a request to cancel the removal.</p><p><i>Contributing: Jon Seidel</i></p>

title: HUD, whistleblower says CHA has violated disability and civil rights laws for years
summary: <p>Before her daughter died, Lynya Cooper spent more than two years submitting documents to the Chicago Housing Authority explaining why she needed a wheelchair accessible unit.</p><p>Cooper’s daughter, Trebora Talbert, had a progressive neurological disease preventing her from walking or performing everyday activities on her own. The pair lived on the second floor of a building without an elevator, which meant Cooper often had to call a private ambulance company or the Chicago Fire Department to help Talbert get to and from her frequent medical appointments.</p><p>Cooper requested an emergency move in 2020 to an accessible CHA apartment, but found many units didn’t fit her family’s needs or she was told the family didn’t meet the requirements for the unit.</p><p>Talbert died just over two years later, with the family still living in the second-floor unit, according to court documents.</p><p>Cooper declined an interview request through her attorney.</p><p>Records show the CHA violated federal disability laws and the civil rights of residents like Talbert for at least eight years — leading to negotiations for a voluntary compliance agreement between the CHA and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.</p><p>Court records show the CHA paid Cooper $525,000 last year to settle a 2023 lawsuit that accused the agency of failing “to provide her and her late daughter, Trebora Talbert, with reasonable alternative housing conditions.”</p><p>It’s not the first instance of the CHA neglecting its legal requirements to accommodate residents with disabilities. </p><p>And a senior manager of compliance at the housing authority is now sounding the alarm, again.</p><p>“Black, brown, and elderly CHA residents languished and died, their names sitting on a de facto waiting list for nearly a decade before their much needed and deserved reasonable accommodations were ever made available,” whistleblower Amanda Motyka wrote in her complaint.</p><p>The complaint, viewed by the Chicago Sun-Times, was sent last week to the agency’s operating chairman, board, members of senior leadership and filed with the CHA’s inspector general and HUD.</p><p>Motyka wrote that she submitted her letter to “shine a light on the dysfunction of CHA’s handling of public housing’s reasonable accommodations,” and three senior leaders were “complicit in the denial and violation of hundreds of CHA residents’ civil rights.”</p><p>She was met with “a fabricated Performance Improvement Plan, a hostile work environment, and retaliation,” when she brought these issues to the attention of her supervisors in the property and asset management division, including Interim Chief Property Officer Leonard Langston.</p><p>The housing authority rescinded the performance improvement plan three days after she filed the complaint, an email obtained by the Sun-Times shows.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/15/cha-residents-frustrated-housing-agency-permanent-ceo" >CHA residents grow frustrated as agency marks one year without permanent CEO</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The CHA declined an interview request. Matthew Brewer, the agency’s board chair and interim operating chairman, didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p><p>CHA spokesperson Matthew Aguilar said in a statement that the agency is taking the complaint “very seriously,” having escalated it to its ethics officer and the Office of the Inspector General for investigation.</p><p>He confirmed Motyka’s continued employment at the CHA and said they “remain in active dialogue to understand and address the complaint as necessary.” He declined to comment further on personnel matters.</p><p>The housing authority also decided to transition the accessibility team — which reviews reasonable accommodations requests and oversees unit accessibility and compliance — from the property and asset management department to the resident services department, effective immediately, Aguilar said.</p><p>It launched a Reasonable Accommodations Task Force to “conduct a top-to-bottom review of our past practices, compared against best practices, to ensure we are improving the quality, consistency, and transparency of our services going forward,” he said.</p><p>HUD declined to comment.</p><p>The mayor’s office didn’t respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Motyka’s complaint has been forwarded to HUD’s Office of the Inspector General, according to a HUD source who wasn’t authorized to speak on the record.</p><h3>Longstanding disability violations</h3><p>In 2018, CHA residents filed a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/news/2018/07/16/cha-seniors-file-complaint-over-missing-grab-bars" target="_blank" >federal complaint</a> against the housing authority saying the agency had failed to install grab bars in their public housing units.</p><p>While grab bars were installed for many residents soon after the complaint was filed, Emily Coffey, attorney for the complainants, said the intention with continuing to pursue the complaint was to reform the CHA more broadly.</p><p>“The goal is to get CHA back to a place where they are approving reasonable accommodations and complying with disability law as a matter of course, rather than the status that we are still in where residents face a real uphill battle into getting reasonable accommodations met,” Coffey said.</p><p>Following the complaint, HUD launched its own investigation and found in 2022 that the CHA had “removed accessibility features during a renovation … relocated Complainant to a unit without the accessibility features present in their previous unit … failed to install the accessibility feature for Complainant after their request for a reasonable accommodation.”</p><p>The federal agency also initiated a comprehensive investigation into the housing authority’s overall compliance with disability and civil rights laws.</p><p>It said the CHA was in violation of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and the Americans with Disabilities Act, records obtained by the Sun-Times show. Section 504 is a part of the federal civil rights law that prohibits discrimination against people with disabilities in programs that receive federal funds.</p><p>The housing authority agreed to settle its issues through a compliance agreement.</p><p>The CHA and HUD have been negotiating a voluntary compliance agreement for years to resolve the issues related to the 2018 complaint and broader disability discrimination issues, according to public records and sources involved in the negotiations. The agency was previously under a compliance agreement from 2006 to 2013 for Section 504 and ADA violations.</p><p>A former HUD official involved in the investigations said negotiations were initially slow because CHA’s in-house attorneys “stalled.” The source spoke on the condition of anonymity given the ongoing negotiations.</p><p>The CHA said it has been “consistently engaged and responsive” to HUD since it agreed to a voluntary compliance agreement in 2023. Aguilar said the CHA moved forward with the agreement “in the spirit of creating long-term sustainability and transparency around its Reasonable Accommodations process.”</p><p>A draft of the agreement, reviewed by the Sun-Times, said the CHA must address its unlawful deficiencies through actions including:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-711b8b22-0773-11f1-8706-e1913bd3c4b8"><li>hiring a “disability rights coordinator”</li><li>retain a “neutral accessibility consultant” to survey the disability-related needs of existing residents and the accessibility of housing units</li><li>create an accessibility plan outlining how the agency will come into compliance</li><li>update its reasonable accommodation policy</li><li>maintain a policy for disability-related grievances, including investigating and responding to all grievances within 30 days after they're received</li><li>annual disability-related training for staff</li></ul><p>The agreement would become effective for 10 years once approved by the regional director of HUD’s Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, records show. The agreement could be terminated early, or extended, depending on the CHA’s adherence to HUD’s demands.</p><p>Negotiations over the agreement stalled due to staffing changes at HUD, but an email, obtained by the Sun-Times, from Elizabeth Silas, CHA’s interim general counsel, said talks have picked back up.</p><p>In December, Silas wrote in her email to senior agency leaders that a new HUD investigator hoped to have updated drafts of their agreement by the end of 2025.</p><p>The CHA, which has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/15/cha-residents-frustrated-housing-agency-permanent-ceo" >without a permanent CEO</a> for over a year, confirmed it provided feedback to HUD on the draft agreement in 2024 and hasn’t received an updated version.</p><h3>Motyka, residents speak out</h3><p>The Sun-Times reported last year that CHA residents are frustrated, saying property conditions remain dire, including for disabled residents who say their accessibility needs aren’t being met.</p><p>Residents with disabilities make up about 35% of the housing authority’s 135,000 clients, agency records show.</p><p>Motyka told the Sun-Times that 35% is likely an undercount because of residents’ disinclination to report disabilities, due to the housing authority’s negligence.</p><p>The CHA acknowledged in a statement that disability data “across housing systems nationwide is inherently limited by voluntary self-reporting” and said residents are not required to disclose a disability.</p><p>Motyka rejoined the CHA in June 2025, after working for years on disability and civil rights compliance at the Federal Emergency Management Agency and HUD. She previously worked at the CHA from 2004 to 2015 in the accessibility office, when it was under the first voluntary compliance agreement with HUD.</p><p>She said the division has been mismanaged for years and the CHA was warned by HUD that staffing levels were inappropriate given the housing authority’s size. The CHA is the third-largest public housing authority in the country.</p><p>About one year ago, the housing authority launched a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/02/27/cha-year-of-renewal-staff-changes/" target="_blank" >“year of renewal”</a> and Aguilar, of the CHA, said it included expanding its reasonable accommodations team with two more full-time employees.</p><p>The CHA is “committed to strengthening our reasonable accommodation process,” Aguilar said in a statement. “When the process does not work as intended, it creates real barriers for residents seeking support, and we must do better.”</p><p>Motyka said her goal with her letter is to have the accessibility department “moved to a place of prominence.”</p><p>“People need to know what is happening,” Motyka said in an interview. “It is a right and duty as a civil servant to be a voice for residents who are basically voiceless at this point.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/02/06/chicago-housing-authority-contracts-commissioner-debra-parker-daughter-lovie-diggs" >Chicago Housing Authority backs off ban on contracts with commissioner’s daughter</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/10/10/chicago-housing-authority-debra-parker-cha-contracts-investigation" >CHA has paid $22 million to companies tied to board member</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/12/15/chicago-housing-authority-hud-oig-audit-immigration-criminal-activity" >Chicago Housing Authority subject of HUD audit citing immigration and criminal activity, records show</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

title: Agentes dijeron ‘es hora de ser agresivos’ en video que contradice las afirmaciones contra Marimar Martínez
summary: <p>El agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza que le disparó a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/04/marimar-martinez-baleada-por-agentes-de-migracion-se-pronuncia-contra-asesinatos" target="_blank" >Marimar Martínez</a> en octubre parece haber girado el volante hacia la izquierda, en dirección del automóvil de Martínez, en un video de cámara corporal del incidente, divulgado el martes por fiscales federales en Chicago.</p><p>El agente hizo esto justo después de que los agentes dentro de la Chevrolet Tahoe que él manejaba dijeran, “es hora de ser agresivos” y “vamos a hacer contacto, estamos atrapados”.</p><p>Después de que la Tahoe chocara con la Nissan Rogue de Martínez, se escuchó a un agente diciendo “nos han golpeado, nos han golpeado” mientras el agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza Charles Exum se bajana del vehículo.</p><p>Se escuchan luego cinco disparos hechos fuera de cámara.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-320000" name="module-320000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p></p><p>A medida que continúa el video, otro agente sale del vehículo, apunta su arma y grita “no te muevas, maldita sea” mientras parece asegurar el área.</p><p>El video parece contradecir la afirmación inicial del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) de que Martínez y otro hombre “embistieron” la Tahoe conducida por Exum, que también llevaba a dos agentes adicionales. También parece respaldar la afirmación de Martínez de que Exum giró su Tahoe en dirección de ella.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/nXGuQ7FrC38?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Border Patrol footage contradicts claims against Marimar Martinez"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Ahora se espera que Martínez anuncie una nueva demanda derivada del tiroteo en una conferencia de prensa hoy miércoles con sus abogados. Dicen que la nueva evidencia del caso mostrará que Exum mintió al Buró Federal de Investigaciones (FBI) sobre haber disparado los cinco balazos al parabrisas delantero de Martínez.</p><p>Se ha afirmado anteriormente que al menos una bala probablemente fue disparada desde atrás.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Martínez fue acribillada por agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza el 4 de octubre en Chicago. Más tarde, DHS declaró que ella embistió el auto de los agentes.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Oficina del Fiscal de Estados Unidos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A Martínez, de 30 años de edad, le dispararon cinco veces y sufrió siete heridas. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/26/marimar-martinezhttps://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/01/27/mujer-a-la-que-le-disparo-la-patrulla-fronteriza-en-chicago-pide-al-juez-que-le-permita-liberar-pruebas" target="_blank" >Recientemente solicitó permiso</a> al juez federal Georgia Alexakis para liberar evidencia de su caso después de que agentes de inmigración dispararan fatalmente a Renee Macklin Good y Alex Prettiel el mes pasado en Minneapolis.</p><p>Martínez es asistente de maestro en una escuela Montessori. Recientemente le dijo al Chicago Sun-Times y a WBEZ que tiene la intención de hablar porque Good y Pretti no pueden.</p><p>“Soy su voz”, dijo Martínez. “Estoy aquí por una razón”.</p><p>Los fiscales federales se habían opuesto a la liberación de alguna de la evidencia. Pero finalmente liberaron los registros el martes después de que Alexakis <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/02/09/jueza-federal-permitira-a-marimar-martinez-publicar-mensajes-de-texto-enviados-por-el-agente-que-le-disparo" target="_blank" >fallara en su contra el viernes</a>. Un portavoz de la oficina del fiscal de Estados Unidos, Andrew Boutros, se negó a comentar.</p><p>Christopher Parente, el abogado de Martínez, dijo que le pareció “irónico que, después de meses de luchar contra la liberación de esta evidencia, la oficina del fiscal federal la libere en el último momento en un intento erróneo de minimizar cuán dañina es para el gobierno”.</p><div
